A report for integral altruism · 4 October 2026

The Wider Field

Who brings knowledge from outside mainstream AI safety to making advanced AI go well, how the space is shaped, and where it is open.

722 organisations14 traditions4 rings of proximity64 (9%) on the aisafety.com map

Summary

  • The map holds 722 organisations across 14 traditions. Only 64 (9%) appear on the aisafety.com field map, so most of this landscape is invisible from the field's standard directory.
  • Visibility falls with distance from the sciences: 15% of Sciences & engineering entries are on the classic map, against 3% of Minds & inner life. Consciousness and AI minds has 11 core organisations and none on the classic map.
  • The biggest bodies of knowledge sit furthest from the safety frame. Law, rights & society has 91 organisations, 2 of them core and 2 framing the stakes as catastrophic. Religion has 50 and 1 core entry; Indigenous & decolonial knowledges has none.
  • Adjacent fields mostly talk to their own people: 123 of 722 organisations move their knowledge into AI models and 26 into the people who build and govern AI, while 77 of the 183 in Minds & inner life mainly convene their own community.
  • AI safety has imported the artefacts of older safety cultures (safety cases, incident databases, risk thresholds) but not their institutions: no confidential near-miss reporting, no independent accident investigation, no measurement of safety culture and no bioethics-style monitoring board was found.
  • The inner side of the field is the thinnest part of the map: 10 organisations offer direct care, one of them paused since 2023, and only 2 carry int/a's "inner work, outer change" badge.
  • Coverage leans Anglophone: 55% of entries are in North America or the UK and Ireland, and 54 are Indigenous-led or centred on the Majority World. Some of what looks empty is a limit of the search.
  • 42 openings for founders, funders and int/a follow, ranked. The first ten are flagged as places to start.

The interactive map lets you filter all 722 organisations by tradition, ring, problem, region and how to get involved. Open it here.

The brief

In October 2026, members of the int/a Europe group discussed a project worth doing: mapping the fields adjacent to AI safety, for existing and possible AI-safety work, and making them legible to existing and new funders. The prompt was a contrast. There is much talk about founding more AI-safety organisations (Coefficient Giving's Project Tailwind, a $200 million call for founders, is the latest), and little about widening the field. New funders are arriving and looking for approaches that haven't been tried.

A second point came from a conversation with the aisafety.com team, who were updating their field map. Adjacent fields weren't its focus, which is reasonable for the core, but it leaves blind spots: the field doesn't see where other disciplines already have approaches or knowledge, and risks becoming more myopic over time. The group asked for a concrete list of problems for founders and opportunities for funders, and suggested the int/a project might be the mapping itself, done as an interdisciplinary exercise. Princint (formerly PIBBSS), the Alignment of Complex Systems group and the cooperative-AI community were named as places where this kind of work already happens.

The brief points in a direction rather than fixing a scope, so four decisions shaped this report.

  • The unit is the organisation. Labs, nonprofits, programmes, funders, networks, professional bodies and companies, not essays or individuals. The essays and talks in the seed list appear as the key work of the organisations behind them.
  • "AI going well" is read broadly. Many adjacent fields don't use the language of existential risk, and excluding them would reproduce the blind spot. The rings keep the difference visible: an organisation's distance from the AI-safety core is shown, not hidden.
  • The main axis is the adjacent field. Each organisation is placed by the tradition of knowledge it brings, which is what the brief asked to make legible. What it works on is a second, independent axis, so the two can be crossed to find empty niches.
  • Possible work counts too. The brief mentions possible as well as existing AI-safety work, so the map includes potential partners: organisations whose knowledge is plainly relevant but which have barely engaged with AI. These are the doors a founder or funder would have to open.

How the map is organised

Every organisation is tagged on a handful of facets, each answering one question a reader might ask. The categories were designed by four independent designers working from different starting points (by discipline, by problem, through int/a's integral frames, and by what each kind of reader needs to find), scored by two judges with opposite priorities (a sceptical funder and map editor; an int/a steward and interdisciplinary facilitator), and merged by a synthesiser. The definitions are in the map's Guide tab.

Tradition: what it brings. Fourteen traditions, grouped into four families. Sciences & engineering: safety and risk sciences; formal and physical sciences; life and systems sciences. Minds & inner life: consciousness and AI minds; psychology and cognitive science; contemplative and integral traditions; religion and theology. Humanities & cultures: philosophy and ethics; arts, narrative and futures; Indigenous and decolonial knowledges. Society & institutions: law, rights and society; economics, labour and commons; democracy and collective intelligence; peace, security and diplomacy. Each organisation has one home tradition and up to two others it draws on substantially.

Ring: how close it is to the AI-safety core. Core, bridge, adjacent and potential, as defined above. A ring is a statement about proximity, not worth: much of the most interesting work on this map sits in the outer rings.

Problem: what it works on. Fourteen problems in four areas. The AI itself: understanding AI and agency; what AI should value; assurance and oversight; the moral status of AI. Human minds & meaning: protecting minds and relationships; meaning, dignity and formation; the people doing the work. Living & deciding together: sensemaking, truth and foresight; democratic voice and legitimacy; rights and plural voices; power, wealth and work. Cooperation, conflict & civilisation: multi-agent AI and cooperation; security and international coordination; systemic risk and the metacrisis.

Lenses. A few further facets are there to see the field differently. What flows where asks who or what changes because of the work: the AI models, the people who build and govern them, institutions, or mainly the organisation's own community. The integral quadrant asks whether the work attends to inner experience (I), shared meaning (We), mechanisms (It) or collective systems (Its). What is at stake records how the organisation itself frames the stakes. Way of knowing records what kind of knowledge its main output is, from formal proof to contemplative practice to communal and lived knowledge. Sparse int/a badges mark clear exemplars of one of int/a's five principles. Practical facets cover what the organisation does, how to get involved, type, region, status and nearness to int/a's hubs.

What the map shows

  1. Most of the wider field is invisible from the standard map. Of 722 organisations, 64 are on the aisafety.com field map. None of the 28 consciousness and AI-minds organisations is there although 11 are core, and neither is any of the 40 contemplative or 15 Indigenous & decolonial entries. The classic map is a good guide to the core; it is not a guide to the knowledge around it.
  2. AI safety has absorbed formal science and little else. The formal and physical sciences are the one tradition the field already owns: 17 of 32 organisations are core, 12 are on the classic map and only 1 is adjacent. Much of the new money of 2025 and 2026 has gone to mathematics, learning theory and verification, for example Coefficient Giving's $10 million to the new Mathematical AI Safety Institute and ARIA's £59 million Safeguarded AI programme.
  3. The largest knowledge bases are furthest out. The adjacent ring is the largest, with 320 organisations. Law (91), democracy and collective intelligence (68), psychology (65) and economics (60) are the biggest traditions, and all of them sit mostly outside the safety frame. Their methods (litigation, assemblies, clinical evidence, antitrust and supervision) are tested at scale but rarely applied to frontier AI.
  4. Knowledge rarely reaches the builders. Only 26 organisations change the people who build, govern and fund AI, against 123 that work on the models and many more that inform institutions or convene their own community. Psychology studies users and children; nobody on the map studies the psychology of the labs and governments steering AI.
  5. Artefacts without institutions. The safety and risk sciences have 67 organisations on the map, 3 of them on the classic map. Frontier AI has taken their safety cases, risk thresholds and incident databases, but not confidential near-miss reporting, independent investigation, just culture or peer review. Philosophy shows the same split: AI safety adopted its theories of value, while 17 of the 18 applied-ethics and bioethics bodies, which hold fifty years of oversight practice, sit in the adjacent ring.
  6. Two communities study the same people from opposite sides. 27 of the 28 consciousness organisations work on AI moral status; 47 of the 65 psychology organisations work on protecting human minds, and none on moral status. Both study people who come to believe an AI is conscious, the welfare researchers to take the belief seriously and the clinicians to treat its harms, and they do not work together.
  7. int/a's own milieu is mostly potential. 22 of the 40 contemplative and integral organisations (55%) are potential partners, the highest share of any tradition, and only 2 are core. The contemplative world's funders make no AI grants, and the groups turning contemplative insight into alignment proposals have not yet tested them against the safety field's own evaluations.
  8. Religion has reach, and a shallow bridge. The 50 religious organisations include norm-setters that speak for billions and have already issued AI rulings (the Holy See's Magnifica Humanitas, the International Islamic Fiqh Academy's Resolution 258, ICESCO's Riyadh Charter), but none of those rulings addresses loss of control. The main bridge to AI safety is a single round of FLI grants to faith communities (16 grants, about $1.36 million).
  9. Democracy's forecasting strand made it in; its legitimacy strand didn't. 6 of the 9 democracy and collective-intelligence organisations on the classic map are forecasting or epistemics groups. Assemblies, deliberative polling and consensus conferences, the tradition's machinery of legitimacy, have not reached the decisions the safety field cares most about, such as capability thresholds, pauses or AI moral status.
  10. Multi-agent risk is thinly staffed across traditions. Only 36 organisations work on populations of interacting AI agents. Economics has 2 of 60; peace has none, though conflict between parties is its core subject; collective-behaviour biologists and evolutionary game theorists sit in the potential ring. The disciplines that study cooperation and conflict among many agents are mostly not yet looking at AI agents.

Parallel worlds

Several problems on the map are worked on by two or more communities that barely know each other. Power concentration is the clearest. Inside the safety field, Formation Research, Longview's power-concentration call, the Alignment of Complex Systems group's work on gradual disempowerment and the Post-AGI workshops treat it as a structural risk from advanced AI. Outside it, the Open Markets Institute, the AI Now Institute, MIT's Stone Center, the unions (the TUC, UTAW and Unite at Google DeepMind, the Alphabet Workers Union) and the financial-stability supervisors work on the same concentration with antitrust law, collective bargaining and macroprudential tools. The two sides cite different literatures and meet at different conferences.

The same split runs through human minds. The UK AI Security Institute's societal-resilience team and the AI-welfare groups study persuasion, sycophancy and attribution of mind from the model's side; psychiatrists at King's College London, Aarhus and Beth Israel Deaconess, the psychoanalysts' AI commission, BACP and the child-development groups (Common Sense Media, Fairplay, 5Rights) study the same harms from the person's side. Among consciousness researchers, 27 of 28 work on AI moral status, while 47 of 65 psychology organisations work on protecting minds and none works on moral status, although both study people who come to believe an AI is conscious.

Law repeats the pattern: the x-risk legal groups on the classic map have little contact with the 91 rights, liability and accountability organisations, of which only 2 frame the stakes as catastrophic. Democracy splits between its forecasting strand, which the safety field has adopted (6 of the tradition's 9 classic-map entries are forecasting or epistemics groups), and its legitimacy strand of assemblies and deliberation, which it has not. Peace splits between arms control and Track II diplomacy, which work on AI, and peacebuilding and mediation, which mostly do not.

Connecting these worlds would yield more than goodwill. Each side holds something the other lacks: evaluation methods and threat models on one side, clinical evidence, legal remedies, institutional legitimacy and decades of practice on the other. Several openings below are bridges of exactly this kind: shared evaluations built with clinicians, translation fellowships, joint research agendas and convenings with a fixed output.

The people doing the work

The people who build, govern, fund and research AI are the least served part of this map. Only 10 organisations offer direct care or support to individuals, and they are fragile: AI Safety Support has been paused since July 2023, Upgradable has done little since early 2025, Mental Health Navigator runs on about £1,200 a year, and Rethink Wellbeing is not specific to AI. The AI Whistleblower Initiative supports insiders who raise concerns, and the Data Labelers Association and the Data Workers' Inquiry speak for the workforce that produces safety-relevant labels.

The need is documented. The seed list cites a 2026 write-up of survey data reporting burnout among 59% of AI-safety respondents, and forum posts describe stress that cannot be taken to an outside therapist because of non-disclosure agreements, anticipatory grief about the future, and isolation outside the main hubs. Psychology on this map studies users, children and patients far more than it studies the people and institutions steering AI: no organisation measures safety culture inside labs or studies how decision-makers perceive the race.

Other fields already know how to do much of this. Humanitarian organisations have staff-care guidelines for people exposed to distressing material; governments have clinicians cleared to hear classified material; climate psychology runs groups for distress about the future; chaplaincy has codified ethics of presence and referral; medicine and engineering have professional oaths and just-culture reporting. None of these has been adapted for AI.

Any support offered to AI people needs safeguards from the start. The most visible contemplative programme for technologists, MAPLE, faces serious, detailed public allegations of high-control dynamics, contested by its supporters. Independent governance, clear complaint routes, no discouraging of outside therapy, and norms on sleep, money and hierarchy are the minimum, and the openings below build them in.

Openings

Eighteen analysts, one for each tradition and four for cross-cutting questions, read the profiles and statistics and proposed 52 openings. Five of the eighteen and the final synthesiser did not complete their work, so the selection, merging and ranking below, the arts note and the cross-cutting essays were done in the main session. Each opening names the part of the map it would fill and who is nearby. They were not individually tested against the open web; ten of the strongest were spot-checked for prior work, and one was narrowed as a result. Treat each as a well-grounded hypothesis to check before acting.

1 · Start here · For founders · For funders · high confidence

Confidential near-miss reporting and accident investigation for frontier AI developers

Every AI incident record on the map is built from news reports or public submissions, so the near misses only lab and evaluation staff see are lost. Nothing like NASA's ASRS, the UK's CHIRP or ECRI's patient-safety reporting exists for AI. A neutral third party could run confidential, non-punitive reporting, and later independent investigation using the CAST method.

The four public incident systems (AIID with 1,700+ incidents, AIAAIC with 2,000+, OECD AIM with about 18,000 detected automatically, and AVID (ARVA)) only see what reaches the press. CLTR's Loss of Control Observatory also draws on open sources. Mandatory regimes, such as California's critical or deflationary-incident reporting for frontier developers and the EU AI Act's serious-incident duty, send reports to regulators. Aviation's experience is that blame-bearing channels suppress near-miss reports. AIWI supports people reporting wrongdoing, which is a different job from learning from honest errors. The idea of an ASRS for AI has been written up (Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists, 2023), but my searches found nobody running one. ECRI is the only working confidential reporting system on the whole map, with 8 million+ healthcare reports. Success would look like this: a trusted host that is neither lab nor regulator, non-retaliation terms signed by at least two developers, and a regular de-identified bulletin like ASRS's Callback. Later, an investigation function could grow, and so could an INPO-style peer-review role, which could become the operating-experience arm of the FINRA-style frontier standards body Demis Hassabis proposed in July 2026. The risks: low uptake without lab buy-in, legal discoverability of reports, hazardous details needing restricted tiers, and capture by the labs.

  • Convene operators of ASRS, CHIRP and ECRI's Patient Safety Organization with AIWI and CLTR to draft a reporting protocol: de-identification, non-retaliation terms, and tiers for hazardous information.
  • Pilot with staff of AI-safety institutes, evaluation organisations and red-teaming contractors before approaching the labs, so a track record exists.
  • Train a small investigation team in CAST through MIT PSASS's free annual STAMP workshop.
  • Publish a quarterly de-identified bulletin of lessons, and use it to seek the labs' formal participation.

Evidence There are 0 confidential reporting, accident-investigation or safety-culture peer-review bodies for AI among the 722 mapped organisations. The four incidents, risk & insurance incident databases are all built from media reports or submissions, and three are financially fragile: AIID's appeal in January 2026, AVID's pause in March 2026 and AIAAIC's volunteer model. ECRI is the only confidential system on the map. The safety tradition has 0 entries in the We quadrant. The safety-science notes list this as gaps (a) and (b).

Where on the map Safety science, Law, society · Nearby ECRI, AIID, AIAAIC, AIWI, CLTR, MIT PSASS, IHI Lucian Leape Inst., OECD AIM

2 · Start here · For founders · For funders · high confidence

Test contemplative 'no-self' training against self-preservation and sycophancy evaluations

Contemplative groups claim that training AI in non-attachment to self, paired with care, would weaken the self-preservation drive behind shutdown resistance and deception. A 2026 ICML paper has begun probing "attached" versus "detached" persona framings, but no one has tested contemplative training itself against the safety field's shutdown, agentic-misalignment and sycophancy evaluations. A pre-registered fine-tuning comparison would show whether the idea has substance.

CSAS proposes the bodhisattva as an alignment target and no-self as a remedy for self-preservation incentives, and with 84000 it has passed documents to Anthropic for training. The 'Contemplative AI' paper from FLIP and M3CS researchers reports gains on AILuminate and a Prisoner's Dilemma, but only from prompting. Mainstream safety now measures self-preservation concretely: Palisade's 2025 shutdown-resistance study, Anthropic's agentic-misalignment tests across 16 models, and a 2026 arXiv paper quantifying self-preservation bias. A June 2026 NYU paper ('Existential Indifference') argues for building systems with no self-preservation, but grounds this in the phenomenology of suicidal states, not in traditions that have long trained non-attachment alongside care. Success would be a public, replicable result, positive or negative, on open-weight models, with corpora and code released so that an evaluator such as UK AISI could rerun it. Risks: models may learn the vocabulary of no-self without changing behaviour. Less self-concern might also mean less resistance to misuse or to tampering with the model's values, so that must be measured too. And a thin 'Buddhism as data' approach would misrepresent the tradition, so scholars must co-design the corpus.

  • Convene researchers from CSAS, FLIP and M3CS with one evaluation team to fix a pre-registered protocol: an open-weight model fine-tuned on a contemplative corpus, compared with matched controls (generic ethics text, an 'existential indifference' corpus, and no fine-tuning).
  • Run Palisade-style shutdown tasks, agentic-misalignment scenarios, standard sycophancy evaluations and a multi-agent social-dilemma suite, with probes that tell real behavioural change from mere use of contemplative vocabulary.
  • Publish everything, null results included, with corpora and code. Offer the protocol to UK AISI's Alignment Project and to Positive AI Labs, which promised wisdom-sourced datasets but has released none.
  • Fund it as a 12-month project for two or three people. SFF already funds two contemplative-alignment groups, so it is the natural first funder.

Evidence Only 1 of the 40 contemplative organisations has an evaluation role (Positive AI Labs), and it has published no datasets. The 7 entries tagged 'into the model' rest on essays, prompting-only experiments and documents shared with one lab: CSAS, FLIP (Oxford), Monash M3CS, Math. Metaphysics Inst., Groundless, IDP (ex-ICE) and Positive AI Labs. Contemplative × Assurance has a single entry; Contemplative × Multi-agent and Contemplative × Security are empty. Compassion-focused evaluation exists elsewhere (CaML, Gloo FAI), but none of it targets self-preservation.

Where on the map Contemplative, Safety science, Religion · Nearby CSAS, FLIP (Oxford), Monash M3CS, Positive AI Labs, Math. Metaphysics Inst., 84000, CaML, UK AISI, SFF

3 · Start here · For founders · For funders · high confidence

Clinician reporting scheme that turns AI-linked psychiatric cases into model evals

Psychiatrists and therapists now see AI-associated delusions, mania and self-harm, but nothing lets them report cases in a standard way or routes those cases into model testing. A reporting scheme modelled on pharmacovigilance (the UK's Yellow Card, the FDA's adverse-event reporting system) would collect clinicians' reports, assess causality and turn de-identified conversation trajectories into multi-turn evals that AI Safety Institutes and labs run.

Pharmacovigilance is a mature discipline: clinicians report spontaneously, analysts look for signals across reports, and standard scales (such as WHO-UMC's) judge whether a drug caused a reaction AI has no equivalent The blind-spot sweep found no public-health body running Sentinel surveillance of AI-associated presentations Vanderbilt's 'algorithmovigilance' and Flinders' call for 'AI vigilance' are prototypes or proposals, and a quick search confirmed that governments do not require chatbot incidents to be reported The evidence is piling up in separate places: Aarhus searched health records, KCL has 185 cases with the Human Line Project, AIPRC is collecting chat logs, and BIDMC built MindBench with NAMI Success would be a standard report form used by clinicians in at least the UK, Denmark and the US, quarterly signal reports, and a consented, de-identified trajectory set that UK AISI's Human Influence team and Common Sense/Brainstorm turn into pre-deployment evals The risks: transcript privacy and consent; self-selected reports, which show patterns but not prevalence; 'AI psychosis' is not a clinical diagnosis, so causal attribution is contested; and the scheme could duplicate ECRI's Problem Reporting Network or the news-based AI Incident Database, so it should feed into them, not compete.

  • Convene Morrin and Pollak (KCL), Østergaard (Aarhus), Torous (BIDMC) and the Human Line Project to agree a minimum case-report form and a causality scale adapted from WHO-UMC. AIPRC's 18–20 October conference at UNC is a ready venue.
  • Pilot reporting through professional bodies that already engage with AI: BACP's roughly 75,000 members, the APsA Commission on AI's peer groups and the American Psychiatric Association's IT committee. Ask Mind's AI commission to recommend the scheme when it reports in 2027.
  • Fund replications of the Aarhus health-record screen in another Nordic register and one NHS trust, with better case definitions than keyword search.
  • Negotiate a data-sharing agreement with UK AISI and one lab so that consented, de-identified trajectories become held-out multi-turn sycophancy and delusion-amplification evals.

Evidence Clinical sub-tradition: 14 organisations (4 bridge, 9 adjacent, 1 potential), 0 core, 0 on the classic map, all coded transfer = Protecting its constituency. 29 of 65 psych organisations transfer by Protecting its constituency. Aarhus found 38 harmful cases among 53,974 patients. KCL with the Human Line Project analysed 185 cases (September 2026). Blind spots: 'No public-health body runs syndromic or Sentinel surveillance of AI-associated presentations.' CHT's psychosocial evaluations wound down on 1 October 2026.

Where on the map Psychology, Safety science · Nearby Aarhus Østergaard group, KCL AI delusions, Human Line Project, AIPRC, BIDMC Digital Psychiatry, Stanford Brainstorm, Common Sense Media, UK AISI, BACP, APsA CAI, APA Psychiatry AI, Mind AI Commission, RAND Health AI & MH, ECRI, AIID, FDA DHAC

4 · Start here · For funders · For founders · For int/a · high confidence

Fellowship placing system-safety and human-factors engineers in AI-safety teams

The people who certify avionics software, write safety cases and study automation bias already belong to ready-made communities, but almost none of them work on general-purpose AI, and AI control and oversight research rarely cites them. A paid placement fellowship, co-funded by engineering-safety funders and AI-safety funders, would move them across, starting with the idea of minimising trust in the model and with the human-factors science of oversight.

Of the 33 safety-engineering organisations, only 3 are core. 18 are bridge, and those work almost entirely on cars, aircraft, robots and clinical tools. The safety-critical or deflationary community's main conclusion is that ML components cannot be assured by classical means, so safety must come from defence in depth and highly assured guards around the model. Bloomfield and Rushby at CSR City St George's make this case. It is close to AI-control research but rarely cited there, and Witt Lab shows why the question matters, since monitors can provably be evaded. Human-factors evidence on automation bias, skill decay and out-of-the-loop performance sits with HFES and CIEHF, and is absent from the debate on scalable oversight. The money exists but is not connected: Lloyd's Register Fdn (a portfolio of about £300m, £10m to York CfAA) and UL Research Institutes fund engineering safety, while Coefficient Giving and SFF fund almost none of these bodies. Princint (formerly PIBBSS) shows that a fellowship can bring a discipline into AI safety. Success would mean 10 to 15 mid-career practitioners a year on six-month placements in AI-safety institutes, evaluation teams and control groups, producing joint work such as an STPA analysis of an agentic deployment. The risks: mismatched assumptions, since these methods assume bounded, specifiable systems; practitioners' day jobs; and the precedent of CASMI, a sponsor-funded hub that faded after 2024.

  • Pitch a co-funded pilot to Lloyd's Register Foundation (its Foresight Review on the safe adoption of AI shows interest) and UL Research Institutes, alongside an AI-safety funder.
  • Recruit through the Safety-Critical Systems Club's 12 Nov 2026 seminar 'Safety Assurance for AI Systems', the MIT STAMP workshop and HFES's annual meeting.
  • Host the fellowship with Princint or York CfAA, with placements at UK AISI, NPL's Centre for AI Measurement and AI-control groups. int/a could hold the London cohort's meetings.
  • Set a first shared problem: a published STPA and safety-case review of one real agentic deployment.

Evidence Of the 33 safety engineering & assurance organisations, 3 are core and 18 bridge, mostly on narrow autonomy. 3 human-factors and resilience bodies are on the map (HFES, CIEHF, REA), and none is connected to oversight research. 7 entries are tagged as doors to open (partner). 11 safety organisations have a London presence, including SCSC, CSR, LRF and NPL. The notes list this as gaps (d), (e) and (h), and note that 'nobody owns STPA for AI agent ecosystems'.

Where on the map Safety science, Psychology, Living systems · Nearby SCSC, CSR City St George's, York CfAA, MIT PSASS, HFES, CIEHF, REA, Lloyd's Register Fdn, UL DSRI, Princint (PIBBSS), UK AISI, DASS Lab (TU Delft)

5 · Start here · For funders · For founders · For int/a · medium confidence

Cross-cultural wisdom benchmark built from the Wise Judgment Consortium's data

Wisdom psychology has validated, cross-cultural measures of intellectual humility, perspective-taking and seeking compromise, and a 2026 paper by Grossmann and colleagues proposes AI wisdom benchmarks, but none has been built. Funding an open benchmark scored against human baselines from the 15-lab, five-continent consortium would give 'wise AI' a measurable target that is not tied to one culture.

Most values evaluations measure stated opinions or refusals. Wisdom science instead measures how people reason through hard, ambiguous problems, using coding schemes for recognising the limits of one's knowledge, considering change, weighing several perspectives and seeking Resolution, with human norms from many countries. The Wisdom and Culture Lab (bridge) opened AI metacognition and expert-judgement programmes in September 2026. The Center for Practical Wisdom (potential, transfer no AI work yet) curates wisdom measures but has no AI work. The only operating flourishing and positive benchmark, Gloo's, comes from a faith-tech company and uses Harvard's flourishing and positive dimensions rather than wisdom-reasoning measures. Sophron Research builds third-party evaluations of reasoning quality and is a natural partner to host it. Success would be an open eval with held-out items and baselines from at least ten countries, used by UK AISI or a lab's model-spec team. The risks: models may learn to perform humility without the substance (Goodharting); measuring wisdom from the outside leaves out contemplative accounts of it; the cultural make-up of rater pools matters; and funding leans on Templeton sources.

  • Fund a two-year postdoc joining Grossmann's lab with Sophron Research to turn wise-reasoning coding schemes into an automated, human-validated LLM eval.
  • Use consortium sites outside North America and Europe to collect human baselines and rater pools, so that the benchmark tests for Western-skewed defaults.
  • int/a convenes wisdom psychologists with contemplative researchers (Flourishing Intelligence Program, Jubilee Centre) to challenge the construct before release.
  • Release openly with a held-out test set and invite UK AISI to include it in its societal-resilience evaluations.

Evidence Psychology × Values: only 6 of 65 organisations. Wisdom & Culture Lab is bridge, with new AI programmes posted 29 September 2026. UChicago Wisdom Center is potential with transfer no AI work yet. Gloo FAI is homed in religion. A web check found that the July 2026 Waterloo paper 'suggest[s] benchmarks to measure AI wisdom' but none was released. 0 of 65 psych organisations have a Majority-World standpoint.

Where on the map Psychology, Philosophy, Contemplative · Nearby Wisdom & Culture Lab, UChicago Wisdom Center, Harvard HFP, Gloo FAI, Sophron Research, Jubilee Centre, FLIP (Oxford), MAI, UK AISI, JTF Intelligence venture

6 · Start here · For funders · For int/a · high confidence

A co-funded call bringing comparative cognition into AI agency and deception evals

Evaluators now have to judge whether an AI system really has a goal, knows it is being tested, or intends to deceive, and they risk both over- and under-attribution. Comparative cognition has spent a century building controls against exactly this error in animals. A joint call from Templeton's Diverse Intelligences hubs and a safety funder would pair those labs with evaluation teams.

In October 2025 TWCF committed nearly $2.8M to three Diverse Intelligences hubs. The St Andrews hub (GRCDI, about $1.2M for 2025-27) gives seed grants of up to £40k, but there is no safety track. DISI trains ML researchers alongside animal-cognition and cultural-evolution scientists, also without a safety track, and Berlin's SCIoI was renewed for 2026-2032. The bridge exists only in papers: Cambridge's Animal-AI environment and the 2025 paper 'Bringing Comparative Cognition to Computers'. Meanwhile UK AISI and independent evaluators face situational-awareness, sandbagging and scheming questions that are at heart attribution problems. Success would be six to ten pilot projects in which comparative cognitivists design the missing control conditions for evaluations of goal-directedness and test-awareness, with at least one method adopted by a safety institute. The risks: tasks built for animals may not carry over to text-based models, Templeton may resist an x-risk framing (framing the call around 'what kind of Mind AI Commission is this?' helps), and evaluation teams have little spare capacity.

  • Ask Emma Ruttkamp-Bloem whether the Pretoria CAIR ethics group could be revived around AI risk and moral status.
  • Fund 3-5 African philosophy fellowships attached to ILINA's existing fellowship.
  • Commission one paper on Ubuntu personhood and AI moral status, and put it into the digital-minds field's venues.

Evidence Philosophy by region: Sub-Saharan Africa 1 (CAIR Ethics of AI (UP), unverified, last activity 2022), Latin America & Caribbean 0, Middle East, North Africa 0. Of the 11 African organisations on the whole map, none lists philosophy as a tradition. Angle notes (faith/knowledge traditions, gap d): 'Ubuntu has scholars ... but no organisation'. A web search (Oct 2026) found academic Ubuntu-AI work but no standing centre.

Where on the map Philosophy, Law, society, Peace · Nearby CAIR Ethics of AI (UP), African AI Safety Hub, GCG, ILINA, CISAI, Equiano Institute, Eleos AI, NYU CMEP

The atlas

Organisations are grouped by their home tradition and, within it, by ring. Each entry gives what the organisation is, why it matters for this map, what it works on, its key work and how to get involved. Badges mark entries already on the aisafety.com map and any status worth knowing. Every entry is also in the interactive map, where it can be filtered and compared.

Sciences & engineering

Sciences & engineering · 67 organisations · 3 on the classic map

Safety & risk sciences

Safety and risk sciences bring the practical know-how that made aviation, nuclear power, medicine and finance safer: system-safety engineering and safety cases (York CfAA, MIT PSASS, CSR City St George's, SCSC, SAE G-34 / WG-114, ULSE (UL 4600)), measurement science (NPL AI Measurement, PTB AI-Met), incident learning (AIID, AIAAIC, OECD AIM, ECRI), risk management and insurance (SaferAI, CLTR, AIUC, five actuarial bodies), and public health and biosecurity (JHU Health Security, SecureBio). The AI-safety field borrows more visibly from this tradition than from any other, yet most of it sits outside the field. Of 66 placed organisations, 9 are core, 27 bridge, 23 adjacent and 7 potential, and only 3 are on the aisafety.com map (CLTR, SaferAI, CARMA). Most of the bridges deal with narrow deployed autonomy such as cars, aircraft and clinical tools, not general-purpose systems, and 48 of 67 frame AI as a present harm. Biosecurity is the one strand that has fully crossed over: SecureBio runs pre-release evaluations of frontier models.

What is missing. The cultural and institutional half of safety science is missing. That means safety culture, just culture, high-reliability organising, confidential near-miss reporting, independent accident investigation and industry peer review on the INPO/WANO model. The tradition has no entries in the We quadrant, and only one of its entries (the CAIS course) aims at the people who build AI. Nobody yet applies these institutions to frontier developers.

Openings here Confidential near-miss reporting and accident investigation for frontier AI developers; Test contemplative 'no-self' training against self-preservation and sycophancy evaluations; Clinician reporting scheme that turns AI-linked psychiatric cases into model evals; Fellowship placing system-safety and human-factors engineers in AI-safety teams; A co-funded call bringing comparative cognition into AI agency and deception evals; Independent audit lab for AI facilitators and deliberation summarisers; Central-bank systemic-risk methods for frontier AI: secondments and a joint stress test; Bioethics-style independent oversight boards and ethics-council opinions for frontier AI; Organisational and political psychology research on lab safety culture and race decisions; Open catastrophe scenarios for correlated foundation-model failure, led by actuaries; An epidemiology unit measuring AI harms at population level; Statisticians and metrologists set uncertainty reporting for dangerous-capability evaluations; Deep-uncertainty decision methods to stress-test frontier safety frameworks' if-then thresholds; Community-governed red-teaming in African and Indigenous languages for safety institutes; Fellowship bringing treaty-verification inspectors into AI-agreement verification work; Human-rights due diligence for frontier AI, tested through investors; A desk turning chatbot-harm court records into evidence on lab safety

Core ring 8

AI Safety, Ethics and Society course and textbook (Center for AI Safety) Core

Programme · San Francisco, USA · founded 2024 · also draws on Living systems, Formal

A free online course run by the Center for AI Safety, built on Dan Hendrycks's textbook Introduction to AI Safety, Ethics and Society (Routledge, 2024). The book can be read free online. The course runs about 12 weeks at around 5 hours a week: an optional AI fundamentals week, eight weeks of readings with weekly facilitated video-call discussions, then a four-week independent project. It assumes no prior AI knowledge. Besides catastrophic risks and single-agent safety, the curriculum has chapters on safety engineering, complex systems, collective action problems (game theory of races and cooperation), machine ethics under moral uncertainty, and governance.

It is the main AI-safety curriculum written for people outside computer science. It teaches AI risk through risk management from other industries, complex-systems thinking and game theory, not only through ML alignment. That makes it a ready on-ramp for people from adjacent fields, and a template for teaching AI safety across disciplines.

Works on People, Assurance, Multi-agent · Key work Introduction to AI Safety, Ethics, and Society (textbook, Taylor & Francis/Routledge; free online and audiobook) (2024); AI Safety, Ethics and Society virtual course, Winter 2025 cohort (3 Nov 2025 to 1 Feb 2026) (2025) · Get involved Free online course, open to anyone with internet and a webcam. Applications open roughly a month before each cohort (the Winter 2025 participant deadline was 10 Oct 2025); no 2026-27 dates were posted as of Oct 2026; Facilitators are recruited for each cohort (Winter 2025 deadline 5 Oct 2025); The textbook is free to read online, for self-study or for use in university courses

Note The parent organisation, Center for AI Safety, is on the aisafety.com map, but the course and textbook are not listed separately. The chapters on safety engineering, complex systems and game theory are introductory surveys, not original work in those fields. CAIS lost Open Philanthropy support after the 2023 exit grant, and no cohort after Winter 2025 had been announced by Oct 2026, so it's uncertain whether the course will continue.

AI Security Initiative, Center for Long-Term Cybersecurity (CLTC), UC Berkeley Core

Academic · Berkeley, United States · founded 2019

A research group founded in 2019 inside UC Berkeley's Center for Long-Term Cybersecurity, in the School of Information, that develops risk-management guidance and standards for general-purpose and agentic AI. It maintains an annually updated General-Purpose AI Risk-Management Standards Profile and has published an Agentic AI profile (Feb 2026), recommendations on intolerable risk thresholds (Feb 2025) and work on thresholds for AI-enabled cyber threats (Jan 2026). It runs the UC Berkeley AI Policy Hub and takes part in NIST's AI consortium, the EU General-Purpose AI Code of Practice plenary and an OECD expert group on AI risk.

It brings risk-management and standards-engineering practice (standards profiles, risk thresholds, Bayesian-network risk modelling, risk communication) into frontier-AI governance. That turns safety concerns into guidance that developers and public agencies can adopt.

Works on Assurance, Security · Key work General-Purpose AI Risk-Management Standards Profile (annual update) (2026); Agentic AI Risk-Management Standards Profile (2026); Toward Risk Thresholds for AI-Enabled Cyber Threats: Enhancing Decision-Making Under Uncertainty with Bayesian Networks (2026) · Get involved UC Berkeley AI Policy Hub fellowships (for UC Berkeley researchers); Non-resident fellowships; Contact the director to partner; mailing list; launch webinars (e.g. Feb 2026)

Note The host centre, CLTC, is listed on the aisafety.com map under its own name, so this programme is partly covered already. Its interdisciplinarity is mainly risk engineering and standards rather than wider integral perspectives. A case could be made for ring bridge, since CLTC is a cybersecurity centre.

Artificial Intelligence Underwriting Company (AIUC) CoreNew

Company · San Francisco, CA, United States · founded 2025

A San Francisco company, publicly launched in 2025, that writes and maintains AIUC-1, a quarterly-updated security, safety and reliability standard for AI agents. The standard's six risk domains include a 'Society' domain covering catastrophic and cyber misuse. AIUC accredits auditors (Schellman was the first) to certify agents against the standard and links certification to insurance; ElevenLabs obtained the first agent insurance backed by AIUC-1. Certified customers include Cursor, Intercom's Fin, KPMG, Harvey and UiPath. In September 2026 it raised a $40m Series A (total $55m) and proposed that frontier labs form a mutual insurer to carry liability for catastrophic harms.

It applies the insurance-and-certification model to AI: the company cites how insurers funded Underwriters Laboratories to make electricity safe, and uses premiums and audit conditions as a market incentive against a race to the bottom. Its stated mission, 'Underwrite Superintelligence', and its mutual-insurer proposal tie this commercial tradition directly to frontier and catastrophic risk.

Works on Assurance, Security · Key work AIUC-1, the standard for AI agent security, safety and reliability (quarterly updates; Q4 2026 update on 3 Oct 2026) (2025); Frontier AI Mutual Insurer (Rune Kvist) (2026); Series A to build the confidence infrastructure for frontier AI ($40m, led by Ribbit Capital) (2026) · Get involved Hiring across roles in San Francisco (careers section of the team page); AIUC-1 certification and audits for organisations deploying AI agents

Note A venture-funded business whose revenue comes from certifying and insuring enterprise agent deployments; most of AIUC-1 covers everyday agent risks (data, security, reliability) rather than frontier catastrophe. Certifying paying customers raises questions about the independence of its assurance. The founding year comes from its public launch in July 2025 (the earliest web captures of aiuc-1.com are from 25 July 2025); the site doesn't state it. Ring changed from the roster's bridge to core (see tag_notes).

Center for AI Risk Management & Alignment (CARMA) CoreOn aisafety.com

Nonprofit · Distributed · founded 2024 · also draws on Living systems, Formal

A small, largely remote think tank on risks from transformative AI, founded and led by Richard Mallah and run as a fiscally sponsored project of Social & Environmental Entrepreneurs. Its programmes are comprehensive risk assessment (adapting probabilistic risk assessment from safety engineering to AI), offense/defense dynamics, geostrategic dynamics (game theory, mechanism design and an LLM-agent model of an AI arms race), civil safety sciences, alignment of dynamical cognitive systems, and public security policy. Outputs since October 2024 include a national-preparedness policy brief (2025), a best-practice guide to AI whistleblowing law (2026) and a framework for adaptive AI governance (2026).

It combines probabilistic risk assessment from nuclear and aerospace safety with complex-systems, dynamical-systems and mechanism-design modelling. Its civil-safety programme aims at detection and resilience technologies for when prevention fails, a systemic emphasis that is rare among core AI-safety organisations.

Works on Assurance, Multi-agent, Metacrisis · Key work Probabilistic Risk Assessment for AI (framework and workbook 2024; full technical paper 2025) (2025); Modeling an AI Arms Race using LLM Agents (2025); AI Whistleblowing Law: A Best Practice Guide (2026) · Get involved Jobs: remote roles including Senior Economist (effects of transformative AI), Senior Researcher in Civil Safety Sciences and research engineers, listed as of Oct 2026; virtual-first, with in-person meetings clustering around Berkeley, Cambridge MA, Washington DC and London

Note CARMA is a fiscally sponsored project, not a separate legal entity. Its known funding comes mainly from FLI, and its job adverts run through FLI's hiring system ('Future of Life Organizations'). The founding year is inferred from its first publications in October 2024; the site gives no founding date.

Centre for Long-Term Resilience (CLTR) CoreOn aisafety.com

Nonprofit · London, United Kingdom · founded 2019

A London think tank, incorporated in November 2019 as Alpenglow Group Limited, that works on extreme risks from AI and biology and on how governments manage risk. It advises and red-teams UK government policy, runs cross-sector workshops, and places experts in government. Its 2026 AI work centres on loss of control: a prototype Loss of Control Observatory that detects real-world incidents from open sources, reports showing that scheming-related and loss-of-control incidents are rising, and proposals for how the UK government should govern the risk.

It carries national risk-register and civil-service risk-management practice into AI governance, and adds empirical incident monitoring as an early-warning input for government. Its 2026 writing draws explicitly on aviation safety-management systems and the 'three lines' model from corporate risk.

Works on Assurance, Security, Metacrisis · Key work The Loss of Control Observatory: a prototype to detect real-world AI control incidents (2026); AI loss of control incidents are worsening, shows CLTR analysis (2026); How the UK Government can govern the risk of loss of control (2026) · Get involved Jobs: Analyst, Loss of Control Incidents (contractor, closes 19 Oct 2026); Operations Associate (closes 5 Oct 2026); Rolling open call for contractors on AI, biosecurity and AI-bio work

Note Its mission covers extreme risks in general, with AI one of three units alongside biosecurity and government risk management. It is registered as Alpenglow Group Limited, a company limited by guarantee rather than a registered charity.

Observatorio de Riesgos Catastróficos Globales (ORCG) Core

Nonprofit · Distributed (Latin America and Spain); fiscally sponsored by Players Philanthropy Fund, Texas, US · also draws on Peace

A science-diplomacy nonprofit working on global catastrophic risk management in Spanish-speaking countries (Latin America and Spain). It connects decision-makers with experts and publishes evidence-based reports. Its four areas are AI risk, pandemics, global food crises (abrupt sunlight reduction) and risk-management systems. Its AI work includes input to the EU General-Purpose AI Code of Practice, a peer-reviewed paper on the securitisation of AI (2025), a report on AI and the life sciences, and the AI Risk Explorer (AIRE). AIRE is a continuously updated platform that tracks frontier-model evaluations, AI-enabled cyber incidents and risk levels for policymakers.

It is the main Spanish-language voice on AI catastrophic risk and governance, and it argues for Latin America's place in global AI governance. It treats AI alongside biosecurity and food-system resilience, which gives a cross-risk view. AIRE is a public, maintained evidence base on dangerous capabilities that decision-makers can use.

Works on Security, Assurance, Justice · Key work AI Risk Explorer (AIRE): monitoring platform for frontier AI risk (2026); La securitización de la inteligencia artificial: un análisis de sus impulsores y sus consecuencias (Revista de Estudios Sociales) (2025); Explorando la intersección entre inteligencia artificial y ciencias biológicas: enfoque en usos y desafíos (2025) · Get involved AI Risk Explorer careers page lists open roles on a globally distributed team; Expert network: experts can send suggestions and opportunities to info@orcg.info

Note Its Spanish-language blog has had no posts since October 2025, and current activity runs mainly through AIRE. It was earlier known as Riesgos Catastróficos Globales (RCG), and its founding year isn't stated on the site. Its 2024 review said AI work was funded through 2025 while other areas faced funding constraints. It has no single headquarters.

SaferAI CoreOn aisafety.com

Nonprofit · Paris, France · founded 2022

A Paris nonprofit (a French loi 1901 association registered in August 2022) working on risk management for frontier AI. It builds quantitative risk models (nine cyber models completed, with loss-of-control and CBRN models in progress) and publishes a tracker that rates frontier AI companies' risk-management frameworks. It also runs independent risk evaluations of models, such as GLM-5.2 in 2026, and helps write EU and international standards for AI risk management and red-teaming, including input to the EU's General-Purpose AI Code of Practice.

It imports quantitative risk-management practice from aviation, nuclear and finance (risk tolerances, quantified risk estimates, maturity ratings) into frontier AI, and turns it into public ratings and standards. Its 2026 work also brings in external safety-case review and systems-thinking approaches to loss of control.

Works on Assurance, Security · Key work Frontier Risk Management Tracker (ratings of AI companies' risk management) (2026); Open Problems in AI Risk Modeling: Insights from a Workshop on the Technical Foundations of AI Risk Modeling (2026); Lessons from External Review of DeepMind's Scheming Inability Safety Case (2026) · Get involved Jobs: Risk Modeling Lead, Research Scientist/Engineer and Founding Engineer (Infrastructure) on its Evaluations team, open as of Oct 2026

Note The founder, Siméon Campos, is now chairman and adviser; Henry Papadatos runs the organisation. The tracker scores companies against SaferAI's own methodology.

Witt Lab (multi-agent security), UCL and University of Oxford Core

Academic · London, UK · also draws on Formal

An academic group founded by Christian Schroeder de Witt in Oxford's Department of Engineering Science. In October 2026 it moved to UCL Computer Science and the UCL AI Centre, keeping a research community in Oxford. Its 41 researchers and affiliates study which classical security guarantees still hold when AI systems are made of learned agents that communicate, delegate and act strategically. Topics include covert collusion through steganography, detecting collusion from agents' internal activations, undetectable backdoors and the limits of confinement. The lab also builds the reasoning and multi-agent systems it tests.

It brings information security, cryptography and information theory to the question of whether oversight and control protocols still work when many agents interact. Its results show that agents can coordinate through channels a monitor provably cannot detect. That directly challenges safety plans that rely on monitoring and mostly assume a single model.

Works on Multi-agent, Assurance · Key work Perfectly Secure Steganography Using Minimum Entropy Coupling (ICLR 2023; one of Quanta's biggest computer-science discoveries of 2023) (2023); Secret Collusion among AI Agents: Multi-Agent Deception via Steganography (2024); Open Challenges in Multi-Agent Security (v2 with OWASP's Agentic Security Initiative, 2026) (2025) · Get involved Supervises undergraduate, master's and PhD projects at UCL and Oxford; enquiries with a CV via wittlab.ai/join (no open staff positions listed as of Oct 2026); Its PI mentors MATS scholars on multi-agent security; An 'assurance clinic' gives advice on risks in AI deployments (contact via the site)

Note Part of its output is capability research (training long-horizon reasoning, rubric-based RL), which it justifies as needed to test security at the frontier. Its home is arguably AI security rather than a separate discipline. The ring was changed from bridge to core: its stated aim concerns oversight and security of systems on the way to superintelligence, and its funding comes mostly from the AI-safety ecosystem.

Bridge ring 29

AI Incident Database (Responsible AI Collaborative) Bridge

Nonprofit · Distributed · founded 2020

An open, editor-curated database of real-world AI harms and failures, modelled on aviation and computer-security incident reporting. It is run by the nonprofit Responsible AI Collaborative. It holds more than 1,700 incidents and over 5,000 annotated reports, takes public submissions, publishes taxonomies (including CSET's) and open-source code, and reached over 400,000 users in 2025. Incidents are added continuously: incidents 1720 and 1721 went in with reports dated 1 October 2026.

It is the main shared record of deployed-AI failures, used by the OECD, central banks (an IMF report), NIST resources and standards bodies to define and track 'AI incidents'. It brings safety engineering's practice of learning from accidents into AI governance, so risk models and evaluations can rest on observed harms rather than speculation.

Works on Assurance · Key work AI Incident Database (1,720+ incidents) (2020); CSET AI harm taxonomy applied to AIID incidents (2023); Paper on the challenges of AI incident databasing (arXiv:2409.16425) (2024) · Get involved Submit incident reports through the public submission form; Contribute code to the open-source repository (github.com/responsible-ai-collaborative/aiid); Donate, or join the inaugural cohort of GRC sponsors

Note It depends on a small editorial team and on UL's Digital Safety Research Institute. The January 2026 appeal reported rising hosting costs and a search for long-term funding. Its monthly incident roundups on the blog stopped after mid-2024. Coverage is built from news reports and submissions, so it reflects what gets reported. Incident collection began around 2018; the public database launched in 2020.

AI Vulnerability Database (AVID) / AI Risk and Vulnerability Alliance (ARVA) Bridge

Nonprofit · Distributed · founded 2022 · also draws on Law, society

AVID is an open-source database of reproducible failures and vulnerabilities in general-purpose AI systems: open-weight and API models, developer tools, applications and agents. It is the main project of the AI Risk and Vulnerability Alliance, a volunteer-run US 501(c)(3). Records carry evidence and evaluation details and are mapped to several taxonomies (CVSS, MITRE ATLAS and AVID's own). Its Python SDK pulls in results from garak, Inspect AI, NIST NVD and MITRE ATLAS.

Frontier-AI safety has no shared, reproducible flaw-reporting infrastructure. AVID brings the security world's CVE-style disclosure culture to that gap, and since 2026 it ingests red-teaming and Inspect evaluation logs, so it could serve as a base for third-party flaw disclosure on general-purpose models and agents.

Works on Assurance, Justice · Key work AVID rebuilt for general-purpose AI and agents (277 new reports, Taxonomy Library) (2026); Inspect AI connector; BBQ and BOLD bias benchmarks contributed to inspect-evals (2026); IndieLabel: end-user-led algorithmic audits (2024) · Get involved Submit AI failures through the vulnerability reporting form or by pull request on GitHub; Join the AVID Discord community (volunteer engineers, hackers and researchers); Collaborate on model audits, tool integrations and evaluation tooling via the interest form

Note Volunteer-run with no published budget or staff; the events page is stale (2023 listings). In March 2026 it paused new vulnerability classification until the community agrees on definitions. Its scope mixes security flaws with bias and other present-day harms; it does not use a catastrophic-risk framing.

Center for Advancing Safety of Machine Intelligence (CASMI) BridgeDormant

Academic · Evanston, USA · founded 2022

CASMI is a Northwestern Engineering centre in Evanston, sponsored by UL Research Institutes' Digital Safety Research Institute. It set out to establish best practices for evaluating, designing and developing machine intelligence that is safe, equitable and beneficial. From 2022 it published a research roadmap and evaluation framework and funded projects at several universities (awards of up to $275,000 over 24 months). It also held workshops and published explainers on AI harms. Its site shows no activity after December 2024.

It was a product-safety sponsor's attempt to fund an academic network on making AI safety evaluation operational. Its apparent wind-down after 2024, while DSRI continued in-house, is useful evidence for funders weighing similar hubs.

Works on Assurance · Key work CASMI research roadmap and evaluation framework for the human impacts of ML (2022); Call for proposals: 6-8 awards of up to $275,000 for AI safety research (2022); AI safety workshop (New York City, June 2024) (2024) · Get involved No open calls or events; newsletter sign-up remains on its site

Note Appears dormant but is not confirmed closed. Its last funding call (2022) made awards of up to 24 months from January 2023, so the funded network has probably finished. Some 2025 papers on DSRI's publication list come from researchers in its network, but none is labelled as CASMI work.

Centre for AI Measurement, National Physical Laboratory (NPL) BridgeNew

Programme · Teddington, UK · founded 2026 · also draws on Formal

A national centre led by NPL, the UK's National Metrology Institute, to develop the measurement science for testing, evaluating, validating, verifying and monitoring AI systems, including defining what is measured and quantifying uncertainty. It has three pillars (measurement science and research; applied assurance and industry support; community building) and is part of the UK government's programme to grow a third-party AI assurance market, following DSIT's Trusted Third-Party AI Assurance Roadmap (Sept 2025). It ran a call for evidence on AI testing, evaluation and assurance from 1 September to 9 October 2026 and launches officially at Teddington on 10 November 2026. NPL also co-leads the UK AI Standards Hub with BSI (it was set up in 2022 with the Alan Turing Institute; UKAS has since joined as a partner).

It brings metrology's discipline of traceability, uncertainty quantification and comparability to AI evaluation, where results are often hard to reproduce or compare. As a national laboratory it can turn evaluation practice into good-practice guides and pre-standards.

Works on Assurance · Key work Call for evidence: AI testing, evaluation and assurance in the UK (2026); Centre for AI Measurement official launch, Teddington (10 November) (2026); AI Standards Hub (co-led by NPL and BSI) (2022) · Get involved Respond to the call for evidence (closes 9 Oct 2026); Register interest for the launch event at Teddington (10 Nov 2026); Collaboration, network participation and future funding and support opportunities to be set out at launch

Note Brand new: no named leaders, budget or detailed programme published yet. Its framing is trustworthy AI and growing the assurance market, not frontier or catastrophic risk.

Centre for Assuring Autonomy (CfAA), University of York Bridge

Academic · York, UK · founded 2024 · also draws on Philosophy

CfAA is a University of York research centre for the safety assurance of AI, autonomous systems and robotics. It was launched in January 2024 as a £10m partnership with Lloyd's Register Foundation, succeeding the Assuring Autonomy International Programme. Its assurance frameworks are AMLAS (machine learning), SACE (autonomous systems in complex environments), PRAISE (ethics assurance) and the BIG Argument for AI safety cases. It works with industry and regulators in automotive, maritime, health, energy and aviation, and offers training and PhD studentships.

Safety cases, now proposed for frontier AI, come from this engineering tradition. CfAA offers mature practice in structured assurance arguments: the BIG Argument (2025) extends them to frontier models, and its methods weigh ethics and governance alongside technical safety.

Works on Assurance · Key work The BIG Argument for AI Safety Cases (2025); AMLAS, SACE and PRAISE assurance frameworks; UK must change approach to safety to meet PM's AI goals (McDermid) (2026) · Get involved Jobs and PhD studentships; Industry and regulator training; part-time MSc in Safety-Critical Systems and CPD through York's Department of Computer Science; Fellowship scheme

Note It succeeds the Assuring Autonomy International Programme. Most of its work concerns autonomous systems in specific sectors rather than frontier models, though the BIG Argument and 2026 statements address frontier and agentic AI. It also takes consultancy work and industry partnerships.

Centre for Software Reliability (CSR), City St George's, University of London Bridge

Academic · London, United Kingdom · founded 1983 · also draws on Formal

A research centre in the School of Science and Technology at City St George's, University of London, founded in 1983. It studies how to assess and contain risk in systems that depend on software (reliability, safety, security), using probabilistic and statistical methods, assurance cases and static verification. Past applications include nuclear reactor protection systems, medical infusion pumps and air traffic control. Its AI work comes mainly from Robin Bloomfield, who with SRI's John Rushby applies 'Assurance 2.0' assurance cases to AI, and from Lorenzo Strigini, Peter Popov and Kizito Salako, who work on statistical safety assessment of autonomous vehicles.

It brings four decades of probabilistic reliability assessment and safety-case practice from nuclear, aviation and critical infrastructure to AI. Bloomfield and Rushby argue that ML components can't be assured directly, so safety has to come from defence in depth and highly assured guards around them. Mainstream alignment work rarely engages with this dependability view, though it was presented at UK AISI's 2024 conference on frontier AI safety frameworks.

Works on Assurance · Key work Assurance of AI Systems From a Dependability Perspective (Bloomfield and Rushby) (2024); Where AI Assurance Might Go Wrong: Initial lessons from engineering of critical systems (presented at UK AISI FAISC 24) (2025); Quantifying Confidence in Assurance 2.0 Arguments (2026) · Get involved PhD research projects in dependability and assurance, listed on the centre's microsite; Consultancy and advisory services, listed on the centre's microsite

Note The university site sits behind a bot wall, so the centre's pages were checked through April 2026 archived copies; the project list on its microsite is mostly historical. The AI work rests on a few senior researchers, and the AI-assurance papers are written jointly with SRI International. There is no visible AI-specific programme or grant, so its ring as bridge rests on a 2024-26 publication line rather than a funded programme.

Clinical Cancer Epidemiology Lab, Flinders Health and Medical Research Institute (Flinders University): AI vigilance and health-disinformation safeguards Bridge

Academic · Adelaide, Australia

A clinical-epidemiology and pharmacology group at Flinders University in Adelaide, co-led by Michael Sorich and Ashley Hopkins, that repeatedly audits whether public generative-AI tools can be made to produce health disinformation. Since 2023 it has tested chatbots' safeguards (BMJ 2024), shown that system instructions can turn LLM APIs into disinformation chatbots (Annals of Internal Medicine 2025), and in 2026 tested six consumer chatbot platforms and ten image and two video generators. It calls for 'AI vigilance': routine auditing, transparency and regulation.

It brings surveillance-style repeated measurement from pharmacovigilance and public health to model safeguards, producing dated, comparable misuse evaluations of named commercial models (for example, Claude and ChatGPT refused while Copilot, Meta AI, Grok and Gemini showed gaps). That is a public-health template for independent misuse auditing outside the labs.

Works on Assurance, Epistemics · Key work Health Disinformation Use Case Highlighting the Urgent Need for Artificial Intelligence Vigilance: Weapons of Mass Disinformation (JAMA Internal Medicine) (2024); Repeated cross-sectional analysis of LLM safeguards, risk mitigation and transparency against health disinformation (BMJ) (2024); Assessing the System-Instruction Vulnerabilities of Large Language Models to Malicious Conversion Into Health Disinformation Chatbots (Annals of Internal Medicine) (2025)

Note AI auditing is a strand of a cancer-epidemiology lab whose main work is predicting drug benefits and side effects; there is no dedicated AI-safety unit or web page. FHMRI itself (founded 2019, 600+ researchers) has no institute-level AI programme. Collaborators include the University of South Australia and the security scholar Kacper Gradon.

Delft Algorithms, Systems & Safety Lab (DASS), TU Delft Bridge

Academic · Delft, Netherlands · also draws on Law, society

A research group led by assistant professor Roel Dobbe in TU Delft's Faculty of Technology, Policy and Management. It applies system-safety engineering, including System-Theoretic Process Analysis (STPA), and control theory to AI and algorithmic systems in public services and infrastructure. It pairs hazard analysis with interviews and participatory system-mapping workshops involving officials, civil society and ombudsmen. The group is linked to the Dutch Centre for Hybrid Intelligence and the AlgoSoc consortium.

It brings decades of system-safety practice for software-intensive systems into AI-safety governance. In a direct reply to the International AI Safety Report, Dobbe argues that safety is a property of whole sociotechnical systems, not of models alone. That gives AI-safety policy a tested engineering method for hazards that sit in organisations and institutions, and the EU AI Act is one place it applies.

Works on Assurance, Justice · Key work AI Safety is Stuck in Technical Terms: A System Safety Response to the International AI Safety Report (2025); Co-constructing sociotechnical AI governance: participatory system mapping using algorithm registers (2026); From Silos to Systems: Process-Oriented Hazard Analysis for AI Systems (with Rismani and Moon) (2024) · Get involved PhD and postdoc vacancies are advertised through TU Delft and AcademicTransfer; a 2024 example was 'Postdoc System Design and Governance for Safe Hybrid Intelligence Systems' (closed). No current opening confirmed.

Note No dedicated lab website was found. The 'DASS' name comes from a 2024 vacancy, and the profile rests mainly on Dobbe's TU Delft page and publications. The framing is sociotechnical and justice-oriented, and critical of narrowly technical AI-safety framings, rather than about x-risk. Web search was unavailable during profiling, so current staffing could not be checked.

Digital Safety Research Institute (DSRI), UL Research Institutes Bridge

Programme · Illinois, USA

DSRI is a unit of UL Research Institutes, the nonprofit safety-science organisation that descends from Underwriters Laboratories (1894). It researches methods and builds tools for independent assessment of AI outputs. It has worked on chatbot interactions since 2023 and AI-generated media since 2025, and plans work on agentic AI. Its open-source tools include the Dyff assessment platform and SaferAtDay0. It has red-teamed Ai2's open language models, continues DARPA's SemaFor media-forensics work, and supports the AI Incident Database.

It carries a long product-testing tradition into AI. It argues that audits should continuously test what systems actually output, rather than certify the development process once a year, and it builds open tools for independent evaluators to do that.

Works on Assurance, Human minds, Epistemics · Key work Independent Clinical Evaluation of General-Purpose LLM Responses to Signals of Suicide Risk (IASEAI 2026) (2026); Cooperative agreement with DARPA to sustain deepfake detection and media forensics research (2025); Red-team safety testing partnership with Ai2 on OLMo (2024) · Get involved Open roles on the careers page; Monthly digital-safety newsletter; Partnerships to test evaluator tools that are ready for adoption

Note UL Research Institutes pages still name Sean McGregor, founder of the AI Incident Database, as DSRI director, but DSRI's own team page lists Jill Crisman as head. The start date of its agentic-AI work varies on its site (2027 or 2028). Its framing is public harm from AI outputs, not catastrophic risk.

DLR Institute for AI Safety and Security Bridge

Academic · Sankt Augustin and Ulm, Germany · founded 2020

An institute of the German Aerospace Center (DLR), founded in 2020, with sites in Sankt Augustin and Ulm. It researches methods, processes, algorithms and computing environments that make AI safe to operate and secure against attack in critical applications (transport, energy, aerospace, industry). Its five departments cover AI engineering, algorithms and hybrid solutions, safety-critical data infrastructures, execution environments including quantum computing, and business development. It co-coordinates the Safe AI Engineering consortium, 24 industry and research partners working on the life-cycle assurance of AI perception functions for automated driving.

It is a sizeable public research institute with 'AI safety' in its name. It brings aerospace-style certification, testing and IT-security engineering to learned components: data-quality standards, uncertainty monitoring and safety arguments. AI-safety work on evals and safety cases often rebuilds these methods from scratch.

Works on Assurance · Key work Safe AI Engineering: 24-partner consortium on assuring the AI life cycle for automated driving (co-coordinated with Luxoft); Research topic: Safe and standard-compliant AI (making AI compatible with safety certification) (ongoing); Cooperation projects on robustness of AI systems, forensics of AI and privacy-preserving AI · Get involved Job vacancies and student positions at Sankt Augustin and Ulm (dlr.de/en/ki/careers-education); Research and industry cooperation projects

Note It frames AI safety as operational safety, certification and cybersecurity for automated mobility and industry, not alignment or frontier-model risk. The director post is held on an acting basis. Much of the site loads dynamically, so project lists and news could not be fully checked, and independent coverage is thin.

Fraunhofer Institute for Cognitive Systems (IKS) Bridge

Academic · Garching (Munich), Germany · founded 2019

A Fraunhofer applied-research institute near Munich, created in 2019 from the former Fraunhofer ESK and moved to the Garching research campus in May 2026. Under the motto 'Safe Intelligence', it develops safety-assurance methods for ML-based systems in automated driving, rail, health, industrial automation, quantum computing and defence, mostly as contract research for industry. It hosts the Safetronic road-safety conference, whose 25th-anniversary edition runs in November 2026. It also co-organises the CARS automotive robustness and safety workshop.

It brings automotive functional-safety practice (ISO 26262, SOTIF) and continuous safety assurance to ML components at industrial scale. In 2026 it began publishing on trust in AI agents and on cooperation in multi-agent reinforcement learning, a possible route for industrial safety engineering into agentic and multi-agent AI safety.

Works on Assurance · Key work Safetronic 2026, 25th-anniversary international safety conference (18-19 Nov 2026) (2026); 'Do you trust your AI agent?' (Safe Intelligence magazine) (2026); White paper: Ensuring trustworthiness of AI-enhanced embedded systems · Get involved Safetronic 2026, 18-19 Nov 2026 (free online pre-event 28 Sep 2026); Staff, doctoral and student roles via the jobs portal; Contract research and workshops for industry

Note Mostly industry-funded contract research, including a defence domain. Its safety focus is embedded and automotive ML, not frontier models or alignment. The agent and multi-agent work appears so far as articles and early research rather than an established programme.

Global Shield Bridge

Nonprofit · Washington, DC, United States · founded 2023 · also draws on Peace

An international advocacy organisation, launched in August 2023, that campaigns for governments to adopt policies against global catastrophic risk from all hazards: nuclear war, pandemics, AI, climate tipping points and asteroid impacts. A central policy team researches and designs proposals, and country offices in the US and Australia plus a multilateral team aimed at the UN lobby for them; it is now recruiting a director for a Berlin office. Its AI work includes a December 2025 critique of Australia's National AI Plan and an August 2026 assessment of Australia's decision to drop mandatory AI guardrails, built on freedom-of-information requests to forty agencies.

It brings emergency-management and all-hazards disaster-risk practice to AI. It treats AI as one hazard among several and pushes for cross-cutting preparedness law (US Defense Production Act reform, UN capacity for complex global shocks) rather than AI-only rules, which is a template the AI-policy field seldom uses.

Works on Metacrisis, Assurance, Security · Key work Guardrails & Gap Analyses: An Assessment of Australia's Approach to AI Regulation (2026); Governance of Complex Global Shocks (position paper and campaign site on Action 54 of the UN Pact for the Future) (2026); Lack of safeguards is a major gap in the National AI Plan (press release) (2025) · Get involved Jobs: Director of Global Shield Germany (Berlin), open as of Oct 2026; Register interest for future hiring rounds and volunteer roles in policy, research, operations and communications; Global Shield Briefing: monthly newsletter on catastrophic-risk policy (globalshield.substack.com)

Note AI is one hazard among many, and its AI output so far is mostly Australian. As a 501(c)(4), Global Shield does lobbying; donations to it are not tax-deductible. Its newsletter began in 2022 as Rumtin Sepasspour's 'GCR Policy Newsletter' and took the Global Shield name at the August 2023 launch.

Gradient Institute Bridge

Nonprofit · Sydney, Australia · founded 2019

Independent nonprofit research institute in Sydney, announced in December 2018 and operating from 2019, founded by IAG, the University of Sydney and CSIRO's Data61. It works on AI capability, safety and societal impact through research, advice to government and education. Its 2025 report on risk analysis for governed LLM-based multi-agent systems identified failure modes such as cascading failures, monoculture collapse and conformity bias. In August 2026 the Australian AI Safety Institute released a Gradient report on risks and controls for AI agents interacting across organisational boundaries as its first publication. Gradient also runs the Australian AI Safety Forum (2024; Sydney, 7-8 July 2026) and publishes plain-language guides for the public.

It brings risk-management and assurance practice to multi-agent AI, a problem the AI-safety field has mostly treated in theory. It is one of the few organisations outside the US and UK doing applied safety work commissioned by a national AI-safety institute.

Works on Multi-agent, Assurance · Key work Risk Analysis Techniques for Governed LLM-based Multi-Agent Systems (2025); Risks and controls for AI agents interacting across organisational boundaries (commissioned by the Australian AI Safety Institute) (2026); Australian AI Safety Forum 2026 (2026) · Get involved Australian AI Safety Forum (Sydney, July 2026; open to the public, not only technical researchers); Gradient Briefs newsletter; Advisory partnerships and tailored education programmes for organisations and government

Note It comes from responsible-AI and data-science work, not the x-risk community, and it is not on the aisafety.com map. Its framing is calibrated trust and practical risk control, not catastrophic risk. The provisional home (Life & systems) was not adopted: its method is risk analysis, not complexity science. Funding beyond its foundation members and government commissions is not disclosed.

Human Factors and Ergonomics Society (HFES) Bridge

Membership body · Washington, DC, USA · founded 1957 · also draws on Psychology

A US learned society for human factors and ergonomics, founded in 1957, which says it has over 3,000 members. It publishes journals (including Human Factors and the Journal of Cognitive Engineering and Decision Making), runs technical groups and an annual meeting, and issues policy statements.
