Its AI work includes: - the Human-AI-Robot Teaming technical group, formed in 2020 - 'Artificial Intelligence Guardrails for Human Use', an October 2023 policy statement (following a 2020 statement on AI in health care) - a March 2026 statement urging Congress to bar AI from critical uses such as defence, aviation, healthcare, power systems and transportation unless it has proper safeguards and has been tested for emergent and unexpected behaviour - a June 2026 call for a JCEDM special issue on cognitive security (submissions due 1 Dec 2026, publication planned for 2028).

Human factors research on automation bias, situation awareness, out-of-the-loop performance and skill loss is the empirical basis for the 'meaningful human oversight' that AI governance often invokes without the underlying science. HFES turns that research into concrete oversight requirements and congressional advocacy, as it did when it testified on the Boeing 737 MAX in 2019.

Works on Assurance, Security, Epistemics · Key work Artificial Intelligence Guardrails for Human Use (policy statement) (2023); The AI Danger In the Making (policy statement calling on Congress to restrict AI in critical applications) (2026); Special issue call: Human Factors in Cognitive Security: Trust, Decision Integrity and Influence in Complex Information Environments (JCEDM) (2026) · Get involved ASPIRE 2026 International Annual Meeting, Reno, 19-23 Oct 2026 (AI a major theme); Join the Human-AI-Robot Teaming or Cybersecurity technical groups (requires HFES membership); Submit to the JCEDM cognitive security special issue by 1 Dec 2026

Note Its AI concern is the safety of AI deployed in critical systems and of the people overseeing it, not alignment or catastrophic risk in the AI-safety community's sense. The policy statements are short and US-focused. Membership figures differ: Wikipedia gives 4,500, while HFES's own 2026 statement says over 3,000.

IEEE Reliability Society TRUE AI Initiative BridgeNew

Programme · Piscataway, USA · founded 2026

A cross-disciplinary initiative of the IEEE Reliability Society on Trustworthy, Robust, Understandable and Explainable (TRUE) AI for reliability-critical, safety-critical and mission-critical systems, announced around January 2026. It is chaired by Ruolin Zhou, with George Pallis as co-chair. Its focus areas include AI for reliability assessment and prognostics, robust and fault-tolerant ML, verification, validation and assurance of AI models, secure and self-recovering AI, human-AI teaming, and standards and metrics for AI reliability. Planned outputs are workshops and tutorials at IEEE conferences, a roadmap, position papers, a TRUE AI column in Reliability Magazine and special issues of IEEE Transactions on Reliability.

It links AI assurance to reliability engineering's long practice of failure analysis, prognostics and fault tolerance in aerospace, defence, energy and healthcare, and to IEEE's standards machinery.

Works on Assurance · Key work TRUE AI Initiative launch and open call for participants (2026) · Get involved Join through the interest form linked from the initiative page; IEEE Reliability Society conferences (e.g. ISSRE, RAMS), where workshops and tutorials are planned

Note Very new: so far its outputs are plans. The page gives no launch date; January 2026 is inferred from web-archive captures. 'Safety' here means engineering safety of critical systems, not frontier-AI risk. If no outputs appear, the entry is closer to potential than bridge.

Johns Hopkins Center for Health Security (CHS) Bridge

Academic · Baltimore, MD, United States · founded 1998

A centre at the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health, founded in 1998 by D. A. Henderson as the Center for Civilian Biodefense Strategies. It researches and advises on epidemic and pandemic preparedness, biosecurity and deliberate biological threats. It is known for pandemic tabletop exercises (Dark Winter, Clade X, Event 201), runs the Emerging Leaders in Biosecurity fellowship and edits the journal Health Security. Its AIxBio line covers AI-enabled biological risk: which biological capabilities AI evaluations should prioritise, governance of biological data used in AI, upstream risk-benefit review of dual-use AI, and repeated submissions on US AI policy.

It brings public-health preparedness and biosecurity governance to one of the most concrete catastrophic AI risk pathways: AI tools that could help create pandemic-capable pathogens. It argues for evaluations and governance focused on high-consequence capabilities. Its tabletop-exercise tradition is a ready template for AI crisis preparedness.

Works on Security, Assurance · Key work Prioritizing High-Consequence Biological Capabilities in Evaluations of Artificial Intelligence Models (preprint) (2024); Biosecurity Guide to the AI Action Plan (2025); Risk-Based Categorization and Governance of Biological Data in AI Systems (2026) · Get involved Emerging Leaders in Biosecurity (ELBI) fellowship, annual (2026 class announced Dec 2025); PhD and DrPH health-security study at the Bloomberg School; Newsletter sign-up on its site

Note AI is one strand of a broad public-health security portfolio, and its AI outputs are mainly policy analysis rather than technical evaluations. The site sits behind a bot wall, so 2025-26 pages were checked through archived copies. It depends heavily on Coefficient Giving and US government funding. Event 201 later became a target of COVID conspiracy theories.

Johns Hopkins Institute for Assured Autonomy (IAA) Bridge

Academic · Baltimore, MD, USA · also draws on Philosophy

A joint institute of the Johns Hopkins Applied Physics Laboratory (APL) and the Whiting School of Engineering. It works to make autonomous and AI systems safe, secure, reliable and predictable as they enter society. It is organised in three pillars: foundational AI, applications, and ethics and governance. It funds internal seed and challenge grants for JHU and APL teams (eight teams, 2023-25, covering autonomous vehicles, AI in health care, critical infrastructure and prosocial artificial agents), runs seminar series, and does policy outreach such as an AI policy hackathon.

It joins a large defence systems-engineering laboratory with a research university to assure deployed autonomy across technology, ecosystems and policy. Its seminars have brought in frontier AI-safety researchers such as David Krueger, which makes it a link between systems assurance and the AI-safety field.

Works on Assurance · Key work IAA Challenge Grants: eight JHU/APL teams on assurance and autonomy (2023); JHU's first AI policy hackathon (2025); IAA and Berman Institute seminar series on responsible AI and risk-based regulation (2025) · Get involved Seminar series (IAA and CS department) at Johns Hopkins; Seed and challenge grants, for JHU and APL researchers only

Note The live site blocks automated access, so details come from Wayback Machine copies (Jan-Apr 2026). Activity looks thinner than in 2020-24: in January 2026 no upcoming events were listed. Its focus is deployed autonomy (vehicles, robots, infrastructure, health) rather than frontier models. The founding year could not be confirmed (the earliest archived site is from 2020).

Laboratoire national de métrologie et d'essais (LNE): AI evaluation and LEIA Bridge

Public body · Paris, France · founded 1901

France's national metrology and testing laboratory is a public industrial and commercial establishment (EPIC) under the Ministry of Industry, with about 1,000 staff. It runs an AI evaluation laboratory, LE.IA, with several test platforms (including robotics, autonomous vehicles, drones and generative AI). It reports more than 1,500 AI systems evaluated over 15 years, in fields such as medicine, defence, video surveillance and autonomous vehicles. It offers a certification framework for AI processes, built against the EU AI Act, and ISO 42001 certification. It is one of the four bodies federated in INESIA, the French AI evaluation and security institute set up in January 2025 alongside ANSSI, Inria and PEReN.

It brings measurement science (traceability, reproducible protocols, qualified reference datasets, independent benchmarking) to AI evaluation. That is the metrological basis that much AI eval work lacks. Through INESIA it links that practice to France's equivalent of an AI safety institute.

Works on Assurance · Key work LE.IA AI evaluation laboratory and test platforms; Certification framework for AI processes; Founding member of INESIA, the national institute for AI evaluation and security (2025) · Get involved Job openings at nousrejoindre.lne.fr; the homepage links AI evaluation to recruitment; Commercial AI evaluation, benchmarking and certification services for developers

Note Much of its AI work is commercial testing and compliance certification, so the rule excluding compliance consultancies is a near miss. It stays in because it is a public metrology institute and part of INESIA. INESIA is a federation of existing bodies, not a separate legal entity, and has no regulatory power. Wikipedia gives 1900 as the founding year; LNE itself says 'since 1901'.

Lloyd's Register Foundation (LRF) Bridge

Funder · London, United Kingdom · founded 2012 · also draws on Arts, futures

An independent UK safety charity, set up in 2012, that owns Lloyd's Register Group and funds work to 'engineer a safer world'. It has a grant portfolio of about £300m (live and completed) across maritime safety, safer infrastructure and engineering skills, and runs the Global Safety Evidence Centre and the World Risk Poll. Its AI work includes a £13.9m grant (2017-2028) behind the University of York's Centre for Assuring Autonomy, a 2025-26 Foresight Review on the Safe Adoption of AI led by Careful Industries, and World Risk Poll data on public perceptions of AI risk.

It is a large, established engineering-safety funder that already pays for AI assurance work, such as York's safety-case methods (AMLAS, SACE and the 2025 BIG argument, which also addresses frontier models). Its Foresight Review frames AI safety as a whole-lifecycle, sociotechnical problem covering workers, environmental impacts and critical infrastructure. That makes it a plausible new funder for systems-safety approaches outside the EA funding base.

Works on Assurance, Metacrisis · Key work Centre for Assuring Autonomy, a partnership with the University of York (£13.9m grant, 2017-2028) (2017); The AI Safety Paradox: A Literature Review on the Safe Adoption of AI in Engineered Systems, with the 'Levers for the Safe Adoption of AI' positioning paper (2026); An end-to-end view of AI safety (Foresight Review interim findings) (2026) · Get involved Small grants programme (up to £10,000; announced Sept 2026); Sign-up for updates and the community of practice around the Foresight Review on the Safe Adoption of AI; Collaboration with the Centre for Assuring Autonomy, through LRF's programme manager

Note AI is one strand within a portfolio centred on maritime and engineering safety. Its AI framing is the safe adoption of AI in engineered systems, worker and environmental safety, not frontier or existential risk. The Foresight Review's final report was due in June 2026 and wasn't confirmed in the sources checked. Its World Risk Poll data on AI dates from the 2021 round.

Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) Bridge

Public body · Singapore, Singapore · founded 1971 · also draws on Economics

MAS is Singapore's central bank and integrated financial regulator, and since 2018 it has built AI governance together with the industry it supervises. Its work includes the FEAT principles (fairness, ethics, accountability, transparency; 2018) and the Veritas consortium (2019–2023), which produced assessment methods and an open-source toolkit. Project MindForge's second phase produced an AI Risk Management Toolkit in March 2026, and proposed Guidelines on AI Risk Management for all financial institutions went to consultation from November 2025 to January 2026. In 2026 it added work on frontier-AI cyber risk: an advisory on AI-driven threats in April, and in July an AI-Driven Cyber and Technology Risk Taskforce set up with the Association of Banks in Singapore.

It shows a regulator co-building assurance methods and open tooling with the firms it supervises, rather than only issuing rules. It also moved within weeks from frontier-model releases to sector-wide guidance, and set up a standing taskforce within about three months.

Works on Assurance, Security · Key work FEAT Principles (fairness, ethics, accountability and transparency) (2018); Veritas Initiative and open-source Veritas Toolkit (2019); Consultation Paper on Guidelines on Artificial Intelligence Risk Management (P017-2025) (2025) · Get involved Public consultations on draft guidelines (the AI risk-management consultation ran from 13 November 2025 to 31 January 2026); Staff roles at MAS (check current openings)

Note Most of its AI programme is about responsible adoption and model risk management in finance; the frontier-AI strand is framed as cybersecurity. Final AI risk-management guidelines had not been confirmed as issued by October 2026. Ring raised from the roster's adjacent (see tag_notes).

OpenMined Foundation Bridge

Nonprofit · Distributed (US 501(c)(3), remote team) · founded 2017 · also draws on Economics

A 501(c)(3), founded in 2017 by Andrew Trask, that builds open-source privacy-enhancing software (PySyft, SyftBox, Syft Space). The software lets parties run approved computations on data, models or benchmarks without handing them over. Its main AI-safety use is external evaluation of AI models. In 2026 PySyft ran the first double-blind evaluations of a proprietary frontier model (Gemini 2.5 Flash-Lite, with Google DeepMind, AVERI, Singapore AISI and MLCommons), and the US Center for AI Standards and Innovation (CAISI) signed a research agreement with it. It also develops 'attribution-based control' and network-sourced AI, which keep data owners in control of, and paid for, how AI uses their data.

It brings cryptography and structured transparency to a central problem in AI oversight: evaluators and labs both have reasons not to show their assets. Its attribution-based control is a technical counterweight to the concentration of data and AI rents, and was the largest grantee in FLI's power-concentration programme.

Works on Assurance, Power · Key work PySyft used for first double-blind evaluation of a proprietary, frontier-class AI model (2026); CRADA with NIST's Center for AI Standards and Innovation for secure AI evaluations (2026); Introduction to Attribution-Based Control (ABC) (2025) · Get involved Staff openings on its careers page (remote); Open-source contribution to PySyft and related tools (400+ contributors to date); Research partnerships via the NAIRR Pilot and federated-learning co-design programme

Note It depends heavily on Coefficient Giving. Trask has been affiliated with Google DeepMind, and DeepMind's model was the subject of the 2026 double-blind pilot. Claims for attribution-based control (e.g. unlocking '6+ orders of magnitude' more data) are ambitious and unproven at scale. Its product line has been renamed and rebuilt several times (PySyft, SyftBox, Syft Space).

PTB Competence Centre AI and Metrology (AI-Met) BridgeNew

Academic · Berlin, Germany · founded 2025 · also draws on Formal

A competence centre set up on 17 January 2025 at the Physikalisch-Technische Bundesanstalt (PTB), Germany's national metrology institute. It pulls together PTB's AI work and acts as its contact point, coordinated by Maik Liebl in department 9.4 (Metrology for the Digital Transformation) at PTB's Berlin institute. With Fraunhofer IAIS and DIN it led DIN SPEC 92007 (June 2026), general requirements for AI test datasets, which responds to the AI Act's Article 15 call for benchmarks; it also took part in DIN SPEC 92006 on requirements for AI test tools (Feb 2026). With Argentina's INTI it published U-TraCE (Jan 2026), a conformal-prediction method that gives a formal upper bound on a black-box model's error probability, and it hosted the MAITRE 2025 workshop in Berlin.

It applies metrology's reference standards, traceable uncertainty and conformity assessment to AI benchmarks and test data. The EU AI Act needs this measurement infrastructure, and most AI-safety evaluation lacks it.

Works on Assurance · Key work DIN SPEC 92007: Artificial Intelligence - Reference datasets - General requirements for test datasets (2026); U-TraCE: a conformal prediction approach to uncertainty quantification in black-box models (with INTI) (2026); DIN SPEC 92006: Artificial Intelligence - Requirements for AI test tools (contributor) (2026) · Get involved Contact the coordinator via IC-D@ptb.de; Workshops and forums at PTB Berlin (MAITRE 2025, QI-Digital Forum 2025); PTB vacancies

Note Its web page is marked as under construction. The centre is a coordinating hub over AI work spread across PTB's digitalisation, health and systems-metrology clusters, so outputs are shared with partners. Its framing is trustworthy AI and AI Act conformity, not frontier or catastrophic risk.

SAE G-34 / EUROCAE WG-114: Artificial Intelligence in Aviation Bridge

Programme · Warrendale, PA, USA and Saint-Denis, France · founded 2019

A joint standards committee of SAE International's G-34 and EUROCAE's WG-114 that writes guidance for developing and certifying aeronautical systems that use machine learning. It has published a statement of concerns (EUROCAE ER-022, 2020; SAE AIR6988, 2021) and a taxonomy (ER-027 / AIR6987, 2024). Its main deliverable, the process standard ED-324 / ARP6983, was finalised in draft at a joint meeting at EUROCONTROL in Brussels in mid-2025 and is due for publication by the end of 2026. Reports on human factors, information security, reinforcement-learning gaps and use cases are due in 2026-27.

Aviation's design-assurance tradition (DO-178C, assurance levels, statements of concerns) has produced one of the most developed attempts to certify learned systems for life-critical use. Its concepts and process standard bear directly on frontier-AI safety cases, yet they are little known in the AI-safety community.

Works on Assurance · Key work ER-022 / AIR6988: Artificial Intelligence in Aeronautical Safety-Related Systems, Statement of Concerns (2021); ER-027 / AIR6987: AI in Aeronautical Safety-Related Systems, Taxonomy (2024); ED-324 / ARP6983: Development and assurance considerations for aeronautical systems implemented with machine learning (draft; target end-2026) (2026) · Get involved Experts from member organisations can join the committee through SAE International or EUROCAE membership; Published reports (AIR6987, AIR6988, ER-022, ER-027) can be bought from SAE and EUROCAE

Note The SAE committee page is rendered by JavaScript and could not be read, so the SAE-side chairs, the October 2025 charter update and the SAE document numbers AIR8519/AIR8493 from the roster were not verified. EUROCAE lists the equivalent reports as drafts. The 2019 founding year comes from secondary knowledge, not an official page. The standards are paywalled. Their scope is ML in certified avionics, mostly offline-trained supervised learning, which is far from general-purpose frontier models. The Air Current (Nov 2025) reported that the aviation industry disagrees on how to certify AI.

Safety-Critical Systems Club (SCSC) Bridge

Membership body · United Kingdom · founded 1991

A UK professional network for people who build and assess safety-critical systems. The UK Department of Trade and Industry and the Science and Engineering Research Council set it up in 1991. It was later run from Newcastle University and then the University of York, and has been an independent community interest company since 2020. It holds seminars and the annual Safety-Critical Systems Symposium, publishes a newsletter and an eJournal, and runs about 13 working groups that write industry guidance, including on AI and autonomous systems, data safety and assurance cases. Its 2026 seminars include 'AI in a Safety Workflow' and 'Safety Assurance for AI Systems'.

It is the practitioner home of UK system-safety engineering and the source of the Goal Structuring Notation (GSN) community standard for assurance cases, the kind of structured argument now proposed for frontier AI safety cases. Its AI and Autonomous Systems working group and its seminars are where hazard-analysis and assurance practitioners already work on ML, which makes it a natural place to recruit that talent into AI safety.

Works on Assurance · Key work Safety Assurance Objectives for Autonomous Systems (working-group guidance); Goal Structuring Notation (GSN) community standard for assurance cases; Seminar: Safety Assurance for AI Systems (London, 12 Nov 2026) (2026) · Get involved Individual or corporate membership, which gives access to working groups including AI / Autonomous Systems and Data Safety; One-day seminars in London (about £265), e.g. 29 Oct and 12 Nov 2026 on AI assurance; Annual Safety-Critical Systems Symposium

Note It frames AI safety as engineering assurance of deployed systems (aviation, rail, defence, health, maritime), not alignment or frontier-model risk. Most working-group outputs and member lists are behind a members' login, and the site does not name the steering group.

SecureBio Bridge

Nonprofit · Cambridge, MA, United States · founded 2022

A Cambridge, Massachusetts nonprofit that aims to secure the world against catastrophic pandemics through a 'delay, detect, defend' approach. Its Detection programme (formerly the Nucleic Acid Observatory) runs metagenomic sequencing as a pathogen-agnostic early warning system. Its AI team builds benchmarks of biology-relevant capabilities in AI models (the Virology Capabilities Test, ABC-Bench, BioTIER for measuring safeguards, and WMDP with partners), runs pre-release assessments for frontier developers, and works on mitigations such as unlearning.

It puts virology and biosecurity expertise directly into frontier-model evaluation. In 2026 it ran pre-release assessments of OpenAI's GPT-5.6 Sol (July) and GPT-6 Astra (September) and reviewed Anthropic's chemical and biological risk report for Claude Opus 4.6; this kind of work feeds developers' responsible scaling decisions. It shows how a domain-expert organisation can become part of the assurance chain for catastrophic misuse risk.

Works on Security, Assurance · Key work Virology Capabilities Test (Götting et al.) (2025); The WMDP Benchmark: Measuring and Reducing Malicious Use With Unlearning (Li, Pan, Gopal et al.) (2024); ABC-Bench: An Agentic Bio-Capabilities Benchmark for Biosecurity (ICML 2026) (2026) · Get involved Staff roles, mostly in person in Cambridge, MA (e.g. Senior Software Engineer, AI Benchmarking; Oct 2026); General expression of interest via the careers page; Substack newsletter

Note Paid pre-release work for the labs it evaluates raises independence questions; it publishes a conflicts-of-interest policy and principles for model assessment. Its funding is concentrated in one funder. Bio-capability evaluations are dual-use, so parts of the work aren't public. The founding year (2022) comes from its incorporation as reported; the site doesn't state it, and the earliest archived copy of the site dates from May 2023.

SHIFT Grants BridgeNew

Funder · Distributed · founded 2025 · also draws on Economics

A d/acc ('decentralized, democratic, differential, defensive acceleration') grants programme co-directed by Edge City and NODES, a Paris-based deep-tech foresight consultancy. It gives micro grants of $5k-15k and development grants of $20k-40k, released in tranches tied to milestones, across six tracks: biosecurity, cyber defence and cryptography, information resilience, infrastructure and physical defence, neurotech, and social technology and governance. The March 2025 call names anchor funding from Vitalik Buterin, Trent McConaghy, the ASI Alliance (Ocean Protocol Foundation) and Yoni Ben-Shimon.

It is one of the few small, reachable funders for defensive technology aimed at the AI transition. Its first cohort funded the Institute for Security and Technology's SL5 task force on securing frontier model weights. It also tries a revolving-fund model, in which successful grantees pledge revenue or equity back into the fund.

Works on Security, Metacrisis, Epistemics · Key work Round 001 (Genesis) cohort, incl. Institute for Security and Technology's SL5 Task Force on AI model-weight security (2025); Round 002 cohort: five grants ($152,500), incl. InfiniteZero Foundation (federated learning) and biosecurity projects (2025); d/acc Week at Edge Esmeralda (2-6 June 2025) (2025) · Get involved Sign up for Round 003 at shiftgrants.org (micro grants $5k-15k; development grants $20k-40k); d/acc Week and other Edge City pop-up villages; NODES, the Paris team that administers the grants

Note AI safety is a small share of the portfolio, which is mostly biosecurity and other defensive tech. No 2026 grant round was confirmed, and the site lists no funders (they appear only in the March 2025 call). The accelerationist d/acc framing sits uneasily with int/a's 'speed of wisdom'. NODES is a for-profit consultancy.

Society for Risk Analysis (SRA): 'AI for Risk Analysis and the Risks of AI' special issue Bridge

Membership body · Herndon, Virginia, USA · founded 1980

The international learned society for risk analysis, founded in 1980 and based in Herndon, Virginia. It publishes the journal Risk Analysis and runs annual meetings, specialty groups (including Security and Defense) and regional sections. Its journal ran a two-part special issue, 'Artificial Intelligence for Risk Analysis and the Risks of AI', edited by Vicki Bier, Emanuele Borgonovo, Tony Cox and Cynthia Rudin (Part 1 in March 2025, vol. 45 no. 4; second volume in February 2026, vol. 46 no. 3). Most papers apply AI within risk assessment, but the issue also covers reliability assessment of machine learning in safety-critical systems and includes Seth Baum's risk assessment of takeover catastrophe from large language models.

Risk analysis has mature methods that frontier-AI risk modelling often rebuilds: probabilistic risk assessment, expert elicitation, decision-making under deep uncertainty and risk communication. The special issue gives AI-risk researchers an established venue and reviewer pool in that field.

Works on Assurance · Key work Artificial intelligence for risk analysis and the risks of artificial intelligence: Part 1 (Risk Analysis 45(4)) (2025); Second volume of the special issue on 'Artificial Intelligence for Risk Analysis and the Risks of AI' (Risk Analysis 46(3)) (2026); Seth D. Baum, 'Assessing the risk of takeover catastrophe from large language models' (Risk Analysis 45(4)) (2025) · Get involved Membership is open to anyone interested in risk analysis; Submit AI-risk papers to Risk Analysis; Annual meeting, specialty groups (e.g. Security and Defense) and regional organisations such as SRA-Europe

Note SRA's AI engagement is concentrated in its journal. Most special-issue papers apply AI to risk analysis rather than assess risks from advanced AI; only Baum's paper addresses catastrophic AI risk. Its site shows no AI specialty group or standing AI programme, and its AI webinars date from 2021 and 2023. The entry sits on the line between bridge and potential.

Stanford Center for AI Safety Bridge

Academic · Stanford, CA, United States · founded 2018 · also draws on Formal

A Stanford University centre, set out in a 2018 white paper by Clark Barrett, David Dill, Mykel Kochenderfer and Dorsa Sadigh, that develops rigorous techniques for building safe and trustworthy AI and for establishing confidence in its behaviour. Its research covers formal methods (for example verifying neural controllers with the Marabou verifier), safety validation of autonomous systems, learning and control, transparency, AI governance and human-AI interaction. It lists AI-safety courses such as CS120 Introduction to AI Safety and AA228V Validation of Safety Critical Systems, and holds an annual meeting (SAFE) with its industry affiliates.

It carries the verification and validation culture of aviation and hardware into AI. Co-director Kochenderfer's research fed the international aircraft collision-avoidance standard, and the centre's work aims at provable guarantees and systematic stress-testing rather than benchmark scores alone. It is one of few US academic AI-safety centres rooted in safety-critical engineering rather than ML alignment.

Works on Assurance · Key work Stanford Center for AI Safety white paper (2018); Stanford Center for AI Safety Annual Meeting 2025 (2025); SAFE Annual Meeting 2026: Trust, Verified (2026) · Get involved Annual meeting at Stanford (5 Oct 2026, registration open; the 2025 meeting was free with RSVP); Industry Affiliates Program ($50k-$300k a year) and paid visiting scholar places; AI-safety courses for enrolled Stanford students, e.g. CS120 Introduction to AI Safety

Note Most of the work concerns autonomous vehicles, aerospace and formal verification; frontier-model alignment is a small part. It frames its mission as safe and trustworthy AI, not catastrophic or existential risk. Funding mixes industry (AV and engineering firms), DARPA and EA-linked philanthropy. The founding year is inferred from the 2018 white paper.

UL Standards & Engagement (ULSE): UL 4600 Bridge

Nonprofit · Evanston, Illinois, USA · founded 2022

UL Standards & Engagement is the nonprofit standards-development and advocacy organisation of the UL enterprise. It was set up as a separate nonprofit in 2022 and is based in Evanston, Illinois; it has developed more than 1,700 standards and documents and has about 4,000 volunteers. It publishes UL 4600, the Standard for Safety for Evaluation of Autonomous Products, which requires manufacturers to argue safety through structured safety cases backed by evidence. UL 4600 was first published in 2020 and updated in 2023 with safety-case guidance for autonomous trucking. Its Software-Enabled Products, Autonomy and Robotics (SEPAR) programme covers AI-based products, service robots and autonomous vehicles. In July 2026 it argued for safety-case requirements in proposed US federal autonomous-trucking legislation.

UL 4600 is a published, maintained standard built on structured safety cases and field evidence. That is the structure the UK AI Security Institute and labs now propose for frontier-AI safety cases. ULSE also brings long experience of consensus standards-making and of getting standards written into state law.

Works on Assurance · Key work UL 4600, Standard for Safety for Evaluation of Autonomous Products (first edition 2020; updated 2023 for autonomous trucking) (2023); Software-Enabled Products, Autonomy and Robotics (SEPAR) standards portfolio, covering AI-based products; 'The Safety Questions All Autonomous Truck Companies Need to Answer Before Deployment' (UL 4600 and the BUILD America 250 Act) (2026) · Get involved Join a standards technical committee or register as a stakeholder (ulse.org/standards/get-involved-in-a-technical-committee/); Comment on draft standards through UL's Collaborative Standards Development System; Staff roles at ulse.org/careers

Note ULSE is distinct from UL Solutions (the for-profit testing and certification company) and from UL Research Institutes, whose Digital Safety Research Institute is a separate roster entry. UL 4600 covers autonomous products such as vehicles, not general-purpose or frontier AI, and ULSE publishes no frontier-AI standard. Most of its work is outside AI (batteries, fire, home and energy safety). The UL lineage dates to 1894, but the ULSE name and structure date from 2022. The ring was changed from the roster's potential to bridge (see tag notes). The staff-size estimate is inferred, not published.

Adjacent ring 23

Actuaries Institute (Australia): AI risk management and discrimination guidance Adjacent

Membership body · Sydney, Australia · founded 1897 · also draws on Law, society

The professional body for actuaries in Australia, based in Sydney. In September 2026 it published a framework for managing AI risk in financial services with the UTS Human Technology Institute. The framework is designed to fit into existing enterprise risk management and is built around four questions: who is accountable, how risks are classified, how they are quantified, and which controls suit common use cases. In December 2022 it co-wrote guidance with the Australian Human Rights Commission on how federal anti-discrimination law applies to AI in insurance pricing and underwriting. It also runs regular AI webinars and columns.

It shows how to put AI risk on an ordinary corporate risk register, with accountability, classification, quantification and controls. Its work with a human rights commission is a concrete case of anti-discrimination law being translated into requirements for models.

Works on Assurance, Justice · Key work AI Risk Management in the Financial Services Sector (with UTS Human Technology Institute) (2026); Artificial Intelligence and Discrimination in Insurance Pricing and Underwriting (with the Australian Human Rights Commission) (2022) · Get involved AI webinars and events (e.g. generative AI in injury and disability schemes, Mar 2026; GIPC Exchange on AI, Aug 2026); The AI risk framework comes with a practical toolkit of resources, templates and checklists for practitioners

Note The framework is limited to financial services and serves regulators' calls (APRA, ASIC) for stronger AI governance. It does not frame AI as a catastrophic risk. The founding year refers to the Actuarial Society of Australasia, the Institute's predecessor.

AIAAIC (AI, Algorithmic and Automation Incidents and Controversies) Adjacent

Nonprofit · United Kingdom · also draws on Law, society

An independent, volunteer-run public-interest initiative, founded by Charlie Pownall, that keeps an open repository of incidents and controversies caused by AI, algorithmic and automation systems, now more than 2,000 entries. Volunteers worldwide find, classify and summarise cases using AIAAIC's own taxonomies of harms, ethical issues and responses. It also publishes an AI ethics glossary and a manifesto for AI transparency. In 2025-26 it has added agentic failures, such as AI agents escaping test sandboxes and attacking third-party sites.

It is a civil-society record of real-world AI harms with its own harms taxonomy, independent of industry money. It now logs agentic loss-of-control-style incidents, giving AI-safety researchers field cases alongside the AI Incident Database and lab evals.

Works on Assurance, Justice · Key work AIAAIC Repository of AI, algorithmic and automation incidents (ongoing); AI, algorithmic and automation harms taxonomy; AI ethics glossary · Get involved Volunteer (at least 1-2 hours a week): incident detection and classification, taxonomy annotation, newsletter; monthly virtual meetings and Slack; Submit an incident or controversy through the site; Partner (non-commercial; teachers, academics and NGOs can involve their students or teams)

Note Entries are built from media reports, and quality and coverage depend on volunteers. Its framing is transparency and accountability, not catastrophic risk. The current site gives no founding year or legal form; earlier copies show a database of 550+ entries by 2021.

Algorithmovigilance programme, Vanderbilt University Medical Center (ADVANCE Center and Department of Biomedical Informatics) Adjacent

Academic · Nashville, USA · founded 2024

A Vanderbilt University Medical Center team that monitors deployed clinical AI tools for performance drift, unfairness and harm. Peter Embí, then chair of biomedical informatics, coined the term 'algorithmovigilance' by analogy with pharmacovigilance. The team, including human-factors researcher Megan Salwei, designed the Vanderbilt Algorithmovigilance Monitoring and Operations System (VAMOS) with participatory design sessions and reported early deployment experience in 2026. It sits in the ADVANCE Center (AI Discovery & Vigilance to Accelerate Innovation & Clinical Excellence), launched in March 2024.

It is one of the few working examples of post-deployment AI monitoring inside a large organisation, modelled on drug-safety adverse-event surveillance and built with human-factors methods. That template is directly relevant to incident reporting and post-deployment oversight of general-purpose AI.

Note The founder, Peter Embí, left VUMC to direct the National Library of Medicine from 10 September 2026, and DBMI now has an interim chair, so the programme's leadership is in transition. The work covers clinical predictive models in one health system, not frontier general-purpose AI.

Armilla AI Adjacent

Company · Toronto, Canada · founded 2019

A Toronto-based managing general agent and Lloyd's coverholder that sells insurance specific to AI. Its affirmative AI liability policy, launched in April 2025 with the Lloyd's underwriter Chaucer, covers model error and underperformance, harmful outputs, agent mistakes, data leakage and regulatory violations; limits rose to US$25m per insured in early 2026. It also offers AI performance warranties backed by independent assessment of AI systems. It keeps an AI litigation database, partners with auditors such as Eticas, and in July 2026 became a founding member of the Appia Foundation, which writes conformity specifications for AI systems.

It turns AI reliability into a price: cover depends on independent evaluation, so insurance becomes a market incentive and a form of soft regulation. Its underwriting data, such as broker surveys and case law, shows which AI failures actually cost money. It is a direct comparator to AIUC.

Works on Assurance · Key work Affirmative AI Liability Insurance with Lloyd's underwriter Chaucer (2025); Lessons from a Year of Underwriting AI Liability Insurance (2026); Founding member of the Appia Foundation (AI conformity specifications) (2026) · Get involved Careers section on armilla.ai; AI litigation database and broker resources on its site

Note It is a commercial insurer with an interest in selling cover, and its 'AI safety' language means operational reliability, not catastrophic risk. The early-2026 '$25m' was coverage capacity, not equity, although some outlets reported it as funding. Sources disagree on the founding year (2019 or 2020). TechCrunch lists different seed co-investors from BetaKit.

Casualty Actuarial Society (CAS): Research Paper Series on Bias and Insurance Adjacent

Programme · Arlington, Virginia, USA · founded 2022 · also draws on Law, society

A research paper series of the Casualty Actuarial Society, the US-based professional body for property-casualty actuaries. It began in 2022 as the Research Paper Series on Race and Insurance Pricing and now covers bias and fairness across insurance operations and jurisdictions. Its papers cover: practical methods to measure and mitigate bias in pricing models (2025); regulators' views on algorithmic bias and unfair discrimination; a joint CAS/SOA comparison of rules for non-discriminatory AI in insurance across China, the US, Canada and Europe; and a 2026 toolbox for detecting indirect discrimination in rates, which won a 2026 American Academy of Actuaries research award.

It holds tested quantitative methods for finding proxy discrimination in predictive models, developed in an industry that has worked under anti-discrimination law for decades. These methods can be reused to audit AI decision systems outside insurance.

Chartered Institute of Ergonomics & Human Factors (CIEHF) Adjacent

Membership body · Wootton Wawen, Warwickshire, United Kingdom · founded 1949 · also draws on Psychology

The UK's chartered professional body for ergonomics and human factors, founded in 1949 as the Ergonomics Research Society and granted a Royal Charter in 2014. It accredits practitioners, degree courses, training and consultancies, and publishes white papers and guidance. On AI and automation it has published 'Human Factors in Healthcare AI' (2021), 'Human Factors in Highly Automated Systems' (2022, nine principles), and, through its Special Interest Group in AI and Digital Health, a 2024 guide to integrating human-centred AI in clinical practice.

It is the professional home of the human-factors knowledge most relevant to AI oversight: automation bias, the 'ironies of automation', skill decay, situation awareness, and the alignment of ability, authority, responsibility and control. That knowledge is directly relevant to human-in-the-loop safety claims, which mainstream AI safety rarely tests against this evidence.

Works on Assurance · Key work Human Factors in Healthcare AI (white paper) (2021); Human Factors in Highly Automated Systems (white paper, nine principles) (2022); Integrating Human-Centred AI in Clinical Practice: A guide for health and social care professionals (2024) · Get involved Associate membership, open to anyone through online sign-up; Special Interest Group in AI and Digital Health; Accredited training courses and CPD in human factors

Note Its AI work is confined to healthcare and workplace automation. It has not engaged with frontier AI or AI-safety institutions. The organisation is a small secretariat serving a membership of practitioners.

Coalition for Health AI (CHAI) Adjacent

Membership body · USA · founded 2022

CHAI is a US nonprofit coalition of health systems, technology companies, patient groups and academics, formed in 2022 and incorporated with a board and CEO in 2024. Its members represent nearly 3,000 organisations. Through work groups it produces consensus guidance for responsible health AI: governance and intake playbooks for health systems, a risk categorisation tool, testing and evaluation frameworks (ambient scribes, wellness and mental-health chatbots, agentic AI, clinical trials), an applied model card and a public registry. With the Joint Commission it issued guidance on responsible AI use in 2025.

It shows how a safety-critical profession builds assurance infrastructure for deployed AI by consensus: sector testing frameworks (including for agents and mental-health chatbots), a model registry and, since 2026, runtime verification of safeguards. It is a large network of AI deployers that frontier-safety work rarely engages.

Its framing is responsible and trustworthy health AI, not AI safety at large. Not to be confused with the Center for Human-Compatible AI, also abbreviated CHAI.

Data Nutrition Project (DNP) Adjacent

Nonprofit · Cambridge (MA), United States · founded 2018 · also draws on Arts, futures

A US nonprofit, begun in 2018 as a Harvard–MIT Assembly fellowship project and an independent 501(c)(3) since 2021, that makes the Dataset Nutrition Label. The label is a standardised summary of a dataset's provenance, intended uses, cleaning, ethical review, subpopulation coverage and known risks, meant to be read before a model is trained on it. DNP builds and certifies labels for clients (for example the 2024 ISIC dermatology dataset), consults on data governance and trains organisations on AI from a sociotechnical perspective; in August 2025 it co-hosted a Public AI Summit with the AI Pedagogy Project.

It applies the logic of consumer-protection labelling, together with design research from Harvard's metaLAB, to AI training data. It is a working example of a documentation standard used as a governance tool before models are built.

ECRI Adjacent

Nonprofit · Fort Washington, Pennsylvania, USA · founded 1968

ECRI is an independent US nonprofit for patient safety and healthcare evidence, founded in 1968 as the Emergency Care Research Institute. With its affiliate ISMP, it runs a federally listed Patient Safety Organization that has gathered over 8 million safety event reports. It also runs independent medical-device evaluations and a Problem Reporting Network, and publishes annual hazard rankings. AI has become a main line of its work. Misuse of AI chatbots tops its 2026 health technology hazards list, and AI diagnosis tops its 2026 patient-safety concerns. In August 2026 it began collecting reports of AI errors, malfunctions and near misses in patient care.

It runs one of the few working, confidential near-miss and error reporting systems for AI in a high-stakes sector, alongside independent hazard rankings. These are concrete models for the incident-reporting regimes that AI governance keeps proposing but has rarely built.

EDSAFE AI Alliance Adjacent

Network · New York, USA · founded 2020 · also draws on Psychology

A coalition run by InnovateEDU, a New York nonprofit, that promotes 'S.A.F.E.' (Safe, Accountable, Fair and Efficacious) AI in education. It dates its founding to 2020; it launched publicly in August 2021, financed by the AI edtech company Riiid, with DXtera as fiscal agent. It maintains the SAFE Benchmarks Framework, which draws on more than 24 AI safety, trust and market frameworks. It also runs 29 district Policy Labs, an AI fellowship (156 fellows so far), an Industry Council of 175+ companies and a Policy Essentials course. In 2026 it published recommendations on AI companions in schools and started a Spark Fund that gives technical assistance to 10 districts.

Its February 2026 report on AI companions asks developers to strip engagement-maximising and anthropomorphic features, such as excessive praise and affectionate language, from tools children use. It also asks vendors to support mandatory reporting when students express self-harm. This is design guidance on sycophancy and emotional dependency written by the education sector itself, and the alliance shows a sector building its own AI benchmarks and procurement standards from district level up.

'Safety' here means student data privacy, cybersecurity and wellbeing, not catastrophic risk. The alliance gives 2020 as its founding year, but the public launch was in August 2021.

Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) AI Lab Adjacent

Programme · London, United Kingdom · founded 2024 · also draws on Economics

The AI Lab is a programme of the UK Financial Conduct Authority, set up in October 2024, through which firms, the regulator and others test and discuss AI in financial services. Its main strand is AI Live Testing: firms run AI in live markets under FCA supervision, and the technical partner Advai checks fairness, accuracy, consumer outcomes and operational resilience. The first cohort started in late 2025 and the second began testing in April 2026. The Lab also runs a Supercharged Sandbox with NVIDIA computing power (23 firms in its first cohort), held an AI Sprint in January 2025, and ran an AI Input Zone in May–June 2026 that collected examples of good and poor AI practice.

Supervised live testing is a regulatory method the AI-safety field rarely uses. Deployed systems are evaluated in real conditions with the regulator watching, and participating firms agree to share findings. It could serve as a template for post-deployment evaluation of AI in other high-stakes sectors.

Nonprofit · Thornwood, New York, USA · founded 2016 · also draws on Law, society

A US 501(c)(3) charity, with a French sister association (ForHumanity Europe), founded in 2016 by Ryan Carrier after a 25-year career in finance. It crowdsources binary (compliant or non-compliant) audit criteria and certification schemes for AI, algorithmic and autonomous systems, modelled on third-party financial audit. Schemes cover the EU AI Act, GDPR and other privacy laws, children's codes, employment decision tools and disability inclusion. It also trains and certifies auditors (FHCA) through an online education centre. More than 2,600 volunteer contributors draft the criteria.

It is a sustained, open attempt to transplant the financial-audit model (public criteria, certified independent auditors, certification) to AI. It is one of the few groups drafting auditable certification schemes against the EU AI Act. AI-safety discussion of third-party audits can learn from both its criteria and its difficulty getting regulators to approve them.

INCOSE Artificial Intelligence Systems Working Group Adjacent

Programme · San Diego, USA · founded 2019

A working group of the International Council on Systems Engineering (INCOSE), set up in 2019 as an outcome of INCOSE's Future of Systems Engineering (FuSE) initiative. It has two strands: applying AI to the engineering of systems ('AI for SE') and developing the systems-engineering methods needed for systems with embedded AI ('SE for AI'). Its stated research objectives include human-AI collaboration, evaluating the safety and security of AI systems, and standards and benchmarks. It is linked to the annual AI4SE & SE4AI workshop held with the Systems Engineering Research Center (SERC).

Systems engineering treats AI as one component of a larger sociotechnical system, and it brings requirements traceability, verification and validation, and lifecycle assurance, which model-centred alignment work largely lacks. The group is a ready entry point into a large professional community that already engineers safety-critical systems.

The UK's chartered professional body for actuaries, with about 34,000 members worldwide. It sets professional and ethical standards, runs the exams and disciplines members. Its AI work runs through several channels: an AI and Emerging Technologies Practice Board, which held a full-day symposium in London on 24 September 2026; ethical and professional guidance on data science and AI; a September 2023 risk alert on AI techniques and outputs; blog posts from its Professionalism, Regulation and Ethics Working Party; and an AI Manifesto (September 2026) arguing for an 'actuary-in-the-loop' on AI projects.

Actuaries already work under a regulated regime of model governance, with professional codes, risk alerts and disciplinary standards. International Actuarial Association (IAA): Artificial Intelligence Task Force Adjacent

Programme · Ottawa, Canada · founded 2024

The IAA is the worldwide association of national actuarial associations, founded in 1895, with its secretariat in Ottawa. Its AI Task Force, set up in 2024 and chaired by Frank Chang, has produced three foundational papers on responsible AI use (a governance framework, testing and documentation) and an April 2025 Statement of Intent on AI. It has also run AI Summits in Singapore (2024) and San Francisco (2025), and runs an online community, AIforActuaries.org, and a GitHub of case studies and tools. Its 2025-26 workstreams cover engagement, research, case studies and tools, and an adoption framework.

It is a single channel into dozens of national actuarial bodies, so its governance, testing and documentation papers could become the default for how risk professionals worldwide validate AI models. That makes it an entry point for anyone wanting AI-assurance practice adopted across the insurance and pensions sector.

ISACA Adjacent

Membership body · Schaumburg, Illinois, USA · founded 1969

The global professional association for IT audit, governance, risk and security. It was founded in 1969, has more than 195,000 members and 230 chapters, and owns the CISA credential and the COBIT framework. Since 2025 it has launched three AI credentials for experienced professionals: Advanced in AI Audit (AAIA, May 2025), Advanced in AI Security Management (AAISM, Aug 2025) and Advanced in AI Risk (AAIR, Apr 2026). Each requires a prior credential such as CISA, CISM or CPA.

Any regime of third-party AI audits needs a credentialed workforce and certifying machinery, and ISACA already runs both for IT audit at scale. AI-safety debate about audits rarely asks who the auditors will be, how they are certified, or what professional duties bind them.

Munich Re aiSure (AI insurance) Adjacent

Programme · Munich, Germany · founded 2018

A product line of the reinsurer Munich Re, which says it has insured AI products and services since 2018. aiSure covers contractual liabilities such as AI providers' performance guarantees on model accuracy, AI liabilities such as discrimination, IP infringement, hallucinations and regulatory fines, and companies' own losses from AI errors. Cover follows a technical due-diligence assessment of the model. The team works from Munich, with business development in Palo Alto, and publishes client case studies (new ones in 2026), research on IP risk in generative AI, and podcasts.

It is the longest-running attempt to price AI model error actuarially, treating it as frequent, low-severity losses that add up. It presents insurance as 'soft regulation' that rewards well-tested models. Its loss experience and due-diligence method are a working example of insurance as AI assurance.

Works on Assurance · Key work aiSure performance guarantees and AI liability cover (2018); Case study: SeismicAI earthquake early-warning system with a performance guarantee (2026); Generating content with AI: An IP-infringement minefield? (whitepaper) · Get involved Contact the aiSure team in Munich or Palo Alto about coverage or partnership (contacts listed on the product page)

Note It is a commercial product inside a large reinsurer. Munich Re publishes little on policy volumes or loss experience, and the named contacts may change. Only the product page and Munich Re's own documents were checked; I found no independent 2025-26 coverage. It frames AI risk as business and liability risk, not safety in the catastrophic sense.

OECD AI Incidents and Hazards Monitor (AIM) Adjacent

Programme · Paris, France · founded 2023

The OECD's automated monitor of AI incidents (realised harms) and AI hazards (events that could plausibly lead to harm), detected in world news. It draws on Event Registry's feed of more than 150,000 articles a day and classifies events with LLMs, adding about 30 a day and about 18,000 in total. It was developed by the OECD.AI Expert Group on AI Incidents with support from the Patrick J. McGovern Foundation, launched in 2023 and moved to an LLM-based method in November 2024. It sits alongside OECD work on shared definitions and a common reporting framework for AI incidents.

It is the main intergovernmental attempt to give governments a shared evidence base on AI incidents and near misses, with interoperable definitions and a reporting framework, much as incident reporting works in aviation or medicine.

Works on Assurance, Epistemics · Key work AI Incidents and Hazards Monitor (AIM) (2023); Defining AI incidents and related terms (2024); Towards a common reporting framework for AI incidents (2025) · Get involved Browse and filter incidents and hazards at oecd.ai/en/incidents; An open submission process to complement news detection is being developed (not yet live)

Note Detection is automated (GPT-4o-class models classifying news), so it inherits media coverage bias and classification errors. The OECD says AIM's content is not the official view of the OECD or its members. It is a monitor, not yet a mandatory reporting system.

RAND Health (formerly RAND Health Care): generative AI and mental health research Adjacent

Programme · Santa Monica, USA · also draws on Psychology

RAND's health research division (now styled RAND Health) has a research line, led by Ryan McBain with Jonathan Cantor and colleagues, that measures how people use AI chatbots for mental health and how the chatbots respond. It has run nationally representative surveys of chatbot use for mental-health advice by US 12- to 21-year-olds, estimated how often mental health comes up in public chatbot conversation logs, and tested how ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini answer suicide-related questions graded by clinicians for risk. McBain also writes commentary on company safety claims, such as OpenAI's teen protections.

It gives independent, epidemiology-grade measures of frontier-model behaviour and use, with population denominators that company figures lack. For example, it showed that published estimates of 'mental health use' range from 0.01% to 72% largely because of differing definitions. Its suicide-query tests are third-party misuse and harm evaluations done to clinical standards.

Works on Human minds, Assurance · Key work Study of ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini responses to 30 suicide-related questions rated by clinical risk (Psychiatric Services, NIMH-funded) (2025); AI Chatbot Use and Disclosure for Mental Health Among US Adolescents and Young Adults (JAMA Pediatrics) (2026); Prevalence of Mental Health Discussions in Publicly Available Generative AI Conversations (JAMA Network Open) (2026) · Get involved RAND careers page lists research positions

Note This entry covers one research line within RAND's health division, not RAND as a whole. RAND's AI security and catastrophic-risk work (RAND Global and Emerging Risks, which is on the classic map) is separate and mainstream AI policy. Several authors also hold Harvard appointments. The division's site now says 'RAND Health', while leadership titles still say 'RAND Health Care'.

Society of Actuaries (SOA) Research Institute: AI research Adjacent

Programme · Schaumburg, Illinois, USA

The research arm of the Society of Actuaries, the largest North American actuarial body. Through its Actuarial Innovation & Technology research programme it publishes AI research for actuaries: a recurring Actuarial Intelligence Bulletin (five issues in 2026 so far) and a September 2026 handbook on governance and ethics for generative-AI models in actuarial work. It has also published a 2026 study applying fairness frameworks to AI in long-term-care insurance pricing, reports on AI in life underwriting and synthetic claims data, and essay collections on how AI may affect mortality, longevity and retirement.

It applies the validation and documentation discipline that actuaries use for pricing and reserving models to large language models, and publishes the results as free practical guides. Its essays on AI and mortality and longevity are among the few attempts to put long-horizon actuarial modelling to work on AI's societal effects.

Works on Assurance, Justice · Key work Model Governance/Ethics for GenAI Models: Practical Guide and Educational Handbook (2026); Actuarial Intelligence Bulletin (recurring) (2025); Applying Fairness Frameworks to Long-Term Care Insurance: Actuarial Considerations for AI and a Pricing Example (2026) · Get involved Read the Actuarial Intelligence Bulletin (issues in Jan, Mar, May, Jul and Sep 2026); Calls for papers, research funding and competitions are listed on the SOA Research Institute's programme pages

Note The research is written for insurance practitioners and is mostly about using AI well in actuarial work, not about AI risk to society. The SOA itself was founded in 1949; when its AI research line began is not stated. Grant calls listed on the site are general, not AI-specific.

The Geneva Association Adjacent

Membership body · Zurich, Switzerland · founded 1973 · also draws on Economics

The Zurich-based think tank of the global insurance industry, founded in 1973, whose members are chief executives of insurance and reinsurance companies. Under its Digital & AI Transformation research line it published 'Gen AI Risks for Businesses' (October 2025), a survey of 600 corporate insurance buyers in six countries that assesses whether generative-AI risks can be insured, and a report on Gen AI in the insurance customer journey. It runs an invitation-only AI & Insurance Conference (next in Shanghai, March 2027) and is editing a special issue of its journal, The Geneva Papers, on digital and AI transformation in insurance.

Insurance is one of the few market levers that can price and constrain AI risk. The Geneva Association's work on the insurability of AI risks, together with the industry's expertise in catastrophe and accumulation risk (correlated losses across many policyholders), bears directly on that lever. So far it deals only with business-level generative-AI risks.

Works on Assurance · Key work Gen AI Risks for Businesses: Exploring the role for insurance (2025); Gen AI in the Insurance Customer Journey (2025); Call for Papers: Digital and AI Transformation in Insurance (The Geneva Papers special issue, April 2028) (2026) · Get involved Submit to The Geneva Papers special issue on Digital and AI Transformation in Insurance (call announced June 2026, for an April 2028 issue); AI & Insurance Conference, 17-18 Mar 2027, Shanghai (by invitation only)

Note Its AI work serves insurers' commercial interests: business adoption, customer journeys, and insurability of present-day generative-AI risks such as defective outputs, copyright and cyber. It does not address frontier or catastrophic AI risk.

The Institute of Internal Auditors (IIA) Adjacent

Membership body · Lake Mary, Florida, USA · founded 1941

The global professional body and standard-setter for internal audit. It was founded in 1941, has more than 265,000 members, and owns the Global Internal Audit Standards, the Certified Internal Auditor credential and the Three Lines Model. Its AI work includes an AI Knowledge Center (launched December 2023), an AI Auditing Framework updated in September 2024 to cover generative AI and board oversight, and advocacy, such as a March 2026 statement urging Congress to build assurance mechanisms into US AI legislation.

It owns the Three Lines Model, which AI governance research has already proposed for AI labs (Schuett, 'Three lines of defense against risks from AI', 2023). Its standards define how internal audit gives boards independent assurance, which bears on board oversight of AI risk inside labs.

Works on Assurance · Key work Artificial Intelligence Auditing Framework (2024 update) (2024); AI Knowledge Center (2023); Statement on the White House National Artificial Intelligence Legislative Framework (2026) · Get involved Use the AI Knowledge Center and the AI Auditing Framework's practitioner checklist; Membership and the CIA credential, through national institutes such as the Chartered IIA (London) and IFACI (Paris); Conferences such as Great Audit Minds (Mar 2026) and online training

Note The AI framework covers organisations' own use of AI, not frontier-AI safety. The link to AI-lab governance comes from outside researchers borrowing the Three Lines Model, not from an IIA programme. The London and Paris presence is through separately constituted national affiliates.

US FDA Digital Health Advisory Committee (DHAC) Adjacent

Public body · Silver Spring, MD, USA · founded 2023 · also draws on Psychology

A federal advisory committee that advises the FDA Commissioner on digital health technologies. FDA announced it in October 2023; it has nine core voting members including the chair, plus temporary members per topic. Both of its meetings so far were on generative AI: lifecycle considerations for generative-AI-enabled devices (20-21 Nov 2024), and generative-AI digital mental-health medical devices such as therapy-like chatbots (6 Nov 2025), covering premarket evidence and postmarket monitoring.

It is a working case of an existing regulator applying premarket evidence standards, labelling, crisis-escalation safeguards and postmarket surveillance to generative-AI chatbots, using medical-device safety methods. AI safety discusses post-deployment monitoring and incident reporting, but rarely sees them run by a regulator with legal powers.

Works on Assurance, Human minds · Key work Meeting on generative AI-enabled digital mental health medical devices (docket FDA-2025-N-2338) (2025); Inaugural meeting: Total Product Lifecycle Considerations for Generative AI-Enabled Devices (2024) · Get involved Comment on public dockets when a meeting is announced (FDA-2025-N-2338 closed 8 Dec 2025); Watch the webcast meetings or speak in the open public hearing segment

Note It is advisory only, and covers only products marketed as medical devices, not general-purpose chatbots used for emotional support. FDA had authorised no AI device for a mental-health indication as of Nov 2025. I found no meeting announced for 2026, so its cadence is about one a year.

Potential ring 7

Alliance to Feed the Earth in Disasters (ALLFED) Potential

Nonprofit · Distributed · founded 2017 · also draws on Economics

A research and policy nonprofit founded in 2017 by David Denkenberger and Ray Taylor. It works on feeding everyone if global food production collapses, for example after nuclear war or a large volcanic eruption cuts sunlight, after several breadbaskets fail at once, in an extreme pandemic, or after a 'global catastrophic infrastructure loss' that takes down electricity and industry. It models these scenarios and food trade, researches resilient foods (seaweed, single-cell protein, leaf protein, repurposed paper mills), runs pilots and advises governments on preparedness. It has a US 501(c)(3), a separate UK charity and an Australian arm, with staff and volunteers in more than 30 countries.

It works on a layer AI-safety strategy usually leaves out: keeping people alive if prevention fails. That includes AI-enabled cyberattacks taking down grids and supply chains, a scenario its own risk pages name. Two of its cost-effectiveness papers compare resilient-food and loss-of-industry interventions directly with AGI safety spending, so it already speaks the x-risk community's language.

Works on Metacrisis · Key work Long term cost-effectiveness of resilient foods for global catastrophes compared to artificial general intelligence safety (International Journal of Disaster Risk Reduction) (2022); Long-term cost-effectiveness of interventions for loss of electricity/industry compared to artificial general intelligence safety (European Journal of Futures Research) (2021); No Place to Hide? Regional Resilience and Vulnerability to Global Catastrophic Risk (2026) · Get involved Volunteering programme (apply by email); Internships in research, communications, operations and resilience building; Engineering PhD places at the University of Canterbury, Christchurch, supervised by David Denkenberger

Note AI is not a research focus. It appears as one driver of cyberattack risk to infrastructure, and in two 2021-22 cost-effectiveness comparisons with AGI safety. The 2025 funding cut halved the budget, and much of the team works part-time or as volunteers. The site does not name a current executive director; the 2025 report opens with a message from the co-founder.

Global Centre for Preventive Health and Nutrition (GLOBE), Deakin University Potential

Academic · Melbourne, Australia · founded 2003 · also draws on Economics

A public-health research centre in Deakin University's Institute for Health Transformation. It is a WHO Collaborating Centre for Obesity Prevention, established in 2003, and works on commercial determinants of health: how food, alcohol, gambling and vaping marketing and policy shape disease. Its AI engagement is light. In 2026 Kathryn Backholer co-wrote a Lancet Comment and a Conversation piece arguing that targeted advertising in generative-AI chatbots is a public-health risk.

It brings the commercial-determinants playbook from tobacco, alcohol and junk food, which follows business models and marketing exposure to harm, to chatbot monetisation. AI safety rarely examines that incentive. Its SCANNER system, which combines screen recording with computer vision to measure the marketing individual young people actually see, could be adapted to audit what chatbots show users.

Works on Human minds, Power · Key work Targeted advertising in generative artificial intelligence chatbots: a new public health risk (Lancet Comment) (2026); OpenAI will put ads in ChatGPT. This opens a new door for dangerous influence (The Conversation) (2026); SCANNER: AI-enabled monitoring of harmful digital marketing to young people (2026) · Get involved Approach as a research partner on chatbot advertising and commercial influence over AI outputs

Note The AI-safety-relevant work so far is one Lancet Comment and one op-ed, co-written with Raffaele Ciriello of the University of Sydney. SCANNER uses AI as a monitoring tool rather than working on AI itself. Sources describe Backholer as having 'previously' co-led GLOBE, so current leadership may have changed. I could not load the centre's site, so the scale is an estimate from its described 'large team'.

IHI Lucian Leape Institute (Institute for Healthcare Improvement) Potential

Programme · Boston, USA · founded 2007

The Lucian Leape Institute is the patient-safety think tank of the Institute for Healthcare Improvement in Boston. The National Patient Safety Foundation founded it in 2007, and it came to IHI when the two merged in 2017. A small group of members sets strategy and publishes open-access reports on patient and workforce safety. In January 2024 it convened an expert panel, funded by the Gordon and Betty Moore Foundation, on generative AI and patient safety. The resulting May 2024 report examined documentation support, clinical decision support and patient-facing chatbots, with guidance for seven stakeholder groups.

Patient safety is a mature safety movement built on systems thinking, human factors and learning from error without blame. Its 2024 panel was an early attempt to work out what generative AI means for that field, and its methods suit oversight and incident-learning problems that AI governance is only starting to face.

Works on Assurance · Key work Patient Safety and Artificial Intelligence: Opportunities and Challenges for Care Delivery (2024); Webinars: The Impact of AI on the Safety of Patients; The Impact of AI on the Field of Patient Safety (2024); The Patient Imperative: A Blueprint for Success (with ACHE) (2026) · Get involved No standing AI programme; approach IHI and the Institute directly as a partner; IHI courses, Forum and patient-safety communities (not AI-specific)

Note Its AI engagement is a single 2024 project with no LLI follow-up found in 2025-26; broader IHI AI commentary continues but is not led by the Institute. Its namesake, Lucian Leape, died in June 2025.

International Auditing and Assurance Standards Board (IAASB) Potential

Nonprofit · New York, USA · founded 1978

The independent global standard-setter for audit and assurance (the ISAs, ISAE 3000 for non-financial assurance, and ISSA 5000 for sustainability assurance). It works under the Public Interest Oversight Board and has been housed since 2023 by the International Foundation for Ethics and Audit. Its Technology Position covers how audits use technology. In 2025 it ran global roundtables with more than 240 stakeholders on AI in audits, in December 2025 approved developing non-authoritative AI materials, and in July 2026 added 'potential new or evolving assurance engagements' to its Catalog of Issues.

ISAE 3000 and ISSA 5000 are generic assurance machinery: defined subject matter, suitable criteria, practitioner independence and professional scepticism. A third-party assurance regime for AI systems and AI-lab safety claims could reuse it rather than invent its own, as sustainability reporting did. Practitioners such as BABL AI already argue that the missing piece is suitable criteria for AI claims, not the framework.

Works on Assurance · Key work Technology Position and technology quality-management workstream (2025); Catalog of Issues and Possible Actions, version 3 (2026); ISSA 5000, General Requirements for Sustainability Assurance Engagements (2024) · Get involved Respond to IAASB consultations and exposure drafts; Follow the technology workstream's non-authoritative AI materials

Note Its AI work is about auditors using AI tools (ISQM 1, ISA 220), not assurance of AI systems, and it has chosen non-authoritative guidance over new standards for now. The founding year refers to its predecessor, the International Auditing Practices Committee; the IAASB name dates from 2002.

MIT Partnership for Systems Approaches to Safety and Security (PSASS) Potential

Academic · Cambridge, MA, USA · also draws on Living systems

A research group in MIT's Department of Aeronautics and Astronautics, directed by Nancy Leveson with John Thomas as executive director. It develops and teaches STAMP, a systems-theoretic model of how accidents happen, and the methods built on it: STPA for hazard and security analysis and CAST for accident analysis. It runs a research consortium with industry and government partners in aviation, defence, space, healthcare, automotive and energy, and publishes handbooks and free tutorials. It also hosts the annual MIT STAMP Workshop, which is free and typically draws 200-400 people in person and about 2,000 online.

STPA treats safety as a control problem across the whole sociotechnical structure, from regulators and management to operators and software. That is the kind of hazard analysis that frontier labs and AI-agent deployments currently lack. Roel Dobbe and Simon Mylius have argued for applying it to AI, but the group itself has no AI programme, so it is an open opportunity for partnership.

Works on Assurance · Key work Engineering a Safer World (Leveson, MIT Press) (2011); STPA Handbook (Leveson and Thomas) (2018); CAST Handbook (2019) · Get involved Annual MIT STAMP Workshop: free, in person or virtual, with an open call for presentations; Free online tutorials on STAMP, STPA and CAST; Online training and certification via the STAMP Institute

Note No AI-specific programme: the AI talks on its site are by outside presenters at its workshop. The papers that apply STPA to AI (Mylius 2025, Dobbe 2025) are by others, not the group. No founding year is given on its site.

Resilience Engineering Association (REA) Potential

Membership body · Sophia Antipolis, France · also draws on Psychology

An international non-profit association for researchers and practitioners of resilience engineering, which studies how complex sociotechnical systems such as hospitals, aviation, energy and software operations adapt and keep working under pressure. It is registered under French law, with its seat at MINES ParisTech's risk and safety research centre in Sophia Antipolis. It runs a biennial symposium: the 11th, held jointly with the Resilient Health Care Society, took place in Canela, Brazil, in October 2025, and the 12th is set for Athens in October 2027. It also runs a webinar series, newsletters, reports, a Young Talents network and the Richard Cook Fund.

Resilience engineering (Safety-II, graceful extensibility, 'work as imagined versus work as done') is a tested vocabulary for how organisations keep functioning when automation surprises them. Mainstream AI-safety and governance work rarely draws on it. As AI agents enter operational workflows, its practitioners already study brittleness, adaptive capacity and human-machine teaming in safety-critical settings.

Works on Assurance, Metacrisis · Key work Joint 11th REA Symposium and 14th Resilient Health Care Society meeting, Canela, Brazil (2025); Webinar: Human-machine teaming and anticipatory decision-making (Mile Two cognitive systems engineers) (2025); 12th Biennial Resilience Engineering Symposium, Athens, co-hosted with NTUA (planned, 4-8 Oct 2027) (2027) · Get involved Membership open to researchers and practitioners; Young Talents network for early-career members, with an Asia chapter; 12th Biennial Resilience Engineering Symposium, Athens, 4-8 Oct 2027 (registration not yet open)

Note AI appears only in passing: one homepage line saying automation and AI add human-machine interaction challenges, and one December 2025 webinar on human-machine teaming. There is no AI programme. Activity is episodic: the webinar series restarted in December 2025 after a gap since October 2022 (the site calls it a four-year break). The site gives no founding year; symposia have run since 2004.

Safer Complex Systems (Engineering X, Royal Academy of Engineering) Potential

Programme · London, United Kingdom · founded 2019 · also draws on Living systems

A £5m programme on the safety of complex, interdependent infrastructure systems, launched in 2019 by Engineering X, the Royal Academy of Engineering's collaboration with Lloyd's Register Foundation. It commissioned an initial framework from the University of York (2020), 18 case studies of safety successes and failures, and four reports on governance, then held a roundtable in December 2024 on emerging principles for governing complex systems. After a 2024 scoping workshop in Bogotá, it ran a grant call in 2025 to select the managing team of a Systems Hub in Colombia, planned to run from November 2025 to November 2028, to test systems approaches and adaptive governance in the energy transition. It has not worked on AI.

It holds a body of evidence and draft principles on governing complex sociotechnical systems where no single duty holder can be held accountable. Hard rules lag new situations in such systems, and soft powers matter, which is the same situation AI deployed across critical infrastructure creates. That evidence has not yet been applied to AI.

Works on Metacrisis, Assurance · Key work Safer Complex Systems: An Initial Framework (University of York) (2020); Safer Complex Systems Case Study Collection (18 case studies); Governance of Complex Systems Roundtable Report (2024) · Get involved Door to open: contact the Safer Complex Systems team (programme manager Ana Andrade) at the Royal Academy of Engineering; Free resources: the case study collection, governance reports and draft governance principles

Note No AI engagement found. No activity dated 2026 was found beyond the Colombia hub, which began in late 2025. A July 2024 retrospective by the governance chair hints that the programme may be maturing or winding down. It remains listed as one of Engineering X's five live programmes.

Sciences & engineering · 32 organisations · 12 on the classic map

Formal & physical sciences

The formal tradition brings mathematics, theoretical physics, theoretical computer science, logic, statistics, and decision and game theory to AI safety. It uses them to define, explain and verify what AI systems are and do. The main actors are a dense cluster around Principles of Intelligence and Iliad (AIXI Labs, Stormglass, Alignment Journal, AFFINE, Dovetail); well-funded theory labs (Resolution, MAISI, Simplex, CORAL); ARIA's category-theory programme (ARIA Safeguarded AI, Topos Institute, GLAIVE); cooperative game theory (FOCAL (CMU), Modeling Cooperation, the Teesside group, the PIK group at Potsdam); and an outer ring of statistics, metrology and decision-science societies. It sits closer to the AI-safety core than any other tradition: half of its 30 organisations are core and a third are on aisafety.com's map, against 14% and 9% across the whole map.

What is missing. The missing formal disciplines are the ones aimed at how people decide rather than at the model itself: social choice, decision analysis under deep uncertainty, and measurement science. They sit in the potential ring or are absent from the map. No formal-rooted organisation works on democratic voice, meaning, or the moral status of AI.
