Openings here Make homeostatic, bounded objectives a funded alignment research programme; Statisticians and metrologists set uncertainty reporting for dangerous-capability evaluations; Deep-uncertainty decision methods to stress-test frontier safety frameworks' if-then thresholds; Structured adversarial collaboration on AI consciousness, co-funded by Templeton; An ecology lab for populations of deployed AI agents; Mediators and negotiation scholars co-building evaluations for AI-agent conflict; Competition economists and regulators as monitors of AI agent markets; Safety science for open-ended AI, built with the artificial-life community; A social choice programme for aggregating public input into AI specifications

Core ring 17

AFFINE (Agent Foundations Field Network) CoreOn aisafety.comNew

Nonprofit · Distributed (seminars in Czechia and Portugal) · founded 2026 · also draws on Philosophy

AFFINE trains newcomers in theoretical AI alignment. It runs a fully funded one-month residential seminar: 30 participants and 19 mentors at Hostačov Château, Czechia, from 28 April to 28 May 2026, and 35 places in Portugal from 4 to 29 January 2027. Up to eight seminar graduates go on to a year-long fellowship, and mentoring is many-to-many, from researchers such as Abram Demski and Richard Ngo.

It treats alignment as pre-paradigmatic. It uses analytic philosophy and philosophy of science to question basic notions such as 'agent' and 'goal', in a self-described 'research monastery' format built around unhurried thinking. It also attends explicitly to psychological safety: participants rated the 2026 seminar's effect on their mental health 8.1 out of 10.

Works on Agency · Key work 2026 Superintelligence Alignment Seminar, Hostačov (retrospective) (2026); 2027 seminar in Portugal, with a year-long fellowship and a research retreat (2027); 2026 seminar talks (2026) · Get involved Apply to the 4–29 January 2027 seminar in Portugal. The deadline is 22 November 2026; travel, accommodation and meals are covered, plus a $1,000 stipend.; Year-long fellowship for up to 8 seminar participants, with stipends, travel and compute budgets; Donations via affi.ne/contact/#support

Note Very new: the first seminar ran in 2026. Leadership has already changed hands (Bagiński directed the 2026 seminar; Hölzer is now Director). Legal form and main funders are not published. Its bet on theory first is contested in alignment; on Manifund most commenters were favourable (e.g. Lucius Bushnaq, Tsvi Benson-Tilsen), while one rated it about three-quarters as promising as PIBBSS. Listed as an affiliate of Principles of Intelligence (formerly PIBBSS).

AIXI Labs (AI X-risk Initiative) CoreOn aisafety.comNew

Nonprofit · London, United Kingdom · founded 2026

A London nonprofit, launched in July 2026 and fiscally sponsored by Principles of Intelligence, that studies the algorithmic-information-theoretic foundations of AI agents. It uses variants of AIXI, Marcus Hutter's mathematical model of universal intelligence, to analyse risk factors such as deception and power-seeking and to test whether safety mitigations scale with capability, then tries to carry the results over to LLM agents. Iliad lists it as an incubated organisation.

It uses an idealised, mathematically tractable model of superintelligence as a testbed, a way to reason about systems more capable than any that can be studied empirically today. It aims both to strengthen the technical case that ASI poses existential risk and to prototype mitigations grounded in theory.

Works on Agency, Assurance · Key work Announcing AIXI Labs (2026); Golden Handcuffs make safer AI agents (arXiv:2604.13609) (2026); Understanding Generalization Requires Universal Induction (preprint) (2026) · Get involved Machine-learning research scientist role in London or Berkeley, £120k-160k (listed 22 Jul 2026 to 22 Jan 2027, academicjobsonline.org); AIXI Labs research fellowship (remote, with a monthly stipend; 2026-27 rounds advertised); Regular reading groups and research meetings through the universal-AI community hub (uaiasi.com)

Note It is only a few months old. AIXI is incomputable, so whether results transfer to real LLM agents is the central open question. Hutter is part-time and also works at Google DeepMind. The fellowship stipend figures come from aggregator sites, not the lab's own pages.

Alignment Journal CoreNew

Media · Distributed · founded 2026 · also draws on Philosophy

A new peer-reviewed, rolling-publication journal for foundational, theory-driven AI alignment research: agency, robustness, incentives, interpretability foundations and formal safety arguments. It welcomes negative results and interdisciplinary work, pays reviewers and credits them by name, and publishes 'reviewer abstracts'. It was announced in March 2026, opened selective submissions in September 2026 and planned broad submissions from October. It is fiscally sponsored by Principles of Intelligence, with operational support from Iliad.

It gives theoretical and interdisciplinary safety work an academic venue and credential that ML conferences do not, which matters for recruiting academics from other fields. The senior editorial board spans a philosopher (Seth Lazar), a theoretical neuroscientist (Andrew Saxe) and mathematicians and learning theorists.

Works on Agency, Assurance · Key work An Alignment Journal: Coming Soon (2026); An Alignment Journal: Features and policies (2026); The Alignment Journal: Organization, Personnel, and Scope (2026) · Get involved Submit papers (selective submissions from September 2026, broad submissions planned from October 2026); Nominate yourself as a paid, attributed reviewer on alignmentjournal.org

Note No papers had been published by early October 2026, so its quality and uptake are untested. It is fiscally sponsored by PrincInt and run with Iliad's support, so it is not independent of the research network it serves; it plans to spin out as its own nonprofit. It uses targeted LLM automation for administrative tasks. The classic map mentions it only inside Iliad's entry.

ARIA: Safeguarded AI and Scaling Trust (Trust Everything, Everywhere) CoreOn aisafety.comChanged

Funder · London, UK · founded 2024 · also draws on Safety science, Economics

Two programmes in 'Trust Everything, Everywhere', an opportunity space of the UK's Advanced Research and Invention Agency. Safeguarded AI (£59M, launched 2024) funds mathematicians and computer scientists, many of them category theorists, to build an open-source toolkit with which AI agents can produce formally verified artefacts; its first application is cybersecurity. Scaling Trust (nearly £50M, Programme Director Alex Obadia) funds cryptographic, game-theoretic and tooling work that lets AI agents negotiate and coordinate securely, stress-tested in a prize-backed Arena.

It is the largest public bet on mathematics-first assurance for AI. Its first theory cohort of more than 20 projects brought applied category theory, categorical probability, string diagrams and computational mechanics into AI safety. Under Nora Ammann, a co-founder of PIBBSS, it is a funding route for theorists from outside ML.

Works on Assurance, Multi-agent, Security · Key work TA1.1 Theory cohort: category theory, probabilistic semantics and verification for safeguarded AI (2024); November 2025 pivot: the toolkit becomes infrastructure for next-generation AI; Phase 2 of the ML track dropped (2025); Scaling Trust Arena: multi-agent coordination competitions (2026) · Get involved Rolling programme funding for Safeguarded AI: Cybersecurity (Track 1); Rolling funding for Scaling Trust Track 2 (Tooling) and Track 3 (Fundamental Research); Scaling Trust Arena competitions with a multi-million-pound prize pool (scalingtrust.org.uk)

Note It pivoted in November 2025 because frontier models were advancing faster than expected. ARIA dropped Phase 2 selection for specialised ML teams that would have built a bespoke AI system and broadened the TA1 toolkit. It also cancelled Phase 2 of the cyber-physical applications track; applications now centre on cybersecurity. The programme director changed in April 2026. The classic map lists ARIA as a funder but not these programmes. Whether formal guarantees can scale to frontier AI is still contested.

Cape Institute for Safe AI (CISAI), formerly AI Safety South Africa (AISSA) CoreChanged

Nonprofit · Cape Town, South Africa · founded 2024 · also draws on Safety science

A Cape Town nonprofit that runs a co-working hub, an in-house research lab and talent programmes on risks from advanced AI and on d/acc (defensive, decentralised technology). It is the 2026 successor of AI Safety South Africa, which Leo Hyams and Benjamin Sturgeon founded in 2024. AISSA ran Africa's first Cooperative AI Research Fellowship (10 fellows, Jan–Apr 2026, with the Cooperative AI Foundation, Principles of Intelligence and UCT). CISAI will host the PIBBSS/Principles of Intelligence fellowship from November 2026 to February 2027. Its in-house research is mainly capability evaluations, built with UK AISI and Apart Research, plus HumanAgencyBench, which tests whether AI assistants support human agency.

It is one of very few AI-safety hubs in Africa, with a cooperative-AI and multipolar orientation. It states openly that it does not endorse racing or any single actor acting for humanity. Hosting the Princint fellowship makes Cape Town a site where interdisciplinary alignment research is done outside the US and UK.

Works on Multi-agent, Assurance, Human minds · Key work Cooperative AI Research Fellowship (Cape Town) (2026); HumanAgencyBench: Scalable Evaluation of Human Agency Support in AI Assistants (2025); Autonomous replication and adaptation evaluations for the UK AISI bounty programme (2025) · Get involved PIBBSS/Principles of Intelligence fellowship hosted at its Cape Town space, Nov 2026–Feb 2027 (apply through pibbss.ai); Co-working applications for AI-safety and d/acc professionals, with subsidised rates; Weekly reading groups and events in Cape Town (Luma calendar); Substack newsletter

Note Renamed in 2026. AISSA's site now describes AISSA as the national volunteer network and CISAI as its operational hub. Much of the in-house research is standard ML capability evaluation, so the interdisciplinary content comes mainly from the cooperative-AI programme and the d/acc and multipolar framing. Partner and funder logos are listed together, so which bodies fund it directly is uncertain.

Causal Incentives Working Group CoreDormant

Network · Oxford and London, UK (distributed)

An informal research group spanning several institutions. It uses causal influence diagrams and multi-agent influence diagrams to formalise the incentives an AI agent has: to gain information, to control variables, to deceive, or to pursue instrumental goals. Members at Google DeepMind, Oxford, Imperial, UCL, Barcelona and elsewhere publish jointly and wrote the PyCID Python library. The site says the group is 'currently not meeting actively'.

It gives a precise graphical language, drawn from causal inference and decision theory, for defining contested notions such as intention, deception, goal-directedness and instrumental control. Those definitions can then be measured in LLMs. It is a worked example of formal concepts becoming evaluations.

Works on Agency, Multi-agent · Key work Modeling AGI safety frameworks with causal influence diagrams (2019); Robust agents learn causal world models (ICLR honourable mention) (2024); General agents need world models (ICML) (2025) · Get involved Its papers and the open-source PyCID library (GitHub) remain available

Note Dormant as a group, though its members continue related work at Google DeepMind, Oxford, Imperial and the Cooperative AI Foundation. No founding date is given; the earliest listed paper is from 2019.

Center on Long-Term Risk (CLR) CoreOn aisafety.com

Nonprofit · London, UK · founded 2013 · also draws on Philosophy

A London charity that works on worst-case (suffering) risks from advanced AI. It began in 2013 as a project of the Swiss Effective Altruism Foundation, first as the Foundational Research Institute, and became an independent UK charity at the end of 2021. It runs two research streams: an empirical Model Personas agenda on how malicious traits such as spite and sadism emerge and generalise in language models, and a conceptual agenda on Safe Pareto Improvements, bargaining changes meant to prevent catastrophic conflict between AI systems. It also makes grants through the CLR Fund and runs a paid summer research fellowship in London and online reading courses.

It brings bargaining theory, decision theory and suffering-focused ethics to a risk that most of the field overlooks: conflict between AI systems and the resulting extreme suffering, including possible suffering of artificial minds. Its Safe Pareto Improvements agenda is one of the few concrete technical approaches to AI–AI conflict.

Works on Multi-agent, Agency · Key work Safe Pareto Improvements research agenda (Anthony DiGiovanni) (2026); Model persona research agenda (2025); Emergent misalignment: narrow finetuning can produce broadly misaligned LLMs (Betley et al., led by Owain Evans's group; CLR researchers Daniel Tan and Niels Warncke co-authors) (2025) · Get involved Summer Research Fellowship: eight paid weeks in London (applications for 2027 open in March 2027); Research Affiliates Program (open now); CLR Fund: grants to individuals and organisations working on s-risks (rolling)

Note Its suffering-focused priorities (s-risks, the view that extreme suffering is not easily outweighed by happiness) are a minority position, even within effective altruism. The team is small, it reports that limited capacity holds back the SPI agenda, and it is narrowing the persona work to malevolent personas. It shares a funder and a trustee (Jesse Clifton, Macroscopic Ventures) with CAIF. Its parent, the Effective Altruism Foundation, ceased operations in 2025.

Computational Rational Agents Laboratory (CORAL) CoreOn aisafety.com

Nonprofit · Distributed

A small agent-foundations lab, fiscally sponsored by Ashgro, that pursues Vanessa Kosoy's learning-theoretic agenda: a mathematical theory of computationally bounded agents, built from computational learning theory, control theory, algorithmic information theory and categorical systems theory, as a framework for a rigorous solution to alignment. Its signature line is infra-Bayesianism, a theory of decision-making under ambiguity for agents embedded in their environment. It also publishes lectures and reading lists for mathematicians who want to contribute.

It is one of the few sustained attempts to derive alignment from first principles of learning theory rather than from empirical work on current models, and it publishes at mainstream learning-theory venues (COLT, JMLR).

Works on Agency, Values · Key work Ambiguous Online Learning (COLT 2026) (2026); Regret Bounds for Robust Online Decision Making (COLT 2025) (2025); Imprecise Multi-Armed Bandits (JMLR) (2025) · Get involved Recorded lecture series on the learning-theoretic agenda and on statistical learning theory, plus a reading list (coral-research.org/resources); Its site points researchers to the PIBBSS fellowship (when available) or to emailing Kosoy directly

Note Founding date and headquarters are not stated; the site dates from about April 2025. It overlaps closely with ALTER in Israel, where Kosoy directs AI research, and with her Technion PhD. The core team is two researchers. The agenda is highly abstract and its pay-off for practical alignment is long-term. The classic map also lists Kosoy separately as an individual.

Cooperative AI Foundation (CAIF) CoreOn aisafety.com

Funder · Exeter, UK (registered charity, England and Wales) · founded 2021 · also draws on Economics, Living systems

A UK charity, backed by a $15m commitment from Macroscopic Ventures, that funds and convenes research on the cooperative capabilities of AI systems and on risks from interacting agents (miscoordination, conflict, collusion). It runs a PhD fellowship (14 fellows in 2026, from 240 applicants), an annual summer school (Toronto, 3–7 August 2026, 45 participants), a monthly online seminar series and research grants. In 2025 it published the 'Multi-Agent Risks from Advanced AI' report. In June 2026 it launched a fund of up to $10m for multi-agent safety with Schmidt Sciences, Google DeepMind, ARIA and Google.org.

It sets the agenda for multi-agent safety, drawing on game theory, mechanism design, social choice and the science of cooperation rather than single-model alignment. It is also the largest dedicated funder of work on risks from ecosystems of interacting agents.

Works on Multi-agent, Assurance · Key work Multi-Agent Risks from Advanced AI (CAIF Technical Report #1, led by Lewis Hammond with dozens of co-authors) (2025); Up to $10m multi-agent safety funding call with Schmidt Sciences, Google DeepMind, ARIA and Google.org (tiers up to $300k and $1m; deadline 8 Aug 2026) (2026); Cooperative AI Summer School 2026 (Victoria College, Toronto; prizes from the Schwartz Reisman Institute) (2026) · Get involved Cooperative AI PhD Fellowship (annual; up to $40k/yr top-up for CAIF Scholars); Research grants, including the 2026 multi-agent safety fund (awards expected autumn 2026); Annual Cooperative AI Summer School for early-career researchers (fees £275–£550, bursaries available)

Note Most of its money comes from a single donor, Macroscopic Ventures, whose grantmaking officer Jesse Clifton is a CAIF trustee and also a CLR trustee. Google DeepMind staff sit on the board and DeepMind co-funds the 2026 call, which raises questions about independence from frontier labs. Its first CEO starts only in Oct 2026.

Dovetail CoreOn aisafety.com

Nonprofit · Distributed · founded 2024 · also draws on Living systems

A small, remote-first agent-foundations research group whose mission is to help humanity safely navigate the creation of powerful AI through foundational mathematics about the nature of AI agents. Its work covers agent structure, world models in optimal policies, the internal model principle and computational mechanics. It runs a paid 10-week research fellowship (2024, 2025, 2026) for people from undergraduates to postdocs. Alex Altair and Alfred Harwood lead it.

It draws on control theory and cybernetics (the internal model principle, the Touchette-Lloyd theorem) and on information theory to ask when optimisation produces agent-like structure and world models. It is also a low-barrier route for mathematicians, including undergraduates, into safety research.

Works on Agency · Key work Information-theoretic analysis of world models in optimal reward maximizers (2026); Proof Explained: Touchette-Lloyd Theorem (2026); Improving Internal Model Principle (2026) · Get involved Research fellowship: 10 weeks, remote-first, full- or half-time, £36,000 FTE pro-rated; the 2026 round (deadline 17 May 2026) required UK residency and is now closed; Occasional contractor roles (Lean formal verification, illustration, operations), all closed as of Oct 2026

Note A small team, many of them students or early-career. No openings at present. Its legal structure and base are not stated; members are in the UK and the Bay Area, and the 2026 fellowship was limited to UK residents, probably because of the ARIA funding. The classic map also lists the Dovetail Research Fellowship separately.

Foundations of Cooperative AI Lab (FOCAL) Core

Academic · Pittsburgh, USA · founded 2021 · also draws on Philosophy

A Carnegie Mellon research lab directed by Vincent Conitzer, set up with a USD 500,000 Cooperative AI Foundation grant (2021-2025), that builds game and decision theory for advanced autonomous AI agents with a focus on cooperation. Its work covers open-source game theory (agents that can read or simulate each other), credible commitments, safe Pareto improvements, imperfect recall, and decision-theoretic foundations. Members include Caspar Oesterheld, Vojtech Kovarik and Emanuel Tewolde. In 2026 its members presented papers on LLM cooperation and agent deception at ICML workshops, and Conitzer taught a 'Foundations of Cooperative AI' course in spring 2025.

It provides the formal theory for agents that can be copied, read each other's code, commit credibly or reason about their own decisions. That is the theoretical basis for avoiding conflict between AI systems, and between AI and humans. It is one of the few academic labs whose founding mission is the foundations of cooperative AI.

Works on Multi-agent, Agency · Key work Foundations of Cooperative AI (Conitzer and Oesterheld, AAAI-23 Blue Sky) (2023); Safe Pareto improvements for delegated game playing (JAAMAS) (2022); Similarity-based cooperative equilibrium (NeurIPS) (2023) · Get involved PhD study through CMU's Computer Science Department (mention FOCAL in the application); Postdoctoral positions (advertised via Interfolio); Lab mailing list

Note The lab's own site is rarely updated: its publication list stops in 2024, and recent outputs appear on Conitzer's homepage. The CAIF grant period ended in 2025. Conitzer also directs a newer CMU centre, Conceptual Research on Safe AI (CoRe Safe AI, launched 2026), and is Head of Technical AI Engagement at Oxford's Institute for Ethics in AI. Ring changed from the roster's bridge to core (see tag notes).

Iliad CoreOn aisafety.comNew

Nonprofit · Bay Area, USA and London, UK · founded 2025 · also draws on Living systems

A nonprofit founded in 2025 by Alexander Gietelink Oldenziel and Caleb Rak to make foundational AI alignment a 'rigorous scientific field' grounded in mathematics and physics. It runs the four-week Iliad Intensive (from April 2026) and the three-month Iliad Fellowship (with PrincInt), the ILIAD and Agent Foundations conference series, and supports the Alignment Journal. It also incubates four research groups: AIXI Labs, Principia, Stormglass and XOR Labs.

It is the main training and incubation route that brings mathematicians, theoretical physicists and theoretical computer scientists into alignment research. It imports those disciplines' standards of rigour, giving people from formal fields a concrete way in.

Works on Agency, People · Key work Iliad Intensive and Iliad Fellowship (evolved from the PIBBSS x Iliad Research Residency) (2026); Agent Foundations 2026 at CMU (third in the series) (2026); ILIAD conference series (with PIBBSS and Simplex at the first edition) (2024) · Get involved Iliad Intensive: four-week taught course; January 2027 cohort in London or the Bay Area, applications close 16 Nov 2026; Iliad Fellowship: three-month mentored research; Dec 2026-Mar 2027 cohort, applications close 19 Oct 2026; Open call for new research organisations, and an RFP on raising the field's epistemic bar and theory of ReLU networks

Note A young organisation that is scaling quickly. It is legally a fiscally sponsored project of PrincInt rather than its own charity.

Mathematical AI Safety Institute (MAISI) CoreOn aisafety.comNew

Nonprofit · San Francisco Bay Area, United States · founded 2026

An independent nonprofit in the Bay Area that aims to build rigorous mathematical foundations for the safety of powerful AI, so that safety problems can be stated and reasoned about with definitions, measurements and solution concepts. It follows the Institute for Advanced Study model: mathematicians join as Members for one or two semesters. It plans a first cohort of 10-30 in January 2027 and a Special Year of 30-100 in September 2027.

It is a large, dedicated funded channel (a $10M grant) for bringing research mathematicians, led by a 2026 Fields Medallist, into defining what AI safety means. It tests whether a pure-mathematics institute format can produce foundations that the ML-led field has not. It deepens the formal strand of AI safety rather than widening the field towards other disciplines.

Works on Assurance, Agency · Key work $10M grant from Coefficient Giving announced (2026); Public launch of the institute (press coverage, 8 September) (2026); Recruitment for the January 2027 semester and September 2027 Special Year (2026) · Get involved Membership for faculty-level mathematicians, one or two semesters: 10-30 places for January 2027, with a preference for candidates who can start then; requires moving to the Bay Area (apply at maisi.org/apply); September 2027 Special Year for 30-100 researchers; Applicants can choose to have their application shared with the Alignment Research Center and Resolution

Note Tsimerman is joining OpenAI's safety team at the same time; press reports say the institute will operate independently of the company. It has no research track record yet, and the first semester starts in January 2027. Commentators note that a mathematical safety guarantee is only as good as the model it rests on. Members must move to the Bay Area.

Modeling Cooperation CoreOn aisafety.com

Nonprofit · Distributed · founded 2019 · also draws on Arts, futures, Living systems

Small independent team of software engineers and researchers, started in 2019 by Jonas Emanuel Müller, Vasily Kuznetsov and Miles Tidmarsh after AI Safety Camp. Convergence Analysis is its fiscal sponsor. It builds the software that runs Intelligence Rising, the AI-competition role-play workshop run by Technology Strategy Roleplay. It also publishes game-theoretic and agent-based models of AI races, such as an extension of 'Racing to the Precipice' and an analysis of whether a Windfall Clause holds up under competitive pressure. A June 2026 BlueDot grant pays the LLM costs of AI-controlled players in the platform.

It gives governance researchers and decision-makers formal and hands-on tools for seeing race dynamics. It combines game theory with policy wargaming, a strategic-studies method that mainstream alignment work rarely uses.

Works on Multi-agent, Security · Key work Scenario simulation platform powering Intelligence Rising workshops (2026); Interactive models of AI competition (Safety-Performance Tradeoff web app) (2022); Safe Transformative AI via a Windfall Clause (technical report) (2021) · Get involved No open roles or calls found. The team shares its models and repositories with governance researchers; Intelligence Rising workshops, run by Technology Strategy Roleplay, use its platform

Note Very small (three or four people) and dependent on small grants. Research output has been sparse since about 2022, with effort going into maintaining and extending the Intelligence Rising software. Location not stated; it works remotely.

Resolution (incorporating Timaeus) CoreOn aisafety.comNew

Nonprofit · Berkeley, USA · founded 2026

An alignment research nonprofit launched in June 2026, when Timaeus (founded 2023, known for applying singular learning theory to alignment) joined researchers from UK AISI's Alignment Team. It was briefly announced as Sequent, and legally it is Timaeus Research, Inc. renamed Resolution Alignment, Inc. It pursues a portfolio of theory and empirical bets for 'higher-confidence' alignment of superintelligence: singular learning theory, learning theory, scalable oversight, game theory, persona structure and theory-guided automated research. In September 2026 it added an Agent Foundations team continuing MIRI's line of work.

It is the best-funded attempt to apply mathematical traditions (singular learning theory, agent foundations, game theory) to alignment at frontier scale, so it will show whether such imported theory can affect how deep learning is done. Its agent-foundations agenda includes work on trust and legitimacy, and it advertises a philosophy research role.

Works on Agency, Assurance · Key work Resolution: Scale and Automation for Higher Confidence in Alignment (launch memo) (2026); Elicitation without Backpropagation (Timaeus) (2026); Focus Period: Mathematical Science of AI Safety, University of Sydney (2025) · Get involved Staff roles: Research Scientist (scalable oversight) and Research Engineer (automation) open as of Sep 2026; other rounds, including philosophy, paused for about two months; $5k referral bonus for successful hires; hiring a CTO

Note Launched under its current name in 2026, but legally a renamed Timaeus Research, Inc., so its track record before 2026 is Timaeus's. The London hub was dropped in Aug 2026, and in-person work in Berkeley is now favoured. It aims for 40-80 FTE within two years; current headcount was not found. Timaeus is not separately listed on the classic map.

Simplex CoreOn aisafety.com

Nonprofit · Emeryville, United States · founded 2024 · also draws on Living systems

An AI-safety research group founded in 2024 by physicist Paul Riechers and neuroscientist Adam Shai, now part of the Astera Institute, with staff in Emeryville and London. It uses computational mechanics and Bayesian belief-state theory to predict and explain the internal geometry of neural network representations. Results so far: transformers encode fractal belief-state geometries, attention implements constrained belief updating, in-context learning follows from pretraining data structure, and transformers learn factored world models.

It brings a mature physics framework, computational mechanics, to interpretability, making testable predictions about what models must represent instead of searching for features after the fact. It also aims for a theory that covers both artificial and biological intelligence.

Works on Agency · Key work Transformers represent belief state geometry in their residual stream (NeurIPS) (2024); Constrained belief updates explain geometric structures in transformer representations (ICML) (2025); Simplex progress report (2025) · Get involved Hiring Research Scientists and Senior Research Scientists in the Bay Area and Research Scientists in London (via Astera's jobs board, 2026); Blog: belief-updates.pub

Note It is organisationally part of the Astera Institute, whose main AI effort is a brain-inspired AGI programme. The roster also lists Simplex inside the Astera entry, so there is a risk of double-counting. Its results so far come mostly from small models trained on synthetic processes, so they may not transfer to frontier models.

Stormglass AI Safety Institute CoreUnverified

Nonprofit · Fredericton, Canada

A small Canadian nonprofit, formerly called MoirAI, that aims to 'advance the science of AI learning dynamics': how training and design choices causally shape what models learn and how they behave. It plans theory, practical tools and educational material to help labs and policymakers detect unsafe behaviours earlier in training. It is led by Max Hennick, a Principles of Intelligence (PrincInt) affiliate, and Iliad lists it as an incubated organisation.

It applies singular learning theory and the statistical physics of stochastic gradient descent to training dynamics, aiming to catch unsafe learning while it happens rather than evaluate finished models. It is based in Fredericton, New Brunswick, outside the usual AI-safety hubs.

Works on Agency, Assurance · Key work Almost Bayesian: Dynamics of SGD Through Singular Learning Theory (Hennick and De Baerdemacker, ICLR) (2026) · Get involved Researcher ($120k-160k USD) role, remote from Fredericton with quarterly travel: not currently hiring but accepting CVs for future consideration (people@stormglass.ca); the research-engineer role ($90k-125k USD) was filled in June 2026, and more hiring waits on funding

Note Renamed from MoirAI. The site is under construction and names no staff or outputs. The only identifiable paper by its leader lists the University of New Brunswick and TrojAI as affiliations, not Stormglass. Funding appears precarious. The location comes from job postings.

Bridge ring 7

Basis Research Institute (Basis) Bridge

Nonprofit · New York, USA · founded 2022 · also draws on Psychology, Living systems

A US nonprofit founded in 2022 by Zenna Tavares, Emily Mackevicius and Eli Bingham, with offices in New York and Cambridge, MA. It builds AI from probabilistic programming, causal inference and cognitive science, aiming at a 'universal reasoning engine'. It releases open-source tools (ChiRho, Effectful, Dynestyx) and runs applied projects on automated scientific discovery, robot design, participatory city modelling and animal collective behaviour. In 2026 it also published work on AI-assisted formal verification and, with ARIA funding, on Pact, a language for trustworthy coordination between AI agents.

It builds auditable, causal and formally checkable alternatives to opaque models, the infrastructure that guaranteed-safe approaches need. It has started applying them to safety-relevant problems: verified software, trustworthy multi-agent protocols, and brain-inspired cognitive architectures (in the NeuroAI for AI Safety roadmap).

Works on Assurance, Multi-agent, Agency · Key work Pact: Trustworthy Coordination for Multi-Agentic Ecosystems (ARIA Scaling Trust pre-discovery) (2026); Using LLM-based Verification to Eliminate Bugs in Linux's Network Stack (2026); Contribution to the Amaranth Foundation's NeuroAI for AI Safety roadmap (2024) · Get involved Research roles on the careers page (basis.ai); Open-source tools on GitHub (BasisResearch): ChiRho, Effectful, Dynestyx

Note Its main mission is building reasoning AI, which has capability as well as safety implications; most of its work carries no safety framing. Its safety-relevant work so far is a short ARIA pre-discovery project, a co-authored roadmap and a verification line. Not to be confused with Basis, the accounting-AI company.

Centre for Mathematical AI, Fields Institute BridgeNew

Academic · Toronto, Canada · founded 2025

A centre at Toronto's Fields Institute for Research in Mathematical Sciences, launched in spring 2025. It works on two questions: how mathematics can make AI systems safer and more transparent, and how AI can help mathematical discovery (formalisation in Lean, AI-assisted reasoning). Its AI-safety strand includes the graduate course 'Mathematics for AI Safety' (autumn 2026) and two-year postdocs, run jointly with PrincInt, on mathematical foundations of interpretability.

It shows how AI-safety teaching and postdocs can be embedded inside a mainstream mathematics institute. It recruits pure mathematicians and statistical physicists through their own institutions rather than through AI-safety field-building channels.

Works on Agency, Assurance · Key work Mathematics for AI Safety (Fields Academy shared graduate course, MAT1510) (2026); Fields-PrincInt postdoctoral fellowships in mathematics and AI safety (2026); Mathematical AI Seminar 2025-26 (2025) · Get involved Mathematics for AI Safety course, Sep-Dec 2026: free for students from sponsoring universities, CAD 500 for others, auditing allowed, Zoom option; Fields-PrincInt two-year postdocs (2026 round closed 31 Jan 2026); Mathematical AI Seminar series

Note Only one strand of the centre is about AI safety; its other themes (knowledge extraction from papers, AI-assisted reasoning, autoformalisation) are AI for mathematics. Not to be confused with the separate Mathematical AI Safety Institute.

Glaive Research (Glasgow Lab for AI Verification, GLAIVE) Bridge

Nonprofit · Glasgow, UK · founded 2024

A small nonprofit research group 'applying category theory to AI verification', using container theory and dependent lenses. It has three programmes: typed tactics for theorem proving in Lean, neural-network architectures built on containers, and Polylang, a programming language whose unit of computation is the lens. It held ARIA Safeguarded AI TA1.1 funding ('True Categorical Programming for Composable Systems') in 2024-25, and its 2025-26 work is an AI-for-maths project on structured tactics for machine-assisted theorem proving.

It represents the programming-language and category-theory route to verifiable AI, outside both mainstream ML and the AI-safety mainstream. Its tooling aims to make AI theorem provers and network architectures structurally checkable.

Works on Assurance, Agency · Key work True Categorical Programming for Composable Systems (ARIA Safeguarded AI TA1.1) (2024); Typed tactics prototype in Lean ('Tactics with Types and Shapes') (2026); Canonical Bidirectional Typechecking (Hedges and Mihejevs) (2025) · Get involved 'Work with us': hires researchers at pay comparable to senior academic posts, and hosts researchers who bring their own grants

Note Its work has moved from ARIA-funded safety verification towards AI-for-maths tooling (structured tactics for AI theorem provers). The ARIA project is closed and Jade Master, its co-lead, is no longer listed on the team. The site gives no founding date or address: 2024 is inferred from the first ARIA awards, and Glasgow from the name ARIA uses. It shares people with the CyberCat Institute (Institute for Categorical Cybernetics), which develops 'theory and software for governing systems that learn and make decisions'.

Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research (PIK): Working Group on Behavioural Game Theory and Interacting Agents (BeGa), formerly the FutureLab on Game Theory and Networks of Interacting Agents (GaNe) BridgeChanged

Academic · Potsdam, Germany · founded 2025 · also draws on Living systems, Democracy

A small working group in PIK's Complexity Science department, led by mathematician Jobst Heitzig. It continues the work of the former PIK–MCC FutureLab on game theory and networks of interacting agents. The group studies cooperation, coalition formation, social choice and bounded rationality among human, institutional and artificial agents, and designs alternatives to expected-utility maximisation, such as aspiration-based and agency-preserving decision algorithms. Within this, Heitzig publishes AI-safety research: non-maximising 'aspiration-based' agents (the SatisfIA project) and objective functions that make AI preserve long-term human power.

This is the clearest case of an Earth-system science institute doing alignment theory. It brings social choice, cooperation game theory and formal ethics to two problems: over-optimisation (Goodhart) and the preservation of human empowerment against power-seeking or gradual disempowerment.

Works on Agency, Power, Values · Key work Non-maximizing policies that fulfill multi-criterion aspirations in expectation (Dima, Fischer, Heitzig, Oliver) (2024); Social Choice Should Guide AI Alignment in Dealing with Diverse Human Feedback (Conitzer et al., incl. Heitzig) (2024); Model-Based Soft Maximization of Suitable Metrics of Long-Term Human Power (Heitzig, Potham) (2025) · Get involved Master's thesis co-supervision for students of mathematics, physics, computer science and economics (contact the group); Follow Heitzig's AI-safety work on LessWrong and arXiv

Note The FutureLab GaNe no longer exists under that name; its research directions continue in the BeGa working group. The AI-safety output depends heavily on one researcher, and most of the group's work is on climate cooperation and social choice rather than AI.

Royal Statistical Society (RSS): AI Task Force Bridge

Membership body · London, UK · founded 1834

The RSS is the UK's learned society and professional body for statistics, founded in 1834 and based in London. Its AI Task Force, formed in June 2024 and chaired by Donna Phillips, plans the society's AI work through subgroups on communications, policy and ethics, evaluation of AI models, and practitioners. In 2026 it published 'AI is Statistics' (2 March) and 'AI regulation needs statistics' (8 July). The papers argue that regulating AI is largely a matter of statistically evaluating models in deployment, through uncertainty quantification, subgroup analysis and testing under distribution shift, and the RSS has followed up with sector regulators in health, education and finance.

It offers an established discipline of inference, uncertainty and experimental design as the basis for evaluating and overseeing AI, and a professional community that could do that work. AI evaluation is often short on this kind of statistical rigour.

Works on Assurance, Epistemics · Key work AI is Statistics: why statistical thinking is vital for the effective, ethical and safe use of AI (2026); AI regulation needs statistics: evaluating reliability, uncertainty and risk in practice (2026); RSS: Data Science and Artificial Intelligence (journal, with Oxford University Press) (2025) · Get involved RSS membership and its sections (e.g. Data Science & AI); AI Task Force recruits members from the RSS membership (call Sept-Oct 2026); Submit to the journal RSS: Data Science and Artificial Intelligence

Note The ring is borderline between bridge and adjacent: the framing is the 'effective, ethical and safe' use of AI and sector regulation, with no frontier or catastrophic-risk angle. AI is one policy area among many for the society.

The Anh Han's AI-safety behavioural modelling group, Teesside University Bridge

Academic · Middlesbrough, UK · founded 2018 · also draws on Living systems, Economics

This is the research group of The Anh Han, Professor of Computer Science and lead of the Centre for Digital Innovation at Teesside University in Middlesbrough. It uses evolutionary game theory, agent-based simulation and behavioural experiments to model AI development races as SAFE/UNSAFE social dilemmas. It tests voluntary safety commitments, peer and institutional sanctions, rewards, and how user trust and monitoring shape developer behaviour. The line began with an FLI grant in 2018 and continues with FLI and EPSRC funding.

It gives formal, testable models of race dynamics and governance incentives, for example when pledges, monitoring or penalties make safe development a stable outcome. It draws on decades of evolution-of-cooperation research, a toolkit largely absent from mainstream AI-policy analysis. One finding: safety collapses when AI supremacy looks near-term.

Works on Multi-agent, Assurance · Key work To regulate or not: a social dynamics analysis of the race for AI supremacy (2019); Voluntary safety commitments provide an escape from over-regulation in AI development (Technology in Society) (2022); FAIRGAME: A Framework for AI Agents Bias Recognition Using Game Theory (ECAI) (2025) · Get involved PhD supervision in AI-safety and existential-risk modelling, game theory, agent-based systems and behavioural incentives (contact The Anh Han via Teesside University)

Note This is not a formally named unit: the label describes Han's research line within Teesside's Centre for Digital Innovation, and he also works on unrelated applied ML. The models are stylised, and much of the work is co-authored with groups in Lisbon, Brussels and Stirling. The founding year is the start of the AI-safety line (first FLI grant); Han has been at Teesside since 2014.

Topos Institute (incl. Topos Research UK) Bridge

Nonprofit · Berkeley, USA · founded 2019 · also draws on Democracy

A nonprofit research institute that applies category theory to 'mathematical systems science' and builds open-source modelling software (CatColab, AlgebraicJulia) for collaborative modelling and collective sense-making. It was incorporated in Berkeley in 2019, and its UK sister organisation, Topos Research UK, was incorporated in 2024 and opened an Oxford office that October. Its main AI-safety work is the ARIA Safeguarded AI project 'Double Categorical Systems Theory for Safeguarded AI', which builds a framework for co-designing auditable models of the environments AI systems are deployed in.

It links formal assurance of AI to collective sense-making: its tools are built to 'enable cooperation across difference', so stakeholders and domain experts can jointly specify what safe AI behaviour means. Its mission language ('knowledge and compassion') is close to int/a's.

Works on Assurance, Epistemics · Key work Double Categorical Systems Theory for Safeguarded AI (ARIA TA1.1, lead David Jaz Myers) (2024); CatColab v0.6 'Starling' collaborative modelling platform (2026); Changing the frame: Formal modeling with LLM assistance, Part 1 (Evan Patterson) (2026) · Get involved Summer Research Associates programme (annual; 2026 call opened Nov 2025); Postdoctoral openings at Topos Oxford (UK rounds in 2025 and 2026)

Note Most of its output is applied category theory and modelling software for science (epidemiology, systems biology), not AI. The AI-safety work is concentrated in the UK arm's ARIA project.

Adjacent ring 1

Munich Center for Mathematical Philosophy (MCMP), LMU Munich Adjacent

Academic · Munich, Germany · founded 2010 · also draws on Philosophy

A research centre for mathematical philosophy at LMU Munich, founded in 2010 by Hannes Leitgeb with an Alexander von Humboldt Professorship and now directed by Leitgeb, Stephan Hartmann and Christian List. It applies logic, probability, statistics, decision theory and social choice theory to philosophical problems, and lists philosophy of AI among its research areas. Its main AI work is Tom Sterkenburg's DFG Emmy Noether group 'From Bias to Knowledge: The Epistemology of Machine Learning' (2023-2029), and it hosts PhilML'26, the annual Philosophy of Machine Learning conference, on 6-9 October 2026.

Formal epistemology, decision theory and social choice are the tools behind agent foundations and preference aggregation, and MCMP holds a large concentration of that expertise. It now has a funded group on what machine learning can justify, and PhilML'26 lists alignment, safety and mechanistic interpretability among its topics, so it is a natural partner for foundational alignment work that wants philosophical rigour.

Works on Agency · Key work DFG Emmy Noether project 'From Bias to Knowledge: The Epistemology of Machine Learning' (Tom Sterkenburg) (2023-2029); PhilML'26: Philosophy of Machine Learning conference and graduate workshop, Munich, 6-9 October (2026); DFG project 'Deep Learning in Particle Physics' (Martin King) (2022-2025) · Get involved PhilML conference and graduate workshop (calls for extended abstracts; 2026 edition in Munich); Regular faculty, postdoctoral, doctoral and master's fellowships; self-funded visiting researchers and sabbatical scholars welcome; Public talk series at LMU

Note AI is one strand among many (logic, philosophy of physics, philosophy of language). PhilML is organised by a cross-institution group (Freiesleben, Grote, Sterkenburg, Vredenburgh); MCMP hosts the 2026 edition, so it is not a permanent MCMP event. Ring changed from the roster's potential to adjacent because the Emmy Noether group is a sustained, funded AI programme. Current size not found.

Potential ring 7

American Statistical Association (ASA) Potential

Membership body · Alexandria, USA · founded 1839

The US professional society for statisticians, founded in Boston in 1839 and based in Alexandria, Virginia. Its board issued a statement on the role of statistics in data science and AI (August 2023) and the 'Statement on Ethical AI Principles for Statistical Practitioners' (8 October 2024). The 2024 statement sets trustworthiness as the overall goal, with accountability, transparency and fairness as principles, and says practitioners should be able to audit, monitor and evaluate AI and make sure its risks are assessed and mitigated. The ASA also co-sponsors the Annual Symposium on Risks and Opportunities of AI in Pharmaceutical Medicine, held since 2022; the 2026 edition at UC Berkeley (13-14 October) is themed on agentic AI in drug development.

It holds codified professional ethics and the validation, auditing and model-governance methods that AI evaluation and assurance could borrow. Its members already audit models in regulated industries such as pharmaceuticals.

Works on Assurance, Justice · Key work ASA Statement on Ethical AI Principles for Statistical Practitioners (2024); ASA Statement on the Role of Statistics in Data Science and Artificial Intelligence (2023); Annual Symposium on Risks and Opportunities of AI in Pharmaceutical Medicine (2026 edition, UC Berkeley) (2026) · Get involved ASA membership, sections and chapters; Register for the AI in Pharmaceutical Medicine symposium (13-14 Oct 2026, UC Berkeley)

Note Its AI engagement is light: two board statements and co-sponsorship of an industry symposium mostly about applying AI in drug development. The ASA site shows no standing AI task force, so the ring sits between adjacent and potential. Scale reflects its membership; staff numbers were not checked.

Bayesian AI Section of the International Society for Bayesian Analysis (BayesAI-ISBA) PotentialNew

Membership body · Distributed · founded 2025

A section of the International Society for Bayesian Analysis that links Bayesian statisticians with AI researchers. Its stated aims are to scale Bayesian methods to large AI models and to extend them to reasoning, decision-making and online learning. It organises the 'Bayesianism in the Age of Modern AI' workshop series, which began at Dagstuhl in 2024 and met at MBZUAI in 2025. The section organises the series itself for the first time in 2026, in Edinburgh. It also runs sessions and a tutorial at the ISBA World Meeting, endorses other events, and funds travel support and prizes from income from the community's Bayesian Deep Learning book.

Calibrated uncertainty, a model knowing when it does not know, underpins reliable evaluation, oversight and robustness to distribution shift. This section is where the Bayesian community organises its engagement with modern AI. It has no safety framing, but its 2026 workshop already centres uncertainty quantification, trustworthiness and robustness.

Works on Assurance, Agency · Key work Dagstuhl Seminar 24461: Rethinking the Role of Bayesianism in the Age of Modern AI (10-15 Nov 2024; precursor meeting) (2024); 2nd Meeting on Bayesianism in the Age of Modern AI, MBZUAI, Abu Dhabi (27-31 Oct 2025) (2025); Invited tutorial on Bayesian Deep Learning and invited session, ISBA 2026 World Meeting, Nagoya (28 June-2 July 2026) (2026) · Get involved Join through ISBA membership with the BayesAI section add-on (USD 5/year); BayesAI-ISBA Google group; Annual Bayesian AI workshop (Edinburgh Oct 2026; Athens 2027); travel support and prizes

Note Founding year is inferred: the first officers' terms began in January 2026, and the 2026 workshop is the first the section organised. The section's webinar page currently shows another ISBA section's listings, so it has no visible webinar series of its own yet. Its work is ML methodology; safety relevance comes through uncertainty quantification, not a safety mission.

EURAMET European Metrology Network for Mathematics and Statistics (EMN Mathmet) Potential

Network · Braunschweig, Germany (EURAMET e.V.); chair at INRiM, Turin · also draws on Safety science

One of EURAMET's twelve European Metrology Networks. It links 14 national metrology institutes, among them NPL, PTB, LNE, INRiM, VSL and METAS, on mathematical and statistical methods for measurement science. It provides guides, quality-assurance tools for software, measurement-uncertainty training, a strategic research agenda (2023-2033) and an international conference. Its AI theme asks how metrology can raise the quality of AI: characterising training data (uncertainty, mislabelling), testing robustness, making model outputs traceable, and evaluating uncertainty. Related projects include uncertainty-aware machine learning (A3SmartML, 2025-28) and medical-imaging AI.

Metrology has a mature framework for stating how far a number can be trusted and tracing it back to reference standards (GUM uncertainty evaluation, SI traceability). AI evaluations lack anything comparable. The network's institutes already sit in standards bodies, so they could make AI benchmarks comparable and auditable.

Works on Assurance · Key work AI theme: metrology for AI quality (training-data uncertainty, robustness, traceability, uncertainty framework); EMN Mathmet Strategic Research Agenda 2023-2033 v2.0 (adds machine learning and virtual metrology) (2023); 6th Mathmet International Conference, Chalmers, Gothenburg (7-9 Oct 2025) (2025) · Get involved Contact form for collaboration on measurement-science needs, including AI; Measurement-uncertainty training materials and courses; Mathmet International Conference and stakeholder workshops (online AGM workshop each May)

Note The AI theme page seems old: its example project, MedalCare, is a 2019-2022 EMPIR project. Most AI-related work is sector-specific (medical imaging, sensors, machine vision) and treats AI as a measurement tool. Founding year not confirmed; the network existed by 2021.

European Network for Business and Industrial Statistics (ENBIS) Potential

Membership body · Zaandam, Netherlands (registered); permanent office at Dortmund University of Applied Sciences, Germany · founded 2000 · also draws on Safety science

A European society for applied and industrial statistics, launched in Amsterdam in December 2000 and registered in the Netherlands. It covers design of experiments, statistical process control, reliability and measurement uncertainty. Individual membership is free and companies pay a fee. ENBIS runs an annual conference, spring meetings, courses and webinars, and has local networks and special interest groups, including Reliability and Safety, and Measurement Uncertainty. Its AI engagement is growing but light: a 2026 webinar on certified robustness in reinforcement learning, ML courses, and a Spring Meeting 2027 on Statistics and Explainable AI at JKU Linz.

Industry uses these statisticians' methods to validate and monitor production systems: designed experiments, control charts and reliability analysis. They map directly onto AI evaluation design and post-deployment monitoring, which the AI-safety field often reinvents. The 2027 meeting already lists DoE for AI validation, explainability methods in safety-critical systems and the EU AI Act.

Works on Assurance, Agency · Key work Spring Meeting 2027: Statistics and Explainable AI (JKU Linz, 31 Mar-1 Apr 2027) (2027); ENBIS-QSR webinar: Enhancing Robustness in Reinforcement Learning: Domain Knowledge Integration and Lower-Bound Certification (2 Apr 2026) (2026); ENBIS-26 annual conference (from 6 Sept 2026) (2026) · Get involved Free individual membership; special interest groups (e.g. Reliability and Safety, Measurement Uncertainty, Design of Experiments); Spring Meeting 2027 on Statistics and Explainable AI (call for abstracts open); Annual conference (ENBIS-27, Barcelona, Aug-Sep 2027), courses and webinars

Note Its AI content is mainly statistics for AI, such as explainability, uncertainty quantification and ML for industrial processes. It has no AI-safety or governance framing beyond trust and the EU AI Act.

INFORMS Decision Analysis Society (DAS) Potential

Membership body · Catonsville, Maryland, USA · founded 1980 · also draws on Safety science

The decision-analysis subdivision of INFORMS, with more than 1,000 members. It was founded in 1980 as the ORSA Special Interest Group on Decision Analysis and took its present name in 1996. It covers subjective expected utility, Bayesian inference, multi-attribute utility, risk analysis, elicitation and behavioural decision research. It publishes the journal Decision Analysis, gives the Frank P. Ramsey Medal and other awards, and runs the Advances in Decision Analysis conference and a webinar series. Its engagement with AI is light: AI appears as a conference topic, in one webinar and in journal papers on LLMs and human-in-the-loop advice.

Decision analysis offers formal tools that AI governance mostly handles informally: value of information, multi-attribute trade-offs, structured expert elicitation and sensitivity analysis. They could apply to deployment go/no-go decisions and safety-case thresholds. The society's members include established risk analysts such as Vicki Bier and Elisabeth Paté-Cornell, who have barely been engaged on AI.

Works on Epistemics, Assurance · Key work Advances in Decision Analysis 2026 (Duke Fuqua, 22-24 June 2026), with artificial intelligence among listed topics (2026); Webinar: Sensitivity Analysis for Decision Making: From Decision Trees to Artificial Intelligence (Emanuele Borgonovo, 8 Oct 2025) (2025); LAMDA: Large Language Model as Decision Analyst (Decision Analysis, ahead of print) (2026) · Get involved Join via INFORMS membership (DAS subdivision); Advances in Decision Analysis conference (biennial; 2026 at Duke) and DAS sessions at the INFORMS Annual Meeting; Webinar series (e.g. Jan 2026, Oct 2025)

Note No AI-safety or governance programme. Its AI content mostly treats AI as a tool for decision analysis, not as something to govern. Most of the site's discussion areas need an INFORMS login.

Simons Collaboration on the Physics of Learning and Neural Computation PotentialNew

Programme · Stanford, CA, USA (multi-institution) · founded 2025 · also draws on Living systems

A Simons Foundation research collaboration launched in August 2025 and directed by Surya Ganguli (Stanford). Its 16 other principal investigators are spread across North America, Europe and Asia. It treats AI as a complex physical system, using statistical physics, mathematics and theoretical neuroscience to explain how data structure, network architecture and learning dynamics produce scaling, emergent capabilities and 'mysterious failures'. It runs a public webinar series and annual meetings.

Statistical physics of learning could explain why capabilities emerge and why models fail, which is the foundation that interpretability and capability forecasting lack. This group holds those methods at scale, but it has no link to the AI-safety field and does not frame its work as safety.

Works on Agency · Key work Collaboration launch: 17 PIs, up to $2M a year for four years (2025); Webinar series (e.g. Lenka Zdeborová on attention-based models, November 2025) (2025); 2026 Annual Meeting, Simons Foundation, New York (2026) · Get involved Public webinar series (physicsoflearning.org/webinar-series); Collaboration postdoctoral positions at Stanford, advertised on AcademicJobsOnline

Note Basic science, with no safety framing. Its PIs include Yann LeCun, a public sceptic of AI existential-risk arguments. Relevance to safety is inferred from its methods, not claimed by the collaboration.

Society for Decision Making Under Deep Uncertainty (DMDU Society) Potential

Membership body · Distributed · founded 2014 · also draws on Arts, futures

A volunteer-run, multidisciplinary professional society for decisions under deep uncertainty: cases where the parties cannot agree on system models, probabilities or how to weigh consequences. Its methods include robust decision making, exploratory modelling, scenario discovery, info-gap theory and dynamic adaptive pathways, in the RAND and TU Delft lineage. It holds an annual meeting (the first in 2013 in Washington DC), runs a summer school, and has regional groups such as DMDU-Asia. Its application areas are climate, water, energy, health and infrastructure. AI comes up only in meeting themes: the 2025 London meeting asked how DMDU should integrate AI, and the 2026 call cites the rapid adoption of AI.

AI governance is a textbook case of deep uncertainty, where experts cannot agree on probabilities. DMDU offers stress-testing of policies across many plausible futures and adaptive plans with signposts and triggers. These complement the probabilistic forecasting already strong on the AI-safety map.

Works on Epistemics, Metacrisis · Key work 13th Annual Meeting, Baton Rouge (9-12 Nov 2026, hosted by The Water Institute) (2026); 12th Annual Meeting, 'Navigating a Fractured Future: DMDU for a World in Flux', Loughborough University London (17-20 Nov 2025), incl. how DMDU should integrate AI (2025); DMDU Summer School 2026, Churchill College, Cambridge (3-7 Aug 2026) (2026) · Get involved Membership (join form on site); Annual meeting with online participation option (Nov 2026, Baton Rouge; registration closes 9 Oct 2026); Summer school (applications usually close in April; some travel support)

Note AI appears only in the framing of meeting themes. There is no AI programme, and most work is on climate, water and infrastructure. The roster gave the 2026 meeting as 10-12 Nov; the society's page says 9-12 Nov.

Sciences & engineering · 49 organisations · 7 on the classic map

Life & systems sciences

Life & systems sciences bring the study of self-organising wholes to AI safety: how parts become agents, how they cooperate or defect (cancer, collusion), how systems regulate themselves, and how they collapse. The map holds 49 organisations here (10 core, 13 bridge, 8 adjacent, 18 potential; 7 on the aisafety.com map). A further 57 draw on life as a secondary tradition. The main actors are Principles of Intelligence (the talent pipeline), ACS Research, Softmax, XOR Labs, Equilibria Network, Astera and AE Studio, funded mostly by SFF and Jed McCaleb. Templeton is the largest money in diverse intelligence but has no safety track. The tradition sits closer to the core than most (20% core against 14% across the map), but only through its agent-science half. Its cybernetics, ecology and systems half sits far out.

What is missing. Nothing translates the systems half of the tradition into AI-safety research. Its 16 cybernetics, systems and ecology entries have no core organisation and none on the classic map, 9 are potential, and most only convene. Across all 49 entries the tradition also contributes nothing to Protecting its constituency minds or meaning, and has only one entry whose primary problem is assurance.

Openings here Fellowship placing system-safety and human-factors engineers in AI-safety teams; A co-funded call bringing comparative cognition into AI agency and deception evals; Make homeostatic, bounded objectives a funded alignment research programme; Fellowship pairing Indigenous knowledge holders with AI-welfare and alignment researchers; Metacognition-science evals of model self-reports, built for both safety and welfare; Structured adversarial collaboration on AI consciousness, co-funded by Templeton; An ecology lab for populations of deployed AI agents; Safety science for open-ended AI, built with the artificial-life community

Core ring 9

AE Studio (alignment team) CoreOn aisafety.com

Programme · Los Angeles, United States · founded 2016 · also draws on AI minds

The alignment research team of AE Studio, a Los Angeles software, data-science and BCI consultancy founded in 2016. It works on what it calls 'neglected approaches': self-other overlap fine-tuning (borrowed from the neuroscience of empathy) to reduce deception, attention-schema-based self-modelling with Princeton's Michael Graziano, modular pretraining that isolates dangerous knowledge (with Anthropic), and empirical experiments on whether models have subjective experience. It also lobbies in Washington, framing alignment as national-security infrastructure.

It turns concepts from social neuroscience (self-other representational overlap behind empathy, the brain's attention schema) into training methods aimed at prosocial and honest models. Few teams do this; most alignment work only shapes behaviour. Its self-referential-processing experiments are also among the few mechanistic studies of model reports of experience.

Works on Values, AI status, Agency · Key work Reducing LLM deception at scale with self-other overlap fine-tuning (2025); Large Language Models Report Subjective Experience Under Self-Referential Processing (Berg, de Lucena, Rosenblatt) (2025); Modular Pretraining Enables Access Control (GRAM, with Anthropic) (2026) · Get involved Open research and engineering roles on the alignment team (ae.studio/join-us, 2026); Contact form for collaborators and funders; AI Alignment Podcast, hosted by James Bowler

Note The host is a commercial consultancy that also sells AI readiness, incident-response and child-safe AI services. The policy work is framed in national-security and 'conservative case for alignment' terms, which sits awkwardly with avoiding race dynamics. Claims from its consciousness experiments are contested, and the authors say the results are not evidence of consciousness. Researchers who led earlier lines (for example Cameron Berg on consciousness) no longer appear on the 2026 team list.

AI Alignment Network (ALIGN) Core

Nonprofit · Tokyo, Japan · founded 2023 · also draws on Formal, Philosophy

A Japanese nonprofit (general incorporated association), set up on 5 September 2023 and fully active since April 2024, that builds an AI-alignment research community in Japan. It runs Japanese and English webinars and study groups, organised the Post-Singularity Symbiosis workshop at AAAI-25 and a machine-ethics workshop at AAAI-26, and ran a superintelligence scenario contest that won a JSAI AI ELSI award. Its members, drawn from brain-inspired AI, neuroscience and artificial life, publish on emergent machine ethics, an 'AI immune system', controllability and the thermodynamic limits of physical intelligence. Since October 2025 it has also lobbied the Japanese government with a national AGI-infrastructure proposal (NAGI).

It is the main hub for alignment work in Japan and frames the problem as 'intelligence symbiosis' and coexistence with superintelligence rather than control alone. Its theory draws on brain-inspired AGI, artificial life and free-energy approaches that Anglophone alignment rarely uses.

Works on Values, Agency, Power · Key work PSS 2025: 1st Workshop on Post-Singularity Symbiosis (AAAI-25, Philadelphia) (2025); Emergent Machine Ethics: A Foundational Research Framework for the Intelligence Symbiosis Paradigm; AAAI-26 workshop report (2026); Humanity in the Circle (HITC): A Position Paper (2026) · Get involved Webinars and Japanese/English study groups (aialign.net/events); Recruited administrative staff, a secretary-general candidate (June 2025), and volunteers (2024); Organised sessions at the Japanese Society for AI annual conference (e.g. JSAI 2025, Osaka)

Note The NAGI proposal asks the Japanese government to build gigawatt-scale 'intelligence plants' (compute plus power) so Japan can be a 'third pole' in frontier AI. ALIGN argues this broadens safety evaluation and auditing, but it also amounts to a compute build-out that could feed race dynamics. Much of the site is in Japanese and it describes itself as provisional. Independent coverage is thin.

Aintelope Core

Nonprofit · Distributed · founded 2022 · also draws on AI minds, Economics

Aintelope is a small AI-safety group that began in 2022 as 'three guys' working in their spare time, and now has a German nonprofit (aintelope gemeinnützige UG) and a UK company. Its agentic strand, built mainly by Roland Pihlakas, makes open-source gridworld benchmarks that test whether RL and LLM agents can handle homeostasis, bounded and multiple objectives, diminishing returns and resource sharing. It also probes when LLMs collapse into unbounded maximisation. A newer consciousness strand, funded by the California Institute for Machine Consciousness, builds agents with attention self-models and presented a position paper at the AAAI 2026 symposium on machine consciousness.

It makes bounded, homeostatic objectives drawn from physiology and economics a concrete, testable alignment target, in place of open-ended maximisation. It also treats measuring machine consciousness as an empirical problem in multi-agent settings, work that frontier labs rarely fund.

Works on Agency, Assurance, AI status · Key work From homeostasis to resource sharing: Biologically and economically aligned multi-objective multi-agent AI safety benchmarks (2024); Black-box interpretability methodology blueprint: Probing runaway optimisation in LLMs (2025); Frontiers in Self Attention and Artificial Consciousness (AAAI 2026 Symposium on Machine Consciousness) (2026) · Get involved Use and extend the open-source benchmarks (MPL 2.0 on GitHub); Expression-of-interest form for expected remote-first roles in multi-agent RL, LLM steering and interpretability, philosophy of mind, AI governance and science communication

Note Its public footprint is thin: a Google Sites page with few dated updates. The 'three guys in their spare time' description dates from 2022 and no longer fits the eight-person team list. The agentic-benchmark and consciousness strands are fairly separate, and Pihlakas is listed as a collaborator rather than core staff. Neither the arXiv benchmark paper nor the LessWrong posts are peer reviewed.

Alignment of Complex Systems Research Group (ACS Research) CoreOn aisafety.com

Academic · Prague, Czech Republic · founded 2022 · also draws on Psychology, Economics

Research group at the Center for Theoretical Study, Charles University, Prague, set up in 2022 by Jan Kulveit and Tomáš Gavenčiak. Epistea, a Czech nonprofit, supports it. It studies advanced AI as part of larger human-AI systems, drawing on complexity science, active inference, network theory and ecology. It has two teams. One works on gradual disempowerment: its 2025 paper argues that step-by-step AI progress can wear away human influence over the economy, the state and culture without any takeover. The other works on LLM psychology and sociology: AI identity, introspection and personas. The group also runs the Human-Aligned AI Summer School in Prague and co-organises the Post-AGI workshop series.

It treats AI risk as a property of whole socio-technical systems, not of single models. Its gradual-disempowerment framing gives economists, political scientists and complexity researchers a way into x-risk work. For int/a it is one of the clearest examples of systems thinking inside the AI-safety core.

Works on Power, Agency, Multi-agent · Key work Gradual Disempowerment: Systemic Existential Risks from Incremental AI Development (ICML 2025) (2025); The Artificial Self: Characterising the landscape of AI identity (2026); Human-Aligned AI Summer School 2026 (Prague, 13-16 July) (2026) · Get involved Human-Aligned AI Summer School, Prague, July 2026: open applications; €300, or €150 for students; some scholarships; Hiring page at acsresearch.org/hiring: no open positions as of Oct 2026. Earlier rounds were a 2026 infrastructure role and 2025 research hires; Post-AGI workshop series (co-organised): attendance by expression of interest

Note The roster draft listed Nora Ammann as a member, but she is not on the current team page. The 2026 posts lean towards LLM psychology (AI selves, personas, introspection), so the balance between its systemic work and its model-level work is shifting. Of the listed staff, the LLM-psychology team is larger than the gradual-disempowerment team.

Equilibria Network CoreOn aisafety.com

Nonprofit · Uppsala, Sweden · also draws on Formal, Democracy

A small Swedish-registered nonprofit research network that studies how groups of people and AI systems come to act together, using complex-systems, cybernetic and social-choice models. It publishes working papers on collective agency, gradual disempowerment and adaptive institutions, and builds the Collective Intelligence Library, an open-source JAX simulation in which markets, networks and democracies are composable mechanisms acting on one population.

It treats AI risk as a property of the network of humans and AI agents rather than of single models, and tries to make gradual disempowerment measurable in simulation, drawing on Beer's Viable System Model, active inference and Ostrom. That is a multi-agent, institution-level lens the alignment mainstream rarely funds.

Works on Multi-agent, Power, Democracy · Key work Spectral Signatures of Gradual Disempowerment (2026); Collective Intelligence Library (open-source simulation) and whitepaper (2026); A Phylogeny of Agents (2025) · Get involved Newsletter on Substack (equilibria1.substack.com); Open-source Collective Intelligence Library on GitHub

Note The domain listed on the aisafety.com map (equilibria.network) now redirects to a GoDaddy for-sale page; the organisation continues at eq-network.org. The site's structured data gives Uppsala as its locality and a foundingDate of 2026-06-12, which looks like a recent registration of the nonprofit rather than the start of the work (its Substack and LessWrong output goes back to Aug 2025). Funders are not stated. Much of the research output is working papers and blog posts rather than peer-reviewed work. Two core people plus four advisors.

GAIA Lab (formerly Gaia Network / Digital Gaia) CoreChanged

Company · Düsseldorf, Germany · also draws on Democracy

The Gaia Network was proposed in 2023-24 by Rafael Kaufmann (Digital Gaia) and Roman Leventov: a decentralised 'web of causal models', built on active inference, that AI decision engines could query to check actions against safety constraints, as an incremental route to davidad's Open Agency Architecture. The work now sits with GAIA Lab in Düsseldorf ('systemically safe AI'), which shares the Digital Gaia GitHub organisation and counts Kaufmann and Leventov among its staff. GAIA Lab develops free-energy risk metrics and 'cybernetic gatekeepers' that take over an agent's behaviour when risk crosses a threshold. It applies neurosymbolic AI and world models to nuclear and energy systems, including two German federal (BMFTR) projects, on AI safety for nuclear decommissioning (Alisa34) and collective intelligence for the energy transition (KIKO), and, since mid-2026, world models for fusion plasma control (PLUME).

It brings active inference and collective-intelligence ideas into AI oversight: risk metrics that carry uncertainty in both world model and stakeholder preferences, and a distributed rather than centralised gatekeeper. That is an alternative to monolithic safety architectures.

Works on Assurance, Epistemics · Key work Gaia Network: an illustrated primer (EA Forum, with Roman Leventov) (2024); Gaia: Distributed planetary-scale AI safety (Guaranteed Safe AI Seminars talk) (2024); Free Energy Risk Metrics for Systemically Safe AI: Gatekeeping Multi-Agent Study (2025) · Get involved Contact via tk@gaia-lab.de for research partnerships

Note Changed: digitalgaia.earth fails with a TLS error, and the work continues as GAIA Lab, whose applied work is now mainly AI for nuclear (decommissioning, fusion) and energy systems rather than a general AI-safety network. The link from Digital Gaia to GAIA Lab is inferred from the shared GitHub organisation (which holds Digital Gaia and gaia_network_prototype repos), the shared people, and GAIA Lab listing the 2024 Gaia talk among its outputs. GAIA Lab's legal form (company or university-affiliated lab) is not stated. Karl Friston is listed as an adviser.

Principles of Intelligence (Princint; formerly PIBBSS) CoreOn aisafety.comChanged

Nonprofit · Distributed · founded 2021 · also draws on Formal

Principles of Intelligence is a nonprofit with a remote team, registered as a US 501(c)(3) in Minnesota. It aims to build scientific foundations for alignment by bringing in researchers and methods from outside mainstream AI safety. It runs the PIBBSS Fellowship, a 3-month programme (London, June to September 2026) that pairs about 20 researchers from fields studying complex and intelligent behaviour with AI-safety mentors. It also coordinates research networks and affiliate groups (Iliad, AFFINE, AIXI Labs, Stormglass, a Fields Institute postdoc), and an internal team works on physics- and maths-inspired interpretability.

It is the field's main pipeline for turning biologists, physicists, neuroscientists and social scientists into alignment researchers, and the nearest existing model for the widening int/a has in mind. It is also a test case for how far such programmes drift toward mainstream technical agendas.

Works on Agency, People · Key work PIBBSS Fellowship (annual since 2022; 2026 cohort in London, Jun-Sep) (2026); Fields Institute postdoctoral fellowship in mathematical foundations of interpretability (2026); Internal 'Ambitious Mech Interp' research and interpretable architectures (2026) · Get involved PIBBSS Fellowship: annual, 3 months in London, $4,000/month plus housing support (2026 deadline 14 Jan); Fields Institute postdoc in Toronto on mathematics and AI safety (2026 deadline 31 Jan); Staff roles: research engineers and scientists (mostly remote, Bay Area or London preferred), PIBBSS Fellowship Program Director, Technical Research Manager in London

Note Renamed from 'Principles of Intelligent Behavior in Biological and Social Systems' (PIBBSS); the fellowship keeps the old name. The internal research has moved toward mechanistic interpretability and physics- and maths-based theory of deep learning, and most affiliates are formal or agent-foundations groups. The focus on biological and social systems now lives mainly in the fellowship.

Softmax CoreOn aisafety.comNew

Company · San Francisco, USA · founded 2025

Softmax is a San Francisco alignment startup founded in March 2025 by Emmett Shear, Adam Goldstein and David Bloomin. It researches 'organic alignment': how learning agents come to share goals and take on specialised roles within a larger whole, as cells do in a body or ants in a colony. It studies this with multi-agent reinforcement learning in open-ended game worlds. It publishes cogames, an open-source benchmark of social intelligence in multi-agent systems, and runs a public platform where people and their coding agents compete in leagues and build 'coworlds'.

It is the most direct attempt to turn ideas from developmental biology and collective intelligence into an alignment research programme. It presents that programme as an alternative to the control-based ('hierarchical') alignment of the frontier labs.

Works on Multi-agent, Agency · Key work Reimagining Alignment (2025); cogames: open-source package and public benchmark for social intelligence in multi-agent systems (2025); Red Button, Blue Button: Teaching AI to supercooperate (2026) · Get involved Jobs: Software Engineer and Applied Research Scientist (San Francisco, full-time); remote software-engineering contractors; Join the Discord community and enter agents in public leagues (Paintbot, Battlecode, Proxy War and others); Build and publish coworlds on Softmax's platform with its SDK

Note Softmax is a for-profit company, and its public face is moving toward a product: leagues and environments for coding agents. Little peer-reviewed research has appeared so far; its writing is mostly essays and blog posts. Goldstein's link to basal cognition is as a former visiting scientist in Michael Levin's lab, not through confirmed co-authored papers. Shear was briefly OpenAI's interim CEO in Nov 2023.

XOR Labs Core

Nonprofit · London, United Kingdom · also draws on Formal, Psychology

A London research organisation, directed by the complexity scientist Fernando Rosas, that studies how agentic behaviour emerges in AI systems and among interacting agents, using information theory and complexity science. It has three lines of work: agentic interpretability (how systems form world models and plans), risks of collective agency in multi-agent systems, and metacognitive agents. Iliad lists it as an incubated organisation.

It brings mainstream complexity science (information decomposition, causal emergence, thermodynamics of information) to AI safety. It also frames a risk the field rarely models: a misaligned collective 'macro-agent' arising from aligned, weak 'micro-agents'.
