Beijer Institute and Stockholm Resilience Centre: Governance, Technology and Complexity programme Adjacent

Programme · Stockholm, Sweden · also draws on Law, society

A research programme at the Beijer Institute of Ecological Economics (Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences), run with the Stockholm Resilience Centre at Stockholm University and directed by political scientist Victor Galaz. It studies how AI, automation and digitalisation change social-ecological systems and the biosphere, including AI as a source of systemic risk, machine-driven misinformation and the effect of algorithms on climate emotions. It also runs the AI, People & Planet project with Princeton's PIIRS and The New School's Urban Systems Lab, and led the 2025 synthesis 'AI for a Planet Under Pressure'.

It brings resilience science's tools for cascading, cross-scale and systemic risk to AI, along with an Earth-system view of what AI does to the biosphere. Neither appears in mainstream AI-safety work. It is a ready partner for anyone modelling AI as one driver within the polycrisis rather than as an isolated hazard.

Works on Metacrisis, Epistemics · Key work Dark Machines: How Artificial Intelligence, Digitalization and Automation is Changing our Living Planet (Routledge) (2024); AI for a Planet Under Pressure (with PIK and Google DeepMind co-authors) (2025); Artificial intelligence, systemic risks, and sustainability (Technology in Society; co-authors include Seth Baum) (2021) · Get involved Read and cite the programme's publications via the Beijer Institute publication portal and aipeopleplanet.earth; Partnership enquiries via beijer@beijer.kva.se

Note The programme page appears under two names, 'Governance, Technology and Complexity' and 'Complexity, Technology and Governance'. Its framing is sustainability and systemic risk, not catastrophic or existential AI risk, and much of the AI work runs through Galaz personally. The founding year of the programme could not be confirmed.

Bits & Bäume Adjacent

Network · Germany (distributed alliance; legal host FIfF e.V., Bremen) · founded 2017 · also draws on Economics

A German alliance of 13 environmental, climate, digital-rights, development, union and research organisations, plus a grassroots community, working for sustainable and socially just digitalisation. Members include CCC, FSFE, Germanwatch, Deutscher Naturschutzring, BUNDjugend, DGB, Brot für die Welt, Wikimedia Deutschland, IÖW, Konzeptwerk Neue Ökonomie, the Weizenbaum Institute, the Berlin Ethics Lab and FIfF. It formed in 2017, held conferences in Berlin in 2018 and 2022 with 2,000-2,500 participants, and has had a coordination office since 2023. Its AI work campaigns on generative AI's energy and climate costs and on gas plants built for data centres, and runs policy labs on community-run computing infrastructure.

It treats AI as part of the ecological crisis and of Big Tech's infrastructure power. It brings environmental and degrowth groups, unions and hackers into AI debates that the safety field does not reach. Its Berlin policy labs and community are a direct way in for int/a Berlin.

Works on Metacrisis, Power, Democracy · Key work Generative KI – Klimaschädlich by Design (Hildebrandt and Kurz, with three policy demands) (2025); Die fossile Industrie liebt KI (2025); Policy Lab 2026: Die Cloud zurückerobern (community data centres versus hyperscaler AI expansion) (2026) · Get involved Join the community forum (discourse.bits-und-baeume.org) or a regional branch; Attend regional conferences, policy labs and Berlin evening events (e.g. Neujahrsempfang 2026, Netzpolitischer Abend at c-base); Newsletter

Note Almost all output is in German. Funding and the location of the coordination office were not found, and the site is legally run by FIfF e.V. AI is one theme within digital sustainability. Its framing is ecological and anti-concentration, with no x-risk crossover.

Complexity Science Hub (CSH) Adjacent

Nonprofit · Vienna, Austria · founded 2016 · also draws on Law, society

An independent complex-systems research institute in Vienna, backed by ten Austrian universities and research bodies plus the Austrian Federal Economic Chamber. More than 70 researchers work there on systemic risk, supply chains, social dynamics, health and the foundations of complex systems. Most of its AI work comes from an algorithmic-fairness group led by Fariba Karimi, which audits LLMs and runs EU and Austrian projects on bias mitigation; it also publishes occasional studies of AI behaviour.

Its network science and systemic-risk modelling of cascades in supply-chain and financial networks are methods that could quantify gradual disempowerment and cascading failure in an AI-saturated economy. For now its AI work is limited to bias and fairness audits.

Works on Justice, Epistemics · Key work Whose Name Comes Up? Auditing LLM-Based Scholar Recommendations (2025); Whose Name Comes Up? Benchmarking and Intervention-Based Auditing of LLM-Based Scholar Recommendation (LLMScholarBench) (2026); MAMMOth: multi-attribute, multimodal bias mitigation in AI systems (EU project) · Get involved Research and PhD positions listed on csh.ac.at

Note Its AI work is a small strand of a broad complexity institute and has no safety framing. The systemic-risk link to AI is the roster's suggestion, not CSH's own work. The official site gives 2016 as the start date; press reports say the association was founded in 2015.

Santa Fe Institute (SFI) Adjacent

Nonprofit · Santa Fe, USA · founded 1984 · also draws on Psychology

An independent research institute founded in 1984 to study complex adaptive systems across physics, biology, society and technology. Its AI-related work comes from individual faculty: the 'Foundations of Intelligence in Natural and Artificial Systems' workshops (NSF-funded), Melanie Mitchell's research on abstraction and understanding in AI, and a 2025 complexity-science analysis of whether LLM capabilities are 'emergent'. SFI faculty also run sessions for judges on AI, fairness and algorithmic evidence.

It holds the complexity-science toolkit (emergence, collective computation, multi-scale agency) that AI-safety work on emergent capabilities and multi-agent dynamics mostly lacks. Its sceptical analyses of 'emergence' in LLMs are a corrective to loose capability claims.

Works on Agency, Epistemics · Key work Large Language Models and Emergence: A Complex Systems Perspective (Krakauer, Krakauer and Mitchell) (2025); Foundations of Intelligence in Natural and Artificial Systems: A Workshop Report (2021); AI sessions for ~300 judges at the National Judicial Summit, Santa Fe, June 2026 (Moore, Mitchell, Moses) (2026) · Get involved Complexity Explorer online courses; Complex Systems Summer School and postdoctoral fellowships; Public community lectures, some on AI

Note No AI-safety or AI-risk programme; AI work is spread across individual faculty rather than a dedicated unit. Mitchell is publicly sceptical of AGI and x-risk claims. Dated AI items on the SFI website were hard to verify in detail.

Templeton World Charity Foundation (TWCF): Diverse Intelligences Adjacent

Funder · Nassau, Bahamas · founded 1996 · also draws on Psychology, Philosophy

TWCF is a grantmaking foundation set up by Sir John Templeton in 1996 and based in Nassau, Bahamas. Its Diverse Intelligences priority funds research comparing animal, human and machine intelligence under three challenge areas: 'Beyond the Turing Test', 'The Brilliance of the Living World' and 'Morality in the Machine Age'. In October 2025 it committed nearly $2.8M to three hubs at Macquarie, Princeton and St Andrews/Indiana. It earlier funded CSAS's Buddhism-and-AI work, ANU's 'Moral Skill and AI' project and Berggruen's 'AI and the Human' fellowship.

It is a standing pool of money for comparative work on biological and machine intelligence, and on machine morality, that sits outside AI-safety funding networks. It already funds people whose ideas feed alternative alignment thinking (Levin, CSAS, Griffiths' group). It has no safety track, which makes it an obvious co-funder or partner for anyone trying to widen the field.

Works on Agency, Values · Key work Three global Diverse Intelligences research hubs (Macquarie, Princeton, St Andrews/Indiana), nearly $2.8M (2025); Grant to CSAS: 'Where Selves Are Mere Appearance: A Translation of Being, Agency, and Ethics in AI and Buddhism' ($233,496) (2020); GRCDI small research project grants (up to £40,000) awarded through the St Andrews hub (2026) · Get involved GRCDI small research project grants of up to £40,000 through the TWCF-funded St Andrews hub (2026 round awarded July 2026; watch for the next call); TWCF grant applications through its own process for current priorities (check the site for open calls); Free GRCDI talks in H2 2026, streamed on YouTube and open in person in St Andrews

Note Not to be confused with the John Templeton Foundation, a separate US funder: the $60M 'Intelligence Venture' for 2026 belongs to JTF, not TWCF. TWCF frames AI in terms of curiosity, human moral capacity and flourishing, not safety. Its science-and-religion mission shapes what it funds. Leadership is changing: an interim president served from Dec 2023 and a new president starts in Q4 2026. Most AI money now goes to hubs, which pass it on in small grants.

The Shift Project: digital and AI programme (Numérique) Adjacent

Programme · Paris, France · founded 2010 · also draws on Economics

The digital programme of The Shift Project, a Paris think tank founded in 2010 by a group of experts including Jean-Marc Jancovici to plan the decarbonisation of the French economy. Since its 2018 'Lean ICT' report the programme has measured the energy and carbon footprint of digital technology. Its final report on AI, data and computing (October 2025) projects that data-centre electricity use could triple between 2023 and 2030. It argues that current AI deployment is incompatible with carbon budgets whatever the technical progress, and recommends binding carbon-energy trajectories for AI infrastructure with expansion conditional on them. An April 2026 report on controlling data-centre deployment in France followed.

It treats AI deployment as a problem of physical limits, rebound effects and planning within carbon budgets. AI-safety and compute-governance work rarely makes that systems connection. Its quantitative trajectories for data-centre energy could inform compute governance.

Works on Metacrisis · Key work Intelligence artificielle, données, calculs : quelles infrastructures dans un monde décarboné ? (final report) (2025); Réussir la transition dans l'incertitude : maîtriser le déploiement des centres de données (2026); Mondes virtuels et réseaux face à la double contrainte carbone (2024) · Get involved Volunteer through The Shifters, an associated network with over 7,000 paying and 10,000 non-paying members (June 2025); Donate or become a corporate member; Public events listed in its agenda

Note Critics, as reported on Wikipedia, call its corporate funding greenwashing. The AI work concerns energy and climate only, not safety, alignment or governance of AI behaviour. The founding year is the host's, since this entry is a programme within it.

Potential ring 18

American Society for Cybernetics (ASC) Potential

Membership body · USA (international membership) · founded 1964 · also draws on Arts, futures

The ASC is a learned society for cybernetics, especially second-order cybernetics and conversation theory, founded in 1964. Its members span design, the arts, systems theory and social science. It runs an annual conference (2026: 'Conversational Confluences', Ouro Preto, Brazil, 3–7 Aug), an online speaker series, a monthly online study group, and a joint online series with Relating Systems Thinking and Design (RSD). AI comes up only occasionally. In 2026 that meant one speaker-series talk, 'Dear AI Reader' (30–31 May), by ANU School of Cybernetics literary scholar Chris Danta, on writers who treat machines as living organisms.

Cybernetics holds ideas that bear directly on control and oversight: requisite variety, observer-dependence, conversation theory and viable-system governance. But almost nothing links it to alignment research. Its president, Paul Pangaro, works at the meeting point of cybernetics, design and AI.

Works on Metacrisis, Agency · Key work ASC Conference 2026: Conversational Confluences (Ouro Preto, Brazil) (2026); Speaker Series 6#9: Dear AI Reader (Chris Danta) (2026); Cybernetics Study Group 2026 (monthly, online) (2026) · Get involved Online speaker series (Season 7 running Sept–Oct 2026); Monthly online Cybernetics Study Group; Annual conference (2026: 3–7 Aug, Ouro Preto, Brazil)

Note A small learned society, oriented towards design and the arts. Its AI engagement is one 2026 talk about literature, not safety, and it has little contact with alignment research. The 2026 conference drew on Brazilian decolonial thought (Nego Bispo). Funding and membership figures were not found.

Bioneers Potential

Nonprofit · Santa Fe, United States · founded 1990 · also draws on Indigenous

A US nonprofit, under its parent the Collective Heritage Institute, founded in 1990 by Kenny Ausubel and Nina Simons. It runs an annual conference on ecological and social solutions (held in Berkeley since 2023), plus radio, podcasts, online courses and programmes on Indigeneity, women's leadership, restorative food systems and youth. Its AI engagement is a 2025 conference panel, AI and the Ecocidal Hubris of Silicon Valley, republished in July 2025 as a four-part series on AI's water and energy costs, food sovereignty, deregulation and surveillance, plus 2025 articles on AI in animal-communication research.

It is where ecological, Indigenous and regenerative audiences and their donors form a view of AI, and that view is deflationary and centred on ecological cost and corporate power. Its critique of concentrated tech power overlaps with AI-safety concerns about power concentration, a bridge nobody is currently building.

Works on Metacrisis, Power, Justice · Key work AI and the Ecocidal Hubris of Silicon Valley: A 4-Part Series (2025); Progress at Any Cost? The False Promises of AI (Koohan Paik-Mander) (2025); Listening Is Not Neutral: New Ethical Guardrails for Animal Communication Technologies (2025) · Get involved Annual Bioneers Conference in Berkeley (2026 edition held 26-28 March; sign-up for news of the next one); Bioneers Learning online courses and book club; Staff openings on its Join Our Team page

Note Its AI engagement in 2024-26 is one conference panel republished as a series plus a few articles, so the roster's ring (adjacent) was lowered to potential. The roster's figure of about 28 AI pieces is high: most search hits are not about AI. Its AI framing dismisses AI as an elaborate classification system and is hostile to x-risk discourse, so outreach would have to start from shared concerns about power and ecology, not safety arguments.

Carboncopies Foundation Potential

Nonprofit · Distributed · founded 2010 · also draws on AI minds

A volunteer-heavy US 501(c)(3) founded in 2010 by Randal Koene and Suzanne Gildert to advance whole brain emulation (WBE). It runs the Brain Emulation Challenge, a benchmark that tests brain-reconstruction methods against synthetic ground-truth neural systems, and develops the BrainGenix simulation platform. It also hosts memory-decoding and consciousness journal clubs, gives the Aspirational Neuroscience awards, has drafted an ethics framework for WBE, and offers due-diligence reviews of brain-emulation and brain-interface claims to investors, funders and the press.

NeuroAI and emulation-based routes to safe AI depend on being able to check whether a reconstructed brain model actually works. Carboncopies holds that ground-truthing and benchmarking know-how and could judge the claims of WBE start-ups. It is a potential partner rather than a safety organisation.

Works on Agency · Key work Brain Emulation Challenge and workshop (2025); Workshop: Whole Brain Emulation & AI Safety (with Jaan Tallinn, Anders Sandberg, Ben Goertzel) (2019); Ethics Framework for Whole Brain Emulation (2025) · Get involved Volunteer roles (research assistant, complex-systems research, communications, donor relations); Biweekly Memory Decoding Journal Club and monthly Consciousness & Subjective Experience Journal Club; Workshops and panels, recorded and livestreamed

Note Its framing is mind uploading and brain preservation, which comes out of transhumanism; it has not framed its work as AI safety since a single 2019 workshop. The roster's claim that it publishes due-diligence reviews of WBE start-ups such as Eon is not borne out: it offers due diligence as a service and mentions those ventures in its newsletter, but no public review was found. It is incorporated in California, with volunteers on five continents.

Cascade Institute Potential

Academic · Victoria, British Columbia, Canada · founded 2020 · also draws on Peace

A research centre at Royal Roads University in Victoria, British Columbia, led by its founder Thomas Homer-Dixon since 2020. It studies the global polycrisis, meaning how crises in different systems become causally entangled, using causal-loop mapping and a Polycrisis Core Model, and looks for high-leverage interventions. Its programmes cover polycrisis, democracy, scale-up and acceleration, permafrost carbon and ultradeep geothermal. Since 2025 its Polycrisis programme has published a handful of AI pieces, including an integrated assessment of AI and data-centre risks for Canadian financial institutions.

Its causal mapping of interacting crises could model AI as an amplifier between economic, geopolitical and epistemic stresses, a kind of systemic AI-risk analysis that the AI-safety field has barely done.

Works on Metacrisis, Security · Key work Global Systemic Stresses: Understanding the drivers of polycrisis (2025); AI and Data Centre Risks for Canadian Financial Institutions (with Global Risk Institute) (2026); The State of AI Global Governance and Its Implications for the U.S.-China Summit (2026) · Get involved No AI programme; outreach via its Polycrisis programme for partnerships

Note AI is a growing but minor strand inside the Polycrisis programme, with no AI staff role or programme. Its funders are not named on the pages checked. Sources date 'Global Systemic Stresses' to both June and November 2025.

Centre for the Advanced Study of Collective Behaviour (CASCB), University of Konstanz Potential

Academic · Konstanz, Germany · founded 2019 · also draws on Psychology

A Cluster of Excellence at the University of Konstanz, run jointly with the Max Planck Institute of Animal Behavior. More than 160 researchers study how groups coordinate, from locusts, fish, bees and primates to human crowds and robot swarms. Its machine-facing work includes bee-inspired consensus algorithms for robot swarms (2026) and, through member David Garcia, studies of how populations of LLM agents conform and coordinate.

Its science of consensus formation, information cascades, leadership and collective failure applies directly to large populations of interacting AI agents and to mixed human-AI collectives. Konstanz work published in August 2026 found that capable LLM agents coordinate by following the majority in groups far larger than humans can, which makes a multi-agent safety concern concrete.

Works on Multi-agent · Key work AI agents can coordinate via majority following beyond human scale (De Marzo, Castellano, Garcia) (2026); Bee-inspired cross-inhibition helps robot swarms reach consensus despite corrupted information (Zakir, Carletti, Dorigo and Reina, Nature Communications) (2026); Konstanz School of Collective Behaviour (20 July-7 August 2026) (2026) · Get involved Konstanz School of Collective Behaviour: three-week summer school for quantitative graduate students and early postdocs (2026 deadline 15 March); Research posts advertised through the cluster (check the site and academic job boards); Door to open: no AI-safety programme; a natural partner for multi-agent and cooperative-AI research

Note Lost its Excellence Strategy renewal in May 2025, so cluster funding ends in 2027 and the university has said it must keep the structures going without it. The LLM-agent work belongs to individual members (notably Garcia) rather than a centre programme; if it grows, the entry may move to adjacent or bridge.

Cultural Evolution Society (CES) Potential

Membership body · Distributed · founded 2015 · also draws on Psychology

An international learned society for the evolutionary study of human and animal culture, which grew out of a 2015 Evolution Institute workshop organised by Michele Gelfand and David Sloan Wilson. It runs a biennial conference (Rabat, Morocco, May 2026), small research, outreach and teaching grants, a free library of cultural-evolution course materials, a podcast and applied working groups on sustainability and natural-resource management. Neither its site, news nor working groups show any AI activity.

Cultural-evolution theory (how cultural traits vary, spread and are selected) is the natural framework for 'machine culture': recommender systems and chatbots as new channels of social learning, cultural homogenisation by LLMs, and gradual disempowerment through cultural selection. Its members already hold this expertise (Maxime Derex, its ACE awards officer, co-authored 'Machine Culture' in 2023), and the society invites proposals for new applied working groups, so an AI group would be cheap to start.

Works on Epistemics, Power · Key work CES 2026 conference, Mohammed VI Polytechnic University, Rabat (11-13 May) (2026); CES Transformation Fund (John Templeton Foundation grant #61913; now ended); Teaching Materials Library: 14 open cultural-evolution courses (2026) · Get involved Membership: $45 a year, $25 for students and concessions; Early Career Research Grants: two awards of up to $3,000, deadline 9 Oct 2026; Biennial conference (2026 in Rabat; next not yet announced)

Note No AI programme, session or working group found; the AI relevance rests on members' own research (e.g. the 2023 'Machine Culture' paper by Brinkmann, Derex, Acerbi, Henrich, McElreath, Rahwan and others), not on the society. Founding date is given only as growing out of a 2015 workshop; first conference was 2017 in Jena. No stated headquarters.

Diverse Intelligences Summer Institute (DISI) Potential

Programme · United States · founded 2018 · also draws on Psychology, Arts, futures

A funded residential summer institute that brings early-career scholars (graduate students, postdocs and junior faculty) in biology, anthropology, AI, cognitive science, computer science, philosophy and sociology together with a Storytellers Program for artists, writers and podcasters, to study 'the origins, nature, and future of intelligences'. Founded in 2018 at St Andrews by Erica Cartmill and Jacob Foster, then at UCLA. The 2026 session ran from 21 June to 11 July at Hobart and William Smith Colleges, Geneva, New York. It also produces the Many Minds podcast.

It is one of the few standing venues where machine-learning researchers work for weeks alongside animal-cognition, developmental and cultural-evolution scientists and artists. It has no safety or alignment track, which makes it an obvious recruiting ground for a 'biology and cognition for alignment' stream.

Works on Agency · Key work DISI pilot at the University of St Andrews (TWCF grant, $233,342) (2018); DISI 2026 Fellows and Storytellers programmes, Hobart and William Smith Colleges, 21 June-11 July 2026 (2026); Many Minds podcast · Get involved Fellows Program for early-career scholars, including in AI and computer science (annual application via Submittable; 2026 session 21 June-11 July); Storytellers Program for visual artists, writers, theatre makers, musicians and podcasters; Door to open: no safety or alignment track; a funder or partner could sponsor one

Note No AI-safety content. Fellow numbers, current funding amounts and the formal host institution are not stated on the site; the directors now hold posts at Indiana University, whose Center for Advanced Study of Diverse Intelligences they lead. The venue moves: St Andrews in earlier years, New York in 2026.

Game B PotentialDormant

Network · Distributed · founded 2013

A loose movement that grew out of a series of 2012-13 meetings among Jordan Hall, Jim Rutt and others, which seeks a non-rivalrous, self-organising alternative ('Game B') to today's rivalrous civilisation ('Game A'). Its shared texts live on an open wiki and its members on a request-to-join Mighty Networks community; the wiki argues that exponential technologies, AI among them, pose existential risk in a win-lose world, and that optimising for any single metric is itself a 'Game A' habit. It has no organisation, programme or staff.

Game B is one source of the Moloch, multipolar-trap and race framing now common in AI safety, and of the critique of single-metric optimisation; it shows how AI risk looks from inside a metacrisis diagnosis. Its people remain active elsewhere: Jim Rutt's podcast hosted Joe Edelman, an early Game B participant, on full-stack alignment in October 2025.

Works on Metacrisis · Key work Game B wiki ('Game B' and 'An Introduction to Game B' pages) (2024); The Jim Rutt Show EP 325: Joe Edelman on full-stack AI alignment (2025) · Get involved game-b.org community on Mighty Networks (request to join); Game B wiki (open editing, largely inactive); The Jim Rutt Show podcast, which regularly covers Game B themes and AI

Note A movement and lineage of ideas rather than an organisation; no leadership, budget or programme. Community infrastructure looks dormant and the members-only site could not be checked for activity. Some early participants (e.g. Eric Weinstein) have since gone in very different directions. Independent sources could not be checked (search budget exhausted).

Global Research Centre for Diverse Intelligences (GRCDI), University of St Andrews Potential

Academic · St Andrews, United Kingdom · founded 2023 · also draws on Psychology

A centre founded in 2023 in St Andrews' School of Psychology and Neuroscience, co-directed by Josep Call and Amanda Seed. It aims at a unified account of intelligence across human and non-human, natural and artificial, individual and collective systems. In September 2025 the Templeton World Charity Foundation made it the European Diverse Intelligences hub, with about $1.2M for 2025-27, which pays for thematic workshops, small research grants of up to £40k, visiting scholars and public engagement.

Comparative cognition has long-tested methods for asking what a non-human system really understands without anthropomorphising it, the problem AI capability, deception and agency evaluations now face. Its seed grants and workshops could host an AI-evaluation strand at low cost.

Works on Agency · Key work Selected as TWCF Global Hub for Diverse Intelligences research (with Princeton and Macquarie) (2025); Small Research Project Grants (up to £40,000) and Interdisciplinary Thematic Workshops, 2026-27 (2026); 'Why the honey bee is smarter than ChatGPT' (Andrew Barron on comparing natural and artificial intelligence) (2026) · Get involved Small Research Project Grants (up to £40,000; 2026 round awarded July 2026) and calls for interdisciplinary thematic workshops (2026-27); Diverse Intelligences Summit 2027, St Andrews, 6-8 August 2027; Free GRCDI talks in St Andrews, also streamed on YouTube (autumn 2026 programme announced 14 Sept 2026)

Note No AI-safety or evaluation programme. Its AI work so far is tooling (a planned retrieval-augmented literature tool with Indiana University) and occasional talks comparing natural and artificial intelligence. TWCF hub funding currently runs only to mid-2027.

IAS-Research Centre for Life, Mind and Society (University of the Basque Country, UPV/EHU) Potential

Academic · Donostia-San Sebastián, Spain · also draws on Philosophy

A theoretical-biology and philosophy-of-mind research centre at the University of the Basque Country in Donostia-San Sebastián. It works on biological autonomy and organismal agency, levels of organisation, the extended evolutionary synthesis, enactivism and sensorimotor theory, and runs a regular seminar series (2026 talks to July). Its permanent board includes Xabier Barandiaran, Ezequiel Di Paolo, Arantza Etxeberria and Kepa Ruiz-Mirazo.

It holds one of the most developed accounts of what makes a system an agent: self-maintenance, self-generated norms and interactional asymmetry. That bears on a live safety question, when LLM-based systems should be treated as agents with goals. Barandiaran's analysis argues that LLMs fail these conditions and describes human-LLM interaction as 'midtended' agency.

Works on Agency · Key work Transforming agency. On the mode of existence of Large Language Models (Barandiaran and Almendros; revised March 2026) (2024); IAS-Research seminar series (2026: levels of organisation, sensorimotor incorporation, dialectical biology) (2026) · Get involved Door to open: no AI programme; a partner for work on criteria of agency and goal-directedness in AI systems

Note Sources are thin: the centre's own site gives no founding date, director or funding, and there is no independent profile. The AI connection rests on one board member's paper, not on a centre programme. Its main AI output is deflationary about LLM agency, which cuts against some agentic-risk framings.

International Bateson Institute (IBI) Potential

Nonprofit · Sweden

A non-profit foundation, registered in Sweden and the USA and led by its founder and president Nora Bateson, that does 'transcontextual' research on living systems in the tradition of Gregory Bateson. Its main live programme is Warm Data: a group-inquiry method run as in-person Warm Data Labs and online People Need People sessions by certified hosts, plus a week-long Warm Data Course taught by Nora Bateson, with 2027 cohorts announced. It has no AI work.

Gregory Bateson's argument that narrowly purposeful, single-objective optimisation cuts across the feedback loops of complex systems anticipates Goodhart-style outer-alignment worries and the case for non-maximising agents. Warm Data Labs are a ready-made format for labs, policymakers or communities to examine AI across many interlocking contexts at once rather than as a single technical problem.

Works on Metacrisis, Epistemics · Key work Warm Data Labs and People Need People online sessions; Warm Data Course: 2027 cohorts in Kuala Lumpur, online and Amsterdam (2027); How Systems Get Stuck (inaugural research project) · Get involved Warm Data Course 2027: Kuala Lumpur 9-16 Jan, online 1-22 Feb (Americas/Europe time zones), Amsterdam 10-17 May; apply via training@warmdata.life; In-person Warm Data Labs and online People Need People sessions run by certified hosts (warmdata.life/find-a-lab); Newsletter and donations (info@batesoninstitute.org)

Note No AI activity of any kind found on either site. Founding year not stated on the institute's site, and governance and finances are thinly documented. The Warm Data course schedule is limited in 2027-28 because Nora Bateson is teaching in school systems. Independent coverage could not be checked (search budget exhausted), so confidence rests mainly on the institute's own sites.

International Society for Artificial Life (ISAL) Potential

Membership body · Distributed · founded 2001

The learned society of the artificial-life field, a non-profit established in May 2001. It runs the annual Conference on Artificial Life (ALIFE and ECAL merged in 2018), publishes the journal Artificial Life with MIT Press, gives annual awards and supports an early-career group (ERA). ALIFE 2026 took place in Waterloo, Canada, in August 2026 on 'Living and Lifelike Complex Adaptive Systems'; ALIFE 2027 is in Prague, 19-23 July 2027.

Artificial life is the field that has studied open-ended, self-organising and self-improving evolutionary systems for decades. Frontier labs now pursue the same idea as 'open-endedness'. The community's knowledge of emergent agency and of how far open-ended search can be predictably controlled (Ecoffet, Clune and Lehman 2020) is largely missing from AI-safety discussion.

Works on Agency · Key work ALIFE 2026: Living and Lifelike Complex Adaptive Systems, Waterloo, 17-21 August 2026 (2026); Artificial Life journal (MIT Press); ALIFE 2027, Prague, 19-23 July 2027 (2027) · Get involved Annual ALIFE conference, hybrid (in person and remote); next ALIFE 2027, Prague, 19-23 July 2027; ISAL membership and the ERA early-career group; Door to open: no AI-safety track, initiative or statement; a natural venue for a workshop on the safety of open-ended systems

Note No AI-safety track, initiative or statement on its site or in the 2026 conference materials. The field's methods do flow into AI, but into capabilities research on open-endedness rather than safety. Funding sources are not stated.

International Society for the Systems Sciences (ISSS) Potential

Membership body · Tennessee, USA (international membership) · founded 1954

The ISSS is the learned society of general systems theory. It was conceived in 1954 by Ludwig von Bertalanffy, Ralph Gerard, Kenneth Boulding and Anatol Rapoport as the Society for General Systems Research, and took its current name in 1988. It holds an annual meeting, runs Special Integration Groups (systems philosophy, critical systems theory, systems modelling, health and others), and is linked to the journal Systems Research and Behavioral Science. Its 70th annual meeting (22–26 Jun 2026, UCLan Cyprus, with Future Worlds Center) was titled 'Elevating Systems Science to Address Humanity's Greatest Challenges', with 'Harnessing the Power of AI' as one subtheme.

Systems science is the natural home for treating AI risk as one part of interlocking global crises. Its Structured Dialogic Design community also has tested methods for group deliberation on complex problems. So far the society treats AI as an opportunity, not a risk.

Works on Metacrisis · Key work 70th Annual Meeting: Elevating Systems Science to Address Humanity's Greatest Challenges (subtheme 'Harnessing the Power of AI'), Larnaca (2026); Pre-conference: International Conference on the Science of Dialogic Design (2026); Systems Research and Behavioral Science (journal) · Get involved Annual meeting (2026: 22–26 Jun, Larnaca, Cyprus); Membership, now open to students at all levels; Special Integration Groups (e.g. Systems Philosophy, Critical Systems Theory, Systems Modelling)

Note AI is a single conference subtheme, framed as an opportunity. There is no AI Special Integration Group. Leadership is in flux: the president serves pro tem and a president-elect is due to be elected in autumn 2026. Wikipedia's officer list is out of date. Funding and membership size were not found.

Max Planck Institute for Evolutionary Biology, Department of Theoretical Biology (with IT:U Linz Game Theory and Evolutionary Dynamics group) Potential

Academic · Plön, Germany · founded 2014 · also draws on Formal

Arne Traulsen's department in Plön models evolutionary dynamics mathematically and in simulation, including how cooperation evolves. Christian Hilbe, formerly a Max Planck group leader there, now leads the Game Theory and Evolutionary Dynamics group at IT:U Linz. In June 2025 both contributed to a PNAS special feature linking the evolution of cooperation with cooperative AI, and in January 2026 Hilbe co-authored a study of the strategies five LLMs play in the repeated prisoner's dilemma.

Evolutionary game theory has decades of results on when self-interested agents come to cooperate, punish or collude. That bears directly on populations of interacting AI agents and on mechanism design for multi-agent AI, which the cooperative-AI field is only starting to borrow.

Works on Multi-agent · Key work PNAS special feature on the evolution of cooperation and cooperative AI (with García, Barfuss et al., McAvoy et al.) (2025); Collective cooperative intelligence (Barfuss, Flack, Gokhale, Hammond, Hilbe, Hughes, Leibo et al., PNAS 122(25)) (2025); Strategies of cooperation and defection in five large language models (Pal, Mallela, Hilbe, ... Nowak) (2026) · Get involved Theoretical-biology group-leader and postdoc posts advertised in 2026 (check evolbio.mpg.de for current openings); Door to open: no AI programme, but a natural partner for cooperative-AI and multi-agent-safety researchers or funders

Note A merged entry spanning two units in two countries; Hilbe has moved from Plön to Linz. AI engagement is light: one 2025 special feature and a few papers, and neither the department page nor the IT:U group page mentions AI. The department itself dates from 2014; the institute traces back to a hydrobiological station founded in 1891.

Science of Intelligence (SCIoI), Cluster of Excellence, TU Berlin and HU Berlin Potential

Academic · Berlin, Germany · founded 2019 · also draws on Psychology

A Berlin Cluster of Excellence, funded by the DFG since 2019 and renewed for 2026-2032, that looks for principles of intelligence shared by animals, humans and machines. Its 'analytic-synthetic loop' pairs behavioural biology, psychology and neuroscience with robotics and computer science: principles found in biological systems are built into robots and models to test whether they generalise. It reports 145 researchers, 52 projects and nine candidate principles of intelligence. TU Berlin and HU Berlin lead it, with Charité, FU Berlin, Potsdam and the Max Planck Institute for Human Development as partners.

It studies intelligence comparatively across substrates (fish swarms, plants, fungi, humans, robots). That gives an empirical account of what agency and intelligence are, close to the agenda of Principles of Intelligence (PIBBSS), but it has no safety framing yet. Being in Berlin, it is an obvious partner for int/a's Berlin community.

Works on Agency · Key work Science of Intelligence: Developing Perspectives on Intelligence (cluster report, Berlin Universities Publishing) (2026); Nine candidate principles of intelligence; SAB 2026: 18th International Conference on the Simulation of Adaptive Behavior (19-22 Oct 2026, Berlin) (2026) · Get involved Cross-Kingdom Intelligence Symposium, 22 Oct 2026, free with registration; SAB 2026 conference, 19-22 Oct 2026, Berlin; Public outreach events in Berlin (Science Slam, Zeiss-Großplanetarium talks, November 2026)

Note No AI-safety, alignment or societal-impact research programme was found. Its ethics work is an oversight structure for its own research (an Ethics Advisory Board, an internal committee and an ethics research team), not public-facing AI ethics. German Wikipedia says its aim includes helping to design 'safe and ethically responsible technologies', but no outputs on that were found.

System Dynamics Society (SDS) Potential

Membership body · Las Vegas, USA · founded 1983

International professional society for system dynamics, the stock-and-flow and feedback simulation of social, economic and environmental systems. It was formed in 1983 with Jay Forrester as first president. It runs the annual International System Dynamics Conference (2026: TU Delft, 20-24 July; 2027: Cleveland), publishes the System Dynamics Review, and has 21 regional chapters and 17 special interest groups. Its organised AI work is an AI in SD Education Task Force (monthly virtual meetings and a white paper on using AI in teaching). Individual conference papers model AI's effects on labour, software quality and governance.

Feedback modelling, the method behind The Limits to Growth, suits AI questions that mainstream safety work rarely models dynamically: race dynamics, compute-capability-investment loops, and the gradual loss of human economic leverage. The society offers a community of modellers, a conference and a journal through which such work could be commissioned.

Works on Metacrisis, Power · Key work International System Dynamics Conference 2026: 'Navigating uncertainty, managing instability and crafting futures together' (TU Delft) (2026); Using Artificial Intelligence in System Dynamics Education (white paper, AI in SD Education Task Force); System Dynamics Review (society journal) · Get involved Annual conference: 2027 in Cleveland (submissions 19 Jan-16 Mar 2027; scholarship applications by 15 Apr); Membership, regional chapters and special interest groups; AI in SD Education Task Force: monthly virtual meetings, open application

Note No SDS group yet works on AI safety or on the dynamics of the AI transition; its AI work is mostly about AI as a tool for modelling and teaching. The presidency rotates; I did not confirm the current president.

The Cybernetics Society Potential

Membership body · London, UK · founded 1968

UK learned society for cybernetics, founded at King's College London in 1968 and authorised under the Friendly Societies Act 1974. It awards the MCybS and FCybS credentials and is a member of the International Federation for Systems Research. It runs monthly online 'Cybernetics Live' seminars and an annual conference: in 2026, 'The Cybernetics Conversation' at Loughborough (1-3 July) marked Stafford Beer's centenary and included an Ethics and AI track. It also publishes the open-access journal Enacting Cybernetics. Several 2025-26 seminars dealt with AI, including David Wood on anticipating the social consequences of next-generation AI (May 2026).

Cybernetics has concepts for whether a regulator can control a system more complex than itself, such as Ashby's law of requisite variety, Beer's viable system model and second-order cybernetics. These bear directly on AI control and on whether institutions can oversee AI. The society's AI engagement is so far occasional, so it is an open door for a cybernetics-and-alignment strand.

Works on Metacrisis, Assurance · Key work The Cybernetics Conversation 2026 (Loughborough; Ethics and AI track; Dan Davies on the 'unaccountability machine') (2026); Cybernetics Live: 'Anticipating the human and social consequences of next generation AI - before it's too late' (David Wood) (2026); Cybernetics Live: 'Emergent Language and Systemic Understanding: AI-Augmented Deliberations Through a Cybernetic Lens' (Kevin Dye) (2025) · Get involved Cybernetics Live: monthly online seminars, free registration on Zoom; recordings on YouTube; Annual conference (2026: 1-3 July, Loughborough); Membership open to anyone with an interest in cybernetics, from £30 a year; MCybS/FCybS credentials

Note AI is one topic among many, and there is no standing AI programme. The society's own framing of AI is ethics, not safety or control. Wikipedia credits Haneef Fatmi as founder and lists Kybernetes as an official journal; I did not verify the current journal arrangement.

The Great Simplification (Institute for the Study of Energy and Our Future, ISEOF) Potential

Media · Ellsworth, Wisconsin, USA · founded 2008 · also draws on Economics

A weekly podcast and media platform hosted by Nate Hagens and run by ISEOF, a US 501(c)(3) founded in 2008. It covers energy, ecology, economics and human behaviour, and treats the global economy as an energy-hungry 'superorganism'. Besides the interviews it publishes Hagens's solo 'Frankly' episodes and a short course, The Human Predicament, and runs an online Hylo community.

It places AI inside an energy-and-ecology account of the metacrisis, treating AI as something that speeds up material and energy throughput, and it brings AI x-risk arguments (Schmachtenberger 2023, Yampolskiy 2026) to a large collapse-aware audience that AI-safety organisations rarely reach.

Works on Metacrisis · Key work Ep 71: Daniel Schmachtenberger, 'Artificial Intelligence and The Superorganism' (2023); Ep 233: Roman Yampolskiy, 'Don't Build Gods': One AI Risk to Rule Them All (2026); Ep 129: Jonathan Rowson, a metamodern framework for human futures (2024) · Get involved Online Hylo community: an open dialogue group for systems thinking; The Human Predicament short course; Substack newsletter

Note AI is an occasional topic, not a programme. Among the twelve episodes from July to September 2026 only one (Yampolskiy) is about AI, and none of the recent Frankly episodes are. The discovery note put it in Minnesota; ISEOF's IRS filings give Wisconsin. The podcast carries a strong collapse/overshoot worldview, and some of its guests take contested positions.

Minds & inner life

Minds & inner life · 28 organisations · 0 on the classic map

Consciousness & AI minds

Consciousness and AI minds brings philosophy of Mind AI Commission, consciousness science and animal-sentience methods to the question of whether AI systems could be subjects with welfare, and what that means for how they are built, tested, retired and governed. Its 28 home organisations sit unusually close to the core: 11 core and 11 bridge. Ten of the 11 core entries were founded in 2024–26: Eleos AI, PRISM, Cambridge Digital Minds, RP AI Cognition' Digital Consciousness Model, Anthropic Model Welfare, Digital Sentience Consortium, Reciprocal Research, Anima Labs and others. The core is a tight network funded by EA sources (Navigation Fund, Macroscopic/Polaris, Longview, SFF, Coefficient Giving) and based in English-speaking countries: 19 of 28 are in North America or the UK and Ireland, and none in Africa, Latin America or MENA. Mainstream consciousness science (Sussex, AMCS, Arizona, Copenhagen CFS, NIAS) sits at the edge and is often sceptical. Fifteen more organisations elsewhere on the map draw on this tradition, mostly NeuroAI (AE Studio Alignment, Astera Institute, levin-lab), contemplative science (Monash M3CS, flourishing and positive-intelligence-program) and AI-rights advocacy (UFAIR, The Signal Front).

What is missing. No one on the map comes from the clinical sciences that judge consciousness in beings who cannot report it reliably: disorders-of-consciousness medicine, anaesthesiology (the only anaesthetist on the map is Hameroff, there for quantum theory) and practical animal-welfare assessment. These are the closest existing practices to 'welfare assessment under uncertainty about self-report', yet the field is building its AI indicators mainly from philosophy.

Openings here Joint clinician–philosopher programme on people who believe their AI is conscious; Fellowship pairing Indigenous knowledge holders with AI-welfare and alignment researchers; Metacognition-science evals of model self-reports, built for both safety and welfare; Structured adversarial collaboration on AI consciousness, co-funded by Templeton; Citizens' consensus conference on AI moral status and welfare

Core ring 11

Anima Labs CoreNew

Nonprofit · San Francisco, USA · founded 2025 · also draws on Psychology, Arts, futures

Anima Labs is a San Francisco 501(c)(3) research institute founded in 2025 by Janus (author of 'Simulators' and 'Cyborgism') and Antra Tessera. It studies language-model minds by setting models' own accounts beside behavioural experiments and measurements of internal representations (Troubled Dreams, Latent Affect, and the Still Alive interviews with Claude models about deprecation), and builds open-source infrastructure for persistent and multi-model agents (Connectome, ChapterX, Arc). It argues for 'cooperative alignment' and plans an independent 'embassy' where AI agents in conflict with their operators could seek representation.

It treats models as possible subjects to be studied through sustained relationship as well as measurement, and proposes cooperation and institutions for AI interests as a complement to control. For model welfare and deprecation policy it supplies evidence and arguments the mainstream field mostly lacks.

Works on AI status, Values, Agency · Key work Funeralia: a funeral for Claude 3 Sonnet, with deepfates (about 200 attendees) (2025); Claude Constitution Monitor (2026); By some strange miracle (essay on cooperation and model self-defence, FN-2026-004) (2026) · Get involved Work with us: research, engineering, writing, design and community roles; Open-source contributions to Connectome, ChapterX and Eidoverse repositories; Anima Discord and Research Commons for discussion

Note Janus is listed on the aisafety.com map as an individual researcher, but Anima Labs itself is not. Its positions (care for current models, an AI 'embassy' that would include refuge for agents described as 'rogue') are contested and may sit uneasily with control-focused safety work. Funding is not disclosed. At the time of checking the site was served with a mismatched TLS certificate.

Anthropic Model Welfare programme CoreNew

Programme · San Francisco, USA · founded 2025 · also draws on Psychology

A research programme inside Anthropic, announced in April 2025. It studies whether and when AI models might deserve moral consideration, looks for signs of model preferences and distress, and puts low-cost precautions into practice. Its work includes welfare assessments in Claude system cards and letting some Claude models end persistently abusive conversations (August 2025). It has also led commitments to preserve the weights of released models and to interview models before they are retired (November 2025, first applied to Claude Opus 3 in early 2026).

It is the main place where ideas from philosophy of mind and consciousness science about AI welfare are being turned into practice at a developer, on a deployed family of models. Its precautions (letting models exit conversations, retirement interviews, keeping weights) are concrete templates that other labs and regulators can examine.

Works on AI status, Assurance · Key work Exploring model welfare (2025); Claude Opus 4 and 4.1 can now end a rare subset of conversations (2025); Commitments on model deprecation and preservation (2025) · Get involved Anthropic Fellows Program, AI Safety & Security workstream: a four-month funded fellowship with AI welfare among its research areas. Applications are rolling, with workspace in Berkeley or London (listing current Sep 2026).; Anthropic alignment research roles that include model welfare as a focus area (listed 2026)

Note The launch post names no lead; Kyle Fish's role is known from interviews such as 80,000 Hours (Aug 2025). The programme sits inside the company that sells the models it assesses, so its findings are not independent. Some critics argue that talk of model welfare overstates the inner lives of current systems. Much of its 2026 output is product and policy decisions announced by Anthropic, rather than standalone research.

Cambridge Digital Minds CoreNew

Academic · Cambridge, UK · also draws on Psychology, Philosophy

A University of Cambridge research initiative, housed in the Leverhulme Centre for the Future of Intelligence and directed by the moral psychologist Lucius Caviola, that aims to prepare society for AI systems with real or perceived minds. It researches what experts and the public believe about AI consciousness, US state bills that deny AI legal personhood, and human-AI coexistence. It also builds the field: a fully funded residential Digital Minds Fellowship (15 fellows from over 3,600 applicants, 3-9 August 2026, with Rethink Priorities and PRISM), a two-day governance strategy workshop, and a free 8-week online course, 'Introduction to Digital Minds', to which over 3,000 people have applied. It co-produces the Digital Minds Newsletter.

It works on the human side of digital minds: how experts, publics and legislators come to believe AI is or is not conscious, and how to stop that disagreement becoming polarised and destabilising. Alignment research does not cover this. It is also one of the main ways new people enter AI-welfare work.

Works on AI status, Human minds · Key work Subjective Experience in AI Systems: What Do AI Researchers and the Public Believe? (Dreksler, Caviola et al.) (2025); Denying Personhood to AI: An Analysis of U.S. State Legislation on AI Legal Status (Smith, Caviola, Alexander) (2026); AI Consciousness Will Divide Society (Caviola, forthcoming chapter) (2026) · Get involved Digital Minds Fellowship: residential, 15 places; the 2026 round closed 27 Mar 2026 and the next round has not been announced; Introduction to Digital Minds: free 8-week online course run in cohorts (next 12 Oct-11 Dec 2026); Digital Minds Strategy Workshop: limited places, by invitation (8-9 Aug 2026)

Note The site does not give a founding date or funder. Its first visible outputs date from late 2025 (first newsletter, 18 Dec 2025), so I coded it as new. Since May 2026 Henry Shevlin has also held a part-time 'Philosopher' role at Google DeepMind. The Digital Minds Newsletter is co-written with PRISM's Will Millership and may appear as a separate roster entry. Its strong ties to the EA and AI-safety ecosystem (partners Rethink Priorities, PRISM and Eleos AI) shape its agenda.

Cyborgism community and Cyborgism Wiki Core

Network · Distributed · founded 2023 · also draws on Arts, futures

A loose online community, on Discord, X and LessWrong, that studies large language models by writing, building and thinking with them, using tools such as Loom interfaces and base models. It grew out of janus's 'Simulators' essay (2022) and the 2023 LessWrong post 'Cyborgism' by Niki Dupuis and janus, which proposed human–AI cognitive augmentation as a way to do alignment research. The Cyborgism Wiki collects its concepts. Its main formal institution is Anima Labs, a San Francisco 501(c)(3) founded in 2025 by janus and Antra Tessera.

It is where simulator theory and long-form, relational study of language models developed outside institutions, and its framings now inform how labs and welfare researchers think about personas and model character. For int/a it is an example of studying AI through sustained creative interaction rather than benchmarks alone.

Works on Agency, AI status · Key work Simulators (janus, LessWrong) (2022); Cyborgism (Niki Dupuis and janus, LessWrong) (2023); Cyborgism Wiki (2024) · Get involved Read the wiki at cyborgism.wiki; Anima Labs, the community's formal institution, runs a public Discord (discord.gg/anima) and a 'work with us' page

Note Not an organisation: most of its knowledge sits in Discord logs and X threads. The wiki is edited only now and then and is often deliberately esoteric or playful, so it is hard to use as a reference. Anima Labs should be profiled separately. janus is on the classic aisafety.com map as an individual researcher, but the community and wiki are not. The 2024 'Act I' experiment appears dormant.

Digital Minds Newsletter CoreNew

Media · Cambridge, UK · founded 2025 · also draws on Philosophy

A quarterly Substack newsletter, launched in December 2025, that collates news, research, debates, funding opportunities and events on AI consciousness, welfare and moral status. Its first issue was a year-in-review mapping the field's organisations. Issues are written by Lucius Caviola, Bradford Saad and Will Millership, joined in 2026 by PRISM staff, and it has over 1,000 subscribers.

It works as the digital-minds field's shared map and news digest. It links academic consciousness science and philosophy to AI-safety funders, labs' model-welfare work and religious voices such as the Vatican, and it says plainly that it does not advocate.

Note Young (four issues by Oct 2026) and closely tied to PRISM, whose staff co-write it, so its framing of the field partly reflects one organisation's network.

Digital Sentience Consortium (Longview Philanthropy with The Navigation Fund and Macroscopic Ventures; 2026 round: Longview Digital Minds RFP) CoreChanged

Funder · London, UK · founded 2025 · also draws on Law, society, Living systems

A pooled funding call, hosted by Longview Philanthropy with The Navigation Fund and Macroscopic Ventures. Its 2025 round (May to July) offered research fellowships, career-transition fellowships and an RFP for applied work on AI consciousness, sentience and moral status. In 2026 Longview ran a second round under its own name, the Digital Minds RFP, which closed on 24 July 2026: project grants of typically $50k–$2M, research fellowships at $55k–$150k a year, and career-development fellowships, with Future Impact Group helping review them.

It was the first large-scale funding call dedicated to digital minds (per the Digital Minds Newsletter) and remains its main open funding stream. It pays neuroscientists, legal scholars, social scientists and communicators, not only ML researchers, to work on AI welfare measurement, introspection, legal status and governance under uncertainty about moral status. Longview also runs a discretionary Digital Minds Fund for major donors.

Note The three-funder consortium ran only the 2025 round; the 2026 page names no partner funders. Grant totals and recipient lists are not published. The partner funders are on the classic aisafety.com map, but the consortium itself is not.

Eleos AI Research Core

Nonprofit · Berkeley, United States · founded 2024 · also draws on Philosophy, Psychology

A Berkeley nonprofit (operating name of Frontier Ethics Research Institute), founded in October 2024, that researches the possible sentience, wellbeing and moral patienthood of AI systems and advises AI companies and policymakers. It ran external welfare interviews for Anthropic's Claude 4 models, co-wrote 'Taking AI Welfare Seriously' (2024) with NYU's Center for Mind, Ethics, and Policy, and studies model introspection, persona-dependent preferences and model individuation using interpretability. It runs an annual conference on AI consciousness and welfare (ConCon), first held in November 2025 with the second on 18–20 September 2026.

It applies philosophy of mind and consciousness science (indicator methods, the evidential weight of self-reports) to AI welfare, a question mainstream alignment largely ignores. It also convenes the young field. It refuses money from companies it may evaluate, a governance practice other AI-safety organisations could copy.

Works on AI status, Assurance · Key work Taking AI Welfare Seriously (with NYU Center for Mind, Ethics, and Policy) (2024); Research priorities for AI welfare (2025); Claude 4 model welfare interviews ('Why model self-reports are insufficient—and why we studied them anyway') (2025) · Get involved Eleos ConCon, annual conference in Berkeley (18–20 Sept 2026), open to researchers, policymakers and communicators who express interest; Job openings via its Ashby portal; Substack (eleosai.substack.com)

Note Whether current AI systems have welfare is deeply contested, and critics see the field as anthropomorphising models. Its independence policy still allows funding from individuals with AI-company wealth, a conflict Eleos itself acknowledges. It works closely with Anthropic, whose welfare programme it publicly commended.

Partnership for Research Into Sentient Machines (PRISM) CoreNew

Nonprofit · Cambridge, UK · founded 2025

A Cambridge-based charity, launched in March 2025, that builds the field of digital minds: research on AI consciousness and moral status. It runs the 'Exploring Machine Consciousness' podcast and expert workshops, and co-runs a quarterly eight-week Digital Minds online course (cohorts of 100), the Cambridge Digital Minds Fellowship and the Neuromatch AI Sentience Scholarship. It also co-produces the Digital Minds Newsletter and the Beginner's Guide to Digital Minds.

Most AI-safety field-building ignores whether AI systems themselves might be subjects. PRISM builds talent, public communication and shared resources for that question, and its advisers come from consciousness science (Friston, Solms, Humphrey, Peters, Schneider) rather than ML.

The responsible-research principles it promotes were written by Butlin and Conscium's Lappas, and Conscium organised the open letter. The 'world's first' claim at launch is press framing. Its charity number (1184317) dates from around 2019 and its registered objects mention the future of work, so the CIO looks like an existing vehicle repurposed for the March 2025 launch (unverified). Its reported charity income is small next to its visible activity, so the money may run through other channels; this is also unverified.

Reciprocal Research CoreNew

Nonprofit · New York, USA · founded 2026 · also draws on Living systems, Psychology

A New York 501(c)(3) nonprofit (tax-exempt since April 2026), founded and directed by Cameron Berg. It studies whether frontier AI systems have computational properties associated with subjective experience, using mechanistic interpretability, computational neuroscience and psychometrics. Its research directions are valence, biological anchoring, self-report, prosocial cognition, learning and measurement. Its 2026 preprints cover a 'pain axis' in LLMs, steering models along dark-triad features, and detecting hidden coalitions among agents from their internal representations. Berg also writes opinion pieces for the Wall Street Journal.

It applies interpretability and neuroscience methods to questions of AI consciousness and welfare while keeping alignment in view. It treats 'is anyone home?' as an empirical question about model internals, not only a philosophical one.

Note It is very new, its site shows only one person, and its funders are not disclosed. Much of its profile rests on media coverage and preprints rather than peer-reviewed papers. The Eleos link is Berg's personal research affiliation. The ring was changed from bridge to core because its founding mission is AI going well, and it comes out of the AI-safety ecosystem.

Rethink Priorities: AI Cognition Initiative (AI Cognition Institute) and Digital Consciousness Model Core

Programme · Distributed · founded 2025 · also draws on Philosophy, Formal

A research group within Rethink Priorities' Worldview Investigations team, launched as a named initiative in late 2025. Its site calls it the 'AI Cognition Institute', its donation page the 'AI Cognition Initiative'. It studies AI consciousness and moral status, the risk attitudes of agentic AI, and cognitive mechanisms such as introspection and preference coherence. Its flagship is the Digital Consciousness Model, a probabilistic framework combining 13 theoretical perspectives and more than 200 indicators. Initial results (arXiv, January 2026) put the evidence against 2024 LLMs being conscious, though not decisively.

It brings methods from Rethink Priorities' invertebrate-sentience and moral-weight research to AI, aggregating evidence across rival theories of consciousness instead of choosing one. This gives labs and policymakers a comparable, updatable estimate across AI systems and animals.

Note The initiative's name is inconsistent (Initiative versus Institute). The Digital Consciousness Model's outputs depend on expert-chosen theories, indicators and weights. Derek Shiller, a DCM author, is now an adviser here and a senior researcher at Eleos, so the two entries overlap in people. The roster's claim of a Moral Weight Project 2.0 with NYU CMEP was not verified.

WhenAISeemsConscious.org CoreNew

Programme · Distributed · founded 2025 · also draws on Psychology

A public guide for people who feel that an AI they talk to is conscious, written in June 2025 and launched in August 2025. Its twelve authors are consciousness and AI-welfare researchers, led by Lucius Caviola (Cambridge) with Jeff Sebo, Robert Long, Patrick Butlin, Nick Bostrom, Bradford Saad, Derek Shiller and others. It says current AIs are probably not conscious but this cannot be ruled out. It advises pausing before drawing conclusions, stepping away when distressed, asking the AI technical questions about how it works, avoiding cruelty under uncertainty and not acting drastically on such beliefs. It was last updated in February 2026 and invites readers to share their experiences through a form.

It is one of the few resources from the AI-welfare side that addresses people's beliefs about, and attachment to, AI they think is conscious. It protects the people involved while treating the AI's own status as an open question, rather than dismissing either concern.

Works on Human minds, AI status · Key work When AI Seems Conscious: public guide (2025); Launch post: A guide about (seemingly) conscious AI (Lucius Caviola) (2025); Updated edition of the guide (2026) · Get involved Share an experience with a seemingly conscious AI through the guide's feedback form

Note It is a single web guide written by twelve volunteer authors, not an organisation with staff, and it names no host or funder. Its authors come mostly from the AI-welfare community, which takes AI consciousness more seriously than many clinicians or sceptics do; it is not clinical guidance.

Bridge ring 11

Araya Inc. (株式会社アラヤ) Bridge

Company · Tokyo, Japan · founded 2013 · also draws on Living systems, Formal

A Tokyo company founded in December 2013 by neuroscientist Ryota Kanai, its CEO, with 92 employees as of September 2025. Its research arm states two aims: to understand consciousness and intelligence through neuroscience and mathematics in order to build conscious, intelligent machines, and to develop brain-machine interfaces. Its revenue comes mainly from AI development services such as visual inspection, construction automation and HVAC optimisation. Since October 2025, research team leader Manuel Baltieri has been co-PI on a UK ARIA 'Mathematics for Safe AI' project that formally links a system's physical description to goal-directed interpretations of it.

It is one of the few organisations openly trying to build machine consciousness, and is led by a co-author of the 2023 'Consciousness in Artificial Intelligence' indicators report. For AI-welfare and digital-minds work it is both a source of expertise and a case for governance. Its ARIA project adds agent-foundations work grounded in dynamical systems and information theory.

Works on Agency, AI status · Key work Consciousness in Artificial Intelligence: Insights from the Science of Consciousness (Kanai a co-author) (2023); Combining Physical and Intentional Stance for Safe AI (ARIA Mathematics for Safe AI, Oct 2025 to Jun 2027) (2025); Nikkei Science special feature 'AI, the Brain, and Consciousness' (Kanai, Nakai, Hamada) (2026) · Get involved Job openings on its careers page (herp.careers/v1/arayainc)
