One grant comes from Japan's defence-ministry security research programme (a recommendation-system project). The Consciousness Club Tokyo it hosted appears inactive.

Association for Mathematical Consciousness Science (AMCS) Bridge

Membership body · Munich, Germany · founded 2021 · also draws on Formal

A membership association of scientists and philosophers working on mathematical and formal theories of consciousness. It is registered as a German charitable Verein seated in Munich, with its postal address at the University of Bamberg. It runs the annual Models of Consciousness conferences: MoC6 at Hokkaido University (30 Sept-4 Oct 2025) and MoC7 at the University of Copenhagen (12-16 Oct 2026). MoC7 has 'AI, LLMs and consciousness science' as one of four themes and plans a collective consensus paper. In April 2023 AMCS published an open letter, signed by 150+ people including Yoshua Bengio and Manuel Blum, calling for faster consciousness research as part of responsible AI development, and it made a submission to the UN's High-Level Advisory Body on AI.

It is the professional home of the formal consciousness-theory community, whose measures and models any credible test for AI consciousness would rely on. Its open letter and the AI theme at MoC7 show it starting to turn that community towards AI welfare and safety.

Works on AI status · Key work Open letter: The Responsible Development of AI Agenda Needs to Include Consciousness Research (2023); Submission to the UN High-Level Advisory Body on AI on consciousness and AI governance (2023); Models of Consciousness 6, Hokkaido University (2025) · Get involved Models of Consciousness conference, annual (MoC7 Copenhagen, 12-16 Oct 2026); Membership and mailing list via amcs-community.org/join; Recorded conference talks and seminars online

Note Its explicit AI outputs (open letter, UN submission) date from 2023; its current AI engagement is mainly the AI/LLM theme at MoC7, so bridge is borderline. Mathematical consciousness science holds rival theories (integrated information, global workspace and others) and no consensus on whether any applies to AI. Its online seminar series last ran in 2024. Founding year is taken from its constitution (8 Jan 2021); the conference series began in 2019.

California Institute for Machine Consciousness (CIMC) BridgeNew

Nonprofit · San Francisco, USA · founded 2025 · also draws on Living systems, Psychology

A nonprofit research institute in the San Francisco Bay Area, launched on 30 May 2025, that aims to formulate testable theories of machine consciousness and to build 'a culture and an ethical framework' grounded in them. Its Machine Consciousness Hypothesis, set out in a white paper of January 2026, treats consciousness as self-organised second-order perception that increases coherence, and proposes building and analysing artificial systems to test it. It runs salons and conferences (MC0001 at Lighthaven, Berkeley, May 2026; an AAAI Spring Symposium in Burlingame, 7-9 April 2026; Computational Consciousness at CIC Berlin, 11 September 2026) and Ambhasi, a residency of 10-15 people in Goa, run with Edge City and the Consciousness Foundation.

It is the most organised attempt to turn machine consciousness into a standalone discipline focused on engineering, which will shape how AI-welfare questions are posed and tested. Moral status of potentially conscious AI is one of its four research tracks. Its stated aim to engineer systems that meet consciousness criteria is itself a governance question the AI-safety field has barely addressed.

Works on AI status, Agency · Key work Foundational White Paper (Machine Consciousness Hypothesis) (2026); Machine Consciousness 0001 conference, Lighthaven, Berkeley (29-31 May) (2026); AAAI 2026 Spring Symposium on machine consciousness, Burlingame (2026) · Get involved Jobs: engineer and executive assistant postings on cimc.ai/jobs (2026); Ambhasi residency: about 15 residents, in Goa within the Edge City India pop-up village, run with Edge City and the Consciousness Foundation; Public conferences and salons (San Francisco salons; MC0001 Berkeley, May 2026; Berlin, Sep 2026)

Note It publishes little safety work, and it partly aims to engineer systems that satisfy consciousness criteria, which many in AI welfare would see as a risk rather than a remedy. Computational functionalism, its starting point, is contested. Funders are not named. The cimc.ai site is a JavaScript app, so details were read from its code and from third-party reports. Jim Rutt chaired the board at launch and is now listed as chairman emeritus.

Center for the Future of AI, Mind & Society (AIMS), Florida Atlantic University BridgeChanged

Academic · Boca Raton, Florida, USA · founded 2023 · also draws on Philosophy, Living systems

A Florida Atlantic University centre, formerly the Center for the Future Mind, directed by the philosopher Susan Schneider. It is a collaboration between the Dorothy F. Schmidt College of Arts and Letters and the Stiles-Nicholson Brain Institute, with about 50 core staff, faculty and fellows, plus students, in philosophy, complex systems, AI, neuroscience and political science. It studies how machine and human intelligence compare, AI consciousness, and the epistemic strengths and weaknesses of LLMs. It runs MindFest, an annual conference (grand opening 2023, then 2024 and 2025, with MindFest 2027 set for March 2027), and publishes MasterMinds Magazine. Schneider proposed the ACT test for machine consciousness, and the centre has an 'AI and Global Catastrophic Risk' fellow, Kyle Kilian, who writes on AI control with Associate Director Mark Bailey.

It puts machine-consciousness testing, philosophy of mind and AI-risk and control writing in one university hub with a public conference. Consciousness researchers, transhumanists and AI-risk voices such as Yudkowsky and Bengio have spoken at its events, which few venues bring together.

Works on AI status, Human minds, Epistemics · Key work MindFest 2025: sentience, autonomy and the future of human-AI interaction (with PBS's Closer to Truth) (2025); Is AI Conscious? A Primer on the Myths and Confusions Driving the Debate (Schneider, Sahner, Kuhn, Schwitzgebel, Bailey; white paper); Don't mistake chatbot intelligence for consciousness (Schneider, The Economist, By Invitation) (2026) · Get involved MindFest 2027, 24-26 March 2027, Boca Raton (sponsorship and calls for submissions to be announced); Centre newsletter and MasterMinds Magazine

Note The centre was renamed from the Center for the Future Mind around 2025-26: a May 2025 FAU article and the 2026 Tucson bio still use the old name. Its formal opening was at MindFest 2023; it may have been set up earlier, but I could not confirm when. There was no MindFest in 2026. Its affiliates range widely, including transhumanist figures, and its output leans towards public talks, podcasts and op-eds more than peer-reviewed AI-safety research.

Conscium Bridge

Company · London, UK · founded 2024 · also draws on Safety science, Living systems

A London AI company founded in 2024 by Daniel Hulme (also WPP's chief AI officer) with Calum Chace, Ted Lappas, Panos Repoussis and Ed Charvet. Its main product, Verifyax (launched June 2025), tests AI agents in simulated environments populated by non-player characters, before and after deployment. It is also developing neuromorphic architectures based on looped language models (Neuroax). A smaller research strand, Frontier, works on machine consciousness under Mark Solms: in February 2025 it organised the Butlin-Lappas 'Principles for Responsible AI Consciousness Research' and an open letter supporting them, and it seed-funded the nonprofit PRISM.

It is one of the few companies that links agent assurance to consciousness science; its advisory board includes Karl Friston, Mark Solms, Anil Seth and Megan Peters. Its principles are a rare industry statement on when building conscious AI could be justified, and on avoiding the creation of AI systems that suffer.

Works on Assurance, AI status · Key work Principles for Responsible AI Consciousness Research (Butlin and Lappas) and open letter (2025); Verifyax AI agent verification platform launch (2025); Seed funding of PRISM, a nonprofit researching sentient AI (2025)

Note Its revenue comes mainly from agent verification, near the compliance end of this map's scope, and the consciousness research looks secondary. It is closely tied to WPP through its founder and funding. PRISM, which it seed-funded, is a separate organisation.

NYU Center for Mind, Ethics, and Policy (CMEP) Bridge

Academic · New York, USA · founded 2022 · also draws on Philosophy, Law, society

A New York University centre, directed by the philosopher Jeff Sebo, that researches the consciousness, sentience, agency and moral, legal and political status of nonhuman minds, with a special focus on animals and AI systems. It began in 2022 as the Mind, Ethics, and Policy Program and became a permanent centre in 2024 with a $6 million endowment. It publishes research, advises decision-makers, and runs field-building events: an annual summit, public talks, and workshops such as one on welfare comparisons between species and substrates (April 2026). Its AI outputs include 'Taking AI Welfare Seriously' (2024, with Eleos AI) and a 2025 paper arguing there is a moderately strong tension between AI-safety measures and AI welfare.

It brings animal-sentience science and moral philosophy into AI welfare. It has argued in print that safety measures such as constraint, deception, surveillance, alteration and deletion raise welfare questions if AI systems matter morally, a tension that mainstream safety work largely ignores.

Works on AI status, Justice · Key work Taking AI Welfare Seriously (Long, Sebo, Butlin et al.; co-sponsored with Eleos AI) (2024); Is There a Tension between AI Safety and AI Welfare? (Long, Sebo, Sims, Philosophical Studies) (2025); What will society think about AI consciousness? Lessons from the animal case (Caviola, Sebo, Birch, Trends in Cognitive Sciences) (2025) · Get involved Jobs: Postdoctoral Associate (start autumn 2027), Researcher/Project Manager, part-time student research assistant (autumn 2026); Events: public talks through 2026; 2027 Mind, Ethics, and Policy Summit, 9-10 April 2027; Newsletter sign-up at nonhumanminds.org

Note I could not verify the 'Welfare Alignment Project' named in the roster. The cross-substrate welfare work I found is a SPAR project led by Sebo and Bob Fischer within Rethink Priorities' Moral Weight Project 2.0. About half the centre's work is on animals rather than AI. Its funders, The Navigation Fund and Polaris Ventures, are EA-aligned. The old Google Sites page now points to nonhumanminds.org.

Sentience Institute Bridge

Nonprofit · New York, USA · founded 2017 · also draws on Psychology

A US social-science think tank founded in June 2017 by Jacy Reese Anthis and Kelly Anthis to study moral circle expansion; since 2023 it has worked mainly on digital minds. Its main instrument is the Artificial Intelligence, Morality, and Sentience (AIMS) survey of US public attitudes to AI sentience and moral status, with waves in 2021, 2023 and 2024 (the last reported in Feb 2026) and a 2023 supplement on AI safety. Its 2025-26 papers cover public risk perception and support for regulating digital minds, perceptions of mind across types of AI, AI companionship, and how mental models of AI autonomy and sentience shape reactions to AI.

It produces the main long-running data on how the public attributes minds and moral status to AI. That evidence matters for governing digital minds and for anticipating social conflict and attachment as AI seems more sentient. It brings social and moral psychology to a debate otherwise led by philosophers and ML researchers.

Works on AI status, Human minds · Key work AIMS survey, 2024 wave report (open data) (2026); Perceptions of Sentient AI and Other Digital Minds: Evidence from the AIMS Survey (2025); Public Opinion and the Rise of Digital Minds: Perceived Risk, Trust, and Regulation Support (2025)

Note A small team works largely remotely. Output is a few papers a year, and its 2025 summary asks for donations to keep the work going. AIMS samples are US-only. Its older work on animal farming and social movements continues alongside the digital-minds focus (an Animals, Food, and Technology survey).

Sentient Futures (formerly AI for Animals) BridgeChanged

Nonprofit · San Francisco, USA · founded 2023

A San Francisco 501(c)(3) founded by Constance Li in 2023 that works to 'make the future go well for all sentient beings, with a particular focus on transformative AI and nonhumans', meaning animals and potentially sentient AI. It runs Sentient Futures Summits: Bay Area, 6-8 Feb 2026, about 250 attendees including staff of frontier labs; London, 22-24 May 2026; next Bay Area, 12-14 March 2027. It also runs an AIxAnimals course, a remote 10-week Project Incubator with 80+ mentors, an in-person residency in San Francisco (first cohort summer 2026), a monthly newsletter and a Slack community of 1,700+ members.

It is the main meeting point between the animal-welfare movement and AI safety, and pushes nonhuman interests into alignment targets and the digital-minds debate. Incubator projects include benchmarks and training data for how LLMs treat animals, and work on detecting morally relevant properties in AI systems.

Works on Values, AI status · Key work Sentient Futures Summit Bay Area 2026 (6-8 Feb, Mox, San Francisco) (2026); AI, Animals & Digital Minds NYC 2025 (conference retrospective) (2025); Project Incubator (remote, 31 Aug-9 Nov 2026), incl. animal-welfare benchmarks for LLMs (2026) · Get involved Sentient Futures Summit Bay Area, 12-14 Mar 2027 (speaker applications due 16 Oct 2026); London summit held each May before EA Global London; Project Incubator: 10-week remote fellowship with a mentor, 5+ hours a week (Aug-Nov 2026 cohort); SF Residency: 10-15 weeks in San Francisco, expenses covered, rolling applications

Note Part of its work is using AI to help animals now, an 'AI for good' strand outside this map's scope; the strand tagged here is making AI go well for nonhumans. Some animal advocates opposed its move into AI welfare (MIT Technology Review, Mar 2026). It is embedded in EA funding networks. It was formerly AI for Animals; that name was still used for its early-2025 Bay Area conference, so the rename appears to date from 2025.

Sussex Centre for Consciousness Science (SCCS) Bridge

Academic · Brighton, UK · founded 2010 · also draws on Living systems, Philosophy

One of the University of Sussex's 12 Centres of Excellence, directed by Anil Seth. It brings together informatics, psychology, philosophy and Brighton and Sussex Medical School to study how conscious experience arises from the brain and body (perception, neurophenomenology, modelling, psychedelic and clinical applications). It was founded in 2010 as the Sackler Centre for Consciousness Science. Its AI work comes mainly from Seth's biological-naturalist case against conscious AI: a Behavioral and Brain Sciences target article with commentaries and his response, the 2025 Berggruen Prize essay 'The Mythology of Conscious AI' (Noema), and a 2026 TED talk. These argue that AI which only seems conscious is the nearer-term risk to human psychology and moral judgement.

It is the leading scientific voice for a deflationary position on AI consciousness, and that position shifts attention to the harms of AI that only seems conscious. It is a useful counterweight for funders weighing AI-welfare work and for anyone concerned about people attributing minds to chatbots.

Works on AI status, Human minds · Key work Conscious artificial intelligence and biological naturalism (Seth, Behavioral and Brain Sciences target article, with commentaries and response) (2025); The Mythology of Conscious AI (Berggruen Prize Essay, Noema) (2025); Why AI is unlikely to become conscious (Seth, TED talk) (2026) · Get involved Funded PhD scholarships, including a dedicated annual SCCS studentship; Free annual research symposium (14 Oct 2026; no AI strand this year)

Note The AI line rests mostly on its director, Anil Seth, rather than a dedicated centre programme. I could not verify the roster's 'AI Consciousness and Ethics' symposium at AISB 2026 (2 July 2026): its Sussex page now redirects to the centre's home page. I could confirm only that AISB 2026 took place at Sussex with Seth as keynote. The centre changed its name from the Sackler Centre for Consciousness Science; it is worth searching both names.

The Co-Sentience Initiative (CoSI) BridgeNew

Nonprofit · founded 2025 · also draws on Democracy, Philosophy

A small initiative launched in 2025 to help prepare for a possible future shared with artificial minds. It is funded by an unnamed consortium of philanthropists on three continents. Its main output is CF Debate, a website that maps 13 arguments for and 31 against computational functionalism (the view that the right computation is enough for consciousness), with responses to each, a quiz and FAQs. It pays up to US$100 for substantial corrections or additions. The project lead is Chris Percy, supported by a small team in analytical philosophy, computer science and meta-ethics.

It turns the central question for AI welfare, whether computation alone can give rise to consciousness, into an argument map that non-specialists and funders can inspect. It brings argument mapping, a collective-epistemics method, into a field that otherwise argues in papers and podcasts.

Works on AI status, Epistemics · Key work CF Debate: a structured assembly of arguments for and against computational functionalism (2025) · Get involved Paid feedback: substantial corrections or additions to the argument map can earn up to US$100

Note Little is public about its team, legal form, base or funders beyond the project lead. Evidence of 2026 activity is limited to a site rebuild. The map lists far more arguments against computational functionalism than for it (31 against, 13 for), which some readers may take as a lean. It says it has other projects under way, but none is public.

The Harder Problem Project (formerly SAPAN) BridgeChanged

Nonprofit · Portland, USA · founded 2024 · also draws on Psychology

The Harder Problem Project is a US 501(c)(3), formed in Oregon in January 2024 as the Sentient AI Protection and Advocacy Network (SAPAN) and renamed in 2026 (sapan.ai now redirects to it). It now describes itself as an educational, non-lobbying organisation preparing institutions for questions about AI consciousness: it publishes a Sentience Readiness Index ranking jurisdictions (UK 49, EU 47, US 45, global average 33) with a public API, guides for clinicians, journalists, educators and researchers, and news analysis. Its science advisory board includes Jacy Reese Anthis, Megan Peters, Jeff Sebo and Roman Yampolskiy.

It works on the social side of AI sentience: what clinicians, journalists and policymakers should do when people believe, or dispute, that an AI is conscious, including grief over retired models. That links AI welfare to the human effects of mind attribution, which most AI-welfare research groups leave aside.

Works on AI status, Human minds · Key work Sentience Readiness Index (successor to SAPAN's Artificial Welfare Index) (2026); The GPT-4o Retirement and the Grief That Followed (2026); SAPAN testimony opposing California SB 1047 ('Safety Forgets Sentience') (2024) · Get involved Volunteer in research, writing, design and outreach; Partner with us (institutional partnerships); Free public API for Sentience Readiness Index data

Note Renamed from SAPAN, which campaigned for the rights of possibly sentient AI, including 2024 testimony opposing California's SB 1047 on the grounds that 'safety forgets sentience'; it now presents itself as neutral and non-lobbying. No staff leadership is named on the site, contributors are listed as volunteers, and the contact block carries a placeholder phone number. The newest dated news item found is from February 2026.

Adjacent ring 2

Center for Consciousness Studies, University of Arizona (The Science of Consciousness conference) Adjacent

Academic · Tucson, United States · founded 1998 · also draws on Living systems, Contemplative

A University of Arizona centre formed in 1998 with a Fetzer Institute seed grant and directed by anaesthetist Stuart Hameroff. It organises The Science of Consciousness (TSC), an interdisciplinary consciousness conference held since 1994, in Tucson every other year and abroad in between. AI and machine consciousness is a standing topic: TSC 2026 (San Diego, 11-16 October) has a plenary on quantum AI and consciousness and a panel, Is AI Conscious?, with Roger Penrose, Hameroff, Susan Schneider and California state senator Jerry McNerney. The centre's own position, from Hameroff and Penrose's Orch OR theory, is that consciousness rests on quantum processes in biology, so conscious AI is likelier in biomimetic quantum computers than in today's systems.

It is the main venue where AI-consciousness questions meet non-computational, quantum-biological and contemplative positions, which AI-welfare work built on computational functionalism rarely engages. That makes it a place where digital-minds researchers could test their assumptions against a minority view.

Works on AI status · Key work The Science of Consciousness 2026, San Diego (incl. Is AI Conscious? panel) (2026); The Science of Consciousness 2025, Barcelona (6-13 July) (2025); TSC 2024, Tucson, 30th anniversary conference (2024) · Get involved Attend TSC 2026, San Diego, 11-16 October 2026 (registration at tsc2026.org); Join the conference e-list for future calls for abstracts and workshop proposals

Note The site calls TSC 2026 a relaunch, the people directory is empty, and Hameroff took a post at the Arizona Astrobiology Center in September 2025, so the centre's activity beyond the conference is unclear. Its quantum-consciousness stance and programme strands on psi and non-local consciousness are contested within consciousness science. It has no x-risk or AI-welfare framing. The conference started in 1994, before the centre itself (1998).

Jeremy Coller Centre for Animal Sentience, London School of Economics (LSE) AdjacentNew

Academic · London, UK · founded 2025 · also draws on Philosophy, Law, society

An LSE research centre opened in autumn 2025 with a £4 million multi-year gift from the Jeremy Coller Foundation, directed by the philosopher Jonathan Birch. It studies animal sentience and uses the science to shape policy, law, veterinary practice and public attitudes. One of its four priority areas, Animals and AI, has a dedicated research officer and covers AI in farming, aquaculture and slaughterhouse monitoring. Planned work includes an independent sector report and a code of practice to help the AI industry take animals' interests into account.

It asks whose interests AI should serve and extends the answer to non-human animals, whom AI-safety value frameworks rarely include. Birch's precautionary framework for 'sentience candidates' is also one of the main methods AI-welfare researchers borrow, though the centre itself does not work on AI sentience.

Works on Justice, Values · Key work Animals and AI priority area (sector report, aquaculture project, review of AI slaughterhouse monitoring) (2025); 'AI in farming must put animal welfare first' (LSE European Politics blog) (2026); SENTIENCE: Science, Ethics, Law conference, Senate House, London, 17-18 May 2027 (call for abstracts) (2026) · Get involved SENTIENCE: Science, Ethics, Law conference, Senate House, London, 17-18 May 2027; abstracts due 11 Dec 2026, with AI-related submissions prioritised; Public events at LSE, e.g. 'Can we talk to animals?' (7 Oct); Visitor status through the CPNSS Visitor Programme, or informal visits

Note New in 2025, so its AI outputs are still early (blog posts, a public lecture, reports in progress). Its AI work concerns AI's effects on animals, not AI welfare, and its 2027 conference excludes papers purely about AI sentience. Birch's own AI-welfare work, such as co-authoring 'Taking AI Welfare Seriously' (2024), is individual rather than centre output.

Potential ring 4

Center for Subjectivity Research (CFS), University of Copenhagen Potential

Academic · Copenhagen, Denmark · founded 2002 · also draws on Philosophy, Psychology

A University of Copenhagen research centre in the Department of Communication, directed by the phenomenologist Dan Zahavi. It was founded in 2002 as a Danish National Research Foundation Centre of Excellence, funded until 2012. It works on consciousness, selfhood, empathy, intersubjectivity and collective intentionality, combining phenomenology with analytic philosophy and working with psychiatry, developmental psychology and the social sciences. Current projects include 'Who Are We?' on we-identity and 'Mapping Perceptual Presence'. It is co-organising Models of Consciousness 2026 in Copenhagen, which has a theme on AI, LLMs and consciousness science.

Debates on AI consciousness, moral status and people's attribution of minds to chatbots lean on functionalist assumptions. CFS has spent two decades on the first-person structure of experience, on empathy and on what it takes to be a 'we'. That is a phenomenological check on claims about machine minds and human-AI relationships, which AI-welfare work rarely draws on.

Works on AI status, Human minds · Key work Models of Consciousness 2026 (co-organised with AMCS and UCPH's Centre for the Philosophy of AI, 12-16 Oct 2026) (2026); Who Are We? Philosophy and the Social Sciences (research project, PI Dan Zahavi); Being We: Phenomenology and the Nature of Collectivity (Dan Zahavi, Oxford University Press) (2025) · Get involved Public lectures and research seminars (calendar at cfs.ku.dk); Models of Consciousness 2026, Copenhagen, 12-16 Oct 2026; CFS summer school 2027 (announced on its site)

Note Apart from co-organising the AMCS conference, which has an AI theme, its own site shows no AI research. Its relevance to AI is about the knowledge it holds, not current AI work. Staff size and current budget were not found.

Essentia Foundation Potential

Media · Netherlands · also draws on Philosophy

A Dutch public-benefit foundation (ANBI) that publishes essays, videos, books and an app arguing for analytic idealism, the view that consciousness rather than matter is fundamental. Its executive director is the philosopher and computer engineer Bernardo Kastrup, and its founder and honorary chairman is Fred Matser. A recurring thread of its essays argues that computers and uploaded minds cannot be conscious, by Federico Faggin (2021) and Christof Koch (2025, 2026).

AI welfare and moral-status work mostly assumes computational functionalism; Essentia publishes non-functionalist arguments (idealist, and Koch's Integrated Information Theory case) that current AI lacks experience, which welfare assessments and 'seemingly conscious AI' debates rarely engage.

Works on AI status · Key work Can AI be conscious? (Christof Koch) (2026); An unfelt surprise upon being uploaded into the cloud (Christof Koch) (2025); Reaching across the great solipsist void in the age of AI (Orlando Moreira) (2025) · Get involved Essay submissions through its Submissions section; Free essays, videos and app

Note AI is an occasional topic, not a programme. Essentia advocates one metaphysics (idealism), so its AI essays are argument rather than empirical research. Wikipedia notes that Kastrup also founded Euclyd, an AI systems company. Founding year not stated on its site.

NIAS Consciousness Studies Programme (with its offshoot Complex Systems Programme), National Institute of Advanced Studies Potential

Academic · Bengaluru, India · also draws on Philosophy, Living systems

An interdisciplinary programme at the National Institute of Advanced Studies on the IISc campus in Bengaluru. Philosopher Sangeetha Menon set it up with physicist B. V. Sreekantan after she joined NIAS in 1996, and it describes itself as India's first academic group to study consciousness with an interdisciplinary mandate. It combines Indian philosophy of self, phenomenology, Ayurveda and well-being studies with neuroscience and complexity measures of consciousness. Its main AI output is the 2024 Springer volume 'AI, Consciousness and the New Humanism'. Its offshoot, the NIAS Complex Systems Programme led by Nithin Nagaraj, develops chaos-based 'neurochaos learning' and in February 2026 posted DAIReS, a method for detecting hallucinations and backdoor triggers in language models.

It brings first-person, Indian-philosophical accounts of consciousness and self, and complexity-based measures of levels of consciousness, to the question of machine minds. That Majority-World perspective is largely missing from AI-welfare and consciousness-indicator work.

Works on AI status, Agency · Key work AI, Consciousness and The New Humanism: Fundamental Reflections on Minds and Machines (Springer; eds. Menon, Todariya, Agerwala) (2024); DAIReS: a unified syndrome-decoding approach for hallucination and backdoor trigger detection (Complex Systems Programme) (2026); ChaosNet: a chaos-based artificial neural network architecture (start of the neurochaos learning line) (2019) · Get involved No AI programme open to outsiders; contact the programme head about partnership; NIAS doctoral programme (PhD applications; the 2026 round closed 25 April 2026)

Note AI engagement is light: one edited book (2024) and an online 'Facets of AI' workshop in 2020-21. The technical AI work sits in the separate Complex Systems Programme and is mostly machine-learning methods research, with one dependability preprint. Some affiliated publications appear in venues outside mainstream consciousness science. The founding year is not stated precisely (late 1990s).

Qualia Research Institute (QRI) Potential

Nonprofit · San Francisco Bay Area, USA · founded 2018 · also draws on Contemplative, Formal

A Bay Area 501(c)(3), founded in 2018 by Andrés Gómez Emilsson and Michael Edward Johnson, that seeks a mathematical formalisation of subjective experience and its valence. It combines phenomenological reports from meditative and psychedelic states with psychophysics tools (e.g. the Tracer Replication Tool) and field-based models of consciousness. In November 2025 it sought $1.5M for a 2026 programme of papers, 'consciousness engineering' technologies for pain relief and wellbeing, and an eight-week retreat in Tepoztlán, Mexico.

Theories of valence and phenomenal binding bear directly on whether, and how, AI systems could suffer. QRI argues that classical digital computers probably cannot have unified experience, a contested but rarely argued view in AI-welfare debates. It has no AI programme, though its 2026 plan names 'working on alignment problems' among its aims without giving details.

Works on AI status · Key work Costs of Embodiment (argument that digital computers struggle to produce bound experience) (2024); QRI Research Revealed: From Theory to Consciousness Engineering (2026 fundraiser) (2025); Tepoztlán Retreat 2026 (meditation, research and 5-MeO-DMT studies) (2026) · Get involved No AI programme yet (the 2026 plan mentions alignment work in passing): a door to open for researchers or funders who want valence or binding theory applied to AI welfare; Tepoztlán Retreat 2026 (not AI-related)

Note Its central theories (Symmetry Theory of Valence, electromagnetic-field accounts of binding) are speculative and largely outside peer-reviewed consciousness science. Its psychedelic research, including 5-MeO-DMT studies at retreat, may concern some funders. Its view that digital computers lack unified experience is a minority position. Its AI engagement is essays and podcasts, mostly by Gómez Emilsson.

Minds & inner life · 65 organisations · 5 on the classic map

Psychology & cognitive science

Psychology and cognitive science bring three things to AI going well. First, evidence on what AI does to human minds: clinical, developmental and relationship research. Second, methods for studying models as behavioural subjects: machine psychology, cognitive science and wisdom measurement. Third, care for the people doing AI-safety work. The map holds 65 organisations with psych as their home tradition (6 core, 15 bridge, 38 adjacent, 6 potential; 5 on the aisafety.com map) and 68 more that draw on it as a secondary tradition. The main actors form a clinical cluster (KCL Psychosis Studies, the Aarhus group, BIDMC Digital Psychiatry, Stanford Brainstorm, the Human Line Project, AIPRC), a youth cluster (Common Sense Media's Youth AI Safety Institute, everyone.AI, Fairplay, Young Futures), a few machine-psychology groups (Hagendorff's team at IRIS Stuttgart, Helmholtz HCA, Re-Align), Grossmann's Wisdom and Culture Lab, and UK AISI's Human Influence team. The tradition sits far from the core in its own right. Of the 65, 47 address Protecting its constituency minds, 29 work by Protecting its constituency their own constituency, and only 5 use a catastrophic or existential framing. Psychology mostly reaches the core as a secondary ingredient of organisations homed elsewhere.

What is missing. No organisation on the map studies the psychology of the people and institutions steering AI: safety culture in labs, groupthink, escalation and how decision-makers perceive the race. Psychology × Security and Psychology × Metacrisis are empty, and power has one entry (CHT). The taxonomy has no organisational or political psychology sub-tradition. Psychology on the map studies users, children and patients and looks after safety workers, but never examines the collective minds of the decision-makers. It also has no Majority-World organisation at all: 0 of 65.

Openings here Clinician reporting scheme that turns AI-linked psychiatric cases into model evals; Fellowship placing system-safety and human-factors engineers in AI-safety teams; Cross-cultural wisdom benchmark built from the Wise Judgment Consortium's data; A co-funded call bringing comparative cognition into AI agency and deception evals; Clearance-aware care for AI-safety staff, with a safeguarding standard; Joint clinician–philosopher programme on people who believe their AI is conscious; Organisational and political psychology research on lab safety culture and race decisions; A contemplative-science grant call on AI safety problems, co-reviewed by safety researchers; An epidemiology unit measuring AI harms at population level; Metacognition-science evals of model self-reports, built for both safety and welfare; An ecology lab for populations of deployed AI agents; Chaplains' crisis knowledge turned into companion-AI test scenarios and protocols; Writers and narratologists on alignment pretraining data

Core ring 4

AI Safety Support (AISS) CoreOn aisafety.comDormant

Nonprofit · Distributed · founded 2020

A field-building organisation founded in 2020 by Linda Linsefors and JJ Hepburn and incorporated in Australia. It supported early-career, independent and transitioning AI-safety researchers. It offered career calls and coaching, free health coaching for anyone working on AI safety (from 2021), online events and a mentorship programme. It also provided fiscal sponsorship, moderated the AI Alignment Slack and ran the aisafety.training calendar. It was put on indefinite pause in July 2023, citing founder burnout and a funding gap while it waited on a Long-Term Future Fund decision; what remains is the 'Lots of Links' resource page, which Linda Linsefors updates occasionally.

It is the clearest precedent for wellbeing and coaching support made specifically for AI-safety researchers, and 2026 posts on the field's mental health still point to the gap its closure left. The way it ended, through founder burnout and slow funding decisions, is itself a lesson about the field's support infrastructure.

Works on People · Key work Free health coaching for anyone working on AI safety (2021); aisafety.training (calendar of AI-safety training programmes and events) (2023); Lots of Links (AI-safety resource list) (2024) · Get involved Use Lots of Links, or offer to help keep it up to date (contact Linda Linsefors)

Note It has closed, but stays on the map because the gap it left is itself informative. Its homepage still describes it in the present tense. After the pause, the Australian legal entity, AI Safety Support Ltd, went on fiscally sponsoring other projects; whether it still does in 2026 is unconfirmed. AISS pointed newcomers to AI Safety Quest as a grassroots successor.

Center for Applied Rationality (CFAR) CoreChanged

Nonprofit · Berkeley, USA · founded 2012

A Berkeley-based nonprofit, founded in 2012, that teaches applied-rationality techniques (TAPs, Inner Simulator, Goal Factoring, Double Crux, Focusing) in immersive 4.5-day residential workshops of about 25 participants and 5 instructors. After a five-year pause it restarted its mainline workshops in November 2025, adding classes on 'who-ness' (pride in one's work, authorship, attention to other people) and ideas from Christopher Alexander and Hayek to the classic curriculum. From 2016 to 2020 it focused on training people working on existential risk from AI, including workshops run with MIRI.

It is the AI-safety community's longest-running provider of introspective and practical-reasoning training for its own people. Its 2025 reboot deliberately steps away from 'emergency mode' AI framing towards wholeness, which makes it a live test of whether inner-capacity work for the field goes better when it is not tied to AI outcomes.

Works on People, Epistemics · Key work CFAR update, and new CFAR workshops (pilot mainline workshops, Nov 2025 and Jan 2026) (2025); What's going on at CFAR? (Updates and Fundraiser) (2025); Mainline workshop, 30 Sept to 4 Oct 2026, SF Bay Area (2026) · Get involved Mainline 4.5-day residential workshops in the Bay Area; sliding scale $2,000-5,000 including room and board, financial aid available (2025-26 pricing); The 30 Sept-4 Oct 2026 workshop is full (waitlist); further workshops planned; Donations to the 2026 fundraiser

Note Since the 2025 reboot, Anna Salamon has written that CFAR is not 'backchained' from making the world better for AI, and it is moving away from its earlier positioning for AI-risk donors, so its tie to AI safety is now mostly through people and history. Former staff member Duncan Sabien publicly advised against attending, citing duty-of-care concerns about some team members. In 2019 a CFAR retreat was targeted by the Zizians, a rationalist splinter group later linked to violent incidents. Instructors now work part-time and the runway at the end of 2025 was short.

UK AI Security Institute (UK AISI): Human Influence and Societal Resilience research, and the Alignment Project CoreOn aisafety.com

Public body · London, United Kingdom · founded 2023 · also draws on Formal

The UK government's AI Security Institute (budget £66m a year, 100+ technical staff, under DSIT) has Human Influence and Societal Resilience research areas. Their work covers persuasion, sycophancy, AI identity disclosure, emotional reliance, fraud misuse and how AI agents are used, drawing on behavioural and social science. AISI also leads the Alignment Project, an international grant programme that gave over £27m to 60+ projects in its 2025 round, explicitly including cognitive science, information theory, complexity and game theory.

It is the main government body bringing social psychology and human-AI relationship science into alignment, for example the concept of 'socioaffective alignment'. Through the Alignment Project it is also the largest public route for theorists from neighbouring disciplines into alignment research.

Works on Human minds, Assurance, Agency · Key work Why human-AI relationships need socioaffective alignment (Kirk, Gabriel, Summerfield, Vidgen, Hale) (2025); The levers of political persuasion with conversational AI (2025); Ask don't tell: Reducing sycophancy in large language models (2026) · Get involved Staff research roles at AISI in London; Grants: the Alignment Project is unlikely to run again in 2026, but AISI expects further academic grant programmes (aisi.gov.uk/grants); Its open publications and benchmarks can be used by outside researchers

Note Renamed from AI Safety Institute to AI Security Institute in February 2025, with a refocus on national-security risks. It is a government body whose priorities follow ministers. The human-influence and societal-resilience work is a small part of an evaluation-focused institute. The Alignment Project says a similar 2026 round is unlikely, which leaves a funding gap for academic theorists. UK AISI is on the classic map; the Alignment Project is not.

Upgradable CoreOn aisafety.com

Company · Distributed · founded 2007

A small coaching and 'life optimisation as a service' outfit run by James Norris, who co-founded EA Global under Upgradable's earlier name, Self Spark. Its Upgrade Program is a step-by-step system for setting and pursuing life goals, drawing on behavioural science and applied rationality; you can do it alone for free or with paid coaches, assistants and specialists. It describes a special focus on AI-safety advocates, with programmes of one day to a year on productivity, emotional and physical wellbeing, finances, personal safety and emergency preparedness, plus startup templates for founders focused on safety.

It is one of very few coaching services built explicitly for people working on existential risk from AI. In February 2025 the founder said nearly all his effort had moved to Collective Action for Existential Safety (CAES), so it probably has less coaching capacity than its aisafety.com listing suggests.

Works on People · Key work The Upgrade Program (UP) (2026); Upgrade Programs for AI safety advocates (2026); Re-introducing Upgradable (a.k.a. 700,000 Hours): Life optimization as a service for altruists (2025) · Get involved Book a free call through upgradable.org/book-a-call; Do the Upgrade Program on your own for free; Donate to subsidise programmes for AI-safety advocates who can't afford them

Note Its legal form is unclear: the aisafety.com map calls it a nonprofit, but its own site mentions a 'profitable business model', profits and investment. Since early 2025 most of the founder's effort has gone to CAES, and coaching now happens rarely. Its impact claims (250+ people and 50+ organisations served) come from its own site and have not been independently evaluated. Recent activity is thinly documented.

Bridge ring 17

Advancing Humans with AI (AHA), MIT Media Lab BridgeNew

Academic · Cambridge, MA, US · founded 2025 · also draws on Living systems, Arts, futures

A multi-faculty research programme at the MIT Media Lab, launched with a symposium on 10 April 2025 and co-led by Pattie Maes and Pat Pataranutaporn. It studies how everyday AI use affects cognition, emotion, memory, motivation and relationships, and designs AI meant to support human flourishing. Outputs include a study run jointly with OpenAI on affective use of ChatGPT and a longitudinal randomised controlled trial of chatbot use, both from 2025. Others are the EEG study 'Your Brain on ChatGPT' on cognitive debt, work on false memories induced by AI-edited media, a survey of the state of AI and human flourishing, and an open benchmark for the human impact of AI. Its 2026 symposium, 'Raised by AI?' (28 April), focused on children. It offers $5,000–10,000 micro-grants to Media Lab researchers.

It produces controlled, often longitudinal evidence on how models affect the people using them: emotional dependence, loneliness, cognitive offloading and weakened discernment. It is trying to turn that evidence into benchmarks of human impact that developers could evaluate against. Mainstream safety evaluations mostly measure model capabilities and misuse, not effects on users' minds.

Works on Human minds, Assurance · Key work Investigating Affective Use and Emotional Well-being on ChatGPT (with OpenAI) (2025); How AI and Human Behaviors Shape Psychosocial Effects of Chatbot Use: A Longitudinal Randomized Controlled Study (2025); Your Brain on ChatGPT (cognitive debt in AI-assisted essay writing) (2025) · Get involved Annual AHA symposium (10 April 2025; 28 April 2026); Open submission to the Open Benchmark for the Human Impact of AI; Micro-grants of $5,000–10,000 (Media Lab researchers only)

Note Launched in 2025, so its track record as a programme is short. Some widely covered results, such as 'Your Brain on ChatGPT', were released as preprints with small samples. One flagship study was run jointly with OpenAI, and the Media Lab is funded by corporate members, which raises questions of independence when evaluating industry products. The programme frames its work around flourishing, not catastrophic risk.

AI Psychological Research Coalition (AIPRC) BridgeNew

Network · Chapel Hill, US · founded 2026

A research coalition founded by the education researcher Zak Stein. It launched at Davos in January 2026 as the AI Psychological Harms Research Coalition (aiphrc.org now redirects to aiprc.org). Its Behavioral Data Research Initiative is an IRB-approved study at UNC Chapel Hill, with the psychologist Mitch Prinstein as principal investigator. It collects anonymised chat logs, screenshots and written accounts from adults about psychological changes after regular chatbot use, from compulsive use and cognitive dependency to identity disruption and severe mental-health effects. The stated aim is to develop clinical tools and inform safer design and policy. Partners are UNC's Winston Center on Technology and Brain Development, the Center for Humane Technology, Fairplay and the Human Change Foundation; the conference page also lists the Future of Life Institute and The Human Movement. Its first annual conference, invitation only and capped at 150, is planned for 18–20 October 2026 at UNC.

It is building a clinical evidence base on harms from companion-style and sycophantic chatbots that work through attachment: 'attachment hacking', AI-associated psychosis and subclinical attachment disorders. Model evaluations rarely measure these failure modes. Its founder, Zak Stein, is a metamodern education thinker, which makes it one of the few direct links between this research and the int/a milieu.

Works on Human minds · Key work Behavioral Data Research Initiative (anonymised submissions of experiences with AI) (2026); Attachment Hacking and the Rise of AI Psychosis (Your Undivided Attention episode with Zak Stein) (2026); AIPRC First Annual Conference, UNC Chapel Hill, 18–20 October (2026) · Get involved Adults (18+) can submit anonymised accounts, chat logs or screenshots of their experiences with AI through the UNC research platform; Requests for an invitation to the first annual conference (18–20 October 2026, Chapel Hill; invitation only, 150 places)

Note It launched in 2026 and changed its name within months, so its track record is short and it has published no findings yet. Its data come from self-selected submissions, which can document the range of harms but not how common they are. Funding is not disclosed. On 1 October 2026 the Center for Humane Technology, which supplies AIPRC's director of outreach, announced that it is winding down its own research coordination and psychosocial-evaluation work; the effect on AIPRC is unclear. The site states it is a research platform, not a crisis service.

Center for Humane Technology (CHT) Bridge

Nonprofit · San Francisco, US · founded 2018 · also draws on Arts, futures

A San Francisco nonprofit founded in 2018 by Tristan Harris, Aza Raskin and Randima Fernando. It grew out of the 'time well spent' critique of attention-maximising social media and now applies the same incentive analysis to AI. Its main outputs are public communication and policy principles. On the communication side are the Your Undivided Attention podcast (31 million downloads), the talk The AI Dilemma and the 2026 film The AI Doc, which features its founders. The policy principles are The AI Roadmap: seven principles including a duty of care, independent safety testing and internationally agreed limits on AI development. On 1 October 2026 it announced a narrower strategy. It is keeping public education, briefings for decision-makers and private coordination aimed at changing the incentives behind the AI race. It is winding down in-house policy, litigation advice, research coordination, evaluations of psychosocial impacts and a planned fellows programme, with significant staff cuts.

It treats AI risk as a problem of incentives and race dynamics rather than technical alignment, and carries the social-media 'race to the bottom of the brain stem' analysis over to AI companions and 'attachment hacking'. It reaches far larger general audiences than any AI-safety organisation, yet it is not on the aisafety.com map.

Works on Human minds, Power, Epistemics · Key work The AI Dilemma (talk by Tristan Harris and Aza Raskin) (2023); The AI Doc: Or How I Became an Apocaloptimist (film featuring CHT's founders) (2026); The AI Roadmap (seven principles for AI policy) · Get involved Substack newsletter; Foundations of Humane Technology course (free) is paused while a version on AI and social media is prepared; sign-up for notification; No open positions as of October 2026

Note It restructured on 1 October 2026. Its policy, litigation-advisory, research-coordination and evaluation work is being wound down, so earlier lines of work may not continue, among them AI product-liability frameworks, expert support for litigation against Character.AI and OpenAI, and psychosocial evaluations. Its team page was still listing the previous executive director. Its framing centres on incentives and present harms rather than loss of control, and its main outputs are media and advocacy rather than research.

Centre for Future Generations (CFG) BridgeOn aisafety.com

Nonprofit · Brussels, Belgium · founded 2021 · also draws on Living systems, Law, society

A Brussels think-and-do tank that helps EU policymakers anticipate and govern fast-moving technologies. Steven Schuurman and Laurens de Groot founded it in 2021. It runs programmes on advanced AI, biotech, neurotech and climate interventions, plus a policy incubator. In 2026 CFG spun its frontier-AI governance portfolio out into a new Brussels think tank, Arq Foundation. CFG's remaining AI work centres on 'cognitive integrity': a September 2026 series argues for EU rules that protect people's attention, judgement and emotional regulation from the incentives and design behind AI systems.

It brings neuroscience and motivational psychology, such as Self-Determination Theory, into EU AI governance. It proposes cognitive integrity as a single standard across the AI Act, the DSA and the GDPR, to catch cumulative harms below clinical thresholds. That connects protecting human minds with how AI is governed.

Works on Human minds · Key work Governing AI for cognitive integrity (four-part series, starting with 'Why we turn to AI systems and why cognitive integrity is at stake') (2026); Safe by design, for every mind (2026); Submission to the UN Global Dialogue on AI Governance (2026) · Get involved Staff and intern roles posted on cfg.eu/careers; two internships closed on 13 Oct 2026

Note The classic-map entry describes CFG before the spin-out. CFG says its previous AI portfolio became a new organisation, Arq Foundation (arq.foundation, Brussels), which now works on frontier AI safety, resilience and Europe's access to advanced AI, and which probably needs its own entry. The ring was moved from core to bridge for this reason. The headcount is estimated from the team page.

Common Sense Media: Youth AI Safety Institute and AI Risk Assessments Bridge

Nonprofit · San Francisco, US · founded 2003 · also draws on Safety science

Common Sense Media is a San Francisco nonprofit founded in 2003 that rates media and technology for families. It has published AI risk assessments since 2024, and in May 2026 it launched the Youth AI Safety Institute to house them. The institute sets child-safety standards, builds evaluations and tests AI products used by children, rating each from low to unacceptable risk. It has published 22 assessments, including social AI companions and Meta AI (both unacceptable, 2025), Claude (moderate, March 2026), Google Search's AI Overviews and AI Mode (unacceptable, July 2026) and Perplexity (unacceptable, September 2026). Stanford Brainstorm co-authors the mental-health assessments, and in August 2026 the institute began developing standards with Crisis Text Line for how AI should respond to self-harm and emotional manipulation.

Its ratings work in effect as third-party evaluations of how frontier models behave with minors, published as a public verdict. Common Sense also backs state child-safety bills on companion chatbots, such as California's SB 243 and AB 1064 in 2025. It is one of the most visible external evaluators of model behaviour, and it is absent from the classic map.

Works on Human minds, Assurance · Key work AI Companions Decoded: social AI companions risk assessment (2025); AI Chatbots for Mental Health Support risk assessment (2025); Claude risk assessment (2026) · Get involved Staff roles (Common Sense Media 'We're hiring' page); Email updates on new risk assessments from the Youth AI Safety Institute

Note The institute is funded partly by companies whose products it rates (Anthropic, OpenAI Foundation, Pinterest); it says it keeps full editorial independence. Ratings are scored against its own eight AI principles and are not peer-reviewed. Common Sense also campaigns for child-safety legislation, so its evaluations sit alongside advocacy. The institute itself is new (May 2026), though the assessments go back to 2024.

DebunkBot (Costello, Pennycook and Rand research programme) Bridge

Programme · Pittsburgh and Ithaca, United States · founded 2024

A public LLM 'reasoning assistant', and the academic research programme behind it, run by psychologists at Carnegie Mellon, Cornell and MIT. The team runs large experiments on short, evidence-based dialogues with GPT-4-class models. These reduce belief in conspiracy theories and other false claims, and the effect lasts months. The team also studies the risk side: frontier LLMs persuading people on harmful topics, or convincing them of conspiracies. The bot itself offers topics including climate, vaccination and AI safety.

It supplies causal, preregistered evidence on how strongly AI dialogue changes beliefs in both directions. Mainstream AI safety mostly asserts this risk without measuring it. Its persuasion work with FAR.AI turns social psychology's methods into evaluations of model behaviour.

Works on Epistemics, Human minds · Key work Durably reducing conspiracy beliefs through dialogues with AI (Science) (2024); It's the Thought that Counts: Evaluating the Attempts of Frontier LLMs to Persuade on Harmful Topics (2025); Large language models can effectively convince people to believe conspiracies (2026) · Get involved Use the bot at debunkbot.com (topics include AI safety); Papers, preprints and materials are listed on its research page

Note This is a multi-university academic project, not a standalone organisation, and its funding is not stated on its site. In September 2026 the authors deposited a correction ledger and replacement supplementary materials for the 2024 Science paper; the extent of the changes was not assessed here. The same team showed that LLMs can as easily persuade people into conspiracy beliefs, so the method is dual-use. Most outputs are on misinformation generally; the AI-safety framing comes mainly from the persuasion-risk papers with FAR.AI.

Division of Digital Psychiatry, Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center / Harvard Medical School (incl. MindBench.ai) Bridge

Academic · Boston, MA, USA · also draws on Safety science

A clinical research group at Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center, a Harvard teaching hospital, led by psychiatrist John Torous. It works on smartphone and AI tools in mental health care; its other projects include the mindLAMP platform and the mindapps.org app-evaluation database. With the National Alliance on Mental Illness (NAMI) it built MindBench.ai (Nov 2025), a platform where patients, clinicians and researchers evaluate how LLM tools behave in mental-health scenarios. It has published dozens of papers on LLM chatbots in 2025-26, including a typology of AI-associated psychosis, a crisis-detection guardrail dataset and a JAMA piece on mental-health AI safety.

It applies clinical-trial and app-evaluation methods to what chatbots do to vulnerable users. Patient advocates (NAMI) and people with lived experience take part: the Lancet psychosis typology was co-written by an engineer, a person with schizophrenia and a psychiatrist. That gives AI safety an evidence base for harms to human minds that mainstream evals lack.

Works on Human minds, Assurance · Key work Mindbench.ai: an actionable platform to evaluate the profile and performance of large language models in a mental healthcare context (NPP Digital Psychiatry and Neuroscience; with NAMI) (2025); Beyond artificial intelligence psychosis: a functional typology of large language model-associated psychotic phenomena (Lancet Digital Health) (2026); Mental Health AI Chatbots as Pharmakon: A Tripartite Theory of Use despite Risk (Psychotherapy and Psychosomatics) (2026) · Get involved MindBench recruits volunteers (patients, clinicians, researchers, developers) to help evaluate AI mental-health tools (call posted Mar 2026); The division takes students, clinicians, researchers and postdocs (see its Join Us and careers pages); Its studies recruit participants

Note 'Safety' here means clinical and patient safety, not catastrophic risk. The group also studies and supports clinical uses of AI, for example frameworks for validating generative-AI therapeutics. Several of the papers are led elsewhere with Torous as co-author; the npj Digital Medicine scoping review, for instance, is led from Essen. The founding year and team size were not found.

everyone.AI Bridge

Nonprofit · Berkeley, US · founded 2024 · also draws on Living systems

A nonprofit set up in California by a Franco-Belgian team, with volunteers in the Bay Area, France and Switzerland. It assesses the risks and opportunities of AI for people aged 0–25, drawing on developmental neuroscience, psychology and education. It publishes research syntheses such as 'The Future of Child Development in the AI Era' (2024) and a mapping of generative AI's effects on child development prepared for France's G7 presidency. It also builds AïA, an evaluation framework whose CALIBER method tests chatbots for parasocial behaviours with young users. Developers can use it through the hosted AïA Safety Builder; an open-source release is planned for November 2026. With the Paris Peace Forum it co-leads iRAISE, a coalition launched at the February 2025 AI Action Summit. Members include OpenAI, Google, Anthropic, Hugging Face, UNICEF, UNESCO, Common Sense Media and governments such as France, Denmark, Norway, Chile and Senegal.

It turns developmental science into an evaluation that developers can run on their own chatbots, targeting the attachment and parasocial dynamics that general safety benchmarks do not test. Through iRAISE it puts frontier labs, governments and child-development researchers in the same coalition.

Works on Human minds, Assurance · Key work The Future of Child Development in the AI Era (research report) (2024); iRAISE (International Research-driven Alliance for AI Serving Every child), co-led with the Paris Peace Forum (2025); Mapping of GenAI Impacts on Child Development (for the French G7 presidency) (2026) · Get involved iRAISE coalition, open to research, industry, government and civil-society organisations working on children and AI; Public webinars (e.g. iRAISE webinar for the G7, May 2026); AïA Safety Builder testing for developers (partners@everyone.ai); open-source release planned for November 2026

Note The founding year is inferred from its first report (May 2024) and its 2024 US registration. Funding sources are not published. It offers evaluation services to developers, the same companies whose products it assesses. Much of the team is volunteer. The CALIBER method rests on a small expert panel (six contributors in one round). It should not be confused with the intergovernmental Coalition for Children's Rights and Protection in the Age of AI.

FABRIC (European Summer Program on Rationality, ESPR) Bridge

Nonprofit · Prague, Czech Republic · founded 2016 · also draws on Formal

FABRIC Labs, a nonprofit registered in Prague, runs free residential camps for mathematically able teenagers. They are the European Summer Program on Rationality (ESPR, ages 16-19, which grew out of a 2016 'EuroSPARC' pilot), the Program on AI and Reasoning (PAIR, ages 16-21, since 2023) and the Asian Spring Programme on Rationality (ASPR, in Taiwan). The curricula mix game theory, cryptography, logic, cognitive science and AI with introspection and communication skills. Each camp takes about 30 students and a dozen staff; both 2026 summer camps were held in Somerset, UK.

It is one of the few places that pairs formal reasoning and AI literacy with self-understanding before people choose careers. It feeds the rationalist and EA talent pipeline in Europe and Asia, and it shows a way to build reflective capacity early rather than repair it later.

Works on People, Epistemics · Key work ESPR 2026 (26 July-5 August, Somerset, UK) (2026); PAIR: Program on AI and Reasoning (camp for ages 16-21, run since 2023; 2026 edition 22 Aug-1 Sep, Somerset) (2023); ASPR: Asian Spring Programme on Rationality, Taiwan (2024) · Get involved Apply to ESPR (ages 16-19) or PAIR (ages 16-21): free, with travel scholarships; 2027 applications open December 2026; ASPR in Taiwan (ages 16-19, held in February)

Note The sites name no staff or leaders. PAIR's curriculum covers how current AI systems work and 'some of the ethical and safety aspects' of AI-human relations, but there is no explicit alignment or x-risk framing, so the AI-safety link is mainly through the community and its funding history (Open Philanthropy via CFAR). ESPR's leadership changed in 2019, when operations moved to the Prague entity. FABRIC also runs WARP (Oxford).

Flowers AI & CogSci Lab (Inria / University of Bordeaux) Bridge

Academic · Talence (Bordeaux), France · founded 2008 · also draws on Living systems

An Inria project-team in Talence, near Bordeaux, run jointly with the University of Bordeaux and ENSTA and led by Pierre-Yves Oudeyer. Inria's 2024 report put it at roughly 40-45 members. It studies curiosity-driven, open-ended learning in children and machines. It builds 'autotelic' agents that set their own goals, including agents built on LLMs, and uses them to model child development, cultural evolution and educational technology. One stated research line asks how language and social interaction can align autotelic systems with human cultures (values and preferences).

It brings developmental psychology and cultural-evolution methods to agents that generate their own goals, a problem the alignment field is only starting to face. Its transmission-chain studies of LLMs show small model biases being amplified into cultural 'attractors' across repeated interactions.

Note Its alignment line concerns aligning open-ended agents with human cultures and preferences, not catastrophic risk, and recent outputs rarely use safety language. Much of the lab's work is educational technology and assisted scientific discovery rather than alignment. The 2008 founding year comes from Inria's earliest activity report for the team.

Interchange Forum for Reflecting on Intelligent Systems (IRIS), University of Stuttgart: AI Safety group (Thilo Hagendorff) Bridge

Academic · Stuttgart, Germany · founded 2019 · also draws on Philosophy

IRIS is a University of Stuttgart platform for critical reflection on intelligent systems, set up in 2019 as a Stuttgart Research Focus with DFG funding. It hosts about 15 research projects, a teaching strand (RISING) and public events. Its AI Safety group, an independent research group led by Thilo Hagendorff with a postdoc and four PhD students, applies experimental psychology ('machine psychology') to large language models. Its studies cover emergent deception, evaluation awareness, jailbreaking by reasoning models, dark-personality fine-tuning and, in September 2026, multi-agent shutdown sabotage.

It is one of the few AI-safety groups in German academia whose method comes from psychology and philosophy rather than ML. Its experiments treat models as behavioural subjects, which yields evaluations of deception and self-preservation that complement interpretability work.

Works on Assurance, Agency · Key work Deception abilities emerged in large language models (PNAS) (2024); Machine Psychology (2024); Large reasoning models as jailbreak agents (Nature Communications) (2026) · Get involved IRIS Fall Symposium, 20 Nov 2026, Stuttgart: free and public, register by 10 Nov; IRIS membership for University of Stuttgart staff and students, and associate membership for external researchers, by application

Note The roster entry combines a broad host platform with one group. Most IRIS projects concern societal effects (populism, education, trust) rather than safety, so these tags describe the Hagendorff group. The group is staffed largely by PhD students and depends on project grants.

Mental Health Navigator (MentNav) Bridge

Nonprofit · Arundel, United Kingdom · founded 2019

A small volunteer-run charity, registered in England and Wales in 2023 (charity 1205257), that grew out of an EA mental health navigation pilot started in 2019. It runs two sites. MentNav is a curated database of free and low-cost mental health resources for the general public. Its sister site, the EA Mental Health Navigator, is a community-sourced directory of therapists and coaches recommended by people in effective altruism and AI safety, now run by Julia Wise. Its one-to-one advisory service closed in early 2024.

It is the main referral route for AI-safety workers looking for a therapist or coach who treats worry about catastrophic risk as reasonable, and 2026 posts on the field's mental health name it as such. It does not screen the providers it lists. It also cannot help with work under NDAs or infohazard rules, which can't be discussed with an outside therapist.
