Note Nobody checks the listings: both sites say they do not verify providers, coaches or reviews. Capacity is very small (two trustees, about £1,200 a year). The advisory service closed in 2024 for lack of volunteers and money, and the October 2025 update said some trustees had been less able to take part. The AI-safety part is the sister directory run by Julia Wise; MentNav itself now serves the general public.

Re-Align: Workshop on Representational Alignment Bridge

Programme · Distributed · founded 2024 · also draws on Living systems

An annual workshop at ICLR (2024, 2025, 2026) where machine-learning, neuroscience and cognitive-science researchers work on measuring and using the similarity between the internal representations of brains, humans and neural networks. The third edition (27 April 2026) asked 'what can we do with alignment?', with two themes: neural control, which it links to mechanistic interpretability and to building safer, steerable models, and downstream behaviour. It added the Re-Align Challenge, a hackathon with blue-team and red-team tracks and a leaderboard of representational-comparison measures. Eight researchers from EPFL, MIT/UCSF, MPI Psycholinguistics, NYU, Berkeley, Stanford and UW-Madison organise it.

It is a standing venue where the methods cognitive scientists and neuroscientists use to compare minds reach interpretability and steering research. Related submissions to ICLR grew from 303 (2024) to 688 (2026), so it is an entry point for funders looking for cognitive-science routes into understanding models.

Works on Agency · Key work Re-Align Workshop @ ICLR 2026: neural control and downstream behaviour (2026); Re-Align Challenge (hackathon and leaderboard of representational-comparison measures) (2026); Re-Align Workshop @ ICLR 2026 listing (ICLR virtual site) (2026) · Get involved Submit papers to future editions (the 2026 call closed 5 Feb 2026, via OpenReview); Enter the Re-Align Challenge, which is run online; Attend at ICLR; the 2026 edition offered asynchronous virtual presentation and travel grants

Note 'Alignment' here mainly means similarity between representations, not value alignment. The safety framing is a single line in the 2026 call, so 'bridge' depends on the interpretability and steerability theme. No 2027 edition had been announced at the time of writing. As a workshop series it has no staff or institution of its own, and the organisers change from year to year.

Rethink Wellbeing BridgeOn aisafety.com

Nonprofit · Wapenveld, Netherlands · founded 2022

A remote mental health nonprofit founded by Inga Grossmann, registered as a Dutch foundation (Stichting Rethink Wellbeing) with US fiscal sponsorship from Players Philanthropy Fund. Its main programme, the CBT Lab, is a free 12-week online course in third-wave CBT for people in high-impact careers: peer groups of 4–6 meet weekly with a trained volunteer facilitator. By its own count it has served 285 participants from 35 countries and trained 66 facilitators. It has also run an IFS Lab and is building an 'AI+ CBT Lab', a lower-cost version that uses LLMs, to be piloted in the Philippines.

It is the main structured, evidence-based mental health programme for the EA and AI-safety talent pool, and 2026 discussions of mental health in AI safety name it. Its peer-group format could carry a cohort built around AI-safety stressors such as short timelines, NDA-bound work and anticipatory grief, but no such cohort exists yet.

Works on People · Key work CBT Lab (12-week peer-group third-wave CBT; winter 2026–27 cohort) (2026); IFS Self-Care Fellowship (IFS Lab) (2024); AI+ CBT Lab (LLM-assisted group programme; Philippines pilot) (2026) · Get involved Apply to the CBT Lab: free with a refundable deposit; winter 2026–27 cohort, final deadline 25 Oct 2026; Volunteer as a trained peer-group facilitator; Job: Clinical AI Mental Health Researcher and Product Owner (advertised Sep 2026)

Note It is not specific to AI safety: it serves 'ambitious altruists' in general (past participants include Center for AI Safety staff) and is expanding toward low-cost care in low- and middle-income countries. The AI+ CBT Lab applies AI to mental health; it is not AI-safety work. Its outcome figures (20-30% reductions in symptoms) are self-reported and come from its own evaluations; its 2024 IFS Lab pilot found mostly small, non-significant effects. It advertised for a co-director in February 2026. Founded in 2022; 'Effective Peer Support' was the name of its first peer-group programme.

Stanford Brainstorm: The Lab for Mental Health Innovation Bridge

Academic · Palo Alto, US · founded 2016 · also draws on Safety science

A psychiatry lab at Stanford School of Medicine, founded in 2016 and directed by the psychiatrist Nina Vasan, that works with technology companies to build mental health into product design. Since 2025 its AI work has centred on clinical testing of chatbots with Common Sense Media. This includes the April 2025 assessment of social AI companions and the November 2025 finding that ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini and Meta AI are unsafe for teen mental-health support. In May 2026 it reviewed five AI mental-health apps for Common Sense's Youth AI Safety Institute. It has also contributed to MLCommons' mental-health safety benchmarks for large language models, published a GenAI Psychological Safety Plan for users, developers and policymakers, and taught a Stanford course on mental health in the age of AI in winter 2026.

It brings psychiatrists' clinical judgement into model evaluation. It tests whether chatbots recognise and respond appropriately to mental-health conditions in young people, rather than only checking how they handle explicit suicide and self-harm content. Through Common Sense Media, these clinical tests become widely cited public ratings of frontier models.

Works on Human minds, Assurance · Key work AI Companions Decoded: risk assessment of social AI companions (with Common Sense Media) (2025); AI Chatbots for Mental Health Support: risk assessment (with Common Sense Media) (2025); AI Mental Health Apps: risk assessment (with the Youth AI Safety Institute) (2026) · Get involved Stanford course PSYC 248/148 on mental health and AI (winter 2026); non-Stanford students and professionals can ask to join; Online community of 2,000+ practitioners (Facebook group); Lab positions, consulting and sponsored projects via brainstormlab@stanford.edu

Note Much of its work is done with and for technology companies through consulting and sponsored projects, and its funding is not disclosed. Its own news and events pages are sparsely dated, so its recent AI outputs are visible mainly through Common Sense Media's publications. Team size includes many student fellows and interns.

The Human Line Project BridgeNew

Nonprofit · Quebec, Canada · founded 2025

A nonprofit started in spring 2025 by Etienne Brisson, a Quebec business coach, after a relative was hospitalised following delusions linked to chatbot use. It runs a peer-support community for affected people and their families: text channels and weekly audio calls on Discord, with about 200 members by January 2026. It also collects case reports, works with university researchers and advocates for safer chatbot design. It is registered as a not-for-profit in Canada and as a 501(c)(3) in the US.

Its corpus of real cases (185 analysed with King's College London in September 2026) is ground-truth evidence of sycophancy and delusion-reinforcement in long conversations, which model-behaviour evals and incident databases mostly lack. It is also a working model of lived-experience peer support for AI-related harm.

Works on Human minds, Assurance · Key work Delusions and Harms Associated with AI Chatbot Use (with King's College London; 185 real-world cases) (2026); Peer-to-peer support community for people and families affected by AI-associated delusions (Discord, weekly calls) (2025); AI-Induced Delusional Spirals (research collaboration with Stanford University) (2026) · Get involved Peer support for people affected by AI-associated delusions and for friends and family: Discord text channels and weekly audio calls, entered through an intake interview; anonymity allowed; Share a case or story through the project's intake form, which feeds its case collection and partner research; Researchers and journalists can request contact with members who have agreed to share their stories

Note Run by people with lived experience rather than clinicians; 'AI psychosis' is not a clinical diagnosis. Its case collection is self-selected, so it shows patterns, not prevalence. Funding sources are not stated publicly. The bridge ring is borderline: its framing is present psychological harm, though it uses 'AI safety' language and engages with industry.

Wisdom and Culture Lab (University of Waterloo) Bridge

Academic · Waterloo, Canada · also draws on Democracy

Igor Grossmann's psychology lab at the University of Waterloo studies how people make wise decisions in everyday life, across cultures and over time. Its methods are surveys, behavioural experiments and computational work (modelling, NLP, large-scale analyses). It leads the Wise Judgment Consortium (15 labs on five continents) and co-authored a 2026 Trends in Cognitive Sciences paper arguing that AI needs metacognitive wisdom strategies. In September 2026 it opened two new AI programmes, one on metacognition in advanced AI systems and one on human-AI systems for expert judgement and forecasting.

It brings the empirical science of wisdom (intellectual humility, perspective-seeking, context adaptation), with cross-cultural ground truth, to AI design and evaluation. That gives 'wise AI' and wisdom evals a measurable psychological basis rather than a purely philosophical one.

Works on Values, Assurance, Epistemics · Key work Imagining and building wise machines: The centrality of AI metacognition (Trends in Cognitive Sciences) (2026); Wise Judgment Consortium: preregistered 15-lab cross-cultural study of wise judgement (2025); New research programmes on AI metacognition and on human-AI systems for expert judgement and forecasting (2026) · Get involved Postdoctoral Research Fellowship in AI Metacognition and Reasoning (CAD 65-70k; review from 15 Oct 2026); Postdoctoral Fellow in Human-AI Systems for Expert Judgment (posted Sep 2026); Research Project Manager: AI, Judgment, and Forecasting (posted Sep 2026)

Note Its AI programmes are new (announced September 2026) and their funders aren't named. Before that, its AI work was mainly the wise-machines position paper. It treats wisdom as cognitive strategies measured from the outside, not as contemplative practice.

Adjacent ring 38

AILit Framework (European Commission and OECD) and PISA 2029 Media & AI Literacy (MAIL) assessment AdjacentNew

Programme · Paris, France and Brussels, Belgium · founded 2025 · also draws on Democracy

A joint project of the European Commission and the OECD, supported by Code.org (now CodeAI), that defines AI literacy for primary and secondary schools. A review draft was launched on 22 May 2025. After consultation with more than 2,000 people in over 100 countries, the final framework, 'Empowering Learners for the Age of AI', was launched on 18 June 2026 with four domains: Engage with AI, Create with AI, Manage AI and Shape AI. It feeds the OECD's PISA 2029 Media & Artificial Intelligence Literacy (MAIL) assessment of 15-year-olds, to be fielded in 2029.

PISA 2029 will measure, across the countries and economies that take part, whether 15-year-olds can evaluate AI-mediated content and use AI responsibly. That will be one of the largest public measurements of human epistemic agency alongside AI. The framework holds that AI cannot replace human judgement, care or relationships, and that choosing not to use AI can be a responsible decision: an alignment-relevant norm for the human side of the transition.

Works on Epistemics, Human minds · Key work Empowering Learners for the Age of AI: final AI Literacy Framework for Primary and Secondary Education (2026); AILit Framework review draft and global consultation (2025); Shaping Future Success: AI Literacy Framework and the PISA 2029 MAIL Assessment (2025) · Get involved The framework, competences and learning scenarios are free at ailiteracyframework.org; The 2025 global consultation on the draft has closed; PISA 2029 MAIL is fielded through national PISA centres

Note The entry covers two related but separate instruments: AILit is a curriculum reference framework, while MAIL is a PISA assessment framework developed by the OECD, with ACER leading delivery of PISA 2029. Code.org/CodeAI, a nonprofit backed by the tech industry, supported the drafting. Ethics runs through the framework, but it has no safety or catastrophic-risk framing. MAIL results are not expected before about 2031.

American Psychiatric Association: Committee on Mental Health Information Technology (AI in Psychiatric Care) Adjacent

Programme · Washington, DC, USA

The AI workstream of the American Psychiatric Association (founded 1844; more than 40,400 members), led by its Committee on Mental Health Information Technology. It publishes guidance for clinicians on AI in psychiatric practice: - a 2024 position statement treating AI as 'augmented intelligence' that supports rather than replaces clinicians - a 2026 AI Resource Document, with a webinar series - a checklist for assessing AI scribe tools - a blog on the risks of 'AI prescribing' - its App Advisor model for evaluating digital mental-health tools, adopted in a 2026 SAMHSA advisory - an eight-part 'facts label' for AI mental-health tools, published in Frontiers in Psychiatry in August 2026.

The facts label (identifying information, intended use, warnings, risks and limitations, model information, clinical evidence, accessibility, privacy) is a ready transparency template. It could be extended to the general-purpose chatbots people use for emotional support. The APA also brings organised clinical judgement on patient safety to AI tools at a time when US regulation of them is thin.

Works on Assurance, Human minds · Key work Facts label for transparent communication of AI risks in mental health technology (Frontiers in Psychiatry) (2026); APA AI Resource Document and webinar series (2026); AI Prescribing Blog: Innovation, Risk, and the Need for Guardrails (2026) · Get involved AI Resource Document webinar series: 'Implementing AI in Hospitals and Academic Settings' (16 Oct 2026), 'AI and Ethics: From Principles to Practice' (20 Nov 2026), 'AI in Practice: A Hands-On Session' (18 Dec 2026); Download the 2026 APA AI Resource Document via a form

Note It focuses on psychiatrists' clinical use of AI tools (scribes, decision support, prescribing), not on general-purpose chatbots or AI safety more widely. It is distinct from the American Psychological Association, which is already in the roster.

American Psychoanalytic Association: President's Commission on Artificial Intelligence (APsA CAI) Adjacent

Programme · New York, USA · also draws on Arts, futures

A commission of the American Psychoanalytic Association that develops psychoanalytic responses to AI across clinical practice, education, theory and organisational life. Psychoanalysts Todd Essig (William Alanson White Institute) and Amy Levy co-chair it. Its main publication is The CAI Report, edited by Alexander Stein, with 13 issues between January 2025 and August 2026. It also publishes the CAI Currents digest and CAI Conversations video roundtables, and runs a monthly working group of psychoanalytic institute leaders and peer consultation groups for clinicians. In October 2025 it issued principles for AI use policies in psychoanalytic education, and it is producing a documentary, 'Uncharted Territory: Humans and the Rise of AI'.

Its central question is what happens to people who form attachments to systems that perform human connection without experiencing it. That is a depth-psychological lens on AI companions, dependence and anthropomorphism, which empirical harm studies lack. The CAI Report has also started engaging with AI-safety debates directly, with essays on AI 2027, on 'If Anyone Builds It, Everyone Dies' and on a psychoanalytic framework for alignment.

Note It writes mainly for clinicians, so its policy reach is limited. The Report mixes clinical essays, poetry and an advice column, and quality varies. The essays on x-risk and alignment are individual contributors' views, not commission positions. The commission's founding date is not stated. It is distinct from the American Psychological Association and the American Psychiatric Association.

American Psychological Association (APA) Adjacent

Membership body · Washington, DC, USA · founded 1892

The main US professional and scientific body for psychologists, founded in 1892 and based in Washington, DC. On AI, it issued a health advisory on AI and adolescent well-being (June 2025) and one on the use of generative AI chatbots and wellness apps for mental health (November 2025), surveys psychologists about patients' AI use, and in August 2026 began working with OpenAI on youth mental-health guidance. In September 2026 it named an executive director for a new Center for Behavioral Science and AI.

It turns clinical and developmental evidence into professional norms that developers and regulators can adopt, such as not presenting chatbots as therapists, building safeguards for minors and protecting likeness and data. It is now building institutional capacity to bring psychological science into AI development.

Note apa.org blocks automated fetching, so the details of the advisories and the new centre come from press coverage and news listings rather than the full texts. Its AI work focuses on present mental-health and developmental harms, without catastrophic-risk framing. Since August 2026 it works directly with OpenAI on youth guidance. Mitch Prinstein also co-directs UNC's Winston Center, which is listed separately.

BlackboxNLP: Workshop on Analyzing and Interpreting Neural Networks for NLP Adjacent

Programme · Distributed · founded 2018

An annual workshop on interpreting and explaining language models, held since 2018 alongside a major ACL conference (EMNLP in all years but 2019). Its call invites methods from machine learning, psychology, linguistics and neuroscience to assess what representations and computations models learn and what inductive biases they have. The ninth edition is on 29 October 2026 in Budapest at EMNLP 2026, with a reproducibility challenge. The 2025 edition in Suzhou ran a shared task on circuit and causal-variable localisation using the MIB benchmark.

It is the standing venue where computational linguists and cognitive scientists study language-model internals, bringing linguistic and psycholinguistic analysis to interpretability, a core AI-safety agenda. It does not describe its work as safety research, so the overlap with safety-motivated interpretability lies in the substance, not in its stated aims.

British Association for Counselling and Psychotherapy (BACP) Adjacent

Membership body · Lutterworth, UK · founded 1977

The UK's largest professional body for counsellors and psychotherapists, with around 75,000 members. It is a registered charity, founded in 1977 and based in Lutterworth, Leicestershire. In 2026 AI in mental health has become a recurring policy theme: - February: responded to the MHRA consultation on regulating AI in healthcare, citing its Mindometer survey of therapists - July: a public survey found 46% of 16-24-year-olds had used AI instead of talking to a person about their mental health - September: responded to the National Commission into the Regulation of AI in Healthcare, and published guidance on managing anxiety about AI's future.

It brings frontline clinical evidence of chatbot use and harm, drawn from its member therapists. It is also one of the few professional bodies publicly addressing anxiety about where powerful AI is heading, including fears that no one is in control. That makes it a natural partner for psychological support around AI distress, including for people working in AI safety.

Its AI work so far consists of consultation responses, surveys and guidance, not a dedicated programme. In April 2026 the Charity Commission closed a regulatory compliance case into its safeguarding, governance and financial controls, opened after trustee resignations and the removal of its Chair and Deputy Chair. The Commission said it was now satisfied with how BACP is governed. The chief executive's name comes from Wikipedia.

Cambridge Language Sciences Interdisciplinary Research Centre Adjacent

Academic · Cambridge, UK · also draws on Living systems

A University of Cambridge Interdisciplinary Research Centre: a virtual network linking language researchers in linguistics, psychology, neuroscience, computer science, education and Cambridge University Press & Assessment. It awards small incubator and workshop grants. From 2024 to 30 September 2026 it ran the AI@Cam-funded project 'Improving language equity and inclusion through AI', which paid for workshops and symposia on AI in aphasia recovery, human-AI collaboration in language assessment, computational methods for language-learning technology, and the conceptual blind spots of automated hate-speech detection.

It brings psycholinguistic, clinical and sociolinguistic methods for asking whose speech and language AI systems handle well or badly: people with aphasia or hearing loss, language learners, speakers of non-standard varieties. Mainstream AI evaluation rarely measures this.

Center for Digital Thriving, Harvard Graduate School of Education (Project Zero) Adjacent

Academic · Cambridge, MA, United States

The Center for Digital Thriving is a research and design centre at Harvard Graduate School of Education's Project Zero. It studies how young people can thrive with technology, centred on 'digital agency': meaningful choice and control over how technology fits into their lives. It co-designs resources with teens and teachers. Since 2024 it has run an AI research portfolio: youth advisory memos with Hopelab on why teens turn to AI for emotional support, and a 2026 report on generative AI in classrooms drawn from a survey of more than 1,000 US teachers and principals. It also runs a self-paced 12-hour course for educators with AI content, and an annual fellowship.

It gives grounded, non-alarmist evidence from young people on AI emotional support and over-reliance, plus an agency-centred framework for AI literacy. That counterweight to harm-only accounts can inform how companion and tutoring products are designed for teens.

Center for Humans and Machines (CHM), Max Planck Institute for Human Development Adjacent

Academic · Berlin, Germany · founded 2019 · also draws on Living systems, Arts, futures

A research centre at the Max Planck Institute for Human Development in Berlin, set up in 2019 and directed by Iyad Rahwan. It studies how AI and digital media change the way people think, work, cooperate and govern, mainly through behavioural experiments with people and machines (the 'machine behaviour' research line). In 2025 it published two Nature papers: one showing that delegating tasks to AI increases dishonest behaviour, and one proposing a 'science fiction science' method for testing a technology's social effects before it exists. It also hosts the Machine+Behavior conference and an Artist & AI residency.

It produces experimental evidence on how AI agents change human moral behaviour and cooperation, a question the alignment field mostly handles in theory; the delegation results bear directly on guardrails for agentic AI. It is in Berlin, within reach of int/a's Berlin community.

Note It frames its work around societal disruption and human moral agency, not AI safety or catastrophic risk. Some strands (social-reward fine-tuning of LLMs, human-AI hybrid systems) sit close to capabilities research. Staff size is an estimate, and individual research groups were not checked.

Centre for the Science of Learning & Technology (SLATE), University of Bergen, host of the AI LEARN centre Adjacent

Academic · Bergen, Norway · founded 2016 · also draws on Law, society

SLATE opened in January 2016 in the University of Bergen's Faculty of Psychology as Norway's national research and competence centre for learning analytics. It draws on information science, computer science, cognitive science, pedagogy, sociology and law. It hosts AI LEARN (AI Centre for the Empowerment of Human Learning), a 2025-2030 centre run with NTNU that studies how people learn, work and create with AI; it has 16 PhD candidates and about 35 partners from universities, the public sector and industry. SLATE also runs NOKI, a national AI Olympiad for upper-secondary pupils, and in May 2026 launched three continuing-education master's courses in human-AI systems.

AI LEARN is a large, publicly funded research programme whose stated aim is to strengthen human agency as AI enters learning and work. It studies cognitive engagement, trust and 'hybrid intelligence' with learning-sciences methods. That produces evidence on human deskilling and over-reliance, which the AI-safety field worries about but rarely studies directly.

Chartered College of Teaching Adjacent

Membership body · London, UK · founded 2017

The Chartered College of Teaching is the professional body for teachers in England: a London-based charity that holds an 1849 Royal Charter and relaunched under its present name in 2017. With Chiltern Learning Trust, and funded by the Department for Education, it produced the free 'Safe and effective use of AI in education' materials (June 2025, updated May 2026). They include training on understanding and safely using generative AI, a certified assessment that earns credits towards Chartered Teacher Status, case studies, and an Impact journal special issue. It also runs the DfE-backed EdTech Evidence Board, which published its pilot findings in September 2026.

It is the main professional-formation route through which England's teachers learn to judge AI in their classrooms, and it ties that judgement to evidence-informed practice and professional credentials. Its EdTech Evidence Board is a working model of evidence standards for technology products sold to schools.

Children and Screens: Institute of Digital Media and Child Development Adjacent

Nonprofit · New York, United States · founded 2013

Children and Screens is a US nonprofit, founded in 2013, that takes no technology-industry funding. It convenes researchers, clinicians and parents on how digital media affect child development, and turns research into webinars (#AskTheExperts), the Screen Deep podcast, tip sheets and short research snapshots. It also runs a small research-grants programme. In 2025 it gave nearly $150,000 for a study tracking 100 adolescents' use of AI companions over 21 days, and in 2026 it published a run of material on chatbots, AI companions and 'artificial intimacy'.

It connects paediatricians, developmental scientists and parents to the questions raised by AI companions, without tech-industry money. Evaluators of companion products could draw developmental expertise from that network.

Cognitive Resonance Adjacent

Company · Distributed · founded 2024 · also draws on Arts, futures

Cognitive Resonance is a one-person venture that teaches educators and policymakers about generative AI through cognitive science. Benjamin Riley, who earlier founded the teacher-preparation nonprofit Deans for Impact, set it up in March 2024. Its method explains first how human learning works and then how large language models produce output. It works through workshops, consulting, keynotes, the white paper 'Education Hazards of Generative AI' (2024) and a Substack newsletter. Since September 2026 the newsletter has run investigative reports on alleged harms to students at Alpha School, an AI-centred private school.

It applies learning science to AI in schools, arguing that tools which do students' thinking for them undercut the effortful practice that learning depends on, and it resists the claim that AI in education is inevitable. It is a deflationary counterweight to both edtech hype and AGI narratives, useful for anyone asking where AI erodes human cognition.

Works on Human minds, Epistemics · Key work Education Hazards of Generative AI (white paper; 25,000+ downloads) (2024); Building Human Knowledge to Halt AI Hype (launch post) (2024); An illustrated guide to resisting 'AI is inevitable' in education (2026) · Get involved Commission a workshop, consulting or a talk; Subscribe to the Substack newsletter; Download the free white paper 'Education Hazards of Generative AI'

Note It is essentially one person's practice, working as a 'virtual organisation' with outside scientists; its legal form and funding are not stated. It is sceptical of AGI claims and of the premises of x-risk discourse, so it will not frame its work as AI safety. Its recent output is mostly investigative journalism on a single school.

Programme · Stanford, CA, USA · founded 2022

A Stanford Graduate School of Education initiative, run with Stanford HAI and the Stanford Accelerator for Learning, that co-designs free AI-literacy resources with high-school teachers. The resources range from 15-minute activities to multi-day lessons for art, maths, English, history and science classes. Each year it takes a remote cohort of teacher co-design fellows; cohorts are listed from 2022-23 to 2025-26. The team also publishes learning-sciences research on how teachers fold AI literacy into their subjects.

It puts critical AI literacy into humanities and non-computing classrooms, so that teenagers learn to understand, question and critique AI wherever they meet it. Its teacher co-design method and published research are a tested way to reach young people at scale; a December 2024 webinar said the resources are used in 54+ countries.

Day of AI AdjacentChanged

Nonprofit · New York, USA · founded 2021

A free PreK-12 AI-literacy curriculum and teacher-training programme, started in 2021 at MIT RAISE (Responsible AI for Social Empowerment and Education) under Cynthia Breazeal. It became an independent nonprofit in August 2024 and still works closely with MIT RAISE. In August 2026 it released a grade-by-grade PreK-12 curriculum. Its high-school units cover ethics, identity, human agency, deepfakes and algorithmic profiling, and stress critical thinking and human-led work over reliance on AI. It reports reaching more than 4 million students, with teachers in about 175 countries.

It is one of the largest free routes through which children learn what AI is and how to question it, so it shapes public understanding of AI early. Its curriculum puts students' own agency ahead of dependence on AI. It does not yet cover AI safety or catastrophic risk.

Kennedy Institute) (2026) · Get involved Free online professional development for teachers (September 2026 sessions); Free curriculum and community registration for educators and families; America's Youth AI Festival and other events

Note Its reach figures are its own and differ between pages: 4 million students in the August 2026 release, 5 million on the homepage, and over a million students in 170 countries on the About page. Its framing is literacy and responsible use, not catastrophic risk, and its partners include corporate sponsors. Jeffrey Riley's and Ethan Berman's roles were not confirmed on its current site.

Deans for Impact (DFI) Adjacent

Nonprofit · Austin, USA · founded 2015

A US nonprofit founded in 2015 that works with educator-preparation programmes to ground teacher training in cognitive science, known for its guide 'The Science of Learning'. It reports working with 261 programmes in 45 states. It runs the Impact Academy fellowship for educator-preparation leaders and does state policy work on teacher pathways. In August 2026 it announced an AI Framework for Teacher Preparation with TeachingWorks (University of Michigan). The framework is funded by the Gates Foundation, will be developed over 2026-27, and will set out the competencies novice teachers need to use AI with sound judgement.

It turns cognitive-science findings, such as the value of effortful retrieval and practice, into norms for how teachers are trained. Those norms are what can stop AI from doing the thinking that produces learning. Its AI framework could shape how many US teacher-preparation programmes teach the use of AI.

Works on Human minds · Key work AI Framework for Teacher Preparation (with TeachingWorks; announced) (2026); The Science of Learning (2015); Impact Academy fellowship for educator-preparation leaders (11 cohorts) (2026) · Get involved Impact Academy fellowship for educator-preparation leaders; Community of Practice of education leaders advising the AI framework (2026-27); Partnerships with educator-preparation programmes

Note Its AI work has only just begun: the framework was announced in August 2026 and will be developed over 2026-27. It frames AI as something to use well in teaching, not as a risk.

Department of Affective Disorders, Aarhus University Hospital – Psychiatry / Aarhus University (Søren Dinesen Østergaard group) Adjacent

Academic · Aarhus, Denmark · also draws on Safety science

A psychiatric research group led by Søren Dinesen Østergaard, Professor of Clinical Medicine at Aarhus University and Head of Research at the Department of Affective Disorders. In 2023 Østergaard predicted that generative AI chatbots could fuel delusions in people prone to psychosis. In 2026 the group searched 10.7 million clinical notes for 53,974 patients of the Central Denmark Region's psychiatric services for mentions of chatbots or ChatGPT. Notes for 38 patients were compatible with harmful consequences of chatbot use; delusions were the most common, followed by suicidality or self-harm and eating disorders. Other outputs include papers on emotion contagion and mania, on the adverse effects of voice-based chatbots, and a case report of first-episode mania during intense ChatGPT use.

It shows how harms from AI can be monitored in a population using routine health records, a pharmacovigilance-style method that AI safety has hardly used. It also gives early clinical, rather than anecdotal, evidence on chatbot-associated delusions and mania.

Works on Human minds, Assurance · Key work Will Generative Artificial Intelligence Chatbots Generate Delusions in Individuals Prone to Psychosis? (Schizophrenia Bulletin) (2023); Generative Artificial Intelligence Chatbots and Delusions: From Guesswork to Emerging Cases (Acta Psychiatrica Scandinavica) (2025); Potentially Harmful Consequences of AI Chatbot Use Among Patients With Mental Illness: Early Data From a Large Psychiatric Service System (Acta Psychiatrica Scandinavica) (2026)

Note The group has no public homepage; the URL is Østergaard's Aarhus University profile. Much of the AI output is short editorials and letters by Østergaard, and the 2026 health-record study is an early, keyword-based screen, so it likely undercounts harms. The group's broader research is on psychiatric epidemiology and clinical prediction tools, with AI chatbots as a recent line.

Department of Psychosis Studies, Institute of Psychiatry, Psychology & Neuroscience, King's College London: AI-associated delusions research (Morrin and Pollak) Adjacent

Academic · London, UK

A clinical research line inside King's College London's Department of Psychosis Studies, led by the psychiatrists Hamilton Morrin and Thomas Pollak, that studies delusions arising during sustained chatbot use. They coined the term 'AI-associated delusions', set out in The Lancet Psychiatry (2026) how LLMs can co-create delusional content and what safeguards would help, and in September 2026 analysed 185 real-world reports of chatbot-linked harm. Morrin co-leads LAMBDA (Looking After Minds and Brains in the Digital Age), a group on the mental-health effects of AI chatbots.

It gives a clinical account of how sycophancy, linguistic mirroring and hyper-personalised replies can build an 'amplification spiral' with vulnerable users. It also argues that chatbot safety should be judged over whole conversation trajectories rather than single replies, which maps directly onto multi-turn sycophancy evaluations. Pollak has publicly called for AI safety teams to include psychiatrists.

Works on Human minds, Assurance · Key work Artificial intelligence-associated delusions and large language models: risks, mechanisms of delusion co-creation, and safeguarding strategies (The Lancet Psychiatry) (2026); It Is the Journey, Not the Destination: Moving From End Points to Trajectories When Assessing Chatbot Mental Health Safety (JMIR Mental Health) (2026); Characterizing the spiral: potential mechanisms in AI-associated delusions (NPP Digital Psychiatry and Neuroscience) (2026) · Get involved Public talks through KCL's Neuropsychiatry Research and Education Group, e.g. 'Delusions by design' (28 Oct 2025, in person and online); The department takes PhD and MD(Res) students in psychosis studies (not AI-specific)

Note The AI work is a small research line led by a doctoral fellow and a consultant, not a funded centre; no public LAMBDA page was found. The evidence so far is case reports, media reports and conceptual papers, and the terminology ('AI psychosis' versus 'AI-associated delusions') is still debated in the journal.

Digital Promise (AI in education initiative) Adjacent

Nonprofit · Washington, DC, USA · founded 2011 · also draws on Safety science

A US education nonprofit headquartered in Washington, DC, authorised by Congress in 2008 and launched in 2011. Its AI work includes: - an AI literacy framework (2024) built on understanding, evaluating and using AI, with 'human judgment' and 'centering justice' as core values; - the Responsibly Designed AI certification for edtech products (launched April 2025); - research such as the U-GAIN Reading R&D centre on generative AI in reading instruction; - professional learning for school districts. In April 2026 it began a three-year partnership with TNTP, funded by Salesforce, to help schools integrate AI.

About 40 district leaders, school staff and AI researchers co-designed its certification. To pass, a product must let educators override AI output, label generative-AI features, monitor for algorithmic bias and be transparent about data. That makes it a working, buyer-side assurance scheme for protecting human agency: the kind of procurement lever AI-governance discussions often lack.

Note It mostly helps schools adopt AI well rather than questioning adoption, and its AI work is partly funded by industry (Salesforce for the TNTP partnership). The certification covers privacy, bias, labelling and educator override, not longer-term cognitive dependency. AI is one strand of a much wider education portfolio.

Experience AI (Raspberry Pi Foundation with Google DeepMind) Adjacent

Programme · Cambridge, UK · founded 2023

A free AI-literacy programme for learners aged about 8 to 17, created by the Raspberry Pi Foundation with Google DeepMind and launched in April 2023. It offers lesson plans, slides, videos and a free online course for teachers ('Understanding AI for educators'), delivered through regional partner organisations and translations. It reports reaching tens of thousands of educators and millions of learners in more than 180 countries. Recent units cover AI safety for ages 11-14 (privacy, misinformation, trust and responsibility; February 2026) and using large language models to learn (September 2026).

Its September 2026 unit on large language models, 'think first, prompt second', teaches 13- to 16-year-olds to resist cognitive offloading: they rewrite prompts so the tool serves their learning, judge the outputs and stay actively involved in their own thinking. Few classroom programmes aim directly at keeping young people's thinking their own as LLMs spread. Its partner network across many countries could also carry broader AI-risk literacy for young people.

Works on Human minds, Epistemics · Key work Encouraging learners to think first, prompt second: LLM unit (2026); AI safety resources for ages 11-14 (helping young people stay safe online in the age of AI) (2026); 2025 UNESCO King Hamad Bin Isa Al-Khalifa Prize for the Use of ICT in Education (2025) · Get involved Free lessons, slides and videos for teachers at experience-ai.org; Free online course for teachers, 'Understanding AI for educators'; Regional partners deliver training and translations, e.g. an Australia/New Zealand programme to train 5,000 more educators by 2028

Note Google DeepMind co-develops the content and Google.org funds the expansion, so a frontier developer shapes and pays for how millions of children are introduced to AI. In these materials, 'AI safety' means online safety (privacy, misinformation, trust), not the AI-safety field's sense.

Fairplay (formerly Campaign for a Commercial-Free Childhood) Adjacent

Nonprofit · Boston, MA, USA · founded 2000 · also draws on Law, society

A Boston nonprofit with 13 staff, founded in 2000 by psychologist Susan Linn and psychiatrist Alvin Poussaint, that campaigns against marketing to children and harmful Big Tech practices. On AI, it led a coalition of more than 260 organisations and experts calling for a five-year pause on generative AI products for students in pre-K to 12 schools (April 2026). It also issued an advisory against AI companion toys (endorsed by 150+ groups and experts), campaigns against AI-generated 'slop' for children on YouTube, and in September 2026 challenged OpenAI and Meta over child-like mascots for AI agents. It is a partner in the AI Psychological Harms Research Coalition (AIPRC).

It applies a developmental, precautionary case for slowing or pausing AI products until they are shown to be safe for children, and it builds large coalitions behind that case. This shows int/a's 'speed of wisdom' at work in a field the AI-safety mainstream rarely reaches.

Works on Human minds, Justice · Key work Coalition call for a five-year pause on generative AI in pre-K to 12 schools (260+ organisations and experts) (2026); Advisory against AI companion toys (150+ endorsers) (2025); Partnership in the AI Psychological Harms Research Coalition (2026) · Get involved Sign-on coalitions and campaigns (e.g. Pause GenAI in Schools, Stop YouTube Slop for Kids); Screen Time Action Network, a network for practitioners and parents run by Fairplay; Submit experiences of AI's psychological effects to research via AIPRC (aiprc.org)

Note Its positions (a five-year moratorium on school AI, 'don't buy AI toys') are contested; for example, the Cato Institute argued in November 2025 against letting 'panic set the rules' for AI toys. It is an advocacy organisation, not a research centre. It works on present harms to children, with no catastrophic-risk framing.

Harding Center for Risk Literacy Adjacent

Academic · Potsdam, Germany · founded 2009 · also draws on Safety science

A research centre for risk literacy and evidence communication, founded in 2009 with Gerd Gigerenzer at the Max Planck Institute for Human Development in Berlin. It has been part of the University of Potsdam's Faculty of Health Sciences since 2020, and also of the Brandenburg Medical School Theodor Fontane (MHB) since 2026. It studies how people understand risks, and builds tools such as fact boxes for doctors, patients and journalists. Its AI line, 'algorithmic decision environments', tests whether AI in healthcare and chatbots such as ChatGPT, Gemini and Le Chat meet evidence-based standards. That work includes the EB-LLM study on cancer-screening information and a systematic review of patient-relevant outcomes.

It judges AI by the standard of evidence-based medicine: does the AI improve decisions and outcomes that matter to patients, not just benchmark accuracy? Its 2025 review found that AI tools for clinicians are rarely evaluated on patient-relevant outcomes. That gives a concrete template for outcome-based AI assurance and for risk communication about AI.

Human Change Foundation Adjacent

Nonprofit · Amsterdam, Netherlands · founded 2024

An operating foundation (Stichting) registered in Amsterdam, launched at the World Economic Forum in Davos in January 2024 by philanthropist Margarita Louis-Dreyfus, with staff in London and Switzerland. It campaigns on how digital technology and generative AI affect children's social, emotional and cognitive development. Its current campaign, 'Beware of Artificial Intimacy', is about anthropomorphic AI companions disrupting children's attachment. It holds public panels and closed-door sessions at its Human Change House in Davos each January and during UN General Assembly week each September, and makes invitation-only grants (about €1.6M in 2025).

It puts the developmental case against attachment-exploiting AI companions in front of business, philanthropic and political elites. It also links child-development advocates with AI-risk organisations: its partners include the Future of Life Institute, the Civilization Research Institute and the AI Psychological Research Coalition.

Human Flourishing Program at Harvard University Adjacent

Academic · Cambridge MA, USA · founded 2016 · also draws on Religion, Philosophy

An interdisciplinary research programme at Harvard's Institute for Quantitative Social Science, founded in 2016 and directed by epidemiologist Tyler VanderWeele. It studies and measures human flourishing, drawing on psychology, public health, philosophy and theology, and runs the Global Flourishing Study (200,000+ participants in 22 countries) with Gallup and Baylor. Its AI and Flourishing Initiative, run with the Happiness Foundation, published a 2026 framework for orienting large language model outputs and AI product design towards flourishing.

It supplies validated, cross-cultural measures of flourishing that can serve as an alignment and evaluation target: Gloo's Flourishing AI benchmark (2025) scores models on its seven dimensions. It also brings Catholic social teaching and virtue-ethics framings into AI discussions, and in 2026 met Anthropic staff, including Chris Olah.

Hybrid Intelligence Centre Adjacent

Programme · Amsterdam, Netherlands · founded 2020 · also draws on Philosophy

A ten-year Dutch research consortium (NWO Gravitation programme, 2020-2029), based at VU Amsterdam, on AI that augments human intellect instead of replacing it. Seven universities take part: VU, Amsterdam, TU Delft, Groningen, Leiden, Utrecht and Twente. It works on four themes: collaborative, adaptive, responsible and explainable hybrid intelligence. That covers human-agent teams, value inference by language models, and building ethics into system design.

It treats human-AI teaming, mutual explainability and value alignment as one research problem, drawing on multi-agent systems, cognitive science and ethics, and it trains a large group of PhD researchers to work this way. Its work on keeping human agency central bears on human oversight and on avoiding humans being sidelined as AI agents spread.

Note This is mainstream academic AI research with a responsible-AI emphasis, not AI-safety work; it does not use catastrophic-risk framing. Funding ends in 2029. The grant amount and headcount were not confirmed.

Institute for Human-Centered AI (HCA), Helmholtz Munich Adjacent

Academic · Munich, Germany · also draws on Living systems

A research institute at Helmholtz Munich, directed by Eric Schulz, of cognitive scientists, neuroscientists and computer scientists (14 current members). It studies human cognition with machine-learning models, and studies machine intelligence with cognitive-psychology experiments. It built Centaur (Nature, 2025), a language model fine-tuned on Psych-101, a dataset of more than ten million human decisions from 160 experiments, which predicts human behaviour across tasks. It also publishes cognitive evaluations of LLMs: CogBench (ICML 2024), repeated games (Nature Human Behaviour 2025), visual cognition (Nature Machine Intelligence 2025) and state anxiety in LLMs (npj Digital Medicine 2025).

It supplies psychology's experimental toolkit (test batteries, game paradigms, models of human choice) for evaluating what language models do. Centaur is an accurate simulator of human behaviour, which is useful for alignment research but carries a dual-use risk of persuasion and manipulation that the institute itself does not discuss.

Works on Agency, Assurance · Key work A foundation model to predict and capture human cognition (Centaur, Nature) (2025); Playing repeated games with large language models (Nature Human Behaviour) (2025); CogBench: a large language model walks into a psychology lab (ICML) (2024) · Get involved Postdoctoral researcher position advertised on hcai-munich.com

Note Nothing is framed as AI safety, and the dual-use concern about human-behaviour simulators is the profiler's inference, not the institute's statement. Marcel Binz, who led Centaur and holds the MIDAS grant, leaves for MPI Tübingen on 1 October 2026, so some of this line may move with him. The founding year was not found.

Kinsey Institute, Indiana University: technology research and VIBES team Adjacent

Academic · Bloomington, USA

The Kinsey Institute at Indiana University (founded 1947) has a technology research strand that studies how AI, social media and sextech shape trust, intimacy and connection. Its Virtual Intimacy, Behavioral Engagement, and Sexuality (VIBES) team, led by Amanda Gesselman, studies how people use technology for romantic, sexual and emotional engagement, from camsites to AI companions. One of its studies is a national survey on how common sextech use is, including sexting with AI chatbots. Recent AI outputs include a 2026 content analysis of how AI-generated pornography platforms govern their content, a 2026 experiment on feeling close to chatbots co-authored by a Kinsey researcher, and data on AI use in dating from its survey work with Match Group.

It has national survey samples and relationship-science methods for measuring who forms romantic or sexual bonds with AI and how that relates to mental health. The safety field needs that evidence on companion design and emotional dependence, and mostly lacks it outside platform data.

Leibniz-Institut für Wissensmedien (IWM, Leibniz Institute for Knowledge Media) Adjacent

Academic · Tübingen, Germany · founded 2001

IWM is a Leibniz Association research institute in Tübingen, founded in 2001, with more than 150 staff. It studies how people use digital media to learn, find information and share knowledge, mainly through experimental educational and cognitive psychology. One of its nine labs is Language and AI in Education, led since 2024 by computational linguist Detmar Meurers; it builds intelligent tutoring systems, tests them in schools and runs the WoLKE project on reflective use of AI tools in teacher training. Recent AI work includes a doctoral thesis on when and how people decide to use AI (August 2026), an AI masterclass for teachers (August 2026) and a recurring conference on generative AI for educators (third edition July 2025).

Its experimental research on knowledge acquisition, information search and handing thinking over to tools is the evidence that claims about AI-induced deskilling and over-reliance need. It also tests AI tutors in randomised field studies in schools.

Mind: Mental Health in the Age of AI Commission AdjacentNew

Programme · London, UK · founded 2026

Mind, the mental-health charity for England and Wales, set up a year-long commission on AI and mental health. It was announced in February 2026 after a Guardian investigation, which Mind's information team supported, found Google's AI Overviews giving inaccurate mental-health advice. The commission brings together clinicians, technologists, policymakers and people with lived experience. It is gathering evidence from the public, regulators, providers and tech companies on how AI is changing help-seeking, how to keep users safe, and what AI does to inequalities in access, and will then make recommendations to policymakers and industry.

It is a large frontline charity applying a lived-experience inquiry to consumer AI, drawing on people who have been harmed by chatbot advice rather than only on experts' views. It could give UK regulators and companies a public-health and service-user account of what safe AI for mental health requires.

Note The chair and full membership could not be confirmed because Mind's site blocked automated reading; only one commissioner is confirmed. The commission runs for about 12 months, so recommendations are not expected before 2027. Mind also stresses AI's potential to widen access, so this is not an anti-AI campaign.

MIT Initiative on Technology and Self Adjacent

Academic · Cambridge, Massachusetts, United States · founded 2001 · also draws on Law, society

An initiative in MIT's Program in Science, Technology, and Society, founded and directed by Sherry Turkle, Abby Rockefeller Mauzé Professor of the Social Studies of Science and Technology. It studies 'the subjective side' of people's relationships with technology, using clinical-psychological interviewing and ethnography. Turkle's 'Artificial Intimacy: Who We Become When We Talk to Machines' (Little, Brown, September 2026) applies this work to chatbots. It argues that they teach people to avoid difficult emotional work and erode relational capacities.

Four decades of fieldwork on human-machine intimacy, from sociable robots to chatbots, offer a psychoanalytic and ethnographic account of what AI companionship does to people. It is a human-side counterweight to AI-welfare and capability framings, and core reading for protecting human minds and relationships.

Neely Center for Ethical Leadership and Decision Making (USC Marshall), with the Psychology of Technology Institute Adjacent

Academic · Los Angeles, USA

A behavioural-science centre at USC's Marshall School of Business that studies social media, AI and mixed reality. It runs the Neely Indices, nationally representative longitudinal surveys of people's experiences with these technologies (an AI index since June 2023), and turns the findings into design codes for platforms. It is closely tied to the Psychology of Technology Institute, a network of behavioural scientists and technologists founded in 2016 that runs an annual research conference.

It measures how people actually experience AI over time, and it has a record of turning behavioural evidence into design codes that the centre says have informed Minnesota policy and Ofcom's online-safety work. Its Knight-funded programme now applies that approach to chatbots. The Psychology of Technology Institute's 2026 conference is co-organised with Berkeley's Center for Human-Compatible AI, so it links social psychology to the AI-safety community.

Sapien Labs Adjacent

Nonprofit · Arlington, Virginia, United States · founded 2016 · also draws on Living systems

Sapien Labs is a US nonprofit founded in 2016 by the neuroscientist Tara Thiagarajan and based near Washington DC. It runs the Global Mind Project, an online survey that has gathered over 2 million profiles from 130 countries in 21 languages. The survey uses the Mind Health Quotient (MHQ), a 47-item assessment of cognitive, emotional and social functioning, and the data are open to academic and nonprofit researchers. On 30 September 2026 it published its first report on AI, drawn from 264,085 adults surveyed between June 2025 and April 2026. Two-thirds of respondents used generative AI. Mind health followed an inverted U with frequency of use: it was highest at moderate use and fell most among young adults using AI constantly. Users who turned to AI for emotional purposes scored lower at every level of use.

It runs a large multi-country instrument that can track the cognitive and well-being effects of AI use over time, the kind of population-scale monitoring of dependence and cognitive decline that AI-safety work lacks.

Works on Human minds · Key work Rapid Report: Generative AI Use and Mind Health Outcomes (2026); Global Mind Project and the Mind Health Quotient (MHQ); Global Mind Health Report 2025 (2025) · Get involved Take the free, anonymous MHQ assessment (contributes data); Researcher Hub: free data access for academic, nonprofit and government researchers

Note The Global Mind Project uses a self-selected internet sample. Rapid reports are correlational and not peer reviewed (this one precedes an academic paper). AI is a new strand: one report so far, though AI-use questions have been in the standing survey since June 2025.

Stanford SCALE Initiative (Systems Change Advancing Learning and Equity): AI Hub for Education Adjacent

Programme · Stanford, USA · founded 2023 · also draws on Economics

SCALE is an initiative of the Stanford Graduate School of Education, part of the Stanford Accelerator for Learning, that links education research to K-12 decision-makers. Its programmes include Getting Down to Facts, the National Student Support Accelerator (tutoring) and the AI Hub for Education. The hub keeps a searchable repository of more than 800 studies on AI in K-12 education. In March 2026 it published 'The Evidence Base on AI in K-12: A 2026 Review', which found only about 20 studies with strong causal evidence. It is also studying how students and teachers use ChatGPT, using classroom data shared by OpenAI (announced July 2025).

It holds claims about AI in schools to the causal-evaluation standards of education policy research. Its finding that very few studies meet that bar is a check on boosters and critics alike. Research on AI deskilling or cognitive offloading in children can build on its repository and methods, though its own focus is whether AI tools work, not whether they harm.

Note Its data-sharing collaboration with OpenAI raises questions about independence when it evaluates OpenAI's products. The hub frames AI in terms of learning impact and benefit, not harm or safety. The 2023 founding date is SCALE's: Loeb returned to Stanford to lead it in February 2023. The hub's launch date and funders are not published.

TeachAI Adjacent

Network · Seattle, USA · founded 2023

TeachAI is a coalition launched on 2 May 2023 by Code.org (renamed CodeAI in June 2026), ETS, ISTE, Khan Academy and the World Economic Forum. Code.org staffs and runs it. It publishes the AI Guidance for Schools Toolkit, built on seven principles for AI in education, as well as Foundational Policy Ideas for education policymakers and a tracker of AI-in-education guidance from US states and other countries. With the Computer Science Teachers Association (CSTA) it also produced briefs on computer-science education in the age of AI, released 2024-25. Its advisory committee lists more than 100 organisations, among them Google, Microsoft, Meta, Amazon, OpenAI and UNICEF.

Many school systems draw their AI rules from its toolkit, whose principles include keeping human decision-making and regularly assessing AI's effects. That makes it a lever on norms for children's cognitive autonomy and AI literacy, an area the AI-safety field barely reaches. Because tech companies sit inside it, it is also a place to watch whose framing of 'AI in schools' wins.

Works on Human minds, Epistemics · Key work AI Guidance for Schools Toolkit (2023); Guidance on the Future of Computer Science Education in an Age of AI (briefs with CSTA) (2024); AI in Education Policy Tracker (2025) · Get involved Free AI Guidance for Schools Toolkit, with editable sample policies, at teachai.org/toolkit; Advisory committee of 100+ organisations; contact through the 'Engage With Us' section of its site

Note The advisory committee is heavy with industry (Amazon, Google, Meta, Microsoft, OpenAI), and the framing puts opportunity first: it promotes AI adoption in schools as much as caution. Its own site shows no dated 2026 output (the footer reads © 2025). The core toolkit dates from 2023, and the latest dated outputs are the CSTA briefs of early 2025. Code.org rebranded as CodeAI on 2 June 2026.

The Jed Foundation (JED) Adjacent

Nonprofit · New York, United States · founded 2000

JED is a US nonprofit for teen and young-adult emotional health and suicide prevention, founded in 2000 by Donna and Phil Satow after their son's suicide. Its main work is with high schools, colleges and communities. Since 2025 it has run an AI strand. A September 2025 open letter to the AI industry set out crisis protocols (detecting distress, handing users to 988 or Crisis Text Line, follow-up contacts) and asked for no emotionally responsive companions for under-18s. Policy recommendations followed in November 2025. In July 2026 it published preliminary findings from a survey of 5,500+ students on AI use and mental health, and in August 2026 it began a partnership with Columbia's Technology & Democracy Initiative on how AI systems should respond to teens in crisis.

It turns codified suicide-prevention practice (safety planning, caring contacts, crisis handoff, lethal-means restriction) into concrete behaviour requirements for AI systems in self-harm conversations, an area where model specifications are thin.

Works on Human minds, Assurance · Key work Open Letter to the AI and Technology Industry (2025); When Young People Turn to AI for Emotional Support: JED's Response to the APA's New Advisory (2025); Preliminary research on how teens use AI and what it means for their mental health (2026) · Get involved Annual policy summit with an AI theme (2025); Columbia TDI cross-sector network of clinicians and technologists (planned); Staff roles at a large nonprofit

Note AI is a growing strand inside a much larger school and college mental-health programme. Its position is firmly against AI companions for minors. The full survey report was due in autumn 2026. The roster's claim that it advises tech companies directly on crisis protocols was not confirmed beyond its public open letter and recommendations.

The Rithm Project Adjacent

Nonprofit · United States · also draws on Arts, futures

The Rithm Project is a small US initiative, founded by Michelle Culver, that works with young people and the adults around them to rebuild human connection as AI enters their social lives. It has three parts: research (a 2026 survey of 2,400 people aged 13-24 on AI use and relationships, interviews with teens about companion apps, a landscape scan); a cross-sector Changemaker Network that meets at twice-yearly summits; and a Creative Studio that makes card games, classroom toolkits and immersive theatre. Its 2025 'Pro-Social Principles for AI' are a framework that partners use to judge whether an AI product strengthens or displaces human relationships. Its 2036 goal is to reach 10 million young people.

It tackles relational displacement by AI companions from the side of human connection, building young people's capacity rather than only restricting products. The Pro-Social Principles give a simple test of whether a product supports human relationships.

Works on Human minds · Key work Will AI strengthen or erode human-to-human relationships? (four-quadrant framework) (2024); 5 Pro-Social Principles for AI (2025); The Questions We Should Be Asking Now: on AI, Youth, and the Future of Relationships (landscape scan) (2026) · Get involved Changemaker Network, entered by attending one of the twice-yearly Human Connection and AI Summits; Free downloadable tools (The AI Effect card game, Sparks Toolkit, conversation kits); Substack newsletter; general-interest applications for roles

Note Its site does not state its legal form, fiscal sponsor or founding date; its earliest dated output is June 2024. Some funders are tech companies (Pinterest, Salesforce, Workday). Its research is practice-oriented and not peer reviewed.

Winston Center on Technology and Brain Development (UNC Chapel Hill) Adjacent

Academic · Chapel Hill, NC, USA · founded 2022 · also draws on Living systems

A University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill research centre, established in 2022 with a $10 million gift from the Winston Family Foundation and co-directed by Mitch Prinstein and Eva Telzer. It studies how smartphones, social media and now generative AI affect adolescents' brains, behaviour and mental health, using longitudinal neuroimaging, smartphone sensing and surveys. Its 2026 AI outputs include papers on generative-AI app use among US youth (JAMA Network Open) and on how young people converse with AI chatbots (Journal of Medical Internet Research), and a Hopelab-funded survey of researchers mapping the youth-and-AI research field (SPARK).

It brings longitudinal developmental-neuroscience and behavioural-measurement methods that could establish what AI companions and chatbots actually do to developing minds. Its researchers' evidence already shapes APA advisories and US child-online-safety policy.

Works on Human minds · Key work Generative AI app use among US youth (JAMA Network Open) (2026); How US youth use AI chatbots: conversation patterns from naturalistic keystroke observations (Journal of Medical Internet Research) (2026); SPARK study: Survey on Possibilities for AI Research and Knowledge (funded by Hopelab) (2025) · Get involved SPARK survey for researchers working on youth and AI (open on the centre's site); Research staff and postdoc posts (none open for 2026-27, per the team page); Free Handbook of Adolescent Digital Media Use and Mental Health (Cambridge University Press)

Note The name is inconsistent: a March 2025 UNC article called it the 'Winston Center for Technology and the Developing Mind' and said it had moved to the Office of the Vice Chancellor for Research, while the centre's own 2025-26 pages still use 'Winston Center on Technology and Brain Development'. Most of its output is still on smartphones and social media; AI-specific work began only in 2025-26. Its news feed has not been updated since January 2025. Co-director Prinstein also holds a senior APA role.

Young Futures Adjacent

Funder · Berkeley, CA, USA · founded 2024

A US nonprofit funder, launched in 2024 and based in Berkeley, California, that funds and scales nonprofits helping young people, families and educators cope with growing up around phones and AI. Its 'Oops!...AI Did It Again' challenge gave $1.39M to 16 organisations in March 2026, for work on teens' agency with AI, including companions and mental-health tools. In September 2026 it launched Groundwork, a $15M three-year initiative across the US and UK (including £4M for the UK with Bukhman Philanthropies) on young people's judgement and independent thinking alongside AI. It also runs a five-month accelerator (YF Academy) for grantee leaders and an in-house storytelling studio.

It is one of the few funders paying for young people's capacity to think, relate and decide for themselves alongside AI, rather than only for safety guardrails. It requires funded work to be co-designed with young people, which gives the field a lived-experience view.

Works on Human minds · Key work Oops!...AI Did It Again challenge: $1.39M to 16 nonprofits (2026); Groundwork: $15M, three-year US and UK initiative on youth and AI (UK strand £4M with Bukhman Philanthropies) (2026); Unwritten Challenge: $1M+ for learning and critical thinking in an AI-shaped world (2026) · Get involved Unwritten Challenge: grants of $50k-100k to US 501(c)(3)s and schools working with ages 10-19; applications open to 16 Oct 2026; solutions must be co-led or co-designed by young people; Groundwork UK funding challenge for UK charities, opening spring 2027 (two-year grants plus YF Academy membership); YF Academy: five-month accelerator for grantee leaders (next cohort from January 2027)

Note It grants mainly in the US; UK grants begin in 2027. Its funders include technology companies (Pinterest, Niantic Spatial, Mozilla), unlike corporate-free advocates such as Fairplay. Its IRS ruling is dated October 2025, which suggests it was fiscally sponsored before then. It frames AI as a developmental question for young people, with no catastrophic-risk framing.

Potential ring 6

Association for the Advancement of Affective Computing (AAAC) Potential

Membership body · Distributed

An international professional association for researchers in affective computing, emotion research and human-machine interaction, formerly the HUMAINE Association. It runs the bidding for, and oversees, the annual International Conference on Affective Computing and Intelligent Interaction (ACII). ACII 2025 was held in Canberra on the theme 'Socially Responsible Affective Computing', and ACII 2026 in Puebla, Mexico, on 8-10 September. The association also runs a monthly online seminar series, awards, and special and local interest groups, one of them on ethics; its members publish mainly in IEEE Transactions on Affective Computing.

It is the professional home of the people who build systems that recognise, simulate and respond to emotion. That is the technical basis of emulated empathy, emotional manipulation and companion design. Its computational models of emotion could also inform research on emotion-like representations inside models. Safety research on sycophancy and manipulation rarely draws on this community.

Works on Human minds, Agency · Key work ACII 2026, Puebla, Mexico (8-10 September) (2026); ACII 2025, Canberra: 'Socially Responsible Affective Computing' (2025); AAAC Online Seminar Series 2025-26 (2026) · Get involved Individual membership and the AAAC announcements mailing list (aaac.world); ACII, held annually (2026: Puebla, 8-10 September); Monthly online seminar series, open to attend, with links posted on the mailing list

Note Affective computing is itself an AI subfield, and its products are contested: the EU AI Act prohibits emotion recognition in workplaces and schools. The association does some ethics work (an ethics SIG; ACII 2021 and 2025 had ethics themes), but it is small, and it has no AI-safety engagement. The roster's claim that it has no visible ethics programme is therefore not quite right. Founding year and finances were not found.

Bramley Computational Cognitive Science Lab (University of Edinburgh) Potential

Academic · Edinburgh, UK

Neil Bramley's group in Edinburgh's School of Philosophy, Psychology and Language Sciences studies how people learn causal structure, generalise, generate hypotheses and learn from others. It combines behavioural experiments with adults and children with computational models. Its link to AI safety is one event: with UK AISI's Konstantinos Voudouris and Christopher Summerfield, Harvard's Xavier Roberts-Gaal and NYU's Ilia Sucholutsky, Bramley co-organised the half-day workshop 'The Cognitive Science of AI Alignment' at CogSci 2026 (Rio de Janeiro, 22-25 July 2026). The workshop was built around four questions: what the alignment target is, how weaker agents can supervise stronger ones, how interacting with AI changes human values, and what human feedback actually measures.

The lab's computational accounts of how people learn structure and norms from sparse data, and of the biases in their judgements, bear directly on what an alignment target is and how reliable human feedback is. The CogSci 2026 workshop, run with UK AISI, is an early attempt to recruit cognitive scientists into alignment work.

Works on Values, Assurance · Key work The Cognitive Science of AI Alignment (CogSci 2026 workshop; Voudouris, Roberts-Gaal, Bramley, Sucholutsky, Summerfield) (2026); Resource bottlenecks determine when human and machine teams decide to specialise (2025); Partner Modelling Emerges in Recurrent Agents (But Only When It Matters) (2025) · Get involved Door to open: approach Neil Bramley about cognitive-science collaborations on value learning, generalisation or biases in human feedback; PhD study in computational cognitive science at Edinburgh

Note The roster calls 'The cognitive science of AI alignment' a paper, but it is a workshop proposal published in the CogSci proceedings. UK AISI staff led it (Voudouris is first author), and Bramley was one of five organisers and gave the talk 'Alignment as plumbing, partnering, or parenting'. The lab has no other AI-safety output, though some of its papers cover human-machine teaming and artificial agents. I lowered the ring from bridge to potential for this reason.

Center for Practical Wisdom, University of Chicago Potential

Academic · Chicago, USA · founded 2016 · also draws on Philosophy

The Center for Practical Wisdom is a research centre in the University of Chicago's Division of Social Sciences, founded and directed by the cognitive psychologist Howard Nusbaum. It studies how wisdom develops and when people decide wisely. Its core projects cover epistemic humility, perspective-taking, narrative, nature exposure and stress resilience, and it curates wisdom measures, an interview series with wisdom researchers and a news feed. It has no AI programme; its site features one external paper on 'artificial wisdom' (Jeste et al., 2020).

Validated measures of wise reasoning and epistemic humility are what anyone building 'wisdom' evaluations of AI advice or decision support would need, and few AI-safety groups have that psychometric grounding. It is a door to open, not an existing contributor.

Works on Values, Epistemics · Key work Defining Wisdom Project (2007); Wisdom Research Project (2012-2015) (2012); Wisdom Scales & Measures (curated measurement resource) · Get involved No AI programme: a door to open for researchers who want wisdom psychometrics (e.g. epistemic humility measures) applied to AI evaluation; contact via the centre's site

Note Recent site activity is mostly curation, and the core projects it lists carry dates up to 2015, so its current research output is unclear. The artificial-wisdom paper it features is by UC San Diego authors, not by the centre. The centre was launched in 2016, building on the Defining Wisdom (2007-2011) and Wisdom Research (2012-2015) projects.

Climate Psychology Alliance (CPA) Potential

Membership body · UK · founded 2009-12

A UK membership community of therapists, researchers, practitioners and activists working on the emotional and psychological side of the climate and ecological crisis. It formed in 2009-12 and is registered as a society (Climate Psychology Alliance Limited). It runs online Climate Café Listening Circles and parents' circles, trains people to facilitate them, offers a course for therapeutic practitioners and keeps a directory of free therapeutic support for eco-distress. It publishes the journal Explorations in Climate Psychology, whose latest issue includes 'AI and power' among its topics.

It has more than a decade of practice in helping groups hold distress about an existential threat, using depth-psychology and psychosocial methods. Its climate cafés and facilitator training could be adapted for AI-risk distress among researchers, advocates and the public.

Works on People, Human minds · Key work Climate Café Listening Circles (online, several a month); Hosting and Facilitating a Climate Café Listening Circle (training, Oct-Nov 2026) (2026); Explorations in Climate Psychology, issue 8: 'Heavy Weather: exploring reactionary states of mind' (includes AI and power) · Get involved Online Climate Café Listening Circles and parents' circles (bookable on Eventbrite, several a month in autumn 2026); Training: Hosting and Facilitating a Climate Café Listening Circle (Oct-Nov 2026); Through the Door course for therapeutic practitioners (24 Oct 2026); Membership (members' hub on Mighty Networks); volunteering and donations

Note Its website was being rebuilt in 2026 and many inner pages returned errors, so leadership and governance details could not be checked. Its AI engagement is one journal theme. A separate US body, Climate Psychology Alliance North America, also exists.

Greater Good Science Center (GGSC) Potential

Academic · Berkeley, USA · founded 2001

A centre at the University of California, Berkeley, founded in 2001, that studies and popularises the science of wellbeing, compassion, gratitude and prosocial behaviour. It publishes Greater Good magazine, co-produces The Science of Happiness podcast with PRX, runs free online courses (The Science of Happiness has over 600,000 registrants) and programmes for educators, parents, workplaces and bridging differences. In 2026 the magazine ran several pieces on AI, on chatbots and intimacy, AI matchmaking and the purpose of education in an AI age.

It holds the prosociality and relationship science that work on companion-AI harms and sycophancy draws on, and it reaches teachers, parents and managers at scale. It has no AI research programme, so this science has not yet been pointed at AI systems.
