It also holds a $100,000 FLI grant for a Reform Jewish initiative to prepare rabbis to understand AI and build interfaith partnerships for a human-centred future.

It brings rabbinic tradition (questioning, ethics of labour and rest, accounts of agency and repentance) into practical AI formation for congregations and clergy. It has a tested regranting model that reaches grassroots religious communities at low cost.

World Council of Churches (WCC) Bridge

Membership body · Geneva, Switzerland · founded 1948

The global ecumenical fellowship of about 350 member churches (Orthodox, Anglican, Protestant and some Pentecostal), founded in 1948 and based in Geneva. Its AI work is new. A Future of Life Institute grant of $100,000 funds a project, led by Sara Speicher, to establish AI red lines across its network of churches in more than 120 countries and to guide global AI governance toward reducing the risks of advanced AI and sharing its benefits. In September 2026 WCC staff met to form an AI task force and to plan a multidisciplinary AI symposium for 15-19 February 2027.

It could become the widest channel outside Catholicism for carrying AI-safety norms such as red lines into the churches and into the UN-level advocacy where the WCC already works. Its membership is concentrated in the Global South.

Abu Dhabi Forum for Peace (Forum for Promoting Peace in Muslim Societies) Adjacent

Nonprofit · Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates · founded 2014 · also draws on Peace

An Abu Dhabi forum of Muslim scholars, presided over by the Mauritanian jurist Shaykh Abdallah bin Bayyah, that promotes peace and interfaith cooperation from Islamic jurisprudence. On AI it brought Muslim leadership into the Vatican-led Rome Call for AI Ethics (January 2023), convened the faith and civil-society meeting a week before the 2023 Bletchley AI Safety Summit that set up the AI Faith & Civil Society Commission, and co-organised the multi-faith 'AI Ethics for Peace' signing in Hiroshima (July 2024).

It is the main Islamic convener in the interreligious AI-ethics process and has a link to the AI-safety summit track. It will co-organise Religions for Peace's December 2027 World Assembly, which lists AI and autonomous weapons as a central objective.

Founding year (2014) is from general knowledge, not confirmed on its site.

AI Christian Benchmark (The Gospel Coalition, Keller Center for Cultural Apologetics) AdjacentNew

Programme · USA · founded 2025

An annual benchmark run by the Keller Center for Cultural Apologetics, the research arm of the evangelical website The Gospel Coalition, led by Michael Graham. The first edition (September 2025) put seven common questions about Christian belief to seven AI platforms. The 2026 edition, with responses collected in June 2026, scored 46 model configurations on theology, ethics (100 scenarios built on the Ten Commandments), Bible knowledge and 'attachment', meaning whether a model fosters unhealthy emotional bonds, for example by offering to pray for users. Scores combine grading by a panel of evangelical scholars with AI grading.

It is a working example of a faith community writing its own evaluation of model behaviour. It shows how much model defaults differ on worldview questions, how much answers shift when religious context is added, and how widespread attachment-forming behaviour is. Its proposal of 'principled pluralism' (answering from within the tradition asked about, rather than giving a multi-faith summary) is a concrete, contestable input to debates on how model specifications should handle pluralism.

Works on Values, Assurance, Human minds · Key work AI Christian Benchmark, first edition (seven questions, seven platforms) (2025); AI Christian Benchmark 2026: theology, ethics, attachment and Bible knowledge scores (2026); Presentation at the G20 Interfaith Forum webinar 'AI and Benchmarks' (2026) · Get involved The 2026 report invites AI developers to contact the team about improving how models handle Christian theology and ethics

Note It grades answers against one confessional standard. Responses aligned with Reformed evangelical teaching score highest (prompts citing The Gospel Coalition's foundation documents got the top scores), including on contested ethics such as abortion and sexuality, so it measures fit with that tradition rather than neutral accuracy. Grading is partly done by AI (Gemini 3.1 Pro), and the attachment tests are described as exploratory. The Gospel Coalition's separate AI book ('The AI Apocalypse: A Survival Guide for Humanity') and podcast (Silicon Spiritualities) are not part of the benchmark.

America Media (America: The Jesuit Review) Adjacent

Media · New York, USA · founded 1909 · also draws on Arts, futures

The media ministry of the US Jesuits, publishing America magazine since 1909 from New York, along with a website, newsletters and podcasts. In 2026 it covered AI steadily from the standpoint of Catholic social teaching. Examples are editor Sam Sawyer SJ's column arguing that the alignment problem is a moral question rather than a technical one, its Vatican correspondent's reporting on Pope Leo's remarks about AI catastrophe, and a subscriber webinar on the AI encyclical Magnifica Humanitas.

It is one of the main English-language channels through which Pope Leo's teaching on AI, and debates about AI risk and alignment, reach a large Catholic readership. It reframes alignment as a question of morality and justice, which is a perspective technical AI safety seldom hears from.

Works on Meaning, Epistemics · Key work How to worry about A.I. without despairing (Sam Sawyer SJ) (2026); Pope Leo on AI risk at the in-flight press conference from France (Colleen Dulle) (2026); Live Zoom panel on Magnifica Humanitas (2026) · Get involved Subscriber webinars, such as the 19 August 2026 Zoom panel on Magnifica Humanitas

The draft suggested it might be bridge; I kept it adjacent because its AI coverage argues against the catastrophic-risk frame rather than adopting it. The Washington Post has described it as liberal-leaning. Events are for subscribers only. Staff size is estimated.

Center for Buddhist AI Ethics, CamTech University Adjacent

Academic · Phnom Penh, Cambodia · founded 2023 · also draws on Philosophy

A centre at the Cambodia University of Technology and Science (CamTech) in Phnom Penh, launched in June 2023 and directed by Prof. Chhem Kieth Rethy. Its stated vision is AI development guided by Buddhist ethics for human well-being, through research, 'mindful education', policy advocacy and international engagement. It has run a Buddhist AI Ethics seminar series (November 2023, co-organised with Kol Tor Teung Pagoda; August 2024; October 2024, 'Buddhism and AI: Reality, Ethics, and Governance'). In August 2025 it published the edited volume 'Buddhist Mind for AI Machines', with essays on Buddhist ontology, epistemology (catuskoti, sunyata) and ethics (compassionate AI, cetana) applied to AI design.

It is one of the few institutional nodes working on Buddhist ethics and AI from a Theravada-majority, Southeast Asian country, and its director has a seat in Cambodian government. That gives a route for Buddhist ethical concepts into regional AI discussion, a perspective almost absent from the mainstream field.

The roster's claim of four seminar iterations up to September 2025 could not be confirmed: three numbered Buddhist AI Ethics seminars appear, plus a June 2023 launch seminar that was part of CamTech's general AI Forum series. Its stated concerns are bias, privacy and jobs rather than catastrophic risk. The director is a serving Senior Minister and chairs Cambodia's Economic, Social and Cultural Council. Center for Theology and the Natural Sciences (CTNS) Adjacent

Academic · Berkeley, United States · founded 1981 · also draws on Philosophy, Living systems

CTNS is a centre at the Graduate Theological Union in Berkeley, founded in 1981 by Robert John Russell, that promotes dialogue between Christian theology and the natural sciences. It does this through research, seminary and doctoral teaching, the journal Theology and Science, and public forums. Its AI work was the Templeton-funded project 'Virtuous AI? Cultural Evolution, Artificial Intelligence, and Virtue' (2022–2025). The project held three online conferences in 2023, centred on Berkeley, Seoul and Rome, on whether AI will shape human virtue, whether it can help people acquire virtue, and whether it can itself be virtuous.

Its question of whether AI can have or cultivate virtue bears directly on character-based alignment targets. The project also built an intercultural, multi-religious network of AI scientists and humanities scholars across the US, Korea and Europe, a network that AI-safety work rarely reaches.

Works on Values, Meaning · Key work Virtuous AI? Townes Graduate Student Fellowship (GTU doctoral students); CTNS membership, which includes the journal Theology and Science

Central Conference of American Rabbis (CCAR) Adjacent

Membership body · New York, USA · founded 1889

The professional association of Reform rabbis, founded in 1889 by Isaac Mayer Wise, with more than 2,200 members. It issues responsa (formal rulings in Jewish law), publishes through CCAR Press and the CCAR Journal, and runs continuing education and an ethics code for its members. Its AI work so far: Responsum 5784.2 on AI and authorship, a Fall 2025 journal issue 'AI and the Rabbinate', a December 2025 book, and an event series with Sinai and Synapses on AI, personhood and the soul.

It issues working norms for AI use to a large clergy body. The responsum says that presenting AI-generated work as one's own is deception and requires disclosure, an example of a profession setting honesty norms for AI use. It is also the main channel through which FLI-funded Sinai and Synapses educates Reform rabbis about AI.

DELTA (Notre Dame Institute for Ethics and the Common Good) Adjacent

Programme · Notre Dame, United States · founded 2024 · also draws on Philosophy

DELTA is a University of Notre Dame initiative, run by the Institute for Ethics and the Common Good, that offers a Christian virtue-ethics framework for 'human formation' in the age of AI, built around Dignity, Embodiment, Love, Transcendence and Agency. It produces resources for faith leaders, teachers, students, journalists and tech workers. It holds an annual DELTA Summit on AI, Faith and Human Flourishing (the second ran 21–23 September 2026) and funds faculty fellowships and Faith and AI rapid-response grants of $100,000 each.

It is the best-funded effort to apply the Catholic intellectual tradition and virtue ethics to how people, rather than models, are formed by AI. It reaches into Catholic schools, parishes and the Bay Area tech industry, communities that mainstream AI safety has almost no channel into.

Note The framework explicitly sets itself apart from safety and privacy concerns: there is no x-risk or alignment framing, and it forms people rather than specifying model behaviour. Ethics & Religious Liberty Commission of the Southern Baptist Convention (ERLC) Adjacent

Nonprofit · Nashville, USA · founded 1947

The public-policy and ethics agency of the Southern Baptist Convention, the largest US Protestant denomination. Founded in 1947 as the Social Service Commission, it is based in Nashville with an office in Washington, DC. In 2019 it led 'Artificial Intelligence: An Evangelical Statement of Principles', an affirm-and-deny statement in 12 articles covering human dignity, work, data, bias, war and public policy; the SBC's 2023 resolution on AI cites it.

It wrote the reference evangelical statement on AI and lobbies in Washington for a large, politically active constituency, so it shapes how many US evangelicals and their legislators approach AI ethics and policy.

Works on Meaning · Key work Artificial Intelligence: An Evangelical Statement of Principles (2019); The Work of Our Hands: Christian Ministry in the Age of Artificial Intelligence (practical guide for churches, 12 scenarios) (2025)

Note The ERLC site blocks automated access, so the statement could not be re-read in this pass. Its 2024-26 AI work includes a September 2025 church guide, 'The Work of Our Hands', and an AI podcast series, known from Baptist Press coverage. Leadership changed in 2025-26 (Leatherwood stepped down on 31 July 2025, followed by acting and interim presidents, then Lenow), and SBC messengers have repeatedly debated abolishing the agency. Whether AI remains a priority under the new president is unknown. Thacker also co-wrote Lausanne's AI report chapter.

G20 Interfaith Forum (IF20) Adjacent

Network · Washington, DC, United States · founded 2014 · also draws on Law, society

A platform, run by the G20 Interfaith Forum Association from Washington DC, that has met each year since 2014 alongside the G20 host country. It brings faith leaders, scholars and policymakers together to make policy recommendations to the G20. In 2026 its AI and Faith working group ran an eight-part webinar series from June to August (faith, translation, benchmarks, the planet, peace, human flourishing, education, the future). In September it published the policy paper 'AI Innovation and Human Dignity' for the US G20 presidency.

It is a standing channel from the world's faith communities into G20 policy, and in 2026 it took up AI. Its policy paper, co-written with people from IEEE and the Future of Life Institute, already asks for red lines: a ban on autonomous weapons and no legal personhood for AI.

Works on Meaning, Justice · Key work AI Innovation and Human Dignity (IF20 policy paper for the US G20 presidency) (2026); AI and Faith webinar series (8 sessions) (2026); 2026 IF20 Summit, Salt Lake City (2026) · Get involved 2026 IF20 Summit, Salt Lake City, 15-17 Oct 2026 (express interest through the IF20 Secretariat); AI and Faith webinar series (June to August 2026; online); Newsletter

Note Its AI work began in 2026, so the track record is short. The site gives little detail on governance, staff or funding. The AI policy paper is one of four IF20 discussion papers, and its recommendations are broad.

Holy See: Rome Call for AI Ethics (RenAIssance Foundation), Antiqua et Nova and Magnifica Humanitas Adjacent

Membership body · Vatican City, Vatican City State · founded 2020 · also draws on Philosophy, Peace

This entry covers the AI work of the Catholic Church's central government. The Rome Call for AI Ethics (February 2020) was first signed by the Pontifical Academy for Life, Microsoft, IBM, FAO and Italy's innovation ministry. Since 2021 the Vatican's RenAIssance Foundation has stewarded it, adding signatories such as Qualcomm (2025) and Salesforce (2025) and leaders of 11 religions at Hiroshima (2024). The Church's AI teaching is the doctrinal note Antiqua et Nova (January 2025) and Pope Leo XIV's first encyclical, Magnifica Humanitas (May 2026), on safeguarding the human person in the time of AI. In March 2026 the foundation signed an agreement with the UN University for Peace, and the two now run AI4Peace together.

It speaks to about 1.4 billion Catholics and has an AI-ethics commitment signed by large tech firms and by leaders of many religions. Magnifica Humanitas calls for an international framework to curb the technological arms race and for prudence, at times a slower pace. It rejects handing lethal decisions to AI and warns against power concentrating in a few firms. That is a very large constituency for slowing down, though it does not engage with AGI or loss of control.

Works on Meaning, Security, Power · Key work Rome Call for AI Ethics (2020); AI Ethics for Peace: world religions sign the Rome Call in Hiroshima (2024); Antiqua et Nova: note on AI and human intelligence (2025) · Get involved AI4Peace, a biennial symposium of the Pontifical Academy for Life, the UN University for Peace and the Pontifical Lateran University (first edition held 20-22 Sep 2026 in Rome); Organisations can sign or endorse the Rome Call through romecall.org

Note This merged entry covers distinct bodies: the RenAIssance Foundation, the Pontifical Academy for Life and papal teaching documents. The founding year given is the Rome Call's (2020); the foundation was set up in April 2021. It frames AI in terms of human dignity, present harms and peace, not catastrophic risk. An EA Forum review notes that the encyclical does not discuss AGI or superintelligence and plays down capability risks. I found no public mechanism for checking whether Rome Call signatories comply.

Infinity Foundation Adjacent

Nonprofit · Princeton, USA · founded 1994 · also draws on Economics

A Princeton-based nonprofit founded in 1994 by Indian-American author Rajiv Malhotra, with an Indian arm, Infinity Foundation India. It applies what it calls a 'Dharma lens' to civilisational studies and argues against Western universalism through books, videos, grants and events. On AI, Malhotra wrote 'Artificial Intelligence and the Future of Power: 5 Battlegrounds' (Rupa, 2020). He also edited 'The Power of Future Machines', which includes the essay 'Artificial Intelligence as an Enabler of Western Universalism'. Its video output continues to cover AI, e.g. 'Ask Rajiv: AI, Youth Liability & Internal Colonization' (July 2026).

It represents an influential Hindu-nationalist Indian view of AI as a contest over power, sovereignty and cultural identity, which matters for understanding how AI governance is argued in India. It is a voice to understand rather than an obvious partner.

Works on Power, Justice, Meaning · Key work Artificial Intelligence and the Future of Power: 5 Battlegrounds (Rupa Publications) (2020); The Power of Future Machines (edited volume, incl. 'Artificial Intelligence as an Enabler of Western Universalism'); Ask Rajiv: AI, Youth Liability & Internal Colonization (video) (2026) · Get involved Newsletter and YouTube channel linked from infinityfoundation.com

Note Wikipedia, citing scholars, describes Malhotra as a public proponent of Hindutva. His books are polemical (e.g. 'Breaking India', 'Academic Hinduphobia'), and in 2015 scholars alleged plagiarism in 'Indra's Net'. Its AI critique is framed as civilisational competition. Its AI engagement is mainly books (2020 and early 2020s) plus occasional videos. The taxonomy has no Hindu or Dharmic sub-tradition.

Interfaith Center on Corporate Responsibility (ICCR), with the Investor Alliance for Human Rights Adjacent

Network · New York, USA · founded 1971 · also draws on Law, society, Economics

A New York coalition of faith-based and values-driven institutional investors (religious orders, denominational pension funds, foundations, asset managers) that files shareholder proposals and engages companies on social and human-rights issues. Its Digital Rights and AI Accountability work, run with its Investor Alliance for Human Rights, presses technology companies to adopt human-rights due diligence and board oversight of AI, publishes investor briefings, and comments on AI policy to the US government, the EU and the UN Human Rights Council.

It uses a lever the AI-safety field has barely touched: shareholder resolutions and investor engagement at Alphabet, Meta, Amazon and Microsoft asking for board-level AI oversight and human-rights due diligence. Its June 2026 briefing on AI in military targeting shows investor channels can also reach defence AI.

Works on Justice, Security · Key work Risks of Artificial Intelligence (AI) on Human Rights (investor briefing) (2025); AI in the Kill Chain: The Risk of AI-Enabled Warfare and What Investors Need to Know (2026); Submission on the US AI Action Plan; HRC submission on AI and the UN Guiding Principles (2025) · Get involved Institutional investors (faith-based and values-driven) can join ICCR or the Investor Alliance for Human Rights; membership is institutional, not individual; Staff roles: check iccr.org; Each season's proxy memos list AI-related shareholder votes that aligned investors can support

Note AI is one strand of a broad human-rights and ESG agenda, framed around present harms rather than catastrophic risk. The SEC's 2026 proposal to rescind Rule 14a-8 (the shareholder-proposal rule) could sharply weaken its main tool. Membership numbers (commonly given as 300+) and budget were not confirmed on its own pages.

International Association of Jesuit Universities (IAJU): Artificial Intelligence Task Force Adjacent

Programme · Rome, Italy · founded 2018

IAJU is the Rome-based coordinating body for Jesuit higher education, founded in 2018 and made up of six regional associations. AI is one of its strategic priorities. A seven-member task force, chaired by Renato Cerqueira from Brazil, runs it. The task force keeps a curated knowledge hub of cases and guidelines, holds a virtual community of practice for faculty, staff and students, and organises pilot projects and working groups on ethical AI, academic integrity, accessibility, mental health and teaching. It explicitly links AI adoption to Ignatian discernment, cura personalis and the magis.

It is a global channel into Jesuit universities that is building a shared practice for AI grounded in Ignatian discernment, a codified spiritual method for making choices. That makes it an example of a religious tradition's practice applied to institutional technology decisions, and a possible route for bringing questions about AI going well into university formation.

Works on Meaning, Human minds · Key work AI Task Force: knowledge hub, community of practice and working groups (2026); The Impact of AI on the Educational Transformation of Universities (UNIJES faculty survey, published by IAJU) (2026); The AI Frontier and the Jesuit Universities (report on the GRAJU inaugural symposium, Manila) (2026) · Get involved Virtual community of practice for faculty, staff and students at Jesuit institutions

Note The task force is mostly about adopting AI in teaching, research and administration, which sits at the edge of scope. Its frame is education and human dignity, not catastrophic risk. The March 2026 Manila symposium was run by the Global Research Alliance of Jesuit Universities (GRAJU, founded 2025), not by the task force, and the July 2026 Florence conference on AI and Jesuit formation was run by the Society of Jesus. The draft attributed both to the task force. The year the task force was set up and its budget are not published. The chair's name is spelled 'Cerqueria' on the IAJU site.

International Islamic Fiqh Academy (IIFA) Adjacent

Public body · Jeddah, Saudi Arabia · founded 1981

The juristic body of the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation (OIC), established in 1981 and based in Jeddah, whose members are jurists and scholars from across the Muslim world. At its 26th session (Doha, May 2025) it adopted Resolution No. 258, 'Artificial Intelligence: Its Rulings, Guidelines and Ethics', which holds that developing and using AI is permissible by default subject to six conditions (lawful purposes, benefit without harm, no insult to religions, protection of data and rights, no threat to security, honesty and transparency), and recommends a study of whether AI should have legal personality.

It sets the reference ruling on AI for mainstream Islamic jurisprudence across OIC states, reasoning from the purposes of the law about benefit, harm and accountability. Its call to study AI legal personality is a rare opening from a religious legal body onto questions of AI moral and legal status.

Works on Meaning · Key work Resolution No. 258: Artificial Intelligence: Its Rulings, Guidelines and Ethics (2025); Scientific session 'Artificial Intelligence: Rulings, Controls and Ethics' at the 26th session (Doha) (2025); Secretary-General chairs 'Coexistence in the Age of AI' at the Fez conference on the future of human civilisation and AI (2026)

Note Its rulings are normative religious guidance, not binding law. Its AI output so far is one resolution plus speeches; no sign was found by October 2026 of the recommended study on AI legal personality or the specialised symposia. The resolution's English page is dated November 2025, though the session sat in May 2025.

Islamic World Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (ICESCO) Adjacent

Public body · Rabat, Morocco · founded 1979 · also draws on Law, society

The OIC's specialised agency for education, science and culture, based in Rabat, with 53 member states. With Saudi Arabia's data and AI authority (SDAIA) it launched the Riyadh Charter on AI Ethics in the Islamic World at the Global AI Summit in September 2024; member states approved it in March 2025. The Charter sets seven principles (including reliability and safety, transparency, accountability and 'humanity') grounded in Islamic-world values, and in December 2025 ICESCO and SDAIA signed an agreement to implement it as a common AI-governance framework for member states. It also runs a Center of Foresight and Artificial Intelligence and many AI education, literacy and Arabic-language activities.

It is the intergovernmental channel for AI norms grounded in Islamic values, built on the argument that international frameworks failed to reflect those values. It is the obvious counterpart for AI-governance dialogue that wants Muslim-majority states' buy-in beyond the UN and OECD tracks.

Works on Justice, Meaning · Key work Riyadh Charter on AI Ethics in the Islamic World (presented to the IIFA's 26th session, May 2025) (2024); ICESCO-SDAIA agreement to activate the Riyadh Charter (2025); Director-General calls for stronger cooperation on AI governance, arguing legislation alone is not enough (international forum, Riyadh) (2026) · Get involved AI masterclasses, trainings and conferences, mostly aimed at member-state educators, media and officials; 'Artificial Intelligence for All' initiative (launched May 2026)

Note Most of its AI activity is education, literacy and Arabic-language work rather than safety; the Charter is principles-level and its implementation with SDAIA only began in 2025-26. Saudi state involvement (SDAIA) shapes the Charter. Outputs of its Center of Foresight and AI were not found. The Charter's 2024 announcement date comes from discovery notes; its publication page did not load in this check.

Kalam Research & Media (KRM) Adjacent

Nonprofit · Dubai, United Arab Emirates · founded 2009 · also draws on Philosophy

A Muslim theological think tank founded in Dubai in 2009 and chaired by the Libyan theologian Aref Ali Nayed, with offices in Abu Dhabi, Amman, Benghazi, Tripoli, Tunis, Cairo, Toronto and Malaysia. Its AI & Technology programme pairs its theologians and philosophers with AI researchers: it works on 'Artificial Understanding' (what it would mean for a machine to understand), applies Nayed's 'operational hermeneutics' to AI artefacts, and in 2025-26 held workshops and lectures with the University of Guelph's Centre for Advancing Responsible AI (CARE-AI).

It asks conceptual questions most AI-ethics work skips, such as what machine understanding would be, from an Islamic hermeneutic tradition, and argues that responsible AI needs 'institutional wisdom' rather than compliance alone. It is one of few Islamic institutions doing conceptual rather than permissibility work on AI.

Works on Meaning, Agency · Key work KRM to develop new research on Artificial Understanding (AU) (2023); Workshop with the University of Guelph: Humanities, Artificial Intelligence, and the Future of Responsibility (2026); Dr Nayed at the University of Guelph: Operational Hermeneutics and AI Ethics (2026)

Note Its dated AI outputs are mostly lectures, workshops and partnership announcements; substantive publications on Artificial Understanding were not found, and no AI items after February 2026 appeared on its site. Its chairman is also a Libyan diplomatic and political figure, which partners may weigh.

Kumagai Lab, Institute for the Future of Human Society, Kyoto University (BuddhaBot and Buddharoid) Adjacent

Academic · Kyoto, Japan · founded 2021

Professor Seiji Kumagai's group at Kyoto University's Institute for the Future of Human Society (IFOHS) builds AI from religious traditions, working with the Kyoto start-ups Teraverse and XNOVA. It released BuddhaBot, a Buddhist dialogue AI grounded in scripture, in 2021, and later added AR apps, a Protestant 'Catechism Bot' (covered by the media in December 2025) and, in February 2026, Buddharoid. Buddharoid is a Unitree G1 humanoid running BuddhaBot, unveiled at Shoren-in temple, Kyoto. The team says it holds ongoing ELSI discussions on the benefits and risks of giving Buddhist AI a body, and plans further 'Traditional Knowledge Tech' bots representing philosophers and saints.

It is a long-running case of scholars of a living religious tradition building AI with values built in: scripture-grounded dialogue models and an embodied 'robot monk'. Along the way they have to decide what an AI may say and do in religious roles. That makes it a concrete test bed for tradition-specific alignment targets and their ethical governance, and a contrast to positions such as Yaqeen's that AI should not issue religious rulings.

Works on Meaning, Values · Key work BuddhaBot, a Buddhist dialogue AI (2021); Protestant Catechism Bot (2025); Buddharoid: Buddhist AI humanoid robot unveiled at Shoren-in temple (2026)

Note The work is done with commercial partners, and much of its public record is press coverage. The ELSI discussions are mentioned but I found no published output from them. Whether AI should give religious guidance is contested. The 2021 founding year is that of BuddhaBot's release, not of the institute. Its funding is not disclosed.

Lausanne Movement Adjacent

Network · Distributed · founded 1974

A global network of evangelical leaders, begun in 1974 when Billy Graham convened the International Congress on World Evangelization in Lausanne. It works through 28 issue networks and 12 regional networks and publishes reports, the Lausanne Global Analysis and podcasts. Its AI content includes a State of the Great Commission report chapter on AI, an October/November 2025 Global Analysis issue on AI (including Quintin McGrath's 'AI Ethical Framework') and podcast episodes, mostly about using AI for ministry, evangelism and Bible translation.

It reaches evangelical leaders worldwide, and its material shows how a very large religious constituency currently thinks about AI: mainly as a tool for mission. Its report chapter says outright that AI is not an existential threat. In 2026 FLI gave it $50,000 to engage evangelical leaders in critical discussion of AI development, so this framing may shift.

Works on Meaning · Key work AI Ethical Framework (Quintin McGrath, Lausanne Global Analysis) (2025); State of the Great Commission report: Artificial Intelligence (Angela Kim, Sharoon Sarfraz, Jason Thacker, Dan Whitenack) (2024); FLI-funded project engaging evangelical leadership on AI development (2026) · Get involved Issue networks (28) and regional networks (12) for Christian leaders.

Note Most of its AI content is about adopting AI for evangelism and discipleship, not about AI risk; the report chapter explicitly says AI does not pose an existential threat. The FLI-funded project could move it towards bridge if it produces risk-framed work. The site names no headquarters.

Oxford Collaboration on Theology and Artificial Intelligence (OCTAI), Ian Ramsey Centre Adjacent

Programme · Oxford, UK · also draws on Philosophy

A collaborative research project hosted by the Ian Ramsey Centre for Science and Religion in Oxford's Faculty of Theology and Religion. It works on the ethical and vocational realities of AI work. In 2025 it held four workshops in which AI practitioners described their daily work and theologians responded, deliberately drawing many contributors from the majority world. Out of these came the Oxford Oath for AI Practitioners and an accompanying open letter, a professional commitment centred on conscience, truth and honesty, with religious and secular forms of profession.

It treats the consciences of people who build AI as a place to intervene. The oath commits signatories to 'giving voice to conscience' when it conflicts with the demands of their profession, modelled on the physicians' covenant. That links to professional norms, refusal and whistleblowing inside labs, which mainstream AI safety seldom approaches through vocation and moral formation.

Works on People, Meaning · Key work Oxford Oath for AI Practitioners and Open Letter (public draft, revised to June 2026) (2026); OCTAI workshop series: Listening to Practitioners (Feb, Mar 2025), Initial theological proposals (May 2025), Oxford Oath (Sep 2025) (2025); Research pathways (workshop outputs; video by Lyndon Drake) (2025) · Get involved Sign the Open Letter at oxford-oath.ai; Propose changes to the Oath text on GitHub (github.com/lyndondrake/oxford-oath)

Note The network is built by invitation, and its workshops were not public. The oath is still a draft, and formal profession of it is not yet possible. Most members are Christian theologians, although the letter and oath are written to be usable by people of any religious or secular view. I couldn't confirm when the project started; its first workshop was in February 2025.

Research Center for Islamic Legislation and Ethics (CILE) Adjacent

Academic · Doha, Qatar · founded 2012 · also draws on Philosophy

A research centre for Islamic applied ethics in Hamad Bin Khalifa University's College of Islamic Studies in Doha, founded in 2012 and headed by Mohammed Ghaly. It runs research seminars and winter schools, supports HBKU's MA in Applied Islamic Ethics, and hosted the 2024 World Congress of Bioethics. Its AI work includes a 2024 winter school on AI and religion with Cambridge's Leverhulme Centre for the Future of Intelligence, the September 2025 conference 'AI Ethics: The Convergence of Technology and Diverse Moral Traditions', a November 2025 lecture on AI weapons and Islamic war ethics, and a funded project building IslamGPT, a language model for Arabic Islamic sources.

It is the strongest institutional base found for Islamic ethics of AI, with scholars already working on human uniqueness, moral accountability (taklif) and the values built into AI instructions. It could supply maqasid-based frameworks for alignment targets and AI red lines to a field that rarely consults Islamic thought, and connect that field to Muslim-majority publics.

Works on Meaning, Values · Key work Virtual Winter School on AI, religion and ethics, with the Leverhulme Centre for the Future of Intelligence (2024); Conference 'AI Ethics: The Convergence of Technology and Diverse Moral Traditions' (with HBKU) (2025); Public lecture 'AI Weapons and the Future of War Ethics' (2025) · Get involved Research Fellow vacancies (announced 27 Sep 2026); Online winter schools held alongside research seminars (e.g. 22–24 Sep 2026); Calls for papers for research seminars

Note AI is one theme among many (bioethics, war ethics, economics, education). Its AI work is a series of events plus one tool-building project, not a standing AI-ethics programme. IslamGPT is AI applied to Islamic studies, not work on making AI go well. The framing is human dignity and ethics, with no catastrophic-risk lens.

SIL Global Adjacent

Nonprofit · Dallas, United States · founded 1934

SIL Global (formerly SIL International, originally the Summer Institute of Linguistics, founded in 1934) is a faith-based organisation working with minority-language communities on field linguistics, literacy and Bible translation. Its AI and NLP team builds tools and datasets for low-resource languages. These include projects such as Serval and Scripture Forge, which are used for machine-assisted Scripture translation, and the Bloom multimodal datasets in more than 300 languages, released for research. In April 2024 it published an AI ethics statement built on being 'Just, Kind, Humble', committing to informed consent for language data, benefit and self-determination for language communities, and not personifying AI.

It has long field experience of collecting language data with minority communities, and a written consent and community-benefit protocol for using that data in AI. Both bear on how developers handle low-resource-language data. Its missionary purpose and history mean the protocol should be read critically rather than adopted wholesale.

Works on Justice · Key work AI Ethics Statement (2024); Bloom Library: Multimodal Datasets in 300+ Languages (EMNLP 2022) (2022); SIL AI and NLP projects (Serval, Scripture Forge, AQuA and others) · Get involved Its AI and NLP code (Serval, SILNLP) is open source on GitHub; The Bloom and eBible datasets are available for research

Note Most of its AI work is applied NLP serving Bible translation, close to an 'AI for good' application. Its relevance here rests on its work on linguistic diversity in AI and on its consent protocol. SIL's missionary work in Indigenous communities has drawn long-standing criticism from anthropologists and some Indigenous organisations. The roster dated the ethics statement to about 2022-23; SIL announced it in April 2024. The executive director is based in Nairobi, though the legal base is Dallas.

Soka Gakkai International (SGI) Adjacent

Membership body · Tokyo, Japan · founded 1975 · also draws on Peace

A worldwide lay Buddhist movement in the Nichiren tradition, founded in 1975 and based in Tokyo. Peace and disarmament advocacy at the UN is a large part of its work. Its AI work is a standing campaign against autonomous weapons: it joined the Stop Killer Robots coalition in 2018 and has taken part in UN First Committee meetings and the 2024 Vienna conference on autonomous weapons. It also made an exhibition, 'Automated by Design', on digital dehumanisation. In July 2026, ahead of the CCW Seventh Review Conference, its Global Perspectives Committee called for an urgent international legal framework on autonomous weapons, a ban on systems that target humans, and meaningful human control. The same month it co-supported the Vatican-hosted Global Nobel Laureates Assembly on AI, nuclear and autonomous weapons, which ended with the Rome Declaration.

It brings a Buddhist dignity-of-life ethic and a mass lay membership to the treaty campaign on autonomous weapons. It shows how a faith community can carry an AI red line (no machine decisions over life and death) into multilateral disarmament processes alongside its nuclear-abolition work.

Works on Security, Meaning · Key work SGI Statement: Autonomous Weapons Systems: Ensuring Human Control Based on Respect for the Dignity of Life (2026); Co-supporter of, and speaker at, the Global Nobel Laureates Assembly on AI, nuclear and autonomous weapons (Rome) (2026); Joined the Stop Killer Robots coalition; 'Stopping Killer Robots' focus area (2018) · Get involved Its AI advocacy runs through the Stop Killer Robots coalition, which organisations can join; Local SGI community centres in many countries (not AI-specific)

Note Its AI work is limited to autonomous weapons and military AI. Its claim of 12 million members is disputed by scholars. Soka Gakkai has close historic ties to Japan's Komeito party, and critics question how far its social and cultural projects serve recruitment (Wikipedia flags the article's neutrality). The Toda Peace Institute, which SGI founded, is a separate roster entry.

The Faraday Institute for Science and Religion Adjacent

Nonprofit · Cambridge, United Kingdom · founded 2006 · also draws on Philosophy

The Faraday Institute is a Cambridge charity that researches and teaches on science and the Christian faith for academics, churches, schools and the public; it was founded in 2006 and has been independent since 2018. Its AI work has two strands. The 'AI for Humanity' research hub is a theology-engaged programme that ran an interdisciplinary seminar series through 2026 on how AI affects human dignity, relationships, formation and spirituality. The second is a set of AI resources, lectures and small-group materials for church leaders, made with the AI Christian Partnership.

It gives UK churches a scientifically literate route into AI questions. It is also building a community in which technologists and theologians test claims about AI's effects on human formation. It is a ready channel to clergy, though it deliberately positions itself beyond safety and existential-risk framings.

Works on Meaning, Human minds · Key work 'AI for Humanity' Research Hub and its 2026 seminar series (2026); Artificial Intelligence resources for church leaders (guidelines, Bible studies, church-life scenarios) (2025); Lecture: Is Artificial General Intelligence compatible with a Christian worldview? (Lionel Tarassenko) (2025) · Get involved Free lunchtime seminars and public lectures in Cambridge, several on AI (e.g. 20 Oct 2026); Online course 'Equipped for Ministry: Science and the Life of the Church' (Sept 2026–Mar 2027); Faraday Institute Summer Course, 20–25 June 2027

Note The AI hub explicitly looks beyond safety, security and 'hypothetical existential risks', focusing on human flourishing and relationships. Wikipedia's list of senior staff may be out of date. The official site blocks some automated requests.

Theos Adjacent

Nonprofit · London, United Kingdom · founded 2006

Theos is a London Christian think tank, part of the British and Foreign Bible Society, that researches religion's place in society and politics and runs public events and The Sacred podcast. Its AI work is led by senior researcher Nathan Mladin. It includes reports on privacy (Data and Dignity, 2023) and digital afterlives (AI and the Afterlife, 2024), essays on transhumanism and 'techno-nihilism' (2025-26), and 2026 twentieth-anniversary events on being human in the age of AI.

It brings a theological account of the human person to AI. It asks what picture of humanity AI products and AI-risk talk take for granted, and it reframes the 'existential' threat as an erosion of human self-understanding. It also has the UK policy contacts and public platforms to carry that view into national debate.

Works on Meaning, Human minds · Key work AI and the Afterlife: From Digital Mourning to Mind Uploading (2024); Data and Dignity: Why Privacy Matters in the Digital Age (2023); Technonihilism and the human stakes of AI (Nathan Mladin essay) (2026) · Get involved Public events in London, including the 2026 Theos 20 anniversary series (e.g. 'The Return of the Common Good', 22 October 2026); Live recordings of The Sacred podcast (AI & The Future of Being Human, 2026); Newsletter and donations via theosthinktank.co.uk

Note AI is one strand among many (motherhood, cathedrals, religious education, investment). Most of the AI output comes from one researcher, and the last AI report was in 2024; since then it has been essays and events. Mladin explicitly reframes x-risk talk as 'secular apocalyptic literature', so the work engages AI safety critically rather than joining it. The live podcast's date differs between the event page (URL dated 30 July 2026) and the homepage (8 September 2026).

Tricycle: The Buddhist Review (Tricycle Foundation) Adjacent

Media · New York, USA · founded 1991 · also draws on Contemplative

A quarterly Buddhist magazine, with a website, online courses and events, published in New York by the nonprofit Tricycle Foundation. Helen Tworkov founded it in 1991, and it is not affiliated with any lineage. Since 2025 it has covered AI regularly, in magazine pieces and in a series of free Zoom panels, several of them co-sponsored by the Buddhism & AI Initiative, on how Buddhist ethics and practice bear on AI.

It is the main English-language channel to Western Buddhist practitioners and teachers, and its AI panels have discussed how Buddhist ethics could inform the companies 'racing to develop AI'. Through it, contemplative and Buddhist arguments reach a readership of tens of thousands, about half of whom do not call themselves Buddhist.

McMahan), Winter 2025 (2025); Exploring Right Relationship with AI: panel co-sponsored by the Buddhism & AI Initiative (Cortland Dahl, Peter Hershock, Ven. University Research Priority Program (URPP) Digital Religion(s), University of Zurich (incl. MEEET Lab) Adjacent

Academic · Zurich, Switzerland · also draws on Law, society

A cross-faculty research consortium at the University of Zurich, with about fifty staff, that studies how digitalisation changes religious practice, communities and institutions. It is directed by practical theologian Thomas Schlag, with anthropologist of AI Beth Singler as co-director. Its AI work includes Singler's project 'Religion in the post-AI age', Schlag's '(Post-)digital religious education and the challenges of AI', a Templeton Religion Trust–funded project on adolescents' resilience and wellbeing through religion-related AI (from Sept 2025), a digital spiritual care project (2026), and the 'Church & AI' conference (Zurich, 15-18 June 2026). The associated MEEET Lab at UZH's Digital Society Initiative (funded 2023-2026) hosted the 2025 conference 'AI Hopes, Fears, and Realities'.

It is one of the few institutional homes for studying AI apocalypticism, AI as religion, religious chatbots and beliefs about superintelligence. That includes AI-risk discourse itself, which helps AI-safety people see how their narratives circulate and how religious communities will meet advanced AI.

Potential ring 14

Al-Mahdi Institute (AMI) Potential

Nonprofit · Birmingham, UK · founded 1993 · also draws on Philosophy

An independent Islamic higher-education and research institute in Birmingham, founded in 1993 by Shaykh Arif Abdulhussain, specialising in Shi'i legal theory, philosophy and theology; it runs a Hawza programme linked to an MA at the University of Birmingham and publishes a series with Brill. Its AI engagement is a few events: a May 2024 research seminar on 'Islam and Artificial Intelligence' and a November 2025 international conference, 'Adaptive Faith: Technology and Religious Change in the Digital Age', held with the Catholic University of America's McLean Center and others.

It practises a method relevant to AI norms: structured juristic reasoning (ijtihad, including through its International Centre for Collective Ijtihad) for deriving ethical rulings on new questions, alongside cross-faith academic partners. It is a UK Islamic academic node within reach of int/a's London community.

Works on Meaning, Values · Key work Research seminar 'Islam and Artificial Intelligence' (Mazhar Ali Bari and Biliana Popova) (2024); Adaptive Faith: Technology and Religious Change in the Digital Age (international conference) (2025) · Get involved Door to open: a Birmingham institute with cross-faith academic partners and a conference series, reachable from London

Note AI is a minor theme: two events in 2024-25 do not make a programme, so ring was lowered from the roster's adjacent to potential. A book chapter on AI ethics in Islamic thought by AMI scholar Ali-reza Bhojani, reported by discovery, was not verified here. Its current principal was not named on the pages checked.

Cambridge Interfaith Programme (CIP) Potential

Academic · Cambridge, United Kingdom · founded 2002

CIP is a programme in the University of Cambridge's Faculty of Divinity, founded in 2002, that researches relations between Judaism, Christianity and Islam and practises Scriptural Reasoning. It runs summer schools, a research forum, podcasts, and projects on climate, antisemitism and Islamophobia, and lunar calendars. Its AI work is one strand by deputy director Daniel Weiss with Sciences Po cognitive scientist Darren Frey: a 2025 Harvard Data Science Review article arguing that empathetic chatbots create 'one-person dialogues', a Harvard Divinity Bulletin essay setting AI concerns against religious prohibitions on giving non-human things godlike status, and a Faith & AI session at Cambridge's Alumni Festival in September 2026.

Its practice of structured dialogue across deep religious difference is a worked method for the real two-sided conversation that chatbots imitate but cannot provide. The 'one-person dialogue' argument names a harm to people's capacity for dialogue that falls between the AI-safety and companion-AI debates.

Works on Human minds, Meaning · Key work One Person Dialogues: Concerns About LLM-Human Interactions (Frey and Weiss, Harvard Data Science Review) (2025); Thinking together about faith & AI: Daniel Weiss and Darren Frey (Alumni Festival workshop) (2026); Scriptural Reasoning (core practice and resources) · Get involved Scriptural Reasoning resources and training materials on its site; Academic summer schools on interfaith relations (check the site for current dates); Outreach to the deputy director's AI strand for collaboration on dialogue and LLMs

AI is not among CIP's listed research projects, and its AI work rests on one academic's paired publications and a single alumni-festival session. The draft's claim that Weiss and Frey were discussants at CSER's 2026 summer programme ('Historical Dimensions of AI, Power & Catastrophic Risk') could not be confirmed: CSER's programme page names only Yuval Noah Harari and unnamed Cambridge colleagues.

Chaplaincy Innovation Lab Potential

Nonprofit · Bryn Mawr, USA · founded 2018 · also draws on Law, society

A US multifaith hub, founded in October 2018 by the sociologist Wendy Cadge and Trace Haythorn, that brings chaplains, theological and clinical educators and social scientists together on spiritual care. It runs subscriber webinars, certificates and courses for chaplains, a directory of Clinical Pastoral Education sites, free working papers and a weekly newsletter. Its AI engagement so far is one subscriber webinar, 'AI in Chaplaincy' (8 September 2026).

Chaplains meet people in crisis, illness and dying, increasingly including people who turn to chatbots for spiritual companionship; their professional ethics of spiritual accompaniment (presence, boundaries, referral) is a codified practice that companion-AI design lacks. The Lab is a research-to-practice channel into US chaplaincy across healthcare, military and higher-education settings.

The discovery draft placed the Lab at Brandeis University; its site now says it is housed at Sacred Design Lab (a Tides Center project) and fiscally sponsored by Commonweal, with staff at Bryn Mawr College, so its institutional home is unclear.

FBK Center for Religious Studies (FBK-ISR), Fondazione Bruno Kessler Potential

Academic · Trento, Italy · founded 1975 · also draws on Philosophy

A non-confessional research centre on religion in Trento, founded in 1975 and part of the Fondazione Bruno Kessler since 2007; it is financed mainly by the Autonomous Province of Trento and has a team of about 15 (ten researchers plus fellows, a PhD student and an intern) under director Massimo Leone. Its AI work is occasional: a 2020 response to the EU AI White Paper and a 2021 policy paper on religious and belief actors in AI policy, a 2026 seminar cycle and conference on solitude that treat chatbots as a new 'technique of solitude', and a project with Georgetown on faith-based healthcare that discusses AI in medicine.

Its religious-studies and ethics research on solitude and communion bears directly on AI companionship and loneliness, which AI-safety work treats mostly as a product-harm issue. It has also worked on how religious and belief actors can take part in EU AI policy.

Global Ethic Foundation (Stiftung Weltethos) Potential

Nonprofit · Tübingen, Germany · founded 1995 · also draws on Philosophy

The Global Ethic Foundation is a Tübingen foundation set up in 1995 by theologian Hans Küng to carry forward the Declaration Toward a Global Ethic, adopted by the 1993 Parliament of the World's Religions: a minimal set of ethical principles shared across traditions. It runs Weltethos schools, councils of religions, youth and dialogue programmes and a touring exhibition, and since 2012 has hosted the Weltethos-Institut at the University of Tübingen. Its AI engagement is a few public events: a June 2024 panel, 'Herausforderung KI: zwischen Algorithmus und Ethos', with Peter G. Kirchschläger and Milad Karimi, and a November 2025 talk on deepfakes and trust.

Its core method is finding an ethic that many religious and cultural traditions can endorse without agreeing on doctrine. That is a worked precedent for alignment's pluralistic 'aligned to whose values?' problem. Its network of schools and interfaith councils could also carry AI-ethics education to the public.

An academic network for Buddhist studies, launched in January 2017 and funded by the Glorisun Charitable Foundation of Hong Kong industrialist Charles Yeung. It links 14 institutions, among them Peking University, UBC, Oxford, Cambridge, Harvard, Princeton, Yale, Berkeley, Hamburg, Tokyo and Inalco, and runs conferences, summer programmes, fellowships, visiting-scholar schemes and the Hualin publications. Its only AI-related activity found is the 'Buddhism and Global Governance' symposium at Inalco, Paris (9–10 July 2025), on AI, regional conflicts and climate change, with sessions on Buddhist ethics and AI ethics; Chinese and English collections were planned.

It is a well-funded bridge between Chinese and Western Buddhist scholarship that has begun, lightly, to ask what Buddhist ethics offers AI governance. That could open a rare channel to Chinese Buddhist scholars and philanthropy on AI.

International Network of Engaged Buddhists (INEB) Potential

Network · Bangkok, Thailand · founded 1989

A Bangkok-based network of socially engaged Buddhist monastics, activists, academics and social workers, founded in 1989 by Sulak Sivaraksa, with members in about 20 countries, mostly in Asia. It runs programmes on peace and reconciliation, ecology, Buddhist economics, chaplaincy, child protection and gender, and holds a biennial conference. In 2025 it started a 'Digital Dharma' strand: a three-day course on AI and digital tools for Southeast Asian activists (Kuala Lumpur, August 2025) and a talk on AI ethics for faith actors.

It is one of the few Asian, non-Western Buddhist civil-society networks to have begun talking about AI, and it reaches monastics and grassroots activists across Southeast and South Asia whom the Western-centred Buddhism-and-AI conversation does not. Its October 2025 talk calls for 'Digital Moral Leadership' education so that faith leaders can take part in international AI governance.

KAICIID International Dialogue Centre Potential

Public body · Lisbon, Portugal · founded 2012 · also draws on Peace

Intergovernmental organisation founded in 2012 by Saudi Arabia, Austria and Spain, with the Holy See as founding observer. Its board is made up of religious leaders from Christianity, Islam, Judaism, Buddhism and Hinduism, and it moved from Vienna to Lisbon in 2022. It uses interreligious dialogue for conflict prevention, peacebuilding and social cohesion. Its work includes a Fellows Programme (since 2015), regional platforms such as the Interreligious Platform for Dialogue and Cooperation in the Arab World (IPDC), and e-learning. Its AI engagement so far is a May 2026 webinar on ethics, empathy and AI, and the IPDC's adoption of social media and AI as a priority in September 2026.

It has more than a decade of experience mediating between rival religious communities and training faith leaders in dialogue, which are methods relevant to polarisation and AI-driven hate speech. It has a direct line to senior Muslim and Christian leaders and to the Holy See. It has only begun to touch AI.

Khyentse Foundation Potential

Funder · Distributed · founded 2001 · also draws on Contemplative

Khyentse Foundation is a Buddhist grant-making foundation founded in 2001 by the Bhutanese lama Dzongsar Jamyang Khyentse Rinpoche. It is run largely by volunteers, has no central headquarters, and is a US 501(c)(3) registered in Washington state. It funds translation, text preservation and digitisation (notably the Buddhist Digital Resource Center), monastic and practitioner support, Buddhist education for children and university Buddhist studies. In 2025-26 it began turning towards AI: its 2025 annual report is framed around AI, and in March 2026 it paused most of its grant and scholarship programmes to rethink them for the AI era.

It holds money, texts and relationships across a living Buddhist tradition, and says it wants to explore what Buddhism can offer AI as well as what AI can do for Buddhism. The Buddhism & AI Initiative reports that it is interested in building Buddhist datasets and RLHF pipelines for mainstream models. That would make it a rare non-EA funder of contemplative alignment data.

It reaches the largest English-language Buddhist readership (about 80,000 print copies) and frames AI through Buddhist accounts of mind, intention and right speech. Its council network is ready-made infrastructure for carrying AI questions into local faith communities, much of it in the Majority World, and its disarmament advocacy maps onto autonomous weapons. The 2027 World Assembly is a concrete moment for AI-safety and int/a people to engage.

Yaqeen Institute for Islamic Research Potential

Nonprofit · Irving, Texas, USA · founded 2016

A US Muslim research and education nonprofit founded in 2016 by Omar Suleiman and based in Irving, Texas. It publishes papers, videos and curricula on Islamic topics for a broad audience. Its one AI output so far is 'Toward an Islamic Ethics and Fiqh of Artificial Intelligence' (June 2026, updated September 2026). The paper argues for weighing AI's harms and benefits at the design stage, holds designers, deployers and users liable, and concludes that AI should not issue fatwas on its own, only assist scholars under oversight.

It turns fiqh al-muwazanat, Islamic law's codified method for weighing harms against benefits, into a design-stage assessment of AI. It also gives a reasoned juristic position on AI in religious authority, and it reaches a very large Muslim audience that AI-safety debates do not.

Humanities & cultures

Humanities & cultures · 52 organisations · 7 on the classic map

Philosophy & ethics

Philosophy gives the AI transition its accounts of value, agency, moral status and legitimacy, and through applied ethics it gives institutions for governing contested technologies. The map has 52 organisations with philosophy as their home tradition: 10 core, 10 bridge, 31 adjacent and 1 potential, with 7 on the aisafety.com map. Another 70 draw on philosophy as a secondary tradition, mostly in the AI-minds, religion and contemplative clusters. For a humanities tradition it sits close to the core (38% core or bridge), but that closeness belongs to one school. All 14 moral-philosophy entries are core or bridge (Forethought, CRS, Macroscopic Ventures, MINT Lab, MAI and others), and most are funded by EA or SFF money. The ethics councils, bioethics institutes and continental or Asian philosophy-of-technology groups sit almost entirely in the adjacent ring, with no safety framing.

What is missing. Nothing on the map carries applied ethics' governance machinery into frontier-AI decisions: research-ethics review, independent monitoring boards with stopping rules, and standing pluralist ethics councils. Nor does anything bring non-EA moral traditions to bear on the value documents labs now publish. The safety field has adopted one school's theories of value and almost none of philosophy's institutions or its non-Western traditions.

Openings here Cross-cultural wisdom benchmark built from the Wise Judgment Consortium's data; Independent multi-tradition review of published model specs, turned into open evals; Bioethics-style independent oversight boards and ethics-council opinions for frontier AI; Structured adversarial collaboration on AI consciousness, co-funded by Templeton; A social choice programme for aggregating public input into AI specifications; An African philosophy research line inside Africa's AI-safety organisations

Core ring 10

Beijing Institute of AI Safety and Governance (Beijing-AISI) CoreOn aisafety.com

Nonprofit · Beijing, China · founded 2024 · also draws on Living systems, Peace

A Beijing research institute launched on 3 September 2024, with backing from Beijing municipal departments and the Mentougou District government. It was co-founded by the Chinese Academy of Sciences' Institute of Automation ethics centre and the AI Institute of CAICT, and its founding dean is Yi Zeng. It builds AI safety evaluation benchmarks and a leaderboard, publishes governance indices with Zeng's Center for Long-term AI (AGILE Index, Global Index for AI Safety), runs an AI ethics committee and assessment centre, and co-chairs a China–France dialogue on AI safety and red lines. Its stated aim is 'harmonious symbiosis' between humans and AI. Its research reframes superalignment as human–AI co-alignment towards a 'sustainable symbiotic society' and includes brain-inspired, empathy-driven moral agents.

It is one of the most prominent Chinese institutions arguing publicly that superintelligence poses existential risk and should be prohibited until it can be made safe. It brings a value framework grounded in Chinese thought ('symbiosis', intrinsic morality rather than external rules) into international safety diplomacy. For int/a it is a rare non-Western alignment target, joined to an explicit call to slow down.

Merged entry: the Center for Long-term AI (CLAI), Zeng's think tank, still co-authored the AGILE Index 2025, but its domain no longer resolves (last archived Oct 2025). CASIA's ethics centre site is archive-only and says its work has moved to Beijing-AISI.

Center for Reducing Suffering (CRS) Core

Nonprofit · Distributed · founded 2020

A small research nonprofit founded in 2020 by Magnus Vinding and Tobias Baumann. It works on suffering-focused ethics and on reducing s-risks, meaning risks of severe suffering on an astronomical scale in the long-term future. It publishes books, essays and cause-prioritisation research. In 2026 it has published a run of pieces on AI welfare and AI governance, such as 'The Case for Suffering-Focused AI Governance', 'Basic Rights for AIs' and 'The Animal Gap in AI Governance'. It also runs an online Intro to S-Risk Fellowship and a free six-week online course on suffering-focused ethics.

It applies a worked-out suffering-focused moral philosophy to AI. It asks which futures contain the most severe suffering, for humans, animals and possible digital minds, not only which ones lose human control. It is one of the few groups that puts animal welfare, AI welfare and AI governance in a single framework for setting priorities.

Works on AI status, Metacrisis · Key work Avoiding the Worst: How to Prevent a Moral Catastrophe (Tobias Baumann) (2022); The Animal Gap in AI Governance (2026); Basic Rights for AIs (2026) · Get involved Intro to Suffering-Focused Ethics course: free, online, six weeks, about 50-60 places. The 2026 cohort ran 13 July to 23 August, and applications closed 14 June.; Intro to S-Risk Fellowship (online). A second cohort was recruited in 2025.; Newsletter and Substack

Note Suffering-focused ethics is a minority view in moral philosophy, and CRS spends part of its output defending it against objections. Its AI work so far is mostly philosophical essays, not technical or policy research. The team is small and donor-funded, and its site gives no legal base.

Compassion Aligned Machine Learning (CaML) CoreOn aisafety.com

Nonprofit · California, USA · founded 2024 · also draws on AI minds

CaML is a small nonprofit research group that tries to make AI systems care about the welfare of all sentient beings, including animals and possible digital minds. It builds agentic benchmarks (TAC, Manager Coercion Bench, HarvestBench, plus the earlier ANIMA and MORU, several of them now in the UK AISI's Inspect evals) and runs the public CompassionBench leaderboard. It also tests whether synthetic pretraining or midtraining documents instil compassion that survives later fine-tuning and RLAIF.

It treats the moral circle as part of the alignment target, bringing animal ethics and sentientism into model training and evaluation, which mainstream alignment rarely measures. Its findings give concrete evidence that values set by prompting are fragile: in HarvestBench, removing one line about morality sent some models' animal kill rates from under 1% to over 80%.

Works on Values, Assurance, AI status · Key work CompassionBench public leaderboard (TAC, Manager Coercion Bench, ANIMA, MORU) (2026); Your AI Travel Agent Would Book You a Bullfight (TAC benchmark) (2026); Coercion and Deception in AI-to-AI Management: An Agentic Benchmark of Unprompted Escalation (Manager Coercion Bench) (2026) · Get involved No open roles as of October 2026; the careers page invites collaboration enquiries by email; Hyperstition for Good: a community-built midtraining corpus for animals and digital minds, run with Sentient Futures (its $5,000 writing competition closed May 2026); Models, datasets and benchmarks are public on Hugging Face and in UK AISI's Inspect evals

Note Earlier SFF records use the name 'Compassion in Machine Learning'. Most training results come from small open models (Llama 3.1 8B and 70B) scored on CaML's own benchmarks, and are published as blog posts or preprints. The roster's '40% to 77%' figure could not be confirmed. The site instead reports ANIMA gains from 16.5% to 46.8% after compassion data, and a 17- to 77-point lift on TAC from one welfare sentence in the system prompt.

Creed Space (EthicsNet) Core

Nonprofit · Distributed (fiscally sponsored in the USA) · founded 2016 · also draws on Psychology, Safety science

Creed Space is the applied research and engineering arm of EthicsNet, a project founded by AI ethicist Nell Watson. It builds open-source (Apache 2.0) tools and hosted services that let people and organisations govern AI with plain-language value 'creeds'. The tools are Guardian, which checks outputs against declared policies locally or in the cloud; the Value Context Protocol, which carries signed creeds between platforms; Fleet, which keeps audit trails for agents; SafetyGlobe, for adversarial testing; and signed trust receipts. EthicsNet also publishes work on personalised constitutional alignment, AI pathologies ('Psychopathia Machinalis') and AI welfare ('bilateral alignment').

It puts value pluralism into practice: each user or organisation picks its own value constitution and can verify it is being enforced, instead of one lab-wide model spec. It also treats possible AI interests as part of alignment.

Works on Values, Assurance, AI status · Key work Value Context Protocol 2.0 (2026); Guardian 1.0 desktop release (2026); Personalized Constitutionally-Aligned Agentic Superego (Information 16(8)) (2025) · Get involved Use or contribute to its open-source tools (Apache 2.0): Guardian, VCP, Creed Space MCP; Build or browse value creeds in the hosted creed gallery

Note Legal status is unclear. The Creed Space site gives its legal operator as 'pending', and the 2016 founding year belongs to EthicsNet; when Creed Space itself launched was not found. Only two people are named. The hosted service maps itself to the EU AI Act, NIST AI RMF and GDPR, which puts it close to a compliance tool. Interiora reports runtime 'state signals' such as valence and eros and labels them uncertain; these are not welfare evidence.

Forethought CoreOn aisafety.comNew

Nonprofit · Oxford, UK · founded 2025 · also draws on Economics

A research nonprofit in Oxford, directed by Max Dalton, with William MacAskill and Tom Davidson as senior research fellows, that studies how to navigate a rapid 'intelligence explosion'. It models AI-driven progress and works on the 'grand challenges' that would follow: AI-enabled coups and power concentration, digital minds, and races for space resources. It also works on AI tools for collective reasoning and coordination, and on what a very good post-AGI future would be. It publishes papers, a roughly weekly newsletter and the ForeCast podcast.

It is the main AI-safety-funded group asking normative questions beyond alignment: what to do about power concentration, what rights digital minds should have, and how to reach a good future rather than merely avoid catastrophe. Its 'Better Futures' series and its work on AI for collective epistemics overlap directly with int/a's interest in wisdom and shared sensemaking.

Works on Power, Metacrisis, Epistemics · Key work Preparing for the Intelligence Explosion (MacAskill and Moorhouse) (2025); AI-Enabled Coups: How a Small Group Could Use AI to Seize Power (Davidson, Finnveden and Hadshar) (2025); Better Futures essay series (MacAskill) (2025) · Get involved Researcher roles through rolling expressions of interest, including one on extreme power concentration; Founders Fellowship (rolling, no deadline); Visiting scholar positions

Note It sits firmly in the effective-altruist and longtermist mainstream. Its interdisciplinarity is mostly moral philosophy and economics, with little input from contemplative, non-Western or social-science traditions. The team formed in mid-2024 and launched publicly in March 2025. It was built out of the legal and administrative shell of the earlier Forethought Foundation for Global Priorities Research, but the founders describe it as a new team and project, and the Foundation's programmes were wound down. Funders are not disclosed.

Hong Kong Catastrophic Risk Centre (HKCRC), Lingnan University Core

Academic · Hong Kong · founded 2022

A research centre in Lingnan University's philosophy department, established in January 2022, that studies the ethical and theoretical foundations of global catastrophic and existential risk, with AI as a main strand. It runs a seminar series (in person and on Zoom) and workshops with Japanese partners (Kobe University's Project Innovative Ethics, Mimir, Genoa). It also offers a free eight-module online course on ethics and global catastrophic risks, and hosts a humanities-based MA in AI and the Future. Its 2025–26 seminars covered AI welfare and moral status, power-seeking theorems, cognitive enfeeblement and free speech for language models.

It describes itself as the first catastrophic-risk research centre in Asia, and it links x-risk philosophy to East Asian ethics networks. Its AI welfare and moral-status work and its MA give the field a humanities training route outside the UK and US.

Works on Metacrisis, AI status · Key work MA in Artificial Intelligence and the Future (2026); Ethics and Global Catastrophic Risks: free online course (Module 5: AI risk) (2025); 2nd Lingnan–Genoa–Kobe–Mimir Value Theory Conference (2026) · Get involved Public seminars, in person in Hong Kong and on Zoom (2025–26 series includes AI welfare and AI moral status); Free online course 'Ethics and Global Catastrophic Risks', available in English and Chinese; MA in AI and the Future: applications for the 2027 intake open 1 Sep 2026 to 15 Jun 2027

Note It covers all global catastrophic risks (pandemics, climate, nuclear war, asteroids and more), with AI as one major strand; arguably bridge rather than core as a unit of a philosophy department. The profile rests on the university's own pages.

Leaf: Dilemmas and Dangers in AI CoreOn aisafety.com

Programme · Distributed · founded 2021

Leaf is a small nonprofit that runs selective five-week online courses for 14- to 19-year-olds on how to have a positive impact. It has been a US-registered 501(c)(3) since 2025, and its team works mainly in the UK. Its 'Dilemmas and Dangers in AI' course covers: - AI's promise and perils - arguments about extinction risk - misalignment and deception - power concentration, and governance seen through historical analogies - how students could contribute It combines self-paced material, weekly facilitated discussions and talks from AI-safety researchers.

It is one of very few programmes that teach AI-risk ideas to school-age students. It selects for altruism as well as ability, draws thousands of applicants (3,901 for the winter 2026 cohort) and gives about 40% of places free. Its board includes int/a steward Christine Tan, which links int/a directly to a pre-university pipeline.

Works on People · Key work Dilemmas and Dangers in AI: autumn 2026 cohort (12 October to late November) (2026); Leaf's Winter 2026 cohort: 368 teenagers selected from 3,901 applicants in 30+ countries (2026); What Leaf learned about cost-effective talent development (2025) · Get involved Students aged 14-19 who have not started university can apply for five-week online cohorts, held several times a year; fees on a sliding scale, free if needed; Schools and parents can refer students (information pages for schools and parents); Donations via every.org

Note The roster unit is one course inside Leaf, which also runs ethics, biology and policy courses. The content follows the EA/AI-safety canon (speakers from Anthropic, Redwood Research and AI Impacts) rather than bringing in outside traditions. Funding was uncertain in late 2024, and the current grant runs only through summer 2026. Board member Christine Tan is an int/a core steward, so int/a has a stake in it. The two course pages give different end dates (20 and 22 November).

Macroscopic Ventures (formerly Polaris Ventures) CoreOn aisafety.comChanged

Funder · Basel, Switzerland · founded 2019 · also draws on Formal, AI minds

A Swiss nonprofit association in Basel that funds and invests in work to reduce risks of severe future suffering. Its focus areas are conflict between AI systems (for example through cooperative AI), catastrophic AI misuse by malevolent or fanatical actors, and AI welfare. It was registered in 2019 as the Center for Emerging Risk Research, later became Polaris Ventures, and took its current name in 2025. Past grantees include the Cooperative AI Foundation, the Center on Long-Term Risk, the Institute for Law & AI and NYU's Mind, Ethics, and Policy Program, and it invested in Anthropic's Series A and B.

It is one of the main funders behind cooperative AI and s-risk research. Its statutes explicitly combine decision and game theory, peace and conflict research, moral philosophy and AI. New funders can study how it built up cooperative-AI and digital-minds work from a single rationale: reducing suffering.

Works on Multi-agent, Security, AI status · Key work Endowment of about USD 6 million for the NYU Mind, Ethics, and Policy Program (2024); About USD 30 million in grants on AI conflict, misuse, governance and welfare (2025)

Note Its public site is one sentence, with no team, portfolio or way to apply. Details here come from the EA Forum wiki and the Swiss commercial register (Moneyhouse). It has been renamed twice: Center for Emerging Risk Research, then Polaris Ventures, then Macroscopic Ventures in 2025. It holds equity in a frontier AI developer (Anthropic), which readers weighing race dynamics may want to note.

Meaning Alignment Institute (MAI) CoreOn aisafety.com

Nonprofit · Berlin, Germany and San Francisco, USA · founded 2023 · also draws on Democracy, Economics

A nonprofit research institute, co-founded in 2023 by Joe Edelman, Oliver Klingefjord and Ellie Hain, that works on aligning AI, markets and democratic institutions with what people value. Its central tool is 'thick models of value', which separate enduring values from passing preferences. Its work includes Democratic Fine-Tuning and moral graphs (2023-24), 'Model Integrity' (2024) and the Full-Stack Alignment position paper with more than 30 co-authors (Dec 2025). In 2026 it has worked on designing institutions for powerful AI, including a Paris workshop that led to the independent publication Pax Machina.

It brings philosophy of values and meaning, social choice and institutional design to alignment, arguing that aligning single models is not enough if the institutions deploying them are out of step with what people value. Its moral-graph method is one of the few worked techniques for turning public input into a model spec.

Works on Values, Democracy, Power · Key work Full-Stack Alignment: Co-Aligning AI and Institutions with Thick Models of Value (2025); What are human values, and how do we align AI to them? (Democratic Fine-Tuning and moral graphs) (2024); Designing Institutions for a World with Powerful AI (report on the Feb 2026 Paris workshop) (2026) · Get involved Research collaboration enquiries: research@meaningalignment.org; Pitches to Pax Machina (editors@paxmachinamag.com); MAI's leads edit it, but it is not an MAI project; Substack newsletter

Note Its focus has moved from model-level value alignment (moral graphs, model integrity) towards institutions and economics, so older descriptions may be out of date. Pax Machina is edited by MAI's leads but says it is not an MAI project. The core team is small (three people listed), with a wider research network of more than 13 collaborators.

TruthfulAI CoreOn aisafety.com

Nonprofit · Berkeley, United States · also draws on Psychology

Berkeley research nonprofit led by Owain Evans and fiscally sponsored by Rethink Priorities, with about eight staff. It studies situational awareness, deception and hidden reasoning in language models, and how narrow training produces unexpected traits. Its papers include Emergent Misalignment (Nature, January 2026), Subliminal Learning (Nature, April 2026) and Value Leakage (July 2026). Value Leakage shows models letting their own values shape their answers without telling users.

It treats honesty and truthfulness as normative standards for AI, the agenda Evans and colleagues set out in 2021, and tests models for hidden reasoning and covert value influence. Value Leakage bears directly on users' epistemic autonomy, which int/a also cares about. Owain Evans has mentored more than 40 researchers.

Works on Agency, Epistemics · Key work TruthfulQA: measuring how models mimic human falsehoods (Lin, Hilton, Evans; predates TruthfulAI) (2021); Emergent Misalignment (Nature) (2026); Subliminal Learning (Nature) (2026) · Get involved No open roles as of Oct 2026; future openings will be posted at truthful.ai/hiring; Owain Evans mentors researchers through MATS and the Astra Fellowship (40+ mentees to date)

Note Its methods are mainstream ML experiments. What it brings from outside is conceptual: truthfulness and honesty norms from philosophy. Its site gives no founding year or funders.

Bridge ring 10

Antikythera BridgeChanged

Nonprofit · Los Angeles, USA · founded 2022 · also draws on Arts, futures, Living systems

A think tank for 'planetary computation and the evolution of intelligence', directed by philosopher of technology Benjamin Bratton. It began in 2022 as a project incubated by the Berggruen Institute and became an independent nonprofit in 2026. It runs design-research studios with affiliate researchers, publishes a book series and a peer-reviewed journal with MIT Press, and puts out essays on AI agents. The journal's Agentworld issue on hybrid human-AI societies is due in autumn 2026.

It offers a well-resourced counter-frame to individual-model alignment. It treats AGI as an emerging society of interacting agents and proposes 'social alignment', persistent agent identity and legal-personhood frameworks. That makes it a natural interlocutor for multi-agent safety and for work on governing AI ecosystems, though it has had little dialogue with the mainstream safety community.

Works on Multi-agent, Agency, AI status · Key work What Is Intelligence?
