(Blaise Agüera y Arcas, Antikythera series, MIT Press) (2025); The Silicon Interior (Agüera y Arcas, Bratton, Evans) (2026); Artificial Symbiotic Intelligence (Bratton, Agüera y Arcas, Manyika) (2026) · Get involved Agentworld call for papers (opened June 2026) for essays, technical papers and web-native work; Partnership, collaboration and support enquiries via contact@antikythera.org; Past studio-researcher and affiliate cohorts in 2023 and 2024; no 2025-26 studio call found

Note In 2026 it moved from the Berggruen Institute to independent nonprofit status, and its base since then is not stated. Bratton is openly critical of mainstream alignment and x-risk framings, so it engages the safety field as a critic. Much of its AI output is co-written with Google DeepMind staff.

Berggruen Institute Bridge

Nonprofit · Los Angeles, USA · founded 2010 · also draws on Democracy

A think tank in Los Angeles, founded in 2010 by the investor Nicolas Berggruen and the journalist Nathan Gardels, with centres in Beijing (at Peking University since 2018) and Venice. It publishes Noema magazine, awards the $1m Berggruen Prize for Philosophy and Culture, funds fellows and incubated Antikythera, Benjamin Bratton's programme on planetary computation. Its AI work covers the philosophy of AI and consciousness, AI safety as a US–China public good (it co-hosted the 2024 IDAIS-Venice dialogue with the Safe AI Forum), and digital-democracy pilots such as Engaged California.

It is one of the few well-endowed places where philosophers, including Chinese and East Asian ones, work on what AI means for being human and for governance, and it has already hosted AI-safety diplomacy. Noema gives int/a-style arguments a way to reach policy and intellectual readers outside the AI-safety community.

Works on Meaning, Democracy · Key work Co-hosted, with the Safe AI Forum (FAR.AI), the third International Dialogue on AI Safety (IDAIS-Venice) at Casa dei Tre Oci; Noema essay 'AI Safety Is A Global Public Good' (2024); Antikythera, a programme on planetary computation led by Benjamin Bratton (incubated) (2022); Engaged California, a digital-democracy platform built with the State of California and expanded statewide for AI-policy input (2026) · Get involved Berggruen Research Center at Peking University fellowships and internships (applications opened for 2026–27); Berggruen Prize Essay Competition ($50,000 awards in English and Chinese categories, running since 2024); Public events in Los Angeles and Venice, e.g. 'Consciousness, AI, and the Human Future' (2026)

Note Funded largely by one billionaire founder. Its AI output is broad philosophy and public debate rather than a dedicated safety programme, and Noema publishes deflationary views (e.g. Anil Seth on conscious AI) alongside safety-minded ones. The Transformations of the Human programme (philosophers placed in AI labs) dates from 2019, and I could not confirm it is still running. Engaged California belongs to the state's Office of Data and Innovation; Berggruen is a partner.

Civic AI / 6-Pack of Care BridgeNew

Programme · Oxford, UK · founded 2025 · also draws on Democracy

A project led by Audrey Tang and Caroline Emmer De Albuquerque Green at the University of Oxford's Institute for Ethics in AI, hosted in its Accelerator Fellowship Programme. It turns care ethics (Fisher and Tronto's phases of care) into six testable principles for building and governing AI: attentiveness, responsibility, competence, responsiveness, solidarity and symbiosis. It defines 'civic AI' as AI 'that the people it affects can check, correct and switch off'. Its outputs include a CC0 manifesto, a short instruction set (a 'Kami') that walks groups through oversight questions, a conference at Rhodes House in March 2026, essays, and a Wiley book due in February 2027.

It brings care ethics and Taiwan's civic-tech practice into alignment debates. It reframes alignment as 'horizontal' (AI supporting cooperation between people) as well as 'vertical', and it proposes many local, bounded, time-limited systems as the alternative to a singleton. Few AI-safety groups offer anything like this: a relational, participatory alignment target with concrete governance tests.

Works on Values, Democracy, Power · Key work 6-Pack of Care manifesto and framework (2025); Civic AI Conference, Rhodes House, Oxford (25 March) (2026); 'Let the People Set the Pace of Frontier AI' (Hélène Landemore and Audrey Tang, Noema): proposes a standing Global Citizens' Assembly on AI (2026) · Get involved Propose amendments to the framework through its public GitHub repository and amendment ledger (CC0 licence); Try the Kami instruction set with a community group: it asks who oversees a system, what could fail, who can veto it and when it ends; Book Civic AI: 6-Pack of Care (Wiley, February 2027)

Note Most of what is known comes from the project's own site; independent coverage found was thin (Wikipedia confirms Tang's Oxford Accelerator Fellowship). It works through process, not enforcement: the Kami instructions 'can only ask; they enforce nothing'. Catastrophic risk is addressed only indirectly, by arguing for a plural, federated architecture against a singleton. 6pack.care now redirects to civic.ai.

Cosmos Institute Bridge

Funder · Austin, United States · founded 2024 · also draws on Democracy

A nonprofit founded in 2024 by Brendan McCord, a former US Department of Defense technologist. It backs 'philosopher-builders' who build AI for human autonomy and truth-seeking. It gives fast grants ($1k-10k) for working prototypes in 90 days, including an AI for Truth-Seeking track with FIRE ($1M in cash and compute); 80 new grantees were announced in September 2026. It also funds fellowships, supports Oxford's HAI Lab, and runs seminars, essay prizes and a Substack. In 2025 a Cosmos incubation fellow, Samuele Marro, launched an Institute for Decentralized AI with visiting slots at Oxford and Stanford, and in September 2026 Cosmos announced an investment arm, Cosmos Ventures.

It is a new funder putting money into AI that preserves human judgement and autonomy, drawing on liberal and classical philosophy rather than the x-risk canon. That makes it a potential co-funder or counterpart for int/a-style work on protecting human minds, though its politics differ.

Works on Human minds, Epistemics, Democracy · Key work Cosmos Grants: fast grants for AI tools serving autonomy and truth-seeking (80 new grantees announced) (2026); Cosmos Fellowship: fellows at the AI-philosophy intersection, some at frontier labs (2025); Institute for Decentralized AI (visiting positions at Oxford and Stanford) (2025) · Get involved Cosmos Grants: rolling rounds; the latest closed 26 July 2026, with an expression-of-interest form for future rounds; Cosmos Fellowship: currently closed, expressions of interest accepted; Seminars and symposia, e.g. the AI x Free Speech Symposium with FIRE (Austin, December 2025)

Note Its classical-liberal, pro-market framing (partners include Liberty Fund, FIRE and IHS; Palantir was an event partner) differs from int/a's and from mainstream AI safety, and its essays are sceptical of precautionary pacing. Funders and budget are not published. Organisation type is borderline: it also runs research and seminars.

Institute for Ethics in AI, University of Oxford Bridge

Academic · Oxford, United Kingdom · founded 2021 · also draws on Law, society, Democracy

The Institute for Ethics in AI is part of Oxford's Faculty of Philosophy. It was launched in 2021 with a donation from Stephen A. Schwarzman and is based in the Schwarzman Centre for the Humanities. It does philosophy-led research on AI and human rights, governance, health and care, the family and the foundations of AI. It also runs the five-year Accelerator Fellowship Programme (from 2025; fellows include Alondra Nelson, Joy Buolamwini, Yuval Shany and Audrey Tang), hosts the Human-Centered AI Lab (HAI Lab), offers executive education, and leads Civic AI, a '6-Pack of Care' framework for 'alignment-by-process' in deployed systems.

It brings moral and political philosophy, care ethics and human-rights law into AI governance at a major university. Through Civic AI it offers a bottom-up, care-based account of alignment that complements work on frontier models. It became an affiliate of the International Association for Safe and Ethical AI in June 2026.

Works on Justice, Values, Democracy · Key work Accelerator Fellowship Programme (five-year, Schwarzman Foundation) (2025); Civic AI: the 6-Pack of Care (Audrey Tang and Caroline Green) and the Civic AI Conference, Rhodes House, 25 March (2026); White paper on an International AI Bill of Human Rights (Yuval Shany) and the AI and Human Rights Summit (2025) · Get involved Accelerator Fellowship Programme and visiting fellowships; DPhil scholarships; Oxford Executive Programme in Ethical AI Leadership, 10–12 Nov 2026

Note The ring was moved from adjacent to bridge because Civic AI is framed explicitly as alignment and the mission lists safety; most of the institute's output is still AI ethics and human rights rather than catastrophic risk. Edward Harcourt is now director; the inaugural director was John Tasioulas. Civic AI is a research project of two of its people, with its own site.

Laboratory for Human-Centered AI (HAI Lab), University of Oxford Bridge

Academic · Oxford, United Kingdom · founded 2024 · also draws on Psychology

A lab set up in 2024 in Oxford's Faculty of Philosophy, affiliated with the Institute for Ethics in AI, and directed by Philipp Koralus, McCord Professor of Philosophy and AI (PhD in philosophy and neuroscience, Princeton). It runs a 'philosophy-to-code pipeline' that turns theories of reasoning and inquiry into open-source software for AI that supports human reasoning and autonomy. Projects include PyETR (an implementation of Koralus's Erotetic Theory of Reason), the Inquiry Complex (question frameworks for knowledge-seeking AI), Humans In Humans Out (which human reasoning patterns, sound and fallacious, LLMs reproduce) and Blueprint (an agent sandbox built for human interpretability).

It starts from a philosophical and cognitive-scientific theory of human reasoning, rather than from ML benchmarks, to design AI that strengthens people's own inquiry instead of replacing it. That is a constructive answer to cognitive atrophy and erosion of agency, which safety work mostly treats only as a harm to measure.

Works on Human minds, Epistemics, Agency · Key work PyETR: open-source implementation of the Erotetic Theory of Reason (2024); Humans In Humans Out: how LLMs replicate human reasoning patterns (2025); The Inquiry Complex: question-based frameworks for knowledge-seeking AI (2025) · Get involved Philosophy, AI and Innovation seminar, co-taught by philosophers and technologists each Trinity Term (Oxford); Annual Cosmos HAI Lab Lecture and other public events; Research associate and doctoral positions, several funded through the Cosmos Fellowship

Note Funding depends heavily on one donor network (Cosmos Institute and the McCord Professorship), whose classical-liberal outlook shapes its framing around autonomy rather than risk. Its framing is human flourishing, not catastrophic risk.

Leverhulme Centre for the Future of Intelligence (CFI) Bridge

Academic · Cambridge, UK · founded 2016 · also draws on Arts, futures, Psychology

An interdisciplinary research centre at the University of Cambridge, founded in 2016 with a £10m grant from the Leverhulme Trust, with spokes at Imperial College London and UC Berkeley. Its programmes are Kinds of Intelligence (comparing animal, human and machine cognition, including the Animal-AI testbed), AI: Futures and Responsibility, AI: Trust and Society, AI: Narratives and Justice, and Design, Participation & Praxis. It teaches an MPhil in Ethics of AI, Data and Algorithms and supervises PhD students.

It holds humanities and cognitive-science methods the safety field rarely uses: animal-cognition tasks that separate real competence from benchmark shortcuts, and the main evidence base on how different cultures imagine AI. It sits beside CSER in Cambridge's Institute for Technology and Humanity, so its people already move between x-risk and humanities work.

Works on Agency, Epistemics, Justice · Key work Animal-AI environment and the Animal-AI Olympics (about 900 animal-cognition tasks for testing AI agents) (2019); Global AI Narratives project (2018–22), with the OUP volume 'AI Narratives' (2018); AI: Futures and Responsibility programme (foresight, governance, safety and security) · Get involved MPhil in Ethics of AI, Data and Algorithms (nine months, full-time); PhD study and scholarships; Staff vacancies and visiting positions listed on its site

Note A broad centre: much of its output is on present-day ethics, justice and culture rather than catastrophic risk, so how relevant it is depends on the programme. Global AI Narratives ended in 2022, though the Narratives and Justice programme continues. Its CASP group is on the aisafety.com map, but the centre as a whole is not. I did not confirm how it is funded now that the 2016 founding grant has run its course.

Machine Intelligence and Normative Theory Lab (MINT Lab) Bridge

Academic · Washington DC, USA · founded 2022

A philosophy lab led by Seth Lazar, founded at the Australian National University in 2022 and now based at Johns Hopkins University's School of Government and Policy. It studies whether AI agents can recognise and act on moral reasons ('normative competence'), how societies should govern AI agents, and political philosophy for a world with advanced AI. It runs an AGI Governance Fellowship and holds workshops at venues such as IASEAI.

It turns moral and political philosophy into concrete agendas for evaluating and governing AI agents, a link most alignment groups lack. Its funding (SFF, Templeton, CSET, OpenAI) shows that philosophy-led safety work can attract mainstream AI-safety money.

Works on Values, Assurance, Democracy · Key work AGI Governance Fellowship, co-led with Gillian K. Hadfield and Nicholas Caputo (2026); Workshop on Normative Competence and AGI-Ready Institution Design workshop at IASEAI '26 (2026); AI and Democratic Freedoms public symposium with the Knight First Amendment Institute, Columbia (2025) · Get involved AGI Governance Fellowship (2026 cohort) at Johns Hopkins School of Government and Policy; Workshops and public symposia, e.g. the IASEAI '26 workshops (February 2026)

Note The lab is moving from ANU to Johns Hopkins: Lazar's CV lists him as a JHU professor from 2026, while the lab site dates the move to 2025, so team composition may be changing. Lazar also has industry and sector ties: a 2025 visiting faculty researcher post at Google (0.2 FTE) and a research scientist role at Resolution from 2026. It received a small OpenAI grant.

The Mimir Center for Long Term Futures Research Bridge

Programme · Stockholm, Sweden · also draws on Arts, futures

A research project at the Institute for Futures Studies (IFFS), an independent research foundation in Stockholm, led by philosopher Joe Roussos (principal investigator) and Emma Engström (co-PI), with Anders Sandberg, Karim Jebari and Gustaf Arrhenius among its researchers. It does academic research on long-term futures: global catastrophic and extinction risk, social collapse, decision-making under deep uncertainty, space governance, novel technologies and whole brain emulation. AI-related outputs include a 2025 working paper on the 'time of perils' and world governance, a 2025 paper arguing long-term AI policy should start from today's deep learning, and a January 2025 workshop on the ethics of brain emulation.

It brings population ethics, decision theory and international-relations theory to existential risk, including AI, from an academic home outside the Oxford/Bay Area network, and Anders Sandberg carries over Future of Humanity Institute themes after FHI's closure. Its brain-emulation work links digital-minds questions to futures studies.

Works on Metacrisis, AI status · Key work Jebari & Adler, 'The Time of Perils and a World System of Governance' (IFFS working paper 2025:1) (2025); Workshop on the Philosophy and Ethics of Brain Emulation (27-28 January 2025, organised by Tim Campbell and Anders Sandberg) (2025); Engström, 'AI:s tid som tankeexperiment är förbi' (long-term AI policy should start from deep learning), Tidskrift för politisk filosofi 2025:1 (2025) · Get involved Reading group roughly every three weeks, Fridays 13:30 CET, at IFFS in Stockholm and on Zoom (sign up via the site); Workshops on long-term futures topics (e.g. brain emulation, January 2025)

Note AI is one strand among many (climate, food, animals, space), and AI-specific output is a handful of papers and one workshop, so the bridge ring is on the thin side. No dated activity in 2026 was found, and its founding year and dedicated funder were not established.

VALAWAI (Value-Aware Artificial Intelligence), coordinated by IIIA-CSIC BridgeDormant

Programme · Barcelona, Spain · founded 2022 · also draws on Living systems, Psychology

An EIC Pathfinder project (grant 101070930, €3.93M, October 2022 to September 2026) coordinated by the Artificial Intelligence Research Institute of Spain's CSIC (IIIA-CSIC). Its partners are IMIM (Hospital del Mar), IIT, Ghent University, Sony Europe and Studio Stelluti. It built 'value-aware' AI: an architecture that pairs a Reflective Global Neuronal Workspace, a computational model of consciousness, with a moral framework for representing values and judging actions against them. The partners tested it on social-media moderation, social robots and medical decision protocols, and planned to release it as a developer toolbox. It also convened the 'Awareness in Artificial Agents' conference and an art-science installation at the 2025 Venice Biennale.

It approaches value alignment from moral philosophy, consciousness neuroscience and social psychology rather than from preference learning, and it treats value awareness as an architectural component of AI systems. Its publications and toolbox remain a European reference point for value-aware AI now that the project has ended.

Works on Values, Agency · Key work Value-aware AI toolbox and the Reflective Global Neuronal Workspace architecture (2026); Awareness in Artificial Agents conference and 'Am I a Strange Loop?' installation, Venice (2025); Social Value Alignment in Large Language Models; Encoding ethics to compute value-aligned norms (project publications) · Get involved Publications and the value-aware AI toolbox are listed on the project site; no open calls now that the project has ended

Note The project ended on 30 September 2026, four days before this profile, and no follow-on project was found on IIIA's projects page. Value-aware AI research continues among IIIA staff. Its 'awareness' is a functional architecture, not a claim about AI experience. The project frames itself around trustworthy AI, not catastrophic risk.

Adjacent ring 31

AAC&U Institute on AI, Pedagogy, and the Curriculum Adjacent

Programme · Washington, DC, USA · founded 2024

A seven-month online institute run by the American Association of Colleges and Universities (AAC&U). Campus teams of at least five people get expert sessions, design sessions, an assigned mentor and an online community while they work out how their courses and curricula should respond to AI. Themes include pedagogy, academic-integrity policy, 'the ethical and equity implications of AI', and writing AI competencies into learning outcomes. It began in September 2024 with 124 institutions; the 2025-26 cohort had 192 teams from 176 institutions, and the third cohort runs 10 Sept 2026 to 6 Apr 2027.

It is a large existing channel for reshaping non-computer-science university curricula around AI, reaching senior academic officers and faculty across disciplines. For anyone wanting the ethics or safety of AI taught across higher education, it is a ready route to campus decision-makers. It does not currently carry any safety or catastrophic-risk content.

Works on Epistemics, Meaning · Key work Inaugural institute (124 institutions, Sept 2024 to Apr 2025) (2024); 2025-26 cohort: 192 teams from 176 institutions (2025); 2026-27 institute (10 Sept 2026 to 6 Apr 2027) (2026) · Get involved Campus teams of at least five, ideally including a senior academic officer, apply each spring for the following academic year (the 2026-27 deadline was 9 Jun 2026); Fee-based and fully online; Mohawk College (Canada) has taken part, so non-US teams can apply

Note It is mainly about teaching with AI and adapting curricula. Ethics and equity are one theme among several, and there is no safety, alignment or catastrophic-risk framing, so its relevance to AI going well is indirect. It is a higher-education membership association's paid professional-development product, not a research programme. The institute faculty are not named publicly.

AIMODELS: The Culture of Algorithmic Models (ERC project, Ca' Foscari University of Venice) Adjacent

Programme · Venice, Italy · founded 2024 · also draws on Economics

An ERC Consolidator project (2024 to 2028) on the historical epistemology of AI, based in the Department of Philosophy and Cultural Heritage at Ca' Foscari University of Venice and led by Matteo Pasquinelli. It writes a history of AI through its algorithmic models and models of intelligence, builds a comparative epistemology with the psychology of learning, and studies how large foundation models affect the automation of work and digital culture. It holds yearly symposia: Chat Token Vector in 2025, and The World Algorithm, Dysphoria Mundi and Adversarial Poetry in 2026. It publishes open-access volumes and papers.

It argues that what matters about AI is its epistemic difference from human reason, not its similarity, which directly challenges the anthropomorphic assumptions in much AI-risk talk. It is a source for tracing where the field's ideas of intelligence, and of measuring intelligence, come from.

Works on Agency, Power · Key work Operativism: Labor, Automation, Agitation (eds Pasquinelli and Vogman) (2026); Machine, Organism, and Language: A Comparative Epistemology of AI Models (Pasquinelli) (2026); The Algorithm and the Antichrist: Political Theology and the Sunset of Silicon Valley (Cesarale and Pasquinelli) (2026) · Get involved Symposia and book presentations in Venice (next listed: Algomedia book presentation, 9 Dec 2026); Project newsletter (sign-up on the project site)

Note Its perspective is critical theory with roots in the political economy of labour. It is sceptical of anthropomorphic and Silicon Valley framings of AI and does not share AI-safety premises, so expect productive disagreement rather than alignment. The project ends in Dec 2028.

Association for Computational Linguistics (ACL): Ethics Committee and Responsible NLP Research Checklist Adjacent

Membership body · Kerrville, Texas, United States · founded 1962

The ACL is the international learned society for computational linguistics and natural language processing. It was founded in 1962 and runs the field's main conferences. In March 2020 it adopted the ACM Code of Ethics as its own. Its Ethics Committee (co-chairs Min-Yen Kan, Aurélie Névéol and Zhijing Jin) maintains ethics-review guidelines, reviewer training and teaching materials. Every paper submitted through ACL Rolling Review must complete the Responsible NLP Research Checklist, first developed for NAACL 2022 and revised for the October 2024 cycle. It asks authors about malicious or unintended harms, dual use, risks to marginalised groups, data practices and their use of AI assistants. Papers that are flagged get a separate ethics review.

Ethics review is built into the publication pipeline of the field that produces language models. That makes it a working model of field-wide harm review before publication, which AI-safety venues could copy or extend. It is also the main institutional door into the linguistics community, though that community is now heavily ML-dominated.

Works on People, Justice · Key work ACL Code of Ethics (adoption of the ACM Code) (2020); Responsible NLP Research Checklist (revised for ARR October 2024) (2024); Ethics reviewing guidelines for ACL Rolling Review (2022) · Get involved Volunteer as an ethics reviewer for ACL Rolling Review (training on ethics.aclweb.org); Teaching materials on NLP ethics for BSc, MSc and PhD levels on the ACL ethics site; ACL membership and conferences, which include ethics review

Note Computational linguistics now overlaps heavily with mainstream ML, so the ACL sits close to the AI mainstream. What is distinctive here is the research-ethics apparatus, not linguistic knowledge. The checklist covers research practice (harms, data, reproducibility), not catastrophic risk or alignment. The committee's site gives no founding date; a past co-chair served from 2021 to 2025.

Center for Philosophy of Artificial Intelligence (CPAI), University of Copenhagen Adjacent

Academic · Copenhagen, Denmark · also draws on Psychology, AI minds

CPAI is a research collective in the University of Copenhagen's Department of Communication, led by Anders Søgaard, that works in both directions between AI and philosophy. It uses philosophy to define fairness, explanation and representation for AI, and uses language models to study meaning, understanding and goal-directedness. Its 2025–26 output includes papers on whether language models have semantics, world models in Othello-playing models, explanation design, and an AAAI 2026 alignment-track paper on conceptions of intelligence. It co-hosts the Models of Consciousness 2026 conference (12–16 October 2026).

It is one of the few continental-European centres doing philosophy of language-model understanding together with hands-on NLP experiments. That combination bears on interpretability and on what alignment targets such as 'intelligence' or 'understanding' mean.

Works on Agency, Assurance · Key work Do Language Models Have Semantics? On the Five Standard Positions (ACL) (2025); Realist and Pluralist Conceptions of Intelligence and Their Implications on AI (Alignment) Research (AAAI alignment track) (2026); Models of Consciousness 2026 (MoC7), co-hosted with the Association for Mathematical Consciousness Science (2026) · Get involved Models of Consciousness 2026 conference, 12–16 Oct 2026, Copenhagen; Public talks and seminars listed on its events page

Note Models of Consciousness 2026 is organised by the Association for Mathematical Consciousness Science at the invitation of CPAI and other Copenhagen units, not by CPAI alone, and consciousness is not CPAI's main line of work. Its founding date and funding are not stated; its website was first archived in August 2025. Several outputs are mainstream NLP papers.

Center for Science and Thought (CST), University of Bonn Adjacent

Academic · Bonn, Germany · founded 2017 · also draws on Safety science, Law, society

An interdisciplinary centre in the University of Bonn's philosophy department, directed by the philosopher Markus Gabriel and the physicist Ulf-G. Meißner, that puts philosophy in dialogue with physics, neuroscience, biology and computer science. Its AI work includes the philosophy sub-project of Certified AI (ethical requirements for certifying AI systems, with Fraunhofer IAIS under North Rhine-Westphalia's KI.NRW flagship), Desirable Digitalisation (with Cambridge, funded by Stiftung Mercator) on designing AI for social justice and ecological sustainability, and Polyglot, which builds open foundation models for low-resource languages. It also runs 'AI at a Crossroads', an online seminar series with partners in Brazil, India and Greece on AI in death, intimacy, care and counselling.

It joins philosophy of technology to concrete standard-setting: its catalogue of ethical requirements for AI certification fed into Germany's AI standardisation roadmap. Its partnership with Cambridge's Leverhulme Centre for the Future of Intelligence and its seminar series with Brazilian and Indian partners bring continental, feminist and non-Western perspectives into AI governance.

Works on Assurance, Justice, Meaning · Key work Certified AI: Catalogue of General Ethical Requirements for AI Certification and white paper on the philosophical foundations of AI certification (2023-26); Desirable Digitalisation (with University of Cambridge; Mercator Visiting Professorship) (ongoing); Conference 'Philosophy of Technology and AI: Traditions, Transitions, and Tensions' (with Leverhulme CFI), 4-6 November (2026) · Get involved 'AI at a Crossroads' online seminar series, open via the philosophy_and_ai mailing list (listen.uni-bonn.de); Philosophy of Technology and AI conference, Bonn, 4-6 November 2026; Feminist AI Network for women researchers and students (University of Bonn)

Note Founding year inferred from Gabriel's directorship 'since 2017'; no explicit founding date found. The Certified AI project is extended only to the end of 2026; the Desirable Digitalisation funding period was not found. Huw Price (co-founder of CSER and former director of Leverhulme CFI) was associated with CST only in 2022-23. Its AI work is about responsible design, certification and justice, not catastrophic risk.

Centre for Philosophy and AI Research (PAIR), FAU Erlangen-Nürnberg Adjacent

Academic · Erlangen, Germany

A philosophy-of-AI research centre at Friedrich-Alexander-Universität Erlangen-Nürnberg, set up with Vincent C. Müller's Alexander von Humboldt Professorship in Theory and Ethics of AI. About a dozen researchers work on what AI is, could be and should be, across philosophy of mind and science, epistemology, ethics and political philosophy, and the centre runs a weekly research seminar and workshops (responsibility gaps, agentic AI, AI and mental health). It is linked to the Society for the Philosophy of AI, which Müller chairs, with its diamond open-access journal Philosophy of AI and the biennial conference series (PT-AI).

Müller edited the 2016 collection Risks of Artificial Intelligence and ran an early expert survey on AI timelines and risk with Nick Bostrom, but has since argued (Ratio, 2022) that the standard singularity-plus-orthogonality argument for existential risk is unsound. That makes PAIR a source of informed philosophical scrutiny of the concepts AI safety rests on (intelligence, goals, responsibility), and its society, journal and conference are a meeting point for philosophers of AI that the safety field rarely uses.

Works on Agency, Justice, Human minds · Key work Correspondence in Nature on Gen Z students' scepticism about AI in education (Robertson, Müller, Catena) (2026); Workshop 'Beyond Responsibility: New Gaps with AI Systems?' (2026); Online Workshop on Agentic AI (2025) · Get involved Weekly research seminar in Erlangen; event announcements via the fau-pair mailing list; Visiting fellowships for doctoral students, postdocs and senior visitors; open positions and hosting of independently funded PhD students (pair.fau.eu/jobs); Submit to the diamond open-access journal Philosophy of AI; the biennial Conference on Philosophy of AI (7th edition due 2027)

Note The centre's founding year is not stated; it was created through the Humboldt Professorship announced in November 2021. Müller's AI-risk publications (2014 JETAI special issue, 2016 edited volume, 2016 expert survey with Bostrom) mostly predate PAIR, and his 2022 paper with Michael Cannon is sceptical of the standard existential-risk argument. The 2026 Nature item is a Correspondence, not a research paper. The PhAI journal is hosted by the University of Cologne library.

Centre for Technomoral Futures, University of Edinburgh Adjacent

Academic · Edinburgh, UK · founded 2020 · also draws on Law, society

A research and teaching centre in the Edinburgh Futures Institute that aims to 'unify technical and moral knowledge' in work on AI and data. It runs the MSc in Data and AI Ethics (44 students in 2024-25), a PhD fellowship programme (18 fellows), an affiliates network and industry training, for example a four-day AI and data ethics course for NatWest. Its research covers AI and human agency, the integrity of knowledge ecosystems, surveillance and rights, and corporate influence on AI policy. A 2026 FAccT paper with partners identified 27 patterns of 'Big AI' policy capture.

Shannon Vallor's virtue-ethics work, including 'The AI Mirror' (2024), treats AI as something that can erode or cultivate human moral skill. On that view practical wisdom is a human capacity to protect and train, which bears directly on int/a's claims about wisdom and inner development. The centre also forms a steady stream of AI-ethics practitioners through its MSc and PhD programmes.

Works on Meaning, Power, Epistemics · Key work MSc in Data and Artificial Intelligence Ethics (first cohort graduated October 2023) (2022); Study mapping how 'Big AI' influences AI laws and oversight (FAccT 2026) (2026); Building AI futures worth wanting (feature by Emily Sullivan) (2026) · Get involved MSc in Data and AI Ethics (University of Edinburgh); PhD fellowships (Baillie Gifford studentships); Postdoctoral posts, for example in philosophy of science and machine learning (advertised March 2026)

Note Folds in a duplicate entry for its own site, technomoralfutures.uk. Vallor's work is generally critical of AGI and x-risk framings, and the centre has no safety programme. Some listed affiliates, such as Kasirzadeh, appear to have moved to other institutions.

Chung-Ang University AI Humanities Research Institute (HK+ AI Humanities; 인공지능인문학연구소) Adjacent

Academic · Seoul, South Korea · founded 2017 · also draws on Arts, futures

A Chung-Ang University institute in Seoul that has carried the National Research Foundation of Korea's Humanities Korea Plus (HK+) agenda 'AI Humanities' since 2017. Its aim is to set up AI humanities as a new foundational humanities field. Research runs in five strands: AI relations and communication, AI ethics and norms, hermeneutics of humanities data, technology criticism, and AI society and culture. It publishes the KCI-listed Journal of AI Humanities three times a year (vol. 23, August 2026) and has co-published the international applied-ethics journal JAHR since 2021. It ran the International Conference on AI Humanities (ICAIH) every year from 2018 to at least 2024, and also holds domestic conferences and colloquia.

It is a sustained institutional attempt to make AI a central object of the humanities, with a peer-reviewed publication line. It opens a channel into Korean philosophy, linguistics, media and cultural studies of AI, work that English-language AI-safety research rarely reads.

Works on Meaning, Epistemics · Key work Journal of AI Humanities (인공지능인문학연구), vol. 23, including a paper on what agentic AI products must avoid (2026); 36th domestic conference: future jobs for the AI-native generation (2025); International Conference on AI Humanities (ICAIH), annual series (2018) · Get involved Submit papers to the Journal of AI Humanities (three issues a year); Attend its domestic AI-humanities conferences in Seoul (most recent September 2025)

Note Most output is in Korean. The host's name has shifted: the HK+ agenda sat in the CAU Humanities Research Institute (인문콘텐츠연구소), while 2025 events are billed under the AI Humanities Research Institute. HK+ funding comes in time-limited phases, and the site does not say whether NRF support continues. The framing is human-centred AI ethics and technology criticism, without a catastrophic-risk focus.

Comité consultatif national d'éthique du numérique (CCNEN), formerly CNPEN AdjacentChanged

Public body · Paris, France · founded 2024 · also draws on Law, society

France's statutory advisory committee on the ethics of digital technology and AI. Decree no. 2024-463 of 23 May 2024 created it as the successor to the Comité national pilote d'éthique du numérique (CNPEN), which had worked under the aegis of the bioethics committee CCNE since December 2019. It issues formal opinions, on its own initiative or at the request of government and other institutions. Earlier opinions covered chatbots (2021), autonomous vehicles (2021), AI in medical diagnosis (2023), generative AI (2023), facial and behavioural recognition (2024) and the metaverse (2024). In 2026 it issued a joint opinion with the CCNE on digital neurotechnologies, and the higher-education ministry asked it to examine AI in scientific research.

It is a working model of a standing, pluralist national ethics council for AI. Its 21 members include judges from the Conseil d'État and Cour de cassation, scientists and civil-society representatives, and it borrows its method from bioethics. Its opinions on emotional manipulation by chatbots, cognitive liberty and neurotechnology, and youth and social media cover human-mind harms that AI-safety policy work seldom addresses.

Works on Human minds, Epistemics, Justice · Key work Avis 150 du CCNE & Avis 10 du CCNEN: digital neurotechnologies (2026); CNPEN Avis 7: Systèmes d'intelligence artificielle générative, enjeux d'éthique (2023); CNPEN Avis 3: Agents conversationnels, enjeux d'éthique (2021) · Get involved Public events, e.g. 'Contrôler ou libérer nos cerveaux ?' on neurotechnologies (registration opened Sep 2025); Anyone can follow its opinions and agenda at ccnen.fr

Note Renamed and reconstituted: CNPEN (pilot, 2019-2024) became CCNEN by the May 2024 decree, and members were appointed in September 2025. It is advisory only, with no binding power. Its working-groups page is out of date (it still describes 2021-22 work).

Deutscher Ethikrat (German Ethics Council) Adjacent

Public body · Berlin, Germany · founded 2008 · also draws on Law, society

Germany's statutory national ethics council, set up on 11 April 2008 under the Ethics Council Act as successor to the National Ethics Council of 2001. Its 26 members, appointed by the President of the Bundestag, come from law, medicine, theology, philosophy and the social sciences. It issues opinions and recommendations and holds public hearings and conferences. Its main AI output is the March 2023 opinion 'Humans and Machines: Challenges of Artificial Intelligence', on whether AI expands or diminishes human authorship and responsible action in medicine, schools, public communication and administration. In June 2026 it issued an ad hoc statement on children and adolescents in the digital world.

It shows a pluralist, statutory process for public ethical deliberation on AI, bringing together law, theology, medicine and philosophy, of a kind the AI-safety field has few equivalents for. Its lens of human authorship and responsible agency gives a philosophical-anthropological vocabulary for loss of human agency as AI spreads.

Works on Meaning, Human minds · Key work Humans and Machines: Challenges of Artificial Intelligence (Opinion) (2023); Ad hoc statement on protection, participation and empowerment of children and adolescents in the digital world (2026); Web event 'Power and Images: AI and Political Opinion Formation' (2024) · Get involved Public annual and autumn conferences (2026 annual conference on protecting and strengthening democracy; autumn conference 11 Nov 2026, Leipzig); Public web events and hearings on its topics (AI events in Dec 2023 and Jun 2024)

Note AI is one of many topics. Its dedicated AI output is thin after the 2023 opinion: a 2024 web event and a 2026 statement on children's digital lives whose AI content was not confirmed. Members are appointed and change over time. Only the council's own site was checked.

Digital Humanism Initiative (DIGHUM) Adjacent

Network · Vienna, Austria · founded 2019 · also draws on Law, society

An international community of scholars, policymakers and industry figures, run from TU Wien's Center for Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning (CAIML) in Vienna. It grew out of the 2019 Vienna Manifesto on Digital Humanism, which calls for technology development and policy grounded in human rights, democracy, inclusion and diversity. It runs a fortnightly online lecture series, workshops and annual summer schools. It has also issued public statements on regulating digital technologies, the EU AI Act and ChatGPT, and is linked to a UNESCO Chair and a Vienna doctoral college on digital humanism.

It offers a continental-European humanist frame for AI governance, centred on rights, democracy and the public sphere. Its steering committee is mostly computer scientists, plus philosophers and lawyers (Vardi, Lee, Walsh, Nida-Rümelin, Nowotny, Rotenberg), so it is an established network that seldom talks to the AI-safety community.

Works on Justice, Democracy, Power · Key work Vienna Manifesto on Digital Humanism (2019); DIGHUM Lecture Series (fortnightly, online) (2026); Digital Humanism Summer School 2026 (with the Austrian Parliament, co-located with ESSAI 2026) (2026) · Get involved Fortnightly DIGHUM lectures and panels, online (Tuesdays, 17:00 CET); Annual Digital Humanism Summer School (application-based; 2026 edition run with the Austrian Parliament); Interdisciplinary workshops, e.g. 'Designing Business Models for Digital Humanism', 23 Nov 2026

Note dighum.org now redirects to caiml.org/dighum. The network is led by computer scientists. Its framing is human-centred technology and rights, not catastrophic risk, and its steering committee is large and mostly honorific.

Embedded EthiCS @ Harvard Adjacent

Programme · Cambridge, USA · founded 2017

A Harvard programme in which philosophers teach ethics modules inside computer-science courses, about ten courses a semester. Computer scientist Barbara Grosz and philosopher Alison Simmons piloted it in spring 2017. AI-related modules have covered fairness in model selection, value-laden reward design in reinforcement learning, the precautionary principle under uncertainty in NLP, the ethics of interpretability, deepfakes, autonomous vehicles, and open-source models and power. Modules in 2025-26 included one in 'Software Engineering with Gen AI'. It publishes its modules openly under CC BY 4.0, and Stanford, Toronto, Technion, Nebraska-Lincoln and California State University campuses have started similar programmes.

It is an established way to build normative judgement into the people who build AI while they learn the technical craft, and other universities have copied it. No explicit AI-safety or alignment module could be confirmed, so for the safety field the value lies in the teaching model rather than its current content.

Works on People, Justice · Key work Open repository of Embedded EthiCS teaching modules (CC BY 4.0) (2026); Embedded EthiCS: Integrating Ethics Across CS Education (Communications of the ACM) (2019); 'Technically, it's possible. Ethically, it's complicated' (Harvard Gazette on demand rising with AI use) (2025) · Get involved Open teaching modules for reuse by other universities (CC BY 4.0); Philosophy postdoctoral fellowships with the programme; Invites other institutions to adopt the model

Note Its modules cover present-day issues (fairness, privacy, deepfakes, trust in AI); no explicit AI-safety or alignment module was found. The news page on its site is stale, showing placeholder items from 2023.

Ethics of AI Research Group, Centre for AI Research (CAIR), University of Pretoria AdjacentUnverified

Academic · Pretoria, South Africa

The AI ethics node of South Africa's Centre for AI Research (CAIR), a multi-university network supported by the Department of Science and Innovation and the CSIR. The group sits in the University of Pretoria's Department of Philosophy and is coordinated by Emma Ruttkamp-Bloem, who chaired the UNESCO expert group that drafted the 2021 Recommendation on the Ethics of AI. Its listed topics include machine ethics, artificial moral agency, robot rights, autonomous weapons, data ethics and culturally sensitive AI policy for Africa. It ran the CAIR/UP AI for Society symposium series from 2018 to 2020.

It brings African relational ethics and epistemic- and data-justice arguments into global AI governance. Through its coordinator it reached the UNESCO Recommendation, a perspective largely missing from Northern AI-safety policy work.

Works on Justice, Values · Key work UNESCO Recommendation on the Ethics of AI (drafting group chaired by Ruttkamp-Bloem) (2021); CAIR/UP AI for Society Symposium series (5th edition) (2020); Relationality and Data Justice for Trustworthy AI Practices in Africa (2025) · Get involved Postgraduate supervision in AI ethics through the University of Pretoria Department of Philosophy (per the coordinator's CAIR profile)

Note The group's web presence is stale: the last listed event is from 2020, the last publication from 2022, and only the coordinator is listed as a member. Recent output found is the coordinator's own, so it is unclear whether the group operates as a unit in 2026.

Ethics of Socially Disruptive Technologies (ESDiT) Adjacent

Programme · Enschede, Netherlands · founded 2020

A ten-year Dutch research consortium in the philosophy and ethics of technology, started in 2020 with NWO/OCW Gravitation funding. It brings together more than 60 researchers from seven Dutch universities across nine research lines. Its central question is how technologies such as AI, robotics, gene editing and geo-engineering unsettle the concepts that moral and political thinking relies on (agency, responsibility, personhood, democracy, the line between natural and artificial), and how those concepts should be revised.

Its 'conceptual disruption' and conceptual-engineering work asks how AI changes the meaning of the concepts that alignment and governance assume are fixed, such as responsibility, agency and moral status. Mainstream AI safety rarely asks this. Its intercultural-philosophy line (Ubuntu and Buddhist keynotes, a Yaoundé seminar) also brings in non-Western ethics.

Works on Meaning, Justice · Key work 4TU.Ethics / ESDiT Conference 2026: philosophy and ethics of technology in turbulent times (Wageningen, 4-6 Nov) (2026); Conceptual Disruption research line (incl. PhD project 'Conceptual ethics for socially disruptive technologies', 2025-2029) (2025); Brey and Dainow, 'Ethics by Design for Artificial Intelligence', AI and Ethics (2023) · Get involved 4TU.Ethics/ESDiT Conference, Wageningen, 4-6 Nov 2026 (registration closed 1 Oct 2026); Calls for abstracts, e.g. the 2026 Yaoundé Seminar on Justice, Democracy and Technology; PhD and postdoc vacancies posted on the site (most recent April 2026)

Note This is a time-limited consortium due to end around 2029-30. AI is one of three technology clusters, alongside bio/brain and environmental technologies, and the programme does not frame AI in terms of safety or catastrophic risk. Founding and budget details come from ESDiT's own annual report.

European Group on Ethics in Science and New Technologies (EGE) Adjacent

Public body · Brussels, Belgium · founded 1991 · also draws on Law, society

An independent, multidisciplinary advisory body of ethicists, lawyers and scientists, founded in 1991, that advises the President of the European Commission where ethics, society and fundamental rights meet science and technology. The current group was appointed on 26 January 2025. Its AI-related advice includes a 2018 statement on AI, robotics and 'autonomous' systems, the opinion 'Democracy in the digital age' (2023) and 'Governing neuro-AI' (September 2026). The Commission has said it will request three further AI opinions in 2027: AI in science, fair digital futures, and AI in the energy system. Its secretariat also runs an international dialogue linking national ethics councils from 97 countries.

It is the EU's highest-level ethics advisory body, and its rights-based, infrastructural analyses go straight to the Commission President. Its neuro-AI opinion treats neural data as a political-economic resource and raises concerns about concentration and dual use, a framing the AI-safety field rarely brings into EU policy.

Works on Justice, Democracy, Human minds · Key work Governing neuro-AI (statement) (2026); Democracy in the digital age (opinion) (2023); Statement on Artificial Intelligence, Robotics and 'Autonomous' Systems (2018) · Get involved Members are appointed by the Commission President, with candidates found by an identification committee; Its research support project, SAEGE, holds public sessions, e.g. at a technology-ethics conference on 4 Nov 2026

Note AI is one topic among many; its other recent opinions cover nature, the just green transition, solar geoengineering and ultra-processed foods. Its advice is non-binding and framed around fundamental rights and democracy, not catastrophic risk.

Globethics Adjacent

Nonprofit · Geneva, Switzerland · founded 2004 · also draws on Religion, Law, society

Globethics is a Geneva-based international ethics NGO, founded in 2004 by the ethicist Christoph Stückelberger with 29 ethics experts from 21 countries. It holds ECOSOC consultative status and runs training, consulting, publishing (an open research library and journals) and conferences through regional centres in Accra, Bangalore, Buenos Aires, Cape Town, Nairobi, Tunis and Yogyakarta. 'Ethics of AI and Emerging Technology' is one of its three focus areas. Under it, Globethics runs the Emerging Leaders in Ethical AI Governance Fellowship (14 fellows in 2026, chosen from 1,660+ applications), chairs a UNESCO subgroup on empowering citizens and civil-society organisations in AI governance, and facilitates a UNESCO course for civil society.

It brings two decades of applied-ethics training, multi-faith and church networks, and Global South regional centres into AI governance. In 2026 it co-hosted the first AI for Good panel on religious perspectives, with the Muslim Council of Elders. It offers a route for plural, non-Western ethical voices to reach civil society and policy forums that the AI-safety field rarely engages.

Works on Justice, Democracy, People · Key work Emerging Leaders in Ethical AI Governance Fellowship (Geneva residency during Geneva Digital Week) (2026); Chairing UNESCO's subgroup on Empowering Citizens and CSOs in AI Governance; course 'Empowering CSOs to Lead the Way in Advancing AI Ethics' (2026); WSIS Prizes Champion 2025 for 'Amplifying the Voice of the Global South for Ethical Knowledge and Education' (2025) · Get involved Emerging Leaders in Ethical AI Governance Fellowship: 14 fellows in 2026; applications for the 2027 cohort 'will open soon'; Open Track webinars with the 2026 fellows, online, 26 May–16 Dec 2026; Global Ethics Forum 2026, Bali and hybrid, 20–22 Oct 2026

Note Its website does not disclose funders. Besides its NGO work it sells consulting and advisory services, including to multinational businesses. Its roots are in Protestant ecumenical ethics (the founder and board president are theologians), though it presents itself as a non-confessional ethics organisation. When it says 'safe' AI it means inclusive, rights-based governance, not catastrophic risk.

Hokkaido University Center for Human Nature, Artificial Intelligence, and Neuroscience (CHAIN) Adjacent

Academic · Sapporo, Japan · founded 2019 · also draws on Living systems, AI minds

An interdisciplinary research and graduate-education centre at Hokkaido University in Sapporo. It brings philosophy, especially phenomenology and the Kyoto School thinker Tanabe Hajime, together with neuroscience and AI, around four questions: consciousness, self, sociality and rationality. Since July 2020 it has run a graduate education programme with summer and winter schools; 33 students joined in 2026. It also runs a long seminar series (#63 in Sept 2026). In September 2026 it hosted the international symposium 'Rethinking Humanity in the Age of AI', with Shannon Vallor, David Gunkel and Anna Puzio, on how generative AI changes creativity, communication and moral judgement.

It approaches human nature in the age of AI through Japanese and continental philosophy (phenomenology, enactivism, Tanabe) working alongside neuroscientists and AI researchers. It trains graduate students across these fields. That gives a non-Anglophone lens on meaning, embodiment and moral judgement, and a convening point for AI ethics in East Asia.

Works on Meaning, Agency · Key work International symposium 'Rethinking Humanity in the Age of AI' (4-5 Sept 2026; keynotes Vallor, Gunkel, Puzio, Miyazono) (2026); CHAIN graduate education programme integrating humanities, neuroscience and computer science (since July 2020) (2020); Two AI for Science (SPReAD) grants: AI robot birds for songbird vocal communication; an AI partner for an embodied Turing test (2026) · Get involved Public seminars and international symposia (in person, Sapporo); Graduate education programme (open to Hokkaido University master's and PhD students); Visiting researcher and partner-institution links

Note No AI-safety framing. The AI work spans ethics events, embodied cognition and AI-for-science projects rather than one AI programme. Hokkaido University established CHAIN in July 2019 (inaugural ceremony 23 July 2019); the graduate programme began in July 2020, and CHAIN became a permanent department in April 2024. In Aug 2026 CHAIN warned that a cryptocurrency (memecoin) was misusing its name; it has no connection to the centre.

IEEE 7014 and IEEE 7014.1 Emulated Empathy standards Adjacent

Programme · Distributed · also draws on Psychology, Safety science

Two IEEE Standards Association documents on 'emulated empathy', both sponsored by the Social Implications of Technology Standards Committee. IEEE 7014-2024 (published 28 June 2024) covers autonomous and intelligent systems in general; IEEE 7014.1-2026, a Recommended Practice for partner-based general-purpose AI such as companions, assistants and co-pilots, was approved on 12 February 2026 and published on 12 June 2026. The 7014.1 working group of about 70 people, chaired by Andrew McStay, set out 29 recommendations covering a product's life cycle from concept to decommissioning, and the text is free to read.

It is the only consensus standards track on how AI 'partners' should perform empathy, with recommendations on dependency, manipulation, deception and children. AI-safety work on sycophancy and personas could cite or build on an instrument that regulators, courts and developers can already use.

Works on Human minds, Assurance · Key work IEEE 7014-2024: Standard for Ethical Considerations in Emulated Empathy in Autonomous and Intelligent Systems (2024); IEEE 7014.1-2026: Recommended Practice for Ethical Considerations of Emulated Empathy in Partner-Based General-Purpose AI Systems (2026); 'When is Deception OK?' Developing the IEEE Recommended Practice (IEEE ISTAS paper) (2024) · Get involved Read IEEE 7014.1 free (linked from emotionalai.org/ieee-70141); IEEE 7014-2024 is free for personal use through the IEEE GET Program; For future revisions, contact the working-group officers through IEEE SA; the 7014 page says its chair welcomes enquiries

Note A voluntary recommended practice; company uptake is unknown. The 7014 working group has been inactive since publication, and the 7014.1 group has probably wound down after publication in June 2026. The 7014.1 effort was led from the Emotional AI Lab, which has its own entry. The year the 7014 project began was not confirmed.

IEEE Global Initiative 2.0 on Ethics of Autonomous and Intelligent Systems AdjacentUnverified

Programme · Piscataway, USA · founded 2016 · also draws on Safety science

An IEEE Standards Association Industry Connections activity (IC16-002), renewed in 2023. It builds on the original Global Initiative, which produced Ethically Aligned Design and led to the IEEE 7000 series of standards. The 2.0 plan aims to move AI governance 'beyond risk framing' towards a safety-first, safety-by-design principle. It has four workstreams: new standards for generative AI and large language models, sector toolkits linked to IEEE conformity assessment, an 'AI Safety Champions' community, and wider use of the 7000-series standards.

It is a route by which ethical principles become engineering standards and certification. Its predecessor's Ethically Aligned Design included a chapter on classical and non-Western ethical traditions and fed into wellbeing-metric standards. For the int/a map it shows how pluralist ethics can enter technical standards, though current activity is hard to verify.

Works on Assurance, Values · Key work Ethically Aligned Design, First Edition (predecessor initiative's report) (2019); IEEE 7000 series of standards on ethical concerns in system design; Planned report: 'Beyond Risk Framing in AI Governance' (not yet published) · Get involved Participation open to anyone involved in researching, designing or deciding on intelligent systems, via the interest form on the activity page

Note Activity is unverified: the activity page describes the 2.0 plan agreed in 2023, but no 2024-26 deliverables, meetings or AI Safety Champions outputs were found. It is not listed among current Industry Connections activities, nor among closed ones. 'Safety' here means engineering and product safety, not catastrophic risk. The 2019 date for Ethically Aligned Design 1e and the 2016 founding rest on the predecessor initiative and its IC16 code.

Institut de recherche et d'innovation (IRI), Centre Pompidou Adjacent

Nonprofit · Paris, France · founded 2006 · also draws on Arts, futures, Economics

A Paris research association created at the Centre Pompidou in 2006 on the initiative of the philosopher Bernard Stiegler, independent since 2008. It works on 'digital studies', contributory research and annotation software (Lignes de temps), and runs the annual Entretiens du Nouveau Monde Industriel (ENMI). ENMI 2025 was devoted to generative AI ('artificial synthesis and human contribution'), arguing that models depend on human contribution and calling for a contributory economy of knowledge; ENMI 2026 ('La clinique des objets') includes sessions on physical AI, robotics and computing.

It carries Stiegler's 'pharmacological' philosophy of technology, which analyses how automation erodes human knowledge and attention ('proletarianisation') and proposes a contributory economy in response, a line of thought almost absent from AI-safety discourse. It also convenes philosophers, designers and economists in Paris every year.

Works on Epistemics, Power, Human minds · Key work ENMI 2025: Synthèse artificielle et contribution humaine (CNAM, Paris, 16–17 Dec 2025) (2025); ENMI 2026: La clinique des objets (Cité des sciences, Paris, 14–15 Dec 2026), with a session on physical AI and robotics (2026); ENMI préparatoires 2026 seminars (ENSCI, 25–26 June 2026) (2026) · Get involved ENMI 2026, 14–15 Dec 2026, Cité des sciences et de l'industrie, Paris, with remote participation; ENMI preparatory seminars each June in Paris, joinable remotely via BigBlueButton

Note Founder Bernard Stiegler died in 2020; current leadership is from Wikipedia and may be out of date, and the website's project and team pages are sparse. Its AI work is critical of the AI industry's extractive model rather than framed around safety. Ring changed from the roster's potential to adjacent.

Institute for Technology, Ethics, and Culture (ITEC), Markkula Center for Applied Ethics, Santa Clara University Adjacent

Programme · Santa Clara, United States · founded 2023 · also draws on Religion

ITEC is a collaboration between Santa Clara University's Markkula Center for Applied Ethics and the Vatican's Dicastery for Culture and Education. It helps companies put ethical principles into practice for AI and other disruptive technologies. Its main output is the ITEC Handbook, 'Ethics in the Age of Disruptive Technologies: An Operational Roadmap' (2023), a free five-stage guide with a primer and a set of principles. It also commissioned a November 2023 survey of 3,000 Americans on AI ethics, and it publishes commentary on Catholic perspectives on AI.

It is a standing channel between the Vatican and Silicon Valley firms, turning Catholic social teaching on human dignity and the common good into corporate governance steps. Its director of technology ethics publicly backed slowing advanced AI in 2026 and warned about recursive self-improvement, which makes him a rare Catholic voice on loss-of-control risk.

Works on People, Meaning · Key work ITEC Handbook: Ethics in the Age of Disruptive Technologies: An Operational Roadmap (2023); Ethics in the Age of AI: survey of 3,000 Americans (2023); ITEC Principles (anchoring, guiding and specifying principles) · Get involved The ITEC Handbook, primer and principles are free downloads for organisations; Markkula Center webinar recordings on AI and Pope Leo XIV's encyclical 'Magnifica Humanitas' (2026)

Note The draft dated the survey to 2025; it was fielded on 7 November 2023 (83% wanted clearer federal AI regulation; 70% supported a temporary pause). ITEC was announced on 28 June 2023 together with the Handbook, most of its own outputs date from 2023, and its 2025–26 activity is mainly media commentary by Markkula staff. The Markkula Center is under an interim executive director after Don Heider's departure.

Japanese Society for Artificial Intelligence (JSAI) Ethics Committee (人工知能学会 倫理委員会) Adjacent

Programme · Tokyo, Japan · founded 2014 · also draws on Law, society, Arts, futures

The ethics committee of the Japanese Society for Artificial Intelligence, Japan's main AI learned society. It was relaunched in 2014 under Yutaka Matsuo and deliberately includes outsiders: science-fiction novelists, journalists, legal scholars and philosophers. It wrote the JSAI Ethical Guidelines (approved February 2017), whose ninth clause says that an AI which becomes a member or quasi-member of society must abide by the guidelines too. It also runs the AI-ELSI Award, holds sessions at JSAI meetings and issues statements.

It is an example of a professional society writing a researchers' code through open debate, with science-fiction writers as standing members, and it posed an early, deliberate question about AI as a moral agent bound by its own code. Its third award gave a special prize to the AI Alignment Network's superintelligence scenario contest, a sign that Japan's mainstream AI community is open to safety themes.

Works on People, Human minds · Key work JSAI Ethical Guidelines (with clause 9 on AI abiding by the guidelines) (2017); Third AI-ELSI Award report (prizes incl. Dialogue for Desirable AI and AI Alignment Network scenario contest) (2026); Session 'LLMs, people, AI and ethics' on AI dependence, JSAI joint research meeting (2025) · Get involved Attend its ethics sessions at JSAI annual conferences and joint research meetings (registration required); Apply for the AI-ELSI Award when a call opens (third round took applications Jan-Mar 2025)

Note As a committee of an AI learned society, it is rooted in the AI field rather than an outside discipline, though its members bring law, philosophy, STS and fiction. Its recent statements stress human-AI symbiosis, research competitiveness and security more than risk. Output is mostly in Japanese, and activity is periodic.

Jubilee Centre for Character and Virtues Adjacent

Academic · Birmingham, UK · founded 2012 · also draws on Psychology

A University of Birmingham research centre on character, virtues and values, founded in 2012 with John Templeton Foundation funding and directed by Tom Harrison. It does research, runs a distance-learning MA in Character Education, online professional courses and an annual Oxford conference, and publishes frameworks for character education in schools. Its staff have lectured on AI and practical wisdom since 2024, and in 2026 Harrison published four essays (April to September) arguing that AI makes cultivating judgment, or 'digital phronesis', the central aim of education.

It is the most developed academic home for practical wisdom (phronesis) as a construct with measurement and teaching frameworks, which bears directly on evaluating 'wise AI' and on the moral deskilling of people who hand judgment to AI. It brings neo-Aristotelian virtue ethics to AI's effects on human formation, with no catastrophic-risk framing.

Works on Meaning, Human minds · Key work The AI Era Could Be Character Education's Defining Moment (2026); On the Possibilities and Problematics of AI-Enhanced Character Education (2026); Artificial Intelligence and Phronesis (Liz Gulliford lecture, Madrid) (2024) · Get involved 15th Annual Conference 'Character and Vocation', 6-8 Jan 2027, Oriel and Magdalen Colleges, Oxford; call for papers includes changes in the digital age; MA Character Education (distance learning) and online CPD courses, including professional ethics; PhD supervision

Note Its AI output so far is lectures and short blog essays by the director rather than a funded AI research project. Templeton-funded virtue-ethics centre with a strong advocacy line for character education. Staff size estimated from named staff.

Nishan Forum on World Civilizations (Nishan World Center for Confucian Studies) Adjacent

Programme · Qufu, China · founded 2010 · also draws on Religion

A state-backed international forum on dialogue between civilisations, held near Qufu, Shandong (Confucius's birthplace) since 2010. The Nishan World Center for Confucian Studies organises it with Chinese central and provincial government bodies. AI became one of six sub-topics in 2025 (the 11th forum, July 2025, 'the development of AI and the trajectory of human civilisation') and again in late September 2026 ('Artificial Intelligence and Universal Harmony', overall theme 'Civilization · Order · Justice', 340+ guests from 40+ countries). There, Confucian and Daoist scholars and Tsinghua's Xue Lan argued for Confucian ethics as a basis for responsible AI and global AI governance.

It is the main recurring venue where Confucian and Daoist scholars, Chinese officials and foreign academics discuss AI ethics and governance together. That makes it a window on how Chinese relational ethics (ren, 'do not impose on others what you do not desire') is being put forward as an input to global AI norms, and a possible channel for East-West dialogue on what AI should serve.

Works on Meaning, Values · Key work When AI Meets Confucius: How Ancient Wisdom Responds to Technological Anxiety (2026 'AI and Universal Harmony' sub-topic report) (2026); Xue Lan: Advancing Global AI Governance from Conceptual Consensus to Institutional Practice (2026); 11th Nishan Forum, with sub-topic 'the development of artificial intelligence and the trajectory of human civilization' (2025) · Get involved Participation appears to be by invitation; no open call for the AI sub-topic was found; English-language reports and speaker summaries are published at nishan.chinakongzi.org/en

Note A state-linked platform that promotes China's Global Civilization Initiative and cultural soft power. The AI content is one of six sub-topics and consists of short speeches and a forum consensus, not research. The forum's own pages give different dates for the 2026 edition (28-29 or 29-30 Sep), and the edition numbering after the 11th (2025) is unclear.

Nuffield Council on Bioethics (NCOB) Adjacent

Nonprofit · London, UK · founded 1991 · also draws on Democracy

Independent UK policy and research centre that identifies, analyses and advises on ethical issues in biomedicine and health. It works through expert working groups, horizon scanning, calls for evidence and public deliberation, including a 2024 citizens' jury on assisted dying. Its AI work has been occasional: 2018 briefings on AI in healthcare, and a joint project with the Ada Lovelace Institute on AI and genomics (2023-24), whose final report advised that the NHS should not yet roll out AI-powered genomic health prediction widely. In July 2026 it launched a project on brain-computer interfaces and their convergence with AI and quantum computing.

It has decades of practice in anticipatory governance of contested technologies such as genome editing and neurotechnology, using working groups, horizon scans and public deliberation. These methods could be applied to frontier AI or digital minds. Its new BCI project takes it into questions of autonomy, identity and privacy where AI meets neurotechnology.

Works on Human minds, Justice · Key work Predicting: the future of health? (AI and genomics futures, with the Ada Lovelace Institute) (2024); DNA.I. - Early findings and emerging questions on the use of AI in genomics (2023); Neurotechnology in healthcare: brain-computer interfaces and their convergence with AI and quantum computing (project launch) (2026) · Get involved Respond to calls for evidence, such as the 2026 BCI project's; Follow its annual horizon scans and blog

Note The roster said it had been inactive on AI since 2018. That is not right: it ran an AI and genomics project in 2023-24 and launched a BCI/AI project in 2026. AI is still not one of its standing priorities, and its work is health-focused rather than about frontier AI risk.

Research Network for Philosophy and Technology Adjacent

Network · Distributed · founded 2014

An international academic network founded in 2014 that rethinks philosophy and technology from global and historical perspectives, including non-modern and non-Western traditions. It publishes the open-access journal Technophany and the 'Cybernetics for the 21st Century' volumes (Hanart Press). With Erasmus University Rotterdam, ITS Rio and Hanart Forum it runs the free online 'Dialogues on Philosophy and Technology' seminars, initiated by Yuk Hui, as well as summer seminars and the annual online Bernard Stiegler Memorial Lecture. Generative AI is a recurring topic in its journal and lecture series.

It is the institutional home of Yuk Hui's 'cosmotechnics' and 'technodiversity' critique, which holds that there is no single universal path of technological development. That critique bears directly on monoculture, lock-in and pluralism in how AI is built. It is also rethinking cybernetics, a precursor field that AI safety rarely draws on, for the machine-learning era.

Works on Meaning, Justice, Metacrisis · Key work Cybernetics for the 21st Century (vol. 1; Part II lecture series 'Cybernetics to Come') (2024); Technophany 2026 General Issue (including Coeckelbergh, 'AI Rituals', and Vudka, 'From Golem to GLLM') (2026); Dialogues on Philosophy and Technology 2025–2026 (online seminar series) (2025) · Get involved Dialogues on Philosophy and Technology: online, free and open to all; registration via Erasmus University Rotterdam; Annual Bernard Stiegler Memorial Lecture (online, early August); Technophany calls for papers (2026 General Issue CFP)

Note The network's statement never mentions AI. AI is one recurring topic among many in its journal and lectures, and it does not engage with AI safety or x-risk. The site names no formal leader; Yuk Hui's central role is evidenced by his initiating the Dialogues series and by the network's orientation.

Research Unit for Robophilosophy and Integrative Social Robotics (RISR), Aarhus University Adjacent

Academic · Aarhus, Denmark · founded 2012 · also draws on Psychology, Arts, futures

A research unit in Aarhus University's School of Culture and Society, coordinated by philosopher Johanna Seibt since 2012, working on 'philosophy of, for, and by social robotics' alongside empirical human–robot interaction studies. It developed Integrative Social Robotics, a method that brings humanities expertise into robot design, and runs projects such as DARE (assistive robots for older adults, 2025–27). It coordinates the biennial Robophilosophy conferences (2024 theme: 'Social Robots With AI: Prospects, Risks, and Responsible Methods'; 2026 at University College Dublin) and the TRANSOR research network and webinar series.

It has more than a decade of philosophy and HRI evidence on attachment, anthropomorphism and the moral and social status of artificial agents, and that work predates LLM companions. Its conferences are an existing venue where companion-harm and AI-status questions meet robot ethics and phenomenology.

Works on Human minds, AI status, Meaning · Key work Robophilosophy 2024: Social Robots With AI: Prospects, Risks, and Responsible Methods (keynotes incl. Chalmers, Turkle, Mitchell) (2024); Robophilosophy 2026: Connected Futures: Nature, Robots, and Society (UCD Dublin, 11–14 Aug) (2026); Robophilosophy: Philosophy of, for, and by Social Robotics (MIT Press, ed. Johanna Seibt, Raul Hakli and Marco Nørskov) (2026) · Get involved Robophilosophy conference series (biennial, hybrid); RP2026 ran 11–14 August 2026 in Dublin; Join the TRANSOR network (free) and attend TRANSOR Talks webinars online

Note Its focus is physical social robots rather than language models, and most listed projects ended between 2016 and 2025; the current main project, DARE, is about assistive robots for older adults. The founding date comes from Seibt's Aarhus research profile.

The Hastings Center for Bioethics Adjacent

Nonprofit · Garrison, NY, USA · founded 1969 · also draws on Law, society

The Hastings Center is an independent bioethics research institute founded in 1969 by philosopher Daniel Callahan and psychoanalyst Willard Gaylin. It helped found bioethics as a field and publishes the Hastings Center Report. It has a standing 'Health AI' research area. That area includes a five-year, Donaghue Foundation-funded project on bioethics, AI and trust in health care (Oct 2024–2029), led by president Vardit Ravitsky, and ethics work in two NIH Bridge2AI projects. It also publishes briefings and essays on AI in healthcare, mental-health chatbots and AI agents in scientific research. From 2017 to 2019 it ran an FLI-funded project with Stuart Russell, Bart Selman and Francesca Rossi on control and responsible innovation in AI.

Bioethics built oversight institutions (IRBs, informed consent, clinical ethics committees) for a powerful, fast-moving technology, and frontier AI has no equivalent. Hastings knows that history first-hand and has already engaged with AI control questions.

Works on Assurance, Justice · Key work Putting Bioethics to Work on AI, Trust, and Health Care (Donaghue Foundation, 2024–2029) (2024); AI Agents Are Transforming Scientific Research—but Raise Ethical Red Flags (Hastings Center Report) (2026); Briefing: AI in Healthcare (Jayaram and Owens) (2026) · Get involved Public webinars and events on AI in health and research ethics; Research staff roles (check the site)

Note Its AI work is mostly about health (clinical AI, research ethics, data ethics) and present harms. Its one AI-safety-style project ended in 2019. The site now uses the name 'The Hastings Center for Bioethics'. Staff size is an estimate.

TUM Institute for Ethics in Artificial Intelligence (IEAI) Adjacent

Academic · Munich, Germany · founded 2019 · also draws on Psychology, Law, society

An AI-ethics institute founded in 2019 at the Technical University of Munich, now part of its School of Social Sciences and Technology and directed by the business ethicist Christoph Lütge. It runs interdisciplinary projects on AI and human rights, the psychological impacts of interactive systems (PSAIS), AI-mediated civic participation, and AI for policymakers. It coordinates alignAI, a Horizon Europe doctoral network of 16 PhDs on aligning LLMs with human values in education, mental health and news. It publishes quarterly research briefs and hosts The Responsible AI Forum (TRAIF), the Global AI Ethics Consortium and the RAIN-Africa network.

alignAI pairs a social-science or humanities PhD with a technical PhD on each use case. This is a concrete training model for bringing value questions into LLM alignment work, which the safety field mostly treats as a technical problem. Its work on the psychological effects of chatbots, and on human rights as limits on state use of AI, adds normative depth.

Works on Values, Human minds, Justice · Key work alignAI: Horizon Europe doctoral network on aligning LLMs with human values (2026); Research brief Q3 2026: 'Human Rights as Negative Obligations in the Age of AI' (Julia Howard) (2026); TRAIF 2026: The Responsible AI Forum (19-20 May) (2026) · Get involved Job openings (ieai.sot.tum.de/jobs); Speaker series and The Responsible AI Forum (TRAIF); Thesis projects for TUM students

Note Founded with Facebook money. Press coverage of the leaked contract, cited by German Wikipedia, reported that Facebook could stop funding after the first US$1.5 million without giving reasons, and that replacing the director needed Facebook's written consent. Critics called it marketing for Facebook; Lütge called the arrangement a 'win-win'. Corporate funding continues. Its framing is responsible AI, not AI safety, and 'alignment' in alignAI centres on fairness and explainability in applied use cases.

Uehiro Oxford Institute (UOI) AdjacentChanged

Academic · Oxford, United Kingdom · founded 2024 · also draws on Psychology

The University of Oxford's practical-ethics institute. It was established in 2024 with a benefaction from the Uehiro Foundation on Ethics and Education, as the successor to the Oxford Uehiro Centre for Practical Ethics. It researches applied ethics across medicine, pandemics, war, climate and technology, publishes the Journal of Practical Ethics, and teaches an MSt in Practical Ethics. Its AI work includes an 'AI and Digital Ethics' theme, a series of papers on using large language models to support informed consent in medicine, research on relational norms and credit or blame for AI-generated content, and a scenario-planning network on AI, death and the afterlife.

It brings a large applied-ethics and experimental-moral-psychology group to concrete questions about humans and AI, such as when it is safe to deploy black-box AI in clinical care and whether AI can improve rather than erode moral decision-making. That is practical normative expertise most AI-safety groups lack.

Works on Human minds, Assurance, Values · Key work Allen, Wilkinson and Savulescu, 'When is it safe to introduce an AI system into healthcare? A practical decision algorithm for the ethical implementation of black-box AI in medicine', Bioethics (2026); Allen, Earp and Wilkinson, 'AI-Assisted Consent in Paediatric Medicine', Journal of Medical Ethics (2026); Scenario planning for AI, death and the afterlife (Medical Humanities-Uehiro network) (2024) · Get involved Director post advertised July 2026; research staff vacancies via the University of Oxford; Oxford Uehiro St Cross Visiting Programme and other academic visitor programmes; Public events: Uehiro lectures, Bitesize Ethics, neuroethics lecture (Nov 2026-Jan 2027)

Note Renamed and re-established in 2024 from the Oxford Uehiro Centre for Practical Ethics; the old practicalethics.ox.ac.uk domain is being retired in 2026. Leadership is in transition, with an interim director and a permanent search open. AI is one theme among many, and its AI output is mostly medical and digital ethics rather than AI risk.

WHO Health Ethics & Governance unit Adjacent

Programme · Geneva, Switzerland · also draws on Safety science, Law, society

The World Health Organization's ethics team, part of the Research for Health Department in the Chief Scientist's division in Geneva.
