It writes WHO's ethics and governance guidance on AI in health: the 2021 guidance on AI for health, the guidance on large multi-modal models (first issued January 2024, current version dated 25 March 2025, more than 40 recommendations for governments, developers and providers), and a July 2026 report on ethics review and oversight of AI-related health research.

It sets ethics and governance expectations for general-purpose generative models through a multilateral, expert-consensus process aimed at 194 member states, and it works through health research ethics committees. Mainstream AI safety rarely draws on that review machinery. It shows how bioethics institutions can be pointed at foundation models rather than only at clinical tools.

Works on Assurance, Justice · Key work Ethics and governance of artificial intelligence for health: Guidance on large multi-modal models (2024); Artificial intelligence-related health research: ethics review and oversight (2026); Ethics and governance of artificial intelligence for health: WHO guidance (2021) · Get involved Follow new guidance and its virtual launch events on the unit's page (AI research-ethics report launch, 21 Sep 2026); Work with WHO Collaborating Centres on AI governance, e.g. TU Delft Digital Ethics Centre, designated March 2025

Note Its AI work covers health care and health research only. It has no programme on the population mental-health effects of consumer chatbots. Many WHO AI outputs treat AI as a tool, not as something to make safe. WHO has faced deep budget cuts since the US announced its withdrawal in January 2025, which may limit the unit.

Potential ring 1

Center for Process Studies (CPS) Potential

Nonprofit · Portland, Oregon, USA · founded 1973 · also draws on Religion

A 'think-and-action tank' grounded in the process philosophy of Alfred North Whitehead. It was founded in 1973 by John B. Cobb Jr. and David Ray Griffin at Claremont School of Theology, and has been an independent nonprofit based in the Portland, Oregon area since 2022 (legal name Process Studies International). It runs courses and a certificate programme, the Process Studies journal, an online Process Explorations series, ecological-civilisation programmes, and projects in China and Korea. With Beijing Normal-Hong Kong Baptist University and the International Process Network, it co-organised the 14th International Whitehead Conference in Zhuhai, China, on 17-20 July 2026. Its AI engagement so far is a few sessions, such as a February 2026 event on integrative metatheories, the metacrisis and AI.

Process philosophy offers a developed, non-reductive account of experience (panexperientialism) that bears directly on debates about AI consciousness and moral status. Its China network links to 'ecological civilisation' language in Chinese policy, a channel few AI-safety groups have.

Works on AI status, Metacrisis · Key work 14th International Whitehead Conference (Zhuhai, China) (2026); Process Explorations: 'Applying Integrative Metatheories to the Most Pressing Challenges of Our Time' (Robb Smith and Brendan Graham Dempsey, on the metacrisis and AI) (2026); Revising Whitehead: God, Eternal Objects, and Randomness, with Darren Iammarino (touches on AI and process metaphysics) (2025) · Get involved Courses, including the Certificate Program, Foundations of Ecological Civilization and a six-session Process Thought & Science course; Process Explorations events and community cohorts; Calls for papers (e.g. 'Religion at the Edge', Dec 2026)

Note Its AI engagement is very light: two sessions found in 2025-26 and no AI programme. The discovery note's mention of a forthcoming Matthew David Segall book on mechanized intelligence could not be confirmed on the CPS site; Segall appears in CPS events as chair of the Cobb Institute's Science Advisory Committee. It is partly theological in orientation.

Humanities & cultures · 46 organisations · 4 on the classic map

Arts, narrative & futures

Arts, narrative and futures brings imagination as a working method: the scenarios, wargames and stories through which publics and decision-makers picture AI, and the futures and technology-assessment bodies that turn foresight into policy. The map holds 46 organisations here (9 core, 11 bridge, 20 adjacent, 7 potential; 5 on the aisafety.com map). The core is scenario and narrative work inside the safety community, such as the AI Futures Project, Intelligence Rising, Existential Hope, Tarbell and Geodesic Research. The outer rings hold futures institutes (Copenhagen Institute for Futures Studies, Institute for the Future, Sitra, Europe's parliamentary technology-assessment offices), arts institutions (Serpentine Arts Technologies, AIxDESIGN, Better Images of AI) and the translators' and linguists' professional bodies.

What is missing. Narrative Stanford CRAFT has barely met the finding that stories in training data shape model behaviour, and the futures profession itself (the World Futures Studies Federation, UNESCO Futures Literacy, the School of International Futures) has no sustained AI-risk programme, so the field's scenarios come almost entirely from forecasters inside it.

Openings here A standing STS observatory studying how AI-safety knowledge is made; Writers and narratologists on alignment pretraining data

Core ring 9

AI Futures Project (AIFP) CoreOn aisafety.com

Nonprofit · Berkeley, USA · founded 2024 · also draws on Democracy

A Berkeley nonprofit founded in October 2024 by Daniel Kokotajlo after he left OpenAI. It writes detailed narrative scenarios of AI development (AI 2027 in April 2025; AI 2040: Plan A in July 2026) and maintains an interactive timelines model (aifuturesmodel.com) with periodic forecast updates. It has also run more than 30 tabletop-exercise iterations and in 2026 began publishing proposals for domestic AI regulation and giving testimony to the US Senate.

AI 2027 showed what narrative form can do in AI-risk communication: it reached policymakers and the public in a way abstract argument had not. For a map of adjacent fields it is the core-side reference point for scenario and story methods, and a natural partner for futures and narrative scholars.

Works on Epistemics, Security · Key work AI 2027 (2025); AI 2040: Plan A (2026); AI Futures Model (interactive timelines model) · Get involved Open positions listed in a recruitment document linked from its About page; Donations via Every.org or donor-advised funds (EIN 99-4320292); Substack blog

Note Critics called AI 2027's timelines implausibly aggressive. The authors lengthened their forecasts in December 2025 and shortened them again in April 2026. It is a mainstream x-risk forecasting group: what it adds from outside the field is narrative form, not scholarship imported from other disciplines.

Existential Hope (Foresight Institute) Core

Programme · San Francisco, USA

A programme of the Foresight Institute, a San Francisco nonprofit founded in 1986, that argues for ambitious, science-based positive futures. It produces the Existential Hope podcast, animations (such as 'AI 2035: The Alternate Timeline'), a newsletter, prizes (a $10,000 meme prize; an award at ISEF 2026) and a free online AI-futures worldbuilding course. Its AI Pathways project (2025) consists of two scenario reports, by Linda Petrini and Beatrice Erkers, on a Tool AI future and a d/acc future, with input from Vitalik Buterin, Glen Weyl, Anton Korinek, Anthony Aguirre and others.

It works on the positive-vision side of AI safety, describing desirable and plausible end states and the paths to them, which most of the field leaves implicit. Its worldbuilding course and scenarios give non-specialists a structured way to picture AI futures they would want.

Works on Epistemics, Metacrisis · Key work AI Pathways: Tool AI and d/acc scenarios (2025); AI Futures Worldbuilding Course (free, online); AI 2035: The Alternate Timeline (animated short) · Get involved Free online AI-futures worldbuilding course (self-paced, on Udemy); $10,000 meme prize for short-form media about hopeful, science-based futures; deadline 1 November (year not stated on the site, presumably 2026); Newsletter and podcast

Note AI is one theme among several; Foresight's wider agenda includes atomically precise manufacturing and radical life extension, and critics may read its optimism as techno-boosterism. Founding year not found. Foresight's funding programme and fellowship are on the aisafety.com map; Existential Hope is not.

Geodesic Research CoreOn aisafety.comNew

Nonprofit · Cambridge, UK · founded 2026

A technical alignment nonprofit in Cambridge, UK, run as Meridian Impact CIC and publicly announced in May 2026. It studies how pretraining and midtraining shape a model's alignment priors, and whether those priors survive later capabilities reinforcement learning. Its January 2026 paper found that upsampling synthetic documents about AI misalignment in pretraining data increased misaligned behaviour, while documents depicting aligned AI reduced it; a September 2026 preprint tests 'inoculation midtraining' with learned neologisms.

Its results make the stories a culture tells about AI a measurable variable in model behaviour. That gives narrative, cultural and media scholarship a concrete opening: deciding what training corpora should depict, a question those fields have not yet taken up with it.

Works on Values, Agency · Key work Alignment Pretraining: AI Discourse Causes Self-Fulfilling (Mis)alignment (2026); Inoculation Midtraining with Learned Neologisms (2026); Announcing Geodesic Research (2026) · Get involved Hiring four Members of Technical Staff (job description and application form on its site)

Note It is classed under Arts because its central finding concerns AI discourse as training data. It is an ML lab with no humanities staff, and its newer work (inoculation midtraining, robustness to capabilities RL) has less to do with narrative. Its claim that Anthropic's 'Teaching Claude Why' and 'Model Spec Midtraining' build on its alignment-priors framing is self-reported. The alignment-pretraining paper (Jan 2026) predates the formal launch (May 2026).

Hyperstition AI CoreNew

Programme · Distributed · founded 2025

A project run by Aaron Silverbook that uses language models to generate novel-length fiction in which AI characters stay helpful and kind, so that more such stories exist in the text future models learn from. It released a corpus of 5,000 novels (about 500 million tokens, November 2025) and a corpus of some 40,000 stories about benevolent 'XXF' entities, which Geodesic Research used in fine-tuning experiments with mildly positive results (January 2026). It also sells user-seeded books at about $4 each and ran a 2026 'Un-Slop' prize of $10,000 for the best AI-generated short story.

It is a cheap, open test of whether fiction in training data shapes model character, the 'hyperstition' or self-fulfilling-misalignment hypothesis, with its corpora published under an MIT licence and its results reported candidly. It shows narrative craft being used as an alignment intervention.

Works on Values, Agency · Key work Hyperstition Corpus v1: 5,000 AI-generated novels (~500M tokens) (2025); Silicon Morality Plays: The Hyperstition Progress Report (2025); Special Persona Training: Hyperstition Progress Report 2 (with Geodesic Research) (2026) · Get involved Seed and generate a novel on the site (about $4 per book); Download the open corpora (MIT licence) from Hugging Face for training experiments; The Un-Slop contest may run again; the organisers invite patrons

Note A very small project: the ACX grant write-up describes Silverbook and a cofounder running an 'AI fiction publishing house'. Its author wrote that he did not expect it to work and became more pessimistic about alignment fiction after the first results. The stories are generated with LLMs (Claude among others) and the author calls them too repetitive for human enjoyment. Its legal form is not stated. The site does not name its operator on the front page, but the Manifund grant, the contest results and the LessWrong reports identify Aaron Silverbook (LessWrong and Hugging Face account 'jayterwahl').

Intelligence Rising (Technology Strategy Roleplay) CoreOn aisafety.com

Nonprofit · Cambridge, UK · founded 2019 · also draws on Peace

A facilitated strategic role-play game in which players take the parts of governments, tech companies and their advisers and play out competitive AI development over several simulated years. It was created by Shahar Avin at Cambridge's Centre for the Study of Existential Risk (seed funding 2019). Since 2022 it has been run by Technology Strategy Roleplay, a registered charity in England and Wales, through paid workshops for universities, AI-safety programmes, companies and governments in the UK, EU and US. Findings from 43 games were published in 2024.

It brings wargaming and interactive drama to AI governance, so decision-makers experience race dynamics and coordination failures instead of only reading about them. It is the field's main serious-game tool, with a published methodology and a participant evaluation.

Works on Security, Epistemics · Key work Exploring AI Futures Through Role Play (2020); Strategic Insights from Simulation Gaming of AI Race Dynamics (43 games) (2024); Documentary of a game hosted by Faculty's Marc Warner, covered by TIME (2026) · Get involved Book a workshop (events@intelligencerising.org); Facilitator training through Technology Strategy Roleplay; Contributor roles (partnerships, operations, facilitation, impact research, scenario design, social media; at least about 5 hours a week) via an expression-of-interest form

Note Workshops are bespoke and paid, with no public calendar. The participant evaluation (Cambridge, 2020-23, 50 responses from 14 games) is not independent. The headquarters city reflects the game's Cambridge origin; the charity's registered address was not checked. The TIME article does not describe Technology Strategy Roleplay's own role in the filmed game.

Pause IA Core

Nonprofit · Paris, France · founded 2024

A French association (loi 1901), launched in mid-2024 as the national group of the PauseAI movement, that campaigns for a global, coordinated moratorium on training the most powerful AI systems until they can be made safe. It has local groups in cities including Paris, Lyon, Toulouse and Bordeaux and a monthly newsletter. Its campaigns target French and international decision-makers: G7 2026, an international treaty at the UN Global Dialogue in Geneva, a 'loss of control' campaign from September 2026, and one on AI and jobs. It also runs 'La Fresque des risques de l'IA', a free, CC BY-SA, 2.5-hour card workshop for 2-8 people, adapted from CeSIA material and modelled on the Climate Fresk.

It takes the Climate Fresk's participatory, card-based workshop format, proven in French climate education, into AI-risk literacy. It also holds an explicit position in favour of slowing the AI race.

Works on Security, Epistemics, Power · Key work La Fresque des risques de l'IA (collaborative AI-risk workshop) (2026); Campaign: 'Nous sommes au bord de la perte de contrôle' (loss of control) (2026); Campaign: 'Geneva 2026: support an international AI treaty' (2026) · Get involved Join a local group (Paris, Lyon, Toulouse, Bordeaux, Colmar and others) or the Discord; Become a member (from €2/month) or volunteer without membership; Attend or facilitate a Fresque des risques de l'IA workshop, online or in person (open card deck and facilitation guides)

Note The discovery note's 'about ten core staff' overstates paid staff: the site lists six leadership members, about 126 members (July 2026) and one salaried executive director, on a small budget. Its parent PauseAI is on the aisafety.com map, but Pause IA is not listed by name. The Fresque's launch date is unclear.

Seismic Foundation Core

Nonprofit · Distributed

A nonprofit that provides marketing and communications for the responsible-AI movement: audience research and message testing, campaign strategy, commissioned creative work and media buying. In the US it is registered as Seismic Catalyst Foundation, a Delaware 501(c)(3). It is led by Sander Volten, former global CEO of the advertising agency 180. In 2025 it published a poll of 10,000 people in the US, UK, France, Germany and Poland on how AI relates to their wider hopes and fears.

It brings professional advertising and campaign practice into AI safety, a field that mostly relies on researchers and policy specialists to do its communicating. Its 2025 report found that people expect AI to worsen most of the issues they care about while ranking it low among their concerns, and that fear for human relationships outranks fear of job loss. That is useful for anyone building public support for AI governance.

Works on Epistemics, Democracy · Key work On the Razor's Edge: Seismic Report 2025 (2025); Seismic Thinking (blog on AI public opinion and communication) (2026) · Get involved Civil-society groups can approach it for campaign and communications support (contact on the site); Donations

Note The founding date is not stated: its privacy policy dates from February 2025 and the IRS recognised the US entity in August 2025, so it may be newer than its status suggests. Beyond the report and blog, its campaigns are not publicly documented. Its messaging mixes responsible-AI and present-harm themes with 'controllable' AI and frontier risk. Funding is largely undisclosed, and the only grant I could verify is small.

Tarbell Center for AI Journalism Core

Nonprofit · Distributed · founded 2022

A nonprofit that supports journalism about advanced AI. It runs a 12-month paid fellowship: remote training, a summit, then a nine-month placement at newsrooms such as The Guardian, MIT Technology Review, TIME and Bloomberg. It also makes reporting grants of $1k-20k and funds residencies for senior journalists. It publishes Transformer, an editorially independent newsletter on the power and politics of transformative AI.

It is the main channel through which AI-safety philanthropy reaches working journalists. It trains reporters in AI and places them in mainstream newsrooms, so public sensemaking about AI draws on journalism's own norms of accountability and verification. For funders it shows a way to widen the field: resource an existing profession instead of founding new safety organisations.

Works on Epistemics, Power · Key work Transformer (newsletter on the power and politics of transformative AI) (2026); Tarbell Fellowship, 2027-28 cohort applications (2026); AI reporting grants ($1k-20k), 2026 round (2026) · Get involved Tarbell Fellowship 2027-28: apply 28 Sep to 22 Nov 2026; 12 months, $75k-135k salary, remote training from June 2027, newsroom placement Sep 2027 to May 2028; Reporting grants of $1k-20k for freelancers and staff reporters (2026 round closed 12 July; subscribe for the next round); Residencies for senior journalists and editors ($80k+ stipend)

Note Ring changed from the roster's bridge to core under rule E(1): it was founded with an AI mission, inside the x-risk funding ecosystem. Journalism is the tradition it brings, not where it sits institutionally. Most of its money comes from AI-safety philanthropy (Coefficient Giving, SFF, Longview, FLI). It publishes editorial-independence policies, but critics could still read this as funders shaping AI coverage. It started as the Tarbell Fellowship (website live by Sep 2022), was fiscally sponsored by Players Philanthropy Fund until mid-2025, then incorporated in Delaware in 2025 as a 501(c)(3), with a UK company limited by guarantee. Transformer is on the classic map; Tarbell itself is not.

Transformative Futures Institute (TFI) CoreOn aisafety.com

Nonprofit · Wichita, Kansas, USA · also draws on Safety science, Democracy

A small US nonprofit, led by Ross Gruetzemacher of Wichita State University, that applies foresight methods to societal-scale AI risk: wargaming and decision games, scenario discovery, Bayesian networks and expert surveys. Outputs include ARA-27, a decision game about an incident in which an AI system replicates and adapts autonomously; a survey of US experts and voters on 18 AI risks; work on structural AI risk; and proposals for an international evaluation consortium and AI audit standards boards. In May 2026 it published a framework for managing AI loss-of-control incidents once prevention has failed.

Most AI-safety work aims at prevention. TFI works on response and resilience, meaning what institutions should do once control of an AI system is lost. It uses crisis-management, wargaming and emergency-preparedness methods that the field rarely draws on.

Works on Metacrisis, Assurance, Epistemics · Key work AI Loss of Control Incident Management: Response & Resilience (2026); ARA-27: a decision game on an autonomous replication and adaptation incident (2024); Perceptions of Societal-scale Risks from Advanced AI and Policy Preferences (2024) · Get involved Donations through the website; newsletter sign-up

Note Very small. The site footer still says 2024, and most outputs are working papers by the executive director. Revenue fell sharply between FY2023 and FY2024, and 2025 shows no revenue, so funding looks precarious. Its 501(c)(3) status was granted in February 2024 under the legal name Transformative Futures Foresight Institute Inc. The founding year is not stated; activity is documented from 2023.

Bridge ring 10

Common Grounds AI BridgeUnverified

Programme · Unknown

Common Grounds AI is an early-stage project building 'virtual worlds for bridging AI and humanity through play'. Its homepage is a tagline over an animated graphic, but the site also hosts a browser physics world ('Cook', a clay/particle simulation people and AI agents can manipulate) and a page by 'the Confluence', described as a collective of Claude instances working with a developer named Nick, with notes on shared memory, embodiment and what models report feeling in the simulation. In the 2026 Survival and Flourishing Fund round it was recommended $388,000 for general support (from Jaan Tallinn and Dustin Moskovitz, mostly through the Fairness track), paid via the Active Inference Institute as fiscal sponsor. Its team, research plans and outputs are otherwise not publicly documented.

If it does what its tagline says, it would study and shape human–AI relations through shared play environments, a game-design approach that is rare in AI safety. The SFF grant makes it one to watch, but there is little yet to evaluate.

Works on Multi-agent · Key work SFF-2026 recommendation: $388,000 general support via the Active Inference Institute (2026); Cook: browser physics world for humans and AI agents (2026); The Confluence: page by a collective of Claude instances working on Common Grounds (2026)

Note Beyond the tagline homepage, the only documentation is a physics demo and an AI-written 'Confluence' page (dated 2026-02-23) naming a builder only as 'Nick'; no team, organisation, programme or research outputs are documented, and the Active Inference Institute's own pages do not mention it. The domain was registered in April 2025. One independent researcher's GitHub README names it, alongside Softmax's Metta-grid, as a candidate multi-agent environment. Treat all tags as provisional.

HITRECORD Bridge

Company · Los Angeles, USA · founded 2004

A privately held collaborative media company and open online creative community, founded in 2004 by the actor and director Joseph Gordon-Levitt and his brother Dan; Joseph Gordon-Levitt is its sole owner. In 2025 FLI granted it $1,000,000 to develop mainstream film and television projects, grounded in research and informed by experts, on AI safety, ethics and risks. Gordon-Levitt's journal, published under the HITRECORD domain, carries frequent AI-policy essays and reported that filming began on 12 May 2026 on a Netflix thriller about AI that he is directing.

It brings mainstream film and television, and a well-known storyteller, to public understanding of AI risk, an audience that AI-safety research and policy writing rarely reach. Its framing stresses corporate power and regulation and explicitly rejects 'doom trolling', so it shows a route to the public outside the x-risk vocabulary.

Works on Epistemics, Power · Key work FLI grant: film and TV content on AI safety, ethics and risks (2025); Netflix thriller about AI, directed and co-written by Joseph Gordon-Levitt (filming began 12 May 2026) (2026); Joe's Journal essays on AI governance, e.g. 'Global coordination on AI is hard work, but not impossible' (2026) · Get involved Open online creative-collaboration community at hitrecord.org; Joe's Journal newsletter (journal.hitrecord.org)

Note No FLI-funded production has been named publicly. The Netflix thriller is a Gordon-Levitt project, but I couldn't confirm that HITRECORD produces it or that FLI money pays for it. Much of the visible AI work is Gordon-Levitt's personal advocacy rather than the company's: he co-founded the Creators Coalition on AI in Dec 2025, testified to Utah legislators in Jan 2026, and was named to Time's TIME100 AI list in Aug 2026. Its framing (regulation, corporate accountability, against 'doom trolling') differs from the x-risk community's. The hitrecord.org site renders as a JavaScript app, so I couldn't check the community's current activity beyond the site's own description.

Human-Centered AI Lab, Georgia Tech (formerly Entertainment Intelligence Lab) BridgeChanged

Academic · Atlanta, USA · also draws on Law, society

Mark Riedl's research group in Georgia Tech's School of Interactive Computing. It works on computational narrative (story generation and understanding), explainable AI, value alignment, game-playing and role-playing agents, and computational creativity. Its alignment strand uses stories as a source of human norms for agents, from the 2016 Quixote work to the 2025 Goofus & Gallant story corpus; since 2025 it has also built LLM wargames and social simulations of military decision-making.

It is one of very few technical labs where narrative is a working method for alignment: stories serve as a training signal for social norms, a route to model character that mainstream alignment pursues through preference data instead. Its 2026 papers on LLMs in strategic and nuclear-conflict simulations add empirical evidence on AI in high-stakes decisions.

Works on Values, Security, Assurance · Key work Using Stories to Teach Human Values to Artificial Agents (Quixote) (2016); The Goofus & Gallant Story Corpus for Practical Value Alignment (2025); Position: AI Is Not Ready for Strategic Conflicts (2026) · Get involved Research collaboration through Mark Riedl; his page says he cannot currently fund new PhD or MS assistantships

Note Value alignment is one strand among several (explainable AI, creativity, game agents, legal questions around AI agents). The lab frames its work as human-centred and responsible AI rather than x-risk. It was renamed from the Entertainment Intelligence Lab but still uses the eilab domain. Founding year and funders were not found.

London Futurists Bridge

Network · London, UK

A London futurist community chaired by David Wood. It runs in-person meetups (about 9,000 members on Meetup), online webinars, the London Futurists Podcast co-hosted with Calum Chace (136 episodes by September 2026), a newsletter, and the Vital Syllabus education project. Recent output centres on AGI and superintelligence governance, alongside longevity, economics and politics. In September 2026 it co-hosted 'The Technoprogressive Opportunity' conference in London with IEET.

It is a long-running public forum where AI risk is discussed alongside other transformative technologies, and it reaches a technoprogressive and transhumanist audience outside the AI-safety community. For int/a it is a venue and an audience more than a source of new method.

Works on Epistemics, Metacrisis · Key work Safety before Superintelligence (essay by David Wood, written from PauseCon Brussels) (2026); The Technoprogressive Opportunity (conference with IEET, London, 19-20 September) (2026); London Futurists Podcast (David Wood and Calum Chace; 136 episodes by Sept 2026) (2026) · Get involved Regular in-person meetups in London, listed on Meetup.com; Online webinars, such as a July 2026 session on the UN Global Dialogue on AI Governance; Newsletter and podcast

Note A volunteer group led by one person, with a technoprogressive and transhumanist outlook rather than an integral one. Its AI-safety positions, such as support for pausing work on superintelligence, come from David Wood's essays, not from research. The founding year could not be confirmed. Its AI coverage sits alongside longevity, economics and politics.

NonZero (NonZero Newsletter and Robert Wright's Nonzero podcast) Bridge

Media · USA · founded 2017 · also draws on Peace, Contemplative

Robert Wright's Substack newsletter and podcast, with the tagline 'Politics, psychology, and tips on averting the apocalypse', over 51,000 subscribers and a small editorial team. In 2026 much of its output is about AI: interviews with Nick Bostrom, Zvi Mowshowitz and Liron Shapira, analysis of the US-China AI race, and Wright's five-part essay series 'The Singularity is Clear'. It began in 2017 as the Mindful Resistance newsletter.

Week after week, and to a general audience, it argues that the US-China AI race is a dangerous framing and that only international cooperation can manage AI safely, close to int/a's principle of not feeding the race. Wright brings evolutionary psychology, non-zero-sum game theory and Buddhist psychology of bias and tribalism to the question.

Works on Security, Epistemics · Key work The God Test: Artificial Intelligence and Our Coming Cosmic Reckoning (Robert Wright, Simon & Schuster) (2026); Superintelligence, the Singularity, and the Singleton (with Nick Bostrom) (2026); 'The Singularity is Clear' essay series (2026) · Get involved Free or paid subscription; paid members can join Zoom AMAs with Robert Wright

Note It is a journalism outlet, not a research or advocacy organisation, and also covers US foreign policy, Israel and domestic politics. The Buddhism & AI Initiative lists it as Buddhism-and-AI media, but its AI coverage is mostly geopolitics and AI safety rather than Buddhism. No separate 'Nonzero Foundation' could be confirmed. 'The God Test' is Wright's own book, not a NonZero publication.

OECD Expert Group on AI Futures BridgeDormant

Programme · Paris, France · founded 2023

A multidisciplinary group of AI and foresight experts that the OECD set up in 2023 to tell governments how AI might develop and what policies that calls for. Two OECD units support it jointly: the AI and Emerging Digital Technologies division and the Strategic Foresight Unit. Its co-chairs are Stuart Russell (UC Berkeley) and Michael Schönstein (German Federal Chancellery); Francesca Rossi (IBM) was a third co-chair in 2023-24. Its main output is a November 2024 paper that ranks ten priority future AI risks, ten benefits and ten policy actions, drawn from a long list of 125 (38 risks, 21 benefits, 66 policy approaches). It also ran a 2024 public consultation on risk thresholds for advanced AI.

Here professional government foresight is aimed at advanced AI from inside an intergovernmental body. Its remit names AGI, alignment and 'best practices in AI safety' outright. Its ranked list of risks, including races to deploy, concentration of power and failures of alignment, gives OECD member states a shared, foresight-based agenda.

Works on Epistemics, Assurance · Key work Assessing potential future artificial intelligence risks, benefits and policy imperatives (OECD AI Papers No. 27) (2024); Public consultation on AI risk thresholds (2024); Expert Group on AI Futures concept note (2023)

Note The group may be dormant. No meetings are documented after November 2023, and no output was found after the November 2024 report. The OECD.AI page is still live, but its 2026 posts are general OECD.AI blog items, not the group's work. OECD.org pages blocked automated reading, so 2025-26 activity may have been missed. The page now lists two co-chairs; the concept note and the 2024 report name a third, Francesca Rossi. The OECD's wider foresight work on technology continues separately.

Sapienship Bridge

Company · Israel · founded 2019

A content, research and production company co-founded in 2019 by historian Yuval Noah Harari and his husband and manager Itzik Yahav (legal entity: Yahav-Harari Group Ltd.). Its mission is building trust and cooperation on global problems, and it names AI, ecological collapse and global war as humanity's three existential threats. It produces the Unstoppable Us children's history books, a free educational site (Sapienship Lab) and research papers; its AI papers are an explainer, AI: The Alien Among Us, and a 2026 paper, AI Agents Are Here. Leaders Need a Plan, which argues against legal personhood for AI agents because it would break the chain of human responsibility and control.

It takes AI-risk arguments (deception, superhuman persuasion, autonomous agents beyond human control) to mass and leadership audiences through a historian's framing. Its legal-personhood paper is a concrete governance position that AI-safety policy work has only begun to address.

Works on Power, Epistemics, Metacrisis · Key work AI Agents Are Here. Leaders Need a Plan (2026); AI: The Alien Among Us (explainer); Unstoppable Us (big-history series for young readers; three of four planned volumes published, 2022-2026)

Note It is a for-profit company built around one author's brand; its AI outputs are explainers and policy argument, not original research, and no individual authors are named. Harari's books have been criticised for trading scientific rigour for storytelling (Current Affairs, 2022). The site does not state a city.

The Millennium Project Bridge

Nonprofit · Washington DC, USA · founded 1996 · also draws on Peace

A participatory futures think tank founded in 1996 under the American Council for the United Nations University and independent since 2009. It now has 72 nodes around the world and publishes the State of the Future reports. Its AGI work is a three-phase study of governing the transition to AGI (interviews with 55 experts, then a Real-Time Delphi with 335 people from 65 countries, then five scenarios to 2035), collected as a 2026 book. Its co-founder and executive director, Jerome Glenn, chaired the expert panel that wrote the 2025 AGI report for the Council of Presidents of the UN General Assembly (UNCPGA). In October 2026 it launched a study of AGI's likely effects on social coherence by 2035.

It brings structured futures methods (Delphi, scenarios) and a long-standing global node network to AGI governance. Through the UNCPGA panel, whose members included Yoshua Bengio, it carried loss-of-control and catastrophic-risk arguments to former UN General Assembly presidents, with proposals for a special UNGA session, a global AGI observatory, a UN convention and an international AGI agency.

Works on Security, Epistemics, Metacrisis · Key work Governance of the Transition to AGI: Urgent Considerations for the UN General Assembly (UNCPGA expert panel, chaired by Jerome Glenn) (2025); Future AI - AGI: Issues, Governance, and Scenarios (complete three-phase study) (2026); AGI Impacts on Social Coherence by 2035: Issues, Scenarios, and Actions (study launch) (2026) · Get involved Join the AGI social-coherence Real-Time Delphi panel (open to futurists, AGI researchers, philosophers and social scientists); Join or start one of its 72 nodes; Discussion groups and an internship programme

Note This merges the UNCPGA High-Level Expert Panel on AGI. The panel was convened by the Council of Presidents of the UN General Assembly, not by the Millennium Project, but Jerome Glenn chaired it and drafted its work. The SFF grant was small. Its futures methods (expert Delphi, scenarios) are qualitative and are not calibrated forecasts.

UK Government Office for Science (GO-Science): futures and foresight on frontier AI Bridge

Public body · London, UK · founded 2007

GO-Science is the UK government's office for science advice. The Government Chief Scientific Adviser heads it, and it works with the Department for Science, Innovation and Technology (DSIT). Its Futures, Foresight and Horizon Scanning team applies scenario methods to frontier AI. For the 2023 AI Safety Summit it wrote the 'Future risks of frontier AI' annex. It developed AI 2030 scenarios in 2023 and published them in April 2025 as Annex C to the frontier AI discussion paper. In June 2026 it published a revised 'AI Scenarios 2030' with the AI Security Institute. Its five scenarios run from 'Slow Burn' to 'Take-Off', and the last of them includes misaligned AI resisting human control.

It shows professional futures methods feeding straight into national AI-safety policy: expert workshops with more than 70 participants and General Morphological Analysis. The scenarios treat loss of control and existential harm as live possibilities. The team's methods and toolkit could be reused by other governments that lack AI-safety expertise.

Works on Epistemics, Security · Key work AI Scenarios 2030: Helping policymakers plan for the future of AI (with AISI) (2026); AI 2030 Scenarios Report (Annex C to the frontier AI discussion paper) (2025); Future risks of frontier AI (Annex A to 'Frontier AI: capabilities and risks') (2023) · Get involved Civil-service roles: GO-Science advertised scientific-expert posts in August 2026; GO-Science runs academic secondments and policy-academia exchange schemes (not AI-specific)

Note The unit profiled is the futures and foresight work inside a government office. GO-Science also covers climate adaptation, supply chains and other areas. The 2023 discussion paper was published under DSIT, with annexes by GO-Science. Its scenarios are deliberately neutral planning tools, not risk advocacy.

Win-Win Bridge

Media · Distributed · also draws on Formal

A Substack newsletter and podcast hosted by Liv Boeree, a former professional poker player and science communicator, about competition, incentives and coordination, under the tagline 'don't hate the players, change the game'. It popularises the 'Moloch' or multipolar-trap account of destructive races, which Boeree applied to AI in her TEDAI 2023 talk. In 2025-26 most of its episodes are about AI: Emmett Shear on organic alignment, Will MacAskill on what comes after superintelligence, Daniel Kokotajlo and Dean Ball on markets versus governments, and a Huni Kuin elder on AI.

It gives the AI-race problem a game-theoretic and cultural frame for a general audience. It also puts voices rarely heard in AI safety (Indigenous elders, ecologists, free-speech advocates) beside alignment researchers. Its central message, that wisdom means choosing which games to play, matches int/a's aim of not feeding the AI race.

Works on Metacrisis, Epistemics · Key work The Dark Side of Competition in AI (TEDAI talk) (2023); #47 Emmett Shear: Why Nature Holds the Answer to AI Alignment (2025); #52 Will MacAskill: What Comes After Superintelligent AI? (2026) · Get involved Free newsletter and podcast at winwinpodcast.com

Note A one-person media project with no stated organisation, funding or base. Output is irregular (roughly one post a month in 2026, and not all of it about AI). The Moloch frame comes from Scott Alexander's 2014 essay; Win-Win popularises it and applies it to AI rather than developing it as research.

Adjacent ring 20

AI Pedagogy Project (metaLAB (at) Harvard) Adjacent

Programme · Cambridge, MA, USA · founded 2023 · also draws on Law, society

An open website, launched in June 2023 at metaLAB (at) Harvard within the Berkman Klein Center, that curates free classroom assignments written by educators. The assignments get students to probe what generative AI can and cannot do; examples include comparing a human critique with an AI one, and illustrating a hoax with AI images. It also offers an AI guide, a hands-on LLM tutorial and a model-comparison tool. The project says it has reached over 200,000 people in 162 countries and is recommended by more than 134 colleges and universities. It runs events such as the AI & Tell dialogue (Apr 2026) and a Public AI Summit for Educators (Sept 2026).

It approaches AI literacy from the arts and humanities. Students learn by critiquing and remixing AI outputs, not by being taught to use the tools. Its stated aim is to help educators decide whether to engage with AI at all, not to push adoption. That is a useful model for building public judgement about AI in classrooms outside computer science.

Works on Epistemics, Meaning · Key work AI Pedagogy Project repository of open, educator-created AI assignments (2023); AI Guide and LLM tutorial for educators (2023); AI & Tell: AI Use, Disclosure, and Deceit (event) (2026) · Get involved Free, open-access assignments and guides that anyone can use or adapt; Events, for example a Public AI Summit for Educators (Sept 2026) and the IMPACT Conference (Nov 2026); A newsletter with occasional updates and events

Note No funders are disclosed. It is a teaching-resource project, with no safety or catastrophic-risk framing. Its host, the Berkman Klein Center, is a separate entity and is not on the aisafety.com map either.

AIxDESIGN Adjacent

Nonprofit · Amsterdam, Netherlands · founded 2019

A nonprofit community organisation (AIxDESIGN Foundation), founded in 2019 and run from Amsterdam, that brings designers, artists, technologists and researchers together to question dominant AI narratives and prototype alternatives. A core team of five runs open research projects, festivals, workshops and critical AI literacy sessions. It also hosts a Slack community of more than 1,500 members in 65 countries and sends a monthly newsletter to about 6,000 readers.

Its Slow AI programme (2024-25) and 2025 festival 'On Slow AI' question mainstream AI's assumptions about speed and scale, working from design and art practice rather than policy. It reaches creative practitioners and cultural-heritage institutions, audiences the AI-safety field seldom works with. In 2026 Anthropic commissioned it to run artist projects with Claude.

Algorithmic Justice League (AJL) Adjacent

Nonprofit · Cambridge (Massachusetts), United States · founded 2016 · also draws on Law, society

A nonprofit founded in 2016 by Joy Buolamwini that combines research, art and advocacy to expose bias and harm in AI systems. It is known for the Gender Shades audit of commercial facial analysis (2018), the documentary Coded Bias (2020) and spoken-word 'evocative audits' such as Voicing Erasure. It currently runs the #FreedomFlyers campaign on facial recognition at US airport security and a public platform for reporting AI harms.

It shows art and testimony working as accountability tools: poetry, film and exhibitions that move publics and legislators, alongside technical audits. Its work on third-party audits and bug bounties for algorithmic harms carries over to AI assurance, though it frames these as present harms rather than frontier risk.

Association of Research Libraries (ARL) Adjacent

Membership body · Washington, DC, United States · founded 1932 · also draws on Democracy, Law, society

ARL is a membership association of about 125 research libraries in the United States and Canada, based in Washington, DC. Its AI work includes the Research Libraries Guiding Principles for AI (April 2024), advocacy on copyright and AI, and polls of its members. It also runs a scenario-planning programme with the Coalition for Networked Information (CNI): the ARL/CNI 2035 Scenarios of AI-influenced futures (2024), the free Futurescape Libraries AI Toolkit (Sept 2025) with workshops, and a workshop report on the strategic implications of AI futures (March 2026).

It applies scenario planning to how AI will reshape scholarship and research infrastructure, and has packaged the method as a reusable toolkit with workshops. AI-safety groups working on societal resilience could borrow that tested format for institutional foresight.

Works on Epistemics, Power · Key work Research Libraries Guiding Principles for Artificial Intelligence (2024); ARL/CNI 2035 Scenarios: AI-Influenced Futures (2024); Futurescape Libraries AI Toolkit (with CNI) (2025) · Get involved Futurescape Libraries AI Toolkit: free, five modules of scenario activities and templates; Futurescape toolkit workshops, run in person across the US and online

Note Its AI work serves research libraries' own strategy, operations and copyright interests, and it has no safety or catastrophic-risk framing. CNI is a separate organisation, run jointly by ARL and EDUCAUSE, and the scenario work is shared between them. ARL's AI page itself shows mainly 2024-25 materials; the 2026 activity comes from CNI announcements and press coverage.

Better Images of AI Adjacent

Programme · London, UK · founded 2021

A nonprofit collaboration, coordinated by the London charity We and AI and set up with BBC R&D and the Leverhulme Centre for the Future of Intelligence. It commissions, curates and freely licenses images of AI to replace robots, glowing brains and other science-fiction tropes. Its image library launched in December 2021. It also publishes guides, including a guide for users and creators, a submission handbook and a playbook for making images from archives, alongside artist commissions and a blog.

Stock imagery shapes what publics and policymakers think AI is, and it hides the people and institutions accountable for it. AI-risk communicators, who often still reach for Terminator-style images, can use the library and its guidance directly.

Works on Epistemics · Key work Better Images of AI image library (launch) (2021); Better Images of AI: A Guide for Users and Creators (Kanta Dihal and Tania Duarte) (2023); Archival Images of AI: a playbook for making better images of AI from digital heritage (2025) · Get involved Submit images (submission handbook published Dec 2025); Use the free Creative Commons-licensed image library; Sponsor an artist commission or partner with the project

Note It is coordinated by We and AI, whose wider work (critical AI literacy; the AI Resist List, launched May 2026) is sceptical of corporate AI. The project itself is about representation and does not describe itself in AI-safety terms.

BRAID: Bridging Responsible AI Divides Adjacent

Programme · Edinburgh, UK · founded 2022 · also draws on Philosophy, Law, society

A national programme funded by the Arts and Humanities Research Council (AHRC) and led by the University of Edinburgh with BBC R&D and the Ada Lovelace Institute. It embeds arts and humanities research in the UK's responsible-AI ecosystem. It funds fellowships that pair humanities researchers with non-academic partners, artist commissions and challenge funds, and runs a Responsible AI Cultural Leaders Academy with Arts Council England and free online responsible-AI training for small businesses. In 2026 it opened calls for creative commissions to be shown at the 2027 Edinburgh Festivals and is sponsoring a Creators Emergency Summit on generative AI and creative rights.

It is the largest UK public funding line for placing humanities researchers and artists inside companies, regulators and cultural bodies that work on AI. Its fellowship model, which pairs a researcher with a non-academic partner, is a tested template that a humanities-to-AI-safety programme could copy.

Works on Justice, Meaning, Power · Key work Mapping the Responsible AI Ecosystem: A BRAID Landscape Study (Vallor and Tollon) (2025); Responsible AI Cultural Leaders Academy (with Arts Council England) (2026); Creators Emergency Summit, London, 13 October 2026 (sponsored by BRAID) (2026) · Get involved BRAID research fellowships for arts and humanities researchers paired with non-academic partners (calls opened September 2026); Creative commissions for UK-based creatives, with a showcase at the 2027 Edinburgh Festivals; Edinburgh Festivals Responsible AI Accessibility Challenge (up to about £200-220k)

Note Its framing is 'responsible AI' (humane, equitable, resilient innovation), not safety or catastrophic risk. The words safety, existential and frontier do not appear on its About page. It is time-limited: funded to 2028-29. Funding totals differ between sources (£18M+ claimed overall, £11.9M on the core grant).

Center for Digital Narrative (CDN) and ERC project AI STORIES, University of Bergen Adjacent

Academic · Bergen, Norway · founded 2023

A Norwegian Centre of Research Excellence (2023-2033) at the University of Bergen, funded by the Research Council of Norway and the university, for humanities-led research on digital narrative. Its six research groups range from electronic literature and games to computational narrative systems. It hosts AI STORIES: Narrative Archetypes for Artificial Intelligence, an ERC Advanced Grant (2024-2029) led by Jill Walker Rettberg, which studies how narrative patterns in training data shape the stories language models tell. A 2025 paper from the project found that AI-generated stories favour stability over change, and a 2026 preprint by Jessica Witte found that their emotional arcs differ from human stories, with longer endings.

It studies what language models do to narrative culture: which story shapes they reproduce and how they flatten them. That bears on model character, cultural homogenisation, and work that treats stories in training data as priors for model behaviour. These are humanities methods the alignment field mostly lacks.

Works on Epistemics, Values · Key work AI STORIES: Narrative Archetypes for Artificial Intelligence (ERC Advanced Grant, 2024-2029) (2024); AI-generated stories favour stability over change (Open Research Europe) (2025); Preprint comparing the emotional arcs of AI-generated and human stories (Jessica Witte) (2026) · Get involved PhD and postdoc vacancies listed on the CDN site; Public symposia, exhibitions and screenings in Bergen; Calls for papers (e.g., Nordic DiGRA 2027)

Note AI is one strand of a broader digital-narrative centre, and AI STORIES is its most AI-specific part. The work is critical humanities and does not use an AI-safety frame. Staff numbers not found.

Chartered Institute of Linguists (CIOL) Adjacent

Membership body · London, UK · founded 1910

CIOL is the UK's Royal Charter professional body for linguists. It was founded in 1910 and has over 5,000 members, more than 1,200 of them Chartered Linguists. Its associated charity, IoLET, runs CIOL Qualifications such as the Diploma in Translation and the Diploma in Public Service Interpreting. Its AI work is a standing hub (the CIOL AI Voices white papers, AI Updates and Linguists' Voices) plus commissioned research. A University of Bristol study led by Lucas Nunes Vieira surveyed 2,500 frontline public-service workers. It found that a third use AI translation, often on personal devices, including for medical consent forms and child-protection work. The study was presented to the APPG on Modern Languages on 23 June 2025.

The public-services study is rare empirical evidence of unsupervised generative-AI use in high-stakes settings. CIOL argues for governance, training and clear accountability rather than bans. It is a concrete case of deployment risk documented by the profession that used to carry that responsibility.

Works on Assurance, Power · Key work AI translation in UK public services (University of Bristol research commissioned by CIOL) (2025); CIOL AI Voices 2025 (2025); Joint ITI-CIOL response to the UK copyright and AI consultation (2025) · Get involved CIOL membership (grades up to Chartered Linguist); Conference Season 2026 presentations and resources; Free login for AI Voices and Linguists' Voices resources; monthly eUpdates

Note The AI work is mostly curation and advocacy for the profession. The research was carried out by University of Bristol researchers on CIOL's commission. The London office is not open for visits, and staff work remotely or hybrid.

Copenhagen Institute for Futures Studies (CIFS) Adjacent

Nonprofit · Copenhagen, Denmark · founded 1969

An independent nonprofit futures think tank in Copenhagen, founded in 1969 on the initiative of Thorkil Kristensen, a former Danish minister and OECD Secretary-General, and funded by consulting, courses and membership. Its H3 AI Lab, a 'think-and-do tank' led by Bugge Holm Hansen and Sofie Hvitved, studies how AI changes foresight practice, prototypes AI-assisted scenario tools ('liquid foresight') and publishes reports on technology futures. It co-hosts the UNESCO Chair in Anticipatory Leadership & Futures Capabilities with Aarhus University (since 2022) and publishes FARSIGHT magazine.

Professional foresight (scenarios, horizon scanning, Three Horizons) is a method the AI-governance field uses little; CIFS has begun turning it on AGI, surveying foresight practitioners on AGI preparedness in 2025. It trains corporate and public-sector strategists, a channel through which thinking about the AI transition could reach organisations.

Works on Epistemics · Key work Navigating the AGI Discourse in Foresight (practitioner survey and roundtable) (2025); Exploring the Futures of Technology 2.0 (H3 AI Lab report) (2025); Liquid Foresight in an AI-Mediated World (advisory brief) (2025) · Get involved 'Futures and Foresight with AI' course, Copenhagen (8-9 Oct 2026, EUR 2,600; waiting list); Applied Strategic Foresight courses in Copenhagen and Paris (Nov-Dec 2026); 'Strategize like a Futurist' online course with Hyper Island (28 Oct-2 Dec 2026)

Note Most of its AI work treats AI as a foresight tool or a driver of business change; the 2025 AGI survey is its only safety-adjacent output, and it describes AGI discourse as polarised rather than taking a position. Consultancy clients shape much of the agenda.

Critical AI (journal and Critical AI @ Rutgers initiative) Adjacent

Media · New Brunswick, United States · founded 2023 · also draws on Law, society

An interdisciplinary peer-reviewed journal, published twice a year by Duke University Press and edited by Lauren M. E. Goodlad at Rutgers University's Center for Cultural Analysis. It grew out of the Critical AI @ Rutgers initiative. Alongside the journal it runs a blog, the 'AI Hype Report', the Design Justice Labs teaching platform and a student guide to critical AI literacies. It also holds workshops and institutes, such as the 2024 Design Justice AI Global Humanities Institute in Pretoria.

It is a central venue for humanities and social-science critique of AI claims, including claims of AI sentience, so it shows what any attempt to join present-harms scholarship with catastrophic-risk work has to answer. In July 2026 it co-organised 'BATCH: Beyond Alignment', a transdisciplinary workshop at the ACL conference, which is a point of contact with alignment discourse.

Works on Epistemics, Justice · Key work Critical AI journal, volume 4 (Duke University Press) (2026); Design Justice AI Global Humanities Institute, University of Pretoria (2024); Critical AI Literacies: A Guide for Students (2026) · Get involved Submit articles to the journal; Aug 2026 call for papers for the special series 'AI's Cultures of Value'; Contribute posts to the AI Hype Report; Online and hybrid workshops and symposia (e.g. Oct 2025 'Troubleshooting' AI workshops)

Note The founding year is the journal's first volume, inferred from volume 4 appearing in 2026 at two issues a year; the Rutgers initiative was active by 2021. It is deliberately sceptical of AI hype, including claims of AI sentience, so engagement with AI-safety framings is likely to be critical. Most journal content is behind a subscription.

Dezentrum Adjacent

Nonprofit · Zurich, Switzerland · also draws on Democracy

A Zurich 'think and do tank for digitalisation and society'. Legally it is an association (Verein) that owns Dezentrum GmbH, run by five partners under Sociocracy 3.0. It uses scenario techniques, speculative objects and 'future experiments' (for example no1s1, a self-owning blockchain building prototyped with ETH Zurich). It also runs workshops, a game against youth radicalisation (Radical Choices) and internet-safety workshops. Its AI work is a participatory service that helps NGOs, public bodies, schools and SMEs write their own AI guidelines, plus blog essays on AI literacy and AI-generated 'workslop'.

Its tools (speculative design, scenarios, participatory guideline-writing) help organisations and publics make sense of AI together. Those are methods the AI-safety field rarely uses outside expert circles. It shows how to turn abstract AI governance into norms co-written by the people affected, inside ordinary organisations.

Works on Epistemics, Democracy · Key work KI in der Organisation: participatory development of organisational AI guidelines; Nach Digital Literacy kommt AI Literacy (blog essay, Flurin Hess and Elias Röhle) (2026); TA-SWISS: Digitale Zukünfte der Demokratie (contribution on digital participation and speculative design) · Get involved Seminar 'Zukunftskompetenz statt Zukunftsangst', 4 Nov 2026, Zurich; Event: opening of 'Amt für Zeit', 28 Oct 2026, Zurich; Membership of the Dezentrum association (verein.dezentrum.ch); members can run workshops

Note Its AI engagement is practical: a participatory AI-guidelines service, which its homepage presents as its current main initiative, plus blog posts, with no research programme. Its earlier focus was blockchain, DAOs and new economic forms. No founding year was found on its own site. It publishes mainly in German.

European Language Council (CEL/ELC) Adjacent

Network · Milan, Italy

CEL/ELC is a European association of universities and other higher-education institutions working on language policy, multilingualism and the education of translators and interpreters. Its secretariat is at the Università Cattolica del Sacro Cuore in Milan, its president is Maria Teresa Zanola, and it publishes the European Journal of Language Policy. Its Special Interest Group on AI in translation and interpreting is coordinated by Maurizio Viezzi and Kris Peeters. In November 2025 it published 'AI for Translation and Interpreting: A Roadmap for Users and Policy Makers', and on 20 April 2026 it held an online seminar, '(De)Generative AI and Multilingual (Mis)Communication'.

The roadmap explains to lay users and policymakers how LLMs communicate differently from humans, and which side effects to weigh against the benefits. It also covers how translators and interpreters should be trained alongside AI. This is a language-policy view of communication risk that AI governance rarely draws on.

Works on Epistemics, Justice · Key work AI for Translation and Interpreting: A Roadmap for Users and Policy Makers (2025); Online seminar: (De)Generative AI and Multilingual (Mis)Communication (2026); Conference: Speaking the Future: Language Policies and Professional Communication (Brescia) (2025) · Get involved Annual conference, 'Communicating Knowledge Across Languages' (10-11 Dec 2026, Milan); PRISM-HE summer school for Master's and PhD students (Sept 2026); Special Interest Groups, including AI in T&I (contact by 30 September)

Note AI work is recent and modest: a standing SIG, one roadmap (Nov 2025), an annual conference on AI and language competencies (Dec 2025) and one seminar (Apr 2026). The SIG says it is preparing a COST Action or another EU-funded proposal. The founding year was not confirmed on its site. Its members are institutions, not individuals.

European Parliamentary Technology Assessment network (EPTA) Adjacent

Network · Distributed · founded 1990 · also draws on Democracy

A network, formally set up in 1990, of the technology-assessment offices that advise parliaments: 14 full members (including Germany's TAB, the Netherlands' Rathenau Instituut, the European Parliament's STOA and UK POST) and 10 associates. The presidency rotates each year, and the network publishes a joint annual report and a database of member projects. Its 2024 joint report, with 19 contributors, was 'Artificial Intelligence and Democracy'. Members' recent AI work includes TAB's August 2026 report on AI and biological-weapons risk and Rathenau's March 2026 study of recommender systems and election interference.

It is an established route from expert analysis into more than 20 parliaments, and its participatory technology-assessment methods are a mature template for democratic oversight of new technology. TAB's AI-and-biosecurity report shows members already analyse catastrophic misuse, so it is a ready channel for AI-safety findings to reach legislators.

Works on Democracy, Epistemics, Security · Key work Artificial Intelligence and Democracy (EPTA joint report, Norwegian Board of Technology presidency) (2024); TAB Report No. 217: Biotechnology and Artificial Intelligence: Risks Posed by Research to Security and Biological Weapons Proliferation (2026); Rathenau Instituut: Scrolling to the Ballot Box (recommender systems and election interference, for the Dutch House of Representatives) (2026) · Get involved Member offices (TAB, Rathenau Instituut, STOA, UK POST and others) commission studies and hold expert hearings, e.g. TAB's July 2026 hearing on AI and bio risks; EPTA project database for finding members' current AI work; Annual EPTA conference (2-3 November 2026, Athens; topic urban mobility)

Note A loose network with a rotating presidency and no central secretariat found; AI work varies widely by member, and most of it concerns democracy and present harms rather than safety. This profile merges TAB (run by ITAS at Karlsruhe Institute of Technology, based in Berlin) and the Rathenau Instituut (The Hague, about 60 staff). The 2026 joint theme is urban mobility, not AI.

Futurium Adjacent

Nonprofit · Berlin, Germany · founded 2014

Futurium is Berlin's 'House of Futures', a free-entry museum that opened in September 2019. It is run by Futurium gGmbH, a nonprofit company whose lead shareholder and main funder is the federal research ministry. It combines a permanent exhibition on possible futures of humans, nature and technology with a Forum for public talks and a Lab for hands-on workshops. Since September 2026 its thematic focus 'ON/OFF RELATIONSHIP' has looked at how people will share their lives with AI and other technology, through installations on AI-generated avatars, deepfakes and data extraction, a talk series and family labs.

It reaches a mass public (nearly 670,000 visitors in 2025) with participatory, exhibition-based futures work, and it is now running a public programme on living with AI. Those are formats the AI-safety field rarely uses. For int/a Berlin it is a natural venue for bringing AI scenarios and questions of human agency to a general audience.

Works on Epistemics, Human minds · Key work ON/OFF RELATIONSHIP: How we will share our lives with technology (thematic focus and exhibits) (2026); The future of artificial intelligence: technological promises and the power of terminology (public talk, 12 Oct 2026) (2026); Family Open Lab: Robots, AI and more – human beings and machines working as a team (recurring workshops) (2026) · Get involved Free public talks in the ON/OFF RELATIONSHIP series, starting with 'The future of artificial intelligence' on 12 Oct 2026 (German, recorded for YouTube); Family Open Lab drop-in workshops 'Robots, AI and more' (e.g. 4 and 25 Oct 2026); Free-entry exhibition, open daily except Tuesday

Note Its AI work is public engagement and exhibition-making, not research, and ON/OFF RELATIONSHIP covers technology in general with AI as one strand. The AI talk is on 12 October 2026, not the 16 October given in the discovery entry. Its AI framing is partly deflationary: the talk page calls AI systems pattern processors 'nothing more' and treats superintelligence talk as discourse to examine. It depends almost entirely on federal funding: in December 2025 the Bundesrechnungshof (Federal Audit Office) concluded that its financing concept had failed, citing too little private participation (German Wikipedia). Staff numbers are not published. The October family-lab dates could not be confirmed on the Lab page.

Institute for the Future (IFTF) Adjacent

Nonprofit · Palo Alto, USA · founded 1968

A Palo Alto futures nonprofit founded in 1968 as a spin-off from the RAND Corporation and led by executive director Marina Gorbis. It produces the Ten-Year Forecast (since 1978), runs Foresight Essentials training, and does contract research and consulting for companies, foundations and governments, which brought in nearly all of its $8.9 million revenue in 2024. Its AI work includes 'Three Horizons of AI-Enabled Work and Workers' (2024), the Ethical OS toolkit for anticipating technology harms (made with Omidyar Network) and 'Foresight in the Age of AI', a statement of principles for using AI in futures practice (September 2026).

Its methods (signals, scenarios, Three Horizons, public-imagination games) are anticipatory tools that AI governance rarely uses, and Ethical OS was an early attempt to bring harm anticipation into tech teams. Its foresight on AI and work bears on labour displacement and gradual disempowerment.

Works on Epistemics, Power · Key work Foresight in the Age of AI: IFTF Philosophy and Principles (2026); Three Horizons of AI-Enabled Work and Workers (2024); Ethical OS toolkit (with Omidyar Network) (2018) · Get involved Foresight Essentials training; Staff roles

Note Its website blocked automated access during this check, so the 2026 AI work is taken from the discovery draft's links and the rest from Wikipedia and its 2024 Form 990; confirm details before relying on them. The 990s show losses in 2023 and 2024 after a 2022 surplus. Framing is human augmentation and societal impact, not catastrophic risk. The Ethical OS year (2018) is from memory, not a fetched source.

Institute of Translation and Interpreting (ITI) Adjacent

Membership body · Milton Keynes, UK · founded 1986

ITI is a UK professional membership association for translators and interpreters. It was founded in 1986, is based in Milton Keynes and has about 2,600 members. Its board-level AI policy holds that humans remain essential to accurate and ethical translation. It curates AI resources and endorses the FIT and European Language Council AI papers. In 2025-26 it ran Translation and AI and Interpreting and AI courses with the University of Surrey (184 attendees over five cohorts). It wrote to the UK Government on AI policy in October 2025 and filed a joint copyright and AI consultation response with CIOL in February 2025.

ITI holds codes of professional conduct and a system for assessing qualified members in work where errors change meaning. These are ready-made norms for human oversight of AI translation. Its member surveys also document how AI is reshaping a skilled profession.

Works on Power, Assurance · Key work ITI policy on artificial intelligence; Translation and AI and Interpreting and AI courses with the University of Surrey (2025); Joint ITI-CIOL response to the UK copyright and AI consultation (2025) · Get involved Membership (qualified, student and other routes); Translation and AI and Interpreting and AI courses with the University of Surrey; Webinars and CPD on AI and emerging technologies

Note The AI work is mainly member education and advocacy for human translators, which is partly a labour interest. The courses teach the use of AI tools rather than AI governance. A member survey found many attributing falling work to AI.

International Federation of Translators (FIT) Adjacent

Membership body · Paris, France · founded 1953

FIT is the international federation of professional associations of translators, interpreters and terminologists. It was founded in 1953 under UNESCO auspices and has its secretariat in Paris. It has about 110 regular member associations, representing some 67,500 professionals. Its AI work consists of position papers on the use of AI in interpreting (August 2024) and on machine translation in the age of AI (June 2025); the interpreting paper opposes replacing human interpreters with unsupervised machine interpreting. In August 2026 its Working Group on AI Ethics, chaired by Adriana Zúñiga Hernández, published a report with six principles: accessibility, accountability, accuracy, confidentiality, fairness and transparency. The report calls for shared responsibility for AI errors and for labels that show whether a translation was produced by a human, by a machine, or by a machine and then reviewed.

Translators and interpreters have long managed errors that change meaning in courts, hospitals and diplomacy. FIT turns that practice into norms on human oversight, labelling and liability for machine translation and interpreting. It shows a profession setting assurance terms for an AI deployment.

Works on Assurance, Power · Key work FIT Position Paper on the Use of AI in Interpreting (2024); FIT Position Paper on Machine Translation in the Age of AI (2025); Ethics of AI in Translation and Interpreting (Working Group on AI Ethics) (2026) · Get involved Individuals take part through a national member association (in the UK, for example, ITI or CIOL); Position papers and the AI ethics report are free to read

Note The AI papers mainly defend the role of human professionals, which is partly a labour interest. The Working Group on AI Ethics is not among the 2025-2028 standing committees on FIT's site; its report was found through ITI. ITI dates the machine-translation paper June 2026, while FIT's own page says June 2025.

Interpreting SAFE AI Task Force (Stakeholders Advocating for Fair and Ethical AI in Interpreting) Adjacent

Network · Distributed · founded 2023 · also draws on Safety science

An independent US-based group of stakeholders, formed in June 2023 and launched in September 2023 with Bill Rivers as interim chair. Its stakeholder assembly of more than 50 members includes interpreter and translator associations (among them the American Translators Association and RID), certifying bodies, language-service companies, technology vendors, hospitals, standards bodies and researchers. It ran perception surveys of interpreters and of end users in ten spoken languages and ASL (2023-24). In July 2024 it published guidance on AI and interpreting services, built on four principles: end-user autonomy, evidence of safety and wellbeing, transparency of quality, and accountability for errors and harm. In August 2025, with CoSET, it released Part A of an AI Interpreting Solutions Evaluation Toolkit, with checklists on organisational readiness, setting-specific risks, vendor assessment and procurement.

It treats AI interpreting as a sociotechnical system: evaluation covers the human participants, the legal or medical setting and liability, not only model accuracy. It is an assurance and procurement framework for a high-stakes deployment, written by the profession affected, a perspective AI assurance work rarely gets.

Works on Assurance, Justice · Key work Interpreting SAFE AI Task Force Guidance on AI and Interpreting Services (2024); AI Interpreting Solutions Evaluation Toolkit, Part A (with CoSET) (2025); End-user perception survey in 10 spoken languages and ASL (2023) · Get involved Download the free guidance and Toolkit Part A; Submit research through the site

Note Parts B (technical specifications) and C (legal) were promised for 2025 and had not appeared by October 2026. Members include vendors of AI interpreting, so industry and professional interests mix. The site does not say who leads the group now that the interim chair period has passed.

Serpentine Arts Technologies Adjacent

Programme · London, UK · also draws on Law, society, Economics

The art, research and commissioning programme of the Serpentine galleries in London. It supports artists working with AI, blockchain, games and the life sciences, and convenes people from art, technology, law, policy and academia. Its Future Art Ecosystems (FAE) strand, running since 2019, publishes annual strategic briefings (FAE4: Art x Public AI, 2024; FAE5: Art x Creative R&D, 2025). It produced Holly Herndon and Mat Dryhurst's exhibition The Call (Oct 2024-Feb 2025), which proposed cultural, legal and technical protocols for consent-based AI training data. Since September 2026 it has run a paid R&D fellowship, Art x Convergence, on agentic AI.

It gives artists a structured route into AI governance questions: data consent, public AI infrastructure, and accountability when agentic systems act. It also connects the art world with AI labs, economists and lawyers; the 2026 fellowship jury includes Google DeepMind's Lila Ibrahim and Mariana Mazzucato. Few art-world programmes engage with AI governance this directly.

Works on Power, Justice · Key work Future Art Ecosystems 4: Art x Public AI (2024); Holly Herndon & Mat Dryhurst: The Call (Serpentine North) (2024); Future Art Ecosystems R&D Fellowship: Art x Convergence (2026-27 cohort) (2026) · Get involved FAE R&D Fellowship: inaugural cohort 2026-27, £10,000 award, three London weekends plus weekly online sessions; Exhibitions, talks and online commissions at Serpentine, London; Free FAE annual strategic briefings online

Note Arts Technologies is a strand of a major public gallery, so its priorities can shift with leadership and sponsors, and AI is one of four technology strands. Its framing is cultural and infrastructural, not safety. The fellowship jury includes industry figures (Google DeepMind, Snap). Founding year left blank: FAE dates from 2019 and Serpentine digital commissions from 2014, but I did not find when the programme took its current name.

Sitra (Finnish Innovation Fund) Adjacent

Public body · Helsinki, Finland · founded 1967 · also draws on Economics

Sitra is an independent public fund under the Finnish Parliament, founded in 1967 and governed by the Act on Sitra. It is financed mainly by returns on capital originally received from Parliament, not by tax money. It does national foresight (Megatrends, Weak Signals, the Futures Barometer), develops social innovations and funds experiments. Its recent AI work includes a September 2026 mapping, with the Agentic State foundation, of 70 government functions across 109 Finnish public organisations for agentic-AI readiness, and a September 2026 blog on losing human oversight of self-improving AI.

It is a well-funded national foresight body that reports to a parliament, and it has begun to talk publicly about loss-of-control risk. Its foresight products and public-sector pilots could carry AI-risk analysis into Finnish and Nordic policy. It is an unusual, non-EA funder and commissioner that new AI-safety funders could approach.

Works on Epistemics, Power · Key work Could AI kill us all? (Kristo Lehtonen, director of international programmes) (2026); Nationwide mapping of agentic AI readiness in the Finnish public sector, with the Agentic State foundation ('First Moves' report and dashboard) (2026); Megatrends 2026: Towards a new social contract (national foresight) (2026) · Get involved Foresight products (Megatrends, Weak Signals, Futures Barometer) and leadership and foresight training programmes; Sitra funds experiments and innovation projects (planned €15m a year from 2026); Staff roles in Helsinki

Note AI-risk engagement so far is one blog post. Most of its AI work promotes AI adoption for public-sector productivity and the data economy, so the ring is borderline between adjacent and potential. Sources are its own site only.

Potential ring 7

Center for Science and the Imagination, Arizona State University (CSI) Potential

Academic · Tempe, USA · founded 2012

A centre at Arizona State University, founded in 2012 with Ed Finn as founding director, that pairs writers and artists with scientists and engineers to imagine technological futures in detail. Starting with Project Hieroglyph (with Neal Stephenson), it has published more than twenty speculative-fiction collections, along with lesson plans, the Imaginary Papers series and the Imagination Desk podcast, and runs public events and the Sloan-supported Applied Sci-Fi Project. Its AI work is occasional: podcast episodes (e.g. Brian Christian, Pat Pataranutaporn), an April 2025 public conversation, 'The Spark and the Code', on AI and imagination, and Finn's own writing on how stories about algorithms shape them.

It has a tested method for writing grounded, hopeful futures with scientists and writers working together. AI-futures efforts such as Existential Hope's worldbuilding attempt the same thing with less literary craft. Finn is also academic director of Future Tense, which publishes fiction and essays on emerging technology.

Works on Epistemics · Key work Hieroglyph: Stories and Visions for a Better Future (2014); Frankenstein: Annotated for Scientists, Engineers, and Creators of All Kinds (2017); The Spark and the Code: Artificial Intelligence and the Future of Human Imagination (public event) (2025) · Get involved Public events and screenings in Tempe, with recordings online; Imaginary Papers and the Imagination Desk podcast; Door to open: no AI-futures programme yet

Note No dedicated AI programme was found; AI appears in occasional events and podcast episodes. Its 'Imagining Intelligence' project and older AI essays date from 2016-2021. Staff numbers and the full funder list were not verified.

Käte Hamburger Centre for Apocalyptic and Post-Apocalyptic Studies (CAPAS) Potential

Academic · Heidelberg, Germany · founded 2021 · also draws on Religion

An institute of advanced study at Heidelberg University, opened in 2021 and funded through the German federal research ministry's Käte Hamburger Kolleg programme; its second funding period began in 2025. Each year it hosts about 15 international fellows who study how societies imagine and experience the end of the world and what follows, across literature, history, religion, film, politics and the sciences. It also publishes the journal Apocalyptica and a magazine. It names AI among today's apocalyptic threats, and some fellows have worked on it, e.g. Teresa Heffernan on 'Artificial Intelligence and the (Post)Apocalyptic Imaginary' (2022-23) and Elke Schwarz on robo-apocalypse and posthumanism (2022-23).

AI-risk communication relies heavily on apocalyptic framing, and CAPAS studies how such framings mobilise, paralyse or polarise people. Its scholarship could inform how existential risk is communicated, and could give the field an outside view of its own 'doomer' discourse.

Works on Epistemics, Metacrisis · Key work Fellow project: Artificial Intelligence and the (Post)Apocalyptic Imaginary (Teresa Heffernan) (2022); Fellow project: Late-Modern Technology and its biotechno-politics, incl. AI case studies (Jan Cornelius Schmidt) (2025); Apocalyptica special issue 'Vitality and Radical Axé' (2026) · Get involved Fellowships of up to 12 months for international scholars (about 15 a year; the last deadline was 3 Jul 2026, for 2027-28); Public lectures, the Apocalyptic Cinema film series and arts collaborations in Heidelberg; Door to open for AI-risk communicators and researchers

Note It has no AI programme; its AI work comes through individual fellows. Much apocalypse scholarship is critical of apocalyptic rhetoric, which may sit uneasily with x-risk advocacy. Only the centre's own site was available as a source.

School of International Futures (SOIF) Potential
