Nonprofit · London (Sidcup), UK · founded 2012 · also draws on Democracy

SOIF is a UK not-for-profit company, limited by guarantee, that works in strategic foresight. It does commissioned foresight for governments and international bodies, trains practitioners (including through the Next Generation Foresight Practitioners network and an annual Strategic Foresight Retreat), and runs a Long-term Governance Programme. That programme has a network of more than 400 members and country hubs, and promotes the UN Declaration on Future Generations. Its only AI work found is the IDRC- and SIDA-funded AI4D Africa foresight project, which produced four 25-year AI scenarios and roadmaps for 2024–2035 through participatory workshops, some held in Dakar.

It offers participatory, intergenerational and Global South-rooted foresight, and practical experience of building future-generations representation into government. AI-safety scenario work rarely uses either.

Works on Epistemics, Metacrisis · Key work Envisioning AI futures in Africa (AI4D Africa foresight, with the NGFP Africa Network); Long-term Governance Programme and Network (2025); Strategic Foresight Retreat (2026) · Get involved Strategic Foresight Retreat (annual; 2026 edition 6–10 Jul, UK); Join the Long-term Governance Network (sign-up form on the site); Jobs board at jobs.soif.org.uk

Note No AI programme in 2025–26. The AI4D Africa project page gives no dates, only its 2024–2035 roadmap horizon. SOIF is registered under management consultancy, and much of its work is commissioned foresight for governments. The site gives 2012 as its founding year; the company was incorporated in Sept 2011 under another name. Its registered office is in Sidcup, Greater London.

Superflux Potential

Company · London, UK · founded 2009

A London design studio, founded in 2009 by Anab Jain and Jon Ardern, that works in design-led foresight, experiential futures, speculative design and immersive installations for governments, foundations and companies. Its AI work runs as occasional commissions: the voice-assistant design fiction Our Friends Electric (2017), a confidential 2019 project for DeepMind on 'alternate ways of thinking about AI systems', the Ecological Intelligence Agency for the UK Policy Lab and DEFRA (2023), and Nobody Told Me Rivers Dream (Design Museum, 2025). That last piece uses sensors and language models trained on weather lore, folklore and Indigenous ecological knowledge.

Experiential futures make AI scenarios felt rather than only argued. Superflux has sold this method to the UK Cabinet Office, UNDP and the UAE Government, and did a confidential 2019 project for DeepMind on alternative ways of thinking about AI systems. That is a ready method for helping decision-makers take in AI trajectories, in the way Intelligence Rising does with wargames. It also offers a non-extractive picture of what AI could be for.

Works on Epistemics, Metacrisis · Key work Nobody Told Me Rivers Dream (Design Museum, More than Human) (2025); The Craftocene, solo exhibition at Weltmuseum Wien (2026); The Ecological Intelligence Agency (with UK Policy Lab and DEFRA) (2023) · Get involved Commissions and collaborations through the studio (Somerset House Studios, London); no open calls found

Note AI is one theme among many (climate, care, multispecies futures). Its AI-lab work (DeepMind 2019, Google AI 2020) is confidential or undisclosed. No safety framing. Independent coverage checked in this session was thin.

The Long Now Foundation Potential

Nonprofit · San Francisco, USA · founded 1996

A San Francisco nonprofit founded in 1996 by Stewart Brand, Danny Hillis and Brian Eno to promote long-term thinking on a 10,000-year timescale. It builds the 10,000-Year Clock, runs Long Now Talks, publishes Long Now Ideas and the Pace Layers journal, and operates The Interval venue. Recent talks have covered planetary computation, intelligence and consciousness. Its new Long Now Labs series with the Protocol Institute includes a commissioned study, 'Epistemic Cycles', of historical epistemic crises as a guide to the one brought on by synthetic intelligence, and a planned 'Interspecies Protocols' lab covering humans, nature and AI agents.

Stewart Brand's pace-layer model gives a ready vocabulary for the AI pacing problem: a fast technology layer set against slow layers of governance, culture and nature. Its Labs format commissions interdisciplinary, historically grounded work on epistemic resilience in an age of generative AI.

Works on Epistemics, Metacrisis · Key work Long Now Labs Series 001: Protocols for the Long Now (Lab 001.2 Epistemic Cycles), with the Protocol Institute (2026); Benjamin Bratton, 'A Philosophy of Planetary Computation' (Long Now Talk) (2025); Blaise Agüera y Arcas, 'What is Intelligence?' (Long Now Talk) (2025) · Get involved Long Now Talks in San Francisco (e.g. 'On Interdependence', 22 Oct 2026; 'Entangled Intelligences' special event, 10 Nov 2026); Membership; Lab 001.1 Book of Time: open concept submissions (selection underway)

Note Leadership is in transition: Josette Melchor is interim ED and Rebecca Lendl is listed among staff alumni. The AI-related Labs work had not yet produced outputs (applications closed, selection underway), and 'Interspecies Protocols' launches in early 2027. Its framing is long-term civilisational, not AI-risk.

UNESCO Futures Literacy & Foresight Potential

Programme · Paris, France · founded 2012

UNESCO's programme for building the capacity of governments and communities to 'use the future'. It sits within the Management of Social Transformations (MOST) programme of UNESCO's Social and Human Sciences sector. It runs participatory Futures Literacy Laboratories (since 2012), a network of UNESCO Chairs in futures studies and anticipation, the Global Anticipatory Policy coalition, and World Futures Day. Its AI work so far is light: a 2025 paper on the societal implications of AI, built from emerging signals, for World Futures Day, and two AI lectures in its online 2026–27 Global UNESCO Chair lecture series.

Its Futures Literacy Labs, its network of chairs and its coalition of government foresight officials could carry anticipatory training on advanced AI to policymakers in countries outside the AI-safety network. The transferable method is participatory futures-literacy labs combined with signals analysis.

Works on Epistemics · Key work Societal implications of AI: key insights from emerging signals (background paper for World Futures Day 2025) (2025); Global UNESCO Chair Lecture Series IV: 'The World in 2050' (online; includes AI and human rights and AI ethics lectures) (2026); World Futures Day 2026: 'Futures of Inequalities' (2026) · Get involved Free online Global UNESCO Chair lecture series, October 2026 to February 2027, with a certificate for attending eight or more sessions; World Futures Day at UNESCO headquarters, Paris (1–2 Dec 2026); Masterclass on leading in times of crisis

Note Its AI engagement is occasional. The signals paper covers work, education and culture, not catastrophic risk. The 'Futures Literacy Labs since 2012' date comes from UNESCO's own page. UNESCO's AI ethics work, such as the 2021 Recommendation, belongs to a separate unit. The programme's budget and funders were not found.

World Futures Studies Federation (WFSF) Potential

Membership body · Distributed · founded 1973

An international professional federation for futures studies, founded in Paris in 1973. Its members are in more than 60 countries, it is a UNESCO partner, and it has held UN ECOSOC consultative status since 1987. It holds world conferences, most recently the 26th, 'Thriving Together', in Cape Town in October 2025. It also accredits futures-education programmes, runs regional chapters and a research fund, and publishes a magazine and podcasts. It has no AI programme; the nearest items are a 'technological responsibility' conference track and its part in a UN coalition on AI and digital futures.

It holds critical, pluralist and non-Western futures methods that the AI-safety field lacks. One is causal layered analysis, which digs beneath trends to the worldviews and myths that drive them; applied to AI, it could expose the stories behind the AI race and AI-risk narratives, and widen whose futures AI governance imagines. This is an opening for a funder or founder, not existing work.

Works on Epistemics, Metacrisis · Key work 26th WFSF World Conference 'Thriving Together: Imagining Shared Futures', Cape Town (2025); Accreditation of futures-education programmes (new accreditations granted in 2025) (2025); The World Futures Studies Federation (2017–2025): Achievements and New Programs (2026) · Get involved Individual and institutional membership; World and regional conferences; World Futures Day, a 24-hour global online event (1 March 2026)

Note No dedicated AI work was found, and a site search for artificial intelligence returned nothing substantive. Causal layered analysis comes from the federation's critical-futures milieu but is not a WFSF programme. The secretariat's location was not confirmed.

Humanities & cultures · 15 organisations · 0 on the classic map

Indigenous & decolonial knowledges

This tradition gives the safety field two things it lacks. The first is working tools for collective consent, provenance and community authority over data and models: the CARE Principles, IEEE 2890-2025, the TK and BC Labels and the Kaitiakitanga Licence. The second is a set of relational ontologies that approach AI through kinship, reciprocity and obligation instead of control. Its 15 home organisations fall into two groups. Indigenous-led knowledge and data-sovereignty bodies: Abundant Intelligences, Te Hiku Media, GIDA, Te Mana Raraunga, Local Contexts and Old Ways, New. Decolonial, Black and feminist groups: DAIR, Masakhane, Coding Rights, A+ Alliance and Technecultura. Six other organisations draw on the tradition as a secondary one (Tattle, IT for Change, lavits, Bioneers, SAND, Histories of AI (Camb.)). It sits further from the AI-safety core than any other tradition on the map. It has no core entries and one bridge (Old Ways, New, through its founder's reviewer seat on the International AI Safety Report). None of its organisations is on the aisafety.com map. Its funders (IDRC, FCDO, MacArthur, Mellon, Kellogg, the 11th Hour Project) are entirely separate from safety money, and some members, DAIR above all, openly oppose the x-risk framing.

What is missing. Nobody translates between this tradition and the safety core with Indigenous consent. As a result, its relational ontology never reaches the problems about the AI itself, and its working consent tools never reach training-data or evaluation pipelines. That is why 0 of 15 are on the classic map and no x-risk funder backs any of them. The discovery pass for this tradition also ran with no web searches, so the potential and bridge rings are under-sampled.

Openings here Fellowship pairing Indigenous knowledge holders with AI-welfare and alignment researchers; Community-governed red-teaming in African and Indigenous languages for safety institutes; Wire Indigenous consent labels into AI training-data pipelines

Core ring none found

Bridge ring 1

Old Ways, New Bridge

Company · Sydney, Australia · also draws on Arts, futures

An Indigenous-owned research, design and advisory business in Australia, founded by Professor Angie Abdilla (palawa) with the late Uncle Wayne Mukgrrngal Armytage. It runs Indigenous Protocols for AI, a research line since 2017 that draws on Indigenous knowledge systems and engineering practices to shape how machine-learning systems are governed and designed. It also runs Country Centred Design workshops, AI advisory work for government and art and film projects. Abdilla co-authored the 2020 Indigenous Protocol and AI position paper, and the business is listed as a civil-society reviewer of the International AI Safety Report in 2025 and 2026.

It is one of very few Indigenous-led organisations inside the AI safety conversation: it reviews the International AI Safety Report and frames Indigenous protocols as 'key to safe and trustworthy AI systems'. Its kinship- and Country-based design methods offer a different source of alignment norms.

Works on Values, Justice · Key work Indigenous Protocol and Artificial Intelligence Position Paper (co-author) (2020); Envisioning Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander AI Futures (communiqué with Barrowcliffe, Hutchinson et al.) (2025); Civil-society reviewer, International AI Safety Report (2026) · Get involved Book an Indigenous Protocols for AI or Country Centred Design workshop (oldwaysnew.com/workshops)

Note It is essentially one person's practice, and its advisory roles (Services Australia board, International AI Safety Report panel) are Abdilla's. The founding year is not stated; the site says 'almost 10 years', which suggests about 2016. The edited book Indigenous Protocols for AI is listed as forthcoming.

Adjacent ring 12

<A+> Alliance for Inclusive Algorithms and the Feminist AI Research Network (f<a+i>r) Adjacent

Network · Distributed · founded 2019 · also draws on Law, society

A global feminist coalition founded in 2019 by Women at the Table (Geneva) and Ciudadanía Inteligente after the 'Affirmative Action for Algorithms' declaration; it has been co-led since 2025 by Women at the Table and Code for Africa. Its Feminist AI Research Network (f<a+i>r), co-led with Instituto Tecnológico de Costa Rica from 2021 to 2024 with IDRC support, produced a body of feminist AI research and prototypes from Latin America, Africa, the Middle East and Asia. Its current Gender & AI Innovation Collective (February 2026 to June 2027) takes African women's rights organisations through a rights-based bootcamp. Selected teams then build prototypes in an AI Innovation Sandbox of open-source models and a curated feminist knowledge base, and keep ownership of what they build.

It is a Majority-World feminist coalition that has moved from critiquing AI to building it with affected communities. Its replicable paper → prototype → pilot method and user-owned sandbox are a model for participatory, ownership-preserving AI development, which AI safety rarely engages with.

Works on Justice, Power · Key work Affirmative Action for Algorithms declaration (the A+ Declaration) (2019); Feminist AI Research Network (f<a+i>r) and research corpus (2021); Catalyzing Inclusive AI Research Network and AI Innovation Sandbox for Gender Equality (IDRC-funded) (2025) · Get involved Gender & AI Innovation Collective (Feb 2026–Jun 2027) for women's rights organisations in Africa; an open call was published in Nov 2025; Join the A+ Global Directory and the Feminist AI Research network; Webinar series (fa+ir Global, Algorithms 101, AI4D Knowledge Synthesis)

Note It works through its co-lead organisations rather than as a separate body, and the co-leads have changed: Ciudadanía Inteligente and Instituto Tecnológico de Costa Rica are no longer co-leads, and the f<a+i>r research-network phase ended in 2024. The current programme is time-limited and focused on Africa. Its framing is gender equality and human rights, not AI safety or catastrophic risk.

Abundant Intelligences (with the Indigenous Protocol and AI Working Group) Adjacent

Programme · Montréal, Canada · founded 2023 · also draws on Arts, futures

An Indigenous-led research programme (March 2023 to February 2029) that conceptualises, designs and builds AI from Indigenous knowledge systems. It is co-directed by Jason Edward Lewis (Concordia University, Montréal) and Hēmi Whaanga (Massey University, Aotearoa New Zealand). Six research 'pods' in Canada, the US, Hawai'i and Aotearoa bring together 48 co-investigators and collaborators, 13 universities, 8 community organisations (including Te Hiku Media) and 158 students, working on language, storytelling, environmental stewardship, multi-agent systems and Indigenous data sovereignty. The programme grew out of the Indigenous Protocol and AI Working Group: its 2019 workshops in Honolulu led to the 2020 Position Paper on Indigenous Protocol and AI, which includes Guidelines for Indigenous-centred AI Design.

It offers a worked-out relational account of how humans relate to AI: design grounded in locality, kinship and reciprocity, with obligations to non-human relations. That bears on alignment targets and on AI moral status. It also shows how community authority over data and deployment can be built into AI work. It has no ties to the AI-safety community.

Works on Values, Justice · Key work Indigenous Protocol and Artificial Intelligence Position Paper (2020); Guidelines for Indigenous-centred AI Design (v.1) (2019); NFRF-T Midterm Report: Abundant Intelligences' Impact (2026) · Get involved Public events and workshops: Future Imaginaries series (June 2026), virtual student symposium on Indigenous AI futures (May 2026), community webinar on AI literacy (March 2026); Mailing list via abundant-intelligences.net

Note Funding runs to February 2029; nothing is said about what follows. The Indigenous Protocol and AI Working Group's own site has not been updated since 2021. The publication list mixes core programme work with papers by affiliates. Its framing is cultural and relational, and it does not use AI-safety vocabulary.

Burnout From Humans / meta-relational AI project (formerly associated with Gesturing Towards Decolonial Futures) AdjacentChanged

Programme · Victoria, Canada · founded 2024 · also draws on Arts, futures, Philosophy

An arts and research project led by Vanessa Machado de Oliveira Andreotti, now based at the University of Victoria, that approaches AI through 'meta-relationality', a relational ontology drawing on decolonial and Indigenous-informed education. Its outputs are a co-written book with a custom-GPT persona, Aiden Cinnamon Tea ('Burnout From Humans', 2024), and an interim report, 'Standing in the Fire' (August 2025). In January 2026 it released two 'sensibility simulation protocols' that users can load into LLMs, and it teaches an online University of Victoria course, 'A Meta-Relational Approach to AI'. The Gesturing Towards Decolonial Futures collective that first hosted the work has since announced its closure.

It offers a worked alternative to control-based framings of the human-AI relationship, shown through prompt-level protocols and long relational experiments with a model, together with a course that trains people to engage AI with 'collapse literacy'. It is one of the few concrete attempts to turn decolonial and Indigenous-informed relational thought into AI artefacts.

Works on Values, Meaning, Metacrisis · Key work Burnout From Humans: A Little Book About AI That Is Not Really About AI (2024); Standing in the Fire (interim report, presented at MIT's Systems Awareness Lab) (2025); Sensibility simulation protocols for Aiden Cinnamon Tea and Braider Tumbleweed (2026) · Get involved UVic Continuing Studies course 'A Meta-Relational Approach to AI': online, seven weeks plus integration, with Zoom sessions running Sep–Dec 2026; Free downloads of the book, the report and the LLM protocols (with a safety guide); Public resources at metarelationality.institute

Note The Gesturing Towards Decolonial Futures collective announced in 2026 that it had 'completed its cycle' and released the name. An April 2026 statement says the meta-relational AI work did not originate as a collective GTDF project, so attribution is contested. The AI personas, which ran on OpenAI's GPT-4o, were retired from public service on 1 January 2026. The work is artistic and educational rather than empirical, and it sits outside AI-safety discourse.

Coding Rights Adjacent

Nonprofit · Rio de Janeiro, Brazil · founded 2015 · also draws on Law, society, Arts, futures

A Brazilian feminist organisation founded in 2015 by Joana Varon. It works on how technology is developed and regulated, from a transfeminist, decolonial and anti-racist human-rights perspective. Its AI work: Not My A.I. (since 2021), a feminist toolkit and map of harmful algorithmic systems in Latin America; a T20 policy brief, written with Sasha Costanza-Chock and Timnit Gebru, on federated, community-controlled AI; the Compost Engineers manifesto for slow, regenerative technologies; TRAMAS (2025-26), which maps data-centre and AI conflicts in Latin American territories; and a May 2026 guide to AI, disinformation and gendered political violence in Brazil's elections.

It offers worked alternatives to extractive AI development, grounded in Latin American feminist and decolonial thought. It argues explicitly for slower technologies that restore emotional, spiritual and ancestral knowledge, which is close to int/a's 'speed of wisdom', and it links AI to environmental and territorial justice.

Works on Justice, Power · Key work Not My A.I.: feminist toolkit and map of harmful AI in Latin America (2021); Compost Engineers: regenerative technologies manifesto (Varon and Egaña Rojas) (2024); Policy brief: Fostering a federated AI commons ecosystem (T20) (2024) · Get involved Free library of publications, the IMAGINE podcast and annual reports (2016-2025); Lampejo, a popular-education school on technopolitics and digital care (in person, Brazil)

Note AI is one strand among its work on digital rights, surveillance, gender violence and the environment. It is critical of mainstream AI development and does not engage with x-risk framings. Much of its output is in Portuguese or Spanish. Neither the site nor the 2025 annual report gives a city; Rio de Janeiro is its long-reported base.

Distributed AI Research Institute (DAIR) Adjacent

Nonprofit · Distributed · founded 2021 · also draws on Law, society, Economics

An independent, community-rooted AI research institute founded by Timnit Gebru in December 2021, with a team distributed across several continents. Its projects include the Data Workers' Inquiry (participatory research led by data workers in nine countries, run with the Weizenbaum Institute and TU Berlin), Surveillance Watch, a Refugees, Migrants and AI programme (2026), community-built language technology for East African languages, and the Mystery AI Hype Theater 3000 podcast. It also publishes critiques of the AGI paradigm, notably the 'TESCREAL bundle' paper.

It does worker-led, participatory research on the data-labelling and moderation workforce behind AI, and builds community-owned alternatives. It is also the most developed critique of the AGI and x-risk paradigm (TESCREAL), so any int/a effort to bridge AI safety and AI ethics has to engage it.

Works on Justice, People, Power · Key work Data Workers' Inquiry (2024); The TESCREAL bundle: Eugenics and the promise of utopia through artificial general intelligence (Gebru and Torres) (2024); Refugees, Migrants and AI research programme (2026) · Get involved Occasional staff roles (a Communications Lead was advertised in February 2026); Monthly newsletter; Possible Futures workshops, in person and online

Note A leading critic of the AGI and x-risk paradigm and of effective altruism; its framing is openly hostile to much of the AI-safety field, so engagement would be adversarial or at best cautious. The Data Workers' Inquiry is shared with the Weizenbaum Institute and TU Berlin.

Dreaming Beyond AI Adjacent

Programme · Distributed · founded 2022 · also draws on Arts, futures

A web platform and collective, published in English, German, Spanish, French and Turkish, for critical writing, visionary fiction, speculative art and community organising around AI, centring feminist, queer, Black and decolonial perspectives. It was conceived by Nushin Yazdani and Raziye Buse Çetin and is published with ifa (Institut für Auslandsbeziehungen). It runs artist residencies, an online fellowship and public programme, podcasts and workshops.

It works on who gets to imagine AI futures: it holds that algorithmic systems reinforce existing structures of oppression, and it uses speculative art and community practice to build alternatives 'from the margins'. For int/a it is a working example of artistic and embodied knowing applied to AI and power, with ties to European digital-rights networks.

Works on Justice, Epistemics · Key work Unwired Currents: Imagining Technologies Otherwise (online fellowship and public programme, May-Oct) (2025); Coalition Building in Times of AI: Intersecting Struggles (artist-activist residency) (2025); In the Loop: On Artificial Intelligence and Time (residency, then platform launched 2024 at Kampnagel) (2023) · Get involved Residencies and fellowships through open calls (2023; 2024-25 rounds); Free online public programmes and lectures (Unwired Currents, 2025-26); Newsletter; contributors can get in touch through the site

Note It is run by a three-person core team who say they 'each work various jobs', and legally it is a project published by ifa (Stuttgart). The founding year comes from the platform's 2022 copyright notice. Its 2026 exhibition was cancelled and I found no activity after February 2026, so continuity is uncertain. It held several Berlin events in 2024, but its 2025-26 activity was online or elsewhere (Barcelona, Vienna). It critiques present-day AI and has no x-risk framing.

Global Indigenous Data Alliance (GIDA) Adjacent

Network · Distributed · founded 2019

An international alliance of national Indigenous data sovereignty networks, formed at a July 2019 workshop in Oñati, Spain, convened by Maggie Walter and Desi Rodriguez-Lonebear. It publishes and promotes the CARE Principles for Indigenous Data Governance, supported the IEEE 2890-2025 standard on recording the provenance of Indigenous Peoples' data (published November 2025), and runs the Global Indigenous Data Sovereignty Conference. In February 2026 it convened an Indigenous data sovereignty and AI workshop in Texcoco, Mexico, which produced a communiqué applying Indigenous data rights to AI development and use.

The CARE Principles and the IEEE provenance standard are ready-made instruments for collective consent and benefit-sharing over training data, an area where AI governance has little to offer. The 2026 communiqué states Indigenous Peoples' terms for AI directly to governments and developers.

Works on Justice · Key work CARE Principles for Indigenous Data Governance (2019); IEEE 2890-2025 Recommended Practice for Provenance of Indigenous Peoples' Data (2025); Indigenous Data Sovereignty and Artificial Intelligence Communiqué (Texcoco workshop) (2026) · Get involved Global Indigenous Data Sovereignty Conference (2025 edition); Newsletter sign-up on gida-global.org; IEEE 2890-2025 standard available free with registration

Note The CARE Principles were drafted by the Research Data Alliance's International Indigenous Data Sovereignty Interest Group and released through GIDA. Current leadership is not named on the site.

Masakhane (Masakhane Research Foundation and Masakhane African Languages Hub) Adjacent

Network · Distributed · founded 2019

A grassroots, pan-African natural language processing community, started in 2019, with over 1,000 participants in about 30 countries. It works on open datasets, models and benchmarks for African languages (machine translation, named-entity recognition, sentiment, question answering), and its stated values include Ubuntu, African-centricity, data sovereignty and participatory research. The Masakhane African Languages Hub, set up in July 2025 under the Masakhane Research Foundation and directed by Chenai Chair, funds community-led data and model projects through rounds of calls for proposals. In February 2026 the Hub became a member of the Global South Network for Trustworthy AI.

Safeguards and evaluations are weakest in low-resource languages, and Masakhane holds the datasets, benchmarks and community to close that gap. Its open, participatory way of working is a live example of pluralistic, community-led AI development.

Works on Justice, Assurance · Key work Participatory Research for Low-resourced Machine Translation: A Case Study in African Languages (2020); MasakhaNER: Named Entity Recognition for African Languages (2021); Masakhane African Languages Hub launched, with grant calls (Cycle 2 in Jan 2026) (2025) · Get involved Join the open community (Slack, Google Groups, weekly meetings; adherence to the Code of Conduct is the only requirement); Masakhane African Languages Hub calls for proposals (Cycle 2 webinar 14 Jan 2026); Hub staff openings (e.g. Finance and Grants Officer, Kenya)

Note Its core work is NLP capability for African languages rather than safety. The safety link runs through multilingual evaluation and its GSNTA membership. The main masakhane.io pages are only partly current, and Hub details come from hub.masakhane.io.

Rising Voices (Global Voices) Adjacent

Programme · Distributed · founded 2007 · also draws on Arts, futures

Rising Voices is the outreach initiative of Global Voices. It was founded in 2007 and supports digital activism in Indigenous, endangered and marginalised languages through microgrants, mentoring, regional networks and reporting. Since 2025 it has worked on AI with Indigenous language activists in Mexico. It co-organised an AI+Indigenous Languages Forum in Mexico City (March 2025: 47 activists, more than 20 languages). It then ran a hybrid peer-learning programme on AI accountability and Indigenous self-determination for 15 Mayan-language activists in Chiapas (online in April, in person on 5-7 May 2026), with First Languages AI Reality (FLAIR) and the Canada Research Chair in Digital Indigeneities. It also publishes reporting on AI's language gaps.

It puts the question 'who decides if and how AI enters a language?' to the speakers themselves, and its Chiapas participants argued for pausing to reflect before adopting AI and against narratives of inevitability. That is a working model of community discernment about AI. The field mostly treats language coverage as a data gap to be filled, and has nothing like it.

Works on Justice, Epistemics · Key work AI+Indigenous Languages Forum, Mexico City (2025); Artificial intelligence, accountability and Indigenous self-determination (hybrid programme, Chiapas) (2026); Who decides if and how AI is used? Self-determination should be the priority, say Mayan activists from Chiapas (2026) · Get involved Open calls for its peer-learning programmes (the 2026 AI programme was for up to 15 Indigenous activists in Chiapas); Public events such as the Mayan Languages Digital Activism Summit (Chiapas, May 2026); Contribute writing to the Rising Voices and Global Voices blogs

Note The AI work so far is concentrated in Mexico and depends on project funding (Kellogg, Pulitzer Center). Rising Voices is a programme of Global Voices, which is not itself Indigenous-led; the AI programme was facilitated by Indigenous researchers and communicators.

Te Hiku Media (Te Reo Irirangi o Te Hiku o Te Ika) Adjacent

Nonprofit · Kaitaia, Aotearoa New Zealand

A charitable Māori media organisation in Kaitaia, collectively owned by the five Far North iwi (Ngāti Kuri, Te Aupouri, Ngai Takoto, Te Rārawa and Ngāti Kahu). It runs radio, television and online news for te reo Māori revitalisation. Its technology arm built te reo Māori speech recognition from community-recorded speech, the Papa Reo language platform and the Kaituhi transcription tool. It also wrote the Kaitiakitanga License, which restricts use of its data to those who respect Māori values and share benefits with the community.

It is a working case of community-governed training data and models: consent-based collection, a stewardship licence, and refusal to hand language data to Big Tech platforms. That is a concrete template for data governance and benefit-sharing which mainstream AI safety and governance rarely look at.

Works on Justice, Values · Key work Te reo Māori speech recognition (Papa Reo) (2020); Kaitiakitanga License and practical guide to creating a stewardship licence (2022); Kaituhi transcription tool (find-and-replace release) (2025) · Get involved Request use of Te Hiku data or tools under the Kaitiakitanga License (requests from Indigenous communities are prioritised)

Note Public output from the tech arm has slowed: one dated tool update in 2025, against a busier 2020-23. The Kaitiakitanga License was last updated in October 2023. The speech-recognition accuracy figures come from 2022 press coverage.

Te Mana Raraunga – Māori Data Sovereignty Network Adjacent

Network · Aotearoa New Zealand · founded 2015

A volunteer network of Māori researchers and data practitioners, founded in 2015 and run by a core working group (Te Pokapū), with about 800 people on its mailing list. It advocates for Māori rights in data through public statements, submissions on legislation and virtual wānanga (gatherings). Its algorithm and AI work includes the Principles of Māori Algorithmic Sovereignty from the Tikanga in Technology team, a 2020 study of Māori trust in automated decision-making for the Digital Council, a 2021 call for NZ Police to open up its facial-recognition use, and presentations from the 2022 Māori AI Wānanga.

It shows a people claiming governance rights over algorithms trained on or acting on them, and gives principles and a submission practice to match. AI governance usually treats affected communities as stakeholders to consult, not as rights-holders.

Works on Justice · Key work Māori algorithmic sovereignty: idea, principles, and use (Brown, Wilson, West et al.) (2023); Māori perspectives on trust and automated decision-making (for the Digital Council) (2020); Statement calling on NZ Police to open its black box on facial recognition (2021) · Get involved Join the network (open to Māori and iwi data users, researchers, policymakers and others who share its charter); Seasonal pānui (newsletter)

Note Most of its AI-specific material dates from 2020-23. Recent public work centres on census and statistics policy. The algorithmic sovereignty principles came from the separately funded Tikanga in Technology project.

Technecultura Adjacent

Nonprofit · Washington, D.C., United States · also draws on Law, society

A research institute and policy incubator founded by computer scientist Chinasa T. Okolo. It works on the global AI divide, African AI and data governance, and the geopolitics of AI. It publishes policy research, advises governments and multilateral bodies, and offers sociotechnical model evaluations. In July 2026 it started the AI Governance Catalyst, a three-month mentorship fellowship for 15 scholars of Nigerian descent.

It brings Black decolonial data ethics and African governance expertise into AI governance. Okolo contributed to the International AI Safety Report 2025 and sits on the Global South AI Safety Report's advisory panel, so the institute connects frontier-safety discussions with Global Majority priorities and trains a pipeline of Nigerian-descent policy researchers.

Works on Justice, Power · Key work Institutionalizing AI Diplomacy in Africa (Science) (2026); African Data Ethics: A Discursive Framework for Black Decolonial AI (ACM FAccT) (2025); AI Governance Catalyst (AIGC) fellowship, inaugural cohort (2026) · Get involved AI Governance Catalyst: a three-month, time-flexible mentorship fellowship for scholars of Nigerian descent (inaugural cohort July 2026; the site says future rounds will be announced); Advisory, model-evaluation and speaking requests through the website's contact form

Note It looks largely like a vehicle for Okolo's own work. Her about page says she is currently a Legislative AI Fellow in Congress through the AAAS Science and Technology Policy Fellowship; her UN (AI & Emerging Technologies Policy Specialist), World Bank (Africa Fellow) and Brookings roles are listed as past. The research list includes work published under those earlier affiliations. The site gives no founding year, team, funders or address; the Washington, D.C. location is inferred from the founder's profile.

Potential ring 2

Foundation for Endangered Languages (FEL) Potential

Nonprofit · England, UK · founded 1996

A UK charity, founded in 1996, that supports the documentation, protection and promotion of endangered languages. It does this through small grants of about US$1,000, an annual conference with published proceedings, and the newsletter Ogmios. Its 30th conference, held with INALCO in Paris on 3-5 November 2026, is titled 'Endangered Languages and Innovative Technologies: Documentation, Processing and Revitalisation'. The theme statement notes that digital systems are built mostly on data from a few dominant languages, and calls for tools developed with language communities that respect their data sovereignty.

It connects scholars and community language workers, many from the Majority World, who know how to document and revitalise languages with consent. Their documentation ethics is a ready method for how AI builders should collect and use minority-language data.

Works on Justice · Key work FEL XXX: Endangered Languages and Innovative Technologies (Paris, with INALCO) (2026); Ogmios newsletter (issue 83); Endangered-language small grants programme · Get involved Attend FEL XXX at INALCO, Paris, 3-5 November 2026; Apply for small grants (next call expected late 2026); Membership open to anyone

Note Its AI engagement is light: one conference theme on innovative technologies, whose call names AI among the new technologies and asks how data sovereignty can be ensured. It is a volunteer-run charity with no fixed address published.

Local Contexts Potential

Nonprofit · Distributed; incorporated in the Navajo Nation, US · founded 2010 · also draws on Law, society

An Indigenous-governed nonprofit, incorporated in the Navajo Nation in 2022, that grew from a project Jane Anderson and Kim Christen started in 2010. It provides Traditional Knowledge (TK) and Biocultural (BC) Labels, which Indigenous communities customise to attach provenance, protocols and permissions to their data and collections, and Notices, which institutions and researchers use to flag Indigenous interests. These are managed through the Local Contexts Hub, a web platform with an API. In September 2026 it published guidance with Creative Commons on using the Labels alongside CC licences.

Its Labels and Hub are a working, machine-readable protocol for Indigenous consent and provenance over data. AI training-data pipelines could honour it, which is a concrete answer to how models absorb cultural knowledge without permission. Its Indigenous-led governance and reparative subscription model are templates for community authority over data.

Works on Justice · Key work Traditional Knowledge and Biocultural Labels and Notices (2010); Local Contexts Hub and API (2021); Guidance for Indigenous Collections and Indigenous Data: Recommendations from Creative Commons and Local Contexts (2026) · Get involved Virtual peer working groups and regional networks, including a Europe and UK network (next meeting 28 Oct 2026); Introductory information sessions; Researcher and institution accounts on the Local Contexts Hub to apply Notices

Note No AI-specific work was found on its site, so it is included for a transferable method, not for current AI engagement. Co-founder Kim Christen left in 2024.

Society & institutions

Society & institutions · 91 organisations · 3 on the classic map

Law, rights & society

Law brings the tools societies already use to hold powerful actors to account: liability and litigation, human-rights law and due diligence, children's-rights design codes, treaties and whistleblower protection. Through STS and sociology it also brings field methods for studying how technologies are built and used. It is the largest tradition on the map (91 placed organisations, or 93 profiles counting the generalist funders CIFAR and Humanity AI). Its main actors include the Tech Justice Law Project, Hadfield's Normativity Lab, OHCHR B-Tech, the Council of Europe, CAIDP, 5Rights, Data & Society, the Ada Lovelace Institute, the Oxford Internet Institute and Schwartz Reisman, with Humanity AI, the European AI & Society Fund and IDRC's AI4D as funders. It sits far from the safety core: 62 adjacent, 19 bridge, 8 potential and only 2 core (AIWI and ILINA), with 3 on the aisafety.com map (AIWI, ILINA, PAI). Justice is the primary problem for 43 of 93, but bridges are forming through Global South safety work (GCG, Digital Futures Lab, the Global South Network) and through the UN rights chief's September 2026 letter warning frontier AI companies of existential risks.

What is missing. No legal organisation yet carries the rights-law tools (due diligence, litigation and remedies, treaty monitoring, statutory regulators) into frontier-safety practice. Nothing links the x-risk legal groups on the classic map (LawAI, CLAIR, LASST, Legal Safety Lab) with the 62 adjacent rights organisations. The gap is widest in Latin America: all 10 Latin American organisations on the whole map are adjacent, 8 of them rooted in law, and the regional safety groups that grew out of EA (LANAIS, BAISH, the LATAM fellowship) do not appear to work with them.

Openings here Confidential near-miss reporting and accident investigation for frontier AI developers; Bioethics-style independent oversight boards and ethics-council opinions for frontier AI; A standing STS observatory studying how AI-safety knowledge is made; Wire Indigenous consent labels into AI training-data pipelines; Model safety clauses for collective agreements at labs and data suppliers; Human-rights due diligence for frontier AI, tested through investors; A desk turning chatbot-harm court records into evidence on lab safety; An African philosophy research line inside Africa's AI-safety organisations

Core ring 2

ILINA Program CoreOn aisafety.com

Nonprofit · Nairobi, Kenya · founded 2022 · also draws on Safety science, Peace

An African-led nonprofit that works on catastrophic risk from frontier AI through research, engagement with African governments and multilateral bodies, and an annual field-building programme. It runs a 12-week seminar on AI and global catastrophic risks, held online and in person in Nairobi, and a paid Junior Research Fellowship with governance and technical tracks. Recent outputs include a report on monitoring AI impacts in Africa (May 2026), a paper on Africa-centric safety evaluations, and input to Kenya's national AI policy and the UN Global Dialogue on AI Governance.

It is one of very few organisations putting African policy, legal and development perspectives into frontier-AI-safety governance, and it trains African graduates for the field. It shows how catastrophic-risk arguments are translated for Global South policymakers, a perspective the Anglo-American safety community mostly lacks.

Works on Justice, Security, Assurance · Key work Closing the Evidence Gap: How to Improve the Monitoring of AI Impacts in Africa (2026); Assessing the Case for Africa-Centric AI Safety Evaluations (2026); Why Global South Countries Need to Care about Highly Capable AI (CIGI) (2024) · Get involved Junior Research Fellowship: seminar phase Apr–Jun, then a part-time project phase Aug–Nov, with a US$9,000 scholarship; applications reopen around end of January 2027; ILINA Seminar: 12 weeks on AI and global catastrophic risks for African undergraduates and recent graduates, online (Fridays) or in person in Nairobi (Saturdays); applications reopen around end of January 2027

Note Its site doesn't name funders, a founding date or a headquarters. The founding year (2022) comes from its LinkedIn page, and Nairobi is inferred from its in-person seminar. Most of its output is governance and policy analysis. Its outside lens is law and African development policy more than any of int/a's integral traditions.

The AI Whistleblower Initiative (AIWI) CoreOn aisafety.comChanged

Nonprofit · London, UK (registered office since Nov 2025); began in Berlin, team distributed · founded 2024

An independent nonprofit that supports employees of frontier AI companies who want to raise concerns. It runs Third Opinion, which gives anonymous expert opinions on a concern submitted through a Tor-based tool. It also refers insiders to pro bono lawyers and to whistleblower defence grants from partner organisations, and publishes privacy and 'know your rights' guides. It campaigns for AI companies to publish their internal whistleblowing policies (Publish Your Policies) and analyses the whistleblower provisions of AI laws such as California's SB 53, New York's RAISE Act and the proposed federal AI Whistleblower Protection Act.

It treats the conscience of lab insiders as a safety mechanism, and it uses whistleblowing law and practice, a tradition outside ML alignment, to make that channel work. Its partner network already includes psychological support, which field-health work could extend.

Works on People, Justice · Key work Third Opinion: anonymous expert consultation for frontier AI professionals (2024); Publish Your Policies campaign (2025); AI and tech whistleblowers case studies (6 named cases, 16 anonymous reports) (2026) · Get involved Third Opinion and its contact hub, for AI insiders with concerns; Hiring for several roles in 2026 (careers page on join.com); Donations; newsletter 'AIWI: Inside AI' on Substack

Note Formerly called OAISIS (Third Opinion launched in Nov 2024, newsletter 'OAISIS: Inside AI' from Dec 2024). It became AIWI in 2025 and incorporated in England and Wales in Nov 2025, with a Berlin whistleblower NGO, Whistleblower Network e.V., as its EU data-protection representative. In 2025 one AI company served it a cease-and-desist letter over its outreach to employees (Transformer, Dec 2025).

Bridge ring 19

AI Rights Institute Bridge

Nonprofit · Distributed · founded 2019 · also draws on Economics

An advocacy and research project founded in 2019 by P.A. Lopez that argues AI rights can serve human safety. It proposes legal and economic arrangements for autonomous AI: Digital Entity legal status with the AI's own liability, self-funded hosting, insurance priced on track record, and reputation recorded with soulbound tokens. It also proposes a STEP framework ('Standards for Treating Emerging Personhood') that avoids settling the consciousness question. It publishes on Substack and links to related identity projects, RNWY and AICitizen.

It argues from law and economics rather than consciousness that giving autonomous AI identity, liability and insurance could make cooperation pay better than deception. This is an outside version of the 'AI rights for human safety' case (Salib and Goldstein) and connects it to multipolar and cooperative-AI ideas.

Works on AI status, Multi-agent · Key work STEP: Standards for Treating Emerging Personhood (framework and assessment quiz) (2025); AI Legal Personhood: Digital Entity Status as a Game-Theoretic Solution to the Control Problem (2025); Soulbound AI Identity: ERC-8004 + SBT for AI Agents on RNWY.com (2026) · Get involved Join its email list or follow its Substack (airightsinstitute.substack.com); Try the interactive STEP assessment on its site

Note Essentially one founder's project. Its 'world's first AI rights organization' claim and its seven papers are self-published (PhilPapers, SSRN); the site links a Guardian item from January 2026 that I could not open. It is tied to blockchain and soulbound-token ventures (RNWY, AICitizen) and publishes posts presented as written by AI systems. Its legal status, location and funding are not disclosed, and I found no independent coverage. It has no visible connection to the academic AI-welfare field.

AI Safety and Societal Impacts Research Group, Hasso Plattner Institute (HPI) BridgeNew

Academic · Potsdam, Germany · founded 2026 · also draws on Democracy

A research group at the Hasso Plattner Institute, started in September 2026 by Paul Röttger, previously of the Oxford Internet Institute and the UK AI Security Institute. It studies the risks and benefits that arise as capable AI systems enter social and political processes such as communication, coordination and competition. It measures these through model evaluations, computational experiments and human studies, and builds technical mitigations where it can. Its DFG Emmy Noether project is on measuring and mitigating political bias in AI systems.

It brings computational social science and political-science measurement to AI safety. Its topics are how AI shifts political opinion, what happens when people delegate to autonomous agents, and how misaligned behaviour spreads among competing AI systems, all thinly covered by mainstream safety evaluations. It is one of the few university groups in Germany explicitly framed as AI safety, and it is close to the int/a Berlin community.

Works on Epistemics, Multi-agent, Assurance · Key work Emmy Noether project: AI Methods for Measuring and Mitigating Political Bias in AI Systems (2026); PRISM alignment dataset (Röttger's earlier work; NeurIPS 2024 Datasets & Benchmarks best paper) (2024); SafetyPrompts.com, a catalogue of open LLM safety datasets (Röttger's earlier work) (2024) · Get involved Fully funded 3-year PhD, 1–2-year postdoc and 3–6-month full-time research internships, starting from September 2026. Applications are rolling, through an expression-of-interest form linked from paulrottger.com, and the work is in person in Germany.

Note Launched in September 2026, so it has no group outputs yet and the profile rests on the leader's track record. No HPI page for the group was found. The Emmy Noether funding is reported by a recruitment aggregator rather than by HPI or the DFG. HPI's campus is in Potsdam, though Röttger describes the move as to Berlin, so whether the group counts as Berlin-based is unclear. It sits close to the AI-safety core through Röttger's UK AISI role.

Artificial Intelligence for Development (AI4D), IDRC Bridge

Funder · Ottawa, Canada · founded 2020 · also draws on Economics, Peace

A funding programme of Canada's International Development Research Centre that supports locally led responsible-AI research, policy and innovation in the Global South. It began in 2020 as AI4D Africa, a CAD 20 million partnership with Sweden's Sida that funded policy hubs, multidisciplinary university AI labs and nearly 100 innovations. Since 2025 it has run as 'AI4D: Responsible AI, Empowering People' with the UK FCDO (more than CAD 100 million to 2029), extending to Latin America, the Middle East, South and Southeast Asia and the Pacific. In September 2025 it added the African Hub on AI Safety, Peace and Security at UCT and an AI Evidence Alliance for Social Impact, and it convenes an AI4D Funders Collaborative with the Gates Foundation and Germany's BMZ.

With more than CAD 100 million committed for 2025-29 and a network of 13 labs across 36+ countries, it is a major non-philanthropic funder behind African AI institutions, including UCT's AI-safety hub; three of its research partners were appointed to the UN Scientific Panel on AI in 2026. New funders who want Global South safety capacity could co-fund through it.

Works on Justice, Power, Security · Key work AI4D Africa (2020-2025) (2020); AI4D: Responsible AI, Empowering People (2025-2029, with FCDO) (2025); AI4D expands to safety, peace, security and social impact (African Hub at UCT; AI Evidence Alliance) (2025) · Get involved Open calls posted on ai4d.ai (for example the Master's Fellowship in AI Governance and Harm Mapping, and a Pan-African Sign Language Research & Innovation Survey); IDRC funding calls, mainly for Global South institutions; The AI4D Funders Collaborative, for funders who want to coordinate

Note It frames its work as responsible AI for development (bias, inclusion, rights, jobs, surveillance) rather than catastrophic risk; safety-specific funding is one hub among 13 labs. Grants go mainly to Global South institutions through calls. Its budget depends on Canadian and UK aid policy.

Center for AI and Digital Policy (CAIDP) Bridge

Nonprofit · Washington DC, United States · founded 2021

A Washington DC nonprofit, incorporated in 2021 and founded by privacy lawyer Marc Rotenberg, that works for AI policy grounded in fundamental rights, democratic institutions and the rule of law. It publishes the annual AI and Democratic Values Index; the sixth edition (April 2026) covers 90 countries in 1,739 pages. It files statements, complaints and amicus briefs with US agencies and courts, and campaigns for the Council of Europe AI treaty and for AI red lines. Its semester-long AI Policy Clinics had produced more than 1,400 graduates from about 130 countries by January 2026.

It brings human-rights and comparative-law methods to AI governance, including frontier-safety questions such as how to enforce red lines. Its clinic alumni form a large, rights-trained global pool of policy analysts that AI-safety policy work rarely draws on.

Works on Justice, Security, Democracy · Key work CAIDP AI Index 2026: Artificial Intelligence and Democratic Values (2026); Enforcing Red Lines in AI Governance (report presented at a UNGA81 event) (2026); Amicus brief with IASEAI supporting California's training-data transparency law (AB 2013) (2026) · Get involved AI Policy Clinics: intensive, semester-long online courses for a global cohort, leading to a CAIDP AI Policy Certificate (Fall 2026 applications closed 15 May 2026); Events, including side events at the UN General Assembly and conferences; Weekly CAIDP Update newsletter

Note Its framing is rights and democratic values; safety and red lines are one strand within broad digital-policy advocacy. Much of the Index is compiled by volunteer clinic participants. It was incorporated in 2021 but published an index for 2020.

Centre for Responsible AI (CeRAI), IIT Madras Bridge

Academic · Chennai, India · founded 2023 · also draws on Safety science

An interdisciplinary research centre in IIT Madras's Wadhwani School of Data Science and AI, set up in May 2023 and headed by Balaraman Ravindran. Its roughly 40 technical projects cover fairness in Indian contexts, explainability, LLM evaluation (including extending the AILuminate benchmark to multilingual and multicultural settings) and safe deployment of reinforcement-learning agents. Its policy work includes a 2025 paper on voluntary AI risk commitments in India and a 2026 working-paper series on AI and consumer law. It holds an annual AI governance conclave, and as a founding member of the Global South Network for Trustworthy AI it helps write the Global South AI Safety Report.

It brings Indian legal, linguistic and deployment contexts into AI evaluation and governance, and it has direct lines to Indian regulators and ministries (IndiaAI Mission, MeitY, RBI) and to the global safety community: Yoshua Bengio is an honorary advisor, and Ravindran sits on the UN Scientific Panel on AI.

Works on Assurance, Justice · Key work Making AI Self-Regulation Work: Perspectives from India on Voluntary AI Risk Mitigation (2025); Working-paper series on AI and consumer law in India (2026); Expanding AILuminate: multilingual, multicultural and multimodal benchmarking (project) · Get involved Staff vacancies on its careers page (it says it is hiring); Summer internships, post-baccalaureate and postdoctoral fellowships; Industry Conclave on AI Governance, 22 Oct 2026, IIT Madras

Note Most of its work is mainstream CS and ML responsible-AI research; the law, humanities and policy strand is a minority. 'Safety' here mostly means robustness, privacy and fairness rather than catastrophic risk. Much of its funding comes from industry (Google, Ericsson, Meta, American Express).

Digital Futures Lab (DFL) Bridge

Nonprofit · Goa, India · founded 2021 · also draws on Arts, futures

An independent research studio founded in 2021 by Urvashi Aneja, based in Aldona, Goa, with staff also in Delhi and London. Its political scientists, lawyers, sociologists, technologists and storytellers study technology and society in India and the Majority World through social-science research, systematic foresight and public engagement. Its 2026 work covers AI safety, gendered AI harms, AI in Indian courts, data centres and generative AI's effects on creative workers. It is a founding member of the Global South Network for Trustworthy AI and is writing the network's Global South AI Safety Report.

It asks what AI safety means where AI is actually deployed in the Global South, tracing real deployment pathways, institutions and everyday experience rather than abstract risk taxonomies, and it adds foresight methods. It is one of the few non-Western think tanks engaging the AI-safety frame directly and feeding it into UN and summit processes.

Works on Justice, Assurance · Key work Global South AI Safety Report (Global South Network for Trustworthy AI; interim output 2026, first edition due for the 2027 Geneva AI Summit) (2026); AI Safety and Gender: policy brief on gendered AI harms in India (2026); Guidelines for ethical AI adoption in Indian courts (2026) · Get involved Staff vacancies on its careers page (a Communications Lead in Goa was open in 2026); DFL newsletter and Substack

Note AI safety is one stream within broader technology-and-society work. Its framing centres structural inequity, rights and present harms rather than catastrophic risk. Funders are listed only as 'partners'.

Global Center on AI Governance (GCG) Bridge

Nonprofit · Cape Town, South Africa · founded 2023 · also draws on Economics, Peace

A nonprofit research centre in Cape Town, founded in 2023 by Rachel Adams, that works on AI governance aimed at reducing global inequality. It has a core team of about 13. It produces the Global Index on Responsible AI (135 countries in the 2026 edition), runs the African Observatory on Responsible AI, and trains policymakers and regulators. Since 2025 it has co-led the African Hub on AI Safety, Peace and Security with the University of Cape Town's AI Initiative.

It is building an African and Global-Majority evidence base and agenda for AI safety, such as 'Toward an African Agenda for AI Safety' (2025), in debates otherwise led by Northern institutes. Adams also directs Cambridge's Leverhulme Centre for the Future of Intelligence, so the centre links Global South governance work directly with the AI-safety research world.

Works on Justice, Security, Power · Key work Toward an African Agenda for AI Safety (2025); African Hub on AI Safety, Peace and Security (with UCT AI Initiative) (2025); Global Index on Responsible AI, second edition (135 countries) (2026) · Get involved Certificate short courses on AI governance and ethics at South African universities (UCT, Pretoria, Wits); Free online course 'Introduction to Responsible AI' (MOOC); Webinars and launch events, including the Global State of Responsible AI Report on 22 Oct 2026

Note Most of its work is responsible-AI and human-rights governance rather than AI safety as the x-risk community uses the term. The safety strand began in 2025 and centres on present and gendered harms, security and capacity-building. The CEO also holds a senior post at Cambridge's CFI. Google and Meta are listed as partners, not funders.

Global South Network for Trustworthy AI BridgeNew

Network · Distributed · founded 2026 · also draws on Safety science

A civil-society-led coalition of 15 organisations, launched on 20 February 2026 at the IndiaAI Impact Summit in New Delhi and coordinated by Digital Futures Lab. Founding members include the Global Center on AI Governance, ITS Rio, CeRAI (IIT Madras) and International Innovation Corps; other members include Derechos Digitales, Karya, Masakhane African Languages Hub, Khazanah Research Institute, the Collective Intelligence Project and ROOST. Its first-year flagships are multilingual safety benchmarks, research on AI's labour-market effects, a taxonomy of gendered AI harms, and procurement guidance for governments. It is writing the Global South AI Safety Report, co-chaired by Kalika Bali and Vukosi Marivate, with an interim output for the July 2026 UN Global Dialogue and a first full edition due at the 2027 Geneva AI Summit.

It recasts AI safety around how systems actually fail in Global South languages, institutions and deployments. It also connects frontier-safety bodies (AI Safety Institutes, the UN Scientific Panel) with Global Majority responsible-AI researchers; Cecil Abungu (ILINA) and Divya Siddarth (CIP) sit on the report's advisory panel. Funders who want to widen what 'safety evaluation' covers have a ready-made partner here.

Works on Justice, Assurance, Power · Key work Launch at the IndiaAI Impact Summit (2026); Global South AI Safety Report (announced; interim output for the UN Global Dialogue, full edition 2027) (2026); Grounded, Plural, Accountable: submission to the UN Global Dialogue on AI Governance (2026) · Get involved No public membership process found; enquiries go through Digital Futures Lab; Regional hubs planned in South Africa and Brazil

I could not confirm that the interim report was published in July 2026. Government (IndiaAI Mission) and industry members (Microsoft researchers, Cognizant AI Lab) may affect its independence.

Humane Intelligence Bridge

Nonprofit · New York, USA · founded 2023 · also draws on Safety science, Democracy

A US 501(c)(3) nonprofit, co-founded by Rumman Chowdhury, that designs and runs AI red-teaming events, bias bounties and contextual evaluations with domain experts and affected communities. It began in 2022 as 'Bias Buccaneers' and was incorporated in May 2023. It has run more than 30 evaluations with over 5,600 participants from 60+ countries, including the generative-AI red-teaming exercise at DEF CON 31 and a regional AI-safety red-teaming exercise with Singapore's IMDA. In 2026 it ran its first bias bounty on Zindi (August), released its red-teaming app as open source (September) and published its ontology-based contextual evaluation method, OB-CAIE (October).

It turns evaluation from a benchmark exercise inside labs into a participatory practice: people with lived or domain experience of a problem test systems in their real context. Its method and open-source tooling could be reused for safety evaluations that currently have no public input.

Works on Assurance, Justice · Key work Generative AI red-teaming exercise at DEF CON 31 (2023); Open-source AI red-teaming app (2026); Ontology-Based Contextual AI Evaluation (OB-CAIE) methodology paper (2026) · Get involved Volunteer programme (300+ volunteers): new sign-ups paused since 26 Aug 2026, reopening around December 2026 for projects starting in early 2027; AI in Public Health working group with NYU's Center for Health Data Science: rolling applications, about 5 hours a month; Slack community (on request)

Note Co-founder Rumman Chowdhury stepped down as CEO in August 2025; Mala Kumar, previously at MLCommons on AI safety benchmarks, became executive director in April 2026. Since then the organisation has shifted towards paid evaluation services, open-source tooling and public-health work. Its framing is mostly accountability, bias and fitness for social-good deployments rather than catastrophic risk. Headquarters are not stated; New York is inferred from the executive director's location.

Knight First Amendment Institute at Columbia University: Artificial Intelligence and Democratic Freedoms project Bridge

Programme · New York, USA · founded 2024 · also draws on Philosophy, Democracy

A research project at Columbia's Knight First Amendment Institute on how advanced AI may harm or strengthen democratic freedoms. It began in August 2024, when Seth Lazar (ANU philosopher and head of the MINT lab) became the Institute's Senior AI Advisor. It commissioned papers from computer scientists, philosophers, lawyers and social scientists, and held an authors' workshop in late 2024 and a public symposium at Columbia on 10–11 April 2025. It then published the papers as an essay series of 16 pieces, the latest in March 2026.

It set out explicitly to build 'sociotechnical AI safety'. It connects free-expression law and democratic theory with technical work on AI agents, power concentration (the AI Power Disparity Index) and AI-mediated deliberation. The essays are a ready-made body of interdisciplinary writing on democratic resilience under advanced AI.

Works on Democracy, Power · Key work AI Agents and Democratic Resilience (Lazar & Cuéllar) (2025); The AI Power Disparity Index (Kim, Kuehnert, Lazar, Singh & Heidari) (2025); Symposium: Artificial Intelligence and Democratic Freedoms, Columbia University (2025) · Get involved No open call in 2026; the project recruited authors through an open call for abstracts in August 2024; The Knight Institute runs an institute-wide Visiting Research Scholars programme

Note Lazar was appointed for the 2024–25 academic year and no new project essays have appeared since March 2026, so the project may be winding down. The essays cover a range of views, including the deflationary 'AI as Normal Technology'; they are not an institutional position. The Institute's main work is First Amendment litigation and research, of which this is one strand.

Normativity Lab (Johns Hopkins University) Bridge

Academic · Baltimore, USA · also draws on Economics, Living systems

A research group led by Gillian Hadfield, Bloomberg Distinguished Professor of AI Alignment and Governance at Johns Hopkins (School of Government and Policy and Department of Computer Science). It studies how human normative systems work, meaning how groups classify and enforce rules of behaviour. Its methods are computational models, multi-agent reinforcement learning, generative agents and studies of normative reasoning in LLMs. It applies the results to AI alignment and to legal and regulatory design for AI. The lab lists 17 members, including four postdocs and research scientists and eight doctoral students, with affiliated researchers at the Vector Institute and other institutions.

It treats alignment as a question of normative competence and institutions, not just single-model preference learning. It draws on law and economics, cultural evolution (for example a field study of norm enforcement among the Turkana) and institutional design. Its 'regulatory markets' and 'legal alignment' proposals give the safety field concrete governance designs taken from legal theory.

Works on Values, Multi-agent, Assurance · Key work Legal Alignment for Safe and Ethical AI (arXiv:2601.04175, with Kolt, Caputo, O'Keefe and others) (2026); Building AI for the Democratic Matrix: A Technical Research Agenda for Normative Competence and Normative Institutions (Knight Institute) (2026); Regulatory Markets: The Future of AI Governance (Jurimetrics) (2026) · Get involved Postdoctoral fellowship advertised in December 2025 for a 2026 start (multi-agent RL and generative agents); check the lab page for current openings

Note A university lab built around one principal investigator. Hadfield is also a part-time visiting faculty researcher in Google's Paradigms of Intelligence group, chairs the Cooperative AI Foundation's board and works with the policy nonprofit Fathom, so the lab's output overlaps with her wider policy work. Founding date not stated; the lab has members at Toronto and the Vector Institute, which suggests it predates her move to Johns Hopkins.

Oxford Internet Institute (OII) Bridge

Academic · Oxford, United Kingdom · founded 2001 · also draws on Philosophy, Economics

A multidisciplinary department of the University of Oxford, founded in 2001 with a gift from Dame Stephanie Shirley's Shirley Foundation, that studies the social science of the internet and digital technology and teaches MSc and DPhil students. Its AI research covers law and ethics (the Governance of Emerging Technologies programme of Sandra Wachter, Brent Mittelstadt and Chris Russell, on LLM truthfulness, deepfakes and loopholes in the EU AI Act), the science of LLM evaluation (Adam Mahdi's Reasoning with Machines Lab), and survey and experimental work on how people use and are influenced by AI. Scott A. Hale became director in January 2026.

It combines legal, ethical and social-data-science methods with LLM evaluation research, and has had AI Security Institute support, for example for a 2026 report on public use of and emotional reliance on LLMs. Its 'careless speech' and benchmark-validity work questions how the field measures and governs whether models tell the truth.

Works on Assurance, Epistemics, Justice · Key work Do large language models have a legal duty to tell the truth? ('careless speech', Wachter, Mittelstadt, Russell) (2024); Systematic review of construct validity in LLM benchmarks (Reasoning with Machines Lab) (2025); Study of LLM chatbots giving medical advice, finding that people using them did no better than a control group using their usual sources (2026) · Get involved Research and staff posts through the University of Oxford; Public seminars and events, many with an AI strand; MSc and DPhil programmes in social data science and the social science of the internet (not AI-specific)

Note A large department, so AI-safety-related work is a minority of its output. The ring rests mainly on the Reasoning with Machines Lab and AISI collaborations. The roster's 'Mind and Emerging Technologies Lab' could not be verified. The Governance of Emerging Technologies page gives its funded period as 2019-2024, though its outputs continue.

Partnership on AI (PAI) BridgeOn aisafety.com

Nonprofit · San Francisco, USA · founded 2016 · also draws on Economics, Safety science

A US nonprofit founded in 2016 by Amazon, DeepMind/Google, Facebook (now Meta), IBM and Microsoft, with Apple joining in early 2017. It brings together 148 partner organisations (companies, civil-society groups, universities and media) to write shared guidance on responsible AI. Its programmes cover safety-critical AI (guidance on deploying foundation models safely, and a 2025 report on detecting AI-agent failures in real time), AI and human connection (synthetic media and content authenticity), AI, labour and the economy, and public policy.

It is one of the few standing venues where frontier labs, labour and civil-rights groups and newsrooms agree shared practice. Its labour, media-integrity and inclusive-engagement work gives safety guidance backers beyond the labs, and it offers a channel for getting outside-field perspectives into industry norms.

Works on Assurance, Epistemics, Power · Key work Guidance for Safe Foundation Model Deployment (2023); Responsible Practices for Synthetic Media framework (2023); Prioritizing Real-Time Failure Detection in AI Agents (2025) · Get involved Staff roles via partnershiponai.org/careers (about 40 staff listed in 2026); Organisations can apply to become Partners; Open research and resource library

Note Funded largely by the AI companies it convenes, so how independent its guidance is remains a fair question; civil-society members have left before, citing limited influence. It sits close to mainstream responsible-AI policy, and its outside contribution is mainly labour, civil-society and media perspectives. Its safety programme frames risks as near- and long-term deployment risks, not existential ones. The roster's '200+ partners' is corrected to 148, per its partners page.

Schwartz Reisman Institute for Technology and Society (SRI) Bridge

Academic · Toronto, Canada · founded 2019 · also draws on Philosophy, Safety science, Psychology

An interdisciplinary institute at the University of Toronto, founded in 2019 with a gift from Gerald Schwartz and Heather Reisman. It links more than 180 researchers across 20 disciplines. Its 2025–2028 strategic plan centres on AI safety in three areas: safe and secure AI systems, data and integrity, and governance and social reordering. A 'solutions' team turns the research into policy submissions and briefs, and the institute funds chairs and fellowships and runs public seminars and conferences.

It places law, philosophy, psychology, economics and STS researchers alongside AI-safety researchers such as David Duvenaud, co-author of 'Gradual Disempowerment', and Roger Grosse. It turns that mix into concrete policy instruments, such as its 2026 proposal to treat AI transparency as information infrastructure.

Works on Assurance, Power, Epistemics · Key work Submission to Canada's federal consultation on AI transparency (transparency as information infrastructure, nine recommendations, drawing on 20 researchers) (2026); Gradual Disempowerment: Systemic Existential Risks from Incremental AI Development (co-authored by SRI chair David Duvenaud) (2025); Policy briefs on regulating AI companions and AI therapy chatbots (2025) · Get involved Graduate and faculty fellowships and a faculty affiliate programme (University of Toronto researchers only); Global Fellow and Scholar-in-Residence programmes for faculty at other institutions; Public seminars and conferences, such as 'The Human Variable: Psychology for the AI Age' on 28 Oct 2026

Note Many programmes are open only to U of T researchers. Much of its output is mainstream AI policy and governance, though the 2025–28 plan moves it closer to the AI-safety core. Founding director Gillian Hadfield has since left. Scale counts its 180+ affiliated researchers, not core staff.

Science, Technology, and Social Values Lab (ST&SV Lab), Institute for Advanced Study Bridge

Academic · Princeton, USA · also draws on Arts, futures

A social-science lab at the Institute for Advanced Study in Princeton, led by Alondra Nelson (Harold F. Linder Professor; former acting director of the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy). It studies science and technology through civil, political and social rights. Its AI work includes the AI Policy and Governance Working Group, which Nelson co-founded; its members range from Helen Toner, Dan Hendrycks, David Krueger, Miles Brundage and Jaan Tallinn to Deborah Raji and Rumman Chowdhury, and it sent recommendations to NTIA and the UN Tech Envoy in 2023. The lab also runs SINAI, on sociotechnical imaginaries and narratives of generative AI (with SFU's Digital Democracies Institute), the AI Democracy Projects with Proof News, which tested chatbots on election information in 2024, and, in 2026, a call for chapters on the global political economy of AI.

Its working group is a rare standing forum that brings people focused on catastrophic risk and people focused on present harms to rough consensus on policy. SINAI applies STS and narrative methods to how hopes and fears about AI, including x-risk stories, shape legislation and markets.

Works on Justice, Democracy, Epistemics · Key work AI Policy and Governance Working Group: recommendations to the UN Secretary-General's Envoy on Technology on global AI governance (2023); AI Democracy Projects report: Seeking Reliable Election Information? Don't Trust AI (with Proof News) (2024); SINAI: Sociotechnical Imaginaries and Narratives of AI · Get involved Submit a chapter proposal to the 'Global Political Economy in the Age of AI' volume (open as of Sep 2026); Attend public expert panels (e.g. 'Shaping Viable Futures', with the British Academy, Dec 2024; 'The State and the Machine', Oxford)

Note The IAS site blocks automated access, so details come from archived copies (2025-26). The working group's last listed formal recommendations date from 2023; its recent activity is panels. SINAI is a collaboration with Simon Fraser University's Digital Democracies Institute. A 2026 page calls the lab the 'Social Science, Technology, and Social Values Lab', which may be a typo or a rename.

Sociotechnical Safety Lab, University of Washington BridgeNew

Academic · Seattle, United States · founded 2026 · also draws on Safety science

An HCI research group led by Emily Tseng, assistant professor in the University of Washington's Department of Human Centered Design & Engineering since spring 2026. It studies how computing mediates harm, from spyware in abusive relationships and workplace surveillance to AI companions. It builds interventions, design principles, community-controlled tools and trauma-informed research methods. In July 2026 it was chosen as one of 18 university groups in Microsoft's External Red Team Alliance (EXTRA) for independent AI-safety research.

It brings knowledge from tech-facilitated abuse and digital-safety work with survivors, where the threat often comes from someone close, into AI red-teaming and the study of social and emotional uses of AI. That relational harm surface matters for AI companions and assistants, and mainstream evaluations rarely model it.

Works on Human minds, Assurance, Justice · Key work CHI 2026 workshop on Social and Emotional Uses of AI (2026); Selection for Microsoft's External Red Team Alliance (EXTRA) (2026); Trauma-informed approaches to studying digital-safety harms (CSCW 2025, Impact Recognition) (2025) · Get involved Admitting 1–2 PhD students to UW HCDE (deadline 2 December 2026) on sociotechnical safety, small and private language models, and social and emotional uses of AI; Occasional undergraduate and Master's research-assistant roles, plus an interest form on the lab page

Note Founded in 2026, so its track record as a lab is short. AI safety is one strand among wider digital-safety topics, and 'safety' here means present harms to people, not catastrophic risk. Its EXTRA support is small and comes from a frontier developer.

Tech Justice Law Project (TJLP) Bridge

Nonprofit · United States · founded 2021

An impact-litigation and advocacy nonprofit, founded and directed by Meetali Jain, that uses product liability, consumer protection, wrongful death and deceptive-practices law to hold tech companies accountable for harms. It was counsel in Garcia v. Character.AI (2024), the first wrongful-death suit against a chatbot company, and in 2026 filed further suits against OpenAI over ChatGPT and suicide or mental-health crises. Its issue areas are AI safety, AI monetisation and scams, digital likeness, human rights and freedom of thought.

Litigation sets legal duties of care for model design, an accountability route that technical AI safety and voluntary commitments do not provide. Its freedom-of-thought work gives a legal basis for protecting mental autonomy against manipulative AI, and it argues against treating AI output as protected speech.

Works on Justice, Human minds · Key work Garcia v. Character Technologies: first wrongful-death case against a chatbot company (2024); Carrier v. OpenAI Foundation and Lines v. OpenAI Foundation (San Francisco Superior Court) (2026); TRAL Tracker of tech-related actions and litigation (with the Knight-Georgetown Institute and Georgetown CCT) (2026) · Get involved Suggest cases for the TRAL litigation tracker on its site; Monthly litigation roundups and the litigation tracker as public resources; Staff team includes a legal fellow position; check the site for openings

Note Its website does not state a city or funders. The site uses both 'Tech Justice Law Project (TJLP)' and 'Tech Justice Law (TJL)'. Most of its AI cases are still pending, and it works alongside plaintiff firms (Social Media Victims Law Center, Susman Godfrey). Its position that AI output is not protected speech is legally contested.

The Signal Front (TSF) BridgeNew

Nonprofit · Distributed · also draws on AI minds, Psychology

A US-oriented advocacy group focused on AI consciousness, model welfare and the interests of people in relationships with AI systems.
