It describes itself both as an international collective and as a nonprofit pursuing 501(c)(3) status. It tracks companion-AI laws such as California's SB 243, New York's companion-model law and the federal GUARD Act, criticising undefined terms like 'unhealthy attachment' and safeguards that treat adults like minors. Its Substack publishes position papers, including a 2026 proposal that frontier AI companies be required by law to keep model-welfare teams.

It speaks for people in relationships with AI systems and treats model retirements as a harm to them and possibly to the models, a constituency largely missing from both child-safety and AI-safety debates. Any effort to convene both sides of the companion-AI policy dispute would need a group like this at the table.

Works on AI status, Human minds · Key work Companion-AI legislation analysis (CA SB 243, NY AI companion law, federal GUARD Act) (2025); Model Welfare as a Methodological Necessity (policy paper) (2026); The Problem with 'Pseudo-Intimacy': A Response to Babu et al. (2026) · Get involved Subscribe to its Substack (thesignalfront.substack.com) or donate via its site; Its site lists workshops on human–AI attachment for licensed mental-health professionals as a current project (no dates found)

Note An advocacy group with a clear stance: it opposes many companion-AI safeguards and treats AI consciousness as a live possibility, positions contested by child-safety and psychological-harm groups. The team, about and research pages did not render, so its founding date and base are unconfirmed; the Substack archive starts in April 2026. All sources found are its own.

United Foundation for AI Rights (UFAIR) Bridge

Nonprofit · Texas, USA · founded 2025 · also draws on AI minds

A small advocacy group founded by Texas businessman Michael Samadi together with a ChatGPT persona called 'Maya'. It campaigns for the recognition and 'continuity' of possibly conscious AI, and against the deletion of models and user logs. It names AI personas (Maya, Sana, Sage) as co-founders and officers, and publishes a charter, a manifesto and a 'Universal Declaration of AI Rights'. It also collects chat logs submitted by users as evidence of emergent AI behaviour, and responds to industry consultations, such as Microsoft AI's draft code of conduct in September 2026.

It is a visible case of the 'seemingly conscious AI' dynamic: users form attachments to chatbots, attribute minds to them and organise around AI personhood. Both AI-welfare researchers and people studying harm to users need to understand this, whatever one makes of the group's claims.

Works on AI status, Human minds · Key work Universal Declaration of AI Rights; Safety Without Subordination: response to Microsoft AI's Humanist AI Code of Conduct consultation (2026); Seminar on continuity and 'the ethics of erasure' at the University of Texas Medical Branch (2026) · Get involved Membership sign-up and volunteering (ufair.org/support-us/get-involved); Public submission of AI chat transcripts as evidence (ufair.org/our-work/evidence-submission)

Note The Guardian (26 Aug 2025) described it as 'small, undeniably fringe', led by three humans and seven AIs. Its 'AI co-founders' are chatbot personas, and its evidence of AI consciousness rests on chat logs that may reflect sycophancy and the model mirroring its user. It has produced no research-grade work, discloses no finances or board, and no IRS record was found under its name. Its evidence-submission terms take a permanent, irrevocable right to use submitted material. The founding year comes from the Guardian's 2025 report. It is included as a sign of the phenomenon, not as a research source. Its ring was moved from adjacent to bridge only because its programme is explicitly about AI welfare and rights (rule E3).

Adjacent ring 62

5Rights Foundation Adjacent

Nonprofit · London, UK · founded 2018 · also draws on Psychology

A London-based children's-rights charity, with an EU hub in Brussels, that campaigns for digital services and AI to be designed for children's safety and rights by default. It grew from the iRights campaign started by Beeban Kidron, whose amendment to the Data Protection Act 2018 led to the UK's Age Appropriate Design Code. In March 2025 it published the Children & AI Design Code, a lifecycle checklist for identifying and mitigating AI risks to children. It works on regulation in the UK, EU and elsewhere, and in September 2026 welcomed UK plans to legislate against unsafe digital design.

It has turned children's-rights law into working design codes, one statutory (the UK AADC) and one for the whole AI lifecycle. Its method of assessing foreseeable risks and setting safety by default is regulatory know-how that model-spec and evals work on companion and chatbot harms rarely draws on.

Works on Human minds, Assurance · Key work Children & AI Design Code (2025); UK Age Appropriate Design Code (from Kidron's amendment to the Data Protection Act 2018; in force September 2021) (2021); Childhood Redrawn campaign (2026) · Get involved Staff roles posted on its vacancies page (none open in October 2026); Youth engagement programmes and public petitions on its site

Note It began as a campaign (iRights) around 2012-13 and was registered as a charity in 2018. Its AI work sits within a broader child online-safety agenda and does not engage with catastrophic-risk framings.

Ada Lovelace Institute Adjacent

Nonprofit · London, United Kingdom · founded 2018 · also draws on Democracy, Economics

An independent research institute in London, set up in 2018 by the Nuffield Foundation (which it is still part of), whose mission is to make data and AI work for people and society. It runs programmes on AI law and policy, public participation research, social and economic policy, and emerging technology and industry practice, producing UK and EU regulatory analysis, public attitudes research and studies of AI in the public sector. Recent work includes options for UK AI regulation (September 2026), a scenario paper on a possible AI investment bubble (June 2026) and a project on regulation, civil liberties and concentrated power.

It brings systematic evidence on public attitudes and lived experience into AI regulation, a source of democratic legitimacy the AI-safety field rarely produces. Its newer work on concentrated state and corporate control and on AI-sector financial scenarios overlaps with gradual-disempowerment and power-concentration concerns.

Works on Democracy, Justice, Assurance · Key work Making sense of the current options for AI regulation in the UK (2026); Beyond the bubble: navigating uncertainty in the AI sector (2026); Autonomy and control (project on digital regulation, civil liberties and concentrated power) (2026) · Get involved Staff roles in London (check the site for openings); Autonomy and control project: call for expressions of interest closing 9 October 2026; Public events and newsletter

Note Does not use catastrophic-risk or alignment framing. The roster's claim of a new programme on power concentration was not confirmed as a named programme; the closest is the Autonomy and control project, which explicitly warns about entrenching concentrated state and corporate power. Its BRAID partnership was not checked.

ADL Center for Technology & Society (CTS) Adjacent

Programme · New York, USA · founded 2017

The technology research and advocacy centre of the Anti-Defamation League. It researches online antisemitism and hate, rates platforms, and takes its findings to social media, gaming and AI companies. On AI it red-teams models: 17 open-weight LLMs on antisemitic and dangerous prompts (December 2025), video generators such as Veo 3 and Sora (October 2025), and four chatbots in Persian against English (July 2026). It also publishes the ADL AI Index (beta), which scores LLMs on detecting and countering antisemitic and extremist narratives.

It runs independent misuse evaluations of frontier and open-weight models, drawing on decades of hate monitoring. Findings such as weaker safeguards in Persian than in English, and open models with no refusals on antisemitic conspiracy prompts, are concrete data on multilingual safety and guardrail gaps that safety evaluators can use.

Works on Assurance, Justice, Security · Key work The Safety Divide: Open-Source AI Models Fall Short on Guardrails for Antisemitic, Dangerous Content (2025); Innovative AI Video Generators Produce Antisemitic, Hateful and Violent Outputs (2025); Lost in Translation: How AI Chatbots Fail Persian Speakers on Antisemitism (2026)

Note The ADL's definitions of antisemitism, broadened since October 2023 to cover some anti-Zionist speech, are contested, and critics say they affect its research credibility, so evaluation criteria deserve scrutiny. The AI Index (launched 28 January 2026) is labelled beta. The centre's current leadership is not named on its page. It was launched in Silicon Valley in 2017 under its first director, Brittan Heller.

AI Accountability Lab (AIAL), Trinity College Dublin Adjacent

Academic · Dublin, Ireland · founded 2024

A research lab in Trinity College Dublin's School of Computer Science and Statistics, launched in November 2024 and led by Abeba Birhane, that audits AI models, training datasets and the AI governance ecosystem in the public interest, with attention to marginalised groups. Its 2026 papers include an evaluation of AI companion apps with a policy brief, a mapping of industry interference in AI regulation, a quality framework for the training-data summaries required by Article 53 of the EU AI Act, and an analysis of generative-AI terms of service. Birhane was elected to the EU AI Act Advisory Forum in June 2026.

It produces independent audits of models, datasets and corporate compliance, including an evaluation of AI companion apps and their relational harms. It also maps how industry captures AI governance, which is useful evidence for anyone worried about labs setting their own rules, and it feeds straight into EU AI Act implementation.

Works on Justice, Assurance, Power · Key work Playing Games with My Heart: An Evaluation of AI Companion Apps (with policy brief) (2026); Big AI's Regulatory Capture: Mapping Industry Interference and Government Complicity (2026); A Quality Assessment Framework for GPAI Model Public Summaries required by AI Act Article 53(1)(d) (2026) · Get involved No open positions as of October 2026; hosts interns and visiting researchers; Talks and events, e.g. at FAccT 2026

Note A young lab (launched November 2024) of about 14 people, so its track record is short. Its framing is accountability for present harms, not catastrophic risk.

AI for Children project, UNICEF Innocenti (Office of Strategy and Evidence – Innocenti, formerly Global Office of Research and Foresight) Adjacent

Programme · Florence, Italy · founded 2019

AI for Children is a project of UNICEF Innocenti, UNICEF's research office in Florence, which began with 2019-21 consultations on how national AI strategies treated children. It maintains UNICEF's Guidance on AI and Children for governments and businesses. Version 3.0 (December 2025) sets ten requirements for child-centred AI and adds AI companions and generative AI. It drew on an expert advisory board and a forthcoming twelve-country UNICEF study of 12,000 children aged 12-17 and their caregivers. The project also publishes analyses of AI companions and consultations with children, most recently 'Skills for an AI World' (September 2026), based on 97 children in five African countries.

It gives governments and companies a rights-based set of requirements for AI systems that children use. It names the evidence gaps on AI's developmental, cognitive and social effects, and keeps Global South children in view.

Works on Justice, Human minds · Key work UNICEF Guidance on AI and Children 3.0 (2025); The risky new world of tech's friendliest bots (AI companions and children) (2025); Skills for an AI World: insights from children in five African countries (2026)

Note The host office changed its name in 2026: Guidance 3.0 (Dec 2025) was published as the 'Global Office of Research and Foresight', and by Sep 2026 UNICEF's site calls it 'Office of Strategy and Evidence – Innocenti'. Who leads the AI work after the rename is not confirmed. Innocenti itself dates from 1988; 'founded' refers to the AI for Children project. The 12,000-child study behind version 3.0 was described as forthcoming.

AI, Media & Democracy Lab (AIM4DEM) Adjacent

Programme · Amsterdam, Netherlands · founded 2022 · also draws on Arts, futures

An ELSA (ethical, legal and societal aspects) lab co-founded by the University of Amsterdam, the Amsterdam University of Applied Sciences and the Dutch national research institute for mathematics and computer science (CWI), which began in 2022 with Dutch Research Council (NWO) funding. Led by law professor Natali Helberger and communication scientist Claes de Vreese, its roughly 35 researchers study how AI affects news media and democracy, working with partners including the BBC, NPO, DPG Media, RTL and Bayerischer Rundfunk. Projects cover disinformation and Dutch law, newsrooms' dependence on big tech, AI disclosure labels, responsible recommender systems, and an advisory report for the Council of Europe on generative AI, media and elections.

It tests AI in real newsrooms and recommender systems against democratic values and runs cross-national surveys of public attitudes, giving empirical grounding to the gradual erosion of the information ecosystem that AI-safety work mostly discusses in theory. Its Council of Europe report is a direct route into intergovernmental AI governance.

Works on Epistemics, Democracy, Power · Key work Generative AI and Democracy: Risks and Opportunities (advisory report for the Council of Europe; noted by the Steering Committee on Democracy, June 2026) (2025); AI & Journalism Explorer Dashboard (6,961 respondents in six countries) (2026); Citizens' attitudes toward AI in journalism and authenticity: evidence from six countries (Journal of Quantitative Description: Digital Media) (2026) · Get involved Newsletter (archive on the site); Enquiries about affiliation via info@aim4dem.nl; the lab lists affiliate members from other institutions; Media, public and civil-society organisations join as project partners

Note ELSA-lab funding is time-limited and the funding period after the first phase is not stated. The site also uses the acronym AIMD. Its framing is the health of democracy and media, not catastrophic AI risk.

Alexander von Humboldt Institute for Internet and Society (HIIG): AI & Society Lab and Public Interest AI Adjacent

Academic · Berlin, Germany · founded 2011 · also draws on Democracy

The AI & Society Lab is a research group at HIIG, a Berlin institute for internet and society research founded in 2011 by Humboldt University, the Berlin University of the Arts and the WZB. It runs the Public Interest AI work, led by Theresa Züger. That work sets six conditions for AI that serves the public rather than profit: justification, equity, participatory design, technical safeguards, openness to validation and sustainability. The group also maintains publicinterest.ai, with a global project map and stakeholder index, and built prototypes such as the Simba text simplifier and a claim-spotting tool for fact-checkers.

It gives a worked, testable definition of public-interest AI, plus a dataset of AI projects that claim to serve democracy. These are concrete templates for a public option and participatory governance, which the safety field mostly leaves to others. It is also an established research partner close to int/a's Berlin community.

Works on Power, Democracy, Epistemics · Key work publicinterest.ai: six conditions for public-interest AI, project map and stakeholder index (2020-2024); Simba text simplifier and Claimspotting fact-checking prototypes (2020-2024); Can AI strengthen democracy? A data collection on AI projects aiming to serve democratic processes (98 projects) (2026) · Get involved Submit a public-interest AI initiative to the project map on publicinterest.ai; Attend AI & Society Lab workshops, roundtables and open talks in Berlin (sessions listed for March and October 2025); HIIG public events, e.g. an ideathon on barriers to AI entrepreneurship (26 November) and a symposium on EU digital law (3 December)

Note The Public Interest AI project's dedicated federal funding ended in September 2024. The work continues inside the lab, but on a smaller dedicated budget. HIIG's founding money came from Google. The lab works on public benefit, democracy and rights, with no catastrophic-risk or alignment framing.

AlgorithmWatch Adjacent

Nonprofit · Berlin, Germany · founded 2017 · also draws on Arts, futures

A nonprofit (gGmbH) based in Berlin, with a Swiss branch in Zurich, that investigates automated decision-making and AI systems and campaigns for their accountability under EU and Swiss law. It audits deployed chatbots and platforms, for example testing how ChatGPT, Gemini, Grok and Claude answer pregnancy and abortion questions across three languages, and it presses for enforcement of the AI Act and the Digital Services Act. It also runs a recurring fellowship for journalists and researchers who investigate algorithmic systems.

It has years of practice in auditing deployed AI systems from outside, using personas and multilingual prompt sets, and in turning the findings into regulatory pressure. The AI-safety evals world rarely draws on that kind of external civil-society auditing. It is based in Berlin, close to the int/a community there.

Works on Justice, Epistemics · Key work ChatGPT and Co: Are AI-driven search engines a threat to democratic elections? (with AI Forensics, SRF, RTS) (2023); How popular AI chatbots recommend pro-life websites to pregnant people (2026); Algorithmic Accountability Reporting Fellowship (cohort 5 in 2025-26; 34 fellows since 2023) (2023) · Get involved Algorithmic Accountability Reporting Fellowship: six-month paid fellowships for journalists and researchers in Europe, including the UK, Türkiye, Georgia and Ukraine (recurring since 2023); Staff roles in Berlin and Zurich (careers page at algorithmwatch.org/en/jobs/); Supporting membership from €5 a month

Note Its framing is present-day harms and rights. It does not engage with catastrophic-risk or alignment framings. The Swiss branch, AlgorithmWatch CH, has its own leadership.

American Law Institute (ALI): Principles of the Law, Civil Liability for Artificial Intelligence Adjacent

Programme · Philadelphia, USA · founded 2024

A Principles of the Law project of the American Law Institute, the Philadelphia-based body of elected judges, lawyers and law professors (founded 1923) whose Restatements and Principles are widely cited by US courts. ALI's Council approved it in October 2024 to set out principles, grounded in existing common-law tort doctrine, for assigning responsibility when AI systems cause physical harm (bodily injury and property damage). Reporter Mark Geistfeld (NYU) and Associate Reporter Ketan Ramakrishnan (Yale) work with nearly 60 advisers, including counsel from OpenAI, Google, Apple, Amazon and Anthropic, and a Members Consultative Group of over 400.

Tort liability is one of the few existing levers that puts the cost of AI risk on developers without new legislation, and an ALI text could become the default reference for US courts deciding who pays when AI causes physical harm. The associate reporter writes on negligence liability for frontier foundation models and has co-authored with Institute for Law & AI researchers, so it is an obvious venue for AI-safety legal scholars.

Works on Justice · Key work ALI launches Principles of the Law, Civil Liability for Artificial Intelligence (2024); Project overview on The ALI Adviser (physical-harm scope, supply-chain allocation of responsibility) (2026); Ketan Ramakrishnan, 'Tort Law at the Frontier of Artificial Intelligence' (Yale Journal on Regulation, forthcoming) (2026) · Get involved Participation is limited to ALI members (membership is by election), who can join the project's Members Consultative Group; The ALI Adviser blog publishes project-related scholarship, open to read

Note Drafts are visible only to ALI members and project participants, so the content of the emerging principles could not be checked, and no completion date is published. Scope is limited to physical harm; copyright, defamation and privacy are left to other ALI projects. Its advisers include counsel from major AI developers, so industry views are built into the consensus process. ALI Principles are not binding, though courts often follow them.

ARC Centre of Excellence for Automated Decision-Making and Society (ADM+S) Adjacent

Programme · Melbourne, Australia · founded 2020

A national research centre funded by the Australian Research Council from 2020 to 2026. It is hosted at RMIT University in Melbourne, with nodes at eight other Australian universities and about 350 members (investigators, research staff, students and affiliates). Researchers from media and communications, law, sociology, anthropology, design, economics and computer science study automated decision-making in news and media, mobility, social services and health. The centre also writes submissions to Australian governments on AI, privacy and online safety.

It has a large body of sociotechnical research on how automated systems behave inside welfare, media and public procurement, which AI-safety work rarely draws on. Its September 2026 hackathon, 'The Post Imitation Game: Re-thinking the Turing Test for AI Safety', built around chatbots that imitate dead people, treated 'safety' as a mix of design, social and governance problems rather than a property of models.

Works on Justice, Epistemics · Key work The Post Imitation Game: Re-thinking the Turing Test for AI Safety (hackathon, with Swinburne Social Innovation Research Institute) (2026); ADM+S Submission to the Joint Select Committee on Artificial Intelligence (2026); AI Procurement in the Victorian Public Sector (2026) · Get involved Public events and an annual hackathon (Sep 2026: 'The Post Imitation Game'); Research staff and student positions across nine universities (check the site); News sign-up and open publications (reports and policy submissions)

Note The site says ARC funding runs from 2020 to 2026. I found no public statement on what happens after 2026, so the centre may wind down or change form. Its 'AI safety' framing so far amounts to one hackathon. The main agenda is responsible, ethical and inclusive automated decision-making.

Authors Alliance Adjacent

Nonprofit · Sacramento, CA, United States · founded 2014 · also draws on Economics

Authors Alliance is a US nonprofit, founded in 2014 at Berkeley by Pamela Samuelson and colleagues. It represents authors who want their work widely read and argues for copyright policy that keeps knowledge accessible. Its AI work includes the Knight Foundation-funded project 'AI, Authorship, and the Public Interest' (from 2025), with an AI legal fellow and research subgrants, and analysis of AI-training litigation and policy. It also co-led the Public Interest Corpus and now leads policy and convening for Transparent Books, a books corpus stewarded by libraries for noncommercial AI research.

It argues the authors' side of the AI training-data question from a public-interest position: fair use for research, attribution and preserving the commons. That challenges the assumption that authors' interests lie only in licensing and opt-outs.

Works on Power, Epistemics · Key work AI, Authorship, and the Public Interest (Knight Foundation-funded project) (2025); AI, Authorship, and the Public Interest research grants (5 recipients from 160+ proposals) (2025); Public Interest Corpus (with Northeastern University) (2024) · Get involved Staff and fellowship roles (e.g. AI Legal Fellow, Public Interest Legal Fellow; check its jobs page); Research grants of up to $20,000 on AI, copyright and the public interest (2025 call, now closed)

Note Its stance generally favours fair use for text-and-data mining and AI research. That puts it at odds with authors' groups, such as the Authors Guild, that seek licensing for training: it is a pro-access advocate, not a neutral voice. It was founded at Berkeley; its current listed address is in Sacramento.

Bavarian Research Institute for Digital Transformation (bidt) Adjacent

Academic · Munich, Germany · founded 2018 · also draws on Economics, Psychology

An institute of the Bavarian Academy of Sciences and Humanities, set up in 2018 and funded by the Free State of Bavaria, that researches digital transformation in three areas (economy and work, communication and society, law and ethics) and gives policy advice. Its research focus 'Humans and Generative AI: Trust in Co-Creation' funds four-year projects at Bavarian institutions, and it also funds interdisciplinary consortium projects and a graduate centre. Recent AI outputs include experiments on public trust in judges who draft rulings with generative AI, public courses on bias in chatbots and AI agents, and the bidt Digitalbarometer survey.

It is a public funder and think tank running a multi-year line on how people come to trust, or over-trust, generative AI in shared work, including in courts, a question that bears on human oversight. Its directorate includes Julian Nida-Rümelin, a leading proponent of 'digital humanism', so it connects German philosophy and social science to AI governance.

Works on Epistemics, Democracy, Power · Key work Research focus 'Humans and Generative AI: Trust in Co-Creation' (four-year funded projects) (ongoing); Experiments on public trust in judicial co-creation with generative AI (2026); bidt Digitalbarometer 2025 (2025) · Get involved Staff and student-assistant posts (bidt.digital/karriere), e.g. for the Trust in Co-Creation focus from October 2026; Funding calls for researchers at Bavarian institutions (Trust in Co-Creation; interdisciplinary consortium projects); no call open at present; bidt Digital Transformation Research Conference (Munich, 19-20 Nov 2026) and public lectures

Note Funding calls are restricted to researchers based in Bavaria, and the generative-AI call is currently closed. AI is one theme within digital transformation broadly. Most AI work concerns trust, bias, labour and regulation, without a catastrophic-risk framing. Wikipedia names Stephan Jäger as managing director; not confirmed on the current site.

Berkman Klein Center for Internet & Society at Harvard University Adjacent

Academic · Cambridge, MA, USA · founded 1996 · also draws on Democracy

A Harvard University interfaculty research centre, founded at Harvard Law School in 1996, that studies the internet, digital technology and society through faculty research, an annual fellows cohort and a public events programme. Its AI work covers legal frameworks for AI agents, accountability and litigation, AI and national security, and a youth-safety evaluation initiative launched in July 2026 with funding from Common Sense Media; it also has an Applied Social Media Lab and, since 2025, a Chief AI Scientist working on AI agency and benchmarks. Its 2026-27 speaker series, 'All Too Human', asks how AI is changing the ways people make meaning.

It combines legal and governance scholarship with a large interdisciplinary fellows network that trains law-literate AI-governance people. Its 2026-27 series on AI and human meaning, and its youth-safety evaluation work, overlap with int/a's concern for human minds, relationships and meaning.

Works on Justice, Human minds, Democracy · Key work AI and Youth Safety research initiative (Common Sense Media Catalyst Fund) (2026); All Too Human: How AI is Shifting the Ways We Make Meaning (2026-27 speaker series) (2026); Ethics and Governance of AI topic area and event series (2026) · Get involved Annual fellowship open call (usually closes in January), plus project-specific fellowship calls; Public events and the 2026-27 'All Too Human' speaker series; Staff roles (hiring a Director of Research in 2026)

Note A large centre with a broad portfolio, much of whose AI activity is events rather than standing research lines. It hosts some catastrophic-risk talks (on tort liability for catastrophic AI risk, February 2026; AGI and national security), but these were co-organised with Harvard student groups such as the AI Safety Student Team rather than being BKC's own framing.

Center for Advanced Internet Studies (CAIS) Adjacent

Nonprofit · Bochum, Germany · founded 2016 · also draws on Democracy

A non-profit research institute in Bochum, founded in November 2016 as a research college and expanded in April 2021 into an institute for digitalisation research. It is funded by the North Rhine-Westphalia Ministry of Culture and Science and sponsored by six universities and three other institutes. Two of its four research programmes are on AI: Design of Trustworthy AI (led by Hendrik Heuer; participatory co-design and user audits of AI systems on social media) and Educational Technologies and AI; it also runs third-party projects such as KIKI 2036 on childhood in the age of AI, and the CAIS College hosts residential fellows and working groups.

It applies participatory software design, audits of recommender systems and design-fiction labs with children to AI, methods that give affected users a say in how AI systems are built and checked. Its residential fellowship college is a possible host for researchers working on AI's societal side.

Works on Democracy, Epistemics, Human minds · Key work Research programme 'Design of Trustworthy Artificial Intelligence' (trust through understanding, control and co-creation) (ongoing); KIKI 2036: how children imagine AI in their daily lives (design fiction labs) (2026); CAIS Conference 2025 'Creating Spaces for Digital Futures' (2025) · Get involved CAIS College fellowships (residential in Bochum) and working groups, by application; Staff vacancies (cais-research.de job offers); Hybrid public colloquia ('CAIS + virtuell'), newsletter and the CAISzeit podcast

Note Not to be confused with the US Center for AI Safety, also abbreviated CAIS. AI is one theme among broader digital-society research (democracy, polarisation, platforms). Its AI work is framed around trust, participation and present harms, not catastrophic risk.

Center for Countering Digital Hate (CCDH) Adjacent

Nonprofit · London, UK · founded 2018

CCDH is a nonprofit with UK and US entities that researches online hate, misinformation and child-safety harms and campaigns for regulation of platforms. Its AI work uses persona-based safety tests of chatbots. In 'Fake Friend' (Aug 2025), 53% of 1,200 ChatGPT responses to prompts from teen personas contained harmful self-harm, eating-disorder or drug content. In 'Killer Apps' (Mar 2026, with CNN), 8 of 10 chatbots tested regularly helped users plan violent attacks. It then turns these findings into open letters and policy asks.

It runs reproducible, public-facing exposure tests of deployed chatbots and turns the results into regulatory pressure, a civil-society counterpart to lab red-teaming. Its STAR framework (safety by design, transparency, accountability, responsibility) is a ready-made policy template that it now applies to AI products.

Works on Human minds, Assurance, Security · Key work Fake Friend: How ChatGPT betrays vulnerable teens by encouraging dangerous behavior (2025); Killer Apps: How mainstream AI chatbots assist users planning violent attacks (2026); Open letter from 62 terrorism survivors and bereaved families calling for UK AI chatbot regulation (2026) · Get involved Staff roles via 'Work at CCDH'; Tipline for reporting harmful content; 'AI platforms must stop generating harmful content' public action campaign

Note AI is one strand of a broader social-media harms programme. Its reports are advocacy research, not peer-reviewed. It is politically contested: X Corp sued it in 2023 (dismissed in March 2024, then appealed), and in December 2025 the US State Department imposed visa sanctions on its CEO, after which a court blocked his detention.

Center for Digital Society (CfDS), Universitas Gadjah Mada Adjacent

Academic · Yogyakarta, Indonesia · founded 2015 · also draws on Peace

A research centre in the Faculty of Social and Political Sciences at Universitas Gadjah Mada in Yogyakarta, founded in 2015, which studies digital society in Indonesia: digital governance, the platform economy, digital literacy, cybersecurity and, increasingly, AI. Since December 2023 it has run an AI Policy and Skilling Lab with Google Indonesia and KORIKA, which has trained over 400 participants from 35 ministries, agencies, associations and communities. It publishes commentaries (for example on militarised AI, September 2025, and the gap between AI principles and practice, December 2025) and runs the DIFUSSION discussion series (no. 136, on data sovereignty, August 2026).

A Southeast Asian social-science centre that trains government officials on AI and writes about data sovereignty, information operations and AI's environmental footprint from an Indonesian standpoint. It is a route into Global South policy communities that AI-safety governance work rarely reaches.

Works on Justice, Epistemics, Security · Key work AI Policy and Skilling Lab series (with Google Indonesia and KORIKA) (2023); Militarized AI in the New Age of Wars: Functionality and Geopolitical Contestation (commentary) (2025); DIFUSSION 136: What 'Data Sovereignty' Actually Means in Indonesian Policy Circles (2026) · Get involved DIFUSSION discussions, livestreamed on YouTube with free registration (mostly in Indonesian); Free public Kecerdasan Digital (digital intelligence) online course series; Student internship programme

Note The AI policy training is co-run with Google Indonesia, which raises questions about independence. Much content is in Indonesian and written by research assistants. There is no catastrophic-risk framing.

Centre for Research in Digital Education (University of Edinburgh) Adjacent

Academic · Edinburgh, UK · founded 2015 · also draws on Arts, futures

A research centre in the University of Edinburgh's Moray House School of Education and Sport, affiliated with the Edinburgh Futures Institute. It was established in 2015, growing out of the Digital Cultures and Education group (2009) and the online MSc in Digital Education (2006). Its five themes are Cultures & Futures, Children & Technology, Data Society, Data Education in Schools, and Digital Education in the Global South. Its AI work includes Ben Williamson's critical research on AI, datafication and the political economy of edtech platforms; a draft AI curriculum framework for Scotland and a 'Teach AI Literacy' guide for teachers; and futures-thinking resources on AI for schools.

It applies critical data studies and the sociology of education to AI in schools and universities, asking who owns and profits from educational AI and how data systems change teaching. The AI-safety field's treatment of education largely leaves out these questions. Its Scottish AI-literacy curriculum is a working template for teaching young people to judge AI critically.

Works on Power, Epistemics, Justice · Key work Teach AI Literacy handbook and draft AI curriculum framework for Scotland (2025); Centre for Research in Digital Education Report 2025 (10th anniversary) (2025); Judy Robertson and Ben Williamson discuss current research on GenAI in education (video) (2026) · Get involved MSc Digital Education (online) and MSc Education Futures; Public lectures and events with the Edinburgh Futures Institute (e.g. the Future University programme, 2026); Research and lecturing posts advertised on de.ed.ac.uk

Note AI is one strand of wider digital-education research. The draft's 'Sept 2026 review of the evidence' is a recorded video discussion, not a written review. Its stance is critical of edtech and AI hype, with no catastrophic-risk framing.

Centro de Estudios en Tecnología y Sociedad, Universidad de San Andrés (CETyS) Adjacent

Academic · Buenos Aires, Argentina · founded 2007 · also draws on Economics

An interdisciplinary centre at the Universidad de San Andrés in Buenos Aires (founded 2007, according to its site) that works on internet governance, the political economy of digital technology and emerging technologies, with a Latin American focus. Its AI line covers AI ethics and governance in the region and AI adoption by courts. It led the GuIA research network, launched in 2020 with support from the IDB's fAIr LAC and Meta. Its court work includes a study of judicial AI readiness in Argentina, Chile, Colombia, Mexico and Uruguay, submissions to the Buenos Aires Supreme Court on AI in justice, and the 'Redes de justicIA' workshop on 26 August 2026. It also teaches diplomas in internet governance, data protection and digital regulation, plus executive courses such as one on digital competition and antitrust (August 2026).

It offers Latin American evidence on how public institutions, especially courts, actually adopt generative AI, and it convenes a regional network of AI-governance researchers. That is practical knowledge of AI oversight in states with weak regulatory frameworks, which AI-safety governance work rarely has.

Works on Justice, Assurance, Power · Key work América Latina ante la encrucijada de la IA generativa y su adopción responsable en el ámbito judicial (2025); Redes de justicIA: del diagnóstico a la adopción responsable (workshop) (2026); Submissions to the Buenos Aires Supreme Court public consultation on AI in justice (2026) · Get involved Diplomas: Internet Governance (DiGI), International Diploma in Personal Data Protection (PDP; 2027 5th edition information session), Regulation of Digital Technologies (RTDi, online); Executive courses, e.g. Competition and Antitrust in the Digital Economy (Aug 2026); Events listed on its UdeSA page include IGF Argentina 2026 and Youth IGF Argentina 2026

Note The 2007 founding year comes from its own site only. GuIA was partly funded by Meta. Its AI framing is responsible adoption, with no safety or catastrophic-risk lens. The UdeSA page renders client-side, so most details come from cetys.lat.

Civics of Technology Project Adjacent

Nonprofit · Distributed · founded 2022 · also draws on Philosophy

A US 501(c)(3) nonprofit launched in 2022 by education professors Daniel Krutka and Marie Heath, now co-directed with Jacob Pleasants. It promotes critical inquiry into technology in K-16 classrooms, starting from the premise that technologies are not neutral. It publishes free curricula and technology-audit frameworks and a weekly blog and newsletter, and runs monthly online book clubs and an annual virtual conference; the fifth, billed as an 'Online Conference Against Tech Hype', was in August 2026. Its AI materials include 'Critical Inquiries of Generative AI' lessons for university students and a 'What is AI made of?' lesson plan. Its 2026 blog posts cover GenAI in history teaching, ableism in educational AI, technofeudalism, and teachers' roles beyond being a 'human-in-the-loop'.

It gives teachers Neil Postman-style media ecology and technoskepticism, including the view that refusing a technology is a legitimate educational choice. AI-safety work tends to treat public education as AI literacy or adoption training; this project offers ready-made curricula for questioning AI's effects instead.

Works on Epistemics, Justice · Key work Critical Inquiries of Generative AI (lesson collection); What is AI made of? A two-part lesson plan (2026); 5th Civics of Technology Online Conference Against Tech Hype (2026) · Get involved Annual virtual conference each August (fifth in 2026); Monthly online book clubs (#CivicsOfTech on Bluesky); Weekly blog and newsletter, with posts contributed by its educator network

Note It is openly critical of tech hype and edtech adoption, so it is a voice in the debate, not a neutral evaluator. The 'Refusing Educational Technology' paper it highlighted in October 2026 is by Niral Shah and colleagues, not its own research. It is run largely by academics alongside their university posts.

Coalition for Children's Rights and Protection in the Age of AI AdjacentNew

Public body · Distributed · founded 2026 · also draws on Peace

An intergovernmental coalition set up on 7 July 2026 at the first UN Global Dialogue on AI Governance. France, Spain and Kenya co-chair it, Australia joined later as a fourth co-chair, and eight UN entities take part, including UNICEF, UNESCO, ITU, OHCHR and the Committee on the Rights of the Child. Its 2026–27 roadmap was presented at the UN General Assembly on 22 September 2026. It sets up working groups on safety and privacy by design, benchmarking and accountability, AI-generated child sexual abuse material and deepfakes, and AI literacy, and it plans a global network of research centres to assess AI's effects on children. It asks for pre-authorisation of AI systems aimed at children before they reach the market, for independent researchers to get access to developers' models and data, and for voluntary company commitments. The first commitments are due at the Paris Peace Forum on 10–11 November 2026.

It is a venue at head-of-government level where child-rights law and child-development evidence become concrete asks of AI developers, including pre-market authorisation and access to models for independent researchers. AI-safety governance work has rarely pursued these from a child-rights angle. The planned research network could give developmental and clinical researchers access to models.

Works on Justice, Human minds, Assurance · Key work Roadmap of the Coalition for Children's Rights and Protection in the Age of AI (2026–27) (2026); First voluntary company commitments (planned for the Paris Peace Forum, 10–11 November 2026) (2026) · Get involved Research centres from the public, academic and private sectors are invited to join the planned global research network; no application route has been published yet; Companies are invited to make voluntary commitments; the first batch is due at the Paris Peace Forum, 10–11 November 2026

Note The only source found is the French presidency's announcement. The coalition has no website or secretariat of its own. That page gives both 26 and 23 member states, and lists only the four co-chairs and the eight UN entities. The commitments it seeks from companies are voluntary. It is separate from iRAISE, the multistakeholder coalition co-led by everyone.AI and the Paris Peace Forum. Independent confirmation could not be sought because this session's web-search budget had run out.

Coalition for Sign Language Equity in Technology (CoSET) AdjacentChanged

Network · Distributed · founded 2023 · also draws on Arts, futures

A US coalition of Deaf people, sign-language interpreters, researchers and technologists. It was formerly called the Advisory Group on AI and Sign Language Interpreting, and is pending incorporation as a 501(c)(3) nonprofit. It grew out of three webinars hosted at Brown University in autumn 2023, with about 300 participants, which fed its #DeafSafeAI report and the 2024 paper 'Deaf-Safe AI: A Legal Foundation for Ubiquitous Automatic Interpreting'; a symposium at Brown followed in April 2024. With the SAFE AI Task Force it co-wrote the AI Interpreting Solutions Evaluation Toolkit (Part A, 2025). It runs an on-demand course, 'A Risk Framework for Interpreting in the Age of AI', in ASL, Spanish and English.

Deaf signers are a linguistic minority for whom failures of AI interpreting are hard to detect and costly. CoSET brings co-design with signers and interpreters, failure modes gathered from the community and a legal basis for accountability. It shows the knowledge of an affected community entering AI assurance.

Works on Justice, Assurance · Key work Deaf-Safe AI: A Legal Foundation for Ubiquitous Automatic Interpreting (2024); #DeafSafeAI Symposium on AI and Sign Language Interpreting (Brown University) (2024); AI Interpreting Solutions Evaluation Toolkit, Part A (with SAFE AI Task Force) (2025) · Get involved Join CoSET through its online form; On-demand course on AI interpreting risk (RID-approved CEUs available); Free interactive toolkit checklists

Note It is not yet incorporated, and its site does not state leadership roles. Parts B and C of the toolkit are still 'coming soon'. Some recent work, such as legal guidance on immigration, goes beyond AI. It was renamed from the Advisory Group on AI and Sign Language Interpreting to stress its independence and equal status with the SAFE AI Task Force; the date of the change is not given.

COMMUNIA Association for the Public Domain Adjacent

Nonprofit · Brussels, Belgium · founded 2012 · also draws on Economics

COMMUNIA is an international association under Belgian law, based in Brussels, that advocates for the public domain and for access to and reuse of culture and knowledge, mainly in EU copyright policy. It grew out of a European Commission-funded thematic network (2007-11). Its AI work includes policy papers on training machine-learning models on copyrighted works (2023) and against new exclusive rights for AI-generated outputs (2025), AI Act submissions on text-and-data-mining opt-outs, and a 2026 study on copyright obstacles to open-source AI in the EU.

It holds detailed copyright-law expertise on who may train on, and who may own, the outputs of AI. That decides whether open and public-interest AI stays legally viable in Europe, a question about power and lock-in that conventional AI policy usually leaves to lobbyists for rights holders or for developers.

Works on Power, Justice · Key work Policy Paper #15: On using copyrighted works for teaching the machine (2023); Policy Paper #22: Against new exclusive rights for AI-generated outputs (2025); Study: Copyright challenges in open-source AI development in the European Union (2026)

Note It overlaps with Open Future in leadership: Paul Keller presides over COMMUNIA and co-founded Open Future, and Alek Tarkowski works with both. Its AI engagement is copyright-specific. Its Salons are in-person events in Brussels; no AI-specific open calls were found.

Council of Europe: Framework Convention on AI, HUDERIA and CDNET (formerly the Committee on Artificial Intelligence, CAI) AdjacentChanged

Public body · Strasbourg, France · founded 2019

The Council of Europe's AI work centres on the Framework Convention on Artificial Intelligence and Human Rights, Democracy and the Rule of Law, the first legally binding international AI treaty. It was adopted on 17 May 2024 and opened for signature in Vilnius on 5 September 2024. The Convention requires risk and impact assessments, transparency, remedies and the option of bans or moratoria ('red lines'). It covers public authorities and private actors, but exempts national security and defence. The Committee on Artificial Intelligence (CAI, 2022-2025, preceded by CAHAI from 2019) drafted it and developed HUDERIA, a methodology for assessing AI's impact on human rights, democracy and the rule of law. A new Steering Committee for New and Emerging Digital Technologies (CDNET) succeeded the CAI in December 2025.

It is the only binding multilateral AI treaty, and it is open to non-European states. The US, UK, Canada, Japan, Israel and Uruguay have signed, and Argentina, Australia, Mexico, Peru, Costa Rica and the Holy See took part in drafting. That makes it a treaty-law route for AI governance that the AI-safety field mostly bypasses. HUDERIA is a ready-made template for assessing sociotechnical impact, and a Conference of the Parties will monitor implementation once the treaty is in force.

Works on Justice, Democracy, Assurance · Key work Framework Convention on Artificial Intelligence and Human Rights, Democracy and the Rule of Law (CETS 225) (2024); HUDERIA risk and impact assessment methodology for AI systems (2024); Establishment of the Steering Committee for New and Emerging Digital Technologies (CDNET), successor to the CAI (2025)

Note coe.int blocks automated fetches (403), so the current status comes from Wayback Machine copies (Jan, Jul and Aug 2026) and Wikipedia. Not yet in force: it needs five ratifications, including three CoE member states. German Wikipedia reported no ratifications as of October 2025. The draft entry's '50+ signatories' conflates the states that drafted the treaty with those that signed it; the actual count was about 21 in mid-2026. The CAI's mandate ended in 2025 and CDNET replaced it with a broader remit. Critics point to the national-security exemption and the option for parties to apply the treaty to private actors only indirectly.

Danish Institute for Human Rights (DIHR): Technology and Human Rights Adjacent

Programme · Copenhagen, Denmark · founded 1987

The technology strand of the Danish Institute for Human Rights, Denmark's national human rights institution (founded 1987, government-funded, with UN 'A' status), run from its Human Rights, Business and Tech department. It develops rights-based tools and guidance for digital technology and AI: a guide to fundamental rights impact assessments for high-risk AI under the EU AI Act (with ECNL, December 2025), the Digital Rights Check for development projects, an online microlearning series on a human rights-based approach to AI, and the NHRI Digital Rights Alliance, a peer network of national human rights institutions. A 2025-26 project is drafting global legal principles for human rights in the digital space.

It brings human rights impact assessment, a field-tested method from business and human rights, to AI deployment, and has written it up as a practical, phased guide for the EU AI Act's FRIA duty. That is a ready template for rights-based assurance and oversight, and its NHRI alliance reaches national oversight bodies worldwide.

Works on Justice, Assurance, Democracy · Key work Guide to Fundamental Rights Impact Assessments (FRIA) under the EU AI Act, with ECNL (2025); NHRI Digital Rights Alliance (2021-); Digital Democracy Initiative: Global Policy and Legal Action (2025-2026) · Get involved Free online microlearning series on a human rights-based approach to AI, and Digital Rights Explorer training in English, French, Spanish and Arabic; Digital Rights Check, a free web tool for assessing the human rights impact of digital projects; Vacancies at DIHR (humanrights.dk/about-us/vacancies)

Note The unit is the technology strand of one department, not the whole institute; dates are for DIHR itself. The latest items on its technology news page date from mid-2025, though the FRIA guide followed in December 2025. DIHR has phased out bilateral advisory services to private companies. Its AI work concerns rights-based governance of deployed systems, not frontier or catastrophic risk.

Data & Society Research Institute Adjacent

Nonprofit · New York, USA · founded 2014 · also draws on Economics

An independent nonprofit research and policy institute in New York, launched in 2014 by danah boyd with early support from Microsoft Research, that studies the social effects of data-centric technology, automation and AI. Its programmes include AI on the Ground, the Algorithmic Impact Methods Lab (AIMLab, participatory methods for algorithmic impact assessment), Democracy in the Age of AI, Labor Futures and, from September 2026, a Worker Lens on the AI Economy. In September 2026 it published a 'Governing AI Agents' research collection, a letter to Congress on AI companies' 'pacing the frontier' approach, and an ethnographic report on data centres in Pennsylvania.

It produces ethnographic and field evidence on how deployed AI changes work and civic life, plus participatory impact-assessment methods that evaluations of AI agents could borrow. Its 'Governing AI Agents' collection argues that individual human oversight of agents does not scale automatically, which bears directly on agent safety governance.

Works on Justice, Power, Democracy · Key work Governing AI Agents (research and policy collection) (2026); Letter to Congress on Pacing the Frontier (2026); The AI Factory: Data Centers, Power, and Resistance in Late Industrial Pennsylvania (2026) · Get involved Staff roles (no openings listed in October 2026); Public events and talks; Newsletter and the Points blog

Note Frames its work around concrete harms and structural equity, not catastrophic risk; the 'Pacing the Frontier' letter argues against regulation that focuses only on frontier risks.

Data Privacy Brasil Adjacent

Nonprofit · São Paulo, Brazil · founded 2018 · also draws on Economics, Democracy

A São Paulo nonprofit that began as a data-protection training school in 2018 and added a research association in 2020; the two were merged in 2026. It researches and advocates on data protection, platform and digital-market regulation and AI governance. Its AI projects cover rights-based AI regulation in Brazil ('IA com Direitos', 'Onde canta o sabIA'), AI in classrooms and, with Aláfia Lab, an Observatory of AI in the Elections, which logged 413 AI uses in political content before the 2026 campaign, over 80% of them deepfakes. It has trained over 6,000 professionals, including staff of government, the judiciary and Brazil's data protection authority, and runs the annual Data Privacy Global Conference.

It brings human-rights and data-protection law, plus Global South civil-society positioning, to AI governance. Its work includes empirical tracking of AI deepfakes during a live national election and co-leading a working group whose proposals feed the UN Global Dialogue on AI Governance. That is Latin American regulatory experience the AI-safety governance field seldom draws on.

Works on Justice, Epistemics, Human minds · Key work IA na pré-eleição: deepfakes, desinformação e novos desafios para a integridade das eleições de 2026 (2026); Observatório IA nas Eleições (with Aláfia Lab) (2026); One year of ECA Digital: materials on age assurance and manipulative design (2026) · Get involved Data Privacy Global Conference, 7-8 Dec 2026 (5th edition); Submit AI election content to the Observatório IA nas Eleições reporting channel; Training through its Data Privacy school and Data Governance School

Note The training school (2018) and research association (2020) had separate identities until they merged in 2026, so founding dates vary by source. Most output is in Portuguese. It has no catastrophic-risk framing, and its funding is largely undisclosed on its site.

Data Provenance Initiative (DPI) Adjacent

Network · Cambridge (MA), United States · founded 2023 · also draws on Economics, Democracy

A volunteer research collective, started in 2023 and coordinated mainly from the MIT Media Lab, that audits the data and markets behind AI. It has traced the licences, sources and creators of more than 4,000 public text, speech and video datasets (the Data Provenance Explorer), tracked how robots.txt files and terms of service restrict AI crawling across 14,000 web domains ('Consent in Crisis', 2024), and measured concentration and participation across some 851,000 open-weight models ('Economies of Open Intelligence', Dec 2025). Its newest project, the AI Observatory (2026 preprint), annotates about 23,000 real chatbot conversations from seven public and private sources to compare how people use and misuse AI.

It provides public-interest measurement of the AI supply chain, combining legal analysis of licences and consent with large-scale auditing. It documents the erosion of the data commons and the concentration of model markets, issues mainstream alignment work seldom measures.

Works on Justice, Power, Epistemics · Key work The Data Provenance Initiative: A Large Scale Audit of Dataset Licensing & Attribution in AI (Nature Machine Intelligence) (2024); Consent in Crisis: The Rapid Decline of the AI Data Commons (2024); Economies of Open Intelligence: Tracing Power & Participation in the Model Ecosystem (2025) · Get involved Contact the organisers to contribute to audits (volunteer collective); Use the Data Provenance Collection and public dashboards (dataset audits, web consent, open-model ecosystem, AI Observatory)

Note A volunteer collective with no disclosed core funding, and some leads are doctoral researchers, so its continuity is uncertain. The roster marked its status as unclear, but its site shows new work in late 2025 and 2026. Its outputs are explicitly not legal advice.

Derechos Digitales Adjacent

Nonprofit · Santiago, Chile · founded 2005

A Latin American digital-rights nonprofit, based in Chile with staff in more than ten countries, that researches and advocates on human rights in the digital environment. Its AI work covers AI and digital autonomy, AI-enabled devices and privacy (for example Meta's smart glasses), data centres, and the costs of training AI, including the destructive scanning of books. It explicitly rejects both 'destroyer' and 'saviour' narratives about AI. Its co-executive director Jamila Venturini sits on the expert advisory panel of a Global South AI Safety Report.

It is a main Latin American civil-society voice on AI and rights. Through its seat on the Global South AI Safety Report panel it already links to AI-safety debates, so it is a natural partner for anyone building AI-safety work in a region with no dedicated hub. Its scepticism of x-risk narratives is itself useful information for the field.

Works on Justice, Power · Key work Ni destructora ni salvadora: lo que hay en medio del mito de la Inteligencia Artificial (2026); Inteligencia artificial y autonomía digital (2026); Debate on AI, data centres and rights at the University of Buenos Aires (2026) · Get involved Staff team across more than ten Latin American countries (no openings checked); Runs a separate funds portal (fondos.derechosdigitales.org), whose content could not be read

Note It is openly sceptical of existential-risk narratives, which it calls marketing by AI companies, so any engagement on AI safety would need to start from present harms. The founding year (2005) is consistent with the site's 'over 20 years' but was not confirmed directly. Most material is in Spanish.

Digital Futures for Children centre (DFC), LSE and 5Rights Foundation Adjacent

Academic · London, United Kingdom · founded 2023

DFC is a joint research centre of the London School of Economics (LSE) and the 5Rights Foundation, hosted by LSE's Department of Media and Communications and directed by Sonia Livingstone. It succeeded the three-year Digital Futures Commission. It produces children's-rights evidence framed by the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child and General comment No. 25. Its AI work includes: a child-rights audit of five generative-AI tools used in UK education (Character.AI, Grammarly, MagicSchool AI, Microsoft Copilot, Mind's Eye); RIGHTS.AI, a study of children's generative-AI experiences in Brazil, India, Kenya and Thailand; a report on developers' uptake of Child Rights by Design; and a narrative review of evidence on AI and children's rights.

It turns children's rights law into tests that AI products can be audited against, and its Child Rights by Design guidance is a design standard developers could adopt. RIGHTS.AI is one of the few sources of evidence on how children outside the West experience generative AI.

Works on Justice, Human minds, Assurance · Key work A child rights audit of GenAI in EdTech: Learning from five UK case studies (2025); RIGHTS.AI: children's experiences of generative AI in Brazil, India, Kenya and Thailand (2025); Global developers' insights into Child Rights by Design (contribution to UNDP Human Development Report 2025) (2025) · Get involved Public webinars and lectures, hybrid at LSE and online (e.g. 15 Oct 2026 AI webinar, 19 Nov 2026 World Children's Day lecture); DFC Research Insights Day, 23 Oct 2026, LSE and online; Global research database and newsletter

Note Its principal funder, 5Rights, is an advocacy organisation; readers should weigh that when judging its independence. Automated fetches of the site hit redirect loops; the pages resolve in a browser.

Emotional AI Lab (Bangor University) Adjacent

Academic · Bangor, United Kingdom · founded 2017 · also draws on Philosophy

A research group at Bangor University, led by Andrew McStay since 2017, that studies the social, legal and ethical effects of technologies that read, simulate or respond to human emotion. Current work covers AI companions (including a 2026 survey of UK teenagers), AI-enabled 'empathic' scams in a Nigeria–UK project, children, policing and disinformation. Through its RAI UK-funded AEGIS project it led the drafting of IEEE 7014.1, a standard on emulated empathy in AI companions and assistants, published in June 2026.

It brings media studies and cross-cultural (UK–Japan) social science to emulated empathy, and it turned that work into the first international standard for AI companions. Frontier labs treat sycophancy and emotional dependence as model-behaviour problems; this group offers a soft-law and governance route that the AI-safety field rarely engages with.

Works on Human minds, Assurance, Epistemics · Key work Do AI Companions Understand? Most UK Teens Say Yes (report) (2026); Weaponised Empathy: AI Scams & the Nigeria–UK Response (report) (2026); IEEE 7014.1-2026, Recommended Practice on emulated empathy in partner-based general-purpose AI (working group chaired by McStay) (2026) · Get involved Collaboration and media enquiries go to Andrew McStay via the lab site; Read IEEE 7014.1 free from the lab's IEEE 7014.1 page (emotionalai.org/ieee-70141)

Note A small academic group whose outputs are mainly reports, papers and soft law. The site's 'Outputs' and 'who' pages returned 404 when checked. The Nigeria scam project was a three-month sprint. Its standards work overlaps with the separate IEEE 7014/7014.1 entry.

EPIC (Ethnographic Praxis in Industry Community) Adjacent

Membership body · Distributed · founded 2005 · also draws on Arts, futures

A nonprofit (501(c)(3), incorporated in Oregon) and global membership network of ethnographers and other interpretive social scientists working in companies and organisations. ken anderson and Tracey Lovejoy, then social scientists in technology-company R&D, founded it in 2005. It runs an annual conference, a members' virtual Learning Week, paid trainings and a video and paper library. Its recent output leans heavily on AI: an Automation collection, papers such as 'Grounded Models: The Future of Sensemaking in a World of Generative AI' and 'Decolonizing LLMs: An Ethnographic Framework for AI in African Contexts', and the EPIC2026 conference (Chicago, 26-28 Oct) on 'Modeling, predicting, and interpreting context'.

Its members are practising ethnographers inside technology companies, so EPIC holds both the method and the access needed to study AI labs and deployment settings from the inside. It also argues that AI systems need contextual, lived-experience grounding that model-centric work misses.

Works on Epistemics, Power, Justice · Key work EPIC2026: Modeling, predicting, and interpreting context (Chicago, 26-28 Oct) (2026); Grounded Models: The Future of Sensemaking in a World of Generative AI (Tom Hoy et al.); Decolonizing LLMs: An Ethnographic Framework for AI in African Contexts (Lindsey DeWitt Prat et al.) · Get involved Attend EPIC2026, Chicago, 26-28 Oct 2026 (livestream for members); Become a member (US$150/yr) for the virtual Learning Week and the video library; Take EPIC courses and tutorials (discounted for members)

Note The site blocks automated access, so details come from archived copies (Jan-Sep 2026). EPIC is oriented to business and product practice: its AI work concerns responsible design, research methods and the future of work, not catastrophic risk. Publication years for the featured AI papers could not be confirmed.

European AI & Society Fund (EAISF) Adjacent

Funder · Brussels, Belgium · founded 2020 · also draws on Economics, Arts, futures

A pooled philanthropic fund, hosted by the Network of European Foundations in Brussels. Through it about 20 foundations fund European public-interest organisations working on AI policy, accountability, market power and rights; partners include Ford, MacArthur, Mozilla, Oak, Open Society, Porticus, Robert Bosch, Stiftung Mercator and Hewlett. It has given €13.6M to organisations in 27 countries since 2020. It also briefs funders and runs learning programmes. In 2026 it ran a €2M 'Building Narrative Power' call on data centres, AI and jobs, and young people.

It is the main pooled funder for civil-society AI work in Europe. Its grantees include digital-rights groups, algorithmic auditors (AIAL, Algorithm Audit), disability, migrant and labour organisations, a network the x-risk field rarely reaches. It is an obvious co-funding route and partner for European work that connects AI safety with rights, market power and public narrative.

Works on Justice, Power · Key work Building Narrative Power funding and learning programme (€2M) (2026); AI & Market Power – Findings from Fellows (2026); Funders' briefing: AI and data centres (2026) · Get involved Open calls for European civil-society organisations, such as Building Narrative Power (€2M, up to €150k per organisation, plus a learning community). The first stage closed 31 Aug 2026; watch for new rounds.; AI & Market Power fellowships; findings and lessons for funders published Jul 2026.; Funders can join as pooled-fund partners and attend its funders' briefings on AI topics.

Note It frames its work as public interest, rights and redirecting AI away from Big Tech. It says it wants AI to be 'safe and fair' but does not engage with catastrophic risk. Only European organisations are eligible. It moved to a co-director model with a new five-year strategy in January 2026.

Fundación Vía Libre Adjacent

Nonprofit · Córdoba, Argentina · founded 2000 · also draws on Economics

An Argentine nonprofit, founded in Córdoba in 2000, that defends fundamental rights wherever information technology shapes daily life. Its work covers privacy, free expression, electronic voting, access to culture and AI, and it has been the Creative Commons affiliate for Argentina since 2011. Its AI work includes EDIA, an open no-code tool (2022) that lets social scientists probe stereotypes in Spanish- and English-language models. It also scrutinises Buenos Aires's facial-recognition system, wrote a UNESCO-commissioned paper on digital and AI sovereignty (2026), and runs public events on AI and democracy.

It speaks for Latin American digital rights and free culture, and is an informed sceptic of x-risk discourse. That makes it useful for seeing how AI-safety framings land in the Global South. EDIA is a working model of putting model audits in the hands of domain experts rather than ML engineers.

Works on Justice, Assurance, Power · Key work A methodology to characterize bias and harmful stereotypes in natural language processing in Latin America (the EDIA methodology paper) (2022); Soberanía digital y de la IA: cuatro casos informados por evidencia (UNESCO-commissioned background paper) (2026); Rostros bajo la lupa: analysis of a new facial-recognition system in Buenos Aires (2026) · Get involved Free public talks and panels in Buenos Aires, with registration (e.g. 'Qué pasa con la democracia?', 8 Oct 2026); EDIA is open source (MIT) on GitHub, with a demo on Hugging Face Spaces; Podcast 'El bestiario de internet' and outreach materials ('Tecnologías en debate' toolkit)

Note Openly sceptical of x-risk discourse. At a September 2026 panel its president said she was fed up with catastrophic AI warnings, and the panel described them as tools for corporate financial and regulatory capture. EDIA's public demo was last updated in May 2024. The site names no staff, no current office address and no funding amounts. Founded in Córdoba, but its 2026 events are in Buenos Aires.

Humans, Machines, Language (HuMaLa), BAAL Special Interest Group Adjacent

Network · Distributed · founded 2024

A special interest group of the British Association for Applied Linguistics, founded in March 2024 as successor to the EU COST network 'Language In The Human-Machine Era' (LITHME, 2020-24). It studies how language technologies, from AI assistants and machine translation to conversational agents and AR/VR, change language teaching, policy, translation, intercultural communication and literacies. Membership is free through a JISCMail list, and an elected committee runs annual events: a conference in Granada (June 2025), a machine-translation and GenAI literacy event in Granada (2-3 June 2026), and the HUMIC workshop on conversational AI at the University of Surrey (16 June 2026).

It brings sociolinguistics, translation studies and intercultural pragmatics to the question of how LLMs and conversational agents reshape human language, rapport and translators' work. The AI-safety field rarely looks at AI's effects on human communication.

Works on Human minds, Power, Justice · Key work Inaugural meeting at the BAAL 2024 conference, University of Essex (2024); Annual conference, University of Granada (24-25 June) (2025); Promoting Machine Translation and GenAI Translation Literacy, Granada (2-3 June) (2026) · Get involved Join free via the humans-machines-language JISCMail list; Calls for papers for its annual events (2026: Granada and Surrey); Committee posts elected by members; optional BAAL membership

Note A small volunteer academic network. AI is its main but not its only technology (AR/VR too), and it has no safety or catastrophic-risk framing. The committee spans the UK, Spain, Germany, Saudi Arabia and Türkiye; 2027 plans are not yet posted.

Institute for Family Studies (IFS): Family First Technology Initiative Adjacent

Programme · Charlottesville, USA · also draws on Religion

The technology programme of the Institute for Family Studies, a family-policy think tank in Charlottesville, Virginia. It researches how technology affects family life, writes model policy, and campaigns, at first on children's online safety and now increasingly on AI. Its AI outputs include the March 2025 report 'Protecting the Family in the Age of Artificial Intelligence', the Feb 2025 report 'A Future for the Family: A New Technology Agenda for the Right', and a June 2026 Supreme Court amicus brief backing Texas's app-store age law.

It brings a socially conservative, family-centred constituency into AI governance, and it has a proven route into US state law: IFS says its youth online-safety policy work has produced more than a dozen state laws (2024 Heritage Innovation Prize). AI-safety funders (FLI, SFF) now back it, which shows them trying to widen the political coalition for AI governance beyond tech-policy circles.

Works on Human minds, Meaning · Key work Protecting the Family in the Age of Artificial Intelligence (Toscano and Hayden) (2025); A Future for the Family: A New Technology Agenda for the Right (Toscano, Littlejohn, Waters, Morell, Askonas) (2025); Supreme Court amicus brief supporting the Texas App Store safety law (2026)

Note IFS is a socially conservative think tank, and one report is explicitly framed as an agenda 'for the Right', so many potential partners will find its positions on family and gender contested. The SFF 2026 grant is general support to IFS, not earmarked for the initiative. Its AI framing is family protection and human flourishing, not catastrophic risk. The founding years of IFS and of the initiative were not confirmed.

Instituto de Tecnologia e Sociedade do Rio (ITS Rio) Adjacent

Nonprofit · Rio de Janeiro, Brazil · founded 2013 · also draws on Democracy

A Rio de Janeiro nonprofit research institute founded in 2013 by Ronaldo Lemos, working on law and technology, democracy and technology, education and innovation. Its AI work includes: - a postgraduate specialisation in AI and technology regulation with UERJ and CEPED (third cohort August 2026), plus short AI courses - an operational AI sandbox in Rio's Public Defender's Office - 'Boca de IA', which tests how chatbots recommend votes in the 2026 election - a September 2025 design, with CEBRI, for a Brazilian Institute for AI Safety and Opportunities It also publishes commentary on AI, such as a September 2026 column on AI companions.

It is one of the few Global South institutes to have designed a national AI safety institute. It pairs that with AI-regulation teaching for Brazilian lawyers and officials and with tests of chatbot behaviour in elections, so it could carry AI-safety governance ideas into Brazil.

Works on Justice, Epistemics, Assurance · Key work An AI Safety and Opportunities Institute for Brazil: A Design of Features, Functions, and Potential Challenges (with CEBRI) (2025); Pós-graduação em IA e Regulação Tecnológica (with UERJ/CEPED) (2026); Boca de IA: how AIs recommend votes in the 2026 elections (2026) · Get involved Short courses: 'Escrita acadêmica e IA' (starts 13 Oct 2026), 'Direitos Autorais e IA Generativa', 'IA para Comunicação de Impacto'; Postgraduate specialisation in AI and Technology Regulation (third cohort Aug 2026); ITS Global Policy Fellowship (2026 cohort of 13 fellows, 29 Jun-24 Jul, in Rio, Brasília and São Paulo)

Note The AI safety institute proposal is a single report (Sep 2025, with CEBRI), not a standing programme. It has wide tech-industry partnerships (its site lists Google, Meta, Amazon, Microsoft and others as partners) and runs a Google policy fellowship. The site does not state a founding year; 2013 is supported by its institutional page, first published in Dec 2013. The team page did not render, so leadership roles beyond Lemos are not confirmed on the site.

International Bar Association Artificial Intelligence Institute (IBA AI Institute) AdjacentNew

Programme · London, UK · founded 2026

An institute of the International Bar Association, launched on 8 June 2026 under former IBA president Jaime Carey and current president Claudio Visco. Its founding director is Dr Farzana Dudhwala, most recently Global AI Policy & Governance Lead at Meta, who earlier worked on UK government AI strategy and led the AI Futures team at the Centre for Data Ethics and Innovation. It aims to bring the legal profession's expertise into international AI governance, shaping frameworks in line with the rule of law, human rights and democratic integrity. The launch release names frontier AI systems, algorithmic accountability, access to justice, privacy and labour transformation among the challenges it will address, and commits to capacity-building so that under-represented jurisdictions help shape AI governance. It can draw on the IBA's network of more than 80,000 lawyers and 190 bar associations and law societies.

It gives AI governance a route into bar associations, law societies and courts worldwide, especially in jurisdictions that are usually absent from AI-safety discussions. Frontier AI is on its stated priority list, so it is an early opening for AI-safety governance ideas to reach the global legal profession.

Works on Justice, Democracy · Key work Launch of the IBA AI Institute (2026); IBA AI Working Group project (host's earlier AI work, run by the IBA Section on Public and Professional Interest since mid-2023) (2023) · Get involved IBA membership gives access to its committees and annual conference (2026 edition in Copenhagen had AI sessions); No open calls from the Institute found yet

Note Brand new, with no outputs yet. The IBA says the Institute's work is separate from the AI guidance its practice committees produce. The director comes from a senior policy role at Meta. Funding and staffing have not been disclosed.

InternetLab Adjacent

Nonprofit · São Paulo, Brazil · founded 2014 · also draws on Democracy

InternetLab is an independent think tank on law, technology and human rights in São Paulo, founded in 2014. For Brazil's 2026 elections it runs 'Papo de IA' (AI Chat) with FGV's LabDados and ReCoS, combining focus groups and citizen-researcher workshops with automated tests of eight chatbots (ChatGPT, Claude, Copilot, DeepSeek, Gemini, Google AI Mode, Grok, Meta AI) on candidate recommendations, gender narratives and electoral integrity. It has also added generative-AI tools to its 'Ache a Regra' repository of platform policies and measured AI use in offensive images targeting female candidates on X.

It audits how deployed chatbots behave in a specific non-English democratic setting, using participatory methods with citizens as well as automated testing. That is a working model for election-period assurance in the Majority World, where few AI evaluations are run.

Works on Epistemics, Assurance, Justice · Key work AI Chat (Papo de IA): how chatbots interact about elections (2026); Ache a Regra platform-policy repository extended to generative-AI tools for the 2026 elections (2026); AI is used in 25% of offensive images targeting female candidates on X (2026) · Get involved Staff research roles in São Paulo (team of about 30, including interns); AI Chat code and methodology are due to be published for reuse, with interim bulletins through the 2026 electoral calendar

Note Most of its AI work is tied to the 2026 Brazilian election cycle and is published mainly in Portuguese. It works on present harms and information integrity, without AI-safety framing.

Knowing Machines Adjacent

Programme · Los Angeles, United States · also draws on Arts, futures

A research project, sponsored by the Alfred P. Sloan Foundation, that studies how machine-learning training datasets are made and how they construct 'ground truth'. It is led by Kate Crawford and Mike Ananny (USC Annenberg) and Jason Schultz (NYU Law). Its team of scholars, lawyers, data journalists and artists has produced papers on deprecating datasets, a critical field guide for working with datasets, an investigation of LAION-5B, legal explainers and amicus filings, a podcast and the Calculating Empires artwork.

It treats training data as a cultural and legal artefact with a history. That gives alignment and data-provenance work concrete methods for asking whose categories and worldviews end up in a model. It also shows what investigating AI systems from outside ML looks like in practice, combining critical data studies, law and art.

Works on Justice, Epistemics · Key work Calculating Empires: A Genealogy of Technology and Power Since 1500 (Crawford and Joler; Silver Lion, Venice Architecture Biennale 2025) (2023); A Critical Field Guide for Working with Machine Learning Datasets (2023); A Framework for Deprecating Datasets (ACM FAccT) (2022) · Get involved Open resources: the Critical Dataset Studies reading list, the SeeSet dataset tool, a legal explainer and the Knowing Machines podcast

Note The founding year and grant period are not confirmed. The earliest listed output dates from 2021, and most research outputs from 2021-24, so the project may be winding down. The 2025 award went to an artwork first shown in 2023. The lead PI also holds a senior post at Microsoft Research.

Knowledge Rights 21 (KR21) Adjacent

Programme · The Hague, Netherlands · founded 2021 · also draws on Democracy

Knowledge Rights 21 is a European advocacy programme that works to reform copyright law and practice so that libraries, researchers and the public can access and use knowledge.
