Arcadia funds it, IFLA manages it, and LIBER and SPARC Europe are partners. It runs from The Hague, with a Brussels lead and national coordinators in 18 countries. 'Research & AI' is one of its four themes: it argues for research-first AI policy, for keeping text-and-data mining open for research, and against the EU's opt-out system for AI training.

It is one of the few organised voices in EU AI and copyright policy speaking for research and libraries. It argues that TDM opt-outs entrench the largest developers and skew training data, which ties copyright rules to power concentration in AI. AI-governance work tends to miss that angle.

Works on Power, Epistemics · Key work Principles on AI, Science and Research; Webinar: Closed Licences, Closed Doors: Open Licensing, AI, and the Future of Research Impact (2026); Copyright and Access in the Age of AI (event in Cyprus) (2026) · Get involved Webinars and national events on copyright, research and AI (listed on its events page); European Rights Retention Community of Practice and the KR21 European e-Books & e-Lending Community of Practice (first meeting Sept 2026), for library and research professionals; Newsletter

Note AI is one of four themes; most of its work is on e-lending, rights retention and secondary publishing rights. It argues for access and against opt-outs, which puts it on the opposite side from creator and rightsholder groups in the EU debate on AI and copyright. The University of Edinburgh Library runs the 9 Oct 2026 webinar; KR21's UK coordinator sits on the panel. The roster placed it in Brussels, but its contact base is IFLA in The Hague, with a Brussels lead.

La Quadrature du Net (LQDN) Adjacent

Nonprofit · Paris, France · founded 2008

A Paris digital-rights association that defends civil liberties online against censorship and surveillance by states and companies. Its AI-related work investigates and litigates against automated systems used by French administrations: the CNAF welfare risk-scoring algorithm, which it is challenging before the Conseil d'État with 24 other organisations, France Travail's profiling of unemployed people, predictive policing and algorithmic video surveillance. It also campaigns against online identity and age verification and runs the Technopolice project on urban surveillance.

It shows, case by case, how machine-learning decision systems are already used against the poorest people in a European state. It also has the tools to contest them: document leaks, freedom-of-information requests, analysis of source code and strategic litigation on data protection and non-discrimination. That is accountability practice the frontier-focused AI-safety field rarely has.

Works on Justice, Democracy · Key work Conseil d'État case against the CNAF discriminatory risk-scoring algorithm (filed Oct 2024 by 15 groups; 10 more joined Jan 2026) (2024); France Travail deploys an algorithmic profiling tool for job-search checks (with Radio France's investigation unit) (2026); Predictive policing in France: against opacity and discrimination, the need for a ban (2025) · Get involved Volunteer: subtitling, translation review, software development, graphics, contacting MPs during campaigns (laquadrature.net/qui-sommes-nous); Donate (the association is mostly funded by individual donors)

Note An activist and adversarial organisation. Its framing is civil liberties and present harms; it does not engage with AI x-risk. Most material is in French. It was an unregistered collective until 2013.

Laboratório de Políticas Públicas e Internet (LAPIN) Adjacent

Nonprofit · Brasília, Brazil · founded 2016

A Brasília nonprofit founded in 2016 that researches and advocates on internet regulation and digital rights. It works on four axes: digital surveillance, AI and emerging technologies, disinformation, and data governance and the digital economy, with dedicated AI and surveillance working groups. Its recent AI work addresses the material footprint of AI. With O Joio e O Trigo and the Heinrich Böll Foundation it held a seminar on AI, environment and socio-environmental justice, reported in February 2026. In June 2026, with IDEC, it sent evidence on AI data centres to the UN Special Rapporteur on climate change and human rights. In August and September 2026 it opposed Brazil's REDATA tax regime for data centres.

It connects the AI infrastructure build-out to water, energy, land and the rights of Indigenous and traditional communities, and calls for free, prior and informed consultation of affected people. AI-safety governance seldom models this resource and territorial side of the AI transition.

Works on Justice, Metacrisis · Key work Report: I Seminário Inteligência Artificial, Meio Ambiente e Justiça Socioambiental (2026); Input to the UN Special Rapporteur on climate change and human rights: the case of AI data centres (with IDEC) (2026); Statement against the approval of REDATA (data-centre tax regime) (2026) · Get involved Newsletter sign-up on lapin.org.br; Contact form for partnerships and joint projects

Note Funding is undisclosed. The AI and environment line is recent (2025-26). It has no catastrophic-risk framing, and its output is mostly in Portuguese. The profile rests on its own site, with no independent source found because search was unavailable.

LIRNEasia Adjacent

Nonprofit · Colombo, Sri Lanka · founded 2004 · also draws on Economics, Democracy

A nonprofit think tank on ICT policy and regulation, based in Colombo. Rohan Samarajiva founded it in 2004, and it works across South and Southeast Asia. Since February 2026 it has led the three-year Asia AI4D Observatory, with the East-West Management Institute and JustJobs Network, funded by Canada's IDRC and the UK's FCDO. The Observatory maps AI enablers, builds a repository of responsible-AI use cases and trains policymakers. Other AI work includes the Asia report for the Global Index on Responsible AI (2025), research on AI exposure in labour markets and on data governance, and misinformation classifiers for Sinhala and Bengali.

It is an established route into evidence-based AI policy research in non-Anglophone Asia, built on nationally representative demand-side surveys. It shows how 'safe, rights-based, inclusive' AI is being defined for countries the AI-safety field rarely consults.

Works on Justice, Power, Epistemics · Key work Asia AI4D Observatory on Responsible AI Innovations for Development (2026); Responsible AI in Asia (regional report for the Global Index on Responsible AI) (2025); Measuring AI exposure in the labour market (2026) · Get involved Staff roles: Senior Researcher (Oct 2026) and Intern, Data Annotation (Sep 2026); The Asia AI4D Observatory plans communities of practice, training and advisory support for policymakers (2026-29)

Note AI is one theme among many (agriculture, social protection, disability, education). Its 'responsible AI' framing includes safety but has no catastrophic-risk or alignment framing. The Observatory began in 2026 and its platform is still being built. Staff numbers were not found.

médialab, Sciences Po Adjacent

Academic · Paris, France · founded 2009 · also draws on Arts, futures

An interdisciplinary research laboratory at Sciences Po in Paris where sociologists, engineers and designers study digital society with digital methods. It also builds open-source research tools: Hyphe, minet and xan, and Spinosa, a local framework for working with LLMs. Its 'Technological Futures' line studies AI from an STS perspective. Projects cover situating AI in the worlds that produce it, LLMs in ordinary work practice (EL2MP), sociologically aware language models, the political and democratic biases of generative AI, and generative AI in citizen participation.

It brings Latourian controversy mapping and large-scale digital methods, which could map how AI-risk debates themselves form, spread and settle. It also does empirical work on how LLMs reshape everyday work and democratic participation. It is in Paris, where int/a has a community.

Works on Epistemics, Democracy, Power · Key work Situer l'intelligence artificielle (situating AI beyond excessive discourse); Écologies des pratiques LLMs (EL2MP): LLMs in ordinary work practice (2025); Spinosa, a local LLM research framework with sub-agents (2026) · Get involved Public research seminars in Paris (e.g. 6 Oct 2026); Jobs section on its website lists openings; Open-source tools on github.com/medialab

Note AI is one of four research lines, not the lab's whole focus. Its stance is to situate AI 'beyond excessive discourse', so it is sceptical of hype in both directions and does not frame its work around safety. The founding year comes from general knowledge, not from its own site.

Rede Latino-Americana de Estudos sobre Vigilância, Tecnologia e Sociedade (LAVITS) Adjacent

Network · Distributed · founded 2009 · also draws on Indigenous, Arts, futures

A network of Latin American researchers, activists and artists, founded in 2009, that studies surveillance, technopolitics, algorithms and AI from a critical and decolonial standpoint. It holds an international symposium: the seventh, in Rio de Janeiro on 26-28 August 2026, drew 350 participants and presented 141 papers chosen from over 300 submissions. It also runs research projects (digital gender violence, public-security technologies, digital peripheries) and publishes commentary under themes including 'Algoritmos & Política' and 'Inteligência Artificial'. A 'Conselho Ciborgue' (Cyborg Council) admits members and decides who speaks for the network.

It brings Latin American surveillance studies and the critique of data colonialism to AI, for example the argument that AI's environmental footprint is structural and falls mostly on the Global South. The AI-safety field's work on power concentration rarely draws on these perspectives. A council member put them before the first UN Global Dialogue on AI Governance in July 2026.

Works on Justice, Power, Metacrisis · Key work VII International LAVITS Symposium: 'Tramar o presente: tecnopolíticas dissidentes e ecologias do Comum' (2026); Jamila Venturini at the 1st UN Global Dialogue on AI Governance (Geneva): manipulative design and AI's environmental footprint (2026); Big techs e eleições (Rafael Evangelista) (2026) · Get involved Newsletter, launched Aug 2026; Membership: researchers, activists and artists apply to the Conselho Ciborgue; members coordinate by email lists and Telegram; Ciclo LAVITS event series, launched June 2026

Note AI is one theme among broader surveillance and technopolitics topics. The network's stance is critical of Big Tech and it does not engage with the AI-safety community. Six symposia ran from 2009 to 2019, then nothing until 2026. The site names few staff. Most sources are its own site.

Research ICT Africa (RIA) Adjacent

Nonprofit · Cape Town, South Africa · also draws on Economics

A digital-policy think tank in Cape Town, registered as a South African nonprofit company, that has run multidisciplinary research on digital governance, data justice and the digital economy across Africa for about two decades. Its Africa Just AI project (2021-2026) produced policy briefs and submissions on AI ethics within human-rights frameworks, agentic AI responsibility, electoral integrity, surveillance and economic justice. In 2026 it is shaping African input to the UN Global Dialogue on AI Governance and publishing on AI's effects on African labour.

It is an established African evidence base on AI labour, data justice and compute access, and it feeds that evidence into UN and African Union processes. AI-governance efforts that want real Majority-World input, beyond a handful of voices, could partner with it for both legitimacy and evidence.

Works on Justice, Power · Key work Africa Just AI project (2021-2026) (2021); A pivotal moment for AI for all: how we focus our research and engagement for the UN Global Dialogue on AI Governance (2026); Policy levers for AI futures: restructuring labour, power and public interest in Africa (2026) · Get involved Staff and research-fellow roles are advertised on its opportunities page; none were open in October 2026; Newsletter and events listed on its site

Note Its own site says it has operated for 'two decades' (nonprofit registration number dated 2009) but gives no founding year, so the field is left blank. Its 2026 UN recommendations deliberately focus on inclusion, labour and data sovereignty rather than frontier or catastrophic risk. No independent source was retrieved: the founding-year and history pages tried (RIA and IDRC) returned 404s, so this profile rests on RIA's own pages.

Responsible AI UK (RAi UK) Adjacent

Programme · Southampton, UK · founded 2023 · also draws on Democracy

A UK research network hosted at the University of Southampton and funded by a £30.7m EPSRC grant running from April 2023 to June 2028. It funds and connects multidisciplinary research on responsible AI: keystone projects such as PHAWM (participatory harm auditing) and PROBabLE Futures (AI in law enforcement), plus enterprise fellowships, skills programmes, research sandpits and international partnerships. Its leaders also publish policy commentary, including a 2026 piece calling for legal powers to require frontier-model assessment after, as the piece reports, Anthropic declined a UK AISI evaluation.

It is a large, publicly funded socio-technical network with participatory auditing methods and expertise in law, social science and HCI. Its leadership has begun commenting on frontier-AI assessment, so it could connect the UK's responsible-AI and AI-safety communities.

Works on Assurance, Justice · Key work PHAWM: Participatory Harm Auditing Workbenches and Methodologies (keystone project); PROBabLE Futures: probabilistic AI systems in law enforcement (keystone project); Anthropic's AISI refusal heralds the end of the road for mutual collaboration on frontier AI assessment (2026) · Get involved Enterprise Fellowships (AIR 26 and AIR 27 cohorts); Research awards, sandpits and live funding calls for UK researchers; UK AI Research Symposium, 24 Nov 2026; RAi UK All-Hands Meeting, 20 Jan 2027

Note A time-limited grant-funded programme (ends June 2028). Its main frame is responsible AI and present harms; frontier-AI commentary and a December 2025 blog on existential risk are occasional.

RIKEN AIP Science, Technology and Society Team (Osamu Sakura) and AI Utilization in Society and Legal System Team (Hiroshi Nakagawa) AdjacentDormant

Academic · Tokyo, Japan · founded 2016 · also draws on Arts, futures

Two societal-implications teams at RIKEN's Center for Advanced Intelligence Project (AIP) in Tokyo. The Science, Technology and Society Team, led by Osamu Sakura (March 2017 to March 2026), studied public images of AI and robots in Japan and East Asia, including science fiction, and contrasted Buddhist and Judeo-Christian views of humans and machines. The AI Utilization in Society and Legal System Team, led by Hiroshi Nakagawa (October 2016 to March 2026), worked on AI ethics, privacy protection, explainability, accountability, trustworthiness and AI agents. Both closed in March 2026, along with AIP's whole AI in Society Research Group, leaving the centre with technical groups only.

Their closure removes Japan's national-lab base for culturally specific East Asian research on how people relate to AI. The niche is open, and researchers such as Sakura, Nakagawa and Arisa Ema remain available to funders who want non-Western perspectives in AI governance.

Works on Meaning, Justice, Epistemics · Key work Research on public images of AI and robots in East Asia and Buddhist versus Judeo-Christian framings of human-AI relations (2017); AI Utilization in Society and Legal System Team wrap-up symposium (Tokyo and online) (2025)

Note Closed. RIKEN AIP's lab list shows no successor unit for ethics, law or social implications. Former members continue at universities and elsewhere.

RInCA (Responsible Innovation with Conscience and Agility), JST-RISTEX Adjacent

Funder · Tokyo, Japan · founded 2020 · also draws on Philosophy

A public R&D funding programme of the Japan Science and Technology Agency's Research Institute of Science and Technology for Society (RISTEX), running since FY2020. It funds research on the ethical, legal and social implications (ELSI) of emerging science and technology, and models of responsible research and innovation. Since then it has supported 25 R&D projects (about JPY 6-12m a year each in direct costs) and 28 feasibility studies. AI-related projects include Kyoto University's 'Autonomy and Affinity in AI Development and Use' (2021-2025) and a 2023 project on the ELSI of intimate relationships between humans and 'co-habitant' robots.

It is a non-Western public funder that has built ELSI and responsible-innovation research into a standing programme. Its AI projects pair philosophers, lawyers and engineers on human autonomy and human-robot intimacy. It offers new funders a model of anticipatory, co-creative ELSI funding, and a route to Japanese perspectives on AI and society.

Works on Human minds, Meaning · Key work Autonomy and Affinity in AI Development and Use (PI Usami Makoto, Kyoto University; Oct 2021-Mar 2025) (2021); Transdisciplinary Study on the ELSI of Building Intimate Relationship between Humans and 'Co-Habitant' Robots (PI Inatani Tatsuhiko, Kyoto University) (2023); RInCA Journal #06 (2026) · Get involved Annual funding calls for R&D projects and feasibility studies (open to Japan-based researchers; FY2025 projects selected Sep 2025); RInCA Journal and essay series

Note AI is a minority strand: of 25 projects, only a few concern AI, robots or data (AI autonomy 2021-25, co-habitant robots 2023, educational data 2022, automated driving 2020). Most concern biomedicine, infectious disease and environmental technology. Calls are for researchers in Japan. No independent source was checked beyond JST's own pages.

Shaping AI (Shaping 21st-Century AI: Controversies and Closure in Media, Policy and Research) AdjacentDormant

Programme · Bremen, Germany · founded 2021 · also draws on Arts, futures

A three-year comparative social-research consortium (Feb 2021 to Feb 2024), funded through the European Open Research Area scheme. It mapped how AI was built up as a scientific paradigm and a contested political issue in the UK, France, Germany and Canada. Teams at Warwick's Centre for Interdisciplinary Methodologies, Sciences Po médialab, ZeMKI Bremen with HIIG Berlin, and Concordia/INRS analysed a decade of AI controversies across media, policy, research and public participation.

It offers a tested method and comparative data for studying how AI controversies form and close, which could be applied to AI-safety and x-risk debates themselves. The French team had already begun, with a paper titled 'Shoggoth with Smiley Face' (named after a meme from AI-safety circles) and one on the Galactica model's withdrawal.

Works on Epistemics, Democracy · Key work 'Shifting AI Controversies' conference, WZB Berlin (2024); Reclaiming AI accounts: a plea for a participatory turn in AI inquiries (Gourlet, Ricci, Crépel, Big Data & Society) (2024); Galactica's dis-assemblage (Chartier-Edwards, Grenier, Goujon, AI & Society) (2024) · Get involved None current: the project ended in Feb 2024. Its publications and event records remain on shapingai.org, and the partner teams (médialab, HIIG, Warwick CIM, ZeMKI) continue related work.

Note A closed, time-limited project. It stays in because its method and outputs are reusable and its teams remain active. Overlaps with the médialab entry, which was its French partner.

Spencer Foundation: Initiative on AI and Education Adjacent

Funder · Chicago, USA · founded 2024 · also draws on Psychology

An initiative of the Spencer Foundation, a Chicago education-research funder founded in 1962. It grew out of a Spencer convening on AI and education in spring 2024. Rather than running a separate grant line, Spencer welcomes AI-focused proposals across its existing grant programmes (Vision Grants, large and small research grants, racial-equity and research-practice partnership grants). It funds research in four areas: AI and learning, AI policy, AI ethics and justice (including data sovereignty, privacy and bias), and how AI will transform education research itself. It also aims to connect researchers, the tech industry, policymakers and practitioners, and to shape public discourse on AI and education.

It is an established funder of research on AI's effects on learners and on equity, with its own review machinery. It backs community-partnered designs, for example AI literacy 'grounded in care and local systems change'. New AI-safety funders interested in AI's effects on young people's minds could co-fund with it.

Works on Justice, Human minds · Key work Spencer Convening on AI and Education (origin of the initiative) (2024); Spencer Vision Grant: 'From Early Encounters to Equitable Futures: Grounding AI Literacy in Care and Local Systems Change' (University at Buffalo team, PI X. Christine Wang) (2026); 2026 Spencer Vision Grant Awardees Workshop, Chicago (2026) · Get involved Open grant programmes that welcome AI-focused proposals: Vision Grants, large and small research grants, racial-equity and research-practice partnership grants (check spencer.org for current deadlines); Partnering or co-funding with the foundation on research about AI and education

Note AI money isn't reported separately from Spencer's general portfolio, so the initiative's size is unclear. Its framing is equity and opportunity in education, not AI safety. Grant amounts beyond the $75,000 Vision Grants weren't confirmed from Spencer's own pages.

Språkrådet (Language Council of Norway) Adjacent

Public body · Oslo, Norway · founded 2005

Norway's state language agency under the Ministry of Culture, established in 2005. It manages the official Bokmål and Nynorsk written standards and oversees state bodies' compliance with the Language Act 2021. Its language technology and AI work does four things. It sets language requirements for public-sector digital products and their procurement, shares Bokmål and Nynorsk language data for building models, advises schools and agencies on AI writing tools, and tests AI output; a September 2026 evaluation found that at least one in three machine-translated Nynorsk sentences needed correcting. In 2026 it also set quality requirements for Nordic language models and warned against Norway's dependence on US AI providers.

It treats AI as a question of linguistic sovereignty and public-sector quality assurance for a small language and its minority written standard, and it acts on models' training data and outputs. It gives the field a state-level example of protecting a language community from homogenising AI.

Works on Justice, Power, Assurance · Key work Language requirements for digital solutions (Krav til språk i digitale løysingar); Er maskin-nynorsken god nok? (evaluation of machine and AI translation into Nynorsk) (2026); Kunstig intelligens og ugunstig avhengighet (AI and unhealthy dependence) (2026) · Get involved Organisations can contribute Bokmål and Nynorsk language data through its 'Bidra med data' page; Its guidance on AI writing tools for schools and the public sector is publicly available

Note Åse Wetås, director since 2015, left in 2026; Nina Teigland is acting director. Much of the AI work is guidance and advocacy; the binding force comes from the Language Act, which applies to state bodies.

SUPERRR Lab Adjacent

Nonprofit · Berlin, Germany · founded 2019 · also draws on Economics, Arts, futures

A Berlin non-profit (Superrr Lab SL gGmbH) founded in 2019 by Julia Kloiber and Elisa Lindinger. It works on feminist digital policy and futures under the line 'digital policy is social policy'. Its AI work includes 'AI Mythbusting: The Zine' (July 2026), drawn from 13 public events in Berlin libraries, and 'Data Workers United' (September 2026, with DAIR), which links data-worker movements in Kenya, Nigeria, Venezuela, the US, Germany and Spain. It also runs feministtechpolicy.org.

It brings the people behind AI training data, and feminist and futures methods, into the question of whose futures AI serves. The safety field rarely looks at the data-labelling workforce or at how the public understands AI. Its Berlin public events on AI power and myths are a ready local partner for int/a Berlin.

Works on Power, Justice, Epistemics · Key work AI Mythbusting: The Zine (2026); Data Workers United (with DAIR) (2026); KI: Macht, Mythen, Missverständnisse (public event series in Berlin libraries) (2026) · Get involved Attend its public events on AI in Berlin (13 library events in early 2026); Use and adapt the AI Mythbusting zine, released with editable files in the public domain; Paid internships (described in an August 2026 post) and staff roles

Note AI is one strand of a broader feminist digital-policy agenda (digital violence, digital fairness, surveillance). Its AI output questions prevailing AI narratives rather than taking a safety or catastrophic-risk view. The team is eight people.

The Neurorights Foundation (NRF) Adjacent

Nonprofit · New York, USA · founded 2022 · also draws on Living systems

A US nonprofit co-founded by the Columbia neuroscientist Rafael Yuste, the human-rights lawyer Jared Genser and Jamie Daves, and run by Executive Director Stephen Damianos. It campaigns for mental privacy, mental identity, free will, fair access to mental augmentation and protection from bias. Its main concern is neurotechnology whose neural data generative AI can increasingly decode. It has backed neural-data laws in Colorado, California and Montana, constitutional changes in Chile and Mexico, and a 2022 UN Human Rights Council resolution. It advised on the US MIND Act (Sept 2025), and in 2024 published a review of consumer neurotech companies' data practices.

It works on the legal frontier where AI meets direct access to human minds, using a human-rights-law method for cognitive liberty that AI-safety work on manipulation and mental autonomy has barely touched. Its model laws are templates that could extend from neural data to other forms of mind inference.

Works on Human minds, Justice · Key work Safeguarding Brain Data: Assessing the Privacy Practices of Consumer Neurotechnology Companies (2024); Expert consultation on the US MIND Act (Schumer, Cantwell, Markey) (2025); Industry accountability workshop and consumer neurotech scorecard at Asilomar for the Brain and Mind (2026) · Get involved 'Get Involved' page on its website (donations, participation); Internships: the staff page lists a current intern cohort (no open call found)

Note Its subject is neurotechnology governance; AI comes in as the technology that makes neural decoding possible. Per the roster, it does not yet address chatbots' cognitive or emotional effects. The founding year is the IRS ruling year (2022); the founders worked on neurorights earlier through Columbia.

The Pranava Institute Adjacent

Nonprofit · New Delhi, India · founded 2020 · also draws on Arts, futures, Psychology

A New Delhi think tank on emerging technology, policy and society, founded in 2020 by Shyam Krishnakumar and Titiksha Vashist, that works from what it calls an 'India-first' perspective. Its 'Feeling Automated' project, whose report launched in February 2026, studies the legal and societal side of social AI (companions and emotionally responsive chatbots). It combined a literature review, multi-stakeholder consultations and tests of selected systems using personas designed with psychologists, then made policy and design recommendations. Other work includes 'Design Beyond Deception', a manual on dark patterns for designers; a responsible-AI fitness check for India's public sector; the Youth Digital Cultures Lab and its Youth for Tech Futures Fellowship; and tech-geopolitics reports.

It brings an Indian, design-aware view of manipulation by companion and emotional AI (addictive design, deceptive anthropomorphism, sycophancy and emotional dependency) and ties dark-patterns practice to regulation, a perspective from outside the US and UK.

Works on Human minds, Justice · Key work Feeling Automated: Ethical Development of Emotional & Interactive AI Systems (report and panel) (2026); Design Beyond Deception: a manual of ethical UI/UX principles against deceptive design; Youth Digital Cultures Lab and Youth for Tech Futures Fellowship (with the University of Leeds) (2026) · Get involved Its careers page lists a Research Analyst (Technology Policy) opening; Youth for Tech Futures Fellowship: first cohort 2025–26, ten fellows aged 18–27 from across India, paid stipend; Mailing list and events, including India AI Impact Summit sessions

Note It is a small team (LinkedIn lists 2–10 employees). Besides research it offers advisory and foresight to organisations entering the Indian market. Its site doesn't state its legal form, and LinkedIn lists it as 'Privately Held', so it may not be a nonprofit. Independent coverage is thin; most details come from its own website and LinkedIn. Its social-AI work is framed around present harms and user safety, not catastrophic risk.

The University of Osaka Research Center on Ethical, Legal and Social Issues (ELSI Center) Adjacent

Academic · Suita (Osaka), Japan · founded 2020 · also draws on Philosophy, Safety science

An interdisciplinary university centre, set up in April 2020, that studies the ethical, legal and social issues (ELSI) of emerging technologies. It works through three divisions: general, practice (industry co-creation) and collaborative (public engagement). Its AI work includes a Value and Privacy Impact Assessment (VPIA) process used for data at Expo 2025 Osaka, an AI risk-assessment methodology developed with the Japanese Standards Association, generative-AI risk assessments with Mitsubishi Electric, and studies of public values on AI in healthcare. It publishes the ELSI NOTE series, whose recent notes cover AI child-abuse risk assessment and the governance of AI agents (No. 77, September 2026), and it is a partner in the Horizon Europe AIOLIA project on operationalising AI ethics.

It offers a worked Japanese model for building humanities and social-science review into R&D together with companies and standards bodies, from impact-assessment processes to risk-assessment methods. Its September 2026 note on keeping governance in step with AI agents shows it beginning to engage with agentic systems.

Works on Assurance, Justice · Key work ELSI NOTE No. 77: 'Can governance keep up with AI agents? Redesigning harnesses and human involvement' (in Japanese) (2026); VPIA: Value and Privacy Impact Assessment for responsible data use at Expo 2025 Osaka (ELSI NOTE 65) (2025); Developing a risk-assessment methodology and implementation process for AI, with the Japanese Standards Association (2025) · Get involved Vacancy: specially appointed assistant professor or researcher, Practice Research Division (posted 29 Sep 2026); Autumn 2026 seminar series (13 Oct–17 Nov); ELSI Forum, which connects companies and academia on ELSI

Note Most output is in Japanese, and the English site lags behind the Japanese one, which lists ELSI NOTE No. 77. Much of its AI work is co-created with and funded by companies, which raises questions about independence. It is one of several university ELSI centres set up in Japan's recent 'ELSI boom'.

UN Human Rights (OHCHR) B-Tech Project Adjacent

Programme · Geneva, Switzerland · founded 2019

A project of the UN Human Rights Office (OHCHR), launched in 2019, that applies the UN Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights to digital technology. It publishes guidance on human-rights due diligence, business models, remedy and a 'smart mix' of regulation. It runs a Community of Practice of large tech companies and a Peer Learning Platform with regional strands in Africa, Asia and Latin America. Its generative-AI project published a taxonomy of human-rights harms across the AI value chain in 2023, and in July 2026 it launched a one-year workstream with BSR on building human-rights due diligence into AI product development.

It applies established legal machinery to foundation-model developers: value-chain responsibility, due diligence, remedy and regulatory 'smart mix'. That gives AI-safety governance a template backed by UN legitimacy and a working channel to the companies. In September 2026 the High Commissioner began addressing frontier AI directly.

Works on Justice, Assurance · Key work Generative AI foundational papers, including a Taxonomy of Generative AI Human Rights Harms (2023); AI product design workstream with BSR: human-rights due diligence in AI product development (2026); 2026 B-Tech Survey on AI and Human Rights (2026) · Get involved B-Tech newsletter (archive on Mailchimp; most recent issue July 2026); Tech companies can join the Company Community of Practice; OHCHR publishes an FAQ on joining; Periodic calls for input, such as the 2026 B-Tech Survey on AI and Human Rights for industry experts

Note The OHCHR site blocks automated access, so the project description comes from an archived copy and from its newsletters. Staff leads and donors were not confirmed. The September 2026 frontier-AI statement came from the High Commissioner, not from B-Tech itself. If OHCHR builds a standing frontier-AI line on top of B-Tech, this entry would move to bridge.

UNESCO Ethics of AI programme (Recommendation on the Ethics of AI, Global Forum on the Ethics of AI) Adjacent

Programme · Paris, France · founded 2021 · also draws on Philosophy

UNESCO's AI-ethics work, based in its Social and Human Sciences sector, centres on the 2021 Recommendation on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence, adopted by all 193 member states. Tools that came out of the Recommendation include a Readiness Assessment Methodology (more than 70 countries have used it or are using it), an Ethical Impact Assessment, and the Global AI Ethics and Governance Observatory with its country profiles. It also runs expert and peer networks: Women4Ethical AI, AI Ethics Experts Without Borders, a Global Network of AI Supervisory Authorities, a civil-society and academia network, and a coalition on linguistic diversity. Since 2022 it has held a Global Forum on the Ethics of AI; the fourth was in Riyadh from 14 to 17 September 2026.

It is the only AI-ethics instrument every UNESCO member state has adopted, and one of the few global AI norms that names environmental and ecosystem flourishing, and cultural and linguistic diversity, as values. Its readiness assessments give it working channels into ministries across the Majority World, which AI-safety policy work rarely reaches.

Works on Justice, Assurance · Key work Recommendation on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence (2021); Readiness Assessment Methodology (RAM, now RAM 2.0), used by more than 70 countries (2023); Global AI Ethics and Governance Observatory · Get involved Global Forum on the Ethics of AI: the 4th edition was in Riyadh, 14–17 Sep 2026, with public livestreams; Civil-society organisations and academics can join UNESCO's Global Civil Society Organizations and Academic Network on AI Ethics and Policy; Women4Ethical AI platform and the AI Ethics Experts Without Borders roster

Note The Recommendation is non-binding soft law, so implementation depends on each member state and is uneven. The United States announced its withdrawal from UNESCO in July 2025. The programme's framing is human rights and present harms; 'AI safety' appeared in 2026 only as one forum topic among many. The work also extends to neurotechnology, under a separate 2025 Recommendation.

WASP-HS (Wallenberg AI, Autonomous Systems and Software Program – Humanity and Society) Adjacent

Funder · Umeå, Sweden · also draws on Democracy, Philosophy

Sweden's largest research programme on AI and society, funded by the Wallenberg Foundations as the humanities and social-science counterpart to the WASP engineering programme. It funds nine multi-university research environments (among them AI, Power and Politics; The AI Welfare State; The Rule of AI; Child Development in the Age of AI; Agentic AI for Humanistic Futures), a graduate school with over 100 PhD students from 19 Swedish universities, guest professorships, and postdoctoral scholarships at MIT and Stanford.

It provides large, long-term humanities and social-science funding on AI, with themes on power, the welfare state and agentic AI that overlap with gradual-disempowerment concerns. Its 100+ PhD students are a pipeline of social scientists and humanists who know AI.

Works on Power, Democracy, Justice · Key work AI, Power and Politics research environment (Stockholm, Umeå, Uppsala, KTH, Gothenburg and others); Agentic AI for Humanistic Futures research environment; Six postdoctoral scholarships at MIT and Stanford (2026) · Get involved Postdoctoral scholarships at MIT (4) and Stanford (2) for Swedish PhD holders, deadline 16 Nov 2026; Project Initiation Grants (open) and Research Initiation Grants for Data-Driven Life Sciences and Society (deadline 4 Nov 2026); Conference 'Digital Sovereignty in the Age of AI', 8–9 Oct 2026; 'Food for Thought' talks

Note Founding year and total budget are not shown on the current site; it is generally reported as launched around 2019, unconfirmed here. Umeå as host is inferred from its newsletter infrastructure. Funding and positions are mostly restricted to Swedish universities and Swedish PhD holders. It has no safety or catastrophic-risk framing.

Weizenbaum Institute (Weizenbaum-Institut e.V.) Adjacent

Academic · Berlin, Germany · founded 2017 · also draws on Democracy, Economics

A Berlin research institute on the networked society, founded in 2017 as a consortium of FU, HU, TU and UdK Berlin, the University of Potsdam, WZB and Fraunhofer FOKUS. It is funded by the federal research ministry and the State of Berlin. Its four focus areas cover digital technologies in society, platform markets and public spheres, organising knowledge (including a 'Working with Artificial Intelligence' group) and digital infrastructures in democracy. Recent AI work covers generative AI and society, democratic control of AI and gendered disinformation, and it continues Joseph Weizenbaum's tradition of computer criticism.

It brings STS, communication science and labour sociology to questions of who controls AI and what it does to democracy and the public sphere. It also offers a critical view of industry narratives, such as its Sept 2026 analysis of the interests behind calls to slow AI, which the safety field rarely examines. It is a large, well-funded research hub in Berlin, close to int/a's community there.

Works on Democracy, Power, Epistemics · Key work Weizenbaum Conference 2026: 'Generative AI and Society: What is at stake?' (2026); Workshop 'The Rulers and the Commons: AI and the Question of Democratic Control' with Cecilia Rikap (23 Oct 2026) (2026); '60 years of ELIZA, 50 years of computer criticism' programme (2026) · Get involved Weizenbaum Conference (annual; 2026 edition on generative AI and society, 10-11 Jun 2026); Public lectures, book presentations and workshops in Berlin (e.g. Distinguished Lecture by Zizi Papacharissi, 16 Sep 2026)

Note Its stance on AI is critical and sociological; it does not use catastrophic-risk framing, and some of its analysis is sceptical of industry calls to slow AI. The 'large' scale is inferred from its budget and 21 research groups in the setup phase. Funding figures after 2025 were not confirmed.

Welsh Language Commissioner (Comisiynydd y Gymraeg) Adjacent

Public body · Caernarfon, UK · founded 2012

The statutory regulator for the Welsh language, created under the Welsh Language (Wales) Measure 2011 and operating since April 2012. It enforces Welsh language standards on public bodies and other organisations in Wales. In July 2025 it published a regulatory policy statement on AI. Organisations that use AI to deliver services must still meet their Welsh-language duties, test AI systems specifically in Welsh and be transparent about how those systems work. They must also follow principles of linguistic fairness, accuracy and naturalness of language, and data security. The Commissioner calls this a precautionary approach.

It is a working template for holding AI deployment to a minority-language rights regime. It works through existing statutory duties rather than new AI law, which shows how a rights regulator can extend its remit to AI without waiting for AI-specific legislation.

Works on Justice, Assurance · Key work Artificial intelligence and the Welsh language: the Welsh Language Commissioner's regulatory policy statement (2025); Managing AI within Welsh language standards (announcement and National Eisteddfod panel) (2025); Response to inquiry on artificial intelligence and the Welsh economy (2024)

Note The AI policy is a single regulatory statement (July 2025) with no announced follow-up found, though it binds every organisation subject to Welsh language standards. The roster placed it in Cardiff; the headquarters is in Caernarfon.

WITNESS Adjacent

Nonprofit · Brooklyn, New York, USA · founded 1992 · also draws on Democracy

WITNESS is a human-rights organisation founded in 1992 by Peter Gabriel. It trains and supports people to use video as evidence of abuses. About 30 staff work on five continents from a Brooklyn base. Its AI programme, 'Prepare, Don't Panic' (since 2018), runs a Deepfakes Rapid Response Force (since 2023) and the TRIED benchmark for AI-detection tools (2025). It co-chairs the C2PA provenance coalition's Threats and Harms task force. In September 2026 it launched a regional rapid-response force in Brazil with Brazilian fact-checkers and Unicamp's Recod.ai, and published lessons on verification from the Nepal floods.

It brings threat models and verification practice from the people most exposed to AI-enabled information attacks, human-rights defenders and journalists, many of them in the Majority World. It also feeds that knowledge into provenance standards and detection benchmarks that the AI field relies on.

Works on Epistemics, Justice · Key work Prepare, Don't Panic: deepfakes and generative AI programme (2018); Deepfakes Rapid Response Force (2023); TRIED (Truly Innovative and Effective AI Detection) benchmark (2025) · Get involved Staff roles (careers page); Journalists and fact-checkers can escalate suspected deepfakes to the Rapid Response Force

Note Most of its work is human-rights video practice in general; AI is one of three priority areas. It frames AI as a matter of present harms and trust, not catastrophic risk.

Potential ring 8

Center for Genetics and Society (CGS) Potential

Nonprofit · Berkeley, USA · founded 2001

A Berkeley-area nonprofit, founded in 2001 by Richard Hayes and Marcy Darnovsky. It works to put social justice, human rights and democratic governance at the centre of debates on human genetic and reproductive technologies: heritable genome editing, assisted reproduction and the resurgence of eugenics. It runs the Missing Voices Initiative on heritable genome editing, an anti-eugenics network of scholars and advocates, the Surrogacy360 resource and an assisted-reproduction working group of 150+ members. It publishes the Biopolitical Times blog and a monthly newsletter, and is a fiscally sponsored project of Tides Center.

It has two decades of civil-society experience pressing for democratic limits on a powerful technology, notably against heritable human genome editing. It also tracks the eugenic and transhumanist ideas that run through some AI-future visions. Its AI commentary is occasional and sceptical of x-risk narratives.

Works on Justice, Democracy, Power · Key work Is AI the End of the World as We Know It? (Pete Shanks, Biopolitical Times) (2026); Missing Voices Initiative on heritable genome editing; Confronting Eugenics to Build a Just Future · Get involved Door to open: no AI programme yet; its anti-eugenics and Missing Voices networks are the natural point of contact; Monthly newsletter, Biopolitical News & Views; Webinars and events on human biotechnology (not AI-specific)

Note Its AI output is light and mostly reposted news plus occasional commentary. That commentary criticises 'AI doomer' narratives as a distraction from concrete harms and corporate power, so it would be a critical partner. The core staff is very small (executive director, coordinator, intern, plus fellows and consultants). The site's address is not stated; the location comes from the roster and its 510 (East Bay) phone number.

Committee on the Anthropology of Science, Technology and Computing (CASTAC), American Anthropological Association Potential

Programme · Distributed · founded 1991

A committee of the American Anthropological Association's General Anthropology Division for anthropologists who study science, technology and computing. It was founded in 1991 as the Committee for the Anthropology of Computing. It runs the Platypus blog (since 2012, about 30 contributing editors), the Platypod podcast, the Assemblage member directory, mentorship, AAA Annual Meeting sessions, and the Diana Forsythe and David Hakken prizes. Its AI output is occasional: tagged Platypus essays such as 'Automating Language, Losing Relationality: Feminist Reflections on African Language AI' (Jul 2026) and 'The Kids Are AI-right' (Aug 2026), and a 2026 series, 'An African Studies Approach to AI'.

It is the organised home of US anthropologists of computing, the community best equipped to do fieldwork on AI labs, AI-safety cultures and everyday AI use. Platypus is an open venue for that work.

Works on Justice, Human minds · Key work Series: An African Studies Approach to AI (Platypus) (2026); Automating Language, Losing Relationality: Feminist Reflections on African Language AI (Mpho Primus, Siri Lamoureaux) (2026); Platypus blog, AI tag · Get involved Join the CASTAC mailing list and the Assemblage directory; Pitch a Platypus post (1,200-1,800 words; open submissions); Attend CASTAC-organised sessions at the AAA Annual Meeting

Note A volunteer-run committee with no budget or staff found. AI is one topic among many, and no CASTAC work on AI safety or AI-lab cultures was found.

Deutsches Museum Research Institute (Forschungsinstitut für Technik- und Wissenschaftsgeschichte) Potential

Academic · Munich, Germany · also draws on Philosophy

The research institute of the Deutsches Museum in Munich, a Leibniz research museum. It works on the history of science, technology and the environment, collection-based and education research, conservation science and digital projects. Two DFG-funded projects in its digital-technology strand touch AI. One is a feminist revision of the ethics of autonomous vehicles (Liliia Zemnukhova). The other, 'Artificial Vision at Work' (2024 to 2027), is a history of how human vision became an information-processing problem and was automated at work. Since January 2026 it has also hosted the Munich office of 'Edition Wissenschaftliche Software', a 21-year academy project to archive and edit scientific software from 1950 to 2010.

It offers a historian's long view of safety-critical automation, a feminist-epistemology analysis of how ethics enters autonomous-vehicle engineering, long-term archival care for software, and a major museum's public reach. None of this is yet framed around advanced-AI safety.

Works on Values, Power · Key work Feministische Revision einer Ethik der autonomen Fahrzeuge (DFG); Artificial Vision at Work (DFG, Jun 2024 to Jun 2027) (2024); Edition Wissenschaftliche Software, Munich office (2026 to 2046) (2026) · Get involved Scholar-in-residence programme: stipends with apartments, plus senior-researcher and guest-scientist routes; Door to open: no AI-safety programme yet; approach the digital-technology researchers directly

Note Its AI work is two individual research projects in a large history-of-technology institute, which puts it on the boundary between potential and adjacent. Research leadership is currently acting. Most of the site is in German, and the institute's founding date is not stated on it.

European Association for the Study of Science and Technology (EASST) Potential

Membership body · Distributed · founded 1981

Europe's learned society for science and technology studies (STS), founded in 1981 and registered as an association in the Netherlands. It holds a biennial conference (jointly with 4S every four years), publishes the open-access EASST Review and, with the Finnish STS association, the journal Science & Technology Studies, and gives awards and small EASST Fund grants. EASST2026 (Kraków, 8-11 Sept 2026, 'More Than Now: Exploring resilient futures') had at least 13 AI panels, including 'The politics of machine learning (ML) evaluation', 'Ground truths and the epistemology of AI' and 'AI cold war and AI nationalism between signals, sovereignty, and imagination'.

STS has well-developed methods for studying how evaluations, benchmarks, 'ground truth' and stories about the future actually work in practice. AI safety depends on all of these and rarely examines them. EASST is the European entry point to the people who use those methods.

Works on Epistemics, Assurance · Key work EASST2026 conference, Kraków: 'More Than Now: Exploring resilient futures' (2026); EASST Fund: Iberoamerican Imaginaries of Technology and Artificial Intelligence symposium (University of Oviedo, 29 May 2026) (2026); EASST Review, Volume 45(1) (2026) · Get involved Join as a member (gives access to the EASST Fund and member rates); Attend the biennial conference; EASST2026 was in Kraków, Sep 2026; Apply to the EASST Fund for workshops and community-building projects

Note The AI panels are proposed by members through the open call. EASST itself has no AI programme or position, and the panels are largely critical of mainstream AI discourse. The roster's count of 16 AI panels could not be reproduced; 13 were found by title.

Future Generations Commissioner for Wales Potential

Public body · Cardiff, United Kingdom · founded 2015 · also draws on Arts, futures

An independent statutory office created by the Well-being of Future Generations (Wales) Act 2015 to act as a guardian for people not yet born. It monitors and advises Welsh public bodies on their legal duty to consider long-term effects, runs Section 20 reviews (the 2026 energy review, Project Ynni), publishes a Future Generations Report every five years and offers futures tools and a leadership academy. Derek Walker has been Commissioner since March 2023.

It is a working legal mechanism that obliges public bodies to weigh long-term and intergenerational effects, with an independent office that reviews and reports on them. That is a ready template for statutory long-term impact assessment of AI adoption by governments, and for representing future generations in AI governance, neither of which exists today.

Works on Metacrisis · Key work Future Generations Report 2025 (2025); Section 20 Review: Project Ynni (energy) (2026); A Year of Impact, Powering Change (annual report 2025-26) (2026) · Get involved No AI programme: a door to open for anyone proposing long-term impact assessment of AI in Welsh public bodies; Cymru Can monthly newsletter; Hwb Dyfodol futures hub (over 90 members, mostly from Welsh public bodies)

Note No AI work found: the 2025 Future Generations Report and the 2025-26 annual report do not mention AI, and site searches for AI, automation and technology returned nothing (the site search looks weak, so absence rests mainly on those two reports). Its 2026 priorities are climate, energy, inequality, health and food. Budget and staff numbers were not found.

Histories of Artificial Intelligence: A Genealogy of Power (Mellon Sawyer Seminar, Cambridge HPS) PotentialDormant

Programme · Cambridge, UK · also draws on Indigenous, Philosophy

An 18-month Mellon Sawyer Seminar in the University of Cambridge's Department of History and Philosophy of Science. It examined the history of AI and its ties to politics, power and control through four threads: hidden labour, encoded behaviour, disingenuous rhetoric and cognitive injustice. It ran a reading group, methods and critical-issues training, community research seminars, 14 fellowships and research awards, a virtual summer school (July 2021) and a winter symposium (December 2021). It published a model graduate syllabus and a community bibliography.

Its syllabus, bibliography and network of AI historians are a ready resource for anyone writing a history of AI-risk ideas or testing the field's assumptions against a longer view of whom AI has served. The seminar has ended, so this is a resource rather than a partner.

Works on Justice, Power, Epistemics · Key work Model Syllabus v1 (Penn, Charbonneau, Moran); Community bibliography v1 (2020); Winter Symposium, Homerton College (2021) · Get involved The site lists a mailing list and a Slack channel; whether they are still active is unknown

Note Closed: no activity after the 2023 BJHS Themes special issue, and the site does not give a start date. It stays in for its reusable outputs and network; drop it if the map lists only live organisations. Some organisers have moved institutions (e.g. Stephanie Dick).

Library Futures (NYU Engelberg Center on Innovation Law & Policy) Potential

Programme · New York, USA · founded 2021 · also draws on Economics

A library-rights initiative, set up as a nonprofit in January 2021, that has been a project of NYU Law's Engelberg Center since September 2022. It works on digital ownership, library e-lending rights and public access to information through advocacy, legal support and amicus briefs, a funded research network, internships and webinars for librarians. Its AI work is light: a four-part webinar series on machine learning and AI for information professionals (autumn 2025), including a session on resisting vendor AI contracts, and a 2025 piece on AI-generated books reaching library shelves.

Transferable method: legal and policy advocacy for the public's right to own, lend and reach digital knowledge, for example through vendor contract terms and controlled digital lending. The same tools could shape how libraries and other public bodies buy AI tools, and who controls access to knowledge through AI.

Works on Power, Epistemics · Key work Machine Learning and Artificial Intelligence for Information Professionals (four-part webinar series) (2025); Can libraries stop AI slop from flooding their shelves? (Jennie Rose Halperin) (2025); 2026 Research Network Grants (2026) · Get involved Webinars and professional education for librarians (autumn 2026 series); Annual internship cohorts; Research Network grants for independent scholars

Note AI is a side topic. Its focus is e-book licensing, digital ownership and library lending, and its AI framing leans critical of vendors and hype. Halperin's title is from a 2024 post and Courtney's role from the 2022 announcement; neither was confirmed for 2026.

Society for Social Studies of Science (4S) Potential

Membership body · Distributed · founded 1975

The main international learned society for science and technology studies, founded in 1975 and incorporated as a 501(c)(3) nonprofit in Virginia. It publishes Science, Technology, & Human Values and the open-access journal Engaging Science, Technology, and Society, runs the Backchannels blog, prizes and small Global Outreach grants, and holds an annual meeting. The 2026 meeting (Toronto, 7-10 Oct, 'TechnoPower · Technoscientific Futures', sold out) has 26 of 244 accepted open panels with 'AI' or 'artificial intelligence' in the title (31 counting machine learning, algorithms and generative models), among them 'Polycentric Futures: Governing AI Beyond Monocentric Control' and 'Contesting AI Futures'. A plenary includes a talk on how AI is framed, including existential-risk discourse.

4S is the largest gathering of scholars trained to study how sciences make knowledge, claims and futures. They could study AI-safety communities, evaluations and forecasts the way STS has studied physics, biomedicine and climate science, and serve as reflexive critics and collaborators.

Works on Power, Epistemics, Democracy · Key work 4S 2026 Toronto meeting: 'TechnoPower · Technoscientific Futures' (accepted open panels list) (2026); Science, Technology, & Human Values (journal); Engaging Science, Technology, and Society (open-access journal) · Get involved Attend the annual meeting; Toronto, 7-10 Oct 2026, has a hybrid option; Join as a member; Apply for Global Outreach small grants (members; the 2026 deadline was 26 Jul, with applicants from Africa, Asia, Latin America and Eastern Europe encouraged)

Note The AI panels are proposed by members; 4S has no society-level AI programme. Much of the AI content is critical of tech power and of AI hype, and only a little of it engages with AI-safety concerns on their own terms.

Society & institutions · 60 organisations · 3 on the classic map

Economics, labour & commons

Economics brings five things to making AI go well: the political economy of power concentration and lock-in, the economics of transformative AI (windfalls, public finance, labour markets), institutional designs for commons, cooperatives and public AI, organised labour, and the macroprudential toolkit that financial supervisors use to watch whole systems of correlated agents. The map has 56 organisations with economics as their home tradition (6 core, 8 bridge, 40 adjacent, 2 potential), and another 62 draw on it as a secondary tradition, including core groups such as Forethought, ACS Research, MAI, AOI and FLF. The main actors are unions (17 labour entries), commons and public-AI groups (17), financial-stability bodies (5 of the 8 bridge entries) and a small x-risk cluster on power concentration (Formation Research, Longview Power RFP, Post-AGI Workshop). The tradition sits well away from the core: 40 of the 56 are adjacent, 35 work by pushing ideas into institutions, only 2 use a catastrophic or existential framing (Convergence Analysis, KIRA Center), and just 3 are on the aisafety.com map.

What is missing. Nothing on the map carries economics into the AI systems themselves or into the agent economies now being built. The Economics × Agency, values and AI moral status cells are empty, only 2 of 56 entries tag multi-agent AI, and the map has no competition authority, industrial-organisation (IO) economist or market-design group, even though LLM pricing agents already collude in experiments and companies are building agent payment rails.

Openings here Central-bank systemic-risk methods for frontier AI: secondments and a joint stress test; Open catastrophe scenarios for correlated foundation-model failure, led by actuaries; Competition economists and regulators as monitors of AI agent markets; Wire Indigenous consent labels into AI training-data pipelines; Model safety clauses for collective agreements at labs and data suppliers

Core ring 6

Convergence Analysis CoreOn aisafety.com

Nonprofit · Distributed · founded 2017 · also draws on Arts, futures, Peace

Nonprofit research organisation founded in 2017 by David Kristoffersson and Justin Shovelain as an existential-risk strategy collaboration. It relaunched in 2024 with a team of about ten, focused on AI scenario and governance research. Its economics work includes: - Threshold 2030: a November 2024 convening of 30 economists, policy experts and forecasters, with a report in February 2025. - The AGI Social Contract essay series, edited by Deric Cheng from April 2025, with contributors including Anton Korinek and Seth Lazar. - Fellowship papers on the AI workforce and on AI and corporate personhood. It also publishes on US-China AI security. In August 2026 it released the AI Readiness Objectives, a framework that sorts about 400 AI-security interventions under seven goals for governments.

It brings economists, forecasters and legal scholars into questions of post-labour economics, wealth distribution and AI legal personhood. It uses worldbuilding and forecasting alongside policy analysis.

Works on Power, Epistemics, Security · Key work Threshold 2030: Modeling AI Economic Futures (convening Nov 2024, report Feb 2025) (2025); Forging a New AGI Social Contract (essay series) (2025); AI and Corporate Personhood: A Comparative Analysis (2025) · Get involved Convergence Fellowship: 12-week team research programme with AI Economic Policy and International Security tracks. Outputs from the 2025 cohort are on the site; no 2026 call found; Newsletter signup on convergenceanalysis.org; AGI Social Contract Substack

Note Its location and funders are not stated, and the most recent report asks for funding. Its 2026 output is security policy, not economics, so the economics strand found by discovery may be less active than in 2025. It relaunched in 2024 after an earlier phase of broad x-risk strategy work. It is the fiscal sponsor of Modeling Cooperation.

Formation Research CoreOn aisafety.comNew

Nonprofit · UK · founded 2025

UK not-for-profit company, founded in 2025 by Alfie Lamerton. It researches lock-in, meaning ways AI could make a distribution of power or values effectively permanent, and works on interventions against it. Its 2025 LessWrong sequence set out lock-in threat models. In 2026 it published a survey of AI-driven power concentration and an empirical paper showing that a narrowly trained secret loyalty in Qwen models evades black-box audits. A $2.15m Coefficient Giving grant, announced in Sep 2026, funds two years of work, starting with model organisms of secretly loyal AI and alignment audits to detect them.

It turns a political-economy concern, entrenchment and illegitimate concentration of power, into testable technical work. That gives labs and auditors concrete defences against AI-enabled power grabs.

Works on Power, Assurance · Key work Lock-In (LessWrong sequence: definitions, threat models, interventions) (2025); A Survey of AI-Driven Power Concentration (2026); Narrow Secret Loyalty Dodges Black-Box Audits (2026) · Get involved Register interest in technical research roles (hiring after the Sep 2026 grant); Newsletter signup on formationresearch.org

Note Young and small. The team page lists only the founder, plus trustees and advisers who work at Anthropic, Thinking Machines, DeepMind and Meta. Its current technical programme (model organisms and alignment audits) is close to mainstream alignment work. What sets it outside the canon is the lock-in and power-concentration framing, not a new discipline. Its UK city is not stated.

KIRA Center (Zentrum für KI-Risiken & -Auswirkungen) Core

Nonprofit · Berlin, Germany · founded 2023

An independent Berlin think tank (a non-profit gUG) that works 'to make AI go well', founded by its executive director Daniel Privitera. Its first outputs date from April 2023. Its focus areas are safety, competitiveness and sovereignty. Privitera was Lead Writer of the International AI Safety Report 2025 and Special Adviser to the Chair for the 2026 edition, on which Philip Fox was a core writer; KIRA also contributed to the Safety and Security chapter of the EU General-Purpose AI Code of Practice. Other outputs include a report on AI compute in Germany (October 2025), which it says informed the national data centre strategy, and an op-ed arguing for a German AI Security Institute (March 2025).

For int/a's Berlin hub it is the main local policy organisation that takes frontier-AI risk seriously, with direct lines into EU and German policy. It brings economic analysis of AGI preparedness and compute to the debate. It is not interdisciplinary in the integral sense.

Works on Assurance, Power, Epistemics · Key work International AI Safety Report 2026 (Privitera Special Adviser to the Chair; Philip Fox core writer) (2026); International AI Safety Report 2025 (Privitera Lead Writer; Fox writer) (2025); AI Compute in Germany (2025) · Get involved Occasional public events in Berlin (e.g. the AI and State Capacity panel with Bertelsmann Stiftung, 17 Mar 2026); No job openings listed on the site

Note Mostly conventional AI policy and economics. It is included because it is the main x-risk-aware policy organisation in int/a's Berlin hub, not for an integral bent. Recent outputs, such as the 2025 FAZ op-ed 'Germany Should Take AGI Seriously', frame AGI mainly through competitiveness and sovereignty. Funders are not disclosed. The site lists only four team members; 2023 as the founding year is inferred from its earliest dated work. Economist Monika Schnitzer (LMU) co-authors several outputs but is not listed as staff.

Longview Philanthropy: Extreme Power Concentration RFP CoreOn aisafety.com

Funder · London, UK · founded 2018 · also draws on Law, society, Peace

Longview Philanthropy was founded in 2018 by Natalie Cargill and is led by CEO Simran Dhaliwal, with offices in London, Washington DC and San Francisco. It advises major donors and runs grant programmes on AI and nuclear risk. Its Extreme Power Concentration RFP opened in May 2026 and closed on 2 July 2026, with proposals assessed on a rolling basis. It offered grants of roughly $100k-$2m a year for 6-18 months, plus career-transition funding, for work on the risk that AI lets a small group gain durable control over everyone else. The twelve priority areas include: - foundational research - AI integrity and secret loyalties - law-following AI - oversight of AI in government - autonomous weapons and mass surveillance - political economy - AI tools that empower citizens - compute in democracies A parallel Digital Minds RFP closed on 24 July 2026.

It is one of the largest funding calls to treat power concentration as a distinct problem. It explicitly invites lawyers, political scientists, economists, national-security veterans and journalists to move into the field, which gives people from adjacent disciplines a direct route in.

Works on Power, Security, Democracy · Key work Request for proposals on extreme power concentration (2026); Request for Proposals: Research and Applied Work on Digital Minds (2026); Frontier AI Fund (2026) · Get involved Extreme Power Concentration RFP: grants and career funding, now closed (deadline 2 July 2026); questions to the RFP inbox; Digital Minds RFP: project grants, research fellowships and career-development fellowships, now closed (deadline 24 July 2026); Staff roles via Longview's careers contact

Note Both 2026 RFPs are closed and no further rounds have been announced. Longview otherwise does not accept unsolicited proposals. Longview Philanthropy is on the aisafety.com map; the RFP is not listed separately. It operates as two entities, a US 501(c)(3) and a UK company limited by guarantee. Its homepage lists Washington DC first among its offices, so its centre of gravity may have moved from London. The roster entry is the RFP, profiled within Longview.

Post-AGI Workshop Series CoreNew

Programme · Distributed · founded 2025 · also draws on Living systems

Workshop series on what stable outcomes that keep humans empowered could look like after AGI. David Duvenaud (University of Toronto) organises it with Raymond Douglas and Jan Kulveit of ACS Research. There have been three editions: Vancouver (July 2025, alongside ICML); San Diego alongside NeurIPS (3 Dec 2025, on post-AGI economics, culture and governance); and Berkeley at Lighthaven (23-24 May 2026, on 'civilizational equilibria'). Speakers have come from ML, economics, philosophy and political science, among them Joe Carlsmith, Richard Ngo, Jacob Steinhardt, Anton Korinek, Iason Gabriel, Paul Christiano, Samuel Hammond, Andrew Critch and Michael Muthukrishna. Attendance is free and by application, and talks are recorded and posted online.

It is one of the few recurring venues where economists and political theorists work with AI-safety researchers on how states and cultures function once human labour is no longer needed. Mainstream alignment work largely leaves that question aside.

Works on Power, Metacrisis · Key work Workshop on Post-AGI Civilizational Equilibria (Lighthaven, Berkeley) (2026); Workshop on Post-AGI Economics, Culture and Governance (San Diego, alongside NeurIPS) (2025); Recorded talks and transcripts from past editions (2025) · Get involved Expression-of-interest form for each edition (attendance is free but selective); Sign up for event updates on post-agi.org; recorded talks are online

Note The roster draft put the first edition at NeurIPS 2024. The series' own site lists Vancouver 2025, and the May 2026 announcement calls Berkeley the third edition, so the series began in 2025. No next edition had been announced by Oct 2026. It is a project of three organisers, not a standing organisation, and funding is not disclosed.

Windfall Trust CoreNew

Nonprofit · Distributed (US-registered 501(c)(3)) · founded 2025 · also draws on Arts, futures

A policy organisation for what it calls 'AI economic preparedness': helping governments plan for transformative AI's effects on jobs, tax bases and the social contract. The Future of Life Institute incubated the idea in 2024 as a proposal for a global trust sharing AI windfall profits, and it became an independent US 501(c)(3) in 2025. Its CEO is Adrian Brown and it has a team of about 15. Its work includes the Windfall Policy Atlas of 40+ policy options (Apr 2026), scenario workshops with economists, the IMF and national partners in the UK, US, Switzerland, Spain and Korea, a 62-country public survey, and the Windfall AI Observatory. The Observatory scores more than 30 countries on their exposure to AI-driven disruption and their capacity to absorb it, and a UK preview was shown at LSE in September 2026.

It works directly on windfall distribution and economic preparedness for transformative AI, a problem the AI-safety field names but rarely staffs. It brings public-finance, welfare-state design and scenario-planning methods, and works with central banks, the IMF and national governments.

Works on Power, Epistemics · Key work Windfall Policy Atlas (2026); Windfall AI Observatory (UK preview at the LSE Global Forum for AI and the Social Sciences) (2026); The Economics of TAI scenario workshop (San Francisco, with Korinek, Brynjolfsson and Agrawal) (2025) · Get involved Staff roles (a 'Hiring' page on its site); Substack newsletter with policy briefs; National working groups and scenario workshops (by invitation)

Note It explicitly distances itself from existential-risk framing and focuses on economic disruption and inequality. It has moved from FLI's original global-trust concept to a broader policy accelerator. OpenAI funding (2026) may raise independence questions, which its published framework addresses. Its headquarters city is not stated. Ring changed from the roster's bridge to core (see tag notes).

Bridge ring 12

Bank for International Settlements (BIS) and Financial Stability Institute (FSI) Bridge

Public body · Basel, Switzerland · founded 1930 · also draws on Safety science

The BIS is owned by member central banks and based in Basel. It has a sustained line of AI analysis for central banks and supervisors. Its 2024 Annual Economic Report chapter argued that shared models, a few dominant providers and cyber attacks could amplify herding, runs and fire sales, and it asked central banks to form a 'community of practice' on AI. The BIS's Financial Stability Institute, which supports supervisors worldwide through policy work and capacity-building, followed with a December 2024 paper on regulating AI in finance and a September 2026 paper on cyber threats from frontier AI.

It turns findings about frontier-AI capabilities into supervisory language for central banks and supervisors around the world, and the FSI's capacity-building carries that framing into national practice. Its 2026 paper argues that frontier AI leaves the foundations of cyber resilience unchanged but greatly raises the speed at which they must be applied. That is a useful counterweight to calls for new AI-specific regimes.

Works on Metacrisis, Security, Power · Key work Artificial intelligence and the economy: implications for central banks (Annual Economic Report 2024, Chapter III) (2024); Regulating AI in the financial sector: recent developments and main challenges (FSI Insights 63) (2024); When machines attack: frontier AI cyber threats and policy responses in the financial sector (FSI Occasional Paper 28) (2026) · Get involved Staff roles at the BIS in Basel (check current openings)

Note Much of the BIS's AI activity, such as Innovation Hub projects and AI tools for central banks, is about adopting AI, not making it safe. Its frontier-AI work is framed as cyber and operational resilience. The FSI was founded in 1998; the BIS in 1930. The FSB, which the BIS hosts, has its own entry.

Bank of England: Financial Policy Committee AI monitoring and AI Consortium Bridge

Public body · London, United Kingdom · founded 1694 · also draws on Safety science

The Bank of England is the UK's central bank, and its Financial Policy Committee treats AI as a risk to financial stability. In April 2025 the committee identified four channels: common weaknesses in widely used models, correlated AI trading, dependence on a few providers, and cyber threats. Its July 2026 Financial Stability Report said rapid progress in frontier AI had significantly raised cyber and operational risks, and flagged stretched AI-related valuations and fast-growing AI credit. With the FCA it runs the AI Consortium, a public–private forum that has met regularly since May 2025. In May 2026 it issued a joint statement on frontier AI models and cyber resilience with the FCA and HM Treasury.

It is one of the few central banks to build frontier-AI capabilities into its systemic-risk assessment and to set supervisory expectations on them. Its surveillance methods (surveys, market intelligence, stress testing) are a template for watching AI risk across a whole sector. It is in London.

Works on Metacrisis, Security · Key work Financial Stability in Focus: Artificial intelligence in the financial system (2025); AI Consortium (with the Financial Conduct Authority) (2025); Joint statement on frontier AI models and cyber resilience (with the FCA and HM Treasury) (2026) · Get involved Staff roles at the Bank of England in London (check current openings); AI Consortium: a public–private forum of firms and observers, run with the FCA; contact details are on the Consortium page

Note Its subject is risk to financial stability, and its frontier-AI concern is framed mainly as cyber and operational resilience. The AI Consortium is also meant to support AI adoption. The Financial Policy Committee dates from 2013; the Bank itself from 1694.

Economics of Transformative AI Initiative (EconTAI), University of Virginia BridgeNew

Academic · Charlottesville, USA · founded 2025

A University of Virginia research centre, launched in August 2025, that studies how AI matching or exceeding human ability would change growth, labour markets, inequality and public finance. Anton Korinek and Lee Lockwood lead it, with Basil Halperin as faculty adviser. It publishes papers on AI take-off, the automation of research and taxation under transformative AI, and co-organises scenario-planning workshops with the IMF, the Windfall Trust and the Stanford Digital Economy Lab.

It is one of the few academic economics groups that takes transformative AI as a premise. It works out practical consequences that AI-safety policy rarely models, for example what happens to the tax base and public finances if labour income collapses. Its scenario workshops bring together labs, labour, the IMF and civil society to plan for more than one possible 2030.

Works on Power, Epistemics · Key work Public Finance in the Age of AI: A Primer (Korinek and Lockwood, Brookings) (2026); Measuring the AI Economy (Korinek and McKelvey, PIIE working paper) (2026); Scenario Planning Workshop on Global Economic and Financial Implications of AI (co-organised with the IMF, with Windfall Trust) (2025) · Get involved Newsletter on the site (econtai.org/newsletter.html); No open fellowships, jobs or public events were listed as of Oct 2026. Its workshops have been invitation-only, under the Chatham House Rule.

Note Launched in Aug 2025, so the track record is short. The core team is three economists and the website is sparse. Korinek's CV lists membership of Anthropic's Economic Advisory Council (2025–), which is a possible conflict of interest for work on lab-economy policy. Funding is not disclosed on the site.

Equiano Institute Bridge

Nonprofit · Nairobi, Kenya · founded 2023 · also draws on Law, society

A small research lab, apparently based in Nairobi with a distributed team, that describes itself as working on AI alignment and responsible AI adoption in Africa. Most of its output is policy analysis of how AI capabilities reach Africa and other low- and middle-income countries: the quarterly 'State of AI Diffusion' newsletter (since July 2026), essays on export controls and jurisdiction-bound models, a review of India's AI diffusion charter, and an Interstate AI Policy Playbook (2024). It has also run an 'Evaluations in Residence' call for volunteers to evaluate language models in Sub-Saharan African languages, and has written on ethnographic approaches to AI safety and on benefit sharing.

It treats access to frontier AI, and who gets its benefits, as an AI-governance problem seen from Africa, which mainstream safety debates on export controls and compute governance rarely do. Its argument for ethnographers in AI labs and ethnographic safety studies names a method the field lacks.

Works on Power, Justice · Key work State of AI Diffusion (quarterly newsletter) (2026); Localised AI Models and Centralised Diffusion (2026); Reviewing Progress on Responsible AI Diffusion (India's AI charter) (2026) · Get involved Subscribe to the quarterly State of AI Diffusion newsletter; Evaluations in Residence: an interest form for contributors evaluating language models in Sub-Saharan African languages (posted May 2025)

Note Its self-description ('pioneering research in AI alignment', 'a global leader in AI governance') outruns the visible output, which is mostly diffusion and access policy rather than alignment research. Team roles, legal status and funders are not published, and I found little independent coverage. The site lists outside work, such as a GovAI benefit-sharing brief, next to its own without clear attribution; GovAI's page does not credit Equiano. The founding year comes from its GitHub organisation (created Aug 2023, location Kenya). Its base is ambiguous: the 2025 review names Nairobi as its primary hub (with links to Paris and Oxford), while the homepage foregrounds London ties (London Data Week, an Alan Turing Institute partnership).

European Systemic Risk Board (ESRB) Bridge

Public body · Frankfurt am Main, Germany · founded 2010 · also draws on Safety science

The ESRB is the EU body responsible for macroprudential oversight of the financial system; the European Central Bank in Frankfurt hosts its secretariat. Report No 16 of its Advisory Scientific Committee, 'Artificial intelligence and systemic risk' (December 2025), ranks the AI features that worsen systemic risk: monitoring difficulty, concentration, model uniformity, overreliance, speed and opacity. It proposes responses including stronger circuit breakers, labels on AI use and skin-in-the-game requirements.
