In July 2026 the ESRB issued a formal warning on systemic cyber risks from frontier AI models, after raising its assessment of systemic cyber risk to 'severe'.

It treats AI as a system-level risk and uses formal instruments against it: warnings, recommendations and quarterly risk assessments. Its scientific committee has mapped the specific ways AI can amplify systemic risk and matched them with concrete tools. The report also names possible loss of human control as an amplifier, which is unusual for a financial regulator.

Works on Metacrisis, Security · Key work Artificial intelligence and systemic risk (Advisory Scientific Committee Report No 16) (2025); Warning on systemic cyber risks stemming from frontier AI models (2026)

Note Its frontier-AI action is framed through cyber risk to the financial system. The December 2025 report is by its Advisory Scientific Committee and does not necessarily represent the ESRB's official position. Ring raised from the roster's potential (see tag_notes).

Financial Stability Board (FSB) Bridge

Public body · Basel, Switzerland · founded 2009 · also draws on Safety science

The FSB is the G20 body that coordinates national financial authorities and international standard-setters. The BIS hosts it in Basel. Its AI workstream looks at how AI adoption could create system-wide weaknesses in finance: concentration on a few third-party providers, correlated models, cyber risk and model risk. Its outputs are a 2017 report, a November 2024 report on AI's implications for financial stability, an October 2025 report on monitoring indicators, a June 2026 consultation on 12 sound practices for responsible AI adoption (final report due October 2026 as a G20 deliverable) and the Chair's letter to G20 ministers of 31 August 2026 on cyber risk from frontier models.

It applies the macroprudential toolkit to AI: watching a whole system for concentration, correlation and contagion. It can also put frontier-model risk in front of G20 finance ministers, as it did in August 2026 when its Chair asked authorities to support safe and responsible model release and deployment. Few AI-safety organisations have a channel like that.

Works on Metacrisis, Security, Assurance · Key work The Financial Stability Implications of Artificial Intelligence (2024); Monitoring Adoption of Artificial Intelligence and Related Vulnerabilities in the Financial Sector (2025); Consultation: Sound Practices for the Responsible Adoption of Artificial Intelligence (2026) · Get involved Public consultations on draft standards: the AI sound-practices consultation ran from 10 June to 22 July 2026, and responses are published; Staff roles in the FSB Secretariat in Basel (check current openings)

Note Its subject is risk to the financial system, not AI safety as such. It frames frontier-model concerns mainly as cyber risk. Its standards are not binding; implementation depends on member authorities. The roster entry is the FSB's AI workstream, not a separate unit.

Funding the Commons (FtC) Bridge

Company · San Francisco, USA · founded 2021 · also draws on Democracy

A network that came out of Protocol Labs in 2021 and is now run by Funding the Commons Inc., a Delaware public benefit corporation based in San Francisco. It works on how shared digital infrastructure is funded and governed, through conferences, hackathons, builder residencies, advice to institutions, fundraising campaigns built on mechanisms such as quadratic and retroactive funding, and the Commons Lab incubator. Its tagline is 'Funding, governance, and coordination for the age of AI'.

It brings public-goods economics and mechanism design, the people who build quadratic funding and community treasuries, to the question of 'where the power AI creates ends up'. It also brings crypto and open-source builders into contact with AI-safety funders and speakers.

Works on Power, Democracy · Key work FtC SF 2026: Intelligence at the Frontier (145 sessions, 155 speakers; hackathon track on AI Safety & Evaluation) (2026); El Salvador Fellowship 'Beyond the Pilot', with an 'AI for Public Use' track (2026); Commons Lab incubator: 'coordination infrastructure for the intelligent economy' (2026) · Get involved Funding the Commons Forum, San Francisco, 13-14 Mar 2027 (speaker applications open); Builder residencies and fellowships (El Salvador, Oct 2026), announced via newsletter; Commons Lab: founders apply via commonslab.ai

Note Its roots and much of its community are in crypto and web3 public goods, and its AI work is newer and mixed in with that. It is legally a public benefit corporation, not a charity. Simocracy, linked in the roster draft, has its own roster entry. Its network page lists names such as Audrey Tang, Glen Weyl and Jaan Tallinn; those people are network members and speakers, not staff.

RadicalxChange Foundation (RxC) Bridge

Nonprofit · Distributed (legal address Moraga, California, USA) · founded 2018 · also draws on Democracy

A US 501(c)(3) founded in 2018 by economist Glen Weyl, out of the ideas in the book Radical Markets. It now describes itself as an international nonprofit advancing participatory governance in the age of AI. It designs and pilots mechanisms such as plural (quadratic) voting, partial common ownership and data coalitions. Its AI-related work includes, with OpenMined, network-sourced AI infrastructure that lets news outlets control and price AI access to their reporting, deployed with AMSI's network of more than 500 outlets in Indonesia and with partners in Uruguay and Denmark. In 2026 it joined the coalition behind 'Reverse Alignment', a programme proposed by Glen Weyl and others that argues for redesigning institutions so that societies can absorb AI; RxC contributes on its democracy dimension.

It brings mechanism design and participatory practice to the side of AI safety that most funding ignores: preparing institutions, economies and democracies to receive AI. It also gives communities such as news publishers and faith groups working tools for collective bargaining and a voice over AI.

Works on Democracy, Power, Justice · Key work Reverse Alignment (Noema paper by a coalition of 27 experts; RxC salon 24 Aug 2026) (2026); Federated data bargaining / network-sourced AI for journalism (with OpenMined and IFPIM) (2025); 'Can AI See Me?' side event and Geneva Reflection principles submitted to the UN Global Dialogue on AI Governance (2026) · Get involved Monthly open community call (first Wednesday, 9am ET / 3pm CET); Autonomous local chapters in 30+ cities; Events such as Community Week NYC (May 2026) and online salons

Note A broad movement organisation: much of its work, such as housing and health deliberations, is not about AI. It is associated with crypto (Buterin on the board, plural money pilots) and has received an FTX Future Fund regrant. The leadership changed in 2025, when Jess Scully succeeded Matt Prewitt. Reverse Alignment is a coalition effort, and RxC is one of its contributors.

Stanford Digital Economy Lab Bridge

Academic · Stanford, USA · founded 2020

A research lab at the Stanford Institute for Human-Centered AI, founded in 2020 by Erik Brynjolfsson. It studies how AI changes the economy through four streams: the economics of transformative AI, new measures of the economy (such as the GDP-B welfare metric), digital platforms, and AI agents (the Loyal Agents project with Consumer Reports). In August 2025 it ran a two-week course on the economics of transformative AI, funded by Open Philanthropy, that included sessions on AI safety and existential risk. In July 2026 it organised the 'We Must Act Now' statement from economists and Nobel laureates.

It trains PhD economists in the theory of explosive growth and in weighing existential risk against growth. Its 'Canaries in the Coal Mine' series measures AI's effect on young workers' jobs, which the AI-safety field rarely tracks. Its Loyal Agents work sets duties of loyalty and care for AI agents acting for consumers, an approach to agent alignment taken from law and markets.

Works on Power, Epistemics · Key work Canaries in the Coal Mine? Six Facts about the Recent Employment Effects of AI (revised Aug 2026: 19% employment gap for young workers) (2025); The Economics of Transformative AI summer course (48 participants; lectures on AI safety and existential risk vs growth) (2025); 'We Must Act Now' statement on preparing for AI's economic transformation (2026) · Get involved Postdoctoral, research and fellowship openings on its careers page; Public seminars and research workshops; Corporate affiliate programme

Note Most of the lab's work is mainstream productivity and labour economics. The TAI stream and course are the parts closest to AI safety, and the course is paused in 2026. It has industry ties through its corporate affiliates. Signatory counts for 'We Must Act Now' differ between sources.

Stripe Economics of AI Fellowship BridgeNew

Programme · San Francisco, USA · founded 2025

A fellowship launched by Stripe in March 2025, led by UVA economist Basil Halperin with Stripe's Emily Glassberg Sands. It gives graduate students and early-career economists a grant of at least $10,000, a conference in San Francisco, a community and possible access to Stripe data. It prioritises research on the economics of transformative AI, meaning AI that brings change on the scale of the industrial revolution. The first cohort of 24 fellows was announced in 2025.

It is one of very few pipelines that bring PhD economists into research on transformative AI. Several 2025 fellows work directly on the economic theory of AI safety, AI-driven growth or software-only take-off. That builds economics capacity the AI-safety field otherwise lacks.

Works on Power · Key work 2025 cohort of 24 fellows (e.g. Eric Chen on the economic theory of AI safety, Parker Whitfill, Zach Mazlish, Lindsey Raymond) (2025); Fellows' conference in San Francisco (2025) · Get involved Fellowship for graduate students and early-career researchers (the 2025 round is closed; no 2026 round announced); Contact: basilh@virginia.edu

Note Whether it continues is unclear: no second cohort or 2026 call could be found, and the page still describes the 2025 round. It is a corporate programme, and part of its offer is access to Stripe and customer data. The roster's '15-20 fellows' was the original plan; 24 were selected.

Systemic Risk Centre (SRC), London School of Economics Bridge

Academic · London, United Kingdom · founded 2013

The SRC is a research centre at the London School of Economics, launched in 2013 with ESRC funding, that studies how financial crises arise and how policy should respond. Since 2019 its co-director Jón Danielsson and collaborators have published on AI. They argue that AI amplifies leverage, liquidity stress and opacity through common data, speed and strategic complementarities, so crises become faster and more severe. Their proposed responses are for authorities to build their own AI, set up AI-to-AI communication with private firms, create automated crisis facilities and monitor AI use.

It gives a formal, game-theoretic account of how many interacting AI agents in a market can produce a crisis: a multi-agent risk argument built on long experience of crisis economics. Its proposal that regulators run their own AI and talk directly to firms' AI is a concrete design for oversight at machine speed.

Works on Metacrisis, Multi-agent · Key work Artificial intelligence and systemic risk (Journal of Banking & Finance 140) (2022); Artificial intelligence and financial crises (Journal of Financial Stability 80; SRC Discussion Paper 133) (2025); How financial authorities best respond to AI challenges (opinion piece) (2025)

Note The AI work is mainly by Danielsson and his co-authors, not a centre-wide programme. Its frame is financial crises, not AI safety as such. The site credits UKRI as a funder, but the current grant's terms were not confirmed.

United Tech and Allied Workers (UTAW), with Unite the Union: Google DeepMind recognition campaign Bridge

Membership body · London, UK · founded 2020

UTAW is the UK's tech workers' union, a national branch of the Communication Workers Union (CWU), formed in 2020 by activists from the London Tech Workers Coalition. On 4 May 2026, its members at Google DeepMind UK, together with Unite members, asked Google for voluntary union recognition. Google refused but agreed to talks through ACAS, saying bargaining should cover only pay, holidays and hours. The members' demands cover AI safety and Google's AI principles, an end to what they call unethical military contracts, and guarantees against AI-led redundancies. Membership has passed the 10% threshold for a statutory recognition claim. On 2 October 2026 UTAW published an AI Workers' Inquiry on how generative AI is changing tech work.

It was widely reported as the first union drive at a frontier AI lab. A recognised union could give lab staff a legally backed collective channel to bargain over safety and use policies, protect people who raise concerns, and staff safety committees on the model of health-and-safety representatives.

Works on People, Security, Power · Key work Request for voluntary recognition at Google DeepMind UK (with Unite); ACAS talks since May 2026 (2026); AI Workers' Inquiry: how generative AI is changing work in the tech sector (2026) · Get involved Join UTAW (open to anyone who develops or deploys technology, works for a tech company, or studies or teaches tech): utaw.tech/join; Google DeepMind UK staff can join the recognition campaign and its member surveys; Read and support the AI Workers' Inquiry at techworkersinquiry.org/ai

Note Google has refused voluntary recognition and wants bargaining limited to pay, holidays and hours, so it is uncertain whether safety, military-use or automation clauses can be negotiated. Statutory recognition needs majority support, beyond the 10% already reached. The campaign is driven largely by opposition to Google's contracts with the US and Israeli militaries, a politically contested issue. Unite is a co-applicant, but UTAW and the CWU lead public communications.

Adjacent ring 40

Aapti Institute Adjacent

Nonprofit · Bengaluru, India · also draws on Law, society

A Bengaluru research institute on technology and society, founded by Sarayu Natarajan and co-led by Astha Kapoor. Its Data Economy Lab works on data stewardship and participatory data governance, including data cooperatives and collective models for building AI. Its labour work studies the people behind AI. With Karya it published a code of conduct for data workers (Nov 2025), and with Sigla Research Center and Tech Global Institute it co-founded ATLAS, a research coalition on tech labour in Asia (Oct 2025). In 2026 it published reports on labour exploitation in AI supply chains and comments on India's AI governance guidelines.

It offers Global South institutional designs, namely data cooperatives, collective data stewardship and labour standards for data workers, that spread control over AI's inputs and its rents beyond the US and UK. It also documents the workforce that labels and moderates data for AI, which the safety field rarely sees.

Works on Power, People, Justice · Key work Labour standards for data workers: code of conduct (with Karya) (2025); ATLAS: Alliance for Tech Labour across the South (with Sigla Research Center and Tech Global Institute) (2025); Fragmented Responsibility: Labour Exploitation and Governance Gaps in AI Supply Chains (2026) · Get involved Research staff roles (a team of about 35); Feedback on, and business adoption of, the data-worker code of conduct; Newsletter

Note Its AI work is about present-day labour, data governance and Global South equity, with no safety or catastrophic-risk framing. Much of its portfolio is not about AI (digital public infrastructure, finance, migration, climate). The founding year and overall funders were not confirmed.

AFL-CIO Tech Institute and Workers First Initiative on AI Adjacent

Programme · Washington, DC, USA · founded 2021

The AFL-CIO, the US federation of 65 unions representing about 15 million workers, set up its Tech Institute in 2021 to work on technology in the workplace. In October 2025 the federation launched the 'Workers First Initiative on AI', with the report 'Artificial Intelligence: Principles to Protect Workers', an education and mobilisation programme and a state-level AI task force. In April 2026 President Liz Shuler gave a National Press Club speech on AI, and the Tech Institute sent Congress a letter on AI and workers. The Tech Institute, led by former NLRB chair Lauren McFerran with about a dozen staff, publishes research (for example on electronic shelf labels and grocery wages) and the 'Workers Tech Watch' newsletter.

It is the largest US labour coalition arguing that tech firms cannot be trusted to self-regulate AI, and it brings electoral and state-legislative reach that AI-governance advocates lack. It shows mass-membership organisations entering AI politics, though its frame is workplace harms and economic power, not frontier risk.

Works on Power · Key work Artificial Intelligence: Principles to Protect Workers (2025); Launch of the Workers First Initiative on AI (2025); Liz Shuler's National Press Club speech on AI (2026) · Get involved Workers Tech Watch newsletter (sign-up on the Tech Institute site); Workers join through the federation's affiliated unions

Note Frames AI as a workplace and economic-power issue and does not engage with frontier or catastrophic risk; 'AI safety policy' in its task-force announcement refers to workplace protections. Its approach is explicitly electoral, with AI-focused campaigning planned ahead of the 2026 midterms.

AI Economics Institute (AIEI) AdjacentNew

Public body · London, UK · founded 2026

A joint research unit of HM Treasury and the Department for Science, Innovation and Technology, announced on 8 June 2026 and modelled on the AI Security Institute. It builds data infrastructure and does empirical research on how AI affects UK productivity, labour markets, firms, trade and the distribution of income. It also develops economic models and scenarios to support policy decisions under uncertainty, working with GO-Science, AISI and the Bank of England. It absorbs DSIT's Future of Work Unit and is chaired by Simon Johnson. It does not set policy itself.

It puts modelling of AI's economic scenarios inside a finance ministry, which is where the UK would actually decide how to prepare for large-scale labour displacement. For int/a it is a government counterpart to the safety institutes, covering who gains and who loses in the transition.

Works on Power, Epistemics · Key work Introducing the AI Economics Institute (2026); AI Economics Institute Prospectus (2026) · Get involved Staff roles: enquiries about working for the AIEI go to AIEI@dsit.gov.uk (June 2026); Says it will commission external research in priority areas (no open call found yet); An advisory board drawn from academia, business and labour-market institutions is to be announced

Note It is very new. It has published no research yet, and its director, chief economist and advisory board have not been named. As a government unit it says it will publish only 'selected analysis', and its agenda follows ministers' live policy questions. It is framed around growth and adoption as much as around risk.

AI Now Institute Adjacent

Nonprofit · New York, USA · founded 2017 · also draws on Safety science, Law, society

An independent policy research institute in New York, founded in 2017 by Kate Crawford and Meredith Whittaker (originally partnered with NYU), studying the political economy of AI. Its research areas include accountability, markets and competition, labour, geopolitics and industrial policy, data-centre infrastructure and climate, healthcare, and a safety and security strand that argues for safety-critical testing and independent oversight of AI. It publishes annual landscape reports ('Artificial Power', 2025), state and local policy toolkits, and technical security research such as 'Double Agents' (July 2026).

It supplies a political-economy analysis of industry power and of the race narratives behind AI policy. Through its Chief AI Scientist, Heidy Khlaaf, it also makes a safety-critical-engineering case for independent oversight of high-risk AI, drawn from aviation and other regulated industries. It is a principled critic of x-risk framing that any bridge-building between AI safety and AI accountability has to reckon with.

Works on Power, Assurance, Security · Key work Artificial Power: 2025 Landscape Report (2025); Double Agents: Defensive AI Agents Magnify Cyber Risks (2026); North Star Data Center Policy Toolkit (2026) · Get involved Occasional staff and contractor roles (a local policy researcher/land-use expert role advertised in September 2026); Newsletter and publications

Note Openly critical of x-risk discourse: in September 2026 its researchers called 'AI doomerism' unscientific and said it lets labs argue for self-regulation. Its Safety & Security research area means safety-critical engineering and independent oversight, not alignment. The roster's claim that it is a Humanity AI grantee was not confirmed; Humanity AI is not on its current list of funders.

Alphabet Workers Union-CWA Local 9009 (AWU-CWA) Adjacent

Membership body · Distributed · founded 2021

A union of Alphabet workers in the US and Canada, organised as Local 9009 of the Communications Workers of America. It went public in January 2021, is open to full-time staff, temps, vendors and contractors, and has about 1,400 members according to press reports. It set up a Committee on Artificial Intelligence in summer 2024, has organised Google's contracted AI raters (through Appen and, from 2025, GlobalLogic) who evaluate Gemini and AI Overviews, and in September 2025 co-published 'Ghost Workers in the Machine', a survey of US AI data workers, with TechEquity. Its elected board has opposed Google's December 2025 Gemini deal with the US Department of War and backed Anthropic's February 2026 refusal to drop safety guardrails for the Pentagon.

It is organised labour inside the parent company of a frontier AI lab (Google DeepMind) and among the raters who produce human-feedback data. That gives workers a collective channel on military uses of AI and on how alignment data is produced, and makes it one of the few existing structures for worker voice and conscience inside AI developers.

Works on People, Power, Security · Key work Committee on Artificial Intelligence (AI & Labor campaign) (2024); 'Ghost Workers in the Machine' survey of US AI data workers (with TechEquity) (2025); Statement on Google's partnership with the US Department of War (2025) · Get involved Membership is open to Alphabet employees, temps, vendors and contractors in the US and Canada; Members can take part in its Committee on Artificial Intelligence

Note It is a minority union: Google does not bargain with it company-wide, and the joint-employer status of contractor units is still contested (an NLRB decision in April 2026). Its positions on military AI come from its elected board and do not speak for all Alphabet staff. The membership figure comes from press reports, not the union's own site.

Anthropic Economic Futures Program AdjacentNew

Programme · San Francisco, USA · founded 2025

Anthropic's programme on AI's economic effects, launched in June 2025 and extended to the UK and Europe in November 2025. It ran small research awards (USD 10,000-50,000 plus API credits) and policy symposia with Georgetown's McCourt School and the LSE. It draws on the Anthropic Economic Index, which tracks real Claude usage with privacy protections. In July 2026 it published the research agenda for a USD 200 million Economic Futures Research Fund. The fund makes grants of USD 1-30 million on AI in the workplace, retraining, income support for displaced workers and giving workers a stake in AI-driven growth.

It funds research on gradual economic displacement and on how the gains are shared, and supplies data for it. This is part of the AI transition that the safety field mostly leaves to others. Its usage data shows which tasks are being automated as it happens, which outside economists cannot otherwise see.

Works on Power, Epistemics · Key work Introducing the Anthropic Economic Futures Program (2025); Economic Futures Programme in the UK and Europe (LSE symposium) (2025); Economic Futures Research Fund agenda (USD 200m) (2026) · Get involved Economic Futures Research Fund: request for proposals for institutional grants of USD 1-30 million (agenda published 22 July 2026, no deadline stated); Anthropic Fellows Program, Anthropic Institute (Economics & Policy) workstream: a four-month funded fellowship. Applications are rolling for the cohort starting January 2027.; Research economist roles in San Francisco, London and Singapore (listed Aug 2026)

Note This is a company programme studying the effects of its own products, so the Economic Index data and the research agenda depend on Anthropic's choices. The original small research awards are closed. Anthropic does not say exactly where the programme sits within the Anthropic Institute, which launched in March 2026.

Association des traducteurs littéraires de France (ATLF) Adjacent

Membership body · Paris, France · founded 1973 · also draws on Law, society

The French association of literary translators, founded in 1973. Its members translate from more than 60 languages for publishing, the press, theatre and audiovisual work. Since 2022 it has campaigned against generative AI in translation. Its model publishing contract now commits publisher and translator not to use AI for the translation itself or when exploiting the rights (for example AI-narrated audiobooks), and lets the translator refuse the use of their work for AI training. It also issues joint statements, for example on the publisher Harlequin's move to AI translation in December 2025.

It shows a profession governing AI from below through contracts: a standard clause on training-data opt-out and AI substitution, which members negotiate book by book. This is a working, copyable instrument for consent over training data, and one the AI-safety field rarely looks at.

Works on Power, Justice · Key work Generative-AI clauses in the ATLF model translation contract (2024); Deux ans de lutte contre l'IA (two years of campaigning against AI) (2024); Harlequin passe à l'IA (joint statement with Collectif En chair et en os) (2025) · Get involved Membership open to practising literary translators; Its model contract, AI clauses included, is published for any translator to use in negotiations; Staff recruitment announced February 2026 ('L'ATLF recrute !')

Note Its stance is refusal of AI in translation and protection of its members' rights, not engagement with AI safety. Sources give slightly different dates: a July 2024 ATLF article describes two AI clauses (articles 1.2 and 10) added to the model contract, while the clauses page refers to three clauses adopted in December 2024. Wikipedia still lists Corinna Gepner as president.

Bertelsmann Stiftung: reframe[Tech] – Algorithms for the Common Good (now Digitalisierung & Gemeinwohl) AdjacentChanged

Programme · Gütersloh, Germany · also draws on Law, society

A digital-policy programme of the Bertelsmann Stiftung, the large German operating foundation founded in 1977. It writes analyses and policy proposals to steer digital technology towards the common good, for policymakers, public administrations and civil society. Recent work covers a European public AI option, practical implementation and simplification of the EU AI Act, interoperability standards, decentralised social media, and public attitudes to platform power. Its old domain, reframetech.de, now redirects to a site called Digitalisierung & Gemeinwohl.

It argues for a public AI option and against dependence on a few private AI companies, and it reaches EU and German policymakers in a way most AI-safety groups do not. Its surveys of German public opinion on platform power give evidence on the structural, power-concentration side of the AI transition.

Works on Power, Assurance, Democracy · Key work Public AI in Europa / European Public AI (policy brief) (2026); A Public Alternative to Private AI Dominance (2025); Fragile Foundations: Hidden Risks of Generative AI (2025) · Get involved Read and cite its policy briefs and studies (German and English); Staff roles at the Bertelsmann Stiftung (check its careers pages)

Note Name: reframetech.de now redirects to digitalisierung-und-gemeinwohl.de. The foundation's own project page still uses the reframe[Tech] name, lists Kirsten Witte as director and shows 2026 publications. This looks like a 2026 rebrand with the same team and mission, but no announcement was found. The programme's start year was not confirmed. The foundation has long been criticised over its political influence and its ownership stake in the Bertelsmann media group. It does not give grants. There is no safety or catastrophic-risk framing.

Collectif En chair et en os Adjacent

Network · Distributed · founded 2023 · also draws on Arts, futures

A volunteer collective of French translators, founded in September 2023, whose slogan is 'Oui à l'humain, non à l'IA' (yes to the human, no to AI). Its manifesto and Change.org petition ask publishers, studios and media not to use AI for translation or creative work, to tell the public when AI was used, and to deny public funding to AI-generated works; ATLF reported more than 15,000 signatures by mid-2024. In 2026 it held an 'anti-summit' in Lille (13 June) against the Hauts-de-France regional AI summit. With the translators' union Stef and IA-lerte générale it also co-organised an international translators' strike day on 30 September, with events in Aubervilliers and Lyon and support from groups in Spain, Italy, Germany, Switzerland and Portugal.

It is organised refusal: workers whose jobs are already being automated deciding together whether, and how fast, AI enters their field. Its anti-summit linked AI to extraction, militarisation and labour, a systemic critique rarely heard in AI-safety venues.

Works on Power, Meaning · Key work Manifesto and petition 'Non à des traductions sans âme' (2023); Anti-sommet de l'IA, Lille (2026); International day of action for translators (strike), 30 September (2026) · Get involved Sign the manifesto petition on Change.org; Attend its public events (Lille anti-summit, June 2026; strike-day workshops, September 2026); Donate to the support fund for its actions

Note Its site names no spokespeople and gives no figures for membership. The collective rejects generative AI outright rather than seeking to shape it, so it is a counter-voice to the AI-safety field rather than a partner within it. Evidence comes mainly from its own site and from ATLF, which works with it.

Creative Commons (CC): CC signals and AI and the Commons Adjacent

Nonprofit · Distributed · founded 2001 · also draws on Law, society

Creative Commons is the US nonprofit, run by a distributed team, that stewards the CC licences. Its AI and the Commons work includes CC signals, a framework announced in June 2025 that lets creators and collection holders state how AI systems may reuse their work. In April 2026 CC said that preference signals without enforcement do not shift power. By September 2026 it was exploring an experimental legal tool that could set conditions on bulk access to large data collections. In 2025-26 it also published guidance on using CC licences in an AI ecosystem, on open heritage in the age of AI and on Indigenous collections.

It holds global norm-setting infrastructure for sharing, through licences used on a vast body of works, and is testing how a commons can set terms for AI developers that neither law nor company policy sets. Its public conclusion that unenforced signals do not change developer behaviour is useful evidence for anyone designing voluntary AI norms.

Works on Power, Justice · Key work CC signals framework (announced) (2025); Update on CC signals: what changed and why (2026); Guidance on Using CC Licenses in an AI Ecosystem (2026) · Get involved Join the CC signals community through the intake form and Zulip chat; CC Global Network community

Note CC signals changed direction in 2026: in April CC dropped reliance on preference signals, and in September it described an experimental legal tool for conditioning bulk data access. The final design is not yet public. Arcadia's open culture funding ends in 2026. The AI work is one strand of a broader licensing organisation.

Current AI AdjacentNew

Funder · Paris, France · founded 2025 · also draws on Law, society

A Paris-based non-profit (French loi 1901 association) launched at the AI Action Summit in February 2025 to build a 'public option for AI'. It brings together governments, philanthropies and companies. It funds community projects, builds open-source AI infrastructure such as the Suno Sutra offline translation device with India's Bhashini, the AlphaChat open chatbot and a Gap Map of the open AI stack, and convenes a wider public-interest AI movement. It reports $404M pledged towards a five-year goal of $2.5B, and has committed $11.3M in grants across two 2026 rounds, starting with a $3.2M pilot cohort announced in June 2026.

It is a large new funder outside the AI-safety funding circuit, working on power concentration and on who builds and owns AI, including community control over language data. For new funders and founders it is one of the few sizeable pools aimed at public and open AI alternatives.

Works on Power, Justice · Key work Paris Charter on Artificial Intelligence in the Public Interest (2025); Pilot grants: $3.2M to four organisations in Kenya, Lebanon and Brazil (multilingual datasets, cultural digitisation, offline tools, accountability audits) (2026); Multilingual AI will not scale without a shift in power (joint brief with UNDP) (2026) · Get involved Grant rounds (two in 2026) and challenges such as the VYOMA Innovation Challenge for multilingual handheld AI in India (June 2026); Join the AI Potluck, its framework for collaborating on an open AI stack; Staff roles (careers page)

Note There is a large gap between pledges ($404M) and funds actually received ($46M direct for 2025-26). Funders include large tech firms (Google DeepMind, Salesforce, Hugging Face). It was launched at a summit that AI-safety voices criticised for sidelining safety, and it has no safety or catastrophic-risk framing. Governance is still forming: an interim committee guides strategy while the board is recruited. Staff numbers were not published.

Data Labelers Association (DLA) AdjacentNew

Membership body · Nairobi, Kenya · founded 2025

A Nairobi-based association of data labellers, annotators and content moderators. It was founded and is run by data workers, and launched officially on 13 February 2025. It reports 878+ members and a wider network of 5,000+, and runs job matching (DLA Connect), mental-health support (DLA Health), training (DLA Academy), and advocacy and collective bargaining (DLA Voice). In 2025-26 it held stakeholder convenings in Nairobi. In September 2026 it published findings from structured interviews with Kenyan labellers and moderators on pay, hours, mental-health support and job security.

Much of the training, RLHF and content-moderation data behind frontier models is produced by workers like DLA's members, including a lot of the safety-relevant labelling. DLA gives that workforce a standing, worker-run body that AI-safety organisations and labs could consult about the conditions under which safety data is made.

Works on People, Power · Key work Official launch of the association (streamed online) (2025); Stakeholder engagement convening with civil society, academia, government, employers and workers (2025); 'Empowering Data Workers: Ethical AI, Rights & Well-Being' community day, Nairobi Arboretum and livestream (2026) · Get involved Data labellers and moderators can register as members (datalabelers.org/register); DLA Academy courses, certifications and workshops for members; Free community events, e.g. 7 Feb 2026 in Nairobi with a YouTube livestream

Note Its own pages give inconsistent figures: the homepage says 878+ members in 3+ countries, while the 2026 report says a network of 5K+ in 15+ countries. The '75% wage improvement' claim is self-reported and unverified. As far as its site shows, it is an association rather than a registered trade union. It has no catastrophic-risk framing. The February 2025 launch was streamed on a TU Berlin Zoom link, which suggests academic partners in Berlin, but this is unconfirmed.

Data Workers' Inquiry (DWI) Adjacent

Programme · Berlin, Germany · founded 2024 · also draws on Law, society

DWI is a participatory research project run jointly by the DAIR Institute, the Weizenbaum Institute and TU Berlin, led by sociologist Milagros Miceli. Data annotators and content moderators research and report on their own workplaces. About 19 community researchers in Kenya, Syria and Lebanon, Venezuela, Brazil, Germany, France, Spain and the UK have produced zines, comics, documentaries, podcasts and reports on pay, trauma, surveillance and organising at firms such as Sama, Telus, Remotasks and Scale AI. It has also published its method (WIRM) and a June 2026 policy report on the ILO platform-work convention.

The human data work behind RLHF, red-teaming and safety filtering rarely appears in AI safety's picture of who does the work; DWI documents its psychological and economic cost from the workers' own vantage. Its workers'-inquiry method shows how affected people can act as researchers rather than subjects.

Works on People, Power, Justice · Key work The Inquiries: worker-produced reports, zines, comics and films from nine countries (2024); Methodological Considerations for Centering Workers' Epistemic Authority in AI Research (AIES) (2025); Data Work in the ILO Platform Labor Convention (policy report) (2026) · Get involved Data workers are invited to contact the team about their experiences and the project; Donations go to the community researchers and their communities; Newsletter and recorded online panels with community researchers

Note It is openly political, rooted in Marxist workers' inquiry and critical of the AI industry, and does not engage with AI-safety framings. Its outputs are testimony and advocacy pieces, not representative surveys. Launch year inferred from its May Day announcement and 2024 talk series.

Education International (EI) Adjacent

Membership body · Brussels, Belgium · founded 1993

Education International is the global federation of teachers' and education workers' unions, based in Brussels: about 383 member organisations representing more than 32 million educators. On AI it argues three things: teachers and their unions must help govern AI in education, the teacher-student relationship stays central, and schools must not become testing grounds for technology companies. It held a global conference on human-centred AI in Brussels in December 2025, launched an AI and Technology Network (first in-person meeting in Madrid, June 2026), and made the case at the 2026 International Labour Conference.

It is the only body speaking for organised educators worldwide on AI. It brings a political-economy critique of AI in schools (commercialisation, data extraction, de-professionalisation) that is largely missing from AI-safety work on education. Its Worlds of Education platform publishes academic critiques of the UNESCO and OECD/European Commission AI-literacy frameworks.

Works on Power, Human minds, Justice · Key work Global conference 'Shaping Our Future: Education Unions Leading for a Human-Centred AI', Brussels (2025); First in-person meeting of the EI AI and Technology Network, Madrid (2026); Intervention at the 114th International Labour Conference on AI and decent work (2026) · Get involved Educators take part through their national union, if it is an EI affiliate; Communications toolkit and network outputs from the AI and Technology Network are public on its site

Note It pursues its AI positions through member unions and global policy forums, not through AI-specific research. The 2024 World Congress resolution on technology and AI is known only from secondary descriptions; its text was not checked. Worlds of Education pieces carry a disclaimer that they are the authors' views, not EI policy. It has no advanced-AI or catastrophic-risk framing.

European Trade Union Committee for Education (ETUCE) Adjacent

Membership body · Brussels, Belgium · founded 1975 · also draws on Law, society

ETUCE is the European federation of education trade unions and the European region of Education International: about 125 unions representing 11 million teachers and other education staff, and the EU social partner for education. Its EU co-funded project 'Balancing AI in EDU' (January 2025 to December 2026) helps unions bargain collectively and lobby on AI. The project includes a survey of unions, a conference in Copenhagen (October 2025), a workshop on collective bargaining in Dublin (May 2026) and a forthcoming guide. In September 2026 ETUCE campaigned against a proposed GDPR Article 88bis that would let companies train AI on students' and educators' data.

It handles AI in schools through collective bargaining and EU data-protection law, organised counter-power over AI training data and deployment that AI-safety work rarely uses. It is a working example of one sector negotiating over AI with employers and EU institutions.

Works on Power, Justice · Key work Balancing AI in EDU: strengthening education trade union capacity for collective bargaining and advocacy on AI (EU co-funded, 2025-26) (2025); ETUCE European Conference on Artificial Intelligence and Education, Copenhagen (2025); Workshop on collective bargaining on AI in education, Dublin (2026) · Get involved Educators take part through their member union; Outputs of 'Balancing AI in EDU', including the AI survey study and a guide for education unions due in 2026, are published on its site

Note Its AI work is EU social dialogue and data-protection advocacy for its sector, with no advanced-AI or catastrophic-risk framing. Membership figures (about 125 unions, 11 million staff) date from 2023. The Stop the Omnibus campaign is run jointly with the school-student union body OBESSU and the European School Heads Association.

European Trade Union Confederation (ETUC) Adjacent

Membership body · Brussels, Belgium · founded 1973 · also draws on Law, society

The European-level trade union confederation, founded in 1973 and based in Brussels, representing about 45 million members through 94 national confederations in 42 countries plus 10 European federations. On AI it campaigns for a dedicated EU directive on algorithmic management and AI at work (circulars in October and December 2025), adopted the resolution 'Artificial Intelligence for Workers, Not Just for Profit' in March 2025, and opposes parts of the AI and Digital Omnibus that it says weaken worker safety and data protection (statements in May and September 2026). It works with the European Trade Union Institute (ETUI), which publishes research on AI and labour.

It is the main worker-side voice in EU AI law, defending the 'human in control' and precautionary principles as the AI Act is implemented and simplified, which is where much binding AI governance is being decided. Its push for a workplace AI directive is a live test of whether AI rules in Europe are extended or rolled back.

Works on Power, Justice · Key work Resolution 'Artificial Intelligence for Workers, Not Just for Profit: Ensuring Quality Jobs in the Digital Age' (2025); 'The EU needs a Dedicated Directive on Algorithmic Management and AI at work' (2025); 'AI Omnibus deal weakens worker safety protections' (2026) · Get involved Staff vacancies and calls for tender on etuc.org (e.g. an expert for the ShapeTech project, Jan 2026); Individuals join through national member unions

Note Its focus is employment, algorithmic management and workers' data; it does not engage with frontier or catastrophic risk. Much of the analytical AI work sits with its research arm ETUI, which may merit its own profile.

Fairwork Adjacent

Nonprofit · Oxford, UK · founded 2018 · also draws on Law, society

Fairwork is an action-research programme founded in 2018 at the Oxford Internet Institute and the WZB Berlin Social Science Center, led by Mark Graham. Country teams in about 40 countries rate platforms and employers against five fair-work principles: pay, conditions, contracts, management and representation. Its AI strand publishes the Fairwork AI Principles and assessments of AI data-work suppliers (Sama with GPAI in 2023; Sama and Appen in 2025; Tinkogroup in 2026). It has now spun out Fairwork Certification, an independent non-profit company limited by guarantee that certifies firms commissioning AI data work, with anonymous worker testimony at the centre of each assessment.

It offers an auditable standard for the labour conditions of the annotators, raters and moderators whose judgements shape model behaviour. AI labs, safety teams and funders could apply it to their own data and red-teaming supply chains. It also ties AI supply chains to due-diligence law such as the EU's CS3D.

Works on People, Power · Key work Fairwork AI Ratings 2023: The Workers Behind AI at Sama (with the Global Partnership on AI) (2023); Fairwork AI Supply Chain Assessments: Sama and Appen (2025); Cloudwork Report 2025: Advancing Standards in Digital Labour and AI Supply Chain Governance (2025) · Get involved Firms can book a free consultation for an AI supply-chain assessment or certification (Onboard, then Endorsed); Organisations can sign the Fairwork Pledge; Jobs listed on the OII Fairwork site

Note The certification arm is paid by the firms it certifies, which raises the usual auditor-independence question, though it is a non-profit with published principles and revocable marks. Its regulation-readiness marketing sits close to the 'compliance' services excluded from scope; it is kept in for its labour research, standards and worker-voice method. Much of Fairwork's wider work concerns gig platforms (delivery, ride-hailing) rather than AI.

Finance Watch Adjacent

Nonprofit · Brussels, Belgium · founded 2011 · also draws on Law, society

A Brussels-based public-interest association (AISBL), set up in 2011 after a cross-party petition by MEPs, that argues for the public interest in EU financial regulation as a counterweight to the financial-industry lobby. Since 2024 its digital-finance team has produced a line of reports and consultation responses on AI in finance. They argue that opaque AI models conflict with the principles of accountability, responsibility and transparency that financial regulation relies on, and they ask for the AI Act to cover all financial services and for the AI Liability Directive to be brought back.

Finance has decades of practice in supervising opaque, automated decision models: model-risk management, named accountability, systemic-risk analysis. Finance Watch carries that practice into AI governance, and it flags the concentration of AI model providers as a financial-stability risk. Mainstream AI policy rarely draws on this regulatory template.

Works on Justice, Assurance, Power · Key work Artificial intelligence in finance: how to trust a black box? (2025); Protecting EU consumers in the age of AI-driven retail finance (2025); Consultation response: robust consumer protection standards are needed for the use of AI in the insurance sector (2025) · Get involved Staff roles are advertised at https://www.finance-watch.org/work-for-us/; Individuals and civil-society organisations independent of the financial sector can become members

Note AI is one strand among many: most of its work is on sustainable finance, banking and retail finance. It has published nothing specifically on AI since July 2025, and the author of the 2025 AI report has since left. Its frame is consumer protection and regulatory accountability, not catastrophic AI risk.

Institute for the Future of Work (IFOW) Adjacent

Nonprofit · London, UK · founded 2018 · also draws on Law, society

An independent London research institute on how new technology, especially AI, affects work. Its co-founders are former employment barrister Anna Thomas, Nobel economist Christopher Pissarides and technologist Naomi Climer. It ran the Nuffield-funded Pissarides Review into automation, work and wellbeing (final report January 2025) and runs a Responsible AI Sandbox where firms test workplace AI. Its research and tools cover good work design, worker voice and accountability in AI adoption. It published an Innovate UK-funded report on good work design and AI adoption in May 2026 and research on worker rights and automation outcomes in September 2026.

It builds concrete mechanisms for worker voice, impact assessment and accountability when AI enters workplaces. These are institutional counterweights to the gradual loss of human leverage in the economy, though IFOW does not frame them that way. It works close to UK government and industry, and the AI Safety Institute appears among its listed funders.

Works on Power, Justice · Key work The Pissarides Review into the Future of Work and Wellbeing: 'Making the Future Work' final report (2025); Good Work Design and AI Adoption (action research across eight organisations) (2026); Responsible AI Sandbox · Get involved Responsible AI Sandbox: open call for industry partners deploying workplace AI; Events and workshops; Staff roles (team page)

Note It works on present and near-term labour effects; it has no catastrophic-risk or alignment framing. The founding year is inferred from its earliest dated activity (July 2018). The nature and size of the AI Safety Institute's funding were not found.

Institutional Data Initiative (IDI), Harvard Law School Library Adjacent

Academic · Cambridge, MA, United States · founded 2024 · also draws on Democracy

The Institutional Data Initiative is a research initiative at Harvard Law School Library. It was incubated at the library's Library Innovation Lab and launched in December 2024. It works with libraries, museums, archives and government agencies to clean, document and publish their collections as open datasets for AI, and it builds open tools for doing so. Its first release, Institutional Books 1.0 (June 2025), holds about 983,000 public-domain books (242 billion tokens, 254 languages) from Harvard's Google Books scans. In 2026 it published 1.47 million historical newspaper pages and a dataset of 186 years of university proceedings.

It treats training data as a commons that knowledge institutions steward, with documented provenance and quality, instead of scraped material. That gives open and smaller developers a well-understood alternative, and gives libraries a say in what models learn from.

Works on Power, Epistemics · Key work Institutional Books 1.0 (983K public-domain books, 242B tokens) (2025); GRIN Transfer: open-source pipeline for libraries to retrieve their Google Books collections (2025); Institutional Proceedings: 186 years of university decisions (2026) · Get involved Open roles: Senior Partnerships Manager; Communications and Community Manager; Invites institutions, researchers and technologists to collaborate on and improve its datasets (contact@institutional.org); Online talks and events (e.g. Oct 2025, with Ruth Okediji, on diversity in AI training data)

Note Microsoft and OpenAI fund it, and its datasets are open to commercial developers, so it also widens the training data available to frontier labs. The books corpus leans heavily towards Western European languages (43% English). It is not framed around AI safety. It launched in December 2024, so its track record is short.

IT for Change Adjacent

Nonprofit · Bengaluru, India · founded 2000 · also draws on Law, society, Indigenous

IT for Change is a non-profit research and advocacy organisation in Bengaluru, founded in 2000, working on digital justice, internet governance, education and gender. Its AI work includes ReGenAI, a 'New Deal for the AI Economy' statement (February 2026) that came out of its 'Towards Regenerative AI' conference (October–November 2025), and the FemFirst Research Observatory, which funds 8–12 women and nonbinary researchers in South and Southeast Asia to write on feminist AI futures. It holds ECOSOC special consultative status and speaks in UN forums such as the WSIS Forum and the Human Rights Council.

It brings a Global South, feminist political-economy analysis of AI (market concentration, precarity, exclusion, ecological harm) into UN and multilateral debates where the AI-safety field has little presence. For funders it is an established Majority-World partner on AI power concentration.

Works on Power, Justice · Key work ReGenAI: A New Deal for the AI Economy (2026); Towards Regenerative AI conference (45 co-creators of the New Deal statement) (2025); FemFirst Research Observatory: call for proposals on feminist AI futures in South and Southeast Asia (2026) · Get involved FemFirst Research Observatory: funded 12-month research places for mid- to senior-career women and nonbinary researchers in South/Southeast Asia (2026 round closed 25 June 2026; about CAD 12,000 each); Organisational or individual endorsement of the ReGenAI New Deal statement; Staff research and policy roles in Bengaluru (team page lists about 110 staff and consultants)

Note It is openly critical of the AI industry and dominant AI paradigms and uses no AI-safety or x-risk language; some positions (e.g. on Big Tech, digital sovereignty, the 'Drop Palantir' campaign) are explicitly political. Funding sources were not visible on the pages checked.

Metagov Adjacent

Nonprofit · Boston, USA · founded 2019 · also draws on Democracy, Law, society

A Boston-based nonprofit that researches and builds tools for the self-governance of online communities and networks. It began in 2019 from a Harvard Law School seminar and became a US 501(c)(3) in 2020. It now describes its work as 'community sovereignty, network governance, and statecraft in the age of AI'. Its AI work includes the Public AI project (it is fiscal sponsor of the Public AI Inference Utility), the 'Collective Governance for AI: Points of Intervention' mapping, Interoperable Deliberative Tools, KOI Pond (LLM-mediated community knowledge infrastructure) and an AI Renaissance residency. It also hosts DAOstar and runs a weekly online seminar.

It brings research on commons, cooperatives and institutional design to the question of who controls AI, and builds working infrastructure as well as papers. Its research directors include Lawrence Lessig, Divya Siddarth, Aviv Ovadya, Nathan Schneider and Primavera De Filippi, with Audrey Tang as adviser, so it links the law, collective-intelligence and cooperative traditions.

Works on Democracy, Power · Key work Collective Governance for AI: Points of Intervention (2025); Public AI Inference Utility (as fiscal sponsor) (2025); Metagov Seminar (weekly, online) (2026) · Get involved Weekly Metagov Seminar, online and open to the public (Wednesdays, registration on Luma); Monthly community orientation calls and a community Slack; Public AI roles: Founding Infrastructure Engineer, Research Engineer, Public AI Fellow (Switzerland) and Public AI Fellow (Open Source), listed 2026

Note AI is one strand among many digital-governance projects. Much of its history and funding come from crypto and web3 (DAOstar, the Ethereum and Filecoin foundations). Its Public AI work overlaps with the separately listed Public AI Network, which shares people, fiscal sponsor and job listings. The people page lists a large network of contributors, so the number of full-time staff is unclear.

MIT James M. and Cathleen D. Stone Center on Inequality and Shaping the Future of Work Adjacent

Academic · Cambridge, Massachusetts, USA · founded 2024

An MIT economics centre, formerly the MIT Shaping the Future of Work Initiative, led by Daron Acemoglu, Simon Johnson and David Autor. It researches how technology, globalisation and policy drive inequality and job quality for workers without degrees. One of its four themes is 'Applying AI to extend worker expertise'. In February 2026 its directors launched 'Building pro-worker AI' (an NBER paper and a Hamilton Project brief), which argues that only AI that creates new tasks clearly benefits workers and proposes nine policies to steer AI in that direction.

It brings the economic history of who captures technology's gains, and the argument that the direction of technology can be steered (Power and Progress), to bear on AI. That gives a concrete research and policy agenda against economic disempowerment. Simon Johnson's appointment in June 2026 to chair the UK's AI Economics Institute links the centre directly to government thinking on AI's economic effects.

Works on Power · Key work Building Pro-Worker Artificial Intelligence (NBER WP 34854; Hamilton Project brief) (2026); Power and Progress: Our Thousand-Year Struggle Over Technology and Prosperity (Acemoglu and Johnson) (2023); What Makes New Work Different from More Work? (2026) · Get involved Predoctoral researcher and staff roles on its Careers page; Public events, e.g. the 'What Happened to Liberal Democracy?' panel (Sep 2026); Affiliates programme for researchers

Note It works within mainstream economics and has no catastrophic-risk or alignment framing. It began as the MIT Shaping the Future of Work Initiative (part of MIT Blueprint Labs, founded with a Hewlett Foundation gift; official launch January 2024) and became the Stone Center on 1 July 2025. AI is one theme among four.

Mozilla Foundation Adjacent

Nonprofit · San Francisco, USA · founded 2003 · also draws on Law, society

The nonprofit parent of Mozilla, founded in 2003. It runs advocacy campaigns, grantmaking, the Common Voice crowdsourced speech dataset, the Mozilla Data Collective and the annual Mozilla Festival (MozFest). Its AI work is about trustworthy and open AI: it funds researchers and builders of alternatives, campaigns on AI bias and platform accountability, and argues for community-governed data and public AI infrastructure. It is a founding member of Humanity AI and a funding partner of the European AI & Society Fund.

It brings the open-source movement's experience of commons-based production and community governance of data to the problem of AI power concentration and lock-in. The x-risk field shares that concern but rarely approaches it through open infrastructure. It also funds and convenes a large public-interest tech community: MozFest drew more than 2,000 people in 2025.

Works on Power, Justice · Key work Mozilla Festival 2026, Barcelona: 'Wilding' (2026); Mozilla Data Collective: community-governed datasets for AI (2025); Common Voice open speech dataset (2017) · Get involved Mozilla Festival, Barcelona, 28–30 Oct 2026; sessions are proposed by the community; Grantmaking: open opportunities and call alerts on the 'What we fund' page; Contribute voice recordings to Common Voice

Note Distinct from Mozilla Corporation (Firefox), Mozilla.ai and Mozilla Ventures, which are separate Mozilla entities. It restructured in late 2024 and redesigned its grantmaking; whether the fellowship programme is currently running was not confirmed. Its AI framing is trustworthy and open AI and the centralisation of tech, not catastrophic risk. The official site blocks automated access, so its pages were read through a proxy; detail on the current AI programme is thinner than for the other entries.

National Education Association (NEA) Adjacent

Membership body · Washington, DC, United States · founded 1857

The NEA is the largest US labour union, representing educators from pre-kindergarten to higher education. Its AI work rests on a June 2024 task force report and the policy statement its Representative Assembly adopted in July 2024. These set five principles: students and educators at the centre, evidence-based tools, ethical use and strong data protection, equitable access, and AI literacy and agency. It runs an AI in Education hub with micro-credentials, independent-study courses, vetting guidance and sample school-board policies.

It sets organised-labour norms for keeping human judgement in high-stakes educational decisions across US public schools. Its task force documented concrete failures: wrong AI-assigned grades, facial recognition failing Black students, opaque data governance. It is the main channel to US teachers, and a test case of a workforce setting terms for how AI enters its profession.

Works on Power, Human minds, Justice · Key work NEA Task Force Report and Policy Statement on Artificial Intelligence in Education (2024); AI in Education hub: micro-credentials in four competency areas and seven independent-study courses (2025); Microsoft Elevate grant to extend AI micro-credentials to 10,000 more members (2025) · Get involved AI micro-credentials and independent-study courses for educators via the AI in Education hub; Membership through state and local affiliates (education employees)

Note It takes Microsoft money to train members and to feed educators' views into Microsoft's products, which sits awkwardly with its stance that tech companies should not lead decisions about AI in schools. Its AI work concerns classroom practice, equity and data protection, not advanced-AI risk. Leadership changed on 1 September 2026.

Omidyar Network Adjacent

Funder · Redwood City, CA, USA · founded 2004 · also draws on Law, society, Democracy

A philanthropic investment firm (foundation plus LLC) founded in 2004 by Pierre and Pam Omidyar, which has committed more than $1.9bn and organises its work around the culture, governance and business of technology. Its AI grantmaking funds groups challenging concentrated tech power, worker voice and online safety (e.g. AI Now, Americans for Responsible Innovation, TechEquity), and it is one of ten founding partners of Humanity AI, a $500m five-year pooled fund. It endorsed New York's RAISE Act and California's 2025 AI bills, and condemned the December 2025 executive order against state AI regulation.

It is one of the few public-interest technology funders that has also publicly backed frontier-safety legislation, so it links the power-and-accountability side of AI governance with safety policy. For new funders it is an established route into political-economy, labour and civil-society work on AI.

Works on Power, Justice, Democracy · Key work Founding partner of Humanity AI ($500m five-year pooled fund); May 2026 announcement of $18m in grants (2026); Endorsement of New York's RAISE Act (2025); Statement condemning the Trump executive order on state AI regulation (2025) · Get involved Humanity AI open call: $10m for US nonprofits working on education, labour and economy, or humanities, arts and culture; deadline 21 Oct 2026 (administered by Humanity AI); Staff roles: https://omidyar.com/who-we-are/our-team/join-our-team/

Note Its own site lists Anthropic among the shareholdings in its Business of Tech portfolio, a possible conflict for safety-policy positions. The May 2026 $18m was granted through Humanity AI, the pooled fund, not by Omidyar alone. Wikipedia reports it ended its India operations in 2024 after government investigations. It took a new CEO in March 2026.

Open Data Institute (ODI) Adjacent

Nonprofit · London, UK · founded 2012 · also draws on Law, society

The ODI is a London nonprofit co-founded in 2012 by Tim Berners-Lee and Nigel Shadbolt. It works on data infrastructure, data stewardship and data institutions such as data trusts. Since November 2023 it has run a data-centric AI programme on AI-ready data, transparency about training data (an AI Data Transparency Index) and responsible data use. The programme also produces policy input such as advice on the UK National Data Library and a recurring DCAI event series. In 2026 it co-launched Data Foundations for AI with the Global Partnership for Sustainable Development Data, and became a joint steward of the Digital Public Goods Alliance's DPG4AI collection.

It treats data as the main lever for governing AI. Its tools are data trusts and stewardship models, transparency indices on training data, and AI-ready public data infrastructure, and it has a direct line into UK government. These institutional tools for accountability and against concentration complement model-centred safety work.

Works on Power, Assurance · Key work Data-centric AI programme (2023); AI Data Transparency Index (first iteration) (2024); Data Foundations for AI (with GPSDD, hosted by the UN Foundation) (2026) · Get involved DCAI (data-centric AI) event series and Data Ethics Professionals sessions on AI (October 2026); ODI training courses on data and AI

Note A large share of its work is consultancy and training for organisations, not only public-interest research. Its AI framing is responsible data and trust rather than safety. Staff size is estimated.

Open Future Adjacent

Nonprofit · Amsterdam, Netherlands · founded 2020 · also draws on Law, society

Open Future is a European think tank for the open movement, registered as a Dutch foundation (stichting), with staff in Amsterdam and Warsaw. Its AI work covers Public AI (AI as commons-based public infrastructure), training-data transparency under the EU AI Act, and the relationship between AI and knowledge commons such as Wikimedia and libraries. It publishes white papers and makes EU policy submissions. In 2024 it hosted an online Alignment Assembly on AI and the Commons, using the Collective Intelligence Project's method.

It develops concrete institutional alternatives to concentrated AI power: public AI infrastructure, library-governed datasets and rules on training-data transparency. Those designs bear directly on concentration and lock-in, which the AI-safety field names as a risk but seldom designs against.

Works on Power, Justice · Key work White Paper on Public AI (2025); European Public AI Policy Brief (2026); European Books Data Commons feasibility study; Wikimedia, the Commons and the New AI Knowledge Loop (2026)

Note Paul Keller and Alek Tarkowski also lead COMMUNIA (president and team member), so the two organisations overlap in people and policy positions. Staff size and budget are not published. No open calls or roles were found on the site.

Open Markets Institute (OMI), incl. OMI Europe Adjacent

Nonprofit · Washington DC, USA · founded 2017 · also draws on Law, society

Washington anti-monopoly think tank of journalists, lawyers, economists and advocates. It became independent in 2017 after eight years as the Open Markets Program at New America. It runs an Artificial Intelligence programme, a Center for Media & Digital Governance (which covers AI and journalism) and a European centre, OMI Europe, which campaigns against Big Tech 'AI lock-in' through EU competition law and the Digital Markets Act (DMA). With Mozilla it published 'Stopping Big Tech from Becoming Big AI' (2024), and in 2026 it published analyses arguing that AI firms' copyright violations amount to unfair competition, along with DMA policy briefs on cloud concentration.

Antitrust is one of the few legal tools that already exist against concentration of AI power, and OMI is one of the most practised users of it on both sides of the Atlantic. Its market-level account of 'AI lock-in' pairs naturally with the AI-safety field's civilisational concerns about lock-in and gradual disempowerment, which so far have few concrete levers.

Works on Power, Epistemics · Key work Stopping Big Tech from Becoming Big AI: a roadmap (with Mozilla; Max von Thun and Daniel Hanley) (2024); License, Please: Mapping the Road Ahead for AI Licensing (webinar) (2026); OMI Europe papers on Google's AI strategy, Gemini lock-in on Android and DMA reform for cloud (2026) · Get involved Public events and webinars, e.g. the AI-licensing webinar (May 2026) and OMI Europe's Paris event (Sep 2026); Staff roles listed on its Careers page; Newsletters, including OMI Europe's 'The Corner'

Note An advocacy organisation with a strongly anti-Big-Tech position. It frames AI as a problem of monopoly and democracy, not of safety or catastrophic risk. The funders list on its site dates from 2021. AI is one of nine programmes, alongside food, health and transport.

Platform Cooperativism Consortium (PCC) Adjacent

Network · New York, USA · founded 2016

A think-and-do tank based at The New School in New York, founded by Trebor Scholz, which supports worker- and user-owned digital platforms worldwide. Its Institute for the Cooperative Digital Economy (ICDE) runs annual research fellowships. Since 2025 it has turned its annual conference and teaching to AI: a 'Cooperative AI' conference in Istanbul (Nov 2025), the online course 'AI Without Bosses' (Aug-Dec 2026) and a 'Solidarity AI' conference at Chulalongkorn University in Bangkok (12-15 Nov 2026). Its 2026-27 ICDE cohort (11 fellows from 10 countries) includes work on AI policy and infrastructure sovereignty.

It represents the other meaning of 'cooperative AI': democratic ownership and governance of AI systems by workers and users, as a counterweight to concentrated control. It has had almost no contact with the game-theoretic cooperative-AI field despite the shared name. Its conferences and fellowships are largely in the Majority World (Kerala, Mombasa, Istanbul, Bangkok), so it reaches cooperative movements the AI-safety field does not.

Works on Power, Democracy · Key work Cooperative AI conference, Istanbul (11-14 Nov 2025) (2025); Solidarity AI conference, Chulalongkorn University, Bangkok (12-15 Nov 2026) (2026); AI Without Bosses: an online course on AI for the co-op movement (2026) · Get involved ICDE research fellowships (annual open call); Annual conference, Solidarity AI, Bangkok, 12-15 Nov 2026; Online course 'AI Without Bosses' (Aug-Dec 2026) and Platform Co-op School courses

Note Its AI work is new (since 2025) and mostly convening and teaching, not research output. It frames AI as a question of ownership and solidarity, not safety. Its name overlaps with the Cooperative AI Foundation's field, but the two are unrelated. Funding sources are not public on its site.

Project Liberty Institute Adjacent

Nonprofit · New York, USA · also draws on Law, society

The research and policy arm of Frank McCourt's Project Liberty: an independent 501(c)(3), formerly the McCourt Institute, led by president Tomicah Tillemann. It backs the Decentralized Social Networking Protocol (DSNP), promoted the Digital Choice Act on data portability and interoperability (enacted in Utah and South Dakota, and extended to AI in Virginia), and runs a responsible-AI investment process with more than 200 investors, which it presented at the OECD in 2026. It also publishes reports on digital infrastructure for 'middle power' governments and on data cooperatives in South-East Asia.

It works against AI-era lock-in and loss of human agency through levers already in use: enacted state law, an open protocol, and steering investment towards a 'pro-human AI stack'. This is concrete counter-power-concentration work that x-risk governance seldom touches.

Works on Power, Democracy · Key work Digital Choice Act (data portability and interoperability), enacted in Utah (2025); Building Digital Infrastructure Ready for the AI Era – Insights from 13 Middle Power Governments (2026); Global responsible-AI investment process, presented at the OECD (2026) · Get involved Project Liberty Alliance: 200+ organisations, monthly virtual pop-ups and a listserv (run by Project Liberty's Alliance division); Careers page: https://www.projectliberty.io/careers/; Newsletter: https://projectlibertynewsletter.substack.com

Note It is closely tied to Frank McCourt's wider Project Liberty (Labs, Alliance), so where the Institute ends is blurred. The site lists 'AI safety' among its research topics, but no specific safety outputs were found. The Institute's founding year and budget were not verified. Protocol Labs (PL) and Protocol Labs R&D (PL R&D) Adjacent

Company · Distributed · founded 2014 · also draws on Living systems, Democracy

Founded in 2014 by Juan Benet as the team behind IPFS, Filecoin and libp2p, Protocol Labs is now an innovation network that says it links more than 750 startups, funds and open-source projects. Its R&D arm works in four areas: digital human rights, economies and governance, AI and robotics, and neurotechnology. The AI area builds open compute, identity, reputation and economic infrastructure for autonomous agents. The neurotech area funds BCI, NeuroAI and whole-organism emulation.

It funds and builds coordination and public-goods infrastructure that AI-governance experiments run on: it led Simocracy and co-ran the Edge City d/acc residency. It also argues that decentralised AI is safer than centralised AI, a view that mainstream AI-safety work rarely tests. For funders it is a large, well-resourced actor in the d/acc and public-goods world, but its AI agenda is mostly infrastructure.

Explicit safety work is thin: a few talks (on the path to AGI, alignment and digital minds in 2023, on machine consciousness in 2024, and on AI safety and governance in October 2025). PL's own timeline says it held the inaugural Funding the Commons (November 2021) and spun it out as an independent company in 2023.

Public AI Network (PAINT) Adjacent

Network · Distributed

A coalition arguing for AI as public infrastructure, 'provisioned like electricity, water, roads, libraries, or the Internet itself', that is publicly accessible and publicly accountable. It runs a Slack community, publishes white papers and policy briefs (from 2024), and runs a weekly online seminar series whose 2026 season ran from August to September. It holds events such as the Public AI Switzerland founding event in Zurich (February 2026) and has chapters in Switzerland, the UK and the US. Its sister project, the Public AI Inference Utility, launched in September 2025 and gives public access to public models such as Switzerland's Apertus.

It offers an answer to AI power concentration that the safety field rarely discusses: AI capacity that is publicly provided and publicly accountable. This is already running as an inference service. It connects national public-AI efforts (the Swiss AI Initiative, AI Singapore, AI Sweden, the Barcelona Supercomputing Center) with civil society and policymakers.

Works on Power, Democracy · Key work Public AI White Paper (2024); Launch of the Public AI Inference Utility (2025); Public AI Switzerland founding event, Zurich (2026) · Get involved Slack community and newsletter (publicai.substack.com); Weekly online seminar seasons (2026 season August to September) and quarterly community calls; Open-source contributions to the Inference Utility and the network's site via GitHub; its definition document is publicly editable

Note The lines between PAINT, Metagov's Public AI project and the Public AI Inference Utility are blurry, since they share people, a fiscal sponsor and links, so the map may count the same work twice. Its site names no leadership or governance structure. Its earliest events date from 2023, but it gives no founding date. Its case rests on public access and accountability, not catastrophic risk. Some proposals in its orbit, such as a public 'Airbus for AI' frontier lab, raise their own race and power questions.

SAG-AFTRA (Screen Actors Guild-American Federation of Television and Radio Artists) Adjacent

Membership body · Los Angeles, USA · founded 2012 · also draws on Law, society

The US union of about 160,000 actors, broadcasters, recording artists and other media professionals, formed in 2012 by the merger of SAG and AFTRA, with national offices in Los Angeles and New York. Its AI framework rests on consent, compensation and control over performances. The 2023 TV/Theatrical contract set consent and pay rules for digital replicas, and the 2026 agreement, ratified on 4 June 2026 by 91.42%, adds rules to keep 'synthetic performers' the exception. It also works on AI law: its president testified before a House Judiciary subcommittee in July 2026, it backs the federal NO FAKES Act, and it publicised a California law, in force by September 2026, requiring disclosure of AI-generated performances.

It has turned public concern about AI copying and replacing people into binding contract terms on consent and likeness, a working model of a membership body governing AI use from the bottom up. Its digital-replica rules are an early template for protecting human identity and presence as generative models improve.

Works on Power, Justice · Key work 2026 TV/Theatrical Agreement, with new restrictions on synthetic performers (2026); A.I. framework (consent, compensation, control) and A.I. policy timeline 2022-2026 (2023); 2023 TV/Theatrical contract: consent and compensation rules for digital replicas (2023) · Get involved Membership is open to qualifying performers and media professionals; Public AI resources page with policy timeline, podcasts and contract bulletins

Note It represents its members' interests: the focus is replacement, likeness and pay, not AI safety. Its website blocks automated fetching, so details were read in a browser. The NO FAKES Act position comes from the roster and SAG-AFTRA's long-standing public support, not a 2026 page read this session.

Software Heritage (incl. CodeCommons) Adjacent

Academic · Paris, France · founded 2016 · also draws on Law, society

Software Heritage is a public archive of publicly available source code, set up in 2016 under Inria with UNESCO's support. It gives every archived file a persistent identifier (SWHID), so provenance can be traced. CodeCommons is a two-year, roughly €5 million consortium funded by France 2030 through Bpifrance and led from Inria with CEA, Tweag and Italian universities. It is turning the archive into a curated, metadata-rich dataset for training code models. Access is conditional on 2023 principles: models trained on the archive must be openly licensed, training data must be documented, and authors can opt out.

It applies archival provenance to training data. Persistent identifiers make it possible to check what went into a model and to attribute generated code. It also offers a working template for a training-data commons that sets conditions on model builders, a governance lever that mainstream AI safety rarely builds.

Works on Power, Justice · Key work Software Heritage statement on large language models for code (transparency, open licensing of trained models, opt-out) (2023); CodeCommons: a traceable, curated code dataset for AI training (2025); Software Heritage 2026 Symposium and Summit at UNESCO (10th anniversary; theme on transparent AI) (2026) · Get involved Staff roles: Head of Communications and DevOps Engineer listed in 2026 (softwareheritage.org/jobs); Annual symposium and summit with UNESCO in Paris, with online attendance (January 2026); Ambassadors programme, profiled on the blog through 2026

Note CodeCommons is a time-limited project, roughly 2025-26, and its own site shows little news after 2024. Whether the curated dataset and opt-out system have been released is unverified.
