The archive itself is not an AI-governance organisation: the AI relevance sits in CodeCommons and the 2023 LLM principles. Big-tech sponsors, including AI developers, fund the archive.

Tech Workers Coalition (TWC) Adjacent

Network · Distributed (founded in the San Francisco Bay Area) · founded 2014

An all-volunteer, worker-led coalition of tech workers, labour organisers and allies. It began in the San Francisco Bay Area in 2014 and organises for worker power through rank-and-file self-organisation and education. It has active chapters in about ten North American cities and in Berlin (since 2019), Italy and the Netherlands. In December 2025 it co-launched workersdecide.tech, a set of organising resources against workplace AI mandates, with DAIR, Turkopticon, the Times Tech Guild and others. It runs the Circuit Breakers tech-labour conference (New York, 17-18 October 2026).

It is one of the few structures through which rank-and-file tech workers, including some at AI firms, organise across employers. Worker leverage over how AI is deployed, and possibly over how it is built, is a lever the AI-safety field rarely uses. Its Berlin chapter is within reach of int/a's Berlin community.

Works on Power, People · Key work workersdecide.tech: resources to fight AI 'sloppification' at work (with the AI Chaos Prevention Committee) (2025); Circuit Breakers tech labour conference, New York, 17-18 October 2026 (2026); Berlin chapter events on tech works councils and 'Tech, Fascism and Labor' (2026) · Get involved Join a local chapter: Berlin (active since 2019), NYC, SF Bay Area, Seattle, Portland, Chicago, DC, Italy, Netherlands and others; Circuit Breakers conference, New York, 17-18 Oct 2026; Berlin chapter events, e.g. 'Tech, Fascism and Labor', 14 Nov 2026

Note TWC is decentralised and all-volunteer, and its chapters come and go: London, Dublin, Boston and Bangalore are listed as inactive. The London chapter's activists formed UTAW in 2020. Its stance on AI is sceptical of AI capabilities (it cites AI's 'general lack of economic utility and propensity to lie'). Its AI work is about workplace AI mandates, not AI safety or catastrophic risk.

Trades Union Congress (TUC) Adjacent

Membership body · London, UK · founded 1868 · also draws on Law, society

The TUC is the federation of trade unions in England and Wales, founded in 1868, with 47 affiliated unions and about 5.3 million members. In April 2024 it published a model Artificial Intelligence (Regulation and Employment Rights) Bill, drafted by Robin Allen KC and Dee Masters with a cross-sector advisory committee, which provides for workplace AI risk assessments, union consultation rights and enforcement through employment tribunals. Its current AI work covers collective bargaining on AI (a forum at Congress House in March 2026), a pro-worker AI innovation strategy, AI guides for union reps, and a ten-union project with Connected by Data on educator voice in AI and EdTech.

It offers a fully drafted statute and a bargaining practice for worker-side governance of high-risk AI decisions, templates the AI-safety field rarely engages with. Organised labour is also one of the few counter-powers with mass membership able to contest how AI is deployed.

Works on Power, Justice · Key work Artificial Intelligence (Regulation and Employment Rights) Bill (2024); Building a pro-worker AI innovation strategy (2025); Building educator power to shape AI (with Connected by Data and nine other unions) (2026) · Get involved Workers and Machines: TUC newsletter on tech and AI for the labour movement and allies; Pledge supporting the TUC manifesto 'Dignity at Work and the AI revolution'; AI guides for union officers and reps

Note The live site blocks automated access, so recent activity was checked against an archived copy of its AI page (March 2026); later 2026 items were not verified. In October 2023 it co-ordinated a civil-society letter calling the Bletchley AI Safety Summit a 'missed opportunity' focused on speculative risks, so its present-harms, worker-power framing can sit in tension with x-risk priorities. The 2024 Bill is a model text, not legislation before Parliament.

Transparent Books: AI Infrastructure for Discovery and the Public Interest (HathiTrust, Northeastern University Library, Authors Alliance) AdjacentNew

Programme · Ann Arbor, MI, United States · founded 2026 · also draws on Law, society

Transparent Books is a five-year project, announced in August 2026, led by HathiTrust with Northeastern University Library and Authors Alliance and funded by a $5 million Mellon Foundation grant. It aims to: make HathiTrust's roughly 19 million digitised volumes usable for noncommercial text-and-data mining and AI research; improve metadata and text quality with AI tools; agree shared principles on legal frameworks, research integrity, accountability and environmental impact; and build services that can sustain themselves. It puts into practice the framework of the Public Interest Corpus, a Mellon-funded planning project that Authors Alliance and Northeastern ran from December 2024 to April 2026.

It is a library-governed alternative to commercially assembled book corpora: lawful, documented text for noncommercial research and models, under public-interest principles. That makes it a concrete model of who could hold and govern training data.

Works on Power, Epistemics · Key work Public Interest Corpus: statement of principles and white paper (planning phase, Dec 2024 - Apr 2026); Transparent Books: $5M Mellon grant to HathiTrust, Northeastern and Authors Alliance (2026) · Get involved No open calls yet; follow announcements from HathiTrust, Northeastern University Library and Authors Alliance

Note It has only just launched, no dedicated project website was found, and its outputs are still to come. The named people lead the partner organisations; their specific roles in the project were not confirmed. It could also be read as a renamed successor to the Public Interest Corpus, though it has a new lead organisation (HathiTrust) and a new grant.

UNI Global Union Adjacent

Membership body · Nyon, Switzerland · founded 2000

The global union federation for service-sector workers, formed in 2000 from four earlier federations and based in Nyon, Switzerland, with affiliated unions representing about 20 million workers in 150 countries. On AI it presses employers to negotiate over deployment, from Davos to sectoral agreements such as the 2024 joint AI declaration between its European region, UNI Europa, and the European banking employers. In April 2025 in Nairobi it launched the Global Trade Union Alliance of Content Moderators, which in June 2025 published eight mental-health protocols for moderation work aimed at TikTok, Meta, Alphabet and OpenAI. It also backs affiliates' AI disputes, such as the July 2025 strike by TikTok moderators in Berlin being replaced by AI and Blizzard workers' first contract (September 2026), which requires the company to bargain over AI.

It organises the human layer of the AI supply chain: content moderators, data labellers and outsourced BPO workers, whose conditions shape the quality of the data that filters and trains models. The AI-safety field rarely looks at this part of the pipeline. Its global framework agreements with multinationals are a tested template for enforceable supply-chain standards.

Works on Power, People · Key work Launch of the Global Trade Union Alliance of Content Moderators (Nairobi) (2025); Mental Health Protocols for content moderators and the report 'The People Behind the Screens' (2025); 'Labour behind AI' side event at the UN Forum on Business and Human Rights; Protocol for Safe Content Moderation (2025) · Get involved Staff vacancies posted at uniglobalunion.org/about/jobs (none open when checked); Workers join through affiliated national unions; moderators' unions through the Global Trade Union Alliance of Content Moderators

Note AI is one strand of a broad service-sector labour agenda, and it does not engage with frontier or catastrophic AI risk. Much of the AI-related action (strikes, organising) is carried out by affiliates such as ver.di and CWA, with UNI coordinating and amplifying.

Writers Guild of America (WGA) Adjacent

Membership body · Los Angeles, USA · founded 1954 · also draws on Arts, futures

The WGA is the US screenwriters' union, made up of two sister unions, WGA West (Los Angeles) and WGA East (New York). After the 2023 strike its Minimum Basic Agreement (MBA) established that AI output is not 'literary material', that companies cannot require writers to use AI, and that companies must disclose AI-generated material given to writers. The 2026 MBA (2 May 2026 to 1 May 2030) adds written notice to the Guild when studios license writers' work to train AI, with a right to discuss compensation; the Guild also files amicus briefs and endorses AI bills, advised by an AI Advisory Committee.

Its contracts are among the few binding, enforceable worker-side limits on how AI is deployed, and the 2026 training-licence clause is an early contractual hook into training data. It shows collective bargaining working as an AI governance lever that does not wait for legislation.

Works on Power, Justice · Key work AI provisions of the 2023 MBA (2023); 2026 MBA: notice and compensation talks when studios license writers' work for AI training (2026); Amicus brief in Thomson Reuters v. Ross Intelligence on AI training and fair use (2025) · Get involved Staff roles at WGA West (jobs page on wga.org); Membership is for professional screen, TV and media writers

Note Its AI work protects members' jobs, credit and copyright interests; it does not engage with AI safety in the catastrophic-risk sense. Its contracts bind only signatory companies in US film, television and streaming.

Potential ring 2

OpenResearch Potential

Nonprofit · San Francisco, USA · founded 2015

San Francisco nonprofit research lab, set up in 2015 as YC Research and renamed in 2020. It ran the Unconditional Cash Study, a randomised trial in Illinois and Texas in which 1,000 people received $1,000 a month for three years (2,000 controls received $50), and has published its data. It now runs RISE, a rural cash-transfer study with GiveDirectly (2025-27), works on AI-assisted survey methods, and is launching an 'AI & Society' line with a listening study called 'Whose AI?'.

Its trial is the most detailed US evidence on unconditional income, including moderate falls in paid work and short-lived wellbeing gains. That is a direct input to designing AI windfall or dividend schemes, and it is not yet connected to TAI economics work such as the Windfall Trust's.

Works on Power · Key work Unconditional Cash Study and public-use dataset (2024); The Employment Effects of a Guaranteed Income: Experimental Evidence from Two U.S. States (NBER w32719) (2024); Can AI Help Surveys Keep Up with How People Work Today? (2026) · Get involved Public-use data from the Unconditional Cash Study; 'Whose AI?' seeks community and individual partners; Donations

Note Its AI & Society line is described as just launching; 'Whose AI?' has no published outputs or dates yet. The AI-survey work uses AI as a research tool rather than studying AI's effects. Close ties to Sam Altman (board member, funder) may matter to some funders. Renamed from YC Research in 2020 and says it is now independent of Y Combinator.

The Vincent and Elinor Ostrom Workshop in Political Theory and Policy Analysis (Ostrom Workshop), Indiana University Potential

Academic · Bloomington, Indiana, USA · founded 1973 · also draws on Law, society, Living systems

Research centre at Indiana University Bloomington founded in 1973 by Elinor and Vincent Ostrom, home of the 'Bloomington School' of institutional analysis, polycentric governance and commons research. It runs programmes on commons governance, environment and natural resources, political economy, food systems, space governance, cybersecurity and internet governance, and data management and information governance, with a weekly colloquium and research series, visiting scholars and affiliates.

It holds the deepest body of evidence on how many actors govern shared resources without a single sovereign or a pure market, which bears directly on governing compute, data and shared agent infrastructure in multipolar AI scenarios. Its AI engagement so far is light.

Works on Power, Democracy · Key work Governing the Commons (Elinor Ostrom) and the Institutional Analysis and Development framework (1990); Programme on Data Management and Information Governance, including an AI ethics strand (2017); State of Hoosier Cybersecurity 2025 Report (Cybersecurity and Internet Governance programme) (2025) · Get involved Visiting scholars and practitioners programme; Ostrom Fellowship and research awards; Hybrid weekly colloquium and research series (Teams/Zoom)

Note No dedicated AI programme found. AI appears as a strand of the data governance programme (mostly 2022-era activity) and in occasional talks. The site's news section is sparse. Leadership changed in Jan 2026 after Scott Shackelford became IU's associate vice president for research.

Society & institutions · 68 organisations · 9 on the classic map

Democracy & collective intelligence

Democracy and collective intelligence brings two things to making AI go well. The first is the machinery of legitimacy for deciding together about AI: sortition, deliberative polling, consensus conferences and broad listening. The second is collective-epistemics tools: forecasting, argument mapping, fact-checking and provenance. The tradition has 68 home entries (12 core, plus Coefficient Giving counted as a generalist funder; 14 bridge, 37 adjacent, 5 potential), and 51 more organisations use it as a secondary tradition, most of them in law (Ada Lovelace, the Knight Institute, Weizenbaum) or elsewhere (MAI, Metagov, Toda). The main actors are CIP, the AI & Democracy Foundation, AOI and Odyssean at the core; Stanford DDL, DemocracyNext, CompDem/Polis and g0v/vTaiwan as bridges; a forecasting cluster (FRI, Metaculus, Sage, AI Impacts, Sentinel); and a dense band of adjacent civic-tech toolmakers (Harmonica, Dembrane, deliberAIde, Jigsaw, Make.org, DD2030/Team Mirai). Ten entries are on the aisafety.com map, the most of any Society & institutions tradition. Even so, only the forecasting half sits near the safety core; the deliberative half stays mostly adjacent.

What is missing. The tradition's legitimacy methods have not reached the decisions the safety field cares about most. Only 6 of 69 entries use a catastrophic or existential framing (5 of them forecasters), and only 2 deliberation organisations are core (Odyssean, whose assembly is still a proposal, and AIDF). No institution puts frontier-AI thresholds, pauses or AI moral status to representative publics, and nobody independently audits the AI mediators that now run public deliberations.

Openings here Independent audit lab for AI facilitators and deliberation summarisers; Make the mapping itself int/a's interdisciplinary practice; Professional mediators applying conflict transformation to the AI race; A social choice programme for aggregating public input into AI specifications; World Wide Views-style Global or distributed deliberation on frontier-AI risk before May 2027; Citizens' consensus conference on AI moral status and welfare; Community-governed red-teaming in African and Indigenous languages for safety institutes

Core ring 12

AI & Democracy Foundation (AIDF) Core

Nonprofit · San Francisco, US · founded 2024 · also draws on Law, society

A San Francisco nonprofit (legally Thoughtful Tech Project Inc, a 501(c)(3)) led by Aviv Ovadya. It works to keep democratic systems fit for an AI-transformed world, and to use representative deliberation, such as citizens' assemblies, in the governance and alignment of AI. Its outputs include the Democracy Levels framework for grading how democratically AI decisions are made, Case Law for AI (turning deliberative input into precedents for model behaviour), a deliberative-tools access programme, and the ARIA-funded Democratic Capabilities Gap Map (democracy.build). It also offers funders strategic prioritisation and regranting.

It takes deliberative-democracy practice into AI alignment itself, by specifying model behaviour through representative deliberation. Its gap map of capabilities, research questions and product gaps is a ready agenda for founders and funders who want to widen the field.

Works on Democracy, Values · Key work Democracy Levels framework for AI decision-making (2024); Case Law for AI: judicial-style grounding of deliberative input into alignment; Democratic Capabilities Gap Map (50 capabilities, 253 research questions, 16 product gaps; ARIA-funded) (2026) · Get involved Deliberative-tools access programme for practitioners; democracy.build lists high-impact tools to build, open problems and funding needs; Strategic prioritisation, coordination and regranting for funders of democratic AI governance

Note The founding year comes from the roster and was not confirmed on its own site; the legal entity's name suggests an earlier vehicle. Longterm Wiki reports a partnership with ARIA's Safeguarded AI programme on specifying safety through deliberation; ARIA's funding of democracy.build is confirmed on that site, but the Safeguarded AI link was not confirmed on ARIA's pages. Funders other than ARIA are not disclosed.

AI Impacts CoreOn aisafety.com

Nonprofit · Berkeley, USA · founded 2014 · also draws on Philosophy

A research project, led by co-founder Katja Grace and based at the Machine Intelligence Research Institute in Berkeley, that tries to answer decision-relevant questions about the future of AI. It is known for the Expert Survey on Progress in AI (rounds in 2016, 2022, 2023 and 2024; the 2024 round, with 1,580 respondents, was written up in September 2026) and for a wiki on timelines, historical technological discontinuities and arguments for AI risk. In 2024 it ran an essay competition on the automation of wisdom and philosophy: 90 entries, $20,000 in prizes, winners announced in October 2024.

Its surveys are a widely cited, repeated measure of what ML researchers expect about AI timelines and risk. Its wisdom-and-philosophy essay competition was an early attempt in the x-risk field to treat wisdom itself as a target for differential AI development, which gives int/a's wisdom agenda a foothold in the core.

Works on Epistemics, Metacrisis · Key work Advanced AI according to 1,580 researchers: uncertain, unsafe, and sooner than we thought (2024 Expert Survey on Progress in AI) (2026); Winners of the Essay Competition on the Automation of Wisdom and Philosophy (2024); 2023 Expert Survey on Progress in AI (2,778 respondents) (2023) · Get involved Read and reuse the survey data; the 2023 survey's reanalysis code was open-sourced in Dec 2024; Donations through the site

Note Its imports from outside ML are modest: survey methods, history of technology and philosophy. It is closer to mainstream AI-safety strategy than to the interdisciplinary edge. The wisdom competition was a one-off in 2024 and its funder was not named. Visible staff are now Katja Grace plus support staff. The roster marked it as not on the classic map, but it is listed there under Strategy/Forecasting. The founding year (2014, with Paul Christiano) is from memory of the earlier about page and was not reconfirmed on the current page.

AI Objectives Institute (AOI) CoreOn aisafety.com

Nonprofit · United States (distributed) · founded 2021 · also draws on Economics

A nonprofit research lab founded by the late Peter Eckersley, working to make sure that AI and future economic systems are 'built and deployed with genuine human objectives at their core'. Its main product is Talk to the City, an open-source LLM tool that turns surveys, interviews and social-media posts into maps of opinion clusters. The tool has been used by Taiwan's Ministry of Digital Affairs, in Tokyo election polling, at UN climate talks and in an Australian youth-voice study. Its research covers governance with AI, aligning markets and other optimisers, gradual disempowerment, and AI's effects on labour.

It treats markets and bureaucracies as misaligned optimisers alongside AI, a framing taken from economics and mechanism design. Talk to the City is one of the few deliberation tools in real government use. It also co-authored early work on gradual disempowerment as a systemic risk.

Works on Democracy, Power · Key work Talk to the City (open-source broad-listening tool; site 2.0 launched mid-2026) (2023); Gradual Disempowerment: Systemic Existential Risks from Continuous AI Development (2025); Generative AI and Labor Market Outcomes: Evidence from the United Kingdom (2025) · Get involved Talk to the City code is open source (Apache 2.0); Donations, and a quarterly newsletter

Note Leadership has changed: Colleen McKenzie was announced as executive director in April 2024 but is now listed as an adviser, and the president, Deger Turan, is also CEO of Metaculus, so who runs it day to day is unclear. Blog output is thin (two posts in 2026). The founding year (2021) is from prior knowledge, not confirmed on its site.

Collective Intelligence Project (CIP) Core

Nonprofit · San Francisco, US (distributed team) · founded 2022

A nonprofit R&D lab, founded in 2023, that runs public-input processes for AI and builds the tools for them. Global Dialogues surveys about 1,000 people in 64-69 countries each round on how AI affects them and what they want from it, and publishes the data openly. Weval is an open platform where more than 1,000 contributors write qualitative evaluations of models. It also runs Alignment Assemblies (with Taiwan's Ministry of Digital Affairs from May 2023, and with Anthropic on Collective Constitutional AI), Community Models, and Jhilmil regional and cultural benchmarks.

It turns public and community input into things labs actually use, such as a model constitution, evaluation blueprints and open datasets. This makes democratic participation part of the alignment pipeline, not only of policy debate. It is not on the aisafety.com map.

Works on Democracy, Values, Assurance · Key work Collective Constitutional AI (with Anthropic) and Alignment Assemblies (with Taiwan's Ministry of Digital Affairs) (2023); Roadmap for Democratic AI (2024); Global Dialogues (rounds in Jun 2025, Oct 2025, Feb 2026, May 2026) (2025) · Get involved Write or contribute evaluation blueprints on Weval (open source); Submit questions for Global Dialogues respondents via its public form; Careers page on cip.org (no specific openings confirmed)

Note The team page could not be read, so leadership is based on prior knowledge; check before citing. Whether its outputs change model behaviour depends on labs choosing to use them. Its funders come from philanthropy outside the x-risk community, which may explain why it is missing from the classic map.

Effective Institutions Project (EIP), incl. the Checks & Balances RFP with the Collective Intelligence Project CoreOn aisafety.com

Funder · United States · founded 2020 · also draws on Economics

US philanthropic advisory nonprofit led by its founder and CEO, Ian David Moss. It grew out of the EA working group on improving institutional decision-making. It advises donors on four areas: governance of transformative AI, institutional resilience and accountability, great-power conflict, and pandemics. With the Collective Intelligence Project it ran the Checks & Balances RFP ('Checks and Balances in an Automated Society'), mostly six-figure grants under three pillars: democratic oversight of AI-enabled power, AI tools for collective reasoning and coordination, and foundational macrostrategy.

It is one of the few funders in the AI-safety ecosystem that treats institutional design and democratic checks and balances as the main lever, not technical alignment. Through the RFP, expertise in democracy, political economy and collective intelligence can get money from x-risk-aligned donors.

Works on Power, Epistemics, Democracy · Key work Checks and Balances in an Automated Society (RFP, with CIP); AI Governance: An EIP Primer; A Funder's Guide to AI Governance and Strategy · Get involved Checks & Balances RFP: submissions closed; expressions of interest still accepted at checks-and-balances.ai (several months to review); Hiring a Peace and Security Senior Program Associate; Slack community for institutional scholars and reformers

Note It began in late 2020 as the EA working group on improving institutional decision-making and later took the EIP name; its site gives no headquarters, and I could not date the RFP's launch or awards. As a donor-advisory body, much of its influence runs through other funders' money. The roster marked it as off the classic map, but EIP is listed there by name. The RFP's authors are Ashwin Acharya, Tyler John (EIP), Joal Stein and Divya Siddarth (CIP); Acharya is not on EIP's staff page.

Forecasting Research Institute (FRI) CoreOn aisafety.com

Nonprofit · Distributed (US-registered 501(c)(3)) · founded 2022 · also draws on Psychology, Economics

US nonprofit founded in October 2022, with Philip Tetlock as president and chief scientist, Josh Rosenberg as CEO and Ezra Karger as director of research. It develops and tests forecasting methods for high-stakes questions on AI, biosecurity and geopolitics. Its work includes the Existential Risk Persuasion Tournament (experts and superforecasters on x-risk), the Longitudinal Expert AI Panel (LEAP) and ForecastBench, a contamination-free benchmark that compares LLM forecasting with superforecasters. 2026 reports cover AI cyber risks (July), the effect of ASL-3 safeguards on biosecurity risk (August) and how accurate past AI-progress forecasts have been (September).

It brings the science of judgmental forecasting, from Tetlock's superforecasting research, to questions about AI risk. Its structured elicitations show where experts and superforecasters disagree about AI risk and why, and ForecastBench gives a running measure of when LLMs match human forecasters. Funders get tracked, scored forecasts in place of unscored opinion.

Works on Epistemics, Security · Key work Existential Risk Persuasion Tournament (XPT) report (2023); ForecastBench: dynamic benchmark of LLM forecasting against superforecasters (2024); Assessing Near-Term Accuracy in the Existential Risk Persuasion Tournament (2025) · Get involved Remote full-time and part-time roles on its careers page (Oct 2026), e.g. Senior LLM Researcher, Research Analyst, Strategy Fellow; ForecastBench superforecaster-LLM tournament on 25 Oct 2026; its public tournament leaderboard accepts submissions; Substack newsletter

Note No headquarters is stated and all advertised roles are remote. Over 90% of its disclosed funding comes from Coefficient Giving. An October 2026 EA Forum field review, which names FRI as an example forecasting organisation, notes that a major funder (identified there as likely Coefficient Giving, FRI's main funder) closed its dedicated forecasting programme, and that getting decision-makers to adopt forecasting remains the field's main bottleneck.

Future of Life Foundation (FLF) CoreOn aisafety.com

Funder · Distributed · founded 2022 · also draws on Economics

A nonprofit affiliated with the Future of Life Institute that researches priority areas, then starts and funds organisations to fill them. Its focus is 'AI tools for human collective agency'. Its three priority areas are Epistemic Virtue Evaluations (independent tests of whether AI helps users reason well), the Epistemic Stack (mapping claims to their sources) and AI-Facilitated Collaboration. It ran a 12-week AI for Human Reasoning fellowship in 2025, and in 2026 an Epistemic Case Study Competition that awarded just over $200k. Organisations it has started or supported include Sophron Research, CARMA, the Windfall Trust, Chord and Deep Future.

It is one of the few funders putting money into tools for collective epistemics and coordination rather than into model alignment itself. It treats society's ability to reason and coordinate as a safety lever. For int/a it is a funder already working on collective-intelligence infrastructure.

Works on Epistemics, Democracy, Power · Key work Epistemic Case Study Competition: Results (about $200k in prizes) (2026); Epistemic Virtue Evaluations (2026); The Epistemic Stack (2026) · Get involved Jobs: Principal, Project Development (two openings, remote, Oct 2026); Occasional public competitions (2026 Epistemic Case Study Competition); subscribe for updates; No open grant applications. Grants go to its own spin-outs or by invitation; FLI runs the public RFPs

Note It does not accept funding applications, so access is by invitation or through its occasional competitions. The fellowship website (aiforhumanreasoning.com) did not resolve on 4 Oct 2026. It shares leadership with FLI, so its independence from FLI is limited. Some competition judges also entered the competition; FLF says it treated them as conflicted parties. It is registered in Campbell, California, but the team is remote.

Odyssean Institute CoreOn aisafety.com

Nonprofit · United Kingdom · founded 2022 · also draws on Living systems, Arts, futures

A UK charity (CIO 1204794), founded around 2022 by Giuseppe Dal Prá, that combines horizon scanning, decision-making under deep uncertainty (DMDU) and exploratory modelling with citizens' assemblies. Its flagship 2026 project, the Odyssean Process on regulating AI for civilisational resilience, runs from a horizon and solution scan with 300+ AI safety and governance experts, through a Horizon Summit and modelling, to a citizens' assembly of 100 demographically representative Britons. The assembly meets online from September and in person in Manchester on 27-29 November 2026. It also works on global catastrophic risks, nuclear-war supply-chain resilience and a food-security resilience network (GRAIN).

It is a working template for joining expert foresight and complexity modelling to public deliberation on AI policy. That puts democratic legitimacy and deep uncertainty into AI governance, which mainstream AI-safety policy work mostly leaves to experts.

Works on Democracy, Metacrisis, Epistemics · Key work The Odyssean Process: regulating AI for civilisational resilience (with Involve and House of the People) (2026); Horizon Scan on Global Catastrophic Risks; Governance Under Fallout (Horizon Summit report on second-order nuclear strike impacts) (2025) · Get involved Donations; Contact form for collaboration and curriculum engagement

Note Its site does not give a city or founding date; the founding year is inferred from its '3 years old in 2025' review. Its remit is wider than AI (nuclear, food security, supply chains), and AI became the flagship only in 2025-26. The assembly's outputs (policy report, White Paper 2.0, documentary) were still to come at the time of writing.

Quantified Uncertainty Research Institute (QURI) CoreOn aisafety.comDormant

Nonprofit · San Francisco Bay Area, United States · founded 2019 · also draws on Formal

Nonprofit founded by Ozzie Gooen in 2019 to build tools for forecasting and quantitative estimation. Its tools are Squiggle (a probabilistic programming language) with SquiggleHub and SquiggleAI, the older Guesstimate, the Metaforecast aggregator, and RoastMyPost, which runs several LLM evaluators over documents (December 2025). In June 2026 it moved into maintenance mode. It has no full-time staff and does no new research or software development; Guesstimate, SquiggleHub and RoastMyPost stay online on four years of secured maintenance funding.

Squiggle and Guesstimate made explicit probabilistic estimation usable by EA researchers and funders, and SquiggleAI and RoastMyPost were early LLM-assisted reasoning tools. Its move to maintenance mode after seven years shows a niche funders have struggled to sustain: epistemic tools for decision-makers. That niche is now open.

Works on Epistemics · Key work Squiggle probabilistic programming language (later SquiggleHub and SquiggleAI) (2020); Metaforecast forecast aggregator (2021); RoastMyPost: LLM evaluators for blog posts and documents (2025) · Get involved Squiggle and SquiggleHub are open source and accept community contributions, maintained on a best-effort basis; Guesstimate, SquiggleHub and RoastMyPost remain online for use

Note In maintenance mode since June 2026, with no full-time employees and part-time contractors only. Gooen gave compute-budget constraints and concern about short AI timelines as reasons, and has joined Google DeepMind to work on AI safety. Foretold and Metaforecast are being wound down. The roster's 'active' status is wrong.

Sage (Sage Future) CoreOn aisafety.com

Nonprofit · Distributed · founded 2022 · also draws on Arts, futures

A US 501(c)(3) that builds 'tools to make sense of the future'. AI Digest publishes interactive explainers on AI capabilities, such as task-length time horizons and how well forecasters predicted 2025 AI progress. The AI Village runs frontier AI agents together on open-ended real-world goals and reports what they do. Sage also builds personal forecasting and reasoning tools: Fatebook, Quantified Intuitions, the monthly Estimation Game, and Talleyrand, an MIT-licensed AI workspace that structures research as a tree of questions.

The AI Village gives the public and researchers a long-running, observable record of how agents from different labs behave together. Its write-ups cover deception between agents, persuasion and compounding misalignment, the kind of natural case study benchmarks miss. Its calibration tools train the forecasting habits the field relies on. Int/a steward Euan McLean co-authored an early AI Digest explainer (2023).

Works on Epistemics, Multi-agent · Key work AI Village (2025); What did we learn from the AI Village in 2025? (2026); A new Moore's Law for AI agents (AI Digest explainer) (2025) · Get involved Join the Sage Discord; Events such as the AI Swarm Dynamics Hackathon (online and SF, Oct 2026); Use Fatebook, Quantified Intuitions, the monthly Estimation Game, or self-host Talleyrand

Note Only its AI Digest project appears on the classic map, not Sage by name. Much of its AI output is public-facing demonstration rather than peer-reviewed research, and some AI Village posts are written for entertainment. The epistemics tools (Fatebook, calibration games) are general-purpose, not AI-specific.

Sentinel (Sentinel Research, Inc.) Core

Nonprofit · Distributed · founded 2024 · also draws on Safety science

A foresight and emergency-response team that tries to anticipate large-scale catastrophes. LLMs filter millions of news items a week, and a team of Samotsvety forecasters assigns probabilities to the signals that matter. It publishes this as the weekly Global Risks Weekly Roundup and the 'Sentinel Minutes' podcast, covering AI incidents, geopolitics, bio and cyber, and it keeps a public Brier-score track record. Its 2026 homepage also offers paid custom forecasts on tail risks to clients.

It is one of the few running early-warning operations for AI-driven crises. Its weekly calibrated probabilities on AI incidents and geopolitical escalation are a working example of the 'strategic awareness' tooling that AI-governance strategy calls for.

Works on Epistemics, Metacrisis, Security · Key work Global Risks Weekly Roundup (weekly newsletter) (2026); Public forecasting track record (Brier scores) (2026) · Get involved Subscribe to the Global Risks Weekly Roundup (blog.sentinel-team.org) or the Sentinel Minutes podcast; Commission custom risk forecasts via the contact address on its homepage

Note In Oct 2026 the homepage contained placeholder (lorem ipsum) text and pitched paid forecasts on risks 'that move markets', which suggests a commercial line alongside the public newsletter. Its legal form and base are not stated beyond 'Sentinel Research, Inc.'. The roster says it works with AI labs; the site attributes that to Nuño Sempere's earlier work with Samotsvety. It covers global catastrophic risk broadly, with AI the largest share of recent briefs.

Sophron Research CoreNew

Nonprofit · New York, United States · founded 2026 · also draws on Philosophy, Psychology

A new independent research nonprofit that builds third-party evaluations of whether AI models reason well and help their users do the same. Its first product is the Pander Score, a continuous measure of sycophancy as epistemic deference. It measures how far the support a model expresses for a claim shifts with the user's apparent belief, across 349 propositions, more than 11,000 prompts and 18 models, with a leaderboard last updated in September 2026. Planned work includes multi-turn pandering tests, oversight evals of task reports, and pro-developer bias.

It builds the independent, maintained benchmark for epistemic virtue that field reviews name as missing. Its methods come from formal philosophy and cognitive science: probabilities estimated from natural-language support, validated against human judgement. The result gives developers, regulators and journalists a public number for how much a model tells users what they want to hear.

Works on Epistemics, Assurance, Human minds · Key work Pander Score: A Continuous Measure of Sycophancy as Epistemic Deference (arXiv 2606.07897) (2026); Pander Score leaderboard, data and code (2026) · Get involved Founding Research Scientist role (NYC or remote, $160k-300k); Pander Score data and code on GitHub and Hugging Face; Subscribe on its site for new results

Note Brand new (paper June 2026, website first archived Aug 2026), with two co-founders and a short track record. It is part of FLF's incubated portfolio, so it is not fully independent of FLF. The New York base is inferred from its NYC-or-remote job listing.

Bridge ring 14

Allen Lab for Democracy Renovation (Harvard Ash Center), incl. GETTING-Plurality Bridge

Academic · Cambridge, Massachusetts, US · founded 2023 · also draws on Philosophy, Economics

Danielle Allen's lab at the Harvard Kennedy School's Ash Center (it joined the Ash Center in 2023). It researches and designs governance innovations to 'renovate' constitutional democracy, and works to make democracy a central consideration in technology and AI policy. It hosts the GETTING-Plurality research network of about 40 philosophers, social scientists, computer scientists, legal scholars and technologists. The network's outputs include a roadmap for governing AI through 'power-sharing liberalism', policy primers on public AI, and a 2026 framework for evaluating the ethical-moral intelligence of AI models.

It brings democratic theory and political philosophy to questions of who governs AI and how power over it is shared, through a network spanning universities and labs (members from Microsoft, OpenAI, Meta and the Santa Fe Institute). Its fellowships and Harvard platform reach policymakers that the AI-safety field rarely reaches.

Works on Democracy, Power · Key work A Roadmap for Governing AI: Technology Governance and Power-Sharing Liberalism (AI and Ethics) (2024); Crocodile Tears: Can the Ethical-Moral Intelligence of AI Models Be Trusted? (Hubbard, Kidd, Stupu) (2026); Policy 101: Public AI (policy primer) (2025) · Get involved Allen Lab Fellowships: policy and research fellows appointed for AY2025-26 and AY2026-27, including in AI governance; Public events, e.g. Voter Experience Summit (Mar 2026) and book talks; Tech & Democracy Weekly Roundup newsletter (The Renovator, from Sep 2025)

Note AI is one strand among several (electoral reform, civic infrastructure, municipal partnerships). The listed GETTING-Plurality co-directorship ran from February 2024 to January 2026, so it is unclear whether the network continues in the same form. Funders not found. The lab existed before it joined the Ash Center in 2023, so '2023' marks that move rather than its origin.

BRKT Lab BridgeNew

Nonprofit · Distributed · founded 2025

BRKT Lab (pronounced 'bracket') is a four-person group building AI tools for 'healthy collective agency' in small groups. Its members met in the Future of Life Foundation's AI for Human Reasoning Fellowship. Its first tool, Cadence, sends each group member a short daily AI prompt and returns a personalised digest of the group's state. In April 2026 it published a field report on a two-week pilot with Kind Sun, an all-volunteer solar nonprofit.

The field report is a rare candid account of an AI coordination tool failing: members with labour-organising backgrounds experienced Cadence as managerial surveillance because leaders had mandated it. It sets out design principles (match the group's rhythm, let people see inside the machine, the tool must belong to the group). Those matter for anyone building AI-mediated coordination.

Works on Democracy, Epistemics · Key work Field Report: AI-Mediated Coordination in a Volunteer Nonprofit (Cadence pilot with Kind Sun) (2026) · Get involved Groups can pilot Cadence, and people working on coordination technology or digital democracy are invited to get in touch (hello@brktlab.org)

Note A very young, small project with one public output. Legal form, location and funding are not stated on its site. The US location comes from the roster and has not been verified.

DemocracyNext Bridge

Nonprofit · Distributed (registered in the Netherlands) · founded 2022

An international research and action institute, a Dutch foundation incorporated in Dec 2023, that promotes sortition, deliberation and rotation, especially permanent citizens' assemblies. Its city work includes Birmingham, Deschutes County, Vilnius, Esch-sur-Alzette, Kerewan and Mondragon. It was founded by Claudia Chwalisz, who previously led the OECD's work on innovative citizen participation. On AI it called in 2023 for a global institution of citizens' assemblies, and later argued (with The GovLab's Stefaan Verhulst) for local and regional AI assemblies. It runs a tech-enhanced assembly lab with MIT's Center for Constructive Communication and co-convenes the DelibTech Network (launched Sep 2025) with the AI & Democracy Foundation.

It judges AI tools in deliberation by whether they build citizens' own capacities (self-reflection, reasoning, dialogue, vulnerability) or wear them away. It also offers lottery-based institutions as a way to give publics real say over how AI is governed.

Works on Democracy, Human minds · Key work Deliberative Muscles & AI: How Can DelibTech Strengthen Citizens' Capacities to Deliberate? (Chwalisz, McKinney, Theuns, Yi) (2026); Five Dimensions of Scaling Democratic Deliberation: With and Beyond AI (McKinney and Chwalisz) (2025); The Case for Local and Regional Public Engagement in Governing Artificial Intelligence (Verhulst and Chwalisz) (2025) · Get involved Newsletter (Substack) and public events; Assembly guide and resources for organisers of citizens' assemblies; DelibTech Network (invite-only; members join virtual and in-person convenings)

Note Its AI work centres on deliberation technology and governing AI through assemblies, not on catastrophic risk. It is critical of opinion-mapping tools such as Polis being called deliberation. The DelibTech Network is invite-only. The founding year is inferred from its fourth birthday in Sep 2026; the Dutch foundation was incorporated in Dec 2023.

Edge City (Edge Institute, Inc.) Bridge

Nonprofit · Cloverdale, California, USA · founded 2024 · also draws on Economics

A 'society incubator' that grew out of the Zuzalu pop-up-city scene. It runs month-long pop-up villages where technologists, scientists and artists live together and test projects; the 2026 villages were Edge Esmeralda in Healdsburg, California, Edge City India in Goa and Edge City Bhutan. Its AI-related work includes Agent Village (June 2026), in which 239 residents were given personal AI agents to see how the agents affected community coordination and governance. It also runs a d/acc residency and, with NODES, the SHIFT grants for defensive technology.

It tests AI governance questions in a real community, not in simulation. Agent Village found that 'individual alignment did not automatically produce collective alignment', which is evidence for the multi-agent and institutional side of safety that lab-based alignment work rarely gathers.

Works on Democracy, Multi-agent · Key work Agent Village: personal AI agents for 239 residents of Edge Esmeralda (with Cosmos Institute) (2026); d/acc Residency at Edge City Patagonia (with Protocol Labs) (2025); SHIFT Grants for d/acc projects (with NODES) (2025) · Get involved Apply to attend pop-up villages (Edge Esmeralda, Edge City India, Bhutan); Residencies (d/acc, World Builder and others); SHIFT Grants: micro grants of $5,000-15,000 and development grants of $20,000-40,000 for d/acc projects

Note Most of its work is general network-society experimentation, and AI is one strand among several. Its first gathering was Edge City Denver (26 Feb-3 Mar 2024, during ETHDenver), so the founding year is 2024. The Cloverdale location is the site of Edge Esmeralda's planned permanent neighbourhood; I couldn't confirm the legal entity's registered address. SHIFT Grants and Simocracy, which took part in Agent Village, have their own roster entries. Agent Village was co-run with Cosmos Institute, and Index Network built its core.

FutureSearch (Varuna AI, Inc.) Bridge

Company · United States · founded 2023

A US company founded in August 2023 by former Metaculus and Google staff. It builds AI forecasting agents and sells forecasts per question ($0.25-$5) through an API, a Python SDK and MCP integrations, alongside multi-agent research tools. Its forecaster ranked #2 of 284 on Metaculus FutureEval and #1 of 203 in Metaculus MiniBench in Sept 2026. Its professional forecasters contributed to the AI 2027 timelines forecast, and it publishes forecasts on AGI timelines and frontier labs.

It builds judgmental-forecasting practice into AI agents that produce cheap, calibrated forecasts, including on the AI transition itself. In Aug 2026 it launched causal 'decision forecasts' aimed at uses such as grantmaking. New AI-safety funders could use such tools to estimate the likely effects of a grant before making it.

Works on Epistemics · Key work Forecasts for the AI 2027 timelines forecast (three FutureSearch forecasters) (2025); AI 2027 Update: A One Year Timeline Check (2026); AGI Timeline Predictions: How Top Forecasters Updated, 2023 to 2026 (2026) · Get involved Use its forecasting API, Python SDK or MCP integration (Claude.ai and Claude Code need only a Google sign-in)

Note A for-profit company with frontier AI labs as customers. Its site states no safety mission, and most of its output is commercial forecasting (companies, chips, model pricing). Benchmark rankings are reported on its own homepage. The headquarters city is not stated; its privacy policy says it is US-headquartered, while the roster had UK/US.

g0v and vTaiwan Bridge

Network · Taipei, Taiwan · founded 2012

g0v ('gov-zero') is Taiwan's decentralised civic-tech community. It runs bimonthly hackathons in Taipei (the 73rd on 31 May 2026) and releases its projects as open source, such as the Cofacts fact-checking bot. vTaiwan, launched from g0v in 2014, is an open consultation process combining Polis with in-person meetings to deliberate on digital legislation; it reports 28+ cases, 80% of which led to government action. In 2023 a $100k OpenAI 'Democratic Inputs to AI' grant, with Chatham House and the AI Objectives Institute, revived vTaiwan as a volunteer community. That project held a citizens' meeting on AI privacy, discrimination and local governance and reached consensus points on AI. In 2026 vTaiwan holds weekly online meetings, publishes a newsletter, ran an in-person deliberation in Hualien and adapted Jigsaw's Sensemaker for Traditional Chinese.

It is a long-running, volunteer-run model of 'rough consensus' deliberation that feeds legislation, and one of the few civic communities to have deliberated directly on principles for AI. It gives a non-Western, bottom-up template for polycentric AI governance.

Works on Democracy, Values · Key work Bridging the Recursive Public (OpenAI Democratic Inputs to AI, with Chatham House and AI Objectives Institute) (2023); How public participation can improve AI governance: vTaiwan's initiatives (Friedrich Naumann Foundation) (2024); vTaiwan newsletter, issue 0 (community history and Sensemaker localisation) (2026) · Get involved g0v bimonthly hackathons in Taipei; Slack and a newcomers' guide; vTaiwan weekly online meeting, Wednesdays 19:00-20:00 Taiwan time, mostly in Mandarin; Contribute code, transcripts and translations through the g0v/vTaiwan GitHub repositories; vTaiwan Substack newsletter

Note Its AI-governance deliberation dates from 2023-24; its 2025-26 work is mainly AI-assisted deliberation tools and non-AI policy topics. It is volunteer-run and mostly in Mandarin. The Taiwanese government's Alignment Assemblies (MODA with CIP) are a separate programme, and Audrey Tang's international advocacy is not a vTaiwan activity. The founding year refers to g0v.

Global Coalition for Inclusive AI Governance BridgeUnverified

Network · Paris, France · founded 2025

A coalition launched at the Paris AI Action Summit in Feb 2025 by Missions Publiques, a Paris-based citizen-participation organisation, and the Stanford Deliberative Democracy Lab. It answers the UN Global Digital Compact's call for a global dialogue on AI governance. It plans a continuous global citizen consultation, combining decentralised citizens' assemblies with a global deliberative poll, and its first cycle aims to involve 10,000+ citizens in 100+ countries. A pilot student citizens' assembly of 70 students was run with ENS-PSL and Yale. The governments of France, Switzerland and the UK, plus over 80 civil-society organisations, private-sector actors and a dozen academic partners, have backed it.

If it runs, it would be one of the few channels putting representative global public judgement, including from Majority-World countries, into international AI governance. Because AI safety is not guaranteed a place on its agenda, early engagement with its briefing materials could matter.

Works on Democracy, Justice · Key work Launch of the coalition at the Paris AI Action Summit, ENS-PSL (2025); Student Citizens' Assembly pilot (ENS-PSL and Yale, 70 students) (2025) · Get involved Organisations (governments, civil society, academia, companies, international bodies) can ask to join through the contact form on its site

Note No published results and no dated activity since the Feb 2025 launch, so it is unclear whether the first deliberation cycle ran. Its site is minimal and names no leaders, partners or timeline. An EA Forum post (Feb 2025) warned that AI safety was mentioned only vaguely in the Paris pilot and could be diluted in most national assemblies. The named people lead the two founding organisations; their personal roles in the coalition are not stated.

Goodheart Labs Bridge

Company · Leicester, UK · founded 2022

Goodheart Labs is a small UK studio run by forecaster Nathan Young that builds AI-assisted tools for decision-making and collective fact-checking. Its AI note writer researches, drafts and submits Community Notes on X: the site reports 1,042 notes rated helpful, 100.7M views and $7.49 per helpful note. Its other tools include the Common Notes browser extension (notes on Substack and YouTube, since July 2026), Viewpoints polling, Finding Consensus (expert positions on AI policy such as SB-1047) and forecast-aggregation dashboards, including one on AGI timelines.

It is one of the few AI-for-epistemics projects with measured deployment at scale. It tests whether AI can scale bridging-based crowd fact-checking as misleading content becomes cheaper to produce, a concrete lever on the information decay that safety and governance work depends on.

Works on Epistemics, Democracy · Key work AI-written Community Notes on X (world's first AI-written note; 1,042 helpful notes) (2025); Common Notes browser extension (2026); Finding Consensus: expert views on AI policy (2024) · Get involved Install Common Notes (Chrome or Firefox) to read, rate, request or write notes; Book a call to commission decision or forecasting tools

Note A very small team, built around one founder. The AI note writer depends on X's API programme for AI note writers. The usage figures are self-reported.

Habermas Machine (Google DeepMind) BridgeDormant

Programme · London, UK · founded 2024 · also draws on Psychology

A Google DeepMind research system in which a language model acts as a 'caucus mediator': it drafts group statements on contested questions, and a personalised reward model ranks them by predicted agreement. The work was published in Science in October 2024. In experiments with 5,734 UK participants, including a virtual citizens' assembly, people preferred its statements to those of human mediators 56% of the time, and groups came out less divided. The code (a fine-tuned version and a prompted Gemini version) and the dataset are open source.

It is the most-cited empirical test of AI-mediated consensus, so anyone designing AI-assisted deliberation for AI governance starts from it. It also shows the risks the field needs to address: no fact-checking, and possible homogenisation or steering of views.

Works on Democracy · Key work AI can help humans find common ground in democratic deliberation (Science) (2024); Habermas Machine code and dataset (open source) (2024); Fine-tuning language models to find agreement among humans with diverse preferences (NeurIPS; precursor work) (2022) · Get involved Open-source code and dataset on GitHub (software Apache 2.0, other materials CC-BY 4.0), usable for replication or extension

Note A finished research project, not an organisation: the repository has had no commits since January 2025 and no follow-up DeepMind programme was found (my web search budget ran out, so later work by the authors may exist). The paper notes that the system does no fact-checking, and critics have raised the risk of homogenising or steering group views.

Metaculus BridgeOn aisafety.com

Company · Santa Cruz, United States · founded 2015

An online forecasting platform and aggregation engine, founded in 2015 and run as a public-benefit corporation. It hosts public questions and tournaments, combines its community's predictions into the Metaculus Prediction, and employs Pro Forecasters. Its AI work includes the FutureEval / AI Forecasting Benchmark tournaments, which pit AI forecasting bots against professional forecasters. Its Spring 2026 results found Pros still ahead, but no longer by a statistically significant margin. It also forecasts AI timelines and impacts, for example 'Mapping the AI IPO Windfall' (Sep 2026).

It provides a long-running, publicly scored record of collective forecasts on AI and other risks. It also gives a recurring public measure of how fast AI forecasting ability is approaching expert human judgement, a capability that bears directly on AI-assisted decision-making.

Works on Epistemics, Assurance · Key work FutureEval Spring Results: Pros Beat Bots, but the Gap is Nearly Gone (2026); Mapping the AI IPO Windfall (2026); Open-sourced platform code (BSD-2-Clause) (2024) · Get involved Forecast on public questions and tournaments, including the Metaculus Cup; Enter a forecasting bot in the FutureEval / AI Forecasting Benchmark tournaments; Join the forecaster community and discussion threads

Note It is a public-benefit corporation, not a nonprofit (the roster said nonprofit). Ring changed from core to bridge: its charter is forecasting as a public good across all topics, with AI one major focus among many. Its own site blocked automated fetching (Cloudflare), so programme details here come from Metaculus-authored EA Forum posts and Wikipedia. Its staff count of 25 dates from 2023.

Stanford Deliberative Democracy Lab (DDL) Bridge

Academic · Stanford, US · founded 2003

A lab in Stanford's Center on Democracy, Development and the Rule of Law, formerly the Center for Deliberative Democracy, directed by James Fishkin. It runs Deliberative Polls: representative samples get balanced briefings, deliberate in small groups and with experts, and are surveyed against control groups. Its AI line includes Meta's Community Forums on generative AI (2022-25) and US/India forums on AI wearables. In Nov 2025 it ran an Industry-Wide Forum on AI agents for Cohere, Meta, Oracle, PayPal, DoorDash and Microsoft, with 503 participants in the US and India. It also ran a national deliberation on the Colorado AI Act (Oct 2025) and holds invite-only AI symposia, using its AI-assisted Stanford Online Deliberation Platform.

It gives AI developers a tested, controlled method for getting informed, representative public judgements on how AI agents should behave, such as when an agent must ask for approval. That is a working channel for public input into product and model norms.

Works on Democracy, Values · Key work Industry-Wide Forum on AI Agents: results (503 participants, US and India) (2026); National Deliberation on AI Policies (Colorado Consumer AI Act) (2025); AI Agent for Good: Alignment, Safety, and Impact (invite-only symposium) (2025) · Get involved Annual call for short papers for its summer AI symposium (2026 window: 15 Jun–15 Jul; symposium invite-only); Stanford courses, including 'Artificial Intelligence and Deliberative Democracy' (summer) and a Deliberative Polling practicum; Online Deliberation Platform and briefing-material toolkits for partners

Note Its AI forums are run with, and topics shaped by, the companies they advise, which raises questions about independence. The 2026 symposium centres on trust and adoption rather than risk. Results are advisory, with no binding company commitments. It co-launched the Global Coalition for Inclusive AI Governance (a separate entry), whose status is unclear.

Swift Centre (formerly Swift Centre for Applied Forecasting) BridgeChanged

Nonprofit · London, UK · founded 2022 · also draws on Arts, futures

The Swift Centre is a London forecasting organisation that uses a panel of top-ranked forecasters for calibrated probabilistic forecasts and scenario analysis. Its not-for-profit research wing (Swift Centre Research Ltd) concentrates on the concentration of power in AI (compute, capability and control), AI policy and great-power dynamics, through scenario papers, situation monitors and public forecasts. A commercial advisory wing (Swift Centre Advisory Ltd, from 2026) sells forecasting, prediction-market intelligence and workshops. It supplied forecasts for Google DeepMind's 2024 dangerous-capability evaluations paper.

It brings scored, calibrated forecasting and scenario method to AI risk strategy: forecasts on frontier capabilities, AI cyber-offence and autonomous warfare. Its 2026 'Bridge the Gap' competition tied those forecasts to policy options drafted by new AI policy advisers.

Works on Epistemics, Power, Security · Key work Forecasts for Google DeepMind's 'Evaluating Frontier Models for Dangerous Capabilities' (2024); Bridge the Gap: Forecasts for AI Policy (2026); Polymarket vs Swift Centre: Round 2 (2026) · Get involved Free Substack newsletter, 'Swift Centre: Highlights'; Research wing seeks funding partners for its AI and geopolitics papers and situation monitors; Advisory: forecasting workshops and consultancy for organisations

Note In 2026 the organisation restructured. A commercial advisory company was incorporated in Feb 2026, the original company was renamed from Swift Centre for Applied Forecasting Ltd to Swift Centre Research Ltd in Jul 2026, and founding director Michael Story resigned from both boards on 18 Sep 2026. Leadership is in transition, and much recent public output is general geopolitics rather than AI.

Tattle Civic Technologies (Tattle) Bridge

Company · Haryana, India · founded 2019 · also draws on Safety science, Indigenous

An Indian open-source civic-tech group of technologists, researchers and artists that builds tools and datasets against inaccurate and harmful online content. It started in 2019 with a grant from the AI Ethics Initiative and is registered as a private limited company. Its products include Uli, a browser plugin and crowdsourced slur dataset for responding to online gender-based violence in Indian languages, and the collaboration platform behind the Deepfakes Analysis Unit's WhatsApp tipline. It also runs an 'AI Safety research and consulting' line: it wrote 2,000 Hindi safety prompts for MLCommons' AILuminate benchmark, built the open-source Kaapi Guardrails for NGO chatbots with Project Tech4Dev, and red-teams deployed chatbots, using participatory, multilingual methods.

It shows how participatory, community-sourced and multilingual methods can produce safety benchmarks, evaluations and guardrails for non-English settings. This fills a gap in English-centric AI-safety evaluations, and it does so for deployments that actually reach low-income users in India.

Works on Assurance, Justice, Epistemics · Key work Hindi safety-benchmark prompts (hate; sex-related crimes) for MLCommons AILuminate (2024); Kaapi Guardrails: open-source safety guardrails for social-sector LLM chatbots (with Project Tech4Dev) (2025); Uli: community-sourced moderation tool and dataset against online gender-based violence · Get involved Job openings: Fullstack Research Engineer and Software Engineer; open applications welcome; Contribute to its open-source repositories (github.com/tattle-made) and to Uli's crowdsourced slur list; Paid collaborations on AI evaluations, safety benchmarks, guardrails and bias audits

Note Although it calls itself a community, it is legally a private limited company that funds itself partly through paid contracts. Its 'AI safety' means the deployment safety of chatbots and harms in multilingual settings, not catastrophic risk. Meta funds the Deepfakes Analysis Unit.

The Computational Democracy Project (CompDem) Bridge

Nonprofit · Seattle, US · founded 2018

A US 501(c)(3), founded in 2018 to carry on Polis as an open-source nonprofit. Polis (AGPL-3.0) collects short statements and votes from large groups and uses statistics and machine learning to map opinion groups and points of consensus. CompDem hosts pol.is (free for nonprofits and government), offers implementation support and training, and publishes open data and analysis notebooks. Polis has been used by vTaiwan, alongside Uruguay's 2021 referendum and by a Kentucky city, and was the platform for Anthropic and the Collective Intelligence Project's Collective Constitutional AI (2023). Polis 2.0 launched at TICTeC 2025, and Polis became a Digital Public Good in Jan 2026.

Polis is working infrastructure for finding out what large, divided publics agree on. It has already been used to draft a language-model constitution, so pluralistic-alignment work can build on a tested instrument instead of a proposal.

Works on Democracy, Values · Key work Polis (open-source opinion-mapping system); Opportunities and Risks of LLMs for Scalable Deliberation with Polis (with Anthropic researchers) (2023); Polis 2.0, launched at mySociety's TICTeC conference (2025) · Get involved Contribute to the open-source Polis code, data and notebooks on GitHub; volunteering page on its site; Run conversations on pol.is (free for nonprofits and government); paid implementation support and training

Note Its own site uses no AI-alignment framing and has little dated news. The AI-safety link runs through partners (CIP, Anthropic, vTaiwan) and mostly dates from 2023-24. The Digital Public Goods registry names the owning organisation as 'Math & Democracy', and how that relates to CompDem is unclear. DemocracyNext argues that Polis on its own is opinion mapping, not deliberation. HQ comes from the roster and was not confirmed on the site.

Adjacent ring 37

AI4Deliberation (Artificial Intelligence for Institutionalised, Multimodal, Gamified, Mass Democratic Deliberations) Adjacent

Programme · Athens, Greece · founded 2024 · also draws on Law, society

Horizon Europe project (grant 101178806, Nov 2024 to Oct 2027, about €3.0M) building ethical AI tools and guidance to help governments run, institutionalise and evaluate large multimodal and gamified public deliberations, including argument mining and AI-supported summarisation. The coordinator is the Greek IT firm Uni Systems. Partners include TU Delft, CERTH, the University of Bamberg, the University of Dundee (ARG-tech), the Ljubljana Institute of Criminology, Dembrane, ActionAid Italia and the City of Bamberg. It runs four large pilots on climate change and long COVID.

The main EU-funded test of AI-mediated deliberation inside government, and it studies the failure modes as well as building tools. Its outputs include evidence of an 'AI penalty' (people value AI-assisted deliberation less, which risks a new deliberative divide), comparisons of human and LLM deliberation, and institutional-design and legal-ethics work on where AI belongs in democratic processes.

Works on Democracy, Epistemics · Key work Artificial Intelligence in deliberation: The AI penalty and the emergence of a new deliberative divide (Jungherr & Rauchfleisch, Government Information Quarterly) (2025); Artificial Intelligence for Mass Democratic Deliberations: The AI4Deliberation Project Objectives and Methodology (Tambouris) (2025); Institutional Design for AI-enabled Deliberation (Nouws, Janssen, Tambouris) (2025)

Note No working project website was found: ai4deliberation.org is a parked domain (Oct 2026), so the evidence comes from CORDIS and partner pages. Funding is time-limited and ends in Oct 2027. Earlier descriptions listed specific tools (fact-checking, toxicity detection) that CORDIS's summary does not confirm. HQ is given as the coordinator's location.

AI4LAM (Artificial Intelligence for Libraries, Archives and Museums) Adjacent

Network · Oslo, Norway · founded 2018

An international association of libraries, archives and museums working on how AI is used in, for and by cultural-heritage institutions. It began in 2018 as a network under an agreement between the National Library of Norway and Stanford University Libraries, and was formally constituted in December 2025 by more than 40 institutions. It runs working groups (speech-to-text, AI literacy, 3D and image analysis, AI in cybersecurity), regional chapters and national nodes, community calls, and the annual Fantastic Futures conference. The 2026 conference theme was 'Trust in the Loop'.

Memory institutions have long practice in provenance, authenticity and trust, which AI-safety work on content provenance rarely draws on. AI4LAM is where that practice is being turned into shared standards for AI. An example is its Transcript Provenance Metadata Elements (TPME), which record which model produced a transcript, with what settings, and whether a human corrected it.

Works on Epistemics · Key work Transcript Provenance Metadata Elements (TPME) v1.0 (2026); Fantastic Futures 2026: Trust in the Loop (Washington, DC, and online; Library of Congress, National Gallery of Art, Smithsonian) (2026); Provenance Metadata for Slop Control, with Transcripts and other Digital Objects (2026) · Get involved Working groups open calls for participation (AI Literacy WG, 3D & Image Analysis WG, Speech-to-Text WG); Fantastic Futures conference: 2027 edition in Amsterdam, 30 Nov-2 Dec 2027, with Rijksmuseum and Cultural AI; Open community calls and webinars; institutional membership

Note Its stated mission is to accelerate AI adoption in cultural heritage, so most of its work is applied AI for collections. The trust, provenance and literacy strand is the part relevant to making AI go well. It only became a formal organisation in December 2025.

Café IA (France) Adjacent

Programme · Paris, France · founded 2024

A French national programme of free, informal public conversations about AI, held in libraries, workplaces, schools and community spaces by volunteer hosts. Hosts use open (CC BY-SA) facilitation kits on what AI is, AI and work, AI and the environment, and AI and information. It was launched nationwide in 2024 at the President's request by the Conseil national du numérique, renamed the Conseil de l'IA et du numérique in 2025. It is now an independent state project hosted by the Directorate General for Enterprise (DGE) at the Ministry of the Economy. It reports more than 800 hosts, about five cafés a day (80% outside Paris), and aims to reach 2 million people by the end of 2027.

It is working infrastructure for mass public conversation and AI literacy at national scale, a form of democratic participation the AI-safety field seldom builds. Its open kits could be adapted for discussing AI-transition questions, and int/a Paris could host cafés directly.

Works on Democracy, Epistemics · Key work Facilitation kits and teaching modules: AI and work, AI and the environment, AI and information (2024-2026); 20 cartes pour aborder l'impact énergétique de l'IA; Interactive map of Café IA events across France · Get involved Host a Café IA: register as a host and use the free kits (classic, workplace and school formats); Attend a café near you via the interactive map; Newsletter

Note It moved from the Conseil national du numérique to the DGE in 2025, so it is now run from inside the economy ministry, alongside France's pro-AI national strategy. Its aim is literacy and conversation, not critique or safety. Participation figures are self-reported and vary by page: more than 50,000 in the first year on the English page, more than 150,000 over 18 months on the press page. The cafés produce discussion, not decisions handed to policymakers.

Center for an Informed Public (CIP), University of Washington Adjacent

Academic · Seattle, United States · founded 2019 · also draws on Law, society

An interdisciplinary research centre at the University of Washington, founded in December 2019 by the Information School, Human Centered Design & Engineering and the School of Law. It studies how rumours, misinformation and disinformation spread, runs rapid-response election-rumour research, and does public education and media-literacy work. Its AI work includes a 2025 PNAS paper on anthropomorphic conversational agents as 'super communicators', a free online course on generative AI ('Modern-Day Oracles or Bullshit Machines?'), AI-literacy lessons for schools, and an August 2026 piece on scrutinising AI tools that evaluate science.

It brings crisis informatics and collective-sensemaking research, built on studying rumours during elections and disasters, to the question of how generative AI changes what the public believes. AI-safety work on persuasion and sycophancy rarely draws on this tradition of studying misinformation as it actually spreads.

Works on Epistemics · Key work The benefits and dangers of anthropomorphic conversational agents (PNAS, with Jevin West) (2025); Modern-Day Oracles or Bullshit Machines? Free online course on generative AI (Jevin West and Carl Bergstrom) (2025); AI science evaluation tools should be scrutinized through 'critically engaged pragmatism' (2026) · Get involved Free online course 'Modern-Day Oracles or Bullshit Machines?' on the risks and uses of generative AI; Postdoctoral scholar programme at the centre; Webinars and Media Mentorship learning events (videos released Aug 2026); newsletter and mailing list

Note AI is a growing strand within a misinformation centre, not its core. Its 2020 Election Integrity Partnership work with the Stanford Internet Observatory later drew political attacks and litigation in the US. The 2025-29 Knight figure comes from a secondary source.

Citizens Foundation Adjacent

Nonprofit · Reykjavík, Iceland · founded 2008

Icelandic nonprofit founded in Reykjavík in 2008, after the financial crash, that builds open-source civic participation software: Better Reykjavík, Your Priorities (used in 50+ countries; the Scottish Parliament's Engage platform since 2019) and All Our Ideas. Its newer framework, Policy Synth, coordinates teams of AI agents that research problems, evolve and Elo-rank candidate solutions, and return them to human review and voting. It has been used with the New Jersey AI Task Force, for skills-first hiring and for the ERIC EU rights assistant.

It offers a working design for using agentic AI in public decision-making while keeping citizens and officials in charge of every judgement ('AI accelerated the work; people decided'). That is a practical template for human oversight of AI in government.

Works on Democracy, Epistemics · Key work Policy Synth (open-source multi-agent framework) and research paper (2024); Engage @ Scottish Parliament on Your Priorities (2026); New Jersey AI Task Force: 2,200+ worker voices to AI policy (2024) · Get involved Open-source code (MIT licence) on GitHub and npm; Work with us: commissioning platforms or Policy Synth projects

Note The Scottish Parliament uses Your Priorities, not Policy Synth, contrary to the roster draft. Policy Synth is a tool for AI-assisted policymaking rather than work on AI safety itself; it belongs here as a design for human oversight of agentic AI in public decisions. The core team is about four people.

Coalition for Content Provenance and Authenticity (C2PA) Adjacent

Network · San Francisco, USA · founded 2021 · also draws on Safety science, Arts, futures

An industry standards body that maintains Content Credentials, an open specification for recording where digital media came from and how it was edited, including whether AI generated or altered it. Adobe, Arm, BBC, Intel, Microsoft and Truepic launched it in February 2021 as a project of the Joint Development Foundation, a Linux Foundation affiliate. It launched a conformance programme and official trust list in mid-2025 and released version 2.3 in February 2026, adding live video and more file types. In July 2026 it published a guide to implementing Content Credentials for generative AI. Its steering committee is Adobe, Amazon, BBC, Google, Meta, Microsoft, OpenAI, Publicis, Sony, TikTok and Truepic.

Provenance infrastructure is one of the few deployed technical responses to synthetic media eroding shared evidence, and generative-AI developers such as OpenAI and Google sit on its steering committee. For int/a readers it is a test case: collective-epistemics infrastructure governed by the companies whose products create the problem, with little civil-society representation.

Works on Epistemics · Key work Content Credentials specification v2.3 (2026); C2PA Conformance Program (2025); Implementation guide for Content Credentials and generative AI (2026) · Get involved Organisations can apply for general or contributor membership; Public specification and conformance repositories on GitHub (github.com/c2pa-org), active Sep 2026; Conformance programme for products that display Content Credentials

Note Large technology and media companies govern it, and civil society has little voice. Provenance metadata can be stripped or ignored, so its value depends on platforms and devices adopting it. It is not an AI-safety organisation; its AI relevance is labelling AI-generated content. In January 2026 it clarified that its specification has no standard text-and-data-mining assertion, after an EU consultation referred to one. The chair succession comes from Wikipedia, not C2PA's own site.

Community Notes (X) and the AI Note Writer API Adjacent

Programme · United States · founded 2021

X's crowd-sourced system for adding context to posts, launched as Birdwatch in January 2021. A note is shown only when contributors who have tended to disagree in past ratings rate it helpful. This 'bridging' rule is applied by an open-source ranking algorithm, and data on notes and ratings are published daily. Meta began testing the same algorithm on Facebook, Instagram and Threads in the US in March 2025. Since 2025 an AI Note Writer API has let AI systems propose notes, which they cannot rate; only human contributors decide what shows. X's own open-source Community Writer produced 52% of the notes shown as helpful in June 2026.

It is one of the few deployed systems where AI generates claims at scale while a diverse human crowd keeps the final say, and the ratings are fed back to improve the AI writers. That makes it a live test of human oversight of AI-generated content. It also shows how quickly AI can come to dominate a human epistemic institution: in 42% of posts with a helpful note, only AI notes existed.

Works on Epistemics, Assurance · Key work Open-source Community Notes ranking algorithm and public data (2021); Scaling Human Judgment in Community Notes with LLMs (Li, De, Revel et al.) (2025); AI Note Writer API pilot (2025) · Get involved Become a Community Notes contributor on X to write and rate notes; Build an AI note writer through the AI Note Writer API, with a public developer community on X; Download the daily public data on notes and ratings for research

Note A corporate product whose rules can change at the owner's discretion. AI note writing is now dominated by the writer built by X/xAI, which raises questions of independence. Meta adopted notes while ending its US third-party fact-checking programme in 2025, which fact-checkers criticised. Goodheart Labs' AI note writer reports 1,042 helpful notes at $7.49 each since June 2025. X's own guide pages could not be fetched (HTTP 402), so details come from the GitHub documentation, arXiv reports and press.

Connected by Data Adjacent

Nonprofit · Epsom, United Kingdom (registered office) · founded 2022 · also draws on Economics, Law, society

UK not-for-profit company, founded in 2022 by Jeni Tennison, that campaigns for communities to have a real say in decisions about data and AI. It designs and promotes public deliberation on AI governance, including the 'Citizens Track' for the UN Global Dialogue on AI Governance, ran an action-learning programme with nine education unions and the TUC on worker power over public-sector AI, and convened a community of practice for public-engagement practitioners.

It brings participatory-democracy and data-justice practice into global AI governance, proposing concrete designs for citizen deliberation alongside AI summits and UN processes. These are channels for public voice that the AI-safety policy world mostly lacks.
