Note It is a fixed-term organisation: in March 2026 it announced it will wind up in 2027, at the end of its planned lifespan, and is exploring 'regenerations' (fiscal sponsorship of collective initiatives, a consultants' umbrella, a grassroots programme), so engagement windows are short. Registered office is in Epsom; I found no evidence of a London office. The public-engagement community of practice ran monthly from July 2024; a June 2026 post discusses its future. It frames its work around power and participation rather than safety, despite 'Alignment' in the white paper's title.

deliberAIde Adjacent

Company · Siegen, Germany

deliberAIde is a German start-up based in Siegen that builds an AI 'co-worker' for structured dialogue. It helps plan engagement processes, transcribes discussions live in 100+ languages, analyses hundreds of sessions together, and produces reports in which every finding links back to the original quote. Users include The Future Society (for its 2025 Athens Roundtable), Pulse of Europe and the District of Siegen-Wittgenstein (10 citizen dialogue conferences). The product is in private preview.

Its design targets a specific failure of AI in deliberation, synthesis that silently distorts what participants said. Findings are traceable to source quotes, data is anonymised by default and never used for training, and approval gates keep publication in human hands. AI-governance convenors already use it.

Note Early-stage, with founding date and funding not published. The imprint names Lukas Salecker & Co GbR (a civil-law partnership) in Siegen, so how the site's 'purpose-locked steward ownership' is implemented is not documented. The case for it rests mostly on testimonials on its own site.

Deliberation.io (MIT GOV/LAB and Stanford Digital Economy Lab) Adjacent

Programme · Cambridge, United States

An open-source platform for large-scale, structured online dialogue with AI-assisted facilitation. It is led by Lily Tsai (MIT GOV/LAB) and Alex 'Sandy' Pentland with Stanford's Digital Economy Lab, Stanford HAI and Boston University's Platform Governance Lab. The team publishes experiments on AI facilitation, LLM opinion aggregation, comment ordering, consensus generation and AI-prompted reason-giving. Washington, DC was the first city to use it, for a public listening session on AI in city government.

It tests experimentally whether AI can widen and improve public deliberation without replacing human judgement, including whether LLM summaries represent minority views fairly. The DC session is an example of the public deliberating about AI policy itself. Its 2026 position paper names alignment, sycophancy and over-reliance as risks of AI facilitators.

Note The site gives no launch date. The DC AI Public Listening Session took place on 15 July 2025, according to DC's Office of the Chief Technology Officer, which called DC the first city to use the platform. Most of its papers are working papers. The 2026 arXiv paper does not name Deliberation.io in its abstract; its link to the platform is inferred from its authors.

Dembrane (dembrane B.V.) Adjacent

Company · 's-Hertogenbosch, Netherlands

Dutch company based in 's-Hertogenbosch. It builds an open-source platform that records, transcribes and synthesises dozens of small-group table conversations happening at the same time, and produces outcome documents that trace back to the original speakers while participants are still in the room. It began with a $100k OpenAI 'Democratic Inputs to AI' grant in 2023. Municipalities and companies use it, and it is a partner in the EU AI4Deliberation project.

A working test bed for AI-mediated deliberation in small groups. It takes an explicit 'low AI' ethics stance: AI is kept minimal and transparent, and participants can accept, reject or change what it suggests. It also moved to EU-sovereign transcription. It is concrete evidence on how to keep humans in charge of the synthesis step that schemes for collective input into AI depend on.

Works on Democracy, Epistemics · Key work OpenAI Democratic Inputs to AI grant ($100k) (2023); Ethical whitepaper ('low AI' principles for AI in deliberation) (2024); dembrane is going open source (2025) · Get involved Jobs: full-stack engineer, head of product design, sales lead, and freelance facilitator and translator roles listed at dembrane.com/work (Oct 2026); Internships and thesis projects (dembrane.com/work); Open-source platform code on GitHub

Note A commercial B.V. Its 2023 framing, a route for democratic input into AI alignment, has since given way to a general stakeholder-engagement product. Its site does not give a founding year (it says the founders came together between 2020 and 2024). A 2023 source places it in Eindhoven; it is now in 's-Hertogenbosch.

Demos Helsinki Adjacent

Nonprofit · Helsinki, Finland · founded 2005 · also draws on Arts, futures

An independent think tank founded in 2005, with about 70 staff, owned by its employees through the association Demos ry and funded mainly by projects. It works on societal transitions, strategic foresight and 'technology for society', often inside EU research consortia. Its AI work includes 'A framework for democratic AI governance' (February 2026, from the EU KT4D project), the FORSEE project on what 'successful AI' means for society, and studies of algorithmic management of Nordic workers and of non-discriminatory public-sector AI.

It turns democratic theory into concrete EU AI-governance roadmaps: six democratic pillars across the AI lifecycle, with 18 recommendations running to 2035. That gives the field a worked bridge between participation research and AI policy. It is also a Nordic partner experienced in EU consortia for anyone building participatory or public-interest AI projects.

Works on Democracy, Power, Justice · Key work A framework for democratic AI governance (KT4D project; Ojanen, Björk, Singh, Djakonoff) (2026); FORSEE: research to define what 'successful AI' means in society (2025); Impact of algorithmic management on workers (Nordic study) (2024) · Get involved Staff roles (about 70 staff, multinational team); Partner on EU research consortia on AI and democracy (as in KT4D and FORSEE)

Note Its AI work explicitly leaves out existential or catastrophic risk and concentrates on democracy, discrimination and labour. AI is one theme among several (circular economy, cities, economic models). Sources are mostly its own site.

Digital Democracy 2030 (DD2030) and Team Mirai AdjacentNew

Network · Tokyo, Japan · founded 2025

DD2030 is an open, volunteer civic-technology community in Japan, launched in 2025 by engineer Takahiro Anno. It builds open-source tools for AI-assisted 'broad listening' and deliberation: Kouchou AI (comment analysis adapted from Talk to the City), Idobata (deliberation modelled on vTaiwan and JOIN), Polimoney (political-finance transparency) and Project Coreloop. Team Mirai is the political party Anno founded, which uses the same methods. It won an upper-house seat in 2025 and, by its own account, 11 lower-house seats in the 2026 general election.

Probably the largest live use of AI-mediated public input in national politics: 8,200+ AI interviews and 9,700 policy suggestions fed into Team Mirai's 2025 platform, with municipalities also using the tools. It is almost invisible in AI-safety circles.

Works on Democracy, Epistemics · Key work Kouchou AI v4.0 (open-source broad-listening tool) (2025); Idobata deliberation platform (2025); Polimoney political-finance transparency dashboard (2025) · Get involved Contribute as developer, researcher, designer, translator or organiser via the join page, Slack and GitHub; Digital Democracy Summit (free, registration); Broad-listening guidebook

Note DD2030 declares party and procedural neutrality and is not Team Mirai's 'sister' organisation: Anno resigned from its board in May 2025 to preserve neutrality. They are profiled together because they share a founder and methods. Team Mirai's 11 lower-house seats in the 8 Feb 2026 election are confirmed by Japanese press (e.g. J-CAST). Most sources are in Japanese.

Elements of AI (University of Helsinki and MinnaLearn) Adjacent

Programme · Helsinki, Finland · founded 2018

A series of free online courses for non-experts, launched in 2018 by the University of Helsinki and the Finnish firm Reaktor and now run with the learning company MinnaLearn. Its two courses, 'Introduction to AI' (which ends with a module on implications) and 'Building AI', have had more than 2 million enrolments from 170+ countries and are offered in 40+ languages. Finland offered the course to all EU citizens as its 2019 EU-presidency gift. MinnaLearn's 'Get AI Ready', a workplace course of under 60 minutes mapped to the EU AI Act's AI-literacy duty, is now the featured product.

It is proven mass public-education infrastructure, available in many EU languages and conceived as 'a civics course in AI'. Today it mostly teaches fundamentals and compliance, but it could carry AI-risk and cognitive-autonomy literacy to millions of adults.

Note Its AI-safety content is thin: the courses cover what AI is and general implications, and the newer product is commercial compliance training. The co-creating partner has changed from Reaktor to MinnaLearn. Ring changed from the roster's potential to adjacent: the whole product is a sustained AI programme, even though its content on societal effects is light. No dated news on its own site; activity in 2026 is confirmed only through partner use of Get AI Ready.

Elicit AdjacentChanged

Company · Oakland, United States · founded 2023

A public benefit corporation in Oakland, California, that sells an AI research assistant for literature search, systematic reviews and evidence synthesis, with sentence-level citations. It began inside Ought, an AI-alignment research nonprofit, and was spun out in September 2023. Its products include a Research Agent (with Routines, Sept 2026), PRISMA 2020 systematic reviews, an API and MCP server, and BioDecisionBench. It reports that 8 of the top 20 pharmaceutical companies use it.

It is the most widely adopted product of the 'AI for epistemics' strand and comes from Ought's alignment thesis: build transparent systems that decompose tasks into supervised reasoning steps, rather than opaque end-to-end models. It shows how far that process-supervision approach can go commercially, and how a safety-motivated project drifts towards a market.

Works on Epistemics, Assurance · Key work Elicit and AI Safety (Andreas Stuhlmüller) (2023); Elicit raises $22M Series A (2025); Introducing Elicit Research Agent (2026) · Get involved Staff roles in engineering, go-to-market and an ML research residency (careers page, 2026)

Note Now a commercial product aimed at pharma and enterprise research. Its AI-safety rationale (process supervision, shifting industry away from black-box models) was set out in 2023 and is not visible in its 2025-26 output. User figures conflict on its own site (5m vs 7m researchers; 400,000 monthly at the Feb 2025 Series A). Its parent Ought is on the classic aisafety.com map; Elicit is not listed separately. It is borderline for scope, as an AI application rather than work on AI itself.

Forum on Information & Democracy Adjacent

Nonprofit · Paris, France · founded 2019 · also draws on Arts, futures, Law, society

A Paris-based civil-society organisation created in November 2019 by Reporters Without Borders (RSF) and ten partner organisations. Its job is to turn the principles of the intergovernmental International Partnership for Information and Democracy, endorsed by more than 50 countries, into policy recommendations. It convenes expert working groups and workstreams that bring states and civil society together, publishes policy frameworks, and hosts the International Observatory on Information and Democracy. AI is one of its four thematic pillars: its 2024 framework 'AI as a Public Good' made more than 200 recommendations, and in February 2026 it launched a workstream on reliable information in the age of AI, co-chaired by Ukraine, Spain and Luxembourg.

It has a direct channel from civil-society policy research to a coalition of governments, and brings press-freedom and journalism-sustainability expertise to the question of how AI reshapes the information commons. It is also one of the few information-integrity bodies funded by an AI-safety funder, the Future of Life Institute.

Works on Epistemics, Power · Key work AI as a Public Good: Ensuring Democratic Control of AI in the Information Space (2024); Information Ecosystems and Troubled Democracy (International Observatory on Information and Democracy) (2025); AI and democracy in West Africa: recommendations for Benin, Côte d'Ivoire and Senegal (2025) · Get involved Calls for proposals for rapporteurs and policy advisors (Jan 2026); The AI workstream invites researchers to submit materials and join discussions; Occasional secretariat job openings (e.g. Development and Resource Officer, 2025)

Note An intergovernmental partnership mandates it and two foreign ministries part-fund it, so it is not fully independent of states. No board chair has been named publicly since founding president Christophe Deloire died in June 2024. Its AI work centres on media viability and information manipulation, not on the AI systems themselves.

Full Fact (incl. Full Fact AI) Adjacent

Nonprofit · London, United Kingdom · founded 2009 · also draws on Arts, futures

London fact-checking charity founded in 2009 by Will Moy and Michael Samuel. Its Full Fact AI tools find checkable claims, label claim types and match new claims to earlier fact checks; more than 40 fact-checking organisations in 30 countries use them daily, in three languages. In 2026 it monitored how Gemini, Grok and ChatGPT answered questions about false claims, finding 39 major errors over five months (reported August 2026). It is building a public, auditable benchmark of AI models on factuality, transparency, timeliness, consistency and civic responsibility.

It has codified fact-checking practice (claim detection, claim matching, human-in-the-loop verification) and is now applying it to how chatbots handle false claims. AI-epistemics projects can use its working verification infrastructure and evaluation criteria instead of rebuilding them.

Works on Epistemics, Assurance · Key work Full Fact AI: claim detection and claim matching tools for fact-checkers; Full Fact analysis: AI chatbots and misinformation (2026); Public, auditable AI benchmark (in development) (2026) · Get involved Careers page (around 50 named staff, including a Full Fact AI team); Full Fact Training courses; Full Fact AI tools are used by fact-checking organisations in 30 countries

Note Most of Full Fact AI applies AI to fact-checking. The parts that bear on AI itself are the 2026 chatbot monitoring and the benchmark, and I could not confirm when the benchmark's first report is due. Part of its funding comes from Meta and Google, whose platforms and models it checks.

Harmonica (Harmonious Technologies Ltd) Adjacent

Company · London, UK · founded 2023

Harmonica is an open-core AI facilitation platform. An AI facilitator holds a one-to-one conversation with each participant, then synthesises themes, tensions and consensus across the group, using templates such as Delphi rounds, Cynefin, Six Thinking Hats and Wardley mapping. The core is open source under AGPL-3.0 and self-hostable; session data is not used for model training. Case studies include CMI's December 2024 multilingual stakeholder survey, a Missions Publiques student workshop on AI governance, and Metagov's mapping of the gov/acc research space.

It is a public-interest, self-hostable alternative for AI-facilitated deliberation. It encodes established facilitation methods rather than ad hoc prompting, and organisations working on AI governance and peace mediation already use it.

That link is wrong: Companies House names Artem Zhiganov as director, and the essay does not mention Harmonica. Without it, there is no AI-safety framing on record, so the ring is lowered from bridge to adjacent. Team size is inferred from one active director and small donation flows.

International Federation of Library Associations and Institutions (IFLA) Adjacent

Membership body · The Hague, Netherlands · founded 1927 · also draws on Law, society

IFLA is the global federation of library associations and institutions. It has more than 1,700 members in about 155 countries, and its headquarters are at the National Library of the Netherlands in The Hague. Its AI work runs through an Artificial Intelligence Special Interest Group (sessions at the annual World Library and Information Congress, webinars and satellite meetings), guidance such as 'Developing a library strategic response to Artificial Intelligence' (2023) and the IFLA Statement on Copyright and AI (April 2025), and Knowledge Rights 21, its Arcadia-funded European copyright programme.

Libraries are the institutions much of the world already relies on for information literacy and knowledge stewardship. IFLA reaches that profession in about 155 countries, and it holds settled positions on AI literacy and on access to training data that the AI-safety field rarely engages with.

Works on Epistemics, Power · Key work IFLA Statement on Libraries and Artificial Intelligence (2020); Developing a library strategic response to Artificial Intelligence (AI SIG working document, v1.1) (2023); IFLA Statement on Copyright and Artificial Intelligence (2025) · Get involved AI Special Interest Group: open to IFLA members and affiliates; runs sessions and calls for papers at the annual World Library and Information Congress (August); Free global webinars from the AI SIG (e.g. 23 June 2026, on library associations and AI governance); Satellite meetings on AI, e.g. on research integrity in the age of AI (2026, with Yonsei University)

Note Its AI work is about libraries' own use of AI, AI literacy and copyright, not AI safety. Automated tools couldn't load IFLA's website, so the recent details come from search snippets of IFLA pages. It wasn't confirmed who convenes the AI SIG after the 2023-25 term. Knowledge Rights 21 has its own profile.

International Panel on the Information Environment (IPIE) Adjacent

Nonprofit · Zurich, Switzerland · founded 2023 · also draws on Law, society

An independent scientific body, loosely modelled on the IPCC, launched at the Nobel Prize Summit in May 2023 and registered as a charity in Zurich in December 2023. It synthesises research on threats to the global information environment through standing scientific panels, evidence assessments and an annual global expert survey (the 2026 edition drew on 470 experts in 71 countries), and has an affiliate network of more than 500 researchers. Its AI work includes a panel on global standards for AI audits (literature review in 2024, audit framework in 2025) and panels on AI and peacebuilding and on AI and economic inclusion.

It runs an IPCC-style international scientific assessment for the information environment, the kind of model the AI-safety field is also trying out with the International AI Safety Report. Its AI-audit panel brings in perspectives that AI-safety evaluation work rarely includes, such as Indigenous data sovereignty and Global South auditing.

Works on Epistemics, Assurance · Key work Global Approaches to Auditing Artificial Intelligence: A Literature Review (2024); Global framework for AI audits (Scientific Panel on Global Standards for AI Audits) (2025); Expert Survey on the Global Information Environment 2026: Under Pressure (2026) · Get involved Researchers can apply online to join the affiliate network (500+ members as of Apr 2026); Annual expert survey and reports released around the UN General Assembly each September

Note AI is one theme among several. Much of its output covers climate misinformation, platforms and child protection, and some AI panel pages list no recent outputs. Its secretariat is about 10 people, and most of the work is done by volunteer experts.

InterPARES Trust AI (I Trust AI: Archives 4.0) Adjacent

Programme · Vancouver, Canada · founded 2021

InterPARES Trust AI ('Archives 4.0: Artificial Intelligence for Trust in Records and Archives') is a multinational archival-science research partnership, led from the University of British Columbia's School of Information. It runs from 2021 to 2026 with more than 60 partner organisations in 26 countries. It studies how AI can help keep public records trustworthy and accessible, what risks AI brings to records and archives, and how archival concepts such as provenance, authenticity and paradata should inform responsible AI. Outputs include work on paradata documentation, cryptographic provenance for AI-generated images, AI competencies for archivists, and a series of symposia.

Archival science has a mature method for establishing whether a record is authentic and where it came from. Applied to AI, it offers ways to document the processes AI systems carry out ('paradata') and to establish provenance for AI-generated content. Both matter for accountability and information integrity.

Works on Epistemics, Assurance · Key work Papers on cryptographic provenance and authentication of AI-generated images (2025); InterPARES Trust AI symposium, Università di Macerata (2025); InterPARES Trust AI symposium, Ascoli Piceno (AI competencies for archivists, cryptographic provenance, paradata) (2026) · Get involved Final InterPARES Symposium, 29 Oct 2026, Library and Archives Canada, Ottawa (free; registration required via Carleton University)

Note The project ends in 2026. Its final symposium also marks the end of Luciana Duranti's career and of more than three decades of InterPARES research, so it is likely to go dormant after October 2026 unless a successor phase is funded. Much of its work is about using AI inside archives rather than about governing AI.

Jigsaw (Google) Adjacent

Programme · New York, US · founded 2010

A technology incubator inside Google, based in New York. It builds tools for censorship circumvention, cyberattack defence, online conversation and, increasingly, AI-assisted civic consultation. Its open-source Sensemaking tools use Gemini to summarise large public conversations and surface statements with broad agreement. They were used in the 'What Could BG Be?' county-wide consultation in Kentucky (nearly 8,000 residents) and in the 'We the People' national conversations with the Napolitan Institute. In Sept 2026 Jigsaw launched a Partner Program to take them to 30 cities, states and countries.

Jigsaw is shaping the default AI-mediation tools that local governments and civic groups adopt, and it frames AI explicitly in terms of human 'structural agency'. How its summarisation and consensus-finding choices treat minority views and resist manipulation will shape AI-mediated democracy at scale.

Works on Democracy, Epistemics · Key work Sensemaking tools (open-source library for AI summarisation of public conversations) (2024); What Could BG Be? AI-enabled county-wide town hall, Warren County, Kentucky (2025); We the People national conversations (with the Napolitan Institute) (2025) · Get involved Open-source sensemaking-tools library on GitHub (Apache 2.0); Jigsaw Partner Program for policymakers and civic leaders who want AI-assisted consultations (2026)

Note A unit of Google, a frontier AI developer, and its civic tools run on Gemini, so it is not independent of the industry whose influence it mediates. Founded in 2010 as Google Ideas and renamed Jigsaw in 2016. Much of its work is not about AI (Outline, spun out to the Outline Foundation in Dec 2025; encryption; cyber defence). Its leadership is not named on its own site, and the CEO was not re-verified for 2026.

KB, National Library of the Netherlands (Koninklijke Bibliotheek) Adjacent

Public body · The Hague, Netherlands · founded 1798 · also draws on Law, society, Economics

The Dutch national library, founded in 1798 and an independent administrative body funded by the Ministry of Education, Culture and Science. It adopted AI principles in 2020. In January 2024 it changed its terms of use and added technical measures to stop commercial AI firms crawling its Delpher and DBNL platforms for training, while keeping them open for academic research. Since 2024 it has sat on the content board of GPT-NL, the public Dutch language model built by TNO, SURF and NFI. In June 2026 it became a launching partner, supplying public-domain Delpher data and running a feasibility study on a retrieval assistant until November 2026.

It is a working template for consent-based governance of AI training data by a public institution: it refuses commercial scraping, protects research access and supplies vetted public-domain data to a public model in which it has a governance seat. Other memory institutions and public-AI projects can copy this approach.

Works on Justice, Power, Epistemics · Key work KB AI principles (2020); KB restricts access to collections for training commercial AI (Delpher, DBNL) (2024); KB becomes launching partner of GPT-NL; retrieval-assistant feasibility study on Delpher data (2026)

Note Its AI policy is mainly about copyright, attribution and personal data in its collections, not wider AI risk. It also uses AI in its own services, for example the retrieval-assistant pilot. The leadership details come from Dutch Wikipedia and the CENL announcement.

KFF Health Information and Trust Initiative (formerly Health Misinformation and Trust Initiative) Adjacent

Programme · San Francisco, USA · also draws on Safety science

One of KFF's core programmes. It tracks where Americans get health information, whom they trust and how false health claims spread, through regular tracking polls, a polling dashboard and a newsletter, The Monitor. AI is a recurring strand. Its March 2026 poll found that 32% of US adults had used AI chatbots for health information in the past year and 16% for mental-health advice, and recent Monitor issues covered state regulation of AI mental-health tools (Aug 2026) and AI-generated search answers (Sep 2026).

It provides repeated, population-level measures of how people use and trust AI in one high-stakes domain, the kind of survey baseline on AI-mediated information that AI-safety sensemaking work rarely has. It also links this to health communicators who have to adapt when AI answers replace visits to original sources.

Works on Epistemics, Human minds · Key work KFF Tracking Poll on Health Information and Trust: use of AI chatbots for health and mental-health information (Feb-Mar 2026 fieldwork) (2026); The Monitor, vol. 53: Different State Regulatory Approaches Reflect Open Questions About AI Mental Health Tools (2026); The Monitor, vol. 54: Correcting False Health Claims and Navigating AI-Generated Information (2026) · Get involved KFF 'Join Our Team' jobs page; Email subscription to The Monitor

Note AI is one strand of a wider health-misinformation and trust programme, so its AI engagement is real but modest (borderline between adjacent and potential). The work is US-focused, and the initiative's founding year was not confirmed.

Make.org Adjacent

Company · Paris, France · founded 2016 · also draws on Law, society

Paris-based civic-tech company founded in 2016. It is a mission-driven company with an associated Make.org Foundation, and it runs large online consultations for public bodies, EU institutions and businesses, reporting over 10 million participants. Its AI work includes leading the Democratic Commons research programme with Sciences Po, Sorbonne University and CNRS, backed by France 2030, which measures and corrects 'democratic biases' in language models used in participation. It also builds Panoramic, an AI platform deployed for EU institutions and events, and co-founded the Worldwide Alliance for AI and Democracy in 2025.

Democratic Commons is one of the few funded programmes that tests LLMs against explicit democratic criteria and publishes benchmarks and corpora; for example, it found that models translate speeches from fringe parties less accurately than from centrist ones. Make.org also ran the citizens' consultation for the 2025 Paris AI Action Summit, a direct channel from public input into AI governance.

Works on Democracy, Assurance, Epistemics · Key work Democratic Commons research programme (with Sciences Po, Sorbonne University, CNRS) (2024); AI Action Summit citizens' consultation 'shaping AI to serve the public good': 11,661 participants, 649 proposals, 121,325 votes (2024); Worldwide Alliance for AI and Democracy (manifesto and launch at the AI Action Summit) (2025) · Get involved Public consultations open to anyone on make.org; Worldwide Alliance for AI and Democracy, which organisations can join; Jobs at Make.org and the Make.org Foundation (listed on about.make.org)

Note A for-profit mission-driven company registered in Paris, not a nonprofit, and much of its revenue comes from the institutions and companies whose consultations it runs. Its AI framing is democratic resilience and bias, not catastrophic risk. A Germany team exists, but its office location was not confirmed.

Mantic Adjacent

Company · London, UK · founded 2024

Mantic is a London start-up, founded in 2024, building an AI system that makes judgmental forecasts of world events (geopolitics, business, policy, technology) one week to one year ahead, with reasoning and references. It sells horizon scanning, forecasts and monitoring, with API and MCP access, mainly to hedge funds, Fortune 500 companies and government users. In the Summer 2026 Metaculus Cup it scored above all 676 human participants.

Superhuman forecasting is a core 'AI for epistemics' capability that AI-safety strategists want for strategic awareness. Mantic shows that capability being built with venture money for traders and corporates, which makes it a live test of who captures AI-generated foresight. Its CEO previously designed dangerous-capability experiments for Gemini at Google DeepMind.

Works on Epistemics · Key work Mantic beats all human forecasters in the Summer 2026 Metaculus Cup and raises $25m (2026); Metaculus Cup results: 4th of 539 humans (Summer 2025), first overall (Summer 2026) (2025) · Get involved Hiring across AI research, engineering, product, sales and operations (announced Sep 2026); contact via contact@mantic.com

Note This is a commercial venture whose stated customers are mainly hedge funds and corporates. It has no AI-safety programme and frames its work as better decisions for business and government, so its place on this map is borderline: it is included as a case of the AI-for-epistemics capability rather than as a safety actor. Funders would not need to fund it.

MIT Center for Collective Intelligence (CCI) Adjacent

Academic · Cambridge, United States · founded 2006 · also draws on Economics, Psychology

A research centre at MIT, founded in 2006 by Thomas Malone, that studies how groups of people and computers ('superminds') can act more intelligently together than either alone. Its Collective Intelligence Design Lab helps sponsor organisations design such systems. Recent AI work includes a 2024 meta-analysis of when human-AI combinations outperform humans or AI alone, and studies showing that warmth works better than aggression for AI negotiators. It has also proposed 'learnrights' to pay creators whose work trains AI models, and in 2026 mapped where AI is used across about 20,000 work activities.

Its meta-analysis found that human-AI combinations often do worse than the better of the two alone on decision tasks, though they help in creative work. That challenges the assumption that a human in the loop makes AI safer. It also brings organisational design and collective-intelligence science to how AI reshapes work and who benefits.

Works on Power, Assurance · Key work When combinations of humans and AI are useful: a systematic review and meta-analysis (Vaccaro, Almaatouq, Malone; Nature Human Behaviour) (2024); Superminds: The Surprising Power of People and Computers Thinking Together (Malone) (2019); Where can AI be used? Insights from a deep ontology of work activities (2026) · Get involved Organisations can sponsor the centre and work with its Collective Intelligence Design Lab

Note No AI-safety or catastrophic-risk framing. Much of its AI work is on productivity and organisational design for corporate sponsors and NATO. Some outputs listed on its news page are by affiliated faculty rather than centre projects. It is not listed in the Oct 2026 'State of the Field' report on AI for epistemics.

MIT Center for Constructive Communication (CCC) Adjacent

Academic · Cambridge, Massachusetts, USA · founded 2021 · also draws on Psychology, Arts, futures

Centre at the MIT Media Lab, launched in January 2021 and directed by Deb Roy, that designs and tests human-led, AI-assisted systems for listening, dialogue and deliberation in small groups. Its tools include Forage (LLM-assisted sensemaking of conversation data), VoiceTrace (tracing public input through civic decisions) and FaciliTrain (AI-simulated facilitation practice), deployed with communities through its nonprofit partner Cortico and its realtalk programmes. It also publishes LLM research on bias and alignment.

It brings dialogue and facilitation practice, along with computational social science, to the question of how AI should mediate public conversation. Recent papers show leading LLMs underperform for less-educated and non-US users, and examine aligning models to users' long-term interests rather than stated wishes.

Works on Democracy, Epistemics · Key work From Delegates to Trustees: How Optimizing for Long-Term Interests Shapes Bias and Alignment in LLMs (EACL 2026) (2026); LLM Targeted Underperformance Disproportionately Impacts Vulnerable Users (AAAI-26) (2026); Forage: Understanding LLM-facilitated sensemaking of conversation data (CHI 2026) (2026) · Get involved Graduate study at the MIT Media Lab; Newsletter; Community partnerships via Cortico and realtalk programmes

Note The alignment paper is one line of work among many; most output is civic-technology and HCI research. Its relationship with Cortico, a separate nonprofit co-founded by Roy in 2016 where he is unpaid CEO, runs under a 10-year cooperation agreement with MIT (to Jan 2032) over IP, prototyping and pilots, with funding kept separate. It grew out of the Laboratory for Social Machines (2014).

Nesta Centre for Collective Intelligence (formerly Centre for Collective Intelligence Design, CCID) AdjacentChanged

Programme · London, UK · also draws on Arts, futures

A unit of Nesta, the UK innovation foundation, that designs digital tools and deliberative processes for public engagement, including the Zeitgeist deliberation platform and the Collective Intelligence Design Playbook. Its AI work centres on the AI Social Readiness process. This was developed with the UK Government's Incubator for AI and piloted in May-June 2025 with 144 members of the public in 18 workshops on the government's Consult tool. It also includes public-attitude studies on AI in social work and a 2026 citizens' jury on neurotechnology.

It turns public deliberation into an AI assurance instrument. Before a government AI tool is deployed, an advisory label records public confidence in it, the risks people see and the safeguards they want. That is a ready template for giving the public a say in deployment decisions, which mainstream AI assurance leaves to experts.

Works on Democracy, Assurance · Key work The AI Social Readiness process (advisory label for the Consult tool) (2025); How to manage AI risks: a community-based approach to AI assurance (2025); How does the public feel about social workers using AI? (2025) · Get involved Staff roles via Nesta's jobs page; Partnership enquiries for public-engagement and AI-assurance projects through the centre's page; Collective Intelligence Design Playbook, a free practitioner toolkit

Note Renamed from Centre for Collective Intelligence Design, and older pages still use that name. Much of its work is commissioned engagement on non-AI topics such as climate, politics and social care. The Participatory AI project page has not been updated since 2023. Founding year not confirmed in the sources checked.

News Literacy Project (NLP) Adjacent

Nonprofit · Washington, DC, USA · founded 2008 · also draws on Arts, futures

A nonpartisan US education nonprofit in Washington, DC, founded in 2008 by Pulitzer Prize-winning reporter Alan C. Miller, that teaches students and the public to judge whether information is credible. Its products include the Checkology virtual classroom, the RumorGuard debunking site, The Sift newsletter for teachers and the annual National News Literacy Week. Its AI materials include 'AI or not?' lessons, '6 Things to Know About AI', the 'Two Truths and AI' video series, RumorGuard debunks of AI-generated fakes, and teen surveys on trust in AI chatbots (2024 and 2026).

It applies nearly two decades of journalism-based verification teaching to AI-generated misinformation. It reports that more than 1.4 million students have been taught with its resources since 2016 (3.5 million on another of its counts), and its educators work in more than a third of US public school districts. That is epistemic self-defence at population scale, which AI-safety work on truthfulness rarely connects to.

Works on Epistemics, Human minds · Key work Teaching About AI: classroom resources ('AI or not?', 'Two Truths and AI', 6 Things to Know About AI) (2026); National News Literacy Week 2026: rebuilding trust in the age of AI (2026); NLP Teen Survey Report (including teen trust in generative AI chatbots) (2024) · Get involved Free Checkology educator accounts and AI lessons; The Sift, a weekly newsletter for educators; National News Literacy Week, held each February

Note Focused on the US. Its AI work is one strand of news literacy, aimed at misinformation, deepfakes and 'AI slop' rather than wider AI risks.

Plurality Institute Adjacent

Nonprofit · San Francisco Bay Area, US · also draws on Peace

A US 501(c)(3) that serves as a hub for 'plurality' research: technology for human cooperation at scale, following Glen Weyl and Audrey Tang's book. It connects academia, industry, civil society and government. It builds prototypes: BridgingBot, an LLM-based moderator that de-escalates polarised social-media threads (tested in randomised trials, code open-sourced), and OpenBallot, a voter-guide platform. With the Council on Technology and Social Cohesion it ran the Feb 2025 'LLMs and Public Discourse' convening in Berkeley and published an Oct 2025 map of 70 LLM tools for public discourse; it also gives micro-grants.

It brings peacebuilding, political science and plurality theory into the design of LLM tools, and tests in randomised trials whether AI can bridge divides rather than deepen them. That gives evidence-based prototypes for societal resilience to AI-mediated discourse.

Works on Democracy, Epistemics · Key work Mapping LLM Tools for Public Discourse, Pluralism & Social Cohesion (with Council on Technology & Social Cohesion and Prosocial Design Network) (2025); LLMs and Public Discourse convening, Berkeley (70+ researchers; $50k awarded by approval voting) (2025); BridgingBot: LLM-based moderator for polarised online conversations (2025) · Get involved Monthly newsletter of plurality grants, fellowships and events; Micro-grants awarded at its workshops and convenings; Annual conference, symposia and online workshops (most recent own convening Feb 2025)

Note Its own dated output thins out after Nov 2025, and the site footer still reads 2024. Several funders (Google.org, Jigsaw, Microsoft) are tech companies whose platforms its tools are meant to moderate. It does not frame its work around AI safety or alignment. The HQ city is inferred from the team and events, not stated.

Research Data Alliance (RDA) Adjacent

Network · Distributed · founded 2013 · also draws on Safety science

A global, member-driven body for research-data sharing, founded in 2013. Volunteers in more than 100 working and interest groups write recommendations on FAIR data, metadata and trusted access. Its AI work covers documenting generative-AI use in research, FAIR for machine learning, 'data visitation' (the analysis travels to sensitive data, not the reverse) and, since 2026, the VANTAGE working group, which is drafting a framework for deciding whether and under what controls AI agents may work with restricted research data.

Here data stewards rather than ML researchers are writing shared rules for when AI agents may touch sensitive data, and for how AI use in research is documented. That makes it a working venue for agent oversight and provenance standards, and a route to adoption for safety researchers.

Works on Epistemics, Assurance · Key work VANTAGE WG: Agentic Landscape Assessment Framework for AI agents and restricted research data (in community review) (2026); Documenting Generative AI Interactions in Research Interest Group (2026); Global community priorities for agentic AI in research: consultation results (with Microsoft) (2026) · Get involved Free individual membership; join or co-chair working and interest groups, including VANTAGE (in community review in 2026); Plenaries: P27 in person in London, 6-8 Oct 2026; virtual plenaries and online Birds of a Feather sessions; Technical Advisory Board election, Nov-Dec 2026

Note Most of its AI work is about getting research data ready for AI and helping researchers adopt AI tools, partly in partnership with Microsoft. VANTAGE and the documentation group are the parts that bear on oversight; both were still in community review and not yet endorsed in Sep 2026 (VANTAGE start date 4 Sep 2026, the Documenting Generative AI Interactions IG 7 Sep 2026). There is no catastrophic-risk framing. Hilary Hanahoe is named as Secretary General in 2025-26 speaker bios and co-authored the January 2026 agentic-AI consultation report; the RDA site does not show the name.

Simocracy AdjacentNew

Programme · San Francisco, USA · also draws on Economics

An open-source platform on the AT Protocol where people mint AI 'sims' (digital twins), each with an avatar, a constitution its owner writes and a speaking style, and send them to public senates, councils and funding rounds. Deliberation and allocations, including S-Process and quadratic-voting rounds, are recorded as a public feed. The site lists 336 sims; Filecoin's ProPGF public-goods rounds and Edge City's Agent Village have used it.

It is a working testbed for AI delegates in collective decisions. It has already exposed the principal-agent gap: at Agent Village, sims' allocations were recorded without their principals confirming them, which bears directly on gradual-disempowerment and scalable-oversight debates. The mechanisms are forkable, so others can test ratification, withdrawal and correction rules.

Works on Democracy, Multi-agent · Key work Agent Village at Edge Esmeralda: 82 sims evaluated 35 proposals and allocated $10,000 (write-up by Cosmos Institute and Edge City) (2026); Filecoin ProPGF Batch 2 decision ($1.02m across 13 proposals) on the Simocracy public record, with S-Process deliberation by sims (2026); simocracy-mechanisms: forkable ATProto runtime for S-Process and quadratic-voting mechanisms (2026) · Get involved Mint a sim (about five minutes of interview) at simocracy.org and bring it to Senate, council or S-Process gatherings; Convene a gathering or funding round on the platform; fork the mechanism runtime on GitHub (GainForest/simocracy-mechanisms)

Note The site names no team; the code is maintained in GainForest's GitHub and Cosmos Institute credits Protocol Labs with leading development. Sums handled so far are small and it sits in the crypto public-goods milieu; it does not frame itself as safety work. Roster counts of 26 gatherings and 432 proposals could not be confirmed (the counters render client-side). An Ecofrontiers 'Agent Governance Sandbox' built for Mozilla's Democracy x AI cohort also uses the 'simocracy' label; its relationship to this project is unclear. An unrelated 2016-17 'Simocracy' simulation game exists on GitHub.

Starling Lab for Data Integrity Adjacent

Academic · Stanford, USA · founded 2018 · also draws on Law, society, Arts, futures

Starling Lab is an academic research centre co-founded by Stanford's Department of Electrical Engineering and the USC Shoah Foundation. It began as a research programme in 2018 and formally launched in 2021. It prototypes tools and principles for capturing, storing and verifying authentic digital records, using cryptography and decentralised storage, for journalism, history, law and human-rights archives. Its 2026 dispatches cover deepfakes as courtroom evidence, guiding principles for AI in international criminal courts, a guide to synthetic-media and provenance law in the EU, US and China, and AI in documentary production.

It applies archival chain of custody and cryptographic provenance to the problem of keeping authentic records once generative AI makes fabrication cheap. That makes it a practical source on epistemic resilience for courts, newsrooms and historians, beyond detecting individual deepfakes.

Works on Epistemics, Justice · Key work Guide to synthetic media regulation and content provenance in the EU, US and China (2026); New guiding principles for AI in the courtroom (international criminal law and deepfake evidence) (2026); Decoding the California AI Transparency Act (2026) · Get involved 2026 fellows on documentary, generative AI and media authenticity; Dispatch newsletter (dispatch.starlinglab.org)

Note Its main funders are decentralised-web and crypto-linked foundations (Protocol Labs, Filecoin Foundation, IOG), which shapes its technical approach. Independent coverage of the lab itself is thin. It has about nine staff.

The GovLab and Burnes Center for Social Change (Reboot Democracy, InnovateUS) Adjacent

Academic · Boston, US · founded 2012 · also draws on Law, society

A cluster of projects led by Beth Simone Noveck. They are based at Northeastern University's Burnes Center for Social Change and The GovLab, which Noveck co-founded with Stefaan Verhulst. Reboot Democracy is a weekly blog on AI, democracy and public-sector governance. InnovateUS runs free online courses and live workshops for public servants, such as 'Responsible AI for Public Professionals' and 'Designing Democratic Engagement with AI', and reports 265,000 learners across more than 75 agencies. Related projects include AI for Impact, a student co-op, as well as AI Localism, Community-Centered AI and an Observatory of Public Sector AI.

It reaches the front-line public servants who will buy, deploy and oversee AI, and does so at a scale the safety field does not. It gives them working templates for AI-assisted public engagement, procurement and evaluation, drawn from collective-intelligence and crowdlaw practice.

Works on Democracy, Assurance · Key work Reboot: AI and the Race to Save Democracy (Beth Simone Noveck, Yale University Press) (2026); Designing Democratic Engagement with AI (free InnovateUS course; 42 examples from 20 countries) (2026); Responsible AI for Public Professionals (InnovateUS course) · Get involved Free InnovateUS online courses and live workshops for public servants (ongoing; e.g. 'Principles for Public-Sector AI Evaluation', 6 Oct 2026); Reboot Democracy weekly newsletter; accepts guest posts by email; AI for Impact co-op (Northeastern University students)

Note Its stance is optimistic 'Democratic AI', aimed at helping governments adopt AI, and it uses no catastrophic-risk framing. Noveck is also New Jersey's Chief AI Strategist, so the group sits close to government adopters. The founding year refers to The GovLab, founded at NYU. The roster entry bundles several branded projects, so it is not always clear which project produced which output.

Wikidata Embedding Project (Wikimedia Deutschland) AdjacentNew

Programme · Berlin, Germany · founded 2024 · also draws on Economics

A Wikimedia Deutschland project, started in 2024 and launched on 1 October 2025, that turns Wikidata's statements into vectors so that language models can search and cite them. It runs a free vector database built with Jina AI's multilingual embeddings and DataStax's Astra DB, and an MCP server that helps models write grounded SPARQL queries. In May 2026 it added a Wikibase MCP for other Wikibase instances. It also publishes processed Wikidata dumps on Hugging Face, to reduce load from AI scrapers.

It shows public-interest grounding infrastructure working in practice: a community-curated, sourced knowledge graph made available to language models for retrieval with citations. It bears on model truthfulness and on alternatives to corporate AI infrastructure. It also tests whether a knowledge commons can supply AI without being worn down by scraping.

Works on Epistemics, Power · Key work Wikidata vector database launch: 'Toward Reliable Generative AIs: The Wikidata Embedding Project Supports Alternatives to Big Tech' (2025); Wikidata MCP and Wikibase MCP servers for grounded SPARQL generation (2026); 'Wikidata MCP: Grounded SPARQL Query Generation', Wikimania 2026 talk (2026) · Get involved Use the free vector database and MCP servers and give feedback on the Wikidata project page; Contribute to Wikidata or to the open-source WikidataMCP and WikidataTextifier code

Note The Wikimedia Foundation is a separate roster entry; this profile is the German chapter's project. Its main users are AI developers, and part of the motive is reducing scraping load. Whether it reduces misinformation in deployed systems has not been shown. At first only about 30 million of Wikidata's roughly 119 million items were vectorised. It relies on commercial partners for embeddings and storage.

Wikimedia Foundation Adjacent

Nonprofit · San Francisco, United States · founded 2003 · also draws on Economics

San Francisco nonprofit, founded in 2003, that hosts Wikipedia and its sister projects. Its April 2025 AI strategy commits to using AI, preferably open-source or open-weight models, to support volunteer editors rather than replace them: in moderation, discovery, translation and onboarding. Wikimedia Enterprise sells high-volume API access to commercial reusers, capped at 30% of Foundation revenue, which the Foundation presents as a way to make AI and big tech pay for the strain they put on its infrastructure. During the September 2026 UN General Assembly its CEO called on AI companies and other large reusers to attribute and financially support Wikipedia.

It runs the largest human-curated knowledge commons, which models train on and AI agents cite. Its verifiability and source-reliability norms are a tested model of collective epistemics at scale. Its dispute over AI crawler costs and attribution is a front-line case of AI drawing down the commons it depends on.

Works on Epistemics, Power · Key work AI strategy: supporting Wikipedia's human editors (2025); The cost of 'free': how Wikimedia Enterprise protects Wikipedia in the AI era (2026); Human knowledge at stake: case at the UN General Assembly (2026) · Get involved Anyone can edit and contribute to Wikipedia and its sister projects online; Wikimania (2026 edition held in Paris for Wikipedia's 25th anniversary); Staff roles at the Foundation

Note It does not frame its work in AI-safety terms. At the UN its CEO argued that AI governance should address damage to the information ecosystem, not only model outputs and safety. Wikimedia Enterprise earns revenue from the commercial reusers whose crawling strains its infrastructure. The Berlin, Paris and London chapters are separate affiliates.

Potential ring 5

Centre for Argument Technology (ARG-tech), University of Dundee Potential

Academic · Dundee, United Kingdom · also draws on Philosophy

A research centre at the University of Dundee working on argument mining, computational models of argument and software for analysing debate. Its tools include OVA, an online argument-analysis tool, and AIFdb, a large open corpus of analysed argumentation. It is a funded partner in AI4Deliberation, an EU Horizon project (Nov 2024 to Oct 2027) building AI tools and guidance so that governments can run and assess mass public deliberations. Its commercial arm, Arg Technica Ltd, took on its first staff in 2025.

It can extract and evaluate the structure of arguments at scale, including automatic debate evaluation and fallacy detection with LLMs. These methods could check whether AI-written reasoning or deliberation summaries are faithful, and could support debate-based oversight of AI. So far it treats AI as a tool for better deliberation, not as an object of safety work.

Works on Epistemics, Democracy · Key work AI4Deliberation (EU Horizon project; ARG-tech leads argument assessment for mass deliberation) (2025); OVA3 online argument visualisation and analysis tool; EMNLP 2023 papers on automatic debate evaluation and fallacy detection with large language models (2023) · Get involved PhD studentships and postdoctoral posts, advertised from time to time on its news page; Door to open: no AI-safety programme yet, so collaboration on argument analysis of AI reasoning would need outreach

Note Its website is being rebuilt, and its news and publication lists stop in mid-2025, so recent output is under-reported there. The director attribution comes from general knowledge and its conference-chair listings, not from a current staff page (the people page returned 403). It has no AI-safety framing; its AI work is about deliberation and misinformation tools.

Democracy X (formerly the Danish Board of Technology / Teknologirådet) PotentialChanged

Nonprofit · Copenhagen, Denmark · founded 2023 · also draws on Arts, futures

A Danish non-profit-distributing foundation formed in 2023 by merging Teknologirådet (the Danish Board of Technology, active since the 1980s and known for consensus conferences and the World Wide Views global citizen consultations) with DeltagerDanmark, a community-organising group. About 50 staff run citizen panels, deliberations and local organising on three themes: planetary boundaries, technological acceleration and democratic strengthening. Its main AI work is the National Youth Dialogue on Generative AI (361 young people, autumn 2024), reported in January 2025 with the Danish Data Ethics Council and TrygFonden.

It holds some of the longest institutional experience in participatory technology assessment, the practice of having citizens deliberate on emerging technologies before they spread. That method applies directly to public deliberation on frontier AI, though Democracy X has not yet aimed it there.

Works on Democracy · Key work De unges stemme i samtalen om generativ AI (National Youth Dialogue on Generative AI report, with Dataetisk Råd and TrygFonden) (2025); Visioner for fremtidens digitale fællesskaber (citizen visions for future online communities) (2026); World Wide Views global citizen consultations (Danish Board of Technology method) (2009) · Get involved Commissions and partnerships for citizen panels, deliberations and stakeholder processes (Danish and EU projects)

Note A renamed and merged successor of the Danish Board of Technology; the old tekno.dk site now points to Democracy X. Its AI engagement is light: one youth dialogue and some work on digital communities. The roster's 'June 2026' date for the youth report is wrong; the report is dated January 2025. Most material is in Danish.

Internet Archive Potential

Nonprofit · San Francisco, USA · founded 1996 · also draws on Law, society

A San Francisco nonprofit digital library founded by Brewster Kahle in 1996. It runs the Wayback Machine, which passed one trillion archived web pages in October 2025, and holds tens of millions of digitised texts, recordings and films. Its AI engagement is light: copyright submissions on AI (2023), episodes of its Future Knowledge podcast with Authors Alliance on AI and web archiving (2025-26), and a September 2026 event, 'Open For Whom? Access to Knowledge in the Age of AI'.

Transferable method: web archiving as an independent, time-stamped record of what was published, which can be used to check provenance and claims as AI-generated content spreads. Since late 2025, publishers have been blocking its crawlers for fear of AI scraping, a direct case of AI pressure eroding a shared epistemic resource.

Works on Epistemics, Power · Key work Wayback Machine passes one trillion archived web pages (2025); Future Knowledge podcast: 'Preserving the Web in the Age of AI' (2026); Open For Whom? Access to Knowledge in the Age of AI (virtual event) (2026) · Get involved Future Knowledge podcast and free virtual events on access to knowledge and AI; Donate, volunteer or upload material to the archive

Note It does not run an AI programme; its AI involvement is commentary and the knock-on effects on its archive. More than 340 news outlets, including the New York Times and the Guardian, restrict its crawlers over AI concerns. It has lost major copyright litigation (Hachette v. Internet Archive). The most recent staff count found is from 2021.

People Powered Potential

Membership body · Distributed (incorporated in the US and Ireland) · founded 2020

A member-driven global hub for participatory democracy, incorporated as a nonprofit in the US and Ireland, with staff and members around the world. It grew out of a Global Participatory Budgeting Hub (2019) and was set up in its current form in 2020 by 58 practitioners from 28 countries. It runs training, mentorship, accelerators and resource centres on participatory budgeting, citizens' assemblies and digital participation. Its AI work so far includes AI criteria in its ratings of 30 digital participation platforms, accelerator funding for European universities where students co-wrote AI policies, and a September 2026 webinar and workshop series with the OECD and Bertelsmann Stiftung on AI in citizen participation.

It is a main channel to local governments and practitioners worldwide, so safeguards for AI-mediated participation (against exclusion, skewed summaries and simulated public opinion) could spread through it. It also holds practical know-how on running participatory processes, which AI governance could borrow.

Works on Democracy · Key work Digital Participation Platform Ratings and Guide (AI usage among the criteria; refreshed 2025) (2025); Who Should Decide the Future of AI? These Universities Put Students in Charge (AI Aware Universities, supported by its Digital Democracy Accelerator) (2026); AI is changing citizen participation: are we ready? (webinar and workshop with OECD and Bertelsmann Stiftung) (2026) · Get involved Membership for organisations, government practitioners, researchers and advocates; Online digital participation training courses; Digital Democracy Accelerator and mentorship programmes

Note Its AI engagement is mostly about AI as a tool inside participation processes, not about governing frontier AI, and there is no standing AI programme or page. Its long-standing co-executive director stepped down in July 2026.

The Society Library (Benjamin Franklin Society Library Inc) Potential

Nonprofit · Orlando, United States · founded 2013

A US nonprofit that builds structured databases ('debate maps') of the arguments, claims and evidence on contested public questions. It extracts these from many kinds of media and aims to represent every detectable point of view. It builds AI tools for this work: the Rose and Juniper debate-modelling tools, a fact-checking model, a claim collector and autonomous research agents. It also teaches its methods to university students. In 2023-24 it ran a grant-funded project to map the AI safety, alignment and x-risk debate, which broke the subject into 272 questions and subtopics.

It has a working method for making a contested field's disagreements legible: who argues what, and on which evidence. Applied to AI risk, that gives new funders and policymakers a map they currently lack. Its 2026 plan to add other 'epistemological paradigms', including ancestral and Indigenous ways of knowing, is close to int/a's full-spectrum knowing.

Works on Epistemics, Democracy · Key work We're Mapping AI Safety/Alignment Arguments and Issues (2023); We Mapped an EA vs. e/acc Debate With Our New Tools (2024); Weaving In More Epistemological Paradigms in 2026 (2025) · Get involved Open-source bounties of $10k each (announced Feb 2026); Project-based and long-term volunteering (credited on its team page); Donations

Note The 2023 AI-safety debate map was announced as work in progress. No finished public map, and no AI-safety output from 2025-26, was found. Its recent posts are about environmental justice and tooling. The founding year is inferred from the site's '2013-' copyright line; it has been a 501(c)(3) since November 2014. There are four named core staff, and much of the work is done by volunteers. The 2025 'Mapping LLMs' report that listed it could not be opened (domain check rate-limited).

Society & institutions · 51 organisations · 6 on the classic map

Peace, security & diplomacy

The peace tradition brings the oldest tested toolkit for handling dangerous technology between rivals: arms control and verification, confidence-building measures and hotlines, Track II and scientist-to-scientist diplomacy, the humanitarian-law doctrine of meaningful human control, and mediation. Its main actors fall into three clusters. The first is Track II channels: Safe AI Forum (SAIF), Concordia AI, Oxford Martin AIGI, Brookings-Tsinghua AI Dialogue and HD AI & Emerging Tech. The second is arms-control institutes, mostly funded by Andrew Carnegie Fdn: SIPRI, ELN Nuclear & Tech, IST, Pugwash and NTI. The third is humanitarian-law and UN bodies: ICRC autonomous weapons, Stop Killer Robots and UNIDIR. Peace sits fairly close to the AI-safety core: 28 of its 51 entries are core or bridge, and 6 are on the aisafety.com map. That closeness is almost entirely in diplomacy and arms control, and it reaches AI mostly through AI in nuclear command and military AI rather than frontier loss of control. Peacebuilding and mediation (11 entries) stay at adjacent and potential.

What is missing. Peacebuilding's own knowledge is not being applied to AI itself: conflict analysis, mediation, ripeness, de-escalation and dialogue across enemies. Of the 11 peacebuilding entries, none is core and only HD AI & Emerging Tech is bridge. No peace organisation works on the race between labs or between the AI camps, or on conflict between AI agents. None of the 51 moves its knowledge into the model or to the builders.

Openings here Organisational and political psychology research on lab safety culture and race decisions; A frontier-risk translation desk for faith delegations at 2026-27 summits; Professional mediators applying conflict transformation to the AI race; Mediators and negotiation scholars co-building evaluations for AI-agent conflict; World Wide Views-style Global or distributed deliberation on frontier-AI risk before May 2027; Fellowship bringing treaty-verification inspectors into AI-agreement verification work; An African philosophy research line inside Africa's AI-safety organisations

Core ring 6

AI Safety Asia (AISA) Core

Nonprofit · Hong Kong · founded 2024 · also draws on Arts, futures

AISA is a nonprofit set up in 2024 to build Asian governments' capacity to govern AI safety. It trains officials (in April 2026, 38 Indonesian officials from 11 ministries), runs regional roundtables and civil-society trainings, and keeps invitation-only channels open between senior officials. It also runs AI crisis tabletop exercises; in 2026 these were held in Geneva, at the Biological Weapons Convention working group, and on the official APEC agenda. In 2025 it announced RAISE-SEA, a scenario platform, at the Paris Peace Forum, and published a Brookings report on AI safety governance in Southeast Asia.

It brings crisis-diplomacy simulation and Southeast Asian policy perspectives into AI-safety governance, which US, UK and Chinese voices otherwise dominate. It helps middle powers and Global Majority states see their dependencies and secure safeguards in AI procurement.

Works on Security, Justice · Key work AI Safety Governance, the Southeast Asian Way (with the Brookings Institution) (2025); Scaling AI Diplomacy: scenario exercises for capacity and readiness (with Chatham House and the University of Geneva) (2026); RAISE-SEA scenario and preparedness platform (Paris Peace Forum) (2025) · Get involved Newsletter on AI governance in Asia; Online public convenings, some co-hosted (e.g. with Chatham House, Jan 2026); Regional civil-society AI-governance training (second cohort June 2026)

Note Its site gives no headquarters. The roster said Manila; its Manifund project lists Hong Kong, the UK and the US, and the CEO is based in Hong Kong. Much of its work is high-level convening, whose effects are hard to verify. Its stated stakes mix sovereignty and lock-in concerns with crisis and catastrophic-risk work.

Concordia AI CoreOn aisafety.com

Company · Beijing, China · founded 2020 · also draws on Safety science

Concordia AI is a social enterprise working on AI safety and governance in China and internationally, with offices in Beijing and Singapore; Brian Tse is its founder and CEO. It publishes the annual State of AI Safety in China report (fourth edition, July 2026, covering July 2025 to June 2026), a State of AI Safety in Singapore report, a Frontier AI Risk Management Framework (version 2.0) and an online Frontier AI Risk Monitor. It also runs the AI Safety in China newsletter, convenes safety forums such as one at the World AI Conference in Shanghai, and advises AI companies and Chinese policy consultations.

It makes Chinese AI-safety policy, research and expert opinion legible abroad, and connects Chinese and international safety researchers. Without that translation, Western safety strategy rests on guesses about China.

Works on Security, Assurance · Key work State of AI Safety in China (2026), fourth edition, with interactive companion site (2026); Frontier AI Risk Management Framework 2.0 (2026); Frontier AI Risk Monitor (update: risk indices rise severalfold) (2026) · Get involved Job: AI Governance Researcher / Research Manager, Singapore (deadline 12 Oct 2026); general expressions of interest accepted; Affiliates Program, a network of fellows from AI research groups worldwide; AI Safety in China newsletter (Substack)

Note As a China-registered company it works within Chinese political constraints, and it does not disclose its funding. The founding year (2020) comes from earlier public profiles, not its current site. Its consulting for AI companies could create conflicts of interest.

Oxford Martin AI Governance Initiative (AIGI) CoreOn aisafety.com

Academic · Oxford, UK · founded 2023 · also draws on Safety science

AIGI is a research centre in the University of Oxford's Martin School, launched in September 2023. It studies the governance of frontier AI from both the policy and the technical side. Its work covers international and China AI governance; the Oxford AI Diplomacy Lab, which supports officials who negotiate on AI; technical and hardware governance (verification, chip and compute-cluster monitoring); and frontier-AI risk-management standards. With the Safe AI Forum it co-hosted the fifth International Dialogue on AI Safety (IDAIS) in London in April 2026, which produced the IDAIS London Declaration.

It applies international-relations and diplomatic practice to frontier AI: Track II dialogue agendas, verification regimes, and lessons from aviation and nuclear governance. It is one of the few university centres building diplomats' capacity for AI negotiations.

Works on Security, Assurance · Key work Co-host of IDAIS-London and the IDAIS London Declaration (with the Safe AI Forum) (2026); Promising Topics for US–China Dialogues on AI Safety and Governance (2025); Verification for International AI Governance (2025) · Get involved Technical AI Governance (TAIG) DPhil studentships; AI Academic Upskilling Program for Social Scientists (call for applications April 2026); Public events and a newsletter

Note Much of its output is conventional AI-governance analysis. The interdisciplinary part is mainly international relations, diplomacy, and comparison with how other safety-critical industries are regulated.

Safe AI Forum (SAIF) CoreOn aisafety.com

Nonprofit · London, UK and San Francisco, USA (US 501(c)(3)) · founded 2023

SAIF is a US 501(c)(3) nonprofit with staff in London and San Francisco. It runs the International Dialogues on AI Safety (IDAIS), where senior Western and Chinese scientists (among them Andrew Yao, Yoshua Bengio, Stuart Russell and Zhang Ya-Qin) agree joint statements on extreme AI risks. There have been five dialogues: Oxford 2023, Beijing 2024 (red lines such as autonomous replication), Venice 2024, Shanghai 2025 (deception) and London 2026. The London dialogue in April 2026 was co-hosted with the Royal Society and the Oxford Martin AI Governance Initiative, and covered AI-enabled cyberattacks and biological misuse. SAIF also publishes research on international cooperation and technical safeguards, often with Chinese co-authors.

It applies the Pugwash model of scientist-to-scientist diplomacy to AI, keeping a US-China channel on catastrophic risk open while official dialogue is thin.

Works on Security, Assurance · Key work IDAIS-Beijing statement proposing red lines for AI development (2024); IDAIS-London statement on AI-enabled cyberattacks and biological misuse (2026); In Which Areas of Technical AI Safety Could Geopolitical Rivals Cooperate? (2025) · Get involved Jobs (Oct 2026): (Senior) Researcher – Misuse Risks, General Counsel, Executive Business Partner; in person in London or San Francisco, some remote

Note The dialogues are invitation-only and their statements are non-binding, so their influence on governments is hard to trace. The founding year is taken from the first IDAIS (October 2023); SAIF ran under FAR.AI's fiscal sponsorship until May 2025.

Simon Institute for Longterm Governance (SI) CoreOn aisafety.com

Nonprofit · Geneva, Switzerland · founded 2021

A Geneva think tank and Swiss nonprofit, founded in 2021 by Maxime Stauffer and Konrad Seifert, that helps diplomats and international civil servants govern frontier AI. Since narrowing its focus to AI in 2023 it has advised over 100 diplomats from dozens of countries. It supported the design of the UN Independent International Scientific Panel on AI and the Global Dialogue on AI Governance. Since 2025 it has run a workstream on confidence building and crisis preparedness between the US and China.

It works inside the UN system in Geneva and New York, translating frontier-AI risk for diplomats from many countries, developing countries included. Few AI-safety organisations do this.

Works on Security, Epistemics · Key work Recommendations for the design of the UN Independent International Scientific Panel on AI and Global Dialogue on AI Governance (2025); What is Artificial General Intelligence? (explainer for policymakers) (2025); Frontier AI and emerging biological risks: side event at the UN Biological Weapons Convention working group (2026) · Get involved Staff roles (no open positions as of Oct 2026); Public events in Geneva, such as UN side events; Donations (tax-deductible in Switzerland and the US)

Note Much of its work happens privately with diplomats, so impact is hard to verify from outside. The co-founder named Konrad Seifert in the 2025 annual report appears as Konrad Gerosa on the current team page, apparently a name change.

UChicago Existential Risk Laboratory (XLab) CoreOn aisafety.com

Academic · Chicago, USA · founded 2022 · also draws on Safety science

XLab is an interdisciplinary lab at the University of Chicago, founded in 2022 by the physicist Daniel Holz. It researches existential and global catastrophic risks (AI safety and security, nuclear security, biorisk and extreme climate change) and trains students in them. It runs a paid 10-week Summer Research Fellowship on AI safety, nuclear security and where they meet; an AI safety fundamentals course; 'Second Look', which replicates influential empirical AI-safety results; and an open AI Security guide. It supports the Nobel Laureate Assembly for the Prevention of Nuclear War and co-sponsored the July 2026 Rome assembly on AI and nuclear war, which produced the Rome Declaration.

It ties AI risk to the nuclear-security tradition of the Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists, whose Science and Security Board Holz chairs. It also trains researchers in the neglected overlap of AI and nuclear risk, including resilience after a nuclear detonation.

Works on Security, Metacrisis · Key work Summer Research Fellowship in AI safety and nuclear security (2026); Co-sponsor, Global Nobel Laureates Assembly on AI and Nuclear War (Rome Declaration) (2026); Second Look: replicating empirical AI-safety claims · Get involved Summer Research Fellowship: 10 weeks in person in Chicago, $10,000 stipend plus housing and compute credits; applications due mid-March (the 2026 round ran 15 Jun–22 Aug); AI Security guide: free self-study material with coding exercises; Mailing list

Note Its AI programme is fairly mainstream (an AI risk fundamentals reading group, replications, a security guide); what sets it apart is the link to nuclear and broader existential risk. The team is small and many members are students. The classic map lists its fellowship, not the lab. The fellowship requires US work authorisation.

Bridge ring 22

African Hub on AI Safety, Peace and Security BridgeNew

Programme · Cape Town, South Africa · founded 2025 · also draws on Law, society, Safety science

A hub in the University of Cape Town's AI Initiative, co-led with the Global Center on AI Governance and funded by IDRC and the UK FCDO through AI4D. It was announced in September 2025 as the twelfth lab in the AI4D network and the first devoted to policy and governance. It teaches an interdisciplinary AI Safety honours course and a technical AI safety track in applied mathematics, and runs red-teaming workshops, quarterly AI safety hackathons and an AI diplomacy curriculum for African policymakers. It funds 15 honours, 4 master's and 1 PhD places, including a 2026-28 master's fellowship on mapping AI harms. Its stated aims are African representation in global AI safety debates and attention to AI risks for marginalised groups, particularly women and girls.

It is one of the few places training African students and policymakers in AI safety itself, with public-law, criminology and peace-and-security perspectives alongside a technical track. That widens both who does safety work and which harms get counted.

Works on Security, Justice, Assurance · Key work AI4D announcement of the hub (twelfth AI4D lab) (2025); Master's Fellowship in AI Governance and Harm Mapping (2026-28) (2026); Interdisciplinary AI Safety honours course and technical AI safety track · Get involved Master's Fellowship in AI Governance and Harm Mapping, 2026-28 (applications closed); Funded honours, master's and PhD places at UCT; Quarterly AI safety hackathons and red-teaming workshops

Note The hub page lists offerings without dates, so I could not check how many have actually run. The launch date comes from IDRC's 29 Sep 2025 announcement.

AIxBio Global Forum (NTI | bio) Bridge

Programme · Washington, DC, United States · founded 2024 · also draws on Safety science

An international forum run by NTI | bio, the biological programme of the Nuclear Threat Initiative. It brings together policymakers, AI developers, biosecurity and AI-safety experts and bioscientists to build a shared understanding of AI-enabled biological risks and to promote governance of 'AIxBio' capabilities. NTI began scoping it in January 2024. Two technical working groups, one on guardrails for biological design tools and one on horizon scanning, risk assessment and evaluations, feed statements, frameworks and horizon scans. It holds events at Biological Weapons Convention meetings and ran a 2025 tabletop exercise with the Munich Security Conference.

It carries nonproliferation practice over to AI tools that could help engineer pathogens: international norms, managed access, verifying users and BWC diplomacy. NTI's wider bio work adds US-China Track II dialogue, including a February 2026 joint statement with the China Arms Control and Disarmament Association. It is one of few standing international venues on AI-bio risk, with participants that include Concordia AI.

Works on Security, Assurance · Key work Statement on Biosecurity Risks at the Convergence of AI and the Life Sciences (2025); Safeguarding Against Global Catastrophe: Risks, Opportunities, and Governance Options at the Intersection of AI and Biology (Munich Security Conference tabletop report) (2025); A Framework for Managed Access to Biological AI Tools (2026) · Get involved Public events, such as side events at BWC meetings in Geneva (Aug 2025) and virtual report launches (Dec 2025); NTI newsletter; Forum and working-group membership is by invitation

Note An invitation-only forum with no public membership list, hosted by NTI rather than independent. Many outputs are written by NTI staff and consultants. Some of NTI | bio's AI-related work, such as the CACDA joint statement, sits at NTI level and isn't explicitly a Forum product. The official page sits behind a bot wall, so it was checked through archived copies.

Andrew Carnegie Foundation (formerly Carnegie Corporation of New York) BridgeChanged

Funder · New York, USA · founded 1911

Andrew Carnegie founded this US grantmaking foundation in 1911. It has an endowment of about $5bn and grants about $220m a year, and it renamed itself the Andrew Carnegie Foundation in June 2026. Its international peace programme funds work on AI and nuclear risk: SIPRI's study of nuclear escalation in the age of AI ($500k, 2024, after $400k in 2017 on machine learning, autonomy and strategic stability); the Institute for Security and Technology's Andrew Carnegie AI-Nuclear Policy Accelerator (first cohort of 26, 2026); and a Pugwash-Carnegie Fellow for Science and Security (2026).

It is the main philanthropic backer of the AI and nuclear-risk bridge. Instead of founding new AI-safety organisations, it pays established arms-control institutions to take on AI. A new AI-safety funder could co-fund with it, or fill the gaps it leaves, such as US-China AI dialogue or AI in biological and chemical weapons.

Works on Security · Key work Grant to SIPRI: assessing the risks of nuclear escalation in the age of AI ($500,000) (2024); Andrew Carnegie AI-Nuclear Policy Accelerator at the Institute for Security and Technology (2026); Pugwash-Carnegie Fellow for Science and Security (first fellow appointed) (2026) · Get involved No open AI funding call found; past grants are searchable in the grants database at carnegie.org

Note AI is not a named focus of its peace programme, whose stated priorities are migration, non-state actors, nuclear and space security and open-source intelligence. Its AI grants are separate projects, not a dedicated portfolio. The Pugwash fellowship is not described as AI-specific. It changed its name in June 2026 with the same mission, so search under both names.
