Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists Bridge

Media · Chicago, USA · founded 1945 · also draws on Arts, futures

A Chicago nonprofit publication founded in 1945 by Manhattan Project scientists. It sets the Doomsday Clock each year: in January 2026 it moved to 85 seconds to midnight, with AI cited alongside nuclear, climate and biological risks. Its Disruptive Technologies desk publishes analysis on AI, autonomous weapons, information warfare and biosecurity. In 2025-26 it ran 'The AI Power Trip', a year-long special project on how AI developers are gaining control over governance, information ecosystems, energy and the military-industrial complex.

It speaks for the nuclear-security community and treats AI as one of several man-made existential threats. It publishes both alarm and scepticism, such as a September 2026 critique of the science behind AI 'doomerism', which helps readers place AI risk among other catastrophic risks.

Works on Security, Power, Epistemics · Key work 2026 Doomsday Clock Statement (85 seconds to midnight) (2026); The AI Power Trip (year-long special project) (2025); How the bad science of AI doomerism is good for big business (Sara Goudarzi) (2026) · Get involved Editorial fellowships, including a Disruptive Technologies Editorial Fellow; Annual 'Conversations Before Midnight' event; Magazine subscription and newsletter

Note Its AI coverage mixes existential-risk framing (the Clock) with critiques of the AI-risk discourse itself. The roster's claim that it co-sponsored the 2026 Nobel Laureates Assembly on AI and Nuclear War was not verified.

Carnegie Endowment for International Peace: Technology and International Affairs Program Bridge

Programme · Washington DC, USA · also draws on Economics

This programme of the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace (Washington DC, founded 1910, with centres worldwide) works on the governance and large-scale risks of AI, biotechnology, cyber and the information environment. It has about 20 staff. Its AI strands cover: the geopolitics and security of the race toward advanced AI; AI and international development; AI governance institutions; and a China AI Initiative that studies Chinese AI safety and US-China dialogue.

It brings international-relations and China expertise, and a century-old institution's access to governments, to questions such as how rival and middle powers should act in an AI race. Its China AI work, for example on China's AI safety and development association, is one of the few close English-language readings of Chinese frontier-AI governance.

Works on Security, Power · Key work If-Then Commitments for AI Risk Reduction (Holden Karnofsky) (2024); How Some of China's Top AI Thinkers Built Their Own AI Safety Institute (Singer, Elmgren, Guest) (2025); AI Breakout Capacity: A Middle-Power Path Between Racing and Dependence (Leicht, Winter-Levy) (2026) · Get involved Research staff roles at the Carnegie Endowment (check its careers page); Public events and the podcast The World Unpacked

Note This is a programme inside a large general-purpose think tank. Not all Carnegie AI output comes from it: AI and democracy work, for example, sits in the Democracy, Conflict, and Governance Program. Its founding year was not found. Its framing is mainly geopolitical competition rather than alignment. The roster's evidence on Scott Singer (a 2024 Lawfare interview) predates his Carnegie role; his current Carnegie profile confirms that role.

Center for Global AI Innovative Governance, Fudan University (CGAIG) BridgeNew

Academic · Shanghai, China · founded 2025 · also draws on Law, society

A Fudan University centre in Shanghai, launched at the World AI Conference (WAIC) on 26 July 2025 with support from the Shanghai municipal government. Its secretariat sits in the Fudan Development Institute. It works in four areas: global AI governance rules, technical governance tools, capacity building, and international agenda-setting. It publishes reports, including a Global AI Governance Index written from a Global South perspective, and a journal. It also runs a visiting scholars programme and training workshops, and takes part in Chinese and UN AI-governance dialogues.

It is a Chinese voice on global AI governance that leads with the Global South and capacity building. That makes it a likely counterpart for Western Track II efforts, and a way to see how China's framing differs from Western safety framing.

Works on Security, Justice · Key work Global AI Governance Index (2026): Perspectives from the Global South and Capacity Building, released at WAIC 2026 (2026); Emerging Trends in Global AI Governance: Observations Since the Shanghai Declaration (bilingual report) (2025); Global AI Innovative Governance journal, first issue (2026) · Get involved Visiting Scholars Programme (regular seminars through 2026); Annual WAIC governance forum in Shanghai each July; Training workshops, e.g. the China–Oman international training workshop (Sep 2026)

Note Almost all sources are the centre's own site. Independent checking was limited because web search was unavailable for this pass. Its framing is development, capacity building and China's Global AI Governance Action Plan, not catastrophic risk, so bridge is a borderline call against adjacent. It is closely tied to official Chinese initiatives (Shanghai government support, a training workshop sponsored by the Ministry of Science and Technology), so read it as part of China's AI diplomacy rather than as an independent voice. Its own pages also call it the 'Center for Global AI Innovation and Governance'.

Center for International Security and Strategy, Tsinghua University (CISS) Bridge

Academic · Beijing, China · founded 2019

A university think tank at Tsinghua University working on international strategy and security, which serves China's foreign and security policy and runs on donations. Its 'AI and International Security' project is China's main Track II counterpart on AI security: with Brookings it has convened the US-China Dialogue on AI and International Security since 2019 and a joint AI Terminology Working Group, and in 2023 it held a dialogue on AI security governance with the Centre for Humanitarian Dialogue. On 14 January 2026 it hosted a forum of about 30 Chinese experts on AI militarisation, misuse by non-state actors and international AI security governance rules; in July 2026 it held a workshop on frontier AI safety and critical-infrastructure protection at the World AI Conference, and in 2026 it launched a podcast series, SinoAI Insights.

It is a working channel into Chinese security thinking on AI risk, and its deputy director also helps lead Tsinghua's Institute for AI International Governance. Western AI-safety efforts aimed at international coordination need counterparts like it, and its framing of AI governance as part of great-power security shows how Chinese experts weigh shared risks against strategic competition.

Works on Security · Key work US-China Dialogue on AI and International Security (with Brookings; eight rounds by late 2023) (2019); CISS-HD dialogue on AI security governance (2023); Forum on Artificial Intelligence and International Security (2026)

Note It is oriented to serving Chinese state diplomacy and security policy, so its positions should be read as close to official thinking. The founding year is inferred from its 2019 start of yearbooks and copyright and from the dialogue beginning in October 2019. Overlaps with the separate Brookings-Tsinghua dialogue entry.

Centre for Humanitarian Dialogue (HD): Artificial Intelligence and Emerging Technologies programme Bridge

Programme · Geneva, Switzerland · founded 1999

HD is a Geneva private-diplomacy organisation, founded in 1999 with more than 300 staff, that mediates armed conflicts. Its Artificial Intelligence and Emerging Technologies programme sits in its Technology and International Security area. The programme aims to help states develop and adopt international measures against the risks AI poses to security and conflict, in both military and civilian uses. Its first AI work was a two-year discreet dialogue among Chinese, American and international experts, which produced a draft Code of Conduct on AI in military systems (2021). Since then it has run dialogues with interested states on codifying risk-reduction measures, and a 2023 dialogue with Tsinghua CISS.

It brings discreet mediation and confidence-building to military-AI risk. HD has used these methods for ceasefires, social-media peace agreements and cyber confidence-building, and they offer a channel that public multilateral processes cannot.

Works on Security · Key work Draft Code of Conduct on Artificial Intelligence in Military Systems (2021); HD–Tsinghua CISS bilateral dialogue on AI security governance (2023); Structured dialogues with interested states on codifying AI risk-mitigation measures (2024) · Get involved Staff roles are advertised at hdcentre.org/careers (none AI-specific in Oct 2026); The Oslo Forum, co-hosted with Norway, is invitation-only

Note The AI work is discreet by design, so public evidence since 2023 is thin. The roster's claim that HD has been expanding military-AI dialogues and hiring advanced-AI advisors since 2025 could not be verified. HD's site blocks automated access, so it was read through a proxy.

European Leadership Network (ELN): Nuclear Weapons and Emerging Technologies Programme Bridge

Programme · London, UK · founded 2011

The ELN is a London charity founded in 2011, with staff in London and Berlin and a network of former senior politicians, diplomats and military officers, working on European security. Its Nuclear Weapons and Emerging Technologies programme studies how AI and other technologies change nuclear risk, through human–machine interaction, automation bias and system vulnerabilities, and proposes risk-reduction measures. Its outputs include a report on P5 views of AI in nuclear command, control and communications (NC3) and a Nuclear Fail-Safe Review project. It is also a partner in Firebreaks, a project with the Arms Control Association and the Berkeley Risk and Security Lab on limiting the risks of putting AI into nuclear operations.

It carries the nuclear risk-reduction toolkit (hotlines, fail-safe reviews, the P5 process, confidence-building measures) into AI governance. It argues for building decision time and human control back in wherever AI shortens crisis timelines.

Works on Security · Key work AI and nuclear command, control and communications: P5 perspectives (2023); Firebreaks: Mitigating the Risks of AI Integration into Nuclear Operations (with Arms Control Association and Berkeley Risk and Security Lab); Nuclear Fail-Safe Review · Get involved Staff roles; Public events and the Ok, Doomer! podcast on emerging technologies and nuclear risk; Younger Generation Leaders Network on Euro-Atlantic Security (YGLN): membership for early-career professionals

Note The ELN holds no institutional policy positions, so commentaries are their authors' views. Its AI work is narrowly about nuclear command and control and strategic stability, not AI risk in general. In Firebreaks, the ELN's role is the second phase, which extends the work to non-US nuclear-armed states.

Global Challenges Foundation (GCF) Bridge

Funder · Stockholm, Sweden · founded 2012

A Stockholm foundation set up in 2012 by the financier László Szombatfalvy to raise awareness of global catastrophic risks and to strengthen global governance to deal with them. It publishes an annual Global Catastrophic Risks report and runs programmes on climate and sustainability and on common security. It funds work through calls for proposals, including, in 2026, a nuclear-risk call made jointly as a member of the Consortium to Reduce Nuclear Dangers. It ran the $5M New Shape Prize for global governance models in 2016-18.

It names AI as one of its four concern areas, alongside climate, biodiversity and nuclear weapons, and argues that these risks cannot be governed in silos. That makes it a non-EA catastrophic-risk funder with a global-governance (UN-reform) lens that the AI-safety field seldom draws on.

Works on Security, Metacrisis · Key work Global Catastrophic Risks 2026 (includes 'AI in military decision-making: the global governance challenge' by Denise Garcia) (2026); Consortium to Reduce Nuclear Dangers, second call for proposals ($50k-$1M) (2026); New Shape Prize for global governance models (2018) · Get involved Consortium to Reduce Nuclear Dangers calls for proposals (second call closed 29 May 2026; decisions expected late autumn/winter 2026)

Note Its AI work is thin: one chapter on military AI in the 2026 report, and AI listed as a concern area. No AI-specific grants were found, so the bridge ring is borderline with potential. The current grant call is about nuclear risk, not AI. Its library page lists the 2024 report as the latest, and a 2025 report could not be checked.

Global Commission on Responsible Artificial Intelligence in the Military Domain (GC REAIM) BridgeDormant

Programme · The Hague, Netherlands · founded 2023 · also draws on Philosophy, Safety science

A commission the Dutch government set up at the first REAIM summit in The Hague in February 2023, for an initial two years. The Hague Centre for Strategic Studies (HCSS) ran its secretariat. Its commissioners and experts came from every region, including Stuart Russell, Michael Horowitz, Marietje Schaake, Toby Walsh and Yi Zeng, with former South Korean foreign minister Yun Byung-se as co-chair. They met across 2024-25. The commission concluded in September 2025 with the strategic guidance report 'Responsible by Design'. Commissioners presented it at the third REAIM summit (A Coruña, February 2026), and the summit's 'Pathways to Action' document referenced it.

It is a worked example of norm-building on military AI by states, industry, academia and civil society together, combining security studies, humanitarian law, ethics-by-design and engineering. Its uneven uptake (40 endorsing states, neither the US nor China) shows the limits of processes led by middle powers.

Works on Security, Assurance · Key work Responsible by Design: Strategic Guidance Report on the Risks, Opportunities, and Governance of AI in the Military Domain (2025); Report presented at the REAIM 2026 summit and referenced in 'Pathways to Action' (2026)

Note The commission has closed. Its continuing relevance is its report and its track record. RSIS (2026) notes that 'Pathways to Action' reflected the commission's guiding principles but left out three of its five core recommendations. Only 40 states endorsed it, against more than 60 for the 2024 Blueprint, and neither the US nor China did. The roster's claim that India abstained was not verified. HCSS continues military-AI work separately.

ICT4Peace Foundation Bridge

Nonprofit · Geneva, Switzerland · founded 2003 · also draws on Law, society

A Geneva foundation, set up in 2003 by the former Swiss ambassador Daniel Stauffacher, that works on ICTs for peacebuilding and crisis management, and since 2007 on norms and confidence-building for a peaceful cyberspace. Since 2025 its main AI line has been a 'Global Compact on Extreme AI Risks' workstream: op-eds, interviews and policy papers arguing for binding minimum standards on frontier models, aimed at the Swiss-hosted Geneva AI Summit in June 2027. It also works on autonomous weapons in the UN GGE, AI and disinformation, and digital sovereignty.

It brings two decades of cyber-norms diplomacy (norms of responsible state behaviour, confidence-building measures, proposals for a state peer-review mechanism and an independent attribution mechanism) to frontier-AI governance. It is one of the few long-standing Geneva peace NGOs that explicitly frames its AI work around extreme risks, and it has a direct line into Swiss preparations for the 2027 summit.

Works on Security, Assurance, Epistemics · Key work Global Compact on Extreme AI Risks (workstream) (2026); Co-hosted the Geneva launch of the Strategic Foresight Group report 'The Essential Convergence: Global Compact on Extreme AI Risks' (with IFRC and GCSP) (2026); NZZ op-ed: 'When It Comes to the Extreme Risks of Artificial Intelligence, Switzerland's Hour Has Come' (2026)

Note A small foundation whose AI output centres on its founder's advocacy (op-eds, interviews, speeches) rather than peer-reviewed research. Its own site gives 2003 as the founding year, while Wikipedia gives 2004 (the concept came out of WSIS 2003 and was endorsed in the 2005 Tunis Commitment). Funding is not disclosed. ICT4Peace Academy trainings found were tailored cyber workshops for governments, not open courses.

Institute for Security and Technology (IST) BridgeOn aisafety.com

Nonprofit · Oakland, USA · founded 2017 · also draws on Safety science

IST is a nonprofit security think tank founded in 2017, with offices in Oakland and Washington DC. It brings technologists, officials and industry together in working groups that produce policy recommendations. Its AI work includes: an AI and NC3 programme on AI in nuclear command, control and communications; a Recursive Self-Improvement Initiative launched with the Future of Life Institute in August 2026; the SL5 Task Force on security standards for frontier models; work towards a US–China AI incident line; and the Andrew Carnegie AI–Nuclear Policy Accelerator for mid-career national-security practitioners. It also runs cyber programmes such as the Ransomware Task Force.

It applies nuclear risk-reduction practice (hotlines, confidence-building, NC3 safeguards) to frontier-AI problems such as loss of control and recursive self-improvement. It also gives nuclear-security practitioners hands-on AI literacy.

Works on Security, Assurance · Key work Recursive Self-Improvement Initiative (with the Future of Life Institute) (2026); Andrew Carnegie AI–Nuclear Policy Accelerator, first cohort of 26 (2026); SL5 Task Force on frontier-model security standards (2025) · Get involved Andrew Carnegie AI–Nuclear Policy Accelerator: a cohort programme for mid-career national-security professionals (first cohort announced Feb 2026); Staff roles on its careers page; Public events and webinars on its events page; newsletter

Note Its founding mission covers technology security in general, and its cyber programmes are large. AI is one of several lines. Some funders are technology companies (Microsoft, Meta, AWS). Its LinkedIn handle still uses an earlier name, Technology for Global Security. I moved its ring from core to bridge.

International Physicians for the Prevention of Nuclear War (IPPNW): AI and nuclear weapons work Bridge

Membership body · Malden (Boston), Massachusetts, USA · founded 1980 · also draws on Safety science

A federation of national medical organisations in 56 countries campaigning to abolish nuclear weapons. It was founded by US and Soviet physicians in 1980 and won the 1985 Nobel Peace Prize. In October 2025, at its 24th World Congress in Nagasaki, it set up a working group on AI and the nuclear threat. Its position is that the nine nuclear-armed states must keep AI out of nuclear command and control and that humans must stay in control. It co-hosted the January 2025 webinar 'Autonomous Armageddon' with ICAN and Pugwash, made a statement to the UN Secretary-General on autonomous weapons, and in July 2026 was a partner in the Global Nobel Laureate Summit on AI and Nuclear Weapons at Castel Gandolfo, which produced the Rome Declaration.

It applies four decades of medical campaigning on nuclear catastrophe to AI in nuclear command and control, and ties AI-risk concerns to the established disarmament coalition (ICAN, Pugwash). It is also a working example of a professional body using clinicians' standing to campaign on an extinction-level risk.

Works on Security · Key work 'Autonomous Armageddon: Nuclear Weapons and AI' webinar with ICAN and Pugwash (speakers incl. Geoffrey Hinton, Connor Leahy, Terumi Tanaka) (2025); Working group on AI and the nuclear threat, set up at the 24th World Congress, Nagasaki (2025); Partner in the Global Nobel Laureate Summit on AI and Nuclear Weapons and its Rome Declaration (2026) · Get involved Contact the AI and nuclear threat working group through Program Director Molly McGinty (mmcginty@ippnw.org); Health professionals and medical students can join national affiliates (56 countries); Peace and Health blog (peaceandhealthblog.com)

Note The AI work is recent (working group since October 2025) and small next to the core abolition mission, and the working group has no dedicated programme budget on public record. IPPNW also argues that nuclear power, including small modular reactors, cannot sustainably power AI expansion, a position not everyone concerned about AI risk shares.

Nuclear Threat Initiative (NTI) Bridge

Nonprofit · Washington DC, USA · founded 2001 · also draws on Safety science

A Washington DC nonprofit founded in 2001 by Sam Nunn and Ted Turner to reduce nuclear and biological threats. Its AI work sits in NTI | bio and in the FutureSafe programme on AI and emerging technologies. It convenes the AIxBio Global Forum on guardrails for AI biodesign tools and publishes AIxBio horizon scans. In January 2026 it published a framework for managed access to biological AI tools, and in August 2026 it launched an international working group with Concordia AI on biological capability evaluations. In July 2026 it held a US–China expert dialogue on AIxBio with Tsinghua CISS. It also runs US–China dialogues on nuclear risk and examines AI in nuclear decision-making.

It applies bio-nonproliferation and biosecurity practice (access controls, norms, international forums) to AI biodesign tools. This is where mainstream AI-safety capability evaluations meet decades of biosecurity governance experience.

Works on Security, Assurance · Key work A Framework for Managed Access to Biological AI Tools (2026); AIxBio Global Forum high-level statement on biosecurity risks at the convergence of AI and the life sciences (2025); NTI and Concordia AI international working group on biological capability evaluations (2026) · Get involved Staff roles (NTI careers); Public events and webinars on AIxBio and emerging technologies; Congressional Leadership Project cohorts for senior congressional staff (second cohort recruiting in 2026)

Note AI is one line of work within a much larger nuclear and biological portfolio, and most of it is specific to biosecurity. The AIxBio evaluation work could also be read as Safety. The roster's claim about a 2026 biological-threats initiative with The Elders was not verified. NTI's site blocks automated access, so pages were read through a proxy and its WordPress API.

Oxford China Policy Lab (OCPL) Bridge

Academic · Oxford, UK · founded 2022

A non-partisan research group of researchers in Oxford and London, founded around 2022, that works to reduce global risks from US-China great-power competition, especially risks from AI and other emerging technologies. It publishes policy analysis on Chinese AI governance and US-China AI diplomacy, for example on China's stance on loss of control, China's proposed World Data Organization, and the 2026 Trump-Xi AI talks. It runs a research fellowship (12 fellows in its fourth cohort, with 35 expert speakers) and held its annual conference in Oxford in late May 2026.

It brings China expertise and international-relations theory, such as status-seeking in the AI race, to a field whose race models are mostly game-theoretic or written from Washington. It also trains a pipeline of US-China specialists for AI governance.

Works on Security · Key work OCPL Research Fellowship (fifth cohort applications open October 2026) (2026); OCPL Annual Conference: great-power rivalry, US-China AI governance and middle powers (2026); China Says It Cares About Loss of Control: But Loss of Whose Control? (2026) · Get involved OCPL Research Fellowship: applications for the fifth cohort open October 2026; Newsletter and analysis: ocpl.substack.com; Staff roles have been advertised (for example a Programme Associate in March 2026)

Note Its exact institutional status is unclear: the Substack describes it as a research group at the University of Oxford, while the website calls it a community of researchers in Oxford and London. No funding information was found. The founding year (around 2022) comes from a February 2024 newsletter that describes OCPL as two years old. It sits near the core ring through its GovAI connections and its listing on effectivealtruism.org.

Pugwash Conferences on Science and World Affairs Bridge

Network · Geneva, Switzerland · founded 1957

An international community of scientists, scholars and current and former policymakers, founded in 1957 after the Russell–Einstein Manifesto. It runs dialogues across political divides on weapons of mass destruction and war, and it has no formal membership. Pugwash and its founder Joseph Rotblat shared the 1995 Nobel Peace Prize. Its Science and Security programme includes a Project on Emerging Technologies and Strategic Stability that covers AI. In 2026 it held a Rome consultation on AI and nuclear weapons, co-organised the Global Nobel Laureates Assembly on AI and Nuclear War, appointed its first Pugwash-Carnegie Fellow for Science and Security, and held a Beijing meeting on nuclear risk reduction and disruptive technologies.

It is the original model of scientist-led dialogue across geopolitical divides, the template IDAIS explicitly borrows. It now brings physicists, international lawyers and arms-control veterans together with AI-industry people on AI and nuclear risk, guided by an ethic of scientists' responsibility.

Works on Security · Key work Rome workshop 'AI and Nuclear Weapons: Risks and Opportunities' (13 Jul 2026) (2026); Global Nobel Laureates Assembly on AI and Nuclear War and the Rome Declaration (organising partner) (2026); Autonomous Armageddon: Nuclear Weapons and AI (co-hosted webinar) (2025) · Get involved Pugwash-Carnegie Fellowships (first appointed June 2026; more planned); International Student/Young Pugwash for early-career scientists; Pugwash Conferences (63rd held in Hiroshima, Nov 2025); participation is open to anyone who shares its values

Note AI is one strand of a nuclear-focused agenda, and the AI work only scaled up in 2026, so its track record there is short. The Rome workshop report says it is not a consensus or policy position. Offices are listed in Geneva, Washington DC and London (the British Pugwash Group); the roster gave Rome.

Stanford Center for International Security and Cooperation (CISAC) Bridge

Academic · Stanford, CA, USA · founded 1983

CISAC is Stanford's international security centre, founded in 1983 and now part of the Freeman Spogli Institute. It is led jointly by a social-science and a natural-science co-director. It is known for nuclear-policy research and for Track II talks with China, North Korea, Pakistan and Russia. Its AI work includes two postdoctoral fellowships and Herbert Lin's research on AI and nuclear escalation. The fellowship on AI in strategic stability and military competition builds datasets for nuclear wargaming scenarios and designs experimental wargames on AI in nuclear command and control and force posture. The other fellowship covers the geopolitics of AI, including US-China competition and the tension between speed and safety.

It brings decades of arms-control and Track II practice, plus wargaming and expert elicitation, to the question of AI in nuclear command and control. That gives the AI-safety field a tested template for US-China dialogue and crisis analysis.

Works on Security · Key work AI in the Information Ecosystem and Its Impact on Nuclear Escalation (Herbert Lin, Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists) (2026); Artificial Intelligence in Strategic Stability and Military Competition Fellowship (AI in nuclear command and control, wargames) (2026); Geopolitics of Artificial Intelligence Fellowship (2026) · Get involved CISAC fellowships, including the two AI fellowships; applications for 2027-28 open 7 Oct 2026; Staff openings listed on its site; Public seminars and events

Note AI is a growing strand, not a dedicated CISAC programme. The AI fellowships are supervised through FSI's Program on Geopolitics, Technology, and Governance and involve Hoover Institution staff, so the AI work is spread across FSI and Hoover. Its Track II record is on nuclear, cyber and space; no AI Track II was found. The current natural-science co-director is not named on the pages checked.

Stockholm International Peace Research Institute (SIPRI) Bridge

Nonprofit · Solna (Stockholm), Sweden · founded 1966

An independent institute founded in 1966, with around 100 staff, that does research on conflict, armaments, arms control and disarmament, and publishes the SIPRI Yearbook and arms-transfer and military-expenditure databases. Its Governance of AI Programme, led by Vincent Boulanin, studies military AI, autonomy in weapons, export controls and responsible innovation. A Carnegie-funded project ($500,000, Sept 2024, 24 months) on AI and inadvertent nuclear escalation held a scenario workshop in Stockholm on 22-23 September 2025 with experts from seven of the nine nuclear-armed states. Recent reports cover responsible procurement of military AI (Feb 2026) and AI in Chinese, Indian and US nuclear postures (Feb 2026).

It brings decades of arms-control practice to AI and nuclear escalation, one of the most concrete catastrophic-risk pathways, and can convene officials from nuclear-armed states, which AI-safety organisations generally cannot. Its work on export controls for models and on military AI procurement translates abstract risk into instruments states already use.

Works on Security · Key work Impact of Military Artificial Intelligence on Nuclear Escalation Risk (2025); Stockholm workshop on military AI and nuclear escalation (experts from seven nuclear-armed states) (2025); Responsible Procurement of Military Artificial Intelligence (Goussac and Boulanin) (2026) · Get involved Staff and research vacancies: sipri.org/about/vacancies; Stockholm Forum on Peace and Development and other public events; Armament and Disarmament Summer School (co-hosted, 2026)

Note AI is one programme in a large arms-control institute. Its framing is lawful and responsible military use rather than opposition to military AI. Its 2017-2020 work on machine learning and strategic stability was an early example of this line.

The Elders Bridge

Nonprofit · London, UK · founded 2007 · also draws on Law, society

The Elders is an independent group of former heads of state, UN officials and Nobel laureates. Nelson Mandela founded it in 2007, and a secretariat in London supports it. Its 2023-27 strategy covers four threats: climate, pandemics, nuclear weapons and conflict. It commissioned a consultancy to scope AI work (December 2025 to May 2026), issued a call to action on AI in March 2026, and has run a dedicated AI programme since July 2026, including a declaration on AI and nuclear weapons. The programme calls on governments to regulate AI, to govern military AI and to negotiate a treaty on autonomous weapons.

It brings political standing that AI-safety groups lack: former presidents and UN human-rights chiefs who can put catastrophic AI risk in front of heads of government. It also explicitly ties AI to the nuclear, pandemic and climate threats it already works on. A new funder could partner with a voice whose credibility comes from outside the AI-safety community.

Works on Security, Metacrisis, Justice · Key work Governments must act now to manage AI for the public good (call to action, backed by Bengio and Russell among others) (2026); ProHuman: Governing the Global AI Revolution (eight-part podcast with Foreign Policy and FLI) (2026); The Elders' AI Principles for Leaders (2026) · Get involved Secretariat roles and consultancies in London, advertised on its site (for example the AI programme scoping consultancy, Nov 2025)

Note The AI programme only launched in 2026. So far its output is statements, a podcast, declarations and co-sponsorship, not research. Its framing mixes catastrophic risk (AI-enabled nuclear and biological weapons) with present harms (rights, inequality, environmental costs). The Elders are retired leaders whose influence runs through access and moral authority, which is hard to measure. Its CEO is not named on the pages checked.

United Nations Institute for Disarmament Research (UNIDIR) Bridge

Public body · Geneva, Switzerland · founded 1980

An autonomous UN institute in Geneva that does independent research on disarmament, arms control and international security. Its Security and Technology Programme (40+ researchers and fellows) runs the Roundtable for AI, Security and Ethics (RAISE), launched with Microsoft in Bellagio in March 2024, and the annual Global Conference on AI, Security and Ethics; the 2026 edition was held at the Palais des Nations on 18-19 June. Other AI outputs: a Framework of Responsible Industry Behaviour for AI in the Military Domain, an AI Policy Portal mapping national policies, a Centre of Excellence on AI, Peace and Security, and a Women in AI fellowship for diplomats.

It is a neutral UN venue where militaries, diplomats from all five UN regional groups, AI labs and defence firms discuss military AI risk together, which few AI-safety organisations can convene. Its industry-behaviour framework is an early voluntary norm aimed directly at defence AI companies.

Works on Security · Key work Roundtable for AI, Security and Ethics (RAISE) (2024); Global Conference on AI, Security and Ethics 2026 (2026); Framework of Responsible Industry Behaviour for AI in the Military Domain · Get involved Annual Global Conference on AI, Security and Ethics (hybrid, Geneva); Women in AI fellowship (UNIDIR Academy); Staff and fellow roles in the Security and Technology Programme

Note As a UN body, its output is consensus-oriented and diplomatic rather than advocacy. Microsoft's partnership in RAISE and the presence of defence firms (Palantir, Helsing) at its conferences may raise questions of industry influence. The roster's claim that the industry framework was co-developed with OHCHR was not verified. The headcount behind the 'large' scale code was not verified.

US-China Track II Dialogue on Artificial Intelligence and National Security (Brookings-Tsinghua CISS) Bridge

Programme · Washington DC, USA / Beijing, China · founded 2019

A non-governmental (Track II) dialogue convened since October 2019 by the Brookings Institution's Foreign Policy programme and Tsinghua University's Center for International Security and Strategy (CISS), bringing US and Chinese experts together on the risks of military AI. Eight rounds had been held by late 2023, alongside a joint AI Terminology Working Group building a shared glossary. In November 2025 delegation members (Melanie Sisson, Colin Kahl, Sun Chenghao and Xiao Qian) jointly published proposals on military AI governance, including a shared failure-mode and incident taxonomy and common definitions of dangerous AI-enabled military actions.

It is one of very few sustained, expert-level channels on AI risk between the two leading AI powers, and it supplies the confidence-building toolkit of Track II diplomacy (shared terminology, incident taxonomies) to the US-China race dynamic that AI-safety work treats as central but rarely engages directly.

Works on Security · Key work Steps toward AI governance in the military domain (joint US-Chinese delegation piece) (2025); From Geneva: AI, security and US-China dialogue (Edelman and Hass) (2026); AI Terminology Working Group, second meeting (joint glossary) (2023)

Note It is invitation-only, and most of its proceedings are not public. The roster's claim that it laid the groundwork for the May 2026 Trump-Xi agreement to resume government AI talks, and for a US incident-alert proposal, could not be confirmed from the cited sources. The joint glossary planned in 2023 was not found published. This entry overlaps with the separate CISS entry; count them once in aggregates.

Adjacent ring 16

AI for Peace Adjacent

Nonprofit · Distributed · also draws on Law, society

A small think tank founded and run by Branka Panic, with a network of volunteer advisers. It aims to make sure peacebuilders, humanitarians and human-rights activists understand AI and are heard in how it is developed, with focus areas in human security, humanitarian action, human rights and democracy, and ethics. Outputs include a non-technical AI guide for policymakers (2020), the book AI for Peace (Routledge, 2024, with Paige Arthur), and blog analysis of topics such as generative AI and mass atrocities, conflict-prediction models and the 2025 Paris AI Action Summit.

It is one of the few organisations dedicated to bringing peacebuilders and humanitarians into AI governance. Its human-security lens covers dual-use risks to vulnerable populations and generative AI's role in mass atrocities, which safety work seldom considers.

Works on Security, Justice · Key work AI for Peace (book, Routledge; Panic and Arthur) (2024); AI Explained: Non-technical Guide for Policymakers (2020); Generative AI and Mass Atrocities: A Real Threat We Can't Ignore (2025) · Get involved Newsletter and mailing list; Its blog invites contributions from people working in peacebuilding, humanitarian action and sustainable development

Note Very small. Its own site was last updated in March 2025 and gives no founding year, location, legal status or funders. Much of its output promotes AI applications for peacebuilding (early warning, hate-speech detection, a pandemic-policy challenge with Omdena), which is closer to 'AI for good' than to making AI go well. It is included for its human-security risk analysis and its work bringing peacebuilders into AI governance.

Build Up Adjacent

Nonprofit · Distributed · founded 2014 · also draws on Democracy

A peacebuilding collective co-founded by Helena Puig Larrauri, working on conflict in the digital age through three legal entities: a California 501(c)(3), a Kenyan subsidiary and a German association. Its digital-conflict programme studies how platforms and AI drive polarisation and violence. The Polarization Footprint ranks large platforms by affective polarisation (Kenya results in 2025). Phoenix is a free, open-source, AI-enabled social-media listening tool for peacebuilders and mediators, built with datavaluepeople and Swiss foreign ministry support. It also publishes monthly Sudan social-media listening reports. It co-organises the annual Build Peace conference (13th edition, Waterloo, Canada, 13-15 Nov 2026) and offers free online courses in digital peacebuilding.

It brings conflict-transformation practice, participatory social-media listening and platform accountability measures to AI's effects on social cohesion. Its work comes from conflict settings in Africa and the Middle East, which the AI-safety field rarely hears from. The Polarization Footprint is a working example of measuring one societal harm across platforms.

Works on Epistemics, Democracy · Key work Polarization Footprint (Kenya results) (2025); Phoenix open-source social-media listening platform; Sudan Social Media Listening monthly reports (2026) · Get involved Build Peace 2026, 13-15 Nov, Waterloo, Canada (with the Kindred Credit Union Centre for Peace Advancement at Conrad Grebel University College); Free self-paced online courses (Digital Peacebuilding 101 and others, in English, Arabic, French and Spanish); Webinars, e.g. Mar 2026 on tech governance, peace and security

Note AI is one part of a wider digital-peacebuilding portfolio, and Build Up has no x-risk framing. It runs as a non-hierarchical collective without a listed executive director. The founding year comes from the roster and matches the 13th Build Peace being held in 2026.

CMI – Martti Ahtisaari Peace Foundation (CMI) Adjacent

Nonprofit · Helsinki, Finland · founded 2000 · also draws on Arts, futures

CMI is a Finnish nonprofit, founded in 2000 by Nobel laureate and former president Martti Ahtisaari, that mediates and supports dialogue in conflicts in over 20 countries. It has 94 staff in Helsinki and Brussels. Its Digital Peacemaking team uses AI in peace processes. In early 2025 it ran an AI-supported consultation of 150 young members of Yemeni political parties over WhatsApp, analysed with the open-source Talk to the City tool. In March 2026 it published principles for responsible AI use in peacemaking, and in September 2026 it convened the Akola Forum for Peace on what AI means for peace and trust.

CMI holds 25 years of mediation practice, and it is one of the few peace organisations to have published AI principles for mediation (no use that escalates tensions or enables surveillance; human judgement keeps responsibility) and field-tested AI consultation in an active conflict. That makes it a practitioner partner for work on AI-facilitated negotiation, and on the risk that AI erodes trust between conflict parties.

Works on Democracy, Security · Key work Principles for responsible use of AI in peacemaking (2026); AI-facilitated youth consultation in Yemen (150 participants, 17 of 21 governorates); won the RTMKM 2026 Innovation Prize (2025); Akola Forum for Peace: what AI means for peace and trust (2026) · Get involved Vacancies page; an open CEO recruitment was announced in Aug 2026; Public webinars, e.g. 'Can AI make peace mediation more inclusive?' (14 Apr 2026); Digital Peacemaking team welcomes partnerships with technology companies and research institutions

Note AI is a small strand within a large peace-mediation organisation. The CEO leaves on 1 Nov 2026 to become Finland's UN ambassador. The roster's claim that CMI's Yemen work used Harmonica is inaccurate: the Yemen consultation used Talk to the City, and Harmonica was used for a December 2024 stakeholder survey for CMI's 2026-29 programme. The State of the Field post cited by the roster does not mention CMI.

Council on Technology and Social Cohesion Adjacent

Network · Washington, DC, US · also draws on Psychology, Democracy

A coalition of peacebuilders, technologists, researchers and civic groups, run with Search for Common Ground. It works to make 'prosocial' technology design, meaning design that builds trust and reduces polarisation, standard practice. It runs thematic hubs, including Deliberative Tech and LLMs and AI Agents, publishes design-governance blueprints and regulation guides, and holds annual Digital Peacebuilding Expos. Its Substack newsletter increasingly covers chatbots and AI-mediated participation.

It brings conflict-transformation practice to AI design questions such as chatbot sycophancy, frictionless agreement and AI-facilitated dialogue. Its policy track (prosocial design regulation, EU platform-design governance) could carry those lessons into AI governance. Peacebuilders' know-how about de-escalation is largely missing from AI safety.

Works on Democracy, Human minds · Key work Blueprint on Prosocial Tech Design Governance (2025); Mapping LLM Tools for Public Discourse, Pluralism & Social Cohesion (with Plurality Institute and Prosocial Design Network) (2025); LLMs and Public Discourse convening, Berkeley (co-hosted with Plurality Institute) (2025) · Get involved Digital Peacebuilding Expo, held annually (May 2026 edition in Kyrgyzstan, Washington DC and online); Thematic hubs, including LLMs and AI Agents and Deliberative Tech (contact via the council's site); Substack newsletter (techandsocialcohesion.substack.com)

Note A coalition with no stated budget or staff of its own, and its membership criteria are not fully documented. At least one report was funded partly by Google (Jigsaw, Google.org). AI is one strand within broader work on social-media design. Founding year not stated; its earliest public output found is from Dec 2023.

DiploFoundation (Diplo), incl. humAInism and the DiploAI ecosystem Adjacent

Nonprofit · Malta (offices in Geneva, Belgrade and Washington DC) · founded 2002 · also draws on Philosophy

A non-profit foundation set up by the governments of Malta and Switzerland. It grew out of a 1992 ICT-and-diplomacy project and became a foundation in 2002. It trains diplomats and officials, mostly online, in digital diplomacy and global governance, and runs the Geneva Internet Platform and its Digital Watch observatory, which tracks AI-governance processes. Its humAInism project (since 2019) works on aligning AI with human values, rights and dignity. Diplo also builds its own 'bottom-up' AI tools (reporting assistants, a GraphRAG chatbot, custom assistants) and teaches a nine-week AI Apprenticeship course.

It reaches diplomats from small and developing states, who are otherwise thinly represented in AI governance, and gives them AI literacy and hands-on tool-building. Its 'bottom-up AI' argument, for community-built models on curated local knowledge as a counter to knowledge monopolies, is a practical alternative to centralised AI that the safety field rarely engages with.

Works on Justice, Security, Power · Key work humAInism project (2019); AI Apprenticeship online course (2026); The DiploAI ecosystem (reporting assistant, Diplo chatbot, MyDepartment) (2026) · Get involved Diplo Academy online courses, incl. the 9-week AI Apprenticeship (EUR 990; scholarships for professionals from developing countries); Courses online and in Geneva, with new cohorts starting 2 Nov 2026; Diplo/GIP events at IGF, AI for Good and WSIS

Note humAInism is framed around human-centred values and rights, not catastrophic risk, and Diplo's leadership argues against centralised AI rather than for AI-safety framings. The discovery draft said Diplo is 'organising' the 2027 Geneva AI Summit. I could only confirm that it tracks the summit on Digital Watch and features it on its homepage; the summit is a Swiss government event. Staff count (about 48 on the staff page) includes consultants.

Doublethink Lab (Taiwan) Adjacent

Nonprofit · Taipei, Taiwan · founded 2019 · also draws on Democracy

A Taipei-based nonprofit, founded in September 2019, that investigates authoritarian (mainly PRC) influence and information manipulation. Its Digital Intelligence team traces AI-generated and cross-platform influence operations with a coalition of OSINT analysts, fact-checkers and journalists, and builds its own AI tools for investigators. Its Global Research team runs the China Index (99 indicators of PRC influence across 101 countries) and the China In The World network. Its Social Engagement team runs audience surveys and focus groups on how propaganda lands in Taiwan. In 2026 it analysed the leaked GoLaxy documents on PRC AI-driven influence operations and a network of 549 fake Threads accounts.

It produces hard evidence on how states already use AI for influence operations, together with OSINT methods and a whole-of-society resilience framework (Taiwan POWER). AI-safety work on persuasion, epistemic security and misuse could draw on all three.

Works on Security, Epistemics · Key work The Rise of AI in PRC Influence Operations: Nine Takeaways from the GoLaxy Documents (2026); Assessing the Borderless Group's Activity on Threads (549 fake accounts) (2026); China Index 2024: Mapping PRC Influence Across 101 Countries (2025) · Get involved Research published on Medium (medium.com/doublethinklab); The China In The World network connects civil-society researchers in 101 countries through an annual Summit and a Community Fund

Note Its work is politically charged and centred on the PRC. In 2025 Taiwanese opposition figures attacked its US funding. Its former chair resigned in February 2025 after a sexual-harassment complaint, which Taipei labour authorities upheld; the organisation publicly apologised for how it handled the investigation. AI is one line of its work, studied as a tool of state influence rather than as a risk in itself.

FIfF – Forum InformatikerInnen für Frieden und gesellschaftliche Verantwortung (Forum of Computer Professionals for Peace and Social Responsibility) Adjacent

Membership body · Bremen, Germany · founded 1984 · also draws on Philosophy

A German association (e.V.) of computer scientists and IT professionals, founded in 1984 out of the peace movement, with Joseph Weizenbaum among its co-founders. It is based in Bremen and has about 700 members. It publishes the quarterly FIfF-Kommunikation, with AI issues in 2024 and 2025. It runs the Cyberpeace campaign against cyberweapons and armed drones, a working group on armed drones and AI targeting, and the Grüne Bits project on the environmental costs of AI data centres. It awards the Weizenbaum Study Prize and Medal, holds an annual conference (Berlin, 30 October to 1 November 2026, 'Resilience in the Polycrisis'), and is the legal host of the Bits & Bäume alliance.

It carries a 40-year tradition of computing professionals taking responsibility for military and social uses of their work, from Weizenbaum onwards. That is a model of conscience among builders which AI-safety culture rarely draws on. Its AI work places autonomous weapons, surveillance and resource use inside a polycrisis frame.

Works on Security, People, Metacrisis · Key work FIfF-Kommunikation 4/2024: Künstliche Intelligenz zwischen euphorischen Erwartungen und dystopischen Szenarien (2024); FIfF-Kommunikation 3/2025: KI – Arbeit – Bildung – Frieden (2025); #FIfFKon42 'Keine Panik! Resilienz in der Polykrise' (includes a track on AI hype and data-centre resource exhaustion) (2026) · Get involved Attend FIfFKon 2026, Theater im Delphi, Berlin, 30 October-1 November 2026 (free tickets available); Join as a member; Submit to FIfF-Kommunikation or for the Weizenbaum Study Prize

Note Almost all output is in German. The Cyberpeace campaign site appears not to have been updated since about 2019. The chair's name comes from Wikipedia and may be out of date. Its AI stance is critical of AI hype and militarisation, not safety-oriented. Its conferences move between cities, so the 2026 Berlin conference does not by itself make it a Berlin-hub organisation.

Geneva Centre for Security Policy (GCSP) Adjacent

Nonprofit · Geneva, Switzerland · founded 1995 · also draws on Law, society, Arts, futures

GCSP is an international foundation in Geneva, set up by the Swiss government in 1995 as Switzerland's contribution to NATO's Partnership for Peace. It trains diplomats, military officers and officials in security policy, and also does research, policy advice and dialogue work. Its Transformative Technologies cluster runs an annual online course on emerging technologies and security and publishes on military AI, for example a 2026 Geneva Paper on the security implications of agentic AI. With UN CTED and the Swiss foreign ministry it runs a project on human-rights-centred use of AI in counter-terrorism, and it hosts the Processes of International Negotiation (PIN) research programme.

It holds decades of negotiation research (PIN) and trains security-policy officials from many states. Both could be used to design international AI agreements and to train the officials who will negotiate them. So far its AI work covers military AI and counter-terrorism, not frontier-AI risk.

Works on Security, Justice · Key work The International Security and Military Implications of Agentic AI (Geneva Paper) (2026); AI in the Military Domain: Multilateralism at a Crossroad (2026); Rule of Law and Human Rights Aspects of Using AI for Counter-Terrorism Purposes (with UN CTED and the Swiss FDFA) (2026) · Get involved Transformative Technologies and Security: two-day virtual course, 14–15 Oct 2026 (applications close 11 Oct); Global Fellowship Initiative; Open-enrolment executive courses and a Master of Advanced Studies in International Security

Note I moved its ring from potential to adjacent. AI is one topic in a broad security-policy portfolio. The link between PIN's negotiation research and AI agreements is a possibility, not current work.

IFSH (Institute for Peace Research and Security Policy at the University of Hamburg): Arms Control and Emerging Technologies Adjacent

Academic · Hamburg, Germany · founded 1971

IFSH is a Hamburg peace-research institute founded in 1971. Its Arms Control and Emerging Technologies area, funded by the German Federal Foreign Office since 2019, studies arms control, verification and escalation, with a growing strand on military AI. The AI work covers autonomous weapons governance at the CCW, AI and nuclear escalation, public opinion on autonomous weapons, and AI assurance in chemical-weapons verification. A separate project, 'Algorithms and Artificial Intelligence as Game Changers?', is funded by the German Foundation for Peace Research (DSF). Through its Berlin office it briefs Bundestag members and ministries.

It brings arms-control expertise in verification, norm-building and escalation dynamics to military AI, and puts it in front of German parliamentarians. Its work on why the CCW talks on autonomous weapons have stalled is directly useful to anyone designing international AI agreements.

Works on Security, Assurance · Key work Anja Dahlmann, 'Contesting control: Mechanisms of norm stagnation in the CCW debate on autonomous weapon systems', Contemporary Security Policy (2026); Alexander Keller, 'Artificial Intelligence Assurance for the OPCW: Governing Trustworthy AI in CWC Implementation', CBWNet Working Paper 20 (2026); Algorithms and Artificial Intelligence as Game Changers? (DSF-funded project) · Get involved Research and PhD positions (IFSH careers page and PhD programme); Public events and IFSH Briefings at the Berlin office; Parliamentary briefings for Bundestag members and staff (by invitation)

Note AI is one strand inside a broader arms-control programme dominated by nuclear issues. The work on AI and nuclear escalation puts it near the bridge line, but its own framing is arms control and norm research, not AI safety. The LLM-psychotherapy paper sits outside the arms-control work. The team size (about 12 core researchers) is for the whole Arms Control and Emerging Technologies project, not just AI. The DSF 'Game Changers' project page gives no dates; the latest related news item found is from 2021, so it may be finished. Keller's OPCW paper appeared in the CBWNet series, a joint project in which IFSH is one partner.

International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC): autonomous weapons and AI Adjacent

Programme · Geneva, Switzerland · founded 1863 · also draws on Law, society

The ICRC, the Geneva-based guardian of international humanitarian law, has a standing legal and policy line on autonomous weapon systems and on AI decision-support systems in military decision-making. It calls for binding rules that prohibit unpredictable autonomous weapons and those designed to target people, restrict all others, and keep human control over life-and-death decisions. In 2026 it issued a joint appeal with UN Secretary-General António Guterres (25 Aug) and a working paper to the CCW expert group (28 Aug) urging negotiations on a legally binding instrument in 2027. It also co-sponsored a forum in New York on 28 Sep calling for treaty talks and submitted a working paper to the UN General Assembly First Committee (Oct).

Its doctrine of human control over force, and its two-tier model of banning unpredictable or anti-personnel systems while restricting the rest, is the most fully developed legal template for limiting AI systems that take irreversible actions. Its neutrality and its role as guardian of the Geneva Conventions give it access to states that AI-safety organisations rarely reach.

Works on Security, Assurance · Key work ICRC position on autonomous weapon systems (2021); Limits on Autonomy in Weapon Systems (with SIPRI) (2020); Renewed joint call by the UN Secretary-General and ICRC President to adopt rules on autonomous weapons (2026) · Get involved Follow its working papers and the Humanitarian Law & Policy blog's autonomous-weapons tag (blogs.icrc.org/law-and-policy)

Note Its focus is military and humanitarian; it takes no position on frontier or general-purpose AI risk. The treaty outcome depends on the November 2026 CCW Review Conference, where the US, Russia, India and Israel have resisted negotiations. The founding year is the ICRC's; the autonomous-weapons line is much younger.

PAX (Netherlands) Adjacent

Nonprofit · Utrecht, Netherlands · founded 1948 · also draws on Law, society

The largest Dutch peace organisation, based in Utrecht, formed by the 2007 merger of Pax Christi Netherlands and the Interchurch Peace Council (IKV) and renamed PAX in 2014. Most of its work is civilian protection, justice and peacebuilding in conflict areas. It has long campaigned against autonomous weapons as a founding member of the Stop Killer Robots coalition. Its 2026 AI outputs include a report with Privacy International on Big Tech becoming military suppliers, investor guidelines against financing autonomous weapons, and advocacy for binding rules on 'digital dehumanisation and automated harm'.

PAX brings humanitarian-disarmament campaigning experience, the coalition model behind the landmine, cluster-munition and nuclear-ban treaties, to military AI. It also uses a lever the AI field rarely touches: research on companies and pressure through investors and financial institutions.

Works on Security, Power, Justice · Key work When Algorithms Go to War (with Privacy International): tech companies' convergence with arms manufacturers (2026); Preventing Investments in Autonomous Weapons: guidelines for financial institutions (2026); Developing rules to counter digital dehumanisation and automated harm (2026) · Get involved Staff vacancies (paxforpeace.nl/who-we-are/vacancies); Supports the Stop Killer Robots campaign, which has its own coalition membership

Note AI is a small part of a large, mostly non-AI peace organisation. Its autonomous-weapons work runs through the Stop Killer Robots coalition, which is already on the roster. The founding year is ambiguous: PAX dates itself from Pax Christi Netherlands (1948); IKV dates from 1966; the merged organisation from 2007; and the PAX name from 2014. Staff size not found.

Peace Research Institute Oslo (PRIO) Adjacent

Nonprofit · Oslo, Norway · founded 1959 · also draws on Philosophy

An independent peace and conflict research institute founded in 1959, with about 80 person-years of staff, that publishes the Journal of Peace Research, Security Dialogue and the Journal of Military Ethics and maintains major conflict datasets. Its AI work includes ERM (Jan 2025 to Jun 2028, Research Council of Norway), a project led by Jovana Davidovic and Gregory Reichberg that builds lifecycle risk-assessment and mitigation tools for AI-enabled weapons with defence practitioners. It also runs AsiaTech (Feb 2026 to Dec 2028, Research Council of Norway) on AI-enabled digital authoritarianism in Asia, and the ERC-funded BRIDGE project (announced Sept 2026, led by Jonas Vestby) on using AI and knowledge graphs to connect conflict data. Its VIEWS early-warning system forecasts conflict with machine learning.

PRIO brings military ethics and quantitative conflict research to two questions the AI-safety field usually treats in theory: how to manage the risks of AI in targeting across a system's whole lifecycle, and how AI entrenches autocratic power. Its conflict-forecasting infrastructure could become an empirical monitor of AI's effects on organised violence.

Works on Security, Democracy · Key work Ethical Risk Management for AI-Enabled Weapons: A Systems Approach (ERM) (2025); AsiaTech: Understanding and countering the advance of AI-enabled digital authoritarianism in Asia (2026); BRIDGE: AI and knowledge graphs for peace and conflict data (ERC Starting Grant) (2026) · Get involved Staff and doctoral positions: prio.org/about/careers; Public events and recorded seminars: prio.org/events; Monthly newsletter, The PRIO Update

Note AI is a minority strand within a broad peace-research portfolio, and its AI topic page is still marked forthcoming. BRIDGE and VIEWS use AI as a research tool rather than studying AI risk. ERM sits close to the bridge ring (risk management for AI weapons) but has no catastrophic or alignment framing.

PRIF Emerging Disruptive Technologies research group, with the Cluster for Natural and Technical Science Arms Control Research (CNTR) Adjacent

Academic · Frankfurt am Main, Germany · founded 2023 · also draws on Safety science

A research group set up in 2023 at PRIF, the Leibniz peace-research institute in Frankfurt, jointly led with PEASEC at TU Darmstadt. It combines political science with natural and computer science to study the military use of AI and machine learning, autonomous weapons, drones, cyber operations and other emerging technologies, and how arms-control verification could work for them. It sits within CNTR, a Federal Foreign Office-funded cluster whose annual CNTR Monitor covered AI in military use, verification, chemistry and biological design in its 2025 edition.

It works on a question AI governance will need answered: how compliance with limits on military AI, and on AI more broadly, could be verified technically. Its mix of physicists, computer scientists and political scientists is a working model for verification research on international AI agreements.

Works on Security, Assurance · Key work CNTR Monitor 2025: how the materialisation of AI is reshaping global security risks and governance (2025); Niklas Schörnig, 'Warfare at Machine Speed: The Growing Use of AI in the Military' (2025); Thomas Reinhold, blog post on autonomous AI cyberattacks as a security-policy warning (2026) · Get involved PRIF Crisis Talks and public panels on military AI; Research positions via the PRIF careers page; CNTR Monitor and PRIF blog

Note CNTR's current funding period ends in December 2026, and I found no confirmation that it continues. The CNTR Monitor 2025 introduction explicitly dismisses 'rogue superintelligence' framings in favour of present security and proliferation risks, so the group is not AI-safety-aligned in framing. The group itself is small (two heads, two fellows, one associate).

Stop Killer Robots Adjacent

Network · Distributed · founded 2012 · also draws on Law, society, Religion

A global coalition of more than 300 NGOs in over 75 countries, set up in October 2012 and publicly launched in 2013. It campaigns for new international law on autonomy in weapons systems, to keep human control over the use of force. A steering committee of NGOs leads it (including Human Rights Watch, Amnesty International, Article 36, ICRAC, PAX and Soka Gakkai International), with a small remote staff under executive director Nicole van Rooijen. In 2026 it lobbied the UN Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons (CCW) expert group, which agreed a text defining lethal autonomous weapons on 6 September. The November Review Conference will decide whether to open treaty negotiations. Its Interfaith Group's June 2026 statement backed Pope Leo XIV's call to 'disarm AI' and called for a legal ban on autonomous weapons that target people.

It is a tested model of a civil-society treaty campaign for binding limits on one AI application, with more than a decade of experience moving states through UN processes. Its 'digital dehumanisation' framing and its interfaith group connect AI governance to human-rights and religious communities that AI safety rarely mobilises.

Works on Security, Justice · Key work 'Disarming AI, Defending Humanity': Interfaith Group response to Magnifica Humanitas (2026); 'Nothing less than negotiations': advocacy at the CCW Group of Governmental Experts, 31 Aug-4 Sep (2026); Youth delegate programme for under-30s at Geneva multilateral meetings (2026) · Get involved NGOs can join as member organisations; Youth network; youth delegate programme (applications opened Jun 2026 for the Sep and Nov Geneva sessions); Petition, e-newsletter, parliamentary pledge and story submissions

Note Focused on weapons, with no position on frontier or general-purpose AI risk. Campaign groups called the September 2026 definitional text too weak, and the US, Russia, India and Israel opposed stronger negotiations. The Interfaith Group sub-entry is folded into this profile.

Toda Peace Institute Adjacent

Nonprofit · Tokyo, Japan · founded 1996 · also draws on Democracy

An independent peace-research institute in Tokyo, founded in 1996 by Daisaku Ikeda, then president of the Soka Gakkai International lay Buddhist movement. It publishes policy briefs and runs projects on peace and conflict. Its Social Media, Technology and Peacebuilding programme, led by Lisa Schirch, tests AI-assisted deliberation platforms (Pol.is, Talk to the City, Deliberation.io, Crowdsmart) in conflict-affected and authoritarian settings, including Afghanistan, Yemen and the ECOWAS early-warning network.

Most AI-for-democracy tools have been tested in stable democracies. Toda's programme gathers field evidence and process-design guidance on using them in peace processes, under authoritarian rule and in early-warning systems, a setting the AI-safety and collective-intelligence communities rarely study.

Works on Democracy, Epistemics · Key work Interoperable Deliberative Technology project (2025); Deliberative Technologies in Afghanistan project (research phase; outputs pending) (2026); Policy Brief No. 306: Deliberative Technologies in Youth, Peace & Security: Promise, Practice, and the Uptake Gap (Lena Slachmuijlder) (2026) · Get involved The programme lead invites researchers who want to contribute to its policy-brief series to get in touch (via the programme page).

Note The programme is small: a few administrative staff plus a network of senior research fellows, several based at other institutions (Schirch is at the University of Notre Dame). Its AI work concerns deliberation tools and social media, not the safety of AI systems.

UN DPPA Innovation Cell Adjacent

Programme · New York, USA · founded 2020 · also draws on Democracy

An interdisciplinary team set up in January 2020 inside the UN Department of Political and Peacebuilding Affairs to pilot and scale new technologies for conflict prevention, mediation and peacebuilding. Its main AI tool is Digital Dialogues, an AI-assisted platform that lets UN officials consult up to 1,000 people at once in their own languages and find areas of consensus on ceasefires, humanitarian measures and peace priorities. It also trains political affairs officers to use generative AI, runs an annual E-Analytics and Innovation course with the Qatar Computing Research Institute (the curriculum covers large language models and agentic AI), and builds tools such as Diplomatic Pulse and the Lisan Arabic-dialect corpus.

It holds years of field experience running AI-mediated, large-scale consultation in real conflict settings: practical evidence on AI-assisted deliberation and bridging that pluralistic-alignment and collective-intelligence work mostly tests only in the lab. Its anonymity-by-design approach to including women in fragile settings is a transferable lesson for public-input processes on AI.

Works on Democracy, Epistemics · Key work Digital Dialogues: AI-assisted consultations of up to 1,000 participants in UN peace processes (2020); Lisan: Yemeni, Iraqi, Libyan and Sudanese Arabic dialect corpora (with Birzeit University and the American University of Beirut) (2022); E-Analytics and Innovation Course (annual, with QCRI), including LLMs and agentic AI · Get involved Contact: DPPA-Innovation@un.org; Diplomatic Pulse and the Peace and Security Data Hub (psdata.un.org) are publicly available tools

Note This is AI applied to peacebuilding rather than work on making AI itself go well; it is included for its method (AI-assisted deliberation in conflict settings). Most of the dated material on the Innovation page is from 2021-2023; Martin Waehlisch and Daanish Masood Alavi co-authored its 2022 research outputs (Lisan, with Mustafa Jarrar and Fadi Zaraket), and the page names no current lead. The platform behind Digital Dialogues has been publicly reported as Remesh, but the DPPA page does not name it. The UN's 2025-26 budget cuts and UN80 restructuring could affect the unit; not verified.

Potential ring 7

African Centre for the Constructive Resolution of Disputes (ACCORD) Potential

Nonprofit · Durban, South Africa · founded 1992

ACCORD is a Durban-based civil-society organisation, founded in 1992, that works on conflict prevention, mediation, peacekeeping and peacebuilding across Africa, often with the African Union and regional economic communities. It trains mediators and officials, convenes dialogues, and publishes the African Journal on Conflict Resolution and Conflict Trends. Its AI engagement is light: a few analysis pieces (on AI early warning and surveillance in the Sudan conflict, and on trustworthy AI for African peace and security), and a June 2026 UN Peacebuilding Week session where its director argued that African conflict experience should shape how AI peacebuilding tools are built and governed.

It holds three decades of African mediation and conflict-transformation practice and working relationships with the AU and regional bodies. AI governance and AI-assisted peacebuilding tools mostly lack that knowledge and an African institutional voice on AI and security.

Works on Security, Justice · Key work Session 'Making Artificial Intelligence Work for Trustworthy and Inclusive Peacebuilding', UN Peacebuilding Week (2026); AI-Powered Early Warning Systems and the Governance of Autonomous Surveillance Technologies in African Conflict Zones: Lessons from the Sudan Crisis (2023–2025) (2026); Trustworthy Artificial Intelligence: How does it matter for African Peace and Security? (2026) · Get involved No AI programme: open to partnerships that bring African peacebuilding experience into AI-and-security governance and AI peacebuilding tools; Staff roles and internships listed on its site

Note Its AI work so far is two 2026 analysis pieces (one by an ACCORD researcher, one by an outside contributor from NUPI) and one UN Peacebuilding Week session; I found no AI staff or programme. I could not confirm from its site the roster's description of it as Ubuntu-informed. Funders are not listed.

Berghof Foundation Potential

Nonprofit · Berlin, Germany · founded 1971

A Berlin-based conflict-transformation NGO, founded in 1971 by Georg Zundel, that works on mediation, dialogue support, peace education and research. Examples include high-level dialogue channels in Yemen, national dialogues and insider mediators. Its digitalisation theme says AI is reshaping armed conflict and names autonomous weapons and digital surveillance, but its digital projects target misinformation, conspiracy narratives and online polarisation (for example Digital.Truth and DesINFORMIERT!). It has no dedicated AI project.

Transferable method: mediation, insider mediation and conflict-transformation practice, which could inform de-escalation of the US-China and lab-to-lab AI race and help bridge polarised AI-risk debates. It sits in int/a's Berlin hub, which makes it a plausible partner for a pilot.

Works on Security, Epistemics · Key work Digitalisation theme: digital technologies, AI and peacebuilding; Digital.Truth: workshops for parents and teachers on conspiracy narratives and misinformation (2023); Supporting social media influencers in Lebanon to counter sectarian messaging · Get involved Staff roles, tenders and training courses listed on its site (not AI-specific); Door to open: no AI programme yet, so engagement would need outreach and a partnership proposal

Note No AI-specific project or publication found. Its only AI content is a framing statement on the digitalisation theme page, and its digital projects (2021-24) are about misinformation and polarisation. Inclusion rests on the transferable method, not on current AI work.

FEST – Forschungsstätte der Evangelischen Studiengemeinschaft Potential

Nonprofit · Heidelberg, Germany · founded 1958 · also draws on Religion

The interdisciplinary research institute of Germany's Protestant church, founded in Heidelberg in 1958 and funded mainly by the EKD, its regional churches, the Kirchentag and the Protestant academies. Its four departments cover peace, sustainable development, religion, law and culture, and theology and natural science. Its AI-related output is thin: a digital-theology research field (digital church, computational theology, the Cursor_ platform) and a 2026 peace-ethics working paper on unmanned weapons.

It holds German Protestant 'just peace' and military ethics and a long theology–science dialogue, and could bring church-backed ethical reasoning on autonomous weapons and human personhood into AI security debates. Through the EKD it also reaches a large church constituency that AI-safety work rarely addresses.

Works on Security, Meaning · Key work Unbemannte Waffen und ihre ethischen Implikationen: Betrachtungen revisited (Heidelberger Forum zur Friedensethik, Working Paper 8, ed. Ines-Jacqueline Werkner) (2026); Digital theology research field (digital church, computational theology, Cursor_, SysLex, Global Network for Digital Theology) · Get involved No AI programme: outreach would go to the Peace department (just peace, military and peace) or the Religion, Law and Culture department (digital theology); FEST Briefing public events (e.g. democracy, 5 Oct 2026; climate-neutral church, 2 Nov 2026), with no AI strand

Note AI engagement is light: the digital-theology pages do not mention AI, and the 2026 working paper concerns unmanned weapons generally rather than AI specifically. No dedicated AI project found. Staff size not published.

Geneva Academy of International Humanitarian Law and Human Rights Potential

Academic · Geneva, Switzerland · founded 2007 · also draws on Law, society

The Geneva Academy is a joint centre of the University of Geneva's law faculty and the Geneva Graduate Institute. Founded in 2007, it teaches and researches international humanitarian law, international criminal law and human rights. It runs LLM and executive master's programmes, summer courses and projects such as War Watch (conflict and civilian-harm tracking), IHL in Focus and Arms TRACK (assessments for the Arms Trade Treaty), and until 2025 RULAC, its classification of armed conflicts. Its AI work so far is a 2024 report on AI decision-support systems in military targeting, from an ICRC-funded project on the digitalisation of armed conflict (2020–2025), and an August 2026 consultation with Oxford's Institute for Ethics in AI on UN human-rights standard setting for AI.

It holds deep, practice-tested expertise in IHL and in how UN human-rights standards are actually made: conflict classification, arms-trade assessment and treaty and Human Rights Council processes. That expertise bears directly on military AI and on any future international AI norms, and the AI-safety governance field mostly lacks it. It has started to apply it to AI, but has no standing programme.

Works on Security, Justice · Key work Artificial Intelligence and Related Technologies in Military Decision-Making on the Use of Force in Armed Conflicts: Current Developments and Potential Implications (Greipl, Davison, Hinds) (2024); Exploring Artificial Intelligence and Human Rights Standard Setting at the United Nations Level (consultation with Oxford Institute for Ethics in AI) (2026); Neurotechnology and Human Rights project (2023–2025) (2025) · Get involved LLM–MAS in International Humanitarian Law and Human Rights; LLM–MAS in International Crimes, Justice and Human Rights; Executive Master in International Law in Armed Conflict; Summer intensive courses and customised professional training; Newsletter and podcasts

Note Its AI engagement is occasional. The project that produced the 2024 military AI report ended in October 2025, and the 2026 item is an account of a small informal consultation, not a full report with findings. Governance changed in 2026: two co-presidents and an executive director replaced the single director. Its partner, Oxford's Institute for Ethics in AI, does not list the consultation in its own news. Scale is estimated from the roughly 70 people listed on its people page, which includes board, committee and visiting faculty.

Geneva Science and Diplomacy Anticipator (GESDA) Potential

Nonprofit · Geneva, Switzerland · founded 2019 · also draws on Arts, futures

A Geneva foundation under private law, set up in 2019 by the Swiss Confederation, the Canton of Geneva and the City of Geneva. Its job is 'anticipatory science diplomacy': it scans for coming scientific breakthroughs and brings scientists and diplomats together to prepare governance for them. It publishes the yearly Science Breakthrough Radar, runs an annual Anticipation Summit and a Science Diplomacy Week, and incubated the Open Quantum Institute, a multilateral body for inclusive access to quantum computing piloted at CERN from 2024 to 2026.

GESDA has already turned a horizon scan into a working multilateral institution for a frontier technology (the Open Quantum Institute), so it has practical experience of the kind of inclusive, shared-access body that 'CERN for AI' proposals describe. Its Geneva platform also links scientists and diplomats, a link AI-safety governance work often lacks.

Works on Security, Epistemics · Key work GESDA Science Breakthrough Radar (includes a 'Quantum Revolution & Advanced AI' platform) (ongoing); Open Quantum Institute, pilot phase hosted at CERN with UBS support (2024); Geneva Science Diplomacy Week 2026, including a simulation on governing lethal autonomous weapons (2026) · Get involved Anticipation Summit, Geneva, 14-15 Oct 2026: high-level and mostly by invitation, with an open-registration evening session ('GESDA Late', 15 Oct); Geneva Science Diplomacy Week (June each year); Staff roles at gesda.global/jobs

Note AI is one theme among many (quantum, neurotech, synthetic biology, space). GESDA has no AI-specific institution or programme, and the 'CERN for AI' parallel is ours, not GESDA's. Its board is dominated by business and diplomatic elites. There is no independent source beyond its own site; an outside article was cited but no longer resolves.

Kofi Annan International Peacekeeping Training Centre (KAIPTC) Potential

Academic · Accra, Ghana · founded 1998

KAIPTC is a training and research centre in Accra. Ghana's Ministry of Defence established it in 1998 and it was commissioned in 2004; it is one of ECOWAS's three peacekeeping training centres of excellence. It trains military, police and civilian personnel for peace operations, runs master's and PhD programmes in peace and security, and does research. Since late 2023 it has offered a fee-paying short course, 'Artificial Intelligence in Peacebuilding', for practitioners in Ghana (the latest edition was 2025). In October 2026 it is running a certificate in cybersecurity, AI and digital resilience that covers AI security and deepfakes.

Its peacekeeping-training curricula and West African network of security practitioners make it a natural channel for building AI-and-security capacity where that capacity is thin. Its AI courses so far teach people to use AI tools, not to govern AI risks.
